q: A matrix contains m rows and n columns. The matrix is called a sparse matrix if
opts: total number of zero elements > (m × n)/2
total number of zero elements = m + n
total number of zero elements = m/n
More than one of the above
exp: A matrix is sparse when more than half of its m × n elements are zero.
concept: A matrix is a table of numbers with m rows and n columns, so it has m × n elements in total. If most of these elements are zero, the matrix is called a sparse matrix. The usual exam definition is: the number of zero elements is more than half of all elements, i.e. zeros > (m × n)/2. Sparse matrices are stored in a compact form (for example a list of (row, column, value) triples) so that memory is not wasted on the zeros.
why: A — Correct. 'More than half of the elements are zero' is exactly the textbook test for a sparse matrix. Example: a 4 × 5 matrix has 20 elements; if 15 of them are zero, it is sparse because 15 > 10.

B — Wrong. m + n is just the number of rows plus the number of columns. It has nothing to do with sparseness: a 10 × 10 matrix with exactly 20 zeros out of 100 elements is mostly non-zero, i.e. a dense matrix.
C — Wrong. m/n is the ratio of rows to columns (it need not even be a whole number). The number of zeros is not compared with this ratio.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Sparse = only a few scattered non-zero values. The opposite is a dense matrix.

q: What is the time complexity of an infix to postfix conversion algorithm?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Infix-to-postfix conversion scans the expression once using a stack, so it takes linear time, O(N).
concept: Infix notation writes the operator between its operands (a + b); postfix writes it after them (a b +). The standard conversion algorithm reads the expression once from left to right: operands go straight to the output, and operators wait on a stack until their turn comes. Each symbol is read once, and each operator is pushed once and popped once, so the total work grows in direct proportion to the length N of the expression.
why: A — Wrong. O(N log N) is the running time of efficient sorting algorithms such as merge sort. The conversion does no sorting; it is a single left-to-right scan.
B — Correct. Each of the N symbols is handled a constant number of times (read once, pushed at most once, popped at most once), so the time is O(N), i.e. linear.
C — Wrong. O(N²) would mean that for every symbol we scan the whole expression again, like the nested loops of bubble sort. The stack algorithm never does that.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is the advantage of the array data structure?
opts: Elements of mixed data types can be stored
Easier to access the elements in an array
Index of the first element starts from 1
More than one of the above
exp: The advantage of an array is easy, direct access to any element through its index.
concept: An array stores elements of the same data type in consecutive (contiguous) memory locations. Because every element has the same size, the address of element i can be calculated directly: address = base address + i × (size of one element). So any element can be reached at once through its index, without visiting the others. This is called random (direct) access, it takes O(1) time, and it is the main advantage of an array.
why: A — Wrong. An array is homogeneous: all its elements must have the same data type (all int, or all float). Mixed types need a structure (struct/record), or a list in languages such as Python.
B — Correct. Elements are easy and fast to access: you can jump straight to arr[i] using its index.
C — Wrong. In C, C++, Java and Python the first index is 0, not 1. (A few languages such as Fortran or MATLAB start at 1, but the starting index is a language rule, not an advantage of arrays.)
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which data structure is mainly used for implementing the recursive algorithm?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Recursion is implemented with a stack (the call stack), because the most recent call must finish first (LIFO).
concept: Recursion means a function calls itself. Each call needs its own copy of parameters, local variables and the return address; this bundle is called an activation record or stack frame. These records are kept on the call stack: a new call pushes a record, and when a call finishes its record is popped. The most recent call is always the first to finish, which is exactly the LIFO (Last In, First Out) rule of a stack.
why: A — Wrong. A queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out). If calls were finished in FIFO order, the first call would try to finish before the calls it is still waiting for, which is impossible.
B — Correct. The run-time system uses a stack (the call stack) to remember pending calls. Like a pile of plates, the latest call is on top and finishes first.
C — Wrong. A binary tree can be used to draw the pattern of recursive calls (a 'recursion tree'), but it is not the structure that implements recursion.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Recursion or function calls → think stack.

q: What is the postfix expression for the infix expression a + b * c + (d * e)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: b*c and d*e are evaluated first, so the postfix form is abc*+de*+.
concept: In postfix (Reverse Polish) notation each operator is written after its two operands, so no brackets are needed. To convert, follow precedence: * and / are done before + and −, brackets first, and operators of equal precedence from left to right. Convert the parts that are evaluated first, then join them in the order they are evaluated.
work:
Grouping method:
b * c (higher precedence) → b c *
(d * e) (bracket) → d e *
Now: a + [bc*] + [de*]; + is left-associative, so the first + is done first:
a + [bc*] → a b c * +
[abc*+] + [de*] → a b c * + d e * +
Stack method (operand → output; operator → stack):
a → out: a
+ → stack: +
b → out: ab
* → higher than + so push → stack: + *
c → out: abc
+ → pop * and + (precedence ≥ +) → out: abc*+ ; push + → stack: +
( → stack: + (
d → out: abc*+d
* → stack: + ( *
e → out: abc*+de
) → pop until ( → out: abc*+de* ; stack: +
end → pop + → out: abc*+de*+
why: A — Correct. abc*+de*+ means: multiply b and c, add a, multiply d and e, then add the two results — exactly a + b*c + (d*e).
B — Wrong. abc+*de*+ means a * (b + c) + d*e: it adds b and c first, ignoring that * has higher precedence than +.
C — Wrong. a+bc*de+* still has an operator between operands ('a+b…'), so it is not a valid postfix expression at all.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Check a postfix answer by evaluating it back: each operator acts on the two values just before it.

q: Which one of the following is not a type of queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Linear, circular and double-ended queues are all types of queue, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: A queue is a linear data structure that follows FIFO: insert at the rear, delete from the front. Its standard types are: (1) simple or linear queue; (2) circular queue, in which the last position is connected back to the first so that freed space is reused; (3) double-ended queue (deque), which allows insertion and deletion at both ends; and (4) priority queue, in which the element with the highest priority leaves first.
why: A — Wrong. A linear (simple) queue is the basic type of queue: insert at the rear, delete from the front, in a straight line.
B — Wrong. A circular queue is a recognised type: the array is treated as a circle so that empty slots at the front can be reused.
C — Wrong. A double-ended queue (deque) is a recognised type that allows insertion and deletion at both ends.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is 'not a type of queue', so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two of them) is false.
E — Correct. All three options are genuine types of queue, so none of them satisfies 'not a type of queue'.
tip: Four standard types of queue: simple (linear), circular, priority and double-ended (deque).

q: The necessary condition to be checked before deletion from the queue is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Before deleting from a queue, check for underflow (empty queue).
concept: Before deleting (dequeuing) an element we must be sure the queue is not empty. Trying to delete from an empty queue is called underflow. Trying to insert into a full queue is called overflow. So underflow is checked before every deletion, and overflow before every insertion.
why: A — Wrong. Overflow means the queue is full. It is checked before insertion (enqueue), not before deletion; a full queue can always give up an element.
B — Correct. Underflow (empty queue) must be checked before deletion; otherwise we would try to remove an element that does not exist.

C — Wrong. The rear is the end where insertion happens. The empty test in an array queue is usually written with front (for example front == −1), and in any case the condition being checked is underflow, not 'rear value'.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Insert → check overflow (full). Delete → check underflow (empty).

q: After performing the following set of operations on a deque, what does the final list contain?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Tracing the operations one by one gives the final deque 10 30 40 15.
concept: A deque (double-ended queue) allows insertion and deletion at both ends. InsertFront adds at the front, InsertRear adds at the rear, DeleteFront removes the front element, and DeleteRear removes the rear element. To solve such questions, write down the contents (front on the left) after every single operation.
work:
Front is on the left.
InsertFront(10) → 10
InsertFront(20) → 20 10
InsertRear(30) → 20 10 30
DeleteFront() → removes 20 → 10 30
InsertRear(40) → 10 30 40
InsertRear(10) → 10 30 40 10
DeleteRear() → removes the last 10 → 10 30 40
InsertRear(15) → 10 30 40 15
display() → 10 30 40 15
why: A — Wrong. 10 30 10 15 would result if DeleteRear removed 40 instead of the last element. DeleteRear always removes the element at the rear end, which at that moment is the second 10.
B — Wrong. This would happen if InsertFront(20) placed 20 behind 10, so that DeleteFront removed 10. But InsertFront puts 20 in front of 10, so DeleteFront removes 20.
C — Correct. Following each operation step by step gives 10 30 40 15.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A linear data structure in which insertion and deletion operations can be performed from both the ends is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The double-ended queue (deque) allows insertion and deletion at both ends.
concept: A deque (pronounced 'deck'), short for double-ended queue, is a linear data structure in which insertion and deletion can be done at both ends, the front and the rear. It can behave like a stack or like a queue. Two restricted forms exist: the input-restricted deque (insertion at one end only) and the output-restricted deque (deletion at one end only).
why: A — Wrong. An ordinary queue inserts only at the rear and deletes only at the front (FIFO), so it does not allow both operations at both ends.
B — Wrong. A circular queue joins the last array position back to the first to reuse space, but it still inserts only at the rear and deletes only at the front.
C — Correct. A deque allows insertion and deletion at both the front and the rear.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue is implemented using an array of size MAX_SIZE with index starting at 0; front points to the first element and rear to the last element. Which condition specifies that the circular queue is empty?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With front pointing to the first element and rear to the last, an empty circular queue is marked by front = rear = −1.
concept: In the common array implementation of a circular queue, front holds the index of the first element and rear holds the index of the last element. When the queue is created, and again when its last element is deleted, both are set to −1, a value that is not a valid index. So front = rear = −1 means the queue is empty. In this convention the queue is full when (rear + 1) mod MAX_SIZE = front.
why: A — Correct. Both pointers are −1 when the queue is empty, because −1 is not a valid array index. The enqueue code tests front == −1 to know it is inserting the very first element.
B — Wrong. front = rear = 0 means the first and the last element are both at index 0, i.e. the queue holds exactly one element. It is not empty.

C — Wrong. In this convention front = rear + 1 (more exactly front = (rear + 1) mod MAX_SIZE) is the test for a FULL circular queue: the rear has come all the way round to just behind the front. (In versions that do not reset the pointers to −1, the same relation also appears when the queue is empty — which is exactly why it cannot be used alone as the empty test.)
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Empty: front = rear = −1. Full: (rear + 1) % MAX_SIZE == front.

q: What is the functionality of the following piece of code (q1 is a queue used to implement a stack)?
opts: Perform push() with push as the costlier operation
Perform push() with pop as the costlier operation
Perform pop() with push as the costlier operation
More than one of the above
exp: q1.offer(x) is a simple O(1) push, so this is the 'pop is costlier' method of building a stack from two queues.
concept: A stack (LIFO) can be built from two queues (FIFO) in two ways. (1) Push costly: after each insertion, move the old elements behind the new one so that the newest element is at the front; then pop is a simple O(1) dequeue. (2) Pop costly: push simply enqueues the element in O(1); pop then moves the first n − 1 elements into the second queue to reach the newest (last) element, which costs O(n). In Java, offer(x) means 'add x at the rear of the queue'.
work:
fun(x) does one thing: q1.offer(x) → add x at the rear of q1, O(1).
It inserts, so fun is push(), not pop().
Example: push 1, 2, 3 → q1 = [1, 2, 3] (front on the left).
pop() must return 3 (the newest), which is at the REAR of q1:
move 1, 2 to q2 → remove 3 → swap the names of q1 and q2 → q1 = [1, 2].
So pop needs n − 1 moves: O(n). Pop is the costlier operation.
why: A — Wrong. In the 'push costly' method, push must also move all older elements behind the new one using the second queue. This function does only one offer, so push is cheap here, not costly.
B — Correct. The function just enqueues x in O(1), so it is push; the work of reaching the newest element is left to pop, which becomes the costlier O(n) operation.
C — Wrong. The function adds an element (offer inserts at the rear) and never removes anything, so it cannot be pop().
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which one of the following techniques is not used in the binary tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Preorder and postorder are standard traversals; 'randomized traversal' is not a binary tree technique.
concept: Traversal means visiting every node of a tree exactly once in a fixed, systematic order. The standard binary tree traversals are preorder (Root, Left, Right), inorder (Left, Root, Right), postorder (Left, Right, Root) and level order (level by level, using a queue). There is no standard technique called 'randomized traversal'.
why: A — Correct. Randomized traversal is not a binary tree traversal technique. A traversal must follow a fixed rule so that its output is predictable; visiting nodes in random order is not a defined method.
B — Wrong. Preorder (Root → Left → Right) is a standard depth-first traversal, used for example to copy a tree or to get the prefix form of an expression tree.
C — Wrong. Postorder (Left → Right → Root) is also standard, used for example to delete a tree or to get the postfix form of an expression tree.
D — Wrong. Only A satisfies the stem (it is the 'not' item); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. A satisfies the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Pre / In / Post tells you when the Root is visited: before, in between, or after its children.

q: Which of the following statements is not true about the doubly linked list?
opts: We can traverse in both the directions
Implementation of doubly linked list is easier than the singly linked list
More than one of the above
exp: A doubly linked list can be traversed both ways and uses extra space, but it is harder, not easier, to implement than a singly linked list.
concept: In a doubly linked list (DLL) every node has three parts: the data, a pointer to the next node and a pointer to the previous node. The extra 'prev' pointer lets you move both forwards and backwards and makes deleting a given node easier. The price is extra memory for one more pointer in every node, and more pointer updates (and more chances of bugs) in every insertion and deletion.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true: with both next and prev pointers a DLL can be traversed in both directions, so it is not the 'not true' statement.
B — Wrong. This statement is true: every node stores an extra prev pointer, so a DLL needs more memory than a singly linked list.

C — Correct. This statement is NOT true. A DLL is harder to implement than a singly linked list, because every insertion or deletion must correctly update both next and prev links (up to four pointers instead of two).
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the 'not' item); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following options is not true about the binary search tree?
opts: The value of the left child should be less than the root node
The value of the right child should be greater than the root node
The left and right subtrees should also be binary search trees
More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are properties of a BST, so none of them is 'not true'.
concept: A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree in which, for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller than the node and all values in its right subtree are larger. This rule must hold at every node, so the left and right subtrees are themselves BSTs. Because of this ordering, an inorder traversal of a BST lists the values in sorted order.
why: A — Wrong. The statement is true: the left child (in fact every node in the left subtree) must be smaller than the node.
B — Wrong. The statement is true: the right child (in fact every node in the right subtree) must be greater than the node.
C — Wrong. The statement is true: the BST rule applies recursively, so every subtree must also be a BST.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is a false statement, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. A, B and C are all true properties of a BST, so none of them satisfies 'not true'.
tip: BST: smaller to the left, larger to the right — at every node.

q: Which one of the following is not an application of the stack data structure?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Asynchronous data transfer is a queue application; string reversal and backtracking use a stack.
concept: A stack is LIFO (Last In, First Out). Typical stack applications are reversing a string, checking balanced brackets, converting and evaluating expressions, function calls and recursion, undo, and backtracking (for example maze solving and depth-first search). A queue is FIFO and is used where items must be handled in their arrival order, such as buffers for asynchronous data transfer, printer spooling and CPU scheduling.
why: A — Correct. Asynchronous data transfer (IO buffers, pipes, the keyboard buffer) must deliver data in the same order it was produced, so it uses a queue, not a stack.
B — Wrong. String reversal is a stack application: push every character, then pop them all; the last character comes out first, giving the reversed string.
C — Wrong. Backtracking is a stack application: the stack remembers the choices made, so the most recent choice can be undone first when a dead end is reached.
D — Wrong. Only A satisfies the stem (it is the 'not' item); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. A satisfies the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Order must be kept → queue. Order must be reversed or undone → stack.

q: Which of the following is the prefix form of A + B * C?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: B * C is grouped first, so the prefix form is +A*BC.
concept: In prefix (Polish) notation each operator is written before its two operands. Convert the higher-precedence operation first (* before +), then place each operator in front of its two operands.
work:
A + B * C
* has higher precedence: B * C → * B C
Now: A + [*BC] → + A [*BC]
Result: +A*BC
Check: + acts on A and (*BC = B × C) → A + B × C ✓
why: A — Correct. +A*BC means 'add A and (B times C)', which is exactly A + B * C.
B — Wrong. ABC+* is a postfix expression (operators at the end), and it means A * (B + C), which is also the wrong grouping.
C — Wrong. +AB*C is not a valid prefix form of this expression: + takes A and B to make A + B, and then '* C' is left with only one operand. It treats A + B as if it were computed first.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which data structure is required to convert the infix to prefix notation?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Infix-to-prefix (and infix-to-postfix) conversion uses a stack to hold operators.
concept: When converting an infix expression to prefix (or postfix), an operator often has to wait until operators of higher precedence and bracketed parts have been handled. A stack holds these waiting operators and brackets. A common method for prefix: reverse the infix expression (swapping '(' and ')'), convert it to postfix using a stack, then reverse the result.
why: A — Wrong. A queue keeps items in arrival order (FIFO), but in this conversion operators must sometimes come out in the reverse of their arrival order, which a queue cannot do.
B — Correct. A stack stores the pending operators and brackets; the most recent operator (on top) is released first when precedence requires it.
C — Wrong. A linked list is only a way of storing data; it may be used to build the stack, but the structure the algorithm needs is the stack itself.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following highly uses the concept of an array?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Arrays store elements contiguously, which is exactly what spatial locality (nearby memory used together) relies on.
concept: Spatial locality means that when a program uses one memory location, it is likely to use nearby locations soon. Computers exploit this: reading one element brings a whole block of neighbouring memory (a cache line) into the fast cache. Array elements are stored next to each other (contiguously), so going through an array makes full use of spatial locality. This is why arrays are cache-friendly and fast to scan.
why: A — Wrong. A binary search tree is usually built from nodes connected by pointers, which may lie anywhere in memory. (A complete tree such as a heap can be stored in an array, but a general BST is not array-based.)
B — Wrong. Process scheduling is based mainly on queues (ready queue, priority queue). A queue can be stored in an array or a linked list, so scheduling does not depend heavily on the array concept.
C — Correct. Spatial locality relies on data being stored in neighbouring memory locations, which is exactly how an array stores its elements.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The necessary condition to be checked before deletion from the queue is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Check for underflow (empty queue) before deleting from a queue.
concept: Deletion (dequeue) removes the element at the front of a queue. If the queue is empty there is nothing to remove; trying anyway is called underflow. So every deletion first checks for underflow, while overflow (queue full) is checked before insertion. This is the same idea as TRE 1 Q80, asked again in TRE 2.
why: A — Wrong. In an array queue the underflow test is often written using front (for example front == −1), but 'front value' is just a variable, not the condition. The condition being checked is underflow (an empty queue).
B — Correct. Before deleting, we must make sure the queue is not empty; deleting from an empty queue is underflow.
C — Wrong. Overflow means the queue is full; it is checked before insertion, not before deletion.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which one of the following is not an application of the queue data structure?
opts: Resource is shared between various systems
More than one of the above
exp: Balancing of symbols uses a stack; asynchronous data transfer and resource sharing use queues.
concept: A queue serves items in the order they arrive (FIFO). It is used when a shared resource must serve requests in turn (CPU scheduling, printer spooling, disk scheduling) and when data is transferred asynchronously, i.e. sender and receiver work at different speeds (IO buffers, pipes, file IO). Balancing of symbols — checking that brackets such as ( ), [ ] and { } match — needs the most recent unmatched opening bracket first, which is LIFO, so it uses a stack.
why: A — Wrong. Asynchronous data transfer is a queue application: data waits in a buffer and is read in the same order it was written.
B — Wrong. Sharing one resource among several users or systems (a printer, the CPU) is a queue application: requests are served in arrival order.
C — Correct. Balancing of symbols is NOT a queue application. Each closing bracket must match the latest unmatched opening bracket, so a stack is used.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the 'not' item); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which one of the following techniques is not used in the binary tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Preorder, inorder and postorder are all standard binary tree traversals, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: The standard ways to traverse (visit every node of) a binary tree are preorder (Root, Left, Right), inorder (Left, Root, Right), postorder (Left, Right, Root) and level order (breadth-first). All three options in this question are standard techniques. (In TRE 1 Q85 the odd one out was 'randomized traversal', which is not a real technique.)
why: A — Wrong. Preorder traversal (Root → Left → Right) is used in binary trees.
B — Wrong. Inorder traversal (Left → Root → Right) is used in binary trees; on a BST it gives the keys in sorted order.
C — Wrong. Postorder traversal (Left → Right → Root) is used in binary trees.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is 'not used', so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three techniques are used in binary trees, so none of the options satisfies the stem.

q: How can we describe an array in the best possible way?
opts: Container that stores the elements of similar types
The array is not a data structure
More than one of the above
exp: An array is best described as a container that stores elements of the same type.
concept: An array is a data structure: a collection of a fixed number of elements of the same data type, stored in contiguous memory and accessed by an index. Its size is usually fixed when it is created, but the values stored in it can be changed at any time.
why: A — Wrong. Arrays are mutable: any element can be changed, e.g. arr[2] = 50. In many languages the size of an array is fixed, but a fixed size is not the same as immutable (unchangeable) contents.
B — Correct. An array is a container that stores elements of the same (similar) type — the best short description.
C — Wrong. An array is one of the most basic data structures: a linear, static data structure.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is another name for the circular queue among the following options?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Another name for the circular queue is ring buffer.
concept: A circular queue is a queue stored in an array whose last position is joined back to the first, so the positions form a ring. When rear reaches the end of the array it wraps around to index 0 using rear = (rear + 1) mod size. Because of this ring shape it is also called a ring buffer or circular buffer; it is widely used for streaming data, keyboard input and network buffers.
why: A — Wrong. 'Rectangle buffer' is not a standard term in data structures.
B — Wrong. 'Square buffer' is not a standard term either.
C — Correct. A circular queue is also called a ring buffer (or circular buffer), because its positions are arranged in a ring.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following determines the need for the circular queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The circular queue is needed to avoid wasting the memory freed at the front of a linear array queue.
concept: In a simple (linear) array queue, rear only moves forward. After some deletions the slots at the front become free, but once rear reaches the last index no new element can be inserted, even though there is empty space at the start of the array. That space is wasted. A circular queue solves this by wrapping rear (and front) around to index 0, so freed slots are reused.
why: A — Wrong. Accessing elements by priority is the job of a priority queue, not a circular queue.
B — Correct. A circular queue exists to avoid wasting memory: slots freed at the front are reused when rear wraps around.
C — Wrong. FIFO is the basic rule of every queue, including the simple linear queue, so it is not the reason a circular queue is needed.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Linear queue problem: it can report 'full' while the front is empty. The circular queue fixes this.

q: Which data structure is the best for implementing a priority queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A binary heap is the best structure for a priority queue: O(log n) insert and delete, O(1) to see the top element.
concept: A priority queue always removes the element with the highest (or lowest) priority first, not the oldest one. A binary heap is a complete binary tree in which every parent has a priority at least as high as its children (max-heap) or at most as high (min-heap). It supports insertion and deletion of the top element in O(log n) time and shows the top element in O(1). A heap is normally stored inside an array: the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
why: A — Wrong. With a linked list, either insertion (keeping the list sorted) or deletion of the top element (searching an unsorted list) takes O(n) time.

B — Wrong. A plain array has the same problem: a sorted array needs O(n) to insert (shifting elements), an unsorted array needs O(n) to find the top element. (A binary heap is usually stored in an array, but it is the heap ordering, not the plain array, that makes it efficient.)
C — Correct. A binary heap gives O(log n) insertion and O(log n) deletion of the top element, the best of the three choices.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following data structures finds its use in recursion?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Recursion uses a stack (the call stack).
concept: Every time a function calls itself, the system pushes a stack frame (parameters, local variables and return address) onto the call stack. When that call returns, its frame is popped and control goes back to the caller. The most recent call always finishes first, so recursion is managed by a stack (LIFO). This is the same idea as TRE 1 Q77.
why: A — Correct. Recursion uses the call stack: calls are pushed as they are made and popped in reverse order as they return.
B — Wrong. A linked list is a general way to store items one after another; recursion does not depend on it. (A stack can be built with a linked list, but the structure recursion needs is the stack.)
C — Wrong. An array is a general storage structure; recursion does not use an array as such. (A stack can be implemented with an array, but again the concept used is the stack.)
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following satisfies the property of the red-black tree (colour given to a newly inserted node)?
opts: Black, if the new node is a root node
Red, if the new node is not a root node
Black, if the new node is not a root node
More than one of the above
exp: A new node is coloured red, except when it is the root, which is black — so both A and B are true.
concept: A red-black tree is a self-balancing binary search tree. Every node is red or black, and the rules are: the root is black; a red node cannot have a red child; and every path from a node down to its empty (NIL) leaves contains the same number of black nodes. A newly inserted node is coloured RED, because adding a red node does not change any path's black count. If the new node is the root (the tree was empty), it is coloured BLACK, because the root must be black. (In Cormen's version the new node is first made red and the fix-up step then recolours the root black; the result is the same.)
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true, but B is true too, so the answer is D, not A alone. If the new node becomes the root (the tree was empty), it is coloured black, because the root of a red-black tree is always black.

B — Wrong. This statement is true, but A is true too, so the answer is D, not B alone. A new non-root node is inserted as red. A red node does not change the number of black nodes on any path; a possible 'red parent – red child' problem is then fixed by recolouring and rotations.
C — Wrong. A new non-root node is not made black: one extra black node would give its path more black nodes than the other paths, breaking the equal-black-count rule.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: New node = red; root = always black.

q: In the deque implementation using a singly linked list, what would be the time complexity of deleting an element from the rear end?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a singly linked list, deleting the last node needs a traversal to find its predecessor, so it is O(N).
concept: A deque allows deletion at both ends. If it is built with a singly linked list, each node has only a 'next' pointer. To delete the rear (last) node we must set the next pointer of the second-last node to NULL, but the second-last node cannot be reached backwards. So we must walk from the head through the list, which takes O(N) time. With a doubly linked list the same deletion is O(1), because each node also points to its previous node.
why: A — Wrong. O(1) is the cost of deleting from the front, or of deleting from the rear in a doubly linked list. In a singly linked list even a tail pointer does not help, because we still need the node before the tail.
B — Wrong. O(N log N) is typical of efficient sorting; nothing is sorted or divided here.
C — Correct. We must traverse the list to find the node just before the last one, which takes O(N) time.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which one of the following is the overflow condition if a linear queue is implemented using an array with a size MAX_SIZE?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A linear array queue overflows when rear = MAX_SIZE − 1, the last valid index.
concept: In a linear queue stored in an array of size MAX_SIZE, the valid indices are 0 to MAX_SIZE − 1. The usual convention starts with rear = −1 and increases rear before each insertion. When rear = MAX_SIZE − 1, the last slot is already used, so another insertion would overflow.
why: A — Correct. rear = MAX_SIZE − 1 means the last valid index is filled, so the queue is full (the overflow condition).

B — Wrong. With indices starting at 0, rear = MAX_SIZE would point outside the array. (It is used only in a different convention where rear stores the next free position; the standard exam answer is rear = MAX_SIZE − 1.)
C — Wrong. rear = front + 1 simply means the queue holds two elements (at front and front + 1); it says nothing about the queue being full.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm; heap sort and bubble sort are not.
concept: Divide and conquer solves a problem in three steps: divide it into smaller subproblems of the same kind, conquer (solve) each subproblem recursively, and combine their solutions into the final answer. Merge sort, quick sort and binary search are classic examples.
why: A — Correct. Merge sort divides the array into two halves, sorts each half recursively and then merges (combines) them — the pure divide-and-conquer pattern.
B — Wrong. Heap sort builds a heap and then repeatedly removes the largest element; it is a selection-based method using a heap, not divide and conquer.
C — Wrong. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbouring elements that are out of order; it is a simple exchange method, not divide and conquer.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following data structures stores elements in a non-linear relationship?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Stack, queue and array are all linear; the non-linear structures (trees, graphs) are not among the options.
concept: In a linear data structure the elements form a single sequence: each element has at most one predecessor and one successor (array, stack, queue, linked list). In a non-linear data structure an element can be connected to several others, forming a hierarchy or a network (tree, graph).
why: A — Wrong. A stack is linear: elements sit one above another in a single sequence.
B — Wrong. A queue is linear: elements stand one behind another, like people in a line.
C — Wrong. An array is linear: elements are stored in consecutive positions 0, 1, 2, ….
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above', which needs at least two true options, is false.
E — Correct. All three listed structures are linear. Non-linear structures are trees and graphs, which are not listed.
tip: Non-linear = tree or graph.

q: Which data structure is used for efficient searching, insertion, and deletion of elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A hash table gives efficient (O(1) average) search, insertion and deletion.
concept: A hash table stores each key in a slot computed directly from the key by a hash function. So search, insertion and deletion take O(1) time on average, however many keys are stored. A stack and a queue allow access only at their ends, so finding an arbitrary element in them takes O(n) time.
why: A — Wrong. A stack gives access only to its top; insertion and deletion happen only there, and searching for an element means going through all of them, O(n).
B — Wrong. A queue allows insertion only at the rear and deletion only at the front; searching for an arbitrary element is O(n).
C — Correct. A hash table supports search, insertion and deletion of any element in O(1) average time.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a binary search tree, which subtree of a node contains elements that are greater than the node's value?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a BST, the values greater than a node are in its right subtree.
concept: In a binary search tree, for every node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller than the node's key and all keys in the right subtree are larger. This makes searching fast: at each node go left for a smaller key and right for a larger one.
why: A — Wrong. The left subtree holds the smaller elements.
B — Correct. The right subtree holds the elements greater than the node's value.
C — Wrong. Only one side can hold the larger values; if both did, the search rule (left = smaller, right = larger) would not work.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The result of evaluating the postfix expression 10 5 + 60 6 / * 8 − is (the '−' at the end was missing in the printed paper)
opts: More than one of the above
concept: A postfix expression is evaluated with a stack. Read from left to right: push every number; when an operator comes, pop the top two numbers (the first one popped is the RIGHT operand), apply the operator and push the result. At the end the single value left on the stack is the answer. (The printed paper missed the final '−'; without it two values, 150 and 8, would be left on the stack.)
why: A — Correct. Evaluating step by step with a stack gives 142.
B — Wrong. 213 does not come from any correct evaluation of this expression; the value is 142.
C — Wrong. 284 is exactly twice the correct value; it does not come from a correct evaluation. The value is 142.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: In postfix, the first number popped is the RIGHT operand — it matters for − and /.

q: In a balanced binary tree, the heights of the two sub-trees of every node cannot differ by more than
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A balanced binary tree allows a height difference of at most 1 between the two subtrees of every node.
concept: A binary tree is height-balanced if, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. This difference (left height − right height) is called the balance factor, so it must be −1, 0 or +1. AVL trees keep this rule using rotations, which keeps the height of the tree O(log n).
why: A — Wrong. A difference of 2 breaks the balance rule; in an AVL tree a balance factor of ±2 triggers a rotation.
B — Correct. In a balanced binary tree the heights of the two subtrees of every node differ by at most 1.
C — Wrong. A difference of 0 at every node would force a perfect binary tree, which is possible only when the number of nodes is 2^h − 1. Balance requires only |difference| ≤ 1.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A queue has configuration a, b, c, d. If you want to get the configuration d, c, b, a, you need a minimum of
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Delete a, b, c and add them back as c, b, a: a minimum of 3 deletions and 3 additions (assuming the deleted items are held aside).
concept: A queue allows deletion only at the front and addition only at the rear. Starting from a, b, c, d (a at the front), we want d, c, b, a. The commonly accepted solution: delete a, b and c (3 deletions), leaving only d; then add c, b and a in that order (3 additions), giving d, c, b, a. This assumes the deleted elements are held somewhere outside the queue (in variables or a stack) so that they can be added back in reverse order. That is why the question is debatable: using nothing but the queue itself, the elements can only be rotated (a, b, c, d → b, c, d, a), never reversed. For the exam, learn the expected answer: 3 deletions and 3 additions.
work:
Queue (front on the left): a b c d
Delete → a out → b c d
Delete → b out → c d
Delete → c out → d   (3 deletions; a, b, c are held aside)
Add c → d c
Add b → d c b
Add a → d c b a   (3 additions)
Why fewer is impossible: d must come to the front, so a, b, c must all be deleted (≥ 3 deletions);
the queue must end with 4 elements again, so those 3 must be added back (≥ 3 additions).
why: A — Wrong. No new elements are created, so every addition must put back an element that was deleted; you cannot add 3 after deleting only 2. Also, d can reach the front only after a, b and c are all deleted.

B — Correct. Delete a, b, c (3 deletions) and add them back as c, b, a (3 additions) to get d, c, b, a. This is the accepted answer, assuming the deleted elements can be kept aside and added back in any order.
C — Wrong. 4 deletions and 4 additions also works (delete everything and add d, c, b, a), but it is not the minimum, because d never needs to be deleted.
D — Wrong. Only B gives the accepted minimum: A is impossible and C is not minimal, so 'More than one of the above' is false.

E — Wrong. B is the expected minimum, so 'None of the above' is not the accepted answer. (Someone could argue for E if no storage outside the queue is allowed, since reversal is then impossible — this is why the question is debatable — but the standard answer is B.)

q: The order of the binary search algorithm is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Binary search halves the search range at every step, so it is O(log N), which is not listed.
concept: Binary search works on a sorted array. It compares the key with the middle element and then throws away half of the remaining elements. After k steps only N/2^k elements remain, so about log₂N steps are enough. Its time complexity is O(log N): for example, 1,000,000 sorted items need only about 20 comparisons.
why: A — Wrong. N (linear time) is the order of linear search, which checks the elements one by one.
B — Wrong. N log N is the order of efficient sorting algorithms such as merge sort and heap sort.
C — Wrong. N² is the order of simple sorting algorithms such as bubble sort and selection sort.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above', which needs at least two true options, is false.
E — Correct. Binary search is O(log N), and log N is not among A–C.
tip: Halving at every step → log N.

q: The preorder traversal of a binary search tree is 15, 10, 12, 11, 20, 18, 16, 19. Which one of the following is the postorder traversal of the tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The BST has root 15, left part 10 → 12 → 11 and right part 20 → 18 → (16, 19); its postorder is 11, 12, 10, 16, 19, 18, 20, 15.
concept: In preorder traversal the root comes first. For a BST, the first value is the root; the values after it that are smaller than the root form the left subtree, and the larger ones form the right subtree (each again in preorder). Build the tree this way, then write the postorder traversal (Left, Right, Root).
work:
Preorder: 15, 10, 12, 11, 20, 18, 16, 19
Root = 15. Smaller (left subtree): 10, 12, 11. Larger (right subtree): 20, 18, 16, 19.
Left subtree: root 10; 12 > 10 → right child of 10; 11 is between 10 and 12 → left child of 12.
Right subtree: root 20; 18 < 20 → left child of 20; 16 → left child of 18; 19 → right child of 18.
Tree: 15(L 10, R 20); 10(R 12); 12(L 11); 20(L 18); 18(L 16, R 19)
Postorder of left subtree of 15: 11, 12, 10
Postorder of right subtree of 15: 16, 19, 18, 20
Then the root: 15
Postorder: 11, 12, 10, 16, 19, 18, 20, 15
why: A — Wrong. 20, 19, 18, 16, 15, 12, 11, 10 is just the keys in descending order (reverse inorder). A postorder traversal must end with the root, 15, and this list does not.
B — Correct. Building the BST from the preorder and visiting Left, Right, Root gives 11, 12, 10, 16, 19, 18, 20, 15.
C — Wrong. 19, 16, 18, 20, 11, 12, 10, 15 is the order Right → Left → Root (a mirror of postorder): it visits the right subtree before the left one.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Preorder always starts with the root; postorder always ends with it.

q: How many distinct binary search trees can be created out of 4 distinct keys?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The number of distinct BSTs on 4 keys is the Catalan number C₄ = 14.
concept: The number of structurally different binary search trees that can be built from n distinct keys is the Catalan number Cₙ = (2n)! / ((n + 1)! · n!). The reason: choose any key as the root; the smaller keys form the left subtree and the larger keys the right subtree, so Cₙ = Σ C(i) × C(n − 1 − i). The first values are C₀ = 1, C₁ = 1, C₂ = 2, C₃ = 5, C₄ = 14, C₅ = 42.
work:
Formula: C₄ = (2·4)! / (5! · 4!) = 40320 / (120 × 24) = 40320 / 2880 = 14
Check by choosing the root among keys 1, 2, 3, 4:
root 1: 0 keys left, 3 right → C₀ × C₃ = 1 × 5 = 5
root 2: 1 key left, 2 right → C₁ × C₂ = 1 × 2 = 2
root 3: 2 keys left, 1 right → C₂ × C₁ = 2 × 1 = 2
root 4: 3 keys left, 0 right → C₃ × C₀ = 5 × 1 = 5
Total = 5 + 2 + 2 + 5 = 14
why: A — Wrong. 8 (= 2³) has no basis in the BST count; the correct count is the Catalan number 14.
B — Wrong. 24 = 4! is the number of insertion orders (permutations) of 4 keys. Different orders can give the same BST (for example 2, 1, 3 and 2, 3, 1), so the number of distinct BSTs is smaller: 14.
C — Correct. 14 = C₄, the 4th Catalan number.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Catalan numbers for n = 0 to 5: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42.

q: Which of the following statements is true about Big-O notation?
opts: It represents the lower bound of an algorithm's runtime
It represents the upper bound of an algorithm's runtime
It represents the average runtime of an algorithm
More than one of the above
exp: Big-O notation represents the upper bound of an algorithm's running time.
concept: Asymptotic notations describe how the running time grows as the input size n grows. Big-O, O(g(n)), gives an upper bound: for large n the running time grows no faster than g(n), up to a constant factor. Big-Omega, Ω(g(n)), gives a lower bound, and Big-Theta, Θ(g(n)), gives a tight bound (both upper and lower).
why: A — Wrong. A lower bound is described by Big-Omega (Ω), not Big-O.
B — Correct. Big-O gives an upper bound on the growth of the running time; it is most often quoted for the worst case.
C — Wrong. 'Average' is a case of analysis (best, average, worst), not a notation; any case can be described with O, Ω or Θ. Big-O itself means an upper bound.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: O = at most (upper bound), Ω = at least (lower bound), Θ = exactly (tight bound).

q: Which of the following is NOT a step in the Divide and Conquer algorithm?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Divide, conquer and combine are the three steps of divide and conquer, so none of them is 'NOT a step'.
concept: Every divide-and-conquer algorithm has three steps. Divide: split the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type. Conquer: solve the subproblems recursively (very small ones directly). Combine: join the sub-solutions into the answer for the whole problem. Merge sort is the standard example: split the array, sort the halves, merge them.
why: A — Wrong. Combine is a step of divide and conquer (in merge sort it is the merge step).
B — Wrong. Conquer is a step: each subproblem is solved recursively.
C — Wrong. Divide is a step: the problem is split into subproblems.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is 'not a step', so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Divide, Conquer and Combine are all steps of divide and conquer, so none of them satisfies the stem.

q: Merge Sort is an example of which algorithm design paradigm?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Merge sort is a classic divide-and-conquer algorithm.
concept: An algorithm design paradigm is a general strategy for designing algorithms. Greedy makes the locally best choice at each step. Divide and conquer splits the problem into independent subproblems, solves them recursively and combines the results. Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems once and stores their answers in a table for reuse. Merge sort splits the array into halves, sorts each half recursively and merges them, so it is divide and conquer.
why: A — Wrong. A greedy algorithm makes one locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it (e.g. Kruskal's, Prim's, Huffman coding). Merge sort makes no such choices.
B — Correct. Merge sort divides, conquers (sorts the halves recursively) and combines (merges) — the divide-and-conquer paradigm.

C — Wrong. Dynamic programming is used when subproblems overlap and their answers are reused (e.g. Fibonacci with a table, 0/1 knapsack). The two halves in merge sort are independent, so nothing is stored for reuse.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many edges does a spanning tree of a graph with N vertices have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A spanning tree of a graph with N vertices has N − 1 edges.
concept: A spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph that contains all N vertices and is a tree: connected and without cycles. Every tree with N vertices has exactly N − 1 edges. With fewer edges some vertex would be disconnected, and adding one more edge would create a cycle.
why: A — Wrong. N edges on N vertices always create a cycle, so the subgraph would not be a tree.
B — Correct. A spanning tree on N vertices always has exactly N − 1 edges.
C — Wrong. N(N − 1)/2 is the number of edges in a complete graph (every pair of vertices joined), the maximum possible in a simple undirected graph.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: A tree with N vertices always has N − 1 edges.

q: Which of the following is NOT a graph traversal algorithm?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Greedy, divide and conquer and dynamic programming are design paradigms, not graph traversal algorithms (BFS and DFS are), so more than one option fits.
concept: Graph traversal algorithms visit all the vertices of a graph in a systematic way; the two standard ones are Breadth-First Search (BFS, uses a queue) and Depth-First Search (DFS, uses a stack or recursion). Greedy, Divide and Conquer and Dynamic Programming are not traversal algorithms at all — they are algorithm design paradigms (general strategies for designing algorithms). Since all three options are 'not a graph traversal algorithm', the answer is 'More than one of the above'.
why: A — Wrong. This option does satisfy the stem, but B and C do too, so the answer is D, not A alone. Greedy is a design paradigm (choose the locally best option at each step, as in Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms), not a graph traversal algorithm.

B — Wrong. This option does satisfy the stem, but A and C do too, so the answer is D, not B alone. Divide and Conquer is a design paradigm (split, solve recursively, combine, as in merge sort), not a graph traversal algorithm.

C — Wrong. This option does satisfy the stem, but A and B do too, so the answer is D, not C alone. Dynamic Programming is a design paradigm (store and reuse the answers of overlapping subproblems), not a graph traversal algorithm.
D — Correct. A, B and C all satisfy the stem ('NOT a graph traversal algorithm'), so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C all satisfy the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Graph traversal = BFS (queue) and DFS (stack).

q: Which of the following is NOT an NP-Complete problem?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Shortest path is solvable in polynomial time, so it is not NP-complete; TSP and SAT are NP-complete.
concept: P is the class of problems that can be solved in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP: no polynomial-time algorithm is known for any of them, and if one were found, every problem in NP could be solved in polynomial time. SAT (Boolean satisfiability) was the first problem proved NP-complete (Cook–Levin theorem), and the decision version of the Travelling Salesman Problem is also NP-complete. The shortest path problem is solved in polynomial time by Dijkstra's or the Bellman–Ford algorithm, so it is in P and is not NP-complete (assuming P ≠ NP, as is widely believed).
why: A — Wrong. The Travelling Salesman Problem (decision version: 'is there a tour of length at most k?') is NP-complete. Its optimisation version, 'find the shortest tour', is NP-hard.
B — Wrong. The Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT) is NP-complete; it was the first problem proved NP-complete.
C — Correct. The shortest path problem is solvable in polynomial time (Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford), so it is not NP-complete.
D — Wrong. Only C satisfies the stem (it is the 'not' item); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. C satisfies the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Shortest path between two points: easy (P). Shortest tour through all cities (TSP): hard (NP-complete).

q: Which of the following is an advantage of using arrays?
opts: Ability to store elements of different data types
Random access to elements using an index
More than one of the above
exp: The advantage of arrays is random (direct) access to any element through its index.
concept: An array stores elements of one type in consecutive memory locations, so the address of any element is base + index × element size. This gives random access: any element can be read or written in O(1) time using its index. The disadvantages are a fixed size and slow insertion or deletion in the middle, because the later elements must be shifted (O(n) time).
why: A — Wrong. Insertion and deletion in an array take O(n) time in general, because later elements must be shifted to open or close a gap (only adding or removing at the end is O(1)). Constant-time insertion and deletion at a known position is an advantage of linked lists.
B — Wrong. An array is homogeneous: all its elements must have the same data type.
C — Correct. Random access to any element by its index in O(1) time is the main advantage of arrays.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a basic operation performed on a data structure?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Encryption is not a basic data structure operation; insertion and deletion are.
concept: The basic operations performed on data structures are traversal (visiting every element), insertion, deletion, searching, sorting and merging. Encryption is a security technique that hides data using a key; it belongs to cryptography, not to the basic operations of a data structure.
why: A — Correct. Encryption converts data into a secret form using a key; it is a cryptography/security technique, not a basic data structure operation.
B — Wrong. Deletion (removing an element) is a basic data structure operation.
C — Wrong. Insertion (adding an element) is a basic data structure operation.
D — Wrong. Only A satisfies the stem (it is the 'not' item); 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy it.
E — Wrong. A satisfies the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Basic operations: Traverse, Insert, Delete, Search, Sort, Merge.

q: A data structure is best described as
opts: A language feature used only for reading input and printing output
A finite sequence of instructions that solves a given problem
A way of organising and storing data so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently
More than one of the above
exp: A data structure is a way of organising and storing data for efficient access and modification; a finite sequence of steps is an algorithm.
concept: A data structure is a way of arranging and storing data in a computer's memory so that we can use it (access it) and change it (modify it) efficiently. Think of a library: books arranged by subject on numbered shelves are easy to find, while the same books thrown in a heap are not. Arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists, trees and graphs are all data structures. Choosing the right one makes a program faster and simpler.
why: A — Wrong. Reading input and printing output are done by input/output (I/O) functions such as scanf() and printf() in C. They are language features for I/O, not ways of organising data.

B — Wrong. A finite sequence of clear steps that solves a problem is the definition of an ALGORITHM. An algorithm works on data; a data structure is how that data is stored. (Niklaus Wirth's famous book title sums it up: 'Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs'.)

C — Correct. This is the standard definition: a data structure organises and stores data (array, list, tree and so on) so that operations such as access, insertion and deletion can be done efficiently.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Algorithm = the steps (the recipe). Data structure = how the ingredients are arranged in the kitchen.

q: An Abstract Data Type (ADT) specifies
opts: the exact memory layout and the C code of every operation
only the hardware device on which the data will be stored
the values and the operations on them, without fixing how they are implemented
More than one of the above
exp: An ADT specifies the values and the operations on them, not how they are implemented.
concept: An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a logical description of a kind of data: which values it can hold, which operations can be done on it, and what each operation does. It deliberately hides HOW it is implemented. For example, the Stack ADT promises push, pop and peek with last-in-first-out behaviour, but it can be built using an array or a linked list. 'Abstract' here means thinking about what, not how.
why: A — Wrong. The exact memory layout and the C code are implementation details. They belong to a concrete data structure (one particular implementation), which is exactly what an ADT keeps hidden.
B — Wrong. An ADT has nothing to do with the hardware device. Where data is physically kept (RAM, disk) is decided by the system, not by the ADT definition.
C — Correct. An ADT = a set of values + a set of operations on those values, described only by their behaviour. The implementation can change without changing the ADT.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: ADT = the 'what' (like the buttons on a TV remote); implementation = the 'how' (the circuit inside).

q: Which of the following is a primitive data structure?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: int is a primitive data type; arrays and linked lists are non-primitive structures built from primitives.
concept: Primitive data structures are the basic data types that the language (and the machine) supports directly, such as int, char, float, double and pointers. Each holds a single value. Non-primitive data structures, such as arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees and graphs, are built from primitive types and hold collections of values.
why: A — Wrong. An array is a collection of many elements of the same type, built from a primitive type. So it is a non-primitive (derived) data structure.
B — Correct. int is a basic built-in type that holds a single integer value and is directly supported by the language and the processor, so it is primitive.
C — Wrong. A linked list is made of nodes, each holding data plus a pointer to the next node. It is built from primitive pieces, so it is non-primitive.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Primitive = a single built-in value (int, char, float, double, pointer).

q: Which of the following are non-primitive data structures?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Array, linked list and tree are all non-primitive, so the answer is 'More than one of the above'.
concept: Data structures are classified as primitive (int, char, float, double, pointer: single basic values supported directly by the language) and non-primitive (collections built from primitive types). Non-primitive structures are further divided into linear ones (array, stack, queue, linked list) and non-linear ones (tree, graph).
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. An array groups many values of one type under one name, so it is a non-primitive (linear) data structure. Since B and C are also true, the answer is D.

B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. A linked list is a chain of nodes connected by pointers; it is a non-primitive (linear) data structure. Since A and C are also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. A tree arranges nodes in a parent-child hierarchy; it is a non-primitive (non-linear) data structure. Since A and B are also true, the answer is D.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: Which of the following is a non-linear data structure?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A tree is non-linear because a node can have several children; stack and queue are linear.
concept: In a linear data structure the elements form one sequence: each element has at most one element before it and one after it (array, stack, queue, linked list). In a non-linear data structure an element can be connected to several others, so there is no single sequence. Trees (one parent, many children) and graphs (any connections) are non-linear.
why: A — Wrong. A queue is a linear structure: elements stand in one line, added at the rear and removed from the front (FIFO), like the line at a railway ticket counter.
B — Wrong. A stack is a linear structure: elements are piled one on top of another and only the top is used (LIFO), like a pile of plates.
C — Correct. A tree is non-linear: a node can have many children, so the elements branch out instead of forming one line.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Linear = one line (array, stack, queue, linked list). Non-linear = branches or a network (tree, graph).

q: Which of the following are linear data structures?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Array, queue and linked list all keep elements in one sequence, so all three are linear: answer D.
concept: A data structure is linear if its elements are arranged in a single sequence, so every element (except the first and the last) has exactly one predecessor (the one before it) and one successor (the one after it). Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are linear; trees and graphs are non-linear. 'Linear' describes the logical order, not the memory layout: a linked list is linear even though its nodes are scattered in memory.
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. An array keeps its elements one after another in index order: a[0], a[1], a[2] and so on. This is a single sequence, so it is linear. Since B and C are also true, the answer is D.

B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. A queue keeps its elements in one line from front to rear, so it is linear. Since A and C are also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. A linked list joins nodes in a chain where each node points to the next one, giving a single sequence. It is linear even though the nodes need not be next to each other in memory. Since A and B are also true, the answer is D.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: Linear is about logical order, not about where the data sits in memory.

q: Hierarchical (parent–child) relationships, such as folders inside folders in a file system, are best represented by a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Hierarchies such as folders within folders are represented by a tree.
concept: A tree is a non-linear data structure that represents a hierarchy. It has one top node called the root; every other node has exactly one parent and may have any number of children. A computer's file system is a perfect example: the root folder contains folders, which contain more folders and files. Family trees and an organisation chart are other examples.
why: A — Wrong. A queue stores items in arrival order (FIFO) in a single line. It cannot express that one folder is inside another.
B — Correct. A tree's parent-child links exactly match 'folder inside folder': each folder (node) has one parent folder and may contain many sub-folders or files (children).
C — Wrong. A stack stores items in a single pile (LIFO). It is used for function calls and undo, but it cannot represent a hierarchy.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In C, which of the following is a static data structure (its size is fixed when it is declared and cannot grow at run time)?
opts: A singly linked list whose nodes are created with malloc()
A binary search tree whose nodes are created with malloc()
An array declared as int a[50];
More than one of the above
exp: int a[50]; has a fixed size, so it is a static data structure; malloc()-based lists and trees are dynamic.
concept: A static data structure has a fixed size that is decided when it is declared (at compile time); it cannot grow or shrink while the program runs. A C array such as int a[50]; is static. A dynamic data structure, such as a linked list or a tree whose nodes are created with malloc() at run time, can grow and shrink as needed.
why: A — Wrong. A linked list whose nodes come from malloc() is dynamic: a new node can be allocated whenever it is needed and freed when it is not.
B — Wrong. A binary search tree (BST) built with malloc() is also dynamic, because its nodes are created and removed at run time.
C — Correct. int a[50]; reserves space for exactly 50 integers when it is declared. This size cannot change during execution, so it is static.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Memory taken with malloc() at run time = dynamic. Fixed size written in the declaration = static.

q: Processing (visiting) every element of a data structure exactly once is called
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Visiting every element exactly once is called traversal.
concept: Traversal means visiting (processing) every element of a data structure exactly once, for example to print all the elements, count them or add them up. Lipschutz lists the basic operations on data structures as traversing, searching, inserting, deleting, sorting and merging.
why: A — Correct. Traversal means going through all the elements one by one and processing each exactly once.
B — Wrong. Merging combines two data structures (for example, two sorted lists) into one. It is not about visiting each element of one structure once.
C — Wrong. Sorting rearranges elements into an order (ascending or descending). It may compare elements many times; its goal is ordering, not simply visiting.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A data structure that represents many-to-many relationships, such as cities connected by roads, is a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Many-to-many relationships such as a road network are modelled by a graph.
concept: A graph is a set of vertices (nodes) joined by edges (links). Any vertex can be joined to any number of other vertices, so a graph models many-to-many relationships: cities and roads, people and friendships, computers in a network. A tree is a restricted kind of graph in which every node except the root has exactly one parent, which gives a one-to-many relationship.
why: A — Wrong. A stack is linear and allows access only at the top (LIFO). It holds a sequence of items, not connections between many items.
B — Wrong. In a binary tree each node has at most two children and only one parent. That is a one-to-many (hierarchical) relationship, not many-to-many.
C — Correct. A graph lets every vertex connect to many others: a city can have roads to many cities, and each of those connects to many more. This is many-to-many.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Hierarchy = tree. Network = graph.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the standard operations performed on data structures?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Encryption is not a standard data-structure operation; merging and searching are.
concept: The standard operations performed on data structures (as listed by Lipschutz) are: traversing (visit each element), searching (find an element), inserting (add), deleting (remove), sorting (arrange in order) and merging (combine two structures into one). Encryption, which scrambles data for security, belongs to cryptography and is not a basic data-structure operation.
why: A — Wrong. Merging IS a standard operation: it combines two structures (for example, two sorted arrays) into one. So A does not satisfy 'NOT a standard operation'.
B — Wrong. Searching IS a standard operation: finding the location of a given key (for example by linear search or binary search). So B does not satisfy the stem.

C — Correct. Encryption converts data into a secret code to protect it. It belongs to computer security (cryptography) and is not one of the standard data-structure operations, so it satisfies the stem.
D — Wrong. Only C (Encryption) is NOT a standard operation; merging and searching are standard, so 'More than one of the above' is false.
E — Wrong. C (Encryption) does satisfy the stem, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Six standard operations: Traverse, Search, Insert, Delete, Sort, Merge.

q: Which of the following can be described as Abstract Data Types (ADTs)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Stack, queue and list are all ADTs, so the answer is 'More than one of the above'.
concept: An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is defined only by its values and its operations, not by its implementation. Stack (push, pop, peek), Queue (enqueue, dequeue) and List (insert, delete, get at a position) are classic ADTs. Each can be implemented with an array or with a linked list, and the user of the ADT does not need to know which.
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. Stack is an ADT: it is defined by push, pop and peek with LIFO behaviour, whatever the implementation. Since B and C are also true, the answer is D.

B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. Queue is an ADT: it is defined by enqueue and dequeue with FIFO behaviour, and can be implemented by an array (often circular) or a linked list. Since A and C are also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. List is an ADT: an ordered collection with operations such as insert, delete and get at a position. It may be built as an array-based list or a linked list. Since A and B are also true, the answer is D.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: Which C construct can group items of DIFFERENT data types (e.g., roll number, name and marks of a student) under one name, with all items stored at the same time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A struct groups items of different types under one name, all stored together.
concept: In C, a structure (struct) groups related items of possibly different data types under one name, and all its members are stored together at the same time, each in its own space.
