For example: struct student { int roll; char name[30]; float marks; };. An array, in contrast, holds items of one type only.
why: A — Wrong. An array is homogeneous: all its elements must be of the same type (all int, or all float). It cannot mix a roll number, a name and marks of different types.
B — Correct. A struct is heterogeneous: its members can have different types (int, char array, float), and all of them exist at the same time in separate memory.
C — Wrong. An enum (enumeration) only defines a set of named integer constants, such as enum day {MON, TUE, WED};. It does not store a group of different data items.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Different types, all stored together = struct. Different types sharing one memory space (only one used at a time) = union.

q: All elements of an array must be
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An array is homogeneous: all its elements are of the same data type.
concept: An array is a collection of a fixed number of elements of the SAME data type, stored in contiguous (adjacent, side-by-side) memory locations and accessed by an index. Because every element has the same size and they lie side by side, the address of any element can be calculated directly.
why: A — Wrong. Grouping elements of different types is the job of a structure (struct), not an array. Arrays are homogeneous.
B — Wrong. This is the opposite of the truth: array elements occupy contiguous memory. Scattered storage connected by pointers is how a linked list works.
C — Correct. All elements of an array must have the same data type (homogeneous), so each has the same size.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The time to access the element A[i] of an array of n elements, given the index i, is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Accessing A[i] by its index takes O(1) time because its address is computed directly.
concept: An array supports random access (also called direct access): any element can be reached directly from its index, without visiting the elements before it. The address is computed by one formula, Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB), where w is the size of one element and LB is the lower bound (first index). One subtraction, one multiplication and one addition take the same time for any i, so access is O(1), constant time.
why: A — Wrong. O(log n) is the time of binary search, which repeatedly halves a sorted array to find a key. Accessing a known index needs no searching at all.
B — Correct. With the index known, the address is computed directly by Base + w × (i − LB). This takes constant time, O(1), whatever the size of the array.
C — Wrong. O(n) is the time to reach the i-th node of a linked list (you must follow the links from the head) or the time of linear search. An array does not need to walk through elements.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Array = random access, O(1). Linked list = sequential access, O(n).

q: For an array declared in C as int a[50];, which of the following statements are TRUE?
opts: Its elements are stored in contiguous memory locations
Its size can be increased at run time by writing a[60] = 5;
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are true (contiguous storage, first element a[0]); C is false because a C array cannot be resized by writing past its end.
concept: A C array declared as int a[50]; has exactly 50 elements, a[0] to a[49], stored in contiguous memory. Indexing starts at 0. Its size is fixed at declaration: writing to a[60] does not grow the array, it writes outside the array's memory, which is undefined behaviour (C does not check bounds).
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. The 50 integers are stored side by side in memory. That is why a[i] can be found at base + 4 × i (for a 4-byte int). Since B is also true, the answer is D.
B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. C arrays are zero-indexed, so the first element is a[0] and the last is a[49]. Since A is also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. This statement is false. The size of int a[50]; cannot change. a[60] = 5; writes to memory outside the array (undefined behaviour): it may corrupt other data or crash the program, but it never enlarges the array.
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: The worst-case time of linear search for a key in an unsorted array of n elements is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Worst-case linear search is O(n), which is not among A–C, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: Linear search checks the elements one by one from the start until the key is found or the array ends. In the worst case (the key is in the last position or not present at all) it makes n comparisons, so its worst-case time is O(n). Its best case is O(1) (key at the first position). Binary search, O(log n), needs a sorted array.
why: A — Wrong. O(1) is the BEST case of linear search (key found at the first position), not the worst case.
B — Wrong. O(log n) is the worst case of binary search, which needs a sorted array. The array here is unsorted, and linear search does not halve the search space.
C — Wrong. O(√n) is the time of jump search (block search) on a sorted array, which jumps √n positions at a time. It is not the time of linear search.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: the worst case of linear search is O(n), which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Which of the following are advantages of an array?
opts: Any element can be accessed in O(1) time using its index
Contiguous storage gives good cache performance (spatial locality)
An element can be inserted in the middle without shifting other elements
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are advantages of arrays; C is false because inserting in the middle needs shifting.
concept: Arrays have two big advantages: (1) random access, meaning any element is reached in O(1) time by its index, and (2) contiguous storage, which gives good cache performance. Spatial locality means that when one memory location is used, nearby locations are likely to be used soon; the CPU cache loads neighbouring elements together, so scanning an array is fast. The main disadvantages are a fixed size and costly insertion or deletion in the middle, which need shifting.
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. Random access by index in O(1) time is the main advantage of arrays. Since B is also true, the answer is D.

B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. Because the elements are side by side, one cache line (a small block the CPU loads from memory at once) brings several elements together. This is spatial locality, and it makes loops over arrays fast. Since A is also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. This statement is false. To insert in the middle, all later elements must first be shifted one place right to make room, which costs O(n) in the worst case. Insertion without shifting is an advantage of a linked list, not an array.
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: Which of the following is NOT a property of a C array?
opts: Random access to any element through its index
All elements are of the same type
More than one of the above
exp: Random access, same type and contiguous storage are all properties of C arrays, so none of them is a 'NOT' item.
concept: A C array has three defining properties: (1) all elements have the same type (homogeneous), (2) the elements are stored in contiguous memory, and (3) any element can be accessed directly (random access) by its index. A 'NOT a property' question asks you to find an option that is false for arrays; if every option is a real property, the answer is 'None of the above'.
why: A — Wrong. Random access IS a property of a C array: a[i] is found at base + w × i in O(1) time. So A does not satisfy the stem.
B — Wrong. Homogeneity IS a property: every element of a C array has the same type. So B does not satisfy the stem.
C — Wrong. Contiguous storage IS a property: the elements lie side by side in memory. So C does not satisfy the stem.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is 'NOT a property' (all three ARE properties), so 'More than one of the above' is impossible.
E — Correct. Random access, same type and contiguous storage are all genuine properties of a C array, so none of A–C satisfies the 'NOT' stem.

q: An array holds 10 elements in positions 1 to 10 and has room for more. To insert a new element at position 4 (so that it becomes the 4th element), how many existing elements must be shifted one place to the right?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Inserting at position 4 among 10 elements shifts positions 4 to 10, i.e. 7 elements.
concept: To insert into an array at position k (positions 1 to n), we must first make room: every element from position k to the end moves one place to the right, starting from the last element so that nothing is overwritten. The number of shifts is n − k + 1. Then the new element is written into position k.
work:
Elements are at positions 1..10 (n = 10). The new element must go to position k = 4.
Elements that move right: positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10.
Count = n − k + 1 = 10 − 4 + 1 = 7.
Order of moves: A[10]→A[11], A[9]→A[10], …, A[4]→A[5]; then the new value is put in A[4].
why: A — Wrong. 6 = 10 − 4. This forgets the '+1': the element already at position 4 must also move out of the way.
B — Correct. Positions 4 to 10 contain 7 elements, and each moves one place right: 10 − 4 + 1 = 7.
C — Wrong. 4 is just the insertion position. The elements at positions 1 to 3 (to the left) do not move at all.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Insert at position k among n elements: n − k + 1 shifts. Delete at position k: n − k shifts.

q: An array holds 15 elements in positions 1 to 15. How many elements must be shifted one place to the left to delete the element at position 6?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Deleting position 6 out of 15 shifts the 9 elements in positions 7 to 15.
concept: To delete the element at position k from an array of n elements (positions 1 to n), every element after it (positions k + 1 to n) moves one place to the left to close the gap. The number of shifts is n − k. The deleted element itself is not shifted; it is simply overwritten.
work:
n = 15, delete position k = 6.
Elements that move left: positions 7, 8, …, 15.
Count = n − k = 15 − 6 = 9.
Moves: A[7]→A[6], A[8]→A[7], …, A[15]→A[14]; the array now has 14 elements.
why: A — Wrong. 10 = 15 − 6 + 1. This wrongly counts the deleted element itself as a shift; that element is simply overwritten.
B — Correct. Positions 7 to 15 hold 9 elements, and each moves one place left: 15 − 6 = 9.
C — Wrong. 6 is the position of the deleted element, not the number of elements that move.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A new value is inserted into a sorted array of n elements so that the array stays sorted. The worst-case time is
opts: O(n), because elements must be shifted even if the position is found by binary search
O(log n), because binary search finds the position
O(1), because the array is already sorted
More than one of the above
exp: Inserting into a sorted array is O(n) in the worst case because of shifting, even if binary search finds the position.
concept: Inserting into a sorted array has two parts: (1) find the correct position, and (2) shift all the larger elements one place right to make room. Binary search can find the position in O(log n), but the shifting can move up to n elements, which takes O(n). The total time is decided by the larger part, so it is O(n) in the worst case (for example, when the new value is the smallest).
why: A — Correct. True: even when binary search (O(log n)) locates the place, up to n elements must still be shifted. O(log n) + O(n) = O(n).
B — Wrong. O(log n) counts only the search step. It ignores the shifting step, which dominates.
C — Wrong. Being sorted does not create a free slot at the right place. O(1) insertion is possible only at the end of an unsorted array (if space exists).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: In arrays the costly part of insertion and deletion is the shifting, not the searching.

q: In C, a loop that visits int a[1000][1000] row by row (outer loop on i, inner loop on j, accessing a[i][j]) usually runs faster than one that visits it column by column, because
opts: C stores 2-D arrays in column-major order
the compiler checks array bounds only for column indices
C stores 2-D arrays in row-major order, so consecutive accesses are adjacent in memory
More than one of the above
exp: Row-wise loops are faster in C because C stores 2-D arrays in row-major order, so consecutive accesses are adjacent in memory.
concept: C stores a 2-D array in row-major order: the whole of row 0 first, then row 1, and so on. So a[i][j] and a[i][j+1] are neighbours in memory. The CPU loads memory in small blocks called cache lines; a row-by-row loop uses every element of each loaded block (good spatial locality), while a column-by-column loop jumps a whole row (1000 ints = 4000 bytes) on every access and keeps missing the cache.
why: A — Wrong. This is false: C (and C++) use row-major order. Column-major order is used by Fortran and MATLAB. If C were column-major, the column-wise loop would be the faster one.
B — Wrong. C does not check array bounds at all, for rows or for columns. Bounds checking has nothing to do with this speed difference.
C — Correct. With row-major storage, the inner loop on j touches consecutive memory addresses, so each cache line that is loaded is used fully.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: C language = Row-major. Fortran = Column-major.

q: An array contains 11 elements. If each element is equally likely to be the one deleted, what is the average number of elements shifted per deletion (the gap is closed by shifting later elements left)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Average shifts per deletion = (n − 1)/2 = (11 − 1)/2 = 5.
concept: When the element at position k (1 to n) is deleted, the n − k elements after it shift left. If every position is equally likely, the average number of shifts is the average of (n − 1), (n − 2), …, 1, 0, which equals (n − 1)/2. For insertion into n elements, with n + 1 equally likely positions, the average is n/2.
work:
n = 11. Deleting position k shifts 11 − k elements.
k = 1 → 10, k = 2 → 9, …, k = 10 → 1, k = 11 → 0.
Total = 10 + 9 + … + 1 + 0 = 10 × 11 / 2 = 55.
Average = 55 / 11 = 5.
Check with the formula: (n − 1)/2 = (11 − 1)/2 = 5.
why: A — Correct. Average = (0 + 1 + … + 10)/11 = 55/11 = 5, which equals (n − 1)/2.
B — Wrong. 5.5 = n/2 = 11/2. That is the average number of shifts for INSERTION into 11 elements (12 equally likely positions with 11, 10, …, 0 shifts: 66/12 = 5.5), not for deletion.
C — Wrong. 6 = (n + 1)/2. This is the average number of comparisons in a successful linear search of 11 elements, a different quantity.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Average shifts: deletion = (n − 1)/2, insertion = n/2.

q: An integer array A[0..99] is stored from base address 1000 and each element occupies 4 bytes. What is the address of A[25]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: The elements of a 1-D array lie side by side, so the address of any element is Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB). Base is the address of the first element, w is the size of one element in bytes, and LB is the lower bound (the first index). (i − LB) is the number of elements that come before A[i].
work:
Formula: Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB)
Base = 1000, w = 4, LB = 0, i = 25
Elements before A[25] = i − LB = 25 − 0 = 25
Bytes to skip = w × 25 = 4 × 25 = 100
Address = 1000 + 100 = 1100
why: B — Wrong. 1104 = 1000 + 4 × 26. This counts 26 elements, as if A[25] itself had to be skipped too. A[25] starts right after the 25 elements A[0]..A[24], so we skip 25, not 26 (1104 is the address of A[26]).
C — Wrong. 1025 = 1000 + 25. This forgets to multiply by the element size (4 bytes): it counts elements, not bytes.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: First count the elements BEFORE the target (i − LB), then multiply by w and add the base.

q: An array A[1..50] has base address 500 (the address of A[1]) and each element occupies 2 bytes. What is the address of A[20]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: For a 1-D array that does not start at index 0, we must subtract the lower bound: Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB). Here the base is the address of A[1], so A[20] has only 19 elements (A[1] to A[19]) before it.
work:
Formula: Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB)
Base = 500 (address of A[1]), w = 2, LB = 1, i = 20
Elements before A[20] = 20 − 1 = 19
Bytes to skip = 2 × 19 = 38
Address = 500 + 38 = 538
why: B — Wrong. 540 = 500 + 2 × 20. This forgets the lower bound: it uses i = 20 instead of i − LB = 19, as if the array started at A[0].
C — Wrong. 520 = 500 + 20. This forgets both the lower bound and the element size (2 bytes).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[−5..10] of 4-byte integers has base address 2000 (the address of A[−5]). What is the address of A[3]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Indices can be negative, as in A[−5..10]. The same formula works: Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB). Be careful with the signs: i − LB = 3 − (−5) = 3 + 5 = 8, because subtracting a negative number is the same as adding it.
work:
Formula: Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB)
Base = 2000 (address of A[−5]), w = 4, LB = −5, i = 3
Elements before A[3] = 3 − (−5) = 8 (they are A[−5], A[−4], …, A[2])
Bytes to skip = 4 × 8 = 32
Address = 2000 + 32 = 2032
why: A — Wrong. 2012 = 2000 + 4 × 3. This ignores the lower bound −5 and treats the array as if it started at index 0.
C — Wrong. 2028 = 2000 + 4 × 7. This is one element short (an off-by-one slip): it counts 7 elements before A[3] instead of 8. 2028 is the address of A[2].
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Minus a negative is plus: 3 − (−5) = 8.

q: In an array A[5..30], A[5] is stored at address 3000 and A[12] at address 3056. How many bytes does each element occupy?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: If we know the addresses of two elements, we can find the element size. The difference of the addresses equals w × (difference of the indices), so w = (Address(A[j]) − Address(A[i])) / (j − i).
why: A — Wrong. With 4 bytes, A[12] would be at 3000 + 4 × 7 = 3028, not 3056. 4 is just the common size of an int; the data does not support it.
B — Correct. 56 bytes separate 7 elements, so each element is 56 / 7 = 8 bytes (for example a double).
C — Wrong. 7 = 56 / 8. This divides by 12 − 5 + 1 = 8, the number of elements from A[5] to A[12] inclusive. But only 7 element sizes separate the START of A[5] from the start of A[12].
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[10..60] of 4-byte elements has base address 1200 (the address of A[10]). Which element is stored at address 1300?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: (1300 − 1200)/4 = 25 elements after A[10], so the element is A[35].
concept: To find which element is stored at a given address, reverse the formula: i = LB + (Address − Base) / w. First find how many elements are skipped from the start, then add the lower bound to turn that count into an index.
work:
Reverse formula: i = LB + (Address − Base) / w
Address − Base = 1300 − 1200 = 100 bytes
Elements skipped = 100 / 4 = 25
i = 10 + 25 = 35, so the element is A[35]
Check: 1200 + 4 × (35 − 10) = 1200 + 100 = 1300
why: A — Correct. 100 bytes / 4 = 25 elements after A[10], so the index is 10 + 25 = 35.
B — Wrong. A[25] forgets to add the lower bound: 25 is the number of elements skipped from A[10], so the index is 10 + 25, not 25.
C — Wrong. A[36] is one element too far (off by one): A[36] is at 1200 + 4 × 26 = 1304.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array of doubles A[−20..20] (8 bytes each) has base address 4000 (the address of A[−20]). What is the address of A[0]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: When the lower bound is negative, A[0] is NOT the first element, so its address is not the base address. In A[−20..20], twenty elements (A[−20] to A[−1]) come before A[0]. Always measure from the lower bound.
work:
Formula: Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB)
Base = 4000 (address of A[−20]), w = 8, LB = −20, i = 0
Elements before A[0] = 0 − (−20) = 20
Bytes to skip = 8 × 20 = 160
Address = 4000 + 160 = 4160
why: B — Wrong. 4000 is the address of A[−20], the first element. It is chosen only if you wrongly assume that A[0] is always the first element.
C — Wrong. 4080 = 4000 + 4 × 20. This uses 4 bytes per element (the size of an int) instead of 8 bytes for a double.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[11..60] of 2-byte elements has base address 100 (the address of A[11]). What is the address of its last element?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The last element A[60] is at 100 + 2 × (60 − 11) = 198.
concept: The last element of A[LB..UB] is A[UB]. The array has UB − LB + 1 elements, and UB − LB of them come before the last one. So Address(A[UB]) = Base + w × (UB − LB).
work:
Last element = A[60]
Formula: Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB)
Base = 100, w = 2, LB = 11, i = 60
Elements before A[60] = 60 − 11 = 49
Bytes to skip = 2 × 49 = 98
Address = 100 + 98 = 198
(The array has 60 − 11 + 1 = 50 elements and occupies addresses 100 to 199.)
why: A — Wrong. 200 = 100 + 2 × 50. This uses the total number of elements (50) instead of the number before the last one (49). 200 is the first address AFTER the array ends.
B — Correct. A[60] is the last element: 100 + 2 × (60 − 11) = 100 + 98 = 198.
C — Wrong. 220 = 100 + 2 × 60. This forgets the lower bound 11 and treats A[60] as if the array started at index 0.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array SALES[1990..2030] stores one 4-byte value for each year, and SALES[1990] is at address 1000. What is the address of SALES[2025]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SALES[2025] is at 1000 + 4 × 35 = 1140, which is not listed, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: Index ranges need not start at 0 or 1; here the indices are years. The rule is the same: Address(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB). (i − LB) is the number of years from 1990 up to, but not including, 2025.
work:
Formula: Address(SALES[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB)
Base = 1000, w = 4, LB = 1990, i = 2025
Elements before SALES[2025] = 2025 − 1990 = 35
Bytes to skip = 4 × 35 = 140
Address = 1000 + 140 = 1140 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. 1136 = 1000 + 4 × 34. This is one element too few (off by one), as if only 34 years came before 2025; it is the address of SALES[2024].

B — Wrong. 1144 = 1000 + 4 × 36. This uses 2025 − 1990 + 1 = 36, which is the number of elements from 1990 TO 2025 inclusive. The '+1' belongs in counting elements, not in the offset; 1144 is the address of SALES[2026].
C — Wrong. 1035 = 1000 + 35. This forgets to multiply by the element size (4 bytes).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: the correct address is 1000 + 4 × 35 = 1140, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: The array int A[3][4] (indices start at 0) is stored in row-major order with base address 1000, and each element occupies 4 bytes. What is the address of A[2][1]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: In row-major order (used by C), a 2-D array is stored row after row: all of row 0, then all of row 1, and so on. To reach A[i][j] we skip (i − lr) complete rows, each with 'cols' elements, and then (j − lc) elements inside row i. Formula: Address = Base + w × [(i − lr) × cols + (j − lc)], where lr and lc are the lower bounds of the row and column indices.
work:
Row-major formula: Address(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [(i − lr) × cols + (j − lc)]
int A[3][4]: rows 0..2, columns 0..3, so lr = 0, lc = 0, cols = 4
Base = 1000, w = 4, i = 2, j = 1
(i − lr) × cols = (2 − 0) × 4 = 8 (two full rows skipped)
(j − lc) = 1 − 0 = 1
Elements before A[2][1] = 8 + 1 = 9
Address = 1000 + 4 × 9 = 1000 + 36 = 1036
why: B — Wrong. 1020 is the COLUMN-major address: 1000 + 4 × [(1 − 0) × 3 + (2 − 0)] = 1000 + 4 × 5. It comes from using the column-major formula instead of row-major.
C — Wrong. 1032 = 1000 + 4 × 8. This skips the two full rows but forgets to add the column offset j = 1 inside row 2; 1032 is the address of A[2][0].
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Row-major: multiply the ROW offset by the number of COLUMNS. Column-major: multiply the COLUMN offset by the number of ROWS.

q: The array int A[3][4] (indices start at 0) is stored in column-major order with base address 1000, and each element occupies 4 bytes. What is the address of A[2][1]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: In column-major order (used by Fortran and MATLAB), a 2-D array is stored column after column: all of column 0, then all of column 1, and so on. To reach A[i][j] we skip (j − lc) full columns, each with 'rows' elements, and then (i − lr) elements down column j. Formula: Address = Base + w × [(j − lc) × rows + (i − lr)].
work:
Column-major formula: Address(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [(j − lc) × rows + (i − lr)]
int A[3][4]: rows 0..2, columns 0..3, so lr = 0, lc = 0, rows = 3
Base = 1000, w = 4, i = 2, j = 1
(j − lc) × rows = (1 − 0) × 3 = 3 (one full column skipped)
(i − lr) = 2 − 0 = 2
Elements before A[2][1] = 3 + 2 = 5
Address = 1000 + 4 × 5 = 1000 + 20 = 1020
why: A — Wrong. 1036 is the ROW-major address: 1000 + 4 × (2 × 4 + 1). It comes from using row-major instead of column-major.
B — Wrong. 1012 = 1000 + 4 × 3. This skips one full column but forgets to add the row offset i = 2 inside column 1; 1012 is the address of A[0][1].
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[1..10][1..15] with 2-byte elements is stored in row-major order starting at address 2000 (the address of A[1][1]). What is the address of A[5][8]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: With 1-based indices we must subtract the lower bound 1 from both indices. In row-major order, four complete rows (rows 1 to 4) of 15 elements come before row 5, and then 7 elements (columns 1 to 7) come before column 8 inside row 5. Formula: Address = Base + w × [(i − lr) × cols + (j − lc)].
work:
Row-major formula: Address(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [(i − lr) × cols + (j − lc)]
A[1..10][1..15]: lr = 1, lc = 1, rows = 10, cols = 15 − 1 + 1 = 15
Base = 2000, w = 2, i = 5, j = 8
(i − lr) × cols = (5 − 1) × 15 = 4 × 15 = 60
(j − lc) = 8 − 1 = 7
Elements before A[5][8] = 60 + 7 = 67
Address = 2000 + 2 × 67 = 2000 + 134 = 2134
why: B — Wrong. 2148 is the COLUMN-major address: 2000 + 2 × [(8 − 1) × 10 + (5 − 1)] = 2000 + 2 × 74. It comes from using column-major instead of row-major.
C — Wrong. 2136 = 2000 + 2 × 68. This forgets to subtract the column lower bound (uses j = 8 instead of j − 1 = 7), so it is one element too far.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[1..10][1..15] with 2-byte elements is stored in column-major order starting at address 2000 (the address of A[1][1]). What is the address of A[5][8]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Column-major order stores columns one after another. Seven complete columns (columns 1 to 7), each of 10 elements, come before column 8; then 4 elements (rows 1 to 4) come before row 5 inside column 8. Formula: Address = Base + w × [(j − lc) × rows + (i − lr)].
work:
Column-major formula: Address(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [(j − lc) × rows + (i − lr)]
A[1..10][1..15]: lr = 1, lc = 1, rows = 10 − 1 + 1 = 10
Base = 2000, w = 2, i = 5, j = 8
(j − lc) × rows = (8 − 1) × 10 = 7 × 10 = 70
(i − lr) = 5 − 1 = 4
Elements before A[5][8] = 70 + 4 = 74
Address = 2000 + 2 × 74 = 2000 + 148 = 2148
why: A — Wrong. 2134 is the ROW-major address of the same element. It comes from using row-major instead of column-major.
C — Wrong. 2150 = 2000 + 2 × 75. This forgets to subtract the row lower bound (uses i = 5 instead of i − 1 = 4), so it is one element too far.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[−3..5][2..9] with 4-byte elements is stored in row-major order, and the address of A[−3][2] is 1500. What is the address of A[2][6]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: With negative lower bounds, first find the number of columns: cols = uc − lc + 1. Then apply the row-major formula, taking care with the signs: Address = Base + w × [(i − lr) × cols + (j − lc)].
why: A — Wrong. 1664 is the COLUMN-major address: 1500 + 4 × [(6 − 2) × 9 + (2 − (−3))] = 1500 + 4 × 41. It comes from using column-major instead of row-major.
C — Wrong. 1656 = 1500 + 4 × 39 = 1500 + 4 × (5 × 7 + 4). This uses 7 columns (9 − 2, forgetting the '+1' in the column count) instead of 8.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[−2..2][−3..3] of 8-byte elements is stored in row-major order with base address 3000 (the address of A[−2][−3]). What is the address of A[1][−1]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Both lower bounds are negative here. Rows run from −2 to 2 (5 rows) and columns from −3 to 3 (7 columns). In row-major order, three complete rows (−2, −1 and 0) come before row 1, and two elements (columns −3 and −2) come before column −1 inside that row.
why: A — Wrong. 3104 is the COLUMN-major address: 3000 + 8 × [(−1 − (−3)) × 5 + (1 − (−2))] = 3000 + 8 × 13. It comes from using column-major instead of row-major.
C — Wrong. 3176 = 3000 + 8 × 22, one element short. It comes from subtracting the ROW lower bound (−2) from the column index: −1 − (−2) = 1 instead of −1 − (−3) = 2.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The array X[20][50] (indices from 0, 4-byte elements) is stored in row-major order and X[0][0] is at address 5000. Which element is stored at address 5420?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 105 elements are skipped: 2 full rows of 50 plus 5, so the element is X[2][5].
concept: To find the element stored at a given address in a row-major array, first find the number of elements skipped: k = (Address − Base) / w. Then row = k ÷ cols (whole-number division) and column = k mod cols (the remainder), and finally add the lower bounds (here both are 0).
work:
Elements skipped k = (5420 − 5000) / 4 = 420 / 4 = 105
Each row has cols = 50 elements
Row = 105 ÷ 50 = 2 (rows 0 and 1 are full: 100 elements)
Column = 105 mod 50 = 5
Element = X[2][5]
Check with the row-major formula: 5000 + 4 × [(2 − 0) × 50 + (5 − 0)] = 5000 + 4 × 105 = 5420
why: A — Wrong. X[5][2] swaps the row and column indices. Its address is 5000 + 4 × (5 × 50 + 2) = 6008.
B — Wrong. X[2][4] is one element short (off by one); its address is 5000 + 4 × 104 = 5416.
C — Correct. 105 elements are skipped = 2 full rows of 50 + 5 more, so the element is in row 2, column 5.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[10..20][5..15] of 2-byte elements is stored in column-major order with base address 200 (the address of A[10][5]). What is the address of A[12][10]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: In column-major order we skip (j − lc) full columns, each having 'rows' elements, and then (i − lr) elements down the column. The number of rows is ur − lr + 1, which is 11 here (do not forget the '+1').
why: A — Wrong. 254 is the ROW-major address: 200 + 2 × [(12 − 10) × 11 + (10 − 5)] = 200 + 2 × 27. It comes from using row-major instead of column-major.
C — Wrong. 304 = 200 + 2 × 52 = 200 + 2 × (5 × 10 + 2). This uses 10 rows (20 − 10, forgetting the '+1') instead of 11.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[1..5][1..4] of 4-byte elements is stored in row-major order. If A[3][2] is at address 1252, what is the base address (the address of A[1][1])?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A[3][2] is 9 elements (36 bytes) after A[1][1], so the base is 1252 − 36 = 1216.
concept: If the address of one element is known, the base address can be found by working backwards: Base = Address(A[i][j]) − w × (number of elements before A[i][j]). The count of elements before A[i][j] is found with the usual row-major formula.
why: A — Wrong. 1196 = 1252 − 4 × 14, where 14 = 3 × 4 + 2. This forgets both lower bounds (uses i = 3 and j = 2 directly instead of 2 and 1).
B — Wrong. 1212 = 1252 − 4 × 10, where 10 = (3 − 1) × 4 + 2. This forgets the column lower bound (uses j = 2 instead of j − 1 = 1).
C — Correct. A[3][2] is 9 elements (36 bytes) after A[1][1], so Base = 1252 − 36 = 1216.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A square matrix A[n][n] (indices from 0) is stored once in row-major order and once in column-major order, with the same base address. Which elements are guaranteed to have the same address in both layouts?
opts: All elements of the first row
All elements of the last column
More than one of the above
exp: Row-major i·n + j equals column-major j·n + i only when i = j, so only the main diagonal is guaranteed to match.
concept: For an n × n matrix with 0-based indices, A[i][j] has offset i × n + j in row-major order and j × n + i in column-major order. These are equal only when i × n + j = j × n + i, that is (i − j)(n − 1) = 0, which means i = j (for n > 1). Hence only the main-diagonal elements A[i][i] are guaranteed to sit at the same address in both layouts.
work:
Row-major offset of A[i][j] = i·n + j; column-major offset = j·n + i
Set them equal: i·n + j = j·n + i
→ i·n − i = j·n − j
→ i(n − 1) = j(n − 1)
→ i = j (when n > 1)
Example n = 3: A[0][1] → row-major 1, column-major 3 (different); A[1][1] → 4 and 4 (same); A[2][2] → 8 and 8 (same)
why: A — Wrong. Only A[0][0] of the first row matches. For A[0][j] the row-major offset is j but the column-major offset is j × n; for example A[0][1] is at offset 1 in one layout and n in the other.
B — Wrong. Only A[n−1][n−1] of the last column matches. For example A[0][n−1] has row-major offset n − 1 but column-major offset (n − 1) × n.
C — Correct. For A[i][i] both formulas give i × n + i, so every diagonal element has the same address in both layouts.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Column-major storage of A is like row-major storage of its transpose, and the transpose never moves the diagonal.

q: The elements of A[1..4][1..5] are stored in column-major order and numbered by their position 0, 1, 2, … in memory (A[1][1] is at position 0). Which element is at position 10?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Position 10 = two full columns of 4 (8 elements) + 2 more, so it is row 3 of column 3: A[3][3].
concept: In column-major order the elements of column 1 are stored first (A[1][1], A[2][1], A[3][1], A[4][1]), then column 2, and so on. With 4 rows, each column takes 4 positions. So position p (counting from 0) is in column p ÷ 4 + 1 and row (p mod 4) + 1.
work:
Rows = 4, so each column holds 4 elements
Positions 0–3: column 1 (A[1][1], A[2][1], A[3][1], A[4][1])
Positions 4–7: column 2 (A[1][2] … A[4][2])
Positions 8–11: column 3 (A[1][3] at 8, A[2][3] at 9, A[3][3] at 10, A[4][3] at 11)
By formula: column = 10 ÷ 4 + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3, row = (10 mod 4) + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 → A[3][3]
why: A — Wrong. A[3][1] is at position 10 in ROW-major order (rows of 5: 10 = 2 full rows + 0, so row 3, column 1). It comes from using row-major instead of column-major; in column-major order A[3][1] is at position 2.
B — Correct. Position 10 = 2 full columns (8 elements) + 2 more, so it is the 3rd element of column 3: A[3][3].
C — Wrong. A[2][3] is at position 9 in column-major order, one place before position 10 (an off-by-one slip).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A C array char A[2][3][4] (1 byte per element) is stored in row-major order starting at address 0. What is the address of A[1][1][2]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Row-major offset = 1 × 12 + 1 × 4 + 2 = 18, so the address is 18.
concept: For a 3-D array A[d1][d2][d3] stored in row-major order (as in C), the LAST index changes fastest. A[i][j][k] has i × (d2 × d3) + j × d3 + k elements before it: skip i whole 2-D 'planes' of d2 × d3 elements, then j whole rows of d3 elements, then k elements.
work:
char A[2][3][4]: d1 = 2, d2 = 3, d3 = 4, w = 1, Base = 0 (all lower bounds 0)
Row-major: Address = Base + w × [i × (d2 × d3) + j × d3 + k]
For A[1][1][2]: i = 1, j = 1, k = 2
i × (3 × 4) = 1 × 12 = 12 (one full 3 × 4 plane)
j × 4 = 1 × 4 = 4 (one full row of the plane)
k = 2
Elements before = 12 + 4 + 2 = 18
Address = 0 + 1 × 18 = 18
why: A — Wrong. 15 is the COLUMN-major address, where the FIRST index changes fastest: k × (2 × 3) + j × 2 + i = 2 × 6 + 1 × 2 + 1 = 15. C does not use this order.
B — Wrong. 16 = 12 + 4. This skips the plane and the row but forgets to add the last index k = 2; 16 is the address of A[1][1][0].
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array A[−3..5][2..9] with 4-byte elements is stored in column-major order, and the address of A[−3][2] is 1500. What is the address of A[2][6]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Column-major address = 1500 + 4 × [4 × 9 + 5] = 1664, which is not listed, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: This is the same array as in the row-major question, but now stored column by column. Skip (j − lc) full columns of 'rows' elements each, then (i − lr) elements down the column. The number of rows is 5 − (−3) + 1 = 9.
work:
Column-major formula: Address(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [(j − lc) × rows + (i − lr)]
A[−3..5][2..9]: lr = −3, lc = 2, rows = 5 − (−3) + 1 = 9, cols = 8
Base = 1500, w = 4, i = 2, j = 6
(j − lc) × rows = (6 − 2) × 9 = 4 × 9 = 36
(i − lr) = 2 − (−3) = 5
Elements before A[2][6] = 36 + 5 = 41
Address = 1500 + 4 × 41 = 1500 + 164 = 1664 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. 1676 is the ROW-major address of A[2][6]: 1500 + 4 × [5 × 8 + 4]. It comes from using row-major instead of column-major.

B — Wrong. 1648 = 1500 + 4 × 37 = 1500 + 4 × (4 × 8 + 5). This multiplies the column offset by 8 instead of 9, either by using the number of columns (8) or by forgetting the '+1' in the row count (5 − (−3) = 8).
C — Wrong. 1660 = 1500 + 4 × 40, exactly one element short of the true 1664. It is an off-by-one slip, for example taking the row offset as 4 instead of 2 − (−3) = 5.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: the correct column-major address is 1500 + 4 × 41 = 1664, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: An array A[−5..5][−5..5] of 2-byte elements is stored in row-major order with base address 1000 (the address of A[−5][−5]). What is the address of A[0][0]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A[0][0] is at 1000 + 2 × (5 × 11 + 5) = 1120, which is not listed.
concept: When the indices run from −5 to 5, A[0][0] sits in the middle of the matrix, not at the start. Count carefully: each dimension has 5 − (−5) + 1 = 11 values (do not forget the zero). Then apply the row-major formula.
work:
Row-major formula: Address(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [(i − lr) × cols + (j − lc)]
A[−5..5][−5..5]: lr = −5, lc = −5, rows = cols = 5 − (−5) + 1 = 11
Base = 1000, w = 2, i = 0, j = 0
(i − lr) × cols = (0 − (−5)) × 11 = 5 × 11 = 55
(j − lc) = 0 − (−5) = 5
Elements before A[0][0] = 55 + 5 = 60
Address = 1000 + 2 × 60 = 1000 + 120 = 1120 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. 1100 = 1000 + 2 × 50 = 1000 + 2 × (5 × 10). It comes from two slips together: using 10 columns (5 − (−5), forgetting the '+1') and leaving out the column offset of 5.
B — Wrong. 1060 = 1000 + 60. This counts the 60 elements correctly but forgets to multiply by the element size of 2 bytes.
C — Wrong. 1110 = 1000 + 2 × 55. This comes from using 10 columns instead of 11 (5 × 10 + 5 = 55), or equally from forgetting to add the column offset (5 × 11 = 55).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: the correct address is 1000 + 2 × 60 = 1120, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: An array of floats A[−10..−1][−5..4] (4 bytes each) is stored in row-major order with base address 800 (the address of A[−10][−5]). What is the address of A[−6][0]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Row-major: 800 + 4 × [4 × 10 + 5] = 980, which is not listed.
concept: Even when all the row indices are negative, the method does not change: count rows and columns with upper − lower + 1, then apply the row-major formula, watching the signs (−6 − (−10) = 4 and 0 − (−5) = 5).
work:
Row-major formula: Address(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [(i − lr) × cols + (j − lc)]
A[−10..−1][−5..4]: lr = −10, lc = −5, rows = −1 − (−10) + 1 = 10, cols = 4 − (−5) + 1 = 10
Base = 800, w = 4, i = −6, j = 0
(i − lr) × cols = (−6 − (−10)) × 10 = 4 × 10 = 40
(j − lc) = 0 − (−5) = 5
Elements before A[−6][0] = 40 + 5 = 45
Address = 800 + 4 × 45 = 800 + 180 = 980 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. 1016 is the COLUMN-major address: 800 + 4 × [(0 − (−5)) × 10 + (−6 − (−10))] = 800 + 4 × 54. It comes from using column-major instead of row-major.
B — Wrong. 960 = 800 + 4 × 40. This skips 4 full rows but forgets to add the column offset 0 − (−5) = 5; 960 is the address of A[−6][−5].
C — Wrong. 976 = 800 + 4 × 44, one element short of 980. It is an off-by-one slip, such as taking the column offset as 4 instead of 0 − (−5) = 5.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: the correct address is 800 + 4 × 45 = 980, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: How many elements does the array A[−5..15] contain?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: The number of elements in A[LB..UB] is UB − LB + 1. The '+1' is needed because both ends are included, just as pages 5 to 15 of a book are 11 pages, not 10. With a negative lower bound, remember that subtracting a negative number adds it.
work:
Number of elements = UB − LB + 1
= 15 − (−5) + 1
= 15 + 5 + 1 = 21
Check by parts: indices −5 … −1 are 5, index 0 is 1, indices 1 … 15 are 15: 5 + 1 + 15 = 21
why: A — Wrong. 20 = 15 − (−5). This forgets the '+1', so one end of the range is not counted.
B — Correct. 15 − (−5) + 1 = 21 elements.
C — Wrong. 15 is only the upper bound. It ignores the negative indices −5 to −1 and the index 0.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Count = upper − lower + 1. Never forget the +1 (the fence-post rule).

q: How many elements does the 2-D array A[−3..5][2..9] contain?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 9 rows × 8 columns = 72 elements.
concept: A 2-D array A[lr..ur][lc..uc] has (ur − lr + 1) rows and (uc − lc + 1) columns, so it holds (ur − lr + 1) × (uc − lc + 1) elements.
why: A — Wrong. 56 = 8 × 7. This forgets the '+1' in BOTH dimensions (5 − (−3) = 8 rows, 9 − 2 = 7 columns).
B — Correct. 9 rows × 8 columns = 72 elements.
C — Wrong. 63 = 9 × 7. This forgets the '+1' only in the column count (9 − 2 = 7 instead of 8).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many bytes of memory does an integer array A[−2..7][4..13] occupy if each integer takes 4 bytes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 10 × 10 = 100 elements × 4 bytes = 400 bytes.
concept: The memory taken by an array = (number of elements) × (size of one element). For a 2-D array, the number of elements = rows × columns, and each of these is found by upper − lower + 1.
why: A — Wrong. 360 = 9 × 10 × 4 (or 10 × 9 × 4). It forgets the '+1' in one of the two dimensions.
B — Wrong. 324 = 9 × 9 × 4. It forgets the '+1' in both dimensions (7 − (−2) = 9 and 13 − 4 = 9).
C — Correct. 10 × 10 = 100 elements, and 100 × 4 bytes = 400 bytes.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In an array A[1..8][1..6] stored in row-major order, how many elements are stored before A[5][4]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 4 full rows of 6 (24) plus 3 elements of row 5 = 27 elements before A[5][4].
concept: In row-major order, the elements stored before A[i][j] are all the elements of the earlier rows plus the earlier elements of row i. This count, (i − lr) × cols + (j − lc), is exactly the number that the address formula multiplies by the element size w.
work:
Row-major: elements before A[i][j] = (i − lr) × cols + (j − lc)
lr = 1, lc = 1, cols = 6, i = 5, j = 4
Complete rows before row 5 (rows 1–4): (5 − 1) × 6 = 24
Elements before column 4 in row 5 (columns 1–3): 4 − 1 = 3
Total = 24 + 3 = 27
why: A — Wrong. 28 counts A[5][4] itself too (it is the position of A[5][4] when counting from 1). It is also the number of elements before A[5][4] in COLUMN-major order: (4 − 1) × 8 + (5 − 1) = 28.
B — Correct. 4 full rows of 6 (24 elements) plus 3 elements of row 5 = 27.
C — Wrong. 30 = 5 × 6 is the number of elements in rows 1 to 5, that is, up to the END of row 5. It wrongly counts the whole of row 5 instead of just its first 3 elements.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many elements does the 3-D array A[5..14][−4..0][1..3] contain?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 10 × 5 × 3 = 150 elements, which is not listed.
concept: For a multi-dimensional array, the number of elements is the product of the sizes of all the dimensions, and each size is upper − lower + 1.
work:
First dimension: 14 − 5 + 1 = 10
Second dimension: 0 − (−4) + 1 = 5
Third dimension: 3 − 1 + 1 = 3
Total = 10 × 5 × 3 = 150 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. 120 = 10 × 4 × 3. This forgets the '+1' in the second dimension (0 − (−4) = 4 instead of 5).
B — Wrong. 180 = 10 × 6 × 3 would need the range −4..0 to have 6 values; it has only 5 (−4, −3, −2, −1, 0). It does not match a correct count.
C — Wrong. 135 = 9 × 5 × 3. This forgets the '+1' in the first dimension (14 − 5 = 9 instead of 10).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: the correct count is 10 × 5 × 3 = 150, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about sparse matrices are TRUE?
opts: Most of their elements are zero
Storing all m × n elements in a 2-D array wastes memory
The triplet form stores only the non-zero elements along with their positions
More than one of the above
exp: All three statements about sparse matrices are true, so the answer is 'More than one of the above'.
concept: A sparse matrix is a matrix in which most of the elements are zero. Storing all m × n elements in a normal 2-D array wastes memory on the zeros, so we store only the non-zero elements together with their positions. Common methods are the triplet (3-tuple) array of (row, column, value) and the linked-list representation.
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. This is the definition of a sparse matrix: most elements are zero. (A matrix with mostly non-zero elements is called dense.) Since B and C are also true, the answer is D.

B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. A 2-D array reserves space for every element, including the many zeros, so most of that memory holds no useful information. Since A and C are also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. The triplet form keeps one (row, column, value) entry for each non-zero element and nothing for the zeros. Since A and B are also true, the answer is D.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: In the triplet (3-tuple) representation of a sparse matrix, each non-zero element is stored as
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Each non-zero element is stored as the triplet (row, column, value).
concept: In the triplet (3-tuple) representation, each non-zero element is stored as (row index, column index, value). Usually the first row is a header holding (number of rows, number of columns, number of non-zero elements), and the entries are kept in row-major order.
why: A — Wrong. (value, next pointer, previous pointer) describes a node of a doubly linked list. It holds no row or column position, so the matrix could not be rebuilt from it.
B — Wrong. (row index, value) is not enough: without the column index we cannot tell where in the row the value belongs.
C — Correct. Each non-zero element needs its row, its column and its value, which is exactly a 3-tuple.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In the linked-list representation of a sparse matrix, each node typically stores
opts: only the value of an element and a link to the next node
the row index, column index and value of a non-zero element, plus link field(s)
every element of the matrix, including the zeros
More than one of the above
exp: Each node holds the row, column and value of a non-zero element along with link field(s).
concept: In the linked-list representation of a sparse matrix, a node is created only for each non-zero element. Each node stores the row index, the column index and the value, plus one or more links (pointers) to the next non-zero node in the same row and/or column. Memory is used only for the non-zero elements.
why: A — Wrong. A node holding only a value and a next link loses the position information (row and column), so the matrix cannot be reconstructed from it.
B — Correct. Each node records where the element is (row, column), what it is (value), and link field(s) to the next non-zero node.
C — Wrong. Storing every element, zeros included, defeats the purpose; it is as wasteful as the full 2-D array (in fact worse, because of the extra pointers).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are TRUE for a diagonal matrix of order n?
opts: Every element A[i][j] with i ≠ j is zero
At most n elements are non-zero
Its non-zero part can be stored in a 1-D array of n elements
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true for a diagonal matrix, so the answer is 'More than one of the above'.
concept: A diagonal matrix is a square matrix in which all elements outside the main diagonal are zero, that is A[i][j] = 0 whenever i ≠ j. Only the n diagonal elements A[1][1], A[2][2], …, A[n][n] can be non-zero (some of them may be zero too). So it can be stored in a 1-D array D of n elements, with D[i] = A[i][i].
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. This is the definition of a diagonal matrix: every off-diagonal element (i ≠ j) is zero. Since B and C are also true, the answer is D.

B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. Only the n main-diagonal positions can hold non-zero values, so at most n elements are non-zero. Since A and C are also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. Keeping D[i] = A[i][i] in a 1-D array of n elements stores all the useful information; any A[i][j] with i ≠ j is known to be 0. Since A and B are also true, the answer is D.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: A square matrix A is called lower triangular if
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Lower triangular means A[i][j] = 0 for i < j (zeros above the diagonal).
concept: A square matrix is lower triangular if every element ABOVE the main diagonal is zero. 'Above the diagonal' means row index < column index (i < j). The non-zero elements sit on and below the diagonal, forming a triangle in the lower-left. An upper triangular matrix is the mirror case: zero for i > j.
why: A — Correct. A[i][j] = 0 for all i < j makes every element above the diagonal zero, which is the definition of lower triangular.
B — Wrong. A[i][j] = 0 for all i > j makes every element BELOW the diagonal zero. That defines an UPPER triangular matrix.
C — Wrong. A[i][j] = 0 whenever |i − j| > 1 keeps only the main diagonal and its two neighbouring diagonals. That defines a tridiagonal matrix.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Lower triangular: values in the LOWER part, zeros above (i < j).

q: What is the maximum number of non-zero elements in a 10 × 10 lower triangular matrix?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Maximum non-zeros = n(n + 1)/2 = 55, which is not listed.
concept: In an n × n lower triangular matrix, row 1 can have 1 non-zero element, row 2 can have 2, …, and row n can have n. So the maximum number of non-zero elements is 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2. The remaining n(n − 1)/2 elements above the diagonal must be zero.
work:
Non-zero elements possible = 1 + 2 + … + 10 = n(n + 1)/2
= 10 × 11 / 2 = 55 (not among the options)
Zeros above the diagonal = n(n − 1)/2 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45
Check: 55 + 45 = 100 = 10 × 10
why: A — Wrong. 45 = n(n − 1)/2 is the number of elements strictly below (or strictly above) the diagonal. It leaves out the 10 diagonal elements.
B — Wrong. 50 = n²/2 = 100/2. Exactly half is wrong, because the diagonal belongs to the lower triangle.
C — Wrong. 100 = n² is the total number of elements, including the 45 that must be zero.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: the maximum is 10 × 11 / 2 = 55, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Triangle including the diagonal: n(n + 1)/2. Excluding it: n(n − 1)/2.

q: A 6 × 5 sparse matrix has 7 non-zero elements. It is stored in triplet form: a header row (number of rows, number of columns, number of non-zeros) followed by one row (row, column, value) per non-zero element. How many integers are stored in total?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: (7 + 1) rows × 3 integers = 24 integers.
concept: In the triplet form with a header, the first row holds (total rows, total columns, number of non-zeros), and then each non-zero element takes one row (row, column, value). So the table has (t + 1) rows of 3 integers, that is 3(t + 1) integers for t non-zero elements.
work:
Non-zero elements t = 7
Header row = (6, 5, 7)
Rows in the triplet table = 1 header + 7 = 8
Integers = 8 × 3 = 24
why: A — Correct. (7 + 1) rows × 3 integers = 24.
B — Wrong. 21 = 7 × 3. It counts the element rows but forgets the header row (3 more integers).
C — Wrong. 30 = 6 × 5 is the number of elements in the full matrix, not the size of the triplet storage.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A 4 × 4 matrix has these rows (indices from 0): row 0 = 0 0 3 0, row 1 = 0 0 0 0, row 2 = 5 0 0 7, row 3 = 0 2 0 0. Its non-zero elements are listed as (row, column, value) triplets in row-major order, with no header row. Which is the third triplet?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The row-major scan gives (0,2,3), (2,0,5), (2,3,7), (3,1,2); the third is (2, 3, 7).
concept: To build the triplet list of a sparse matrix in row-major order, scan row 0 from left to right, then row 1, and so on, writing (row, column, value) for every non-zero element you meet.
work:
Row 0: 0 0 3 0 → (0, 2, 3) is triplet 1
Row 1: 0 0 0 0 → no triplet
Row 2: 5 0 0 7 → (2, 0, 5) is triplet 2, (2, 3, 7) is triplet 3
Row 3: 0 2 0 0 → (3, 1, 2) is triplet 4
Third triplet = (2, 3, 7)
why: A — Correct. Scanning row by row gives (0, 2, 3), (2, 0, 5), (2, 3, 7), (3, 1, 2); the third is (2, 3, 7).
B — Wrong. (2, 0, 5) is the SECOND triplet. You get it if you forget that row 0 contributes (0, 2, 3) first.
C — Wrong. (3, 1, 2) is the fourth (last) triplet.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A 100 × 100 integer matrix (4 bytes per integer) has only 50 non-zero elements. If only the (row, column, value) triplets of the non-zero elements are stored, each as three 4-byte integers and with no header row, how many bytes are saved compared with storing the full matrix?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 40000 − 600 = 39400 bytes are saved.
concept: Memory saved = memory of the full matrix − memory of the compact form. The full matrix stores m × n elements; the triplet form stores 3 numbers (row, column, value) per non-zero element. The saving is large only when the matrix is very sparse.
work:
Full matrix = 100 × 100 = 10000 integers × 4 bytes = 40000 bytes
Triplets = 50 elements × 3 integers × 4 bytes = 600 bytes
Saved = 40000 − 600 = 39400 bytes
why: A — Correct. 40000 − 600 = 39400 bytes.
B — Wrong. 39800 = 40000 − 200. It counts only the 50 values (50 × 4 = 200 bytes) and forgets that the row and column indices are stored too.
C — Wrong. 39600 = 40000 − 400. It counts 2 integers per element (50 × 2 × 4 = 400), leaving out one of the three fields.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a tridiagonal matrix, non-zero elements can appear only on the main diagonal and the diagonals immediately above and below it. What is the maximum number of non-zero elements in a 6 × 6 tridiagonal matrix?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: At most 3n − 2 = 3 × 6 − 2 = 16 non-zero elements.
concept: A tridiagonal matrix of order n can have non-zero elements only on the main diagonal (n elements), the diagonal just above it (n − 1 elements) and the diagonal just below it (n − 1 elements). So at most n + 2(n − 1) = 3n − 2 elements are non-zero.
work:
Main diagonal: 6
Upper diagonal: 6 − 1 = 5
Lower diagonal: 6 − 1 = 5
Total = 6 + 5 + 5 = 16 = 3n − 2 = 3 × 6 − 2
why: B — Wrong. 18 = 3n = 3 × 6. It assumes all three diagonals have 6 elements, but the upper and lower diagonals have only 5.
C — Wrong. 15 = 3(n − 1). It takes all three diagonals as 5 long, forgetting that the main diagonal has 6.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Tridiagonal: 3n − 2. Diagonal: n. Triangular: n(n + 1)/2.

q: Using the rule 'a matrix is sparse if more than half of its elements are zero', what is the maximum number of non-zero elements an 8 × 10 matrix can have and still be sparse?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The zeros must exceed 40, so at least 41 zeros; the non-zeros can be at most 39.
concept: Under this rule a matrix is sparse when the number of zeros is MORE than half of all its elements. So the zeros must be strictly greater than (m × n)/2. When m × n is even, the non-zeros can then be at most (m × n)/2 − 1.
work:
Total elements = 8 × 10 = 80
Half = 80 / 2 = 40
Zeros must be more than 40 → at least 41 zeros
Maximum non-zeros = 80 − 41 = 39
why: A — Correct. At least 41 zeros are needed, so at most 80 − 41 = 39 non-zeros.
B — Wrong. 40 non-zeros leave exactly 40 zeros, which is exactly half, not MORE than half. So the matrix would not be sparse by this rule.
C — Wrong. 41 non-zeros leave only 39 zeros, which is fewer than half.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The non-zero part of a lower triangular matrix A[1..8][1..8] is stored row by row in a 1-D array, starting with A[1][1] at address 1000; each element takes 4 bytes. What is the address of A[5][3]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Offset = 5 × 4 / 2 + (3 − 1) = 12, so the address is 1000 + 48 = 1048.
concept: To save space, only the lower triangle (the diagonal and below) of an n × n matrix is stored row by row in a 1-D array. With 1-based indices, rows 1 to i − 1 contain 1 + 2 + … + (i − 1) = i(i − 1)/2 elements, so A[i][j] (with j ≤ i) is at offset i(i − 1)/2 + (j − 1). Then Address = Base + w × offset.
work:
Row-wise lower triangle, 1-based: offset(A[i][j]) = i(i − 1)/2 + (j − 1)
i = 5, j = 3
Elements in rows 1–4 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 5 × 4 / 2 = 10
Elements before A[5][3] inside row 5 = 3 − 1 = 2 (A[5][1], A[5][2])
Offset = 10 + 2 = 12
Address = 1000 + 4 × 12 = 1000 + 48 = 1048
why: A — Wrong. 1052 = 1000 + 4 × 13. It uses j instead of j − 1 inside row 5 (offset 10 + 3), one element too many.
B — Correct. Offset = 5 × 4 / 2 + (3 − 1) = 12 elements, so the address is 1000 + 4 × 12 = 1048.
C — Wrong. 1068 = 1000 + 4 × 17. It uses i(i + 1)/2 = 15 for the earlier rows, which wrongly includes all 5 elements of row 5 itself.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The three central diagonals of a tridiagonal matrix A[1..n][1..n] (n ≥ 5) are stored row by row in a 1-D array, with positions numbered from 1 (A[1][1] → 1, A[1][2] → 2, A[2][1] → 3, …). At which position is A[4][5] stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Counting row by row (2, 3, 3, then 3 more), A[4][5] is at position 11 = 2i + j − 2.
concept: When the three central diagonals of a tridiagonal matrix are stored row by row, row 1 has 2 elements, every middle row has 3 and the last row has 2. With positions numbered from 1, A[i][j] (where |i − j| ≤ 1) is at position 2i + j − 2. You can also simply list the positions in order.
why: A — Wrong. 12 is one position too far (off by one); it is where A[5][4] is stored.
B — Correct. Rows 1–3 use 2 + 3 + 3 = 8 positions, and A[4][5] is the 3rd element of row 4: 8 + 3 = 11 (also 2i + j − 2 = 11).
C — Wrong. 10 is the position of A[4][4], the diagonal element just before A[4][5].
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The lower triangular part of A[0..6][0..6] (including the diagonal) is stored row by row in an array B, starting at B[0]. At which index of B is A[4][2] stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A[4][2] is at B[4 × 5 / 2 + 2] = B[12], which is not listed.
concept: With 0-based indices, rows 0 to i − 1 of the lower triangle contain 1 + 2 + … + i = i(i + 1)/2 elements. So A[i][j] (with j ≤ i), stored row by row from B[0], is at index i(i + 1)/2 + j.
work:
Index(A[i][j]) = i(i + 1)/2 + j
i = 4, j = 2
Rows 0–3 hold 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 elements, so A[4][0] is at B[10]
A[4][1] → B[11], A[4][2] → B[12]
Formula: 4 × 5 / 2 + 2 = 10 + 2 = 12 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. 10 is the index of A[4][0], the first element of row 4. It forgets to add the column j = 2.
B — Wrong. 14 is the index of A[4][4], the last element of row 4.
C — Wrong. 13 is one too many: it is the 1-based position of A[4][2] (12 + 1), which is also the index of A[4][3].
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: A[4][2] is stored at B[12], which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: 0-based lower triangle: i(i + 1)/2 + j. 1-based: i(i − 1)/2 + (j − 1).

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: In C, the end of a string stored in a character array is marked by
opts: More than one of the above
exp: C strings end with the null character '\0'.
concept: In C, a string is an array of characters that ends with the null character '\0' (a byte whose value is 0). Functions such as printf("%s"), strlen() and strcpy() keep reading characters until they reach '\0'. That is why a string of k characters needs an array of at least k + 1 bytes.
why: A — Wrong. '\n' (newline, ASCII code 10) moves the output to the next line. It can appear inside a string, but it does not mark the end of the string.
B — Correct. Every C string is terminated by '\0', the character with value 0, which tells library functions where the string stops.
C — Wrong. '0' is the digit zero, a printable character with ASCII code 48. It is different from '\0', whose code is 0.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: '\0' has value 0; the digit '0' has value 48.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: What is printed by the following C code?
code:
char s[] = "HELLO";
printf("%d", (int)sizeof(s));
opts: More than one of the above
exp: s holds 5 letters plus '\0', so sizeof(s) = 6.
concept: When a char array is initialised with a string literal and no size is given, the compiler makes it just big enough for the characters PLUS the terminating '\0'. sizeof gives the size of the whole array in bytes, while strlen() counts only the characters before '\0'.
work:
"HELLO" has 5 characters: H E L L O
The compiler adds '\0', so the array holds H E L L O \0 = 6 chars
sizeof(char) = 1, so sizeof(s) = 6 × 1 = 6
Output: 6 (verified by compiling with gcc)
why: A — Correct. s holds 'H', 'E', 'L', 'L', 'O' and '\0', which is 6 bytes, so sizeof(s) = 6.
B — Wrong. 5 is strlen(s), the number of visible characters. sizeof also counts the hidden '\0' at the end.
C — Wrong. 7 has no basis: the array is H, E, L, L, O, '\0', six bytes in all. There is no second terminator or extra byte.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: A dynamic array (such as C++ std::vector) doubles its capacity whenever it becomes full. The amortised time to append one element is
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With doubling, the total copying is less than 2n for n appends, so each append costs O(1) amortised.
concept: Amortised time means the average cost per operation over a long sequence of operations, even if a few operations are expensive. When a dynamic array doubles its capacity, an append occasionally copies all n elements (O(n)), but such copies happen only at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, … So the total copying for n appends is less than 2n, and the average cost per append is a constant: O(1) amortised.
work:
Copies during n appends = 1 + 2 + 4 + … + (largest power of 2 below n) < 2n
Total work = n writes + fewer than 2n copies < 3n
Average per append < 3n / n = 3, a constant, so O(1) amortised
why: A — Wrong. O(log n) is the NUMBER of resizes during n appends (the capacity doubles about log₂ n times), not the average cost of one append.
B — Correct. Over n appends the total copying is less than 2n, so the average (amortised) cost per append is constant, O(1).
C — Wrong. O(n) is the cost of ONE worst-case append (the one that triggers a resize and copies everything). Averaged over all appends, the cost is constant.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: A single append can cost O(n), but the AVERAGE (amortised) cost is O(1).

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: In C, for the declaration int a[10];, what happens when a program reads a[10]?
opts: The compiler always reports an error
The behaviour is undefined, because C does not check array bounds
More than one of the above
exp: a[10] is out of bounds; C does no bounds checking, so the behaviour is undefined.
concept: C does not check array bounds. For int a[10]; the valid indices are 0 to 9. Reading a[10] accesses memory just past the end of the array. The C standard calls this undefined behaviour: anything may happen (a garbage value, a crash, or output that looks correct), and the compiler is not required to report it.
why: A — Wrong. The compiler does not always report an error. It usually compiles the code, at most with a warning, because C has no built-in bounds checking (and indices are often known only at run time).
B — Correct. a[10] is outside the valid range 0..9, and C does no bounds checking, so the result is undefined behaviour.
C — Wrong. No rule makes an out-of-bounds read return 0. The value is whatever happens to be in that memory, or the program may crash.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: int a[N] has valid indices 0 to N − 1.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: What is printed by the following C program?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: strlen gives 5 (B, I, H, A, R) and sizeof gives the declared 20 bytes, so it prints 5 20.
concept: strlen(s) counts the characters before the first '\0' and does not count the '\0' itself. sizeof(s), applied to an array, gives the total size of the array in bytes as declared, no matter how much of it is used. For char s[20] = "BIHAR"; the remaining 15 bytes are filled with '\0'.
work:
char s[20] = "BIHAR";
Memory: B I H A R \0 \0 … (20 bytes in all)
strlen(s) = characters before the first '\0' = 5
sizeof(s) = 20 × sizeof(char) = 20
Output: 5 20 (verified by compiling with gcc)
why: A — Correct. strlen gives 5 (B, I, H, A, R) and sizeof gives the declared 20 bytes, so the output is 5 20.
B — Wrong. 6 20 counts the '\0' in strlen. strlen never counts the terminator.
C — Wrong. 5 6 would be printed for char s[] = "BIHAR"; (size chosen by the compiler = 5 + 1). Here the size is given explicitly as 20.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: strlen = characters actually used; sizeof (on an array) = bytes reserved.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: When a 2-D array is declared as a function parameter in C, which size may be left empty?
opts: Only the second (column) size, as in int a[10][]
Both sizes, as in int a[][]
Only the first (row) size, as in int a[][10]
More than one of the above
exp: Only the first (row) size may be omitted, as in int a[][10].
concept: When a 2-D array is passed to a function, the compiler needs the number of columns to compute the address of a[i][j] in row-major order (base + w × (i × cols + j)). The number of rows is not needed, because the parameter is really a pointer to the first row. So only the first size may be left empty, as in int a[][10].
why: A — Wrong. int a[10][] is invalid. Without the column count the compiler cannot work out where row i begins (gcc reports 'array type has incomplete element type').
B — Wrong. int a[][] is invalid for the same reason: the column size is missing.
C — Correct. int a[][10] gives the column count (needed for the address formula) and leaves out only the row count, which the compiler does not need.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: In a C parameter, only the FIRST dimension may be left blank.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: Which of the following are valid C function headers for a function that receives a 2-D int array having 10 columns?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three headers are valid and equivalent, so the answer is 'More than one of the above'.
concept: In C, an array parameter is automatically adjusted to a pointer to its first element. For a 2-D int array with 10 columns, the first element is a whole row of 10 ints, so the parameter really has the type int (*)[10] (a pointer to an array of 10 ints). Writing int a[][10], int a[5][10] or int (*a)[10] all give this same type; any first size, such as 5, is ignored.
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. int a[][10] is the usual way to write it: rows unspecified, 10 columns. Since B and C are also true, the answer is D.

B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. int a[5][10] is valid; the 5 is ignored by the compiler, so it means the same as int a[][10]. Since A and C are also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. int (*a)[10] spells out the real type: a pointer to an array of 10 ints. The parentheses are essential; without them, int *a[10] would mean an array of 10 pointers. Since A and B are also true, the answer is D.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: What is printed by the following C code?
code:
int a[][3] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
printf("%d %d", (int)(sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])), a[1][2]);
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The array becomes {{1,2,3},{4,5,0}}: 2 rows, and a[1][2] is 0.
concept: When the first size of a 2-D array is omitted, the compiler works it out from the number of initialisers: rows = (number of initialisers ÷ columns), rounded UP. Elements that are not given an initial value are set to 0. sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) gives the number of rows (total size divided by the size of one row).
work:
int a[][3] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};  5 values, 3 per row
Rows = 5 ÷ 3 rounded up = 2
Row 0: 1 2 3
Row 1: 4 5 0   (the missing element is filled with 0)
sizeof(a) = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 bytes, sizeof(a[0]) = 3 × 4 = 12 bytes, 24 / 12 = 2
a[1][2] = 0
Output: 2 0 (verified by compiling with gcc)
why: A — Correct. The array becomes {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 0}}: 2 rows, and a[1][2] is the zero-filled element, so it prints 2 0.
B — Wrong. a[1][2] is not 5. 5 is a[1][1]; a[1][2] is the extra slot in row 1, which is filled with 0.
C — Wrong. 1 row is too few: 5 values need 2 rows of 3. The row count is rounded UP, not down.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: In C, the declaration int *p[10]; declares p as
opts: a pointer to an array of 10 ints
an array of 10 pointers to int
a pointer to a function returning int
More than one of the above
exp: int *p[10]; declares an array of 10 pointers to int.
concept: To read a C declaration, start at the name and remember that [] (array) and () (function) bind more tightly than * (pointer). In int *p[10];, p[10] is read first, so p is an array of 10 elements, and each element is an int * (pointer to int). To get a pointer to an array, use parentheses: int (*p)[10];.
why: A — Wrong. A pointer to an array of 10 ints is declared int (*p)[10]; the parentheses force * to apply first.
B — Correct. [] binds more tightly than *, so p is first an array of 10, and each element has type int *: an array of 10 pointers to int.
C — Wrong. A pointer to a function returning int is declared int (*p)(); it needs () for the function, not [10].
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: No brackets around *p: array of pointers. (*p) in brackets: a pointer to something.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: What is printed by the following C code?
opts: More than one of the above
