exp: p points to a[1], so p + 2 points to a[3] and *(p + 2) is 40.
concept: In C, adding an integer k to a pointer moves it forward by k ELEMENTS (not k bytes): p + k points k elements after p. The name of an array, used in an expression, gives the address of its first element, so a + 1 points to a[1].
work:
a = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}, indices 0..4
p = a + 1 → p points to a[1] (value 20)
p + 2 → points to a[1 + 2] = a[3]
*(p + 2) = a[3] = 40
Output: 40 (verified by compiling with gcc)
why: A — Wrong. 30 is *(a + 2) = a[2]. It forgets that p already starts one element ahead, at a[1].
B — Wrong. 50 is a[4], which would need *(p + 3). It moves one element too far.
C — Correct. p points to a[1], so p + 2 points to a[3], and *(p + 2) is 40.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: For an int array a and an int variable i in C, which of the following expressions refer to the same element as a[i]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: a[i], *(a + i), i[a] and *(i + a) all mean the same element, so the answer is 'More than one of the above'.
concept: In C, the subscript expression a[i] is DEFINED as *(a + i): take the address of the first element, move i elements forward, and read the value there. Since addition is commutative, a + i equals i + a, so *(i + a) and even i[a] (which means *(i + a)) refer to the same element.
why: A — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. *(a + i) is the definition of a[i]: pointer arithmetic moves i elements from the start, then * reads the value. Since B and C are also true, the answer is D.

B — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. i[a] means *(i + a), which equals *(a + i). It looks strange but is legal C and gives the same element. Since A and C are also true, the answer is D.

C — Wrong. On its own this is not the answer, even though the statement is TRUE. *(i + a) is the same as *(a + i), because a + i and i + a give the same address. Since A and B are also true, the answer is D.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: Given the C declarations int a[10], b[10]; int *p;, which of the following statements compiles without error?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An array name is not a modifiable lvalue, so a++, a = b and a = p all fail; the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: In C, an array name is not a variable that can be changed. In most expressions it is converted to the address of the first element, but the array itself is not a modifiable lvalue (an lvalue is something that can appear on the left of =). So you cannot increment an array name or assign another array or a pointer to it. The reverse, p = a;, is fine because p is a pointer variable.
work:
Each statement compiled separately with gcc:
a++;   → error: lvalue required as increment operand
a = b; → error: assignment to expression with array type
a = p; → error: assignment to expression with array type
(p = a; and p++; would compile.)
why: A — Wrong. a++ tries to change where the array starts. An array's address is fixed, so the compiler rejects it.
B — Wrong. C does not allow assigning one whole array to another. To copy, use a loop or memcpy(a, b, sizeof a).
C — Wrong. An array name cannot be made to point elsewhere, so a = p is also an error. Only the opposite direction, p = a, is allowed.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: all three statements are compile-time errors, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Array name = fixed (constant) address. Pointer = variable that holds an address.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: On a 64-bit system where int is 4 bytes and every pointer is 8 bytes, what is printed by the following C code?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: p is an array of 10 pointers (80 bytes); q is one pointer (8 bytes): it prints 80 8.
concept: int *p[10]; is an ARRAY of 10 pointers, so sizeof(p) = 10 × (size of a pointer). int (*q)[10]; is a single POINTER that points to an array of 10 ints, so sizeof(q) = the size of one pointer. The parentheses completely change the meaning.
work:
Pointer size = 8 bytes (64-bit system)
p: array of 10 pointers → sizeof(p) = 10 × 8 = 80
q: one pointer to int[10] → sizeof(q) = 8
Output: 80 8 (verified by compiling with gcc on a 64-bit system)
why: A — Wrong. 8 80 swaps the two: it treats p as a single pointer and q as the array. The parentheses in (*q) are what make q a pointer.
B — Wrong. 40 8 uses 4 bytes per pointer for p (10 × 4). On this 64-bit system every pointer is 8 bytes; the size of the int it points to does not matter.
C — Correct. p is an array of 10 pointers (10 × 8 = 80 bytes) and q is one pointer (8 bytes), so it prints 80 8.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: A dynamic array starts empty with capacity 1. Before an append, if the array is full, its capacity is doubled by allocating a new block and copying all current elements into it. How many element copies are made in total during 17 appends? (Count only elements copied from an old block to a new block.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Resizes at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 copy 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 elements.
concept: With the doubling strategy, the array becomes full (and must be copied into a block twice as big) whenever its size reaches a power of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … Each resize copies all the current elements. The total number of copies, 1 + 2 + 4 + …, is a geometric series that always stays below 2n; this is why appends are O(1) amortised.
work:
Start: capacity 1, size 0
Append 1: not full → no copy (size 1)
Append 2: full (1/1) → capacity 2, copy 1
Append 3: full (2/2) → capacity 4, copy 2
Append 4: room (3/4) → no copy
Append 5: full (4/4) → capacity 8, copy 4
Appends 6–8: room → no copy
Append 9: full (8/8) → capacity 16, copy 8
Appends 10–16: room → no copy
Append 17: full (16/16) → capacity 32, copy 16
Total copies = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31
why: A — Wrong. 16 counts only the last resize (before append 17). Every earlier doubling also copied elements.
B — Wrong. 32 is the final capacity after the last doubling, not the number of copies.
C — Correct. Resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16, copying 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 elements.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In C, the array int a[4][5][6]; is stored in row-major order (the last index changes fastest). Each int takes 4 bytes and the base address (the address of a[0][0][0]) is 1000. What is the address of a[2][3][4]?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: A 3-D array a[d1][d2][d3] can be pictured as d1 'pages', each page being a d2 × d3 table. C stores it in row-major order: all of page 0 first, then page 1, and inside each page row by row, so the last index changes fastest. To reach a[i][j][k] we skip i full pages (i × d2 × d3 elements), then j full rows of that page (j × d3 elements), then k elements. Address = Base + element size × (number of elements skipped).
work:
Row-major (C) formula: Address(a[i][j][k]) = Base + w × [(i × d2 + j) × d3 + k]
Here d1 = 4, d2 = 5, d3 = 6, w = 4, Base = 1000, (i, j, k) = (2, 3, 4)
Full pages skipped: i × d2 × d3 = 2 × 5 × 6 = 60 elements
Full rows skipped in page 2: j × d3 = 3 × 6 = 18 elements
Elements skipped in row 3: k = 4
Elements before a[2][3][4] = 60 + 18 + 4 = 82
Address = 1000 + 4 × 82 = 1000 + 328 = 1328
why: A — Wrong. 1316 = 1000 + 4 × 79. It comes from multiplying j by 5 (the number of rows, d2) instead of by 6 (the length of a row, d3): 60 + 3 × 5 + 4 = 79. Skipping one row means skipping a whole row of d3 = 6 elements.
B — Correct. 82 elements come before a[2][3][4] (60 for two full pages, 18 for three full rows, 4 in the current row), so the address is 1000 + 4 × 82 = 1328.
C — Wrong. 1376 = 1000 + 4 × 94 is the column-major answer, where the FIRST index changes fastest: offset = (k × d2 + j) × d1 + i = (4 × 5 + 3) × 4 + 2 = 94. C does not use column-major order.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Row-major 3-D: offset = (i·d2 + j)·d3 + k. Each index is multiplied by the product of the sizes of the dimensions to its RIGHT.

q: An array A[1..3][−2..2][0..4] of 2-byte elements is stored in row-major order. The base address (the address of A[1][−2][0]) is 500. What is the address of A[3][1][2]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: E1 = 2, E2 = 3, E3 = 2; offset = (2·5 + 3)·5 + 2 = 67; address = 500 + 2 × 67 = 634, which is not listed.
concept: When the index ranges do not start at 0, first find (a) the size of each dimension, size = upper − lower + 1, and (b) how far each index is from its lower bound, E = index − lower. Then use the row-major formula with these distances: Address = Base + w × [(E1 × n2 + E2) × n3 + E3], where n2 and n3 are the sizes of the 2nd and 3rd dimensions.
work:
Sizes: n1 = 3 − 1 + 1 = 3, n2 = 2 − (−2) + 1 = 5, n3 = 4 − 0 + 1 = 5 (75 elements in all)
Distances from the lower bounds: E1 = 3 − 1 = 2, E2 = 1 − (−2) = 3, E3 = 2 − 0 = 2
Elements before A[3][1][2] = (E1 × n2 + E2) × n3 + E3 = (2 × 5 + 3) × 5 + 2 = 13 × 5 + 2 = 67
Address = 500 + 2 × 67 = 500 + 134 = 634 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. 664 = 500 + 2 × 82. It comes from forgetting the lower bounds and using the raw indices: (3 × 5 + 1) × 5 + 2 = 82. The distances must be measured from the lower bounds 1, −2 and 0.
B — Wrong. 582 = 500 + 2 × 41 is the column-major address (first index changing fastest): (E3 × n2 + E2) × n1 + E1 = (2 × 5 + 3) × 3 + 2 = 41. The question says row-major.
C — Wrong. 567 = 500 + 67. The element count 67 is right, but it was not multiplied by the element size of 2 bytes.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true. The correct row-major address is 500 + 2 × 67 = 634, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Always subtract the lower bound first: E = index − lower; size = upper − lower + 1.

q: A character array C[2..5][1..4][0..2] (1 byte per element) is stored in column-major order, so the FIRST index changes fastest. The base address (the address of C[2][1][0]) is 2000. What is the address of C[4][3][1]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Column-major: (E3·n2 + E2)·n1 + E1 = (1·4 + 2)·4 + 2 = 26, so the address is 2026.
concept: In column-major order the first index changes fastest and the last index changes slowest — the opposite of C's row-major order. For a 3-D array: Address = Base + w × [(E3 × n2 + E2) × n1 + E1], where n1 and n2 are the sizes of the first two dimensions and E1, E2, E3 are the distances of the indices from their lower bounds.
why: A — Wrong. 2031 is the row-major address: (E1 × n2 + E2) × n3 + E3 = (2 × 4 + 2) × 3 + 1 = 31. In column-major order it is the LAST index that gets the largest multiplier.
B — Wrong. 2032 = 2000 + 32 comes from using the raw indices 4, 3, 1 without subtracting the lower bounds 2, 1, 0: 1 × 16 + 3 × 4 + 4 = 32.
C — Correct. The distances from the lower bounds are (2, 2, 1) and the column-major offset is (1 × 4 + 2) × 4 + 2 = 26, so the address is 2000 + 26 = 2026.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Column-major = first index fastest; row-major (C) = last index fastest.

q: A two-dimensional array whose rows can have different lengths (for example, row 0 has 3 elements, row 1 has 5 and row 2 has 2) is called a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Rows of different lengths make a jagged (ragged) array — an array of separately sized 1-D arrays.
concept: A jagged (or ragged) array is an 'array of arrays' in which each row is a separate 1-D array with its own length. In C it is usually made as an array of pointers, each pointing to a row allocated separately with malloc; in Java, int[][] a = new int[3][]; followed by a[0] = new int[3]; and so on creates one directly. It saves memory when rows naturally have different sizes, such as a lower-triangular table.
why: A — Correct. Each row is a separate 1-D array of its own length, so the right-hand edge of the table is uneven (jagged).
B — Wrong. A sparse matrix is an ordinary m × n matrix in which most elements are zero; every row still has the same length n. 'Sparse' is about the values, not about rows of different lengths.
C — Wrong. Column-major is a way of storing an ordinary rectangular array in memory (column by column). It says nothing about rows having different lengths.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A jagged array of ints is built in C as an array of 4 row pointers; the rows hold 3, 5, 2 and 6 ints. An int takes 4 bytes. Ignoring the row pointers themselves, how many bytes do the elements occupy, and how many bytes would the smallest rectangular array that can hold every row (int a[4][6]) occupy?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Jagged: 16 × 4 = 64 bytes; rectangular 4 × 6: 24 × 4 = 96 bytes.
concept: In a jagged array each row gets exactly the number of elements it needs. A rectangular array must give every row the length of the longest row, so short rows waste space. Memory for the elements = (sum of the row lengths) × element size for the jagged array, and (rows × longest row) × element size for the rectangular array. (The jagged array also needs one pointer per row, which this question asks you to ignore.)
work:
Jagged: elements = 3 + 5 + 2 + 6 = 16; bytes = 16 × 4 = 64
Rectangular: longest row = 6, so int a[4][6] has 4 × 6 = 24 elements; bytes = 24 × 4 = 96
Saving = 96 − 64 = 32 bytes (less the space for the 4 row pointers)
why: A — Wrong. 96 bytes is the size of the rectangular 4 × 6 array, not of the jagged one. The jagged array stores only 3 + 5 + 2 + 6 = 16 ints, not 24.
B — Wrong. 64 bytes is right for the jagged array, but the rectangular array must reserve 6 places in every row: 4 × 6 × 4 = 96 bytes, not 64.
C — Correct. The jagged array stores 16 ints (64 bytes); the rectangular array stores 24 ints (96 bytes) because every row is padded to the longest length, 6.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Strings, dynamic and multi-D arrays in C
q: Which of the following C declarations of a 2-D array is valid?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only the first (row) dimension may be omitted: int a[][3] = {…} is valid; a[2][] and a[][] are errors.
concept: In C, only the FIRST dimension (the number of rows) of an array may be left empty, and only when an initialiser is given, because the compiler can count the rows from the values. Every other dimension (here the number of columns) must be written, because the compiler needs the row length to find a[i][j] at base + (i × columns + j) × size.
why: A — Correct. The column count 3 is given, so the compiler splits the 6 values into rows of 3 and creates a[2][3].
B — Wrong. The column size is missing. Without it the compiler cannot know how long each row is, so int a[2][] is a compile-time error even though the row count is given.
C — Wrong. Both sizes are missing. The number of rows can be worked out only when the row length is known, so int a[][] is not allowed.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: You may skip the row size, never the column size.

q: A structure declared as struct node { int data; struct node *next; }; is called a
opts: More than one of the above
exp: struct node holds a pointer to its own type, so it is a self-referential structure — the basic node of a linked list.
concept: A self-referential structure is a structure that contains a pointer to a structure of the same type. In struct node, the member next is a pointer to another struct node, so each node can hold the address of the next node. This is the building block of every linked list, like a chain in which every link holds on to the next link.
why: A — Wrong. A nested structure is a structure that has another structure variable as a member (for example, struct student containing a struct date). Here next is only a pointer, and it points to the same type, not to a different structure stored inside.
B — Correct. The structure contains a pointer (struct node *next) to its own type. That is exactly the definition of a self-referential structure.
C — Wrong. A union is declared with the keyword union, and all its members share the same memory location. This is declared with struct, and data and next each have their own memory.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Self-referential = 'refers to itself': the pointer member has the same structure type as the structure that contains it.

q: In a (non-circular) singly linked list, the next field of the last node contains
opts: the address of the first node
the address of the previous node
More than one of the above
exp: In a non-circular singly linked list, the last node's next field is NULL, which marks the end of the list.
concept: In a singly linked list each node stores data and one link, next, to the following node. The last node has no following node, so its next field is set to NULL, a special pointer value that means 'points to nothing'. A traversal loop such as while (p != NULL) uses this NULL to know where the list ends.
why: A — Wrong. If the last node pointed back to the first node, the list would be a circular linked list, not an ordinary (non-circular) one.
B — Wrong. A singly linked node has only a next field; it never stores the previous node's address. A link to the previous node (prev) exists only in a doubly linked list.
C — Correct. The last node's next field is NULL. This marks the end of the list.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a circular singly linked list with two or more nodes, the next field of the last node points to
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a circular singly linked list, the last node's next field points back to the first node.
concept: In a circular singly linked list the last node does not store NULL. Instead its next field points back to the first node, so the nodes form a ring. Starting from any node you can visit every node and come back to where you started, like children sitting in a circle passing a parcel.
why: A — Wrong. A NULL next field in the last node is the feature of an ordinary (linear) singly linked list. A circular list has no NULL link at all.

B — Wrong. The last node points to itself only when the list has exactly ONE node (then the last node is also the first node). With two or more nodes it points to the first node, which is a different node.
C — Correct. The defining feature of a circular list is that the last node's next field links back to the first node.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Each node of a doubly linked list contains
opts: data and a pointer to the next node only
data and pointers to the first and last nodes of the list
data, a pointer to the previous node and a pointer to the next node
More than one of the above
exp: A doubly linked list node has data and two links: prev (to the previous node) and next (to the next node).
concept: A node of a doubly linked list (DLL) has three parts: a data field, a prev pointer to the node before it, and a next pointer to the node after it. Because it has links in both directions, the list can be walked forwards and backwards, like a train in which you can walk from coach to coach in either direction.
why: A — Wrong. Data plus only a next pointer is the node of a singly linked list, which can be traversed in one direction only.
B — Wrong. Nodes do not store the addresses of the first and last nodes of the whole list. Those addresses are kept in separate variables (head and tail) outside the nodes.
C — Correct. Every DLL node has data, a prev pointer (to the previous node) and a next pointer (to the next node).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A singly linked list is accessed through the pointer head. The list is empty when
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A singly linked list is empty exactly when head == NULL.
concept: The pointer head stores the address of the first node. If the list has no nodes, there is no first node, so head is NULL. Always check head == NULL before using head->next or head->data, because following (dereferencing) a NULL pointer is an error that usually crashes the program.
why: A — Wrong. head->next == NULL means a first node exists and it has no successor, so the list has exactly ONE node. Also, if the list really were empty, evaluating head->next would dereference NULL, which is an error.
B — Wrong. The value stored in a node says nothing about whether the list is empty; a node may legally hold the value 0.
C — Correct. An empty list has no first node, so head holds NULL.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: head == NULL → empty list; head->next == NULL → list with one node.

q: A header node of a linked list is
opts: an extra node at the beginning that does not hold a list element (it may store information such as the number of nodes)
the node holding the largest element of the list
the last node, whose next field is NULL
More than one of the above
exp: A header node is an extra node at the start of the list that holds no element (it may store the node count) and simplifies insertion and deletion at the front.
concept: A header node (also called a dummy or sentinel node) is an extra node placed before the first real node. It does not hold a list element; it may store useful information such as the number of nodes. Because this node is always present, inserting or deleting at the front of the list does not need special code that changes head.
why: A — Correct. This is the standard definition: an extra first node that holds no list element and may keep information such as the count of nodes.
B — Wrong. A linked list does not automatically keep its largest element in a special node. (Keeping the largest element at the top is the idea of a max-heap, a different data structure.)
C — Wrong. The last node (whose next is NULL) is sometimes called the tail node. It is an ordinary node that holds a real list element, not a header.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular singly linked list contains exactly one node, pointed to by p. Which condition holds?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a one-node circular list, the node's next field points to itself (p->next == p).
concept: In a circular singly linked list the last node always links back to the first node. When there is only one node, that node is both the first and the last, so its next field points to itself. This self-link is how a one-node circular list is recognised.
why: A — Wrong. A circular list never has a NULL link. p->next == NULL describes a one-node ordinary (linear) list, not a circular one.
B — Wrong. p == NULL would mean the list is empty, but here the list has one node and p points to it.
C — Correct. The only node is the last node and also the first node, so its next field points back to itself: p->next == p.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are TRUE for a circular doubly linked list with at least two nodes?
opts: The prev field of the first node points to the last node
The next field of the last node points to the first node
No node has a NULL link field
More than one of the above
exp: In a circular DLL, first->prev is the last node and last->next is the first node, so no link is NULL. All three statements are true.
concept: A circular doubly linked list joins both of its ends: the last node's next points to the first node, and the first node's prev points to the last node. As a result no link field anywhere in the list is NULL, and you can move round the ring in either direction.
why: A — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so A alone is not the answer (choose D). In a circular DLL the first node's prev link wraps around to the last node.
B — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so B alone is not the answer (choose D). The last node's next link wraps around to the first node.

C — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so C alone is not the answer (choose D). Because both ends are joined, every prev field and every next field points to some node; none of them is NULL.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: Which of the following is a valid declaration of a linked-list node in C?
opts: struct node { int data; struct node *next; };
struct node { int data; struct node next; };
More than one of the above
exp: Only struct node { int data; struct node *next; }; is valid: a structure may hold a pointer to its own type, but not a copy of itself.
concept: A structure in C may contain a pointer to its own type, because a pointer has a fixed size (for example 8 bytes) whatever it points to. It may NOT contain a member of its own type, because then the structure would contain itself, again and again, and its size could never be decided. Also, every member must be declared with a type.
why: A — Correct. next is a pointer to struct node, which is allowed. This is the standard linked-list node declaration.
B — Wrong. struct node next; puts a whole struct node inside struct node. Its size would have to include itself, which is impossible, so the compiler reports an 'incomplete type' error.
C — Wrong. *next has no type written before it, so this is a syntax error. It must be written as struct node *next;.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about linked-list nodes created with malloc() in C is TRUE?
opts: They are always stored in consecutive memory locations
They are released automatically when the function that created them returns
They are allocated in the stack frame of the function that created them
More than one of the above
exp: Nodes made with malloc() live on the heap, usually at non-contiguous addresses, until free() is called; so all three statements are false.
concept: malloc() takes memory from the heap, a pool of memory that the program manages at run time. Heap memory is not part of any function's stack frame, so it stays allocated after the function returns and is released only when the program calls free(). Successive malloc() calls may return addresses that are far apart, which is why each node must store the address of the next node.
why: A — Wrong. malloc() gives memory wherever free space exists in the heap, so nodes are generally scattered. Storage in consecutive locations is a property of arrays, and it is exactly why a linked list needs next pointers.

B — Wrong. Heap memory is never released automatically when a function returns; it stays until free() is called (forgetting to call free() causes a memory leak). Automatic release on return happens only to local (automatic) variables.
C — Wrong. Local variables live in the function's stack frame, but malloc() memory comes from the heap. Only the pointer variable that holds the node's address may be on the stack.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. A, B and C are all false: malloc() memory comes from the heap, is generally not contiguous, and stays allocated until free() is called.

q: What is the time complexity of inserting a new node at the beginning of a singly linked list of n nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Insertion at the front needs only t->next = head; head = t; — constant time, Θ(1).
concept: Inserting at the beginning of a singly linked list needs only two pointer assignments: make the new node point to the old first node, then make head point to the new node. The amount of work does not depend on how many nodes the list has, so it takes constant time, Θ(1). (Θ gives a tight bound: the time grows exactly like the given function, up to constant factors.)
work:
Before: head → 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL; new node t holds 5
Step 1: t->next = head;   (5 → 10)
Step 2: head = t;
After:  head → 5 → 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL
Always 2 assignments, whatever n is → Θ(1)
why: A — Wrong. Θ(n) means the work grows in proportion to the length of the list. That is the cost of inserting at the END when only a head pointer is kept, because the list must be walked. At the front no walking is needed.
B — Wrong. Θ(n log n) is the growth of efficient sorting algorithms such as merge sort. A single front insertion does nothing of that kind.
C — Correct. Only two pointer assignments are made, independent of n, so the time is constant: Θ(1).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The front of a singly linked list is always cheap: insert or delete there in constant time.

q: A singly linked list of n nodes keeps only a head pointer. What is the time complexity of inserting a new node at the end?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With only a head pointer the list must be walked to its last node, so insertion at the end takes O(n) time.
concept: With only a head pointer, the program does not know where the last node is. To insert at the end it must start at head and follow next links until it reaches the node whose next is NULL, visiting all n nodes. The time therefore grows in proportion to n: O(n).
work:
List: head → 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL; insert 40 at the end
p = head; while (p->next != NULL) p = p->next;   visits 10, 20, 30 (all n nodes)
p->next = t;   (t holds 40, t->next = NULL)
After: head → 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → NULL
A walk over n nodes → O(n)
why: A — Correct. A full traversal of the n nodes is needed to reach the last node; then one link is changed. Total O(n).
B — Wrong. O(1) end insertion is possible only when a tail pointer to the last node is also kept. With only head, the last node must be searched for.
C — Wrong. O(log n) needs a way to skip half of the remaining elements at every step, as binary search does on an array. A linked list can only be walked one node at a time.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A singly linked list keeps both head and tail pointers. Inserting a new node at the end takes
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With a tail pointer, end insertion is just tail->next = t; tail = t; — Θ(1) time.
concept: A tail pointer stores the address of the last node. To insert at the end, link the old last node to the new node and then move tail to the new node. Only two assignments are needed, so the time does not depend on n: Θ(1).
work:
Before: head → 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL, tail → 30; new node t holds 40 (t->next = NULL)
tail->next = t;   (30 → 40)
tail = t;
After: head → 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → NULL, tail → 40
2 assignments → Θ(1)
why: A — Wrong. Θ(n) is the cost when there is NO tail pointer, because then the last node has to be found by walking the whole list.
B — Correct. tail gives the last node directly: tail->next = t; tail = t; — constant work, Θ(1).
C — Wrong. Θ(log n) belongs to algorithms that halve the problem at each step (like binary search). Here there is no search at all.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: To access the k-th node of a singly linked list, a program must
opts: follow k − 1 next links starting from head, taking O(k) time
compute the node's address with a formula, taking O(1) time
use binary search, taking O(log k) time
More than one of the above
exp: To reach the k-th node you must follow k − 1 next links from head, which takes O(k) time.
concept: A linked list has no random access: its nodes are scattered in memory, so no formula can give the address of the k-th node. The only way is to start at head and follow next links one by one. Reaching node k needs k − 1 hops, which is O(k) time. An array, in contrast, finds element k by the formula base address + (k − 1) × element size in O(1) time.
work:
Example, k = 4:
start at head = node 1
hop 1 → node 2, hop 2 → node 3, hop 3 → node 4
3 hops = k − 1 → O(k) time
why: A — Correct. Starting from head (node 1), each next link moves one node forward, so k − 1 links reach node k: O(k) time.
B — Wrong. An address formula (base address + offset) works for arrays because their elements are stored one after another. Linked-list nodes are not contiguous, so no such formula exists.
C — Wrong. Binary search must jump straight to a middle element, which a linked list cannot do; and binary search finds a key, it does not reach a position.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a doubly linked list, a pointer p to a node (not necessarily the first or last) is given. Deleting that node takes
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Given a pointer to the node, a DLL deletion uses p->prev and p->next directly, so it takes Θ(1) time.
concept: To delete a node from a doubly linked list, its predecessor must be linked forward past it and its successor must be linked back past it. When we already have a pointer p to the node, p->prev and p->next give both neighbours at once. So only a fixed number of pointer changes are needed, whatever the length of the list: Θ(1).
work:
Before: 10 ⇄ 20 ⇄ 30, p → 20
p->prev->next = p->next;   (10 → 30)
p->next->prev = p->prev;   (10 ← 30)
free(p);
After: 10 ⇄ 30
A fixed number of steps → Θ(1)
why: A — Correct. Both neighbours are reached through p->prev and p->next, so the node is unlinked with two pointer changes and no traversal: Θ(1).
B — Wrong. Θ(n) is the usual cost in a SINGLY linked list, where the predecessor of p has to be found by walking from head. The prev link of a DLL removes that search.
C — Wrong. Θ(log n) belongs to algorithms that halve the problem at each step, such as binary search. Deleting a node we already point to involves no search at all.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is the worst-case time to search for a key in a SORTED singly linked list of n nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Even a sorted linked list must be searched node by node, so the worst case is O(n), which is not listed.
concept: Keeping a linked list sorted does not give it random access. Even when the keys are in order, the program can only move from one node to the next. In the worst case (the key is in the last node, or is larger than every key) all n nodes are checked, so the search takes O(n). Sorting only lets an unsuccessful search stop early when a larger key is met; it does not improve the worst case.
why: A — Wrong. O(1) search would need direct access to the right node, as hashing gives. A linked list must be walked node by node.
B — Wrong. O(log n) is the time of binary search on a sorted ARRAY, which can jump to its middle element in O(1). A linked list cannot jump to its middle.
C — Wrong. O(√n) is the time of jump search on a sorted array, which skips √n positions at a time. In a linked list, 'skipping' still means following every link, so nothing is saved.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The worst-case search time in a sorted singly linked list is O(n) (a linear scan), which is not among A–C.
tip: Sorted array → binary search, O(log n). Sorted linked list → still O(n).

q: Binary search is not efficient on a sorted linked list mainly because
opts: a linked list cannot keep its elements in sorted order
there is no random access, so reaching the middle node requires traversing the list
the keys stored in list nodes cannot be compared
More than one of the above
exp: Binary search needs quick access to the middle element; a linked list must be walked to reach it, so binary search is not efficient on it.
concept: Binary search repeatedly looks at the middle element and throws away half of the remaining elements. This is fast only if the middle element can be reached in O(1) time, which arrays allow (this is called random access). In a linked list, reaching the middle needs a walk through about half of the nodes, so the total work becomes O(n) and the advantage of binary search is lost.
why: A — Wrong. A linked list can certainly keep its elements in sorted order, for example by inserting each new node at its correct place.
B — Correct. A linked list has no random access, so finding the middle node needs a traversal; every 'jump to the middle' costs linear time.
C — Wrong. The keys in list nodes are ordinary values (int, char, and so on) and can be compared exactly like array elements.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A doubly linked list maintains head and tail pointers. Deleting its last node takes
opts: O(1), since tail->prev gives the new last node
O(n), since the second-last node must be searched from head
O(log n), since half of the list can be skipped
More than one of the above
exp: In a DLL with a tail pointer, the last node is deleted in O(1) time using tail->prev.
concept: With a tail pointer, the last node of a doubly linked list is known, and tail->prev gives the second-last node directly. Deleting the last node then needs only a few pointer changes: move tail back, set the new last node's next to NULL, and free the old last node. This takes constant time, O(1).
why: A — Correct. tail->prev gives the new last node, so only a constant number of pointers change: O(1).
B — Wrong. Searching for the second-last node from head is needed in a SINGLY linked list, which has no prev link. In a DLL, tail->prev already gives that node.
C — Wrong. A linked list cannot skip half of its nodes; it can only be walked one link at a time. In any case, no search is needed here.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a singly linked list of n nodes with only a head pointer, which of the following operations take O(1) time?
opts: Inserting a node at the beginning
Inserting a new node just after the node pointed to by a given pointer p
More than one of the above
exp: Insert at the front, delete the front node and insert after a given node each need only a few pointer changes, so all three are O(1).
concept: An operation is O(1), or constant time, when it needs only a fixed number of steps no matter how long the list is. In a singly linked list, any change at the front, or just after a node we already have a pointer to, alters only a couple of links and needs no traversal.
work:
Insert t at the front:      t->next = head; head = t;            (2 steps)
Delete the first node:      x = head; head = head->next; free(x);  (3 steps)
Insert t just after p:      t->next = p->next; p->next = t;      (2 steps)
None of them walks the list → all O(1)
why: A — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so A alone is not the answer (choose D). t->next = head; head = t; — two assignments, O(1).
B — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so B alone is not the answer (choose D). x = head; head = head->next; free(x); — a fixed number of steps, O(1).

C — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so C alone is not the answer (choose D). t->next = p->next; p->next = t; — p already gives the position, so no traversal is needed: O(1).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: By contrast, inserting BEFORE p (or deleting the last node) in a singly linked list needs the predecessor, which normally means a traversal.

q: Inserting a new node immediately BEFORE a given node p takes O(1) time in a doubly linked list because
opts: the nodes of a doubly linked list are stored contiguously
p->prev gives the predecessor directly, so no traversal is needed
a doubly linked list is always kept sorted
More than one of the above
exp: In a DLL the predecessor of p is p->prev, so insertion before p needs no traversal and takes O(1) time.
concept: To insert a new node before p, the node that comes before p (its predecessor) must have its next link changed to the new node. In a singly linked list the predecessor can be found only by walking from head, which takes O(n). In a doubly linked list p->prev gives the predecessor at once, so the insertion needs only a few pointer changes: O(1).
why: A — Wrong. DLL nodes are created with malloc() and lie at scattered addresses, just like singly linked nodes. Contiguous storage is a property of arrays.
B — Correct. p->prev gives the predecessor directly, so no traversal is needed and the insertion takes O(1) time.
C — Wrong. A DLL keeps elements in whatever order they were inserted; it is not automatically sorted, and being sorted would not remove the need to find the predecessor.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Two singly linked lists of lengths m and n are given only by their head pointers. Attaching the second list to the end of the first takes
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The first list (m nodes) must be traversed to find its last node; then one link joins the lists. Time O(m).
concept: To attach list 2 to the end of list 1, the last node of list 1 must be made to point to the first node of list 2. With only head pointers, the last node of list 1 has to be found by walking through its m nodes. After that, a single assignment (last->next = head2) joins the lists. The length n of list 2 does not matter.
work:
List 1 (m = 3): 1 → 2 → 3 → NULL;  List 2 (n = 2): 7 → 8 → NULL
Walk list 1: 1, 2, 3 (m nodes) → last = node 3
last->next = head2;
Result: 1 → 2 → 3 → 7 → 8 → NULL
Cost = O(m); list 2 is never walked
why: A — Wrong. O(n) would be the cost of walking the SECOND list, but the second list is never walked; only its head address is used.
B — Correct. Finding the last node of the first list takes m steps; then one pointer is set. Total O(m).
C — Wrong. O(1) would need a tail pointer to the last node of list 1 (or a circular list held by its last node). With only head pointers, the first list must be traversed.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A singly linked list of n nodes maintains both head and tail pointers. Deleting the last node takes
opts: O(1), because tail points directly to the last node
O(n), because the second-last node must be found by traversal
O(log n), because half of the list can be skipped
More than one of the above
exp: Even with a tail pointer, deleting the last node of a singly linked list needs the second-last node, which must be found by traversal: O(n).
concept: Deleting the last node of a singly linked list is harder than it looks. The tail pointer gives the last node, but after deleting it the second-last node must get next = NULL and become the new tail. A singly linked node has no backward link, so the second-last node can be found only by walking from head: O(n).
work:
Before: head → 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL, tail → 30
Walk: p = 10, then p = 20 (stop when p->next == tail)   ← about n − 1 steps
p->next = NULL; free(tail); tail = p;
After: head → 10 → 20 → NULL, tail → 20
Traversal needed → O(n)
why: A — Wrong. tail does point to the last node, but the deletion must also update the second-last node and move tail to it. tail gives no way to go back to the second-last node.
B — Correct. The second-last node must be found by traversing from head, which takes O(n) time.
C — Wrong. A linked list cannot skip half of its nodes; nodes can be reached only one link at a time.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: In a singly linked list a tail pointer makes INSERT at the end O(1), but DELETE at the end stays O(n).

q: A circular singly linked list is accessed only through a pointer last that points to its last node. Which of the following operations take O(1) time?
opts: Inserting a node at the front
Inserting a node at the end
More than one of the above
exp: Because last->next is the first node, front insertion, end insertion and front deletion are all O(1) in a circular list held through last.
concept: A circular singly linked list is often held by a pointer to its LAST node instead of its first. This is clever because last->next is the first node, so both ends are only one step away. As a result, insertion at the front, insertion at the end and deletion of the first node all take O(1) time.
work:
List: 10 → 20 → 30 → (back to 10), last → 30, so the first node is last->next = 10
(each operation starts from this list)
Insert 5 at front:  t->next = last->next; last->next = t;   → 5 → 10 → 20 → 30 → (5), last → 30
Insert 40 at end:   same two steps, then last = t;          → 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → (10), last → 40
Delete first:       f = last->next; last->next = f->next; free(f);   → 20 → 30 → (20)
Each uses a fixed number of steps → O(1)
why: A — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so A alone is not the answer (choose D). The first node is last->next, so t->next = last->next; last->next = t; puts t at the front in O(1).

B — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so B alone is not the answer (choose D). Do the same two steps and then move last to t (last = t); the new node becomes the last node, still O(1).

C — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so C alone is not the answer (choose D). f = last->next; last->next = f->next; free(f); removes the first node in O(1) (when the list has at least two nodes).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: Hold a circular list by its LAST node: you then reach both ends in one step.

q: Two circular singly linked lists of lengths m and n are each accessed through a pointer to their LAST node (last1 and last2). Joining them into one circular list can be done in
opts: O(1) time, by changing a constant number of pointers
O(m) time, since the first list must be traversed
O(m + n) time, since both lists must be traversed
More than one of the above
exp: With pointers to the last nodes, two circular lists are joined by changing three pointers, so the join takes O(1) time.
concept: When each circular list is held by a pointer to its last node, the first node of each list is simply last->next. Joining two such lists needs only three pointer changes: remember the first node of list 1, make last1 point to the first node of list 2, and make last2 point to the first node of list 1. There is no traversal, so it takes O(1) time.
work:
List 1: 1 → 2 → 3 → (1), last1 → 3;  List 2: 7 → 8 → (7), last2 → 8
first1 = last1->next;         (first1 = node 1)
last1->next = last2->next;    (3 → 7)
last2->next = first1;         (8 → 1)
Result: 1 → 2 → 3 → 7 → 8 → (1), held through last2
3 assignments → O(1)
why: A — Correct. Only three pointers change (see the working), whatever m and n are, so joining takes O(1) time.
B — Wrong. Traversing the first list is needed only when you hold a pointer to its FIRST node and must search for its last node. Here last1 is given directly.
C — Wrong. Neither list needs to be traversed, because both last nodes, and through them both first nodes, are already known.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: To insert the node pointed to by t at the beginning of a non-empty singly linked list whose first node is pointed to by head, which sequence is correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Link first, then move head: t->next = head; head = t;
concept: To insert a node at the front, the ORDER of the two assignments matters. First link the new node to the old first node (t->next = head), and only then move head to the new node (head = t). If head is changed first, the address of the old first node is lost and the rest of the list can no longer be reached.
work:
Before: head → 10 → 20 → NULL; new node t holds 5
Option C: t->next = head;   5 → 10 → 20 → NULL
          head = t;         head → 5 → 10 → 20 → NULL   (correct)
Option A: head = t;         head → 5 (address of 10 is lost)
          t->next = head;   5 → 5 → 5 ... (t points to itself; 10 → 20 is lost)
Option B: t->next = NULL; head = t;   head → 5 → NULL (10 → 20 is lost)
why: A — Wrong. head = t runs first, so the address of the old first node is lost; then t->next = head makes t point to itself. The result is a one-node loop, and the old nodes are lost (a memory leak).
B — Wrong. Setting t->next = NULL and moving head to t leaves a one-node list 5 → NULL. The old nodes are no longer reachable from head.
C — Correct. t is first linked to the old first node, then head is moved to t, so the new list is t → old first node → ...
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: When inserting, always set the NEW node's link first, then change the old links.

q: The iterative reversal of a singly linked list uses three pointers prev, curr and next, with the loop running while curr != NULL. When the loop ends, which pointer points to the first node of the reversed list?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When the loop ends curr (and next) are NULL and prev points to the old last node, which is the first node of the reversed list.
concept: Iterative reversal walks the list once and turns each next link around so that it points to the previous node. prev points to the first node of the part already reversed, curr is the node being processed, and next saves the rest of the list before curr's link is changed. When curr becomes NULL every link has been turned, and prev is at the old last node, which is the new first node. So after the loop we set head = prev.
work:
List: 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL; prev = NULL, curr = 10
iter 1: next = 20; 10->next = NULL; prev = 10; curr = 20   reversed part: 10 → NULL
iter 2: next = 30; 20->next = 10;   prev = 20; curr = 30   reversed part: 20 → 10 → NULL
iter 3: next = NULL; 30->next = 20; prev = 30; curr = NULL  reversed part: 30 → 20 → 10 → NULL
curr == NULL → loop ends; prev → 30 = new first node
why: A — Wrong. The loop stops only when curr is NULL, so at the end curr points to no node at all.
B — Wrong. In the last iteration next was copied from curr->next of the old last node, which is NULL. So next is NULL too.
C — Correct. prev always points to the first node of the reversed part; at the end it is the old last node, which is the new head.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Floyd's cycle-finding (tortoise and hare) algorithm detects a loop in a linked list by
opts: moving one pointer one node at a time and another two nodes at a time; they meet only if there is a loop
changing the data of every visited node to −1 and checking for −1
counting nodes until the count exceeds a fixed limit
More than one of the above
exp: Floyd's algorithm moves one pointer by one node and another by two nodes; they meet only if the list contains a loop.
concept: Floyd's cycle-finding algorithm uses two pointers: slow (the tortoise) moves one node per step and fast (the hare) moves two nodes per step. If the list ends in NULL, fast reaches NULL and the algorithm reports 'no loop'. If there is a loop, both pointers end up going round it, and fast gains one node on slow at every step, so it must land on slow — they meet. It uses only O(1) extra memory and does not change the list, like a faster runner who must eventually lap a slower runner on a circular track.
why: A — Correct. This is exactly Floyd's method: one pointer moves 1 node and the other 2 nodes per step; they can meet only if the list has a loop.

B — Wrong. Marking visited nodes by changing their data is a different, destructive idea: it destroys the stored data and fails when −1 is a genuine value in the list. Floyd's algorithm never modifies the list.
C — Wrong. Counting up to a fixed limit cannot tell a long loop-free list from a list with a loop. Floyd's algorithm uses no length limit.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Tortoise and hare = two runners on a circular track: the faster one always catches up.

q: To insert the node q immediately after node p in a singly linked list, which sequence is correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Insert q after p with q->next = p->next; p->next = q; — in that order.
concept: To insert node q after node p, q must first take over p's old successor (q->next = p->next), and only then p is linked to q (p->next = q). If p->next is changed first, the address of p's old successor is lost. Rule: set the new node's link before changing any existing link.
work:
Before: 10 (p) → 20 → NULL; q holds 15
Option A: q->next = p->next;   15 → 20
          p->next = q;         10 → 15 → 20 → NULL   (correct)
Option B: p->next = q;         10 → 15 (address of 20 is lost)
          q->next = p->next;   15 → 15 (q points to itself); 20 is lost
Option C: q->next = p;         15 → 10
          p->next = q->next;   10 → 10 (p points to itself); 15 and 20 are cut off
why: A — Correct. q first points to p's old successor, then p points to q, giving p → q → old successor.
B — Wrong. After p->next = q, the expression p->next is q itself, so q->next = p->next makes q point to itself. The old successor (and everything after it) is lost.
C — Wrong. q->next = p makes q point backwards to p, and then p->next = q->next makes p point to itself. The list is broken.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: To delete (and free) the node just after node p in a singly linked list, which sequence is correct? (Assume p->next != NULL and t is a struct node *.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Save the node in t, bypass it with p->next = t->next, then free(t).
concept: To delete the node after p: save its address in a temporary pointer t, make p skip over it (p->next = t->next), and only then free it. After free(), the memory of that node must never be read or written again; doing so is called 'use after free' and gives undefined behaviour (the program may crash or give wrong results).
work:
Before: 10 (p) → 20 → 30 → NULL
Option A: t = p->next;        t → 20
          p->next = t->next;   10 → 30
          free(t);             After: 10 → 30 → NULL   (correct)
Option B: free(p->next);       node 20 freed
          p->next = p->next->next;   reads 20's next field after it was freed → undefined behaviour
Option C: t = p->next; free(t); p->next = p;   10 → 10 (points to itself); 30 is lost
why: A — Correct. The node is first bypassed (p->next = t->next) and then safely freed through t.
B — Wrong. p->next->next reads a field of the node that has just been freed. This use-after-free is undefined behaviour, even if it sometimes seems to work.
C — Wrong. After freeing the node, p->next = p makes p point to itself, so the nodes after the deleted one are lost and the list now contains a loop.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Node x is neither the first nor the last node of a doubly linked list. Which pair of assignments unlinks x (before free(x))?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: x is unlinked with x->prev->next = x->next; x->next->prev = x->prev;
concept: To remove a middle node x from a doubly linked list, two links must jump over it: the predecessor's next must point to x's successor, and the successor's prev must point to x's predecessor. After these two assignments no node points to x, so it can be freed.
work:
Before: 10 ⇄ 20 ⇄ 30, x → 20
x->prev->next = x->next;   (10 → 30)
x->next->prev = x->prev;   (10 ← 30)
After: 10 ⇄ 30; now free(x)
why: A — Wrong. x->prev->next = x->prev makes the predecessor point to itself, and x->next->prev = x->next makes the successor point back to itself. The list is broken.
B — Wrong. This changes only x's own fields. Its neighbours still point to x, so after free(x) they would hold dangling pointers to freed memory.
C — Correct. The predecessor now skips forward to x's successor and the successor points back to x's predecessor, so x is unlinked.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A new node t is inserted between two adjacent nodes p and r (r = p->next) of a doubly linked list. How many pointer fields in total (in t, p and r) must be assigned?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Four assignments are needed: t->prev = p, t->next = r, p->next = t and r->prev = t. 4 is not listed.
concept: Inserting a node t between two neighbours p and r of a doubly linked list needs both directions to be fixed. t needs its two links (prev and next), p's next must point forward to t, and r's prev must point back to t. That is 4 pointer assignments in total.
work:
Before: p ⇄ r   (r = p->next)
t->prev = p;   (1)
t->next = r;   (2)
p->next = t;   (3)
r->prev = t;   (4)
After: p ⇄ t ⇄ r
Total = 4 pointer fields
why: A — Wrong. 2 is the count for a SINGLY linked list (t->next and p->next). It forgets the two backward (prev) links of a DLL.
B — Wrong. 3 leaves one link unset, usually r->prev; then going backward from r would skip t.
C — Wrong. 6 counts every link field of the three nodes, but p->prev and r->next do not change.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Exactly 4 pointer fields must be assigned (t->prev, t->next, p->next, r->prev), and 4 is not among A–C.
tip: DLL insertion in the middle = 4 links; SLL insertion = 2 links.

q: A node t is to be inserted at the front of a non-empty doubly linked list whose first node is head (t->prev is already NULL). Which of the following assignments are required?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three assignments are needed: t->next = head; head->prev = t; head = t;
concept: Inserting at the front of a non-empty doubly linked list needs three things: the new node's next must point to the old first node, the old first node's prev must point back to the new node, and head must move to the new node. (t->prev is already NULL because t becomes the first node.) head = t must come after the other two, because they use the old value of head.
work:
Before: head → 10 ⇄ 20; new node t holds 5, t->prev = NULL
t->next = head;    (5 → 10)
head->prev = t;    (5 ← 10)
head = t;
After: head → 5 ⇄ 10 ⇄ 20
why: A — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so A alone is not the answer (choose D). Without t->next = head, moving forward from t would not reach the old nodes.

B — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so B alone is not the answer (choose D). Without head->prev = t, the old first node's prev would stay NULL, so a backward walk would stop there and never reach t.

C — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so C alone is not the answer (choose D). Without head = t, head would still point to the old first node, and t would not be part of the list as seen from head.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

opts: More than one of the above
exp: After 3 iterations the reversed part is 30 → 20 → 10 → NULL, so prev->data = 30 and curr->data = 40.
concept: In iterative reversal, each iteration turns one link around and moves prev and curr one node forward. After k iterations, the first k nodes have been reversed, prev points to the k-th node (the head of the reversed part) and curr points to the (k + 1)-th node (the head of the part not yet touched).
work:
Start: prev = NULL, curr = 10; list 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50 → NULL
iter 1: next = 20; 10->next = NULL; prev = 10; curr = 20   reversed: 10 → NULL;             rest: 20 → 30 → 40 → 50
iter 2: next = 30; 20->next = 10;   prev = 20; curr = 30   reversed: 20 → 10 → NULL;        rest: 30 → 40 → 50
iter 3: next = 40; 30->next = 20;   prev = 30; curr = 40   reversed: 30 → 20 → 10 → NULL;   rest: 40 → 50 → NULL
After 3 iterations: prev->data = 30, curr->data = 40
why: A — Wrong. 40 and 50 are the values after 4 iterations, one iteration too many.
B — Correct. After 3 iterations the reversed part is 30 → 20 → 10, so prev is at 30 and curr is at 40.
C — Wrong. 20 and 30 are the values after only 2 iterations, one iteration too few.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: After k iterations of reversal: prev = k-th node, curr = (k+1)-th node.

opts: More than one of the above
exp: The loop runs 3 times: slow goes 2 → 4 → 6 → 8 and fast becomes NULL, so slow points to 8.
concept: The slow/fast pointer method finds the middle of a list in one pass: fast moves two nodes for every one node of slow, so when fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the list. When the number of nodes is even there are two middle nodes, and the loop condition decides which one slow stops at; with while (fast != NULL && fast->next != NULL) it stops at the SECOND middle node.
work:
List: 2 → 4 → 6 → 8 → 10 → 12 → NULL (6 nodes)
start: slow = 2, fast = 2
check fast = 2, fast->next = 4 (not NULL) → slow = 4, fast = 6
check fast = 6, fast->next = 8           → slow = 6, fast = 10
check fast = 10, fast->next = 12         → slow = 8, fast = 12->next = NULL
check fast == NULL → loop ends; slow → 8
why: A — Correct. The loop ends when fast becomes NULL, with slow at 8, the second of the two middle nodes (6 and 8).
B — Wrong. 6 is the FIRST middle node. slow would stop there only with a different condition, such as while (fast->next != NULL && fast->next->next != NULL).
C — Wrong. slow moves only half as far as fast; after 3 moves it is at the 4th node (8), not the 5th (10).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Starting with an empty singly linked list, these operations are performed in order: insert 5 at the front, insert 10 at the front, insert 15 at the end, delete the front node, insert 20 at the front. What is the final list (from head)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Step by step the list becomes 5; 10 → 5; 10 → 5 → 15; 5 → 15; 20 → 5 → 15. This final list is not listed.
concept: Front insertion puts the new node before the current first node, end insertion puts it after the current last node, and deleting the front node removes the current first node. To answer such questions correctly, write down the full list after EVERY operation.
work:
Start: empty list (head = NULL)
insert 5 at front:   5 → NULL
insert 10 at front:  10 → 5 → NULL
insert 15 at end:    10 → 5 → 15 → NULL
delete front node:   5 → 15 → NULL
insert 20 at front:  20 → 5 → 15 → NULL
Final list: 20 → 5 → 15
why: A — Wrong. 20 → 10 → 5 → 15 is what you get if you forget the 'delete the front node' step, which removes 10.
B — Wrong. 15 was inserted at the END, after 5, so it must come after 5, not before it.
C — Wrong. 10 → 5 → 15 is the list after the third operation only; the delete and the final insertion of 20 are missing.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The final list is 20 → 5 → 15, which does not match A, B or C.

q: The sorted lists 1 → 4 → 7 and 2 → 3 → 8 are merged into one sorted list by the standard method (compare the two front nodes and move the smaller; when one list becomes empty, attach the rest of the other without comparisons). How many key comparisons are made?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Comparisons: 1–2, 4–2, 4–3, 4–8, 7–8 = 5; then 8 is attached without comparison. 5 is not listed.
concept: Merging two sorted lists compares the front nodes of the two lists, moves the smaller one to the result, and repeats. When one list becomes empty, the rest of the other list is attached directly, without comparisons. For lengths m and n the number of comparisons is at least min(m, n) and at most m + n − 1, and the time is O(m + n).
work:
L1: 1 → 4 → 7, L2: 2 → 3 → 8
comparison 1: 1 vs 2 → take 1   result: 1
comparison 2: 4 vs 2 → take 2   result: 1 → 2
comparison 3: 4 vs 3 → take 3   result: 1 → 2 → 3
comparison 4: 4 vs 8 → take 4   result: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
comparison 5: 7 vs 8 → take 7   result: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 7
L1 is empty → attach 8 without comparing
Final: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 7 → 8; comparisons = 5
why: A — Wrong. 6 is the total number of elements (m + n). The last remaining element is attached without a comparison, so at most m + n − 1 = 5 comparisons can occur.
B — Wrong. 4 stops one comparison early; 7 still has to be compared with 8 before L1 becomes empty.
C — Wrong. 3 = min(m, n) is the fewest comparisons possible, which happens only when one whole list is smaller than the other (for example 1 → 2 → 3 with 4 → 5 → 6).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Exactly 5 comparisons are made, and 5 is not among A–C.
tip: Merging sorted lists of sizes m and n: between min(m, n) and m + n − 1 comparisons.

q: Nodes 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 form a list in which node 6's next points back to node 3. Pointers slow and fast both start at node 1; in each step slow moves one node and fast moves two nodes, and then they are compared. At which node do they first meet?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The (slow, fast) positions are (2,3), (3,5), (4,3), (5,5), so they first meet at node 5.
concept: In Floyd's algorithm both pointers start at the head. In every step slow moves one node and fast moves two nodes, and then they are compared. Inside a loop, fast closes the gap to slow by one node per step, so they must meet somewhere inside the loop. The meeting point is generally NOT the first node of the loop.
work:
Links: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → back to 3
start: slow = 1, fast = 1
step 1: slow = 2, fast = 3 (1→2→3)   not equal
step 2: slow = 3, fast = 5 (3→4→5)   not equal
step 3: slow = 4, fast = 3 (5→6→3)   not equal
step 4: slow = 5, fast = 5 (3→4→5)   equal → first meeting at node 5
why: A — Correct. After 4 steps both pointers are at node 5.
B — Wrong. Node 3 is the START of the loop. Floyd's second phase finds it, but it is not where slow and fast first meet.
C — Wrong. When slow first reaches node 6 (step 5) the pointers have already met at node 5 in step 4.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In the list 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 where node 6's next points back to node 3, Floyd's slow and fast pointers (both starting at node 1) first meet at node 5. Now slow is moved back to node 1, and slow and fast each advance one node at a time until they are equal. At which node do they meet?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Moving both pointers one step at a time from node 1 and node 5, they meet at node 3, the start of the loop.
concept: Floyd's algorithm has a second phase that finds where the loop begins. After the first meeting, one pointer goes back to the head and both then move ONE node per step; they meet exactly at the first node of the loop. The reason: the distance from the head to the loop start equals (up to whole turns of the loop) the distance from the meeting point forward to the loop start.
work:
Links: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → back to 3; first meeting at node 5
slow = 1, fast = 5
step 1: slow = 2, fast = 6
step 2: slow = 3, fast = 3 → equal → node 3
Check: head to loop start = 2 links (1→2→3); meeting point to loop start = 2 links (5→6→3)
why: A — Wrong. Node 5 is where slow and fast met in the FIRST phase; the second phase moves away from it.
B — Correct. slow goes 1 → 2 → 3 and fast goes 5 → 6 → 3, so they meet at node 3, the first node of the loop.
C — Wrong. Node 1 is the head of the list. It is not inside the loop, so fast (which stays inside the loop) can never be there.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Floyd phase 1 detects the loop; phase 2 (one pointer back to head, both at speed 1) finds where it starts.

q: Assume struct node { int data; struct node *next; };. What does the function f return when called with the head of a singly linked list?
opts: The data value of the last node
The number of nodes in the list
The sum of the data values of all nodes
More than one of the above
exp: f adds 1 for every node until NULL is reached, so it returns the number of nodes in the list.
concept: This is the basic traversal pattern: start at the first node, do some work for the current node, and move on with h = h->next until h becomes NULL. Here the 'work' is c++, which adds 1 for every node visited, so the function returns the length of the list (0 for an empty list).
work:
List: 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL
h = 10: c = 1, h = 20
h = 20: c = 2, h = 30
h = 30: c = 3, h = NULL
h == NULL → return 3 = number of nodes
why: A — Wrong. The function never reads h->data, so it cannot return any data value; returning the last value would need something like return h->data when h->next == NULL.
B — Correct. c is increased by 1 once per node until the end of the list, so f returns the number of nodes.
C — Wrong. A sum would need c += h->data; here c++ always adds 1, whatever the data is.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is printed by the code below? (struct node has fields int data and struct node *next.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Each push inserts at the front, so the list becomes 40 → 30 → 20 → 10 and that is what is printed.
concept: push() creates a node and inserts it at the FRONT of the list, returning the new head. Inserting each new value at the front reverses the order of insertion: the last value pushed comes first. This is exactly how a stack works (LIFO: Last In, First Out).
work:
head = NULL
i = 1: push 10 → 10 → NULL
i = 2: push 20 → 20 → 10 → NULL
i = 3: push 30 → 30 → 20 → 10 → NULL
i = 4: push 40 → 40 → 30 → 20 → 10 → NULL
Print from head: 40 30 20 10
why: A — Correct. Each value is placed in front of the previous ones, so the list is 40 → 30 → 20 → 10 and it is printed in that order.
B — Wrong. 10 20 30 40 would be printed if each node were inserted at the END of the list. push() inserts at the front (t->next = h).
C — Wrong. The printing loop runs until p is NULL, so it prints every node, not only the first one.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: f(head) is called for the list 1 → 2 → 3 → 4. What is printed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Because printing happens after the recursive call returns, the list is printed in reverse: 4 3 2 1.
concept: In this recursive function the recursive call f(p->next) comes BEFORE printf. So nothing is printed while going down the list; the values are printed while the calls return, last node first. This prints the list in reverse without changing it, using the call stack to remember the nodes.
work:
f(1) calls f(2) calls f(3) calls f(4) calls f(NULL) → returns at once
back in f(4): print 4
back in f(3): print 3
back in f(2): print 2
back in f(1): print 1
Output: 4 3 2 1
why: A — Correct. Values are printed as the calls return, from the last node back to the first: 4 3 2 1.
B — Wrong. 1 2 3 4 would be printed if printf came BEFORE the recursive call (normal forward traversal).
C — Wrong. Every call with a non-NULL p prints its own node, including the call for the first node, so 1 is printed last.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Print before the recursive call → forward order; print after it → reverse order.

q: What does the function f do when it is called with the head of a singly linked list?
opts: Returns a pointer to the last node without changing the list
Frees every node and returns NULL
Reverses the list and returns a pointer to the new first node
More than one of the above
exp: The function reverses the links one by one and returns p, the new first node of the reversed list.
concept: This is the standard iterative reversal of a singly linked list, written with p in the role of prev, h as the current node and q as next. Each iteration saves the next node in q, turns the current node's link back to p, and moves p and h one node forward. At the end p is the old last node, which is the first node of the reversed list.
work:
List: 1 → 2 → 3 → NULL; p = NULL
iter 1: q = 2;    1->next = NULL; p = 1; h = 2     reversed: 1 → NULL
iter 2: q = 3;    2->next = 1;    p = 2; h = 3     reversed: 2 → 1 → NULL
iter 3: q = NULL; 3->next = 2;    p = 3; h = NULL  reversed: 3 → 2 → 1 → NULL
return p → node 3 (new head)
why: A — Wrong. It does return the old last node, but the list IS changed: every next link is reversed (h->next = p).
B — Wrong. There is no call to free() in the function; all nodes are kept and the returned pointer is not NULL for a non-empty list.
C — Correct. Each link is turned around, and p, the old last node, is returned as the new first node.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The code below is run on the list 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7, and then the list is printed from head. What is printed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The data in each pair of adjacent nodes is swapped and the unpaired last node keeps 7, giving 2 1 4 3 6 5 7.
concept: This loop swaps the DATA of each pair of neighbouring nodes, (1st, 2nd), (3rd, 4th), and so on, and then jumps two nodes ahead. The links are not changed, only the values. If the list has an odd number of nodes, the last node has no partner and keeps its value.
work:
Start: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7
p = node 1: swap 1, 2 → 2 1 3 4 5 6 7; p = node 3
p = node 3: swap 3, 4 → 2 1 4 3 5 6 7; p = node 5
p = node 5: swap 5, 6 → 2 1 4 3 6 5 7; p = node 7
p = node 7: p->next == NULL → stop
Printed: 2 1 4 3 6 5 7
why: A — Wrong. No node is deleted; the 7th node simply has no partner, keeps the value 7 and is still printed.
B — Wrong. 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 would be the result of reversing the whole list. The code only swaps neighbouring pairs.
C — Correct. The pairs (1,2), (3,4), (5,6) are swapped and 7 stays at the end: 2 1 4 3 6 5 7.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: head points to the first node of the circular singly linked list 7 → 14 → 21 → 28 → 35 (the node 35 links back to 7). What is printed by the code below?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The do-while loop counts every node once and stops when p returns to head, so it prints 5.
concept: A circular list has no NULL, so a traversal must stop when it comes back to the starting node. A do-while loop is used because its body runs BEFORE the condition is checked; a plain while (p != head) loop would stop at once, since p starts equal to head. The body runs exactly once for each node.
work:
c = 0, p = 7 (head)
body: c = 1, p = 14; 14 != 7 → continue
body: c = 2, p = 21
body: c = 3, p = 28
body: c = 4, p = 35
body: c = 5, p = 7; p == head → stop
Printed: 5
why: A — Wrong. 4 is the number of links followed before reaching the last node (35). The body also runs for the last node, so the count is 5.
B — Correct. The body runs once for each of the 5 nodes, and the loop stops when p returns to head.
C — Wrong. An endless loop would happen if the code waited for NULL in a circular list, but this loop stops as soon as p comes back to head.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Circular list traversal: use do { ... } while (p != head); so the head node is processed too.

q: The code below is run on the list 4 → 9 → 2 → 7 → 7 → 1. Which of the following values are printed?
opts: More than one of the above
