In nested recursion a recursive call is used as an argument of another recursive call, e.g. f(f(n − 1))
In head recursion the recursive call is the last statement executed in the function
More than one of the above
exp: A (tree recursion) and B (nested recursion) are correct; C describes tail recursion, not head recursion.
concept: Recursion is classified in several ways. Direct or indirect: does f call itself, or go round through other functions? Tail or head (non-tail): is the recursive call the last action, or is work done after it? Linear or tree: does each call make one recursive call (a chain of calls) or several (a tree of calls)? Nested: is a recursive call passed as the argument of another recursive call? Tree recursion such as the naive Fibonacci function makes an exponential number of calls.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each call of fib makes two further calls, so the calls branch like a binary tree; this is called tree (or multiple) recursion.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. f(f(n − 1)) passes the result of one recursive call into another recursive call; that is exactly nested recursion (examples: Ackermann's function and McCarthy's 91 function).
C — Wrong. This describes tail recursion. In head recursion the recursive call comes FIRST and the remaining work is done after it returns.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Head: call first, work later. Tail: work first, call last.

q: Which statement correctly compares a register stack with a memory stack?
opts: A register stack is built from a small, fixed number of processor registers, so its capacity is very limited; a memory stack uses a part of main memory and can be much larger
A memory stack is kept inside the CPU registers, so it cannot hold more than a few items
A register stack can hold more data than a memory stack because registers are faster
More than one of the above
exp: Register stack: a few CPU registers, fast but small; memory stack: part of RAM, much larger.
concept: A stack can be organised in hardware in two ways. A register stack is a small set of CPU registers (for example 64) used as a stack, with a stack-pointer register; it is very fast but holds only a few items. A memory stack is a region of main memory (RAM) used as a stack, with a stack-pointer register holding the address of the top; it can be much larger. The call stack of a running C program is a memory stack.
why: A — Correct. Registers are few, so a register stack has a small, limited height; a memory stack lives in RAM and can hold far more data.
B — Wrong. This mixes up the two. A memory stack is in main memory (RAM), not inside the registers; only its stack pointer is a register.
C — Wrong. Speed and capacity are different things. Registers are faster, but there are very few of them, so a register stack holds LESS data than a memory stack.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A queue is a linear data structure that works on which principle?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A queue follows FIFO: the first element inserted is the first one removed.
concept: A queue is a linear data structure (its items are kept one after another, in a line). It works like the line at a railway ticket counter: whoever joins first is served first. New items join at the back, called the rear, and items leave from the front. This rule is called FIFO - First In, First Out.
why: A — Wrong. LIFO (Last In, First Out) is the rule of a stack, like a pile of plates where the plate put on last is the first one taken off.
B — Correct. In a queue the item that has waited the longest leaves first, so the first item in is the first item out (FIFO).
C — Wrong. Removing the highest-priority item first is the rule of a priority queue, a special variant. An ordinary queue ignores priority and goes only by order of arrival.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Queue = line at a ticket counter (FIFO). Stack = pile of plates (LIFO).

q: In a queue, elements are inserted at the ____ end and deleted from the ____ end.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Elements enter a queue at the rear and leave from the front.
concept: A queue has two ends with fixed names. The rear (also called the tail or back) is where new elements are inserted. The front (also called the head) is where elements are removed. Because insertion and deletion happen at opposite ends, the oldest element is always at the front, and this gives FIFO order.
why: A — Correct. Enqueue adds at the rear and dequeue removes from the front, just as a new person joins at the back of a line and the person at the front is served.

B — Wrong. The names are defined by their roles: 'front' is the end from which elements leave and 'rear' is the end where they join. Saying 'inserted at the front, deleted from the rear' mixes up the standard labels.
C — Wrong. Inserting and deleting at the same end (the top) is how a stack works. That gives LIFO order, not FIFO.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Join at the Rear, served at the Front - just like any real line.

q: The operation that adds a new element at the rear of a queue is called:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Enqueue inserts a new element at the rear of the queue.
concept: The basic queue operations are: enqueue (insert an element at the rear), dequeue (remove and return the element at the front), peek or front (read the front element without removing it), and isEmpty / isFull (test the state of the queue). 'En-queue' means put into the queue and 'de-queue' means take out of the queue.
why: A — Wrong. Dequeue removes the element at the front of the queue. It is the opposite of adding.
B — Wrong. Peek only reads the front element. It does not add anything and does not change the queue.
C — Correct. Enqueue is the insert operation of a queue, and it always adds the new element at the rear.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: EN-queue = ENter the line; DE-queue = DEpart from the line.

q: A queue is also referred to as a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A queue is a FIFO (first-come-first-served) list; all three given names belong to a stack, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: Because the element that arrives first is served first, a queue is also called a FIFO list or a first-come-first-served (FCFS) list. The stack, which is the opposite structure, has its own names: LIFO list, pushdown list and last-come-first-served (LCFS) list. Exams often test these alternate names.
why: A — Wrong. A LIFO (Last In, First Out) list is another name for a stack, not a queue.
B — Wrong. 'Pushdown list' is another name for a stack. Think of a spring-loaded plate holder in a canteen: each new plate pushes the others down, and the last plate pushed is the first one taken.
C — Wrong. Last-come-first-served is the LIFO rule, so it describes a stack. A queue is first-come-first-served.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. All three names (LIFO list, pushdown list, last-come-first-served list) describe a stack. A queue is a FIFO or first-come-first-served list, which is not offered.
tip: Queue = FIFO = FCFS. Stack = LIFO = LCFS = pushdown list.

q: Which queue operation returns the element at the front WITHOUT removing it?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Peek (Front) reads the front element without removing it.
concept: Peek (also called front or getFront) returns the value at the front of the queue but leaves the queue unchanged. Dequeue also gives the front value, but it removes that element, so the queue becomes one element shorter. isFull and isEmpty are test operations that only answer true or false about the state of the queue.
why: A — Wrong. Dequeue returns the front element AND removes it from the queue, so it does change the queue.
B — Correct. Peek (Front) only looks at the front element and returns it without removing it.
C — Wrong. isFull only answers true or false (is there any free space left?). It never returns an element.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Peek = peep at the front without taking it.

q: Which of the following is NOT a real-life example of a queue?
opts: Customers waiting in line at a bank counter
Calls on hold at a call centre, answered in order of arrival
A pile of plates in which the plate placed last is taken first
More than one of the above
exp: A pile of plates works on LIFO (a stack), so it is not a queue; the bank line and the call centre are FIFO queues.
concept: A real-life situation is a queue when people or jobs are served in the order they arrived (FIFO). A situation where the last item added is the first one taken is a stack (LIFO), not a queue. In a 'Which is NOT ...' question, the option that counts as 'true' is the one that is NOT a queue.
why: A — Wrong. Customers at a bank counter are served in order of arrival (first come, first served), so this IS a queue. It does not satisfy 'NOT a queue'.
B — Wrong. Calls answered in the order they arrived follow FIFO, so this IS a queue (call centres actually keep a 'call queue').
C — Correct. In a pile of plates the plate placed last is taken first. That is LIFO, the rule of a stack, so this is NOT an example of a queue.
D — Wrong. Only C is not a queue; A and B are genuine queues. 'More than one of the above' would need at least two options that are not queues.
E — Wrong. Option C is not a queue example, so it satisfies the stem, and 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Elements 10, 20, 30, 40 are enqueued (in this order) into an empty queue, and then two dequeue operations are performed. Which element is now at the front?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The two dequeues remove 10 and 20 (FIFO), so 30 is at the front.
concept: Enqueue adds at the rear and dequeue removes from the front. In FIFO order each dequeue removes the oldest element still present. So after k dequeues, the element that was inserted (k+1)-th is at the front.
work:
(Shown in an array Q[0..3] with front = rear = -1 at the start.)
enqueue(10): front was -1 so front = 0; [10, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(20): [10, 20, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(30): [10, 20, 30, _] front=0 rear=2
enqueue(40): [10, 20, 30, 40] front=0 rear=3
dequeue() -> 10: [_, 20, 30, 40] front=1 rear=3
dequeue() -> 20: [_, _, 30, 40] front=2 rear=3
Front element = Q[front] = Q[2] = 30.
why: A — Correct. The two dequeues remove 10 and then 20, so 30 is now first in line.
B — Wrong. 20 is at the front after only ONE dequeue. The second dequeue removes 20 as well.
C — Wrong. 40 is the rear element (the newest). It will be removed last, after 30.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: After k dequeues, the front is the (k+1)-th element inserted.

q: Which of the following statements about the queue ADT is/are true?
opts: Elements leave the queue in the same order in which they entered it
Insertion and deletion take place at different ends of the queue
Performing dequeue on an empty queue is an underflow condition
More than one of the above
exp: All three statements are true: FIFO order, insertion and deletion at different ends, and dequeue on empty = underflow.
concept: Three core facts about the queue ADT (abstract data type: a description of WHAT the operations do, not HOW they are coded): (1) elements leave in the same order in which they entered (FIFO); (2) insertion (enqueue) happens at the rear and deletion (dequeue) at the front, which are different ends; (3) trying to dequeue from an empty queue is called underflow, and trying to enqueue into a full queue is called overflow.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because B and C are also true; so the answer is D. This is the FIFO property: the first element in is the first element out, so the order of leaving equals the order of entering.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A and C are also true; so the answer is D. Insertion is at the rear and deletion at the front. (A stack, by contrast, uses one end, the top, for both.)

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A and B are also true; so the answer is D. Underflow means trying to remove something from an empty structure, so dequeue on an empty queue is underflow.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In the usual array implementation of a linear queue Q[0..MAX_SIZE-1], which initial values of front and rear represent an empty queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: An empty array queue is usually set up with front = rear = -1.
concept: In the usual array implementation of a linear queue, front holds the index of the first element and rear holds the index of the last element. At the start there is no element, so both are set to -1, which is not a valid array index. So front == -1 (with rear == -1) means EMPTY. The first enqueue makes front = 0 and rear = 0. (Some books start with front = 0, rear = -1 instead; this question asks for the usual -1 / -1 form.)
why: A — Wrong. front = 0 and rear = MAX_SIZE - 1 means the first element is at index 0 and the last element is in the final cell, so the array is completely FULL, not empty.
B — Correct. front = rear = -1 means neither index points to any element yet: the queue is empty.
C — Wrong. front = MAX_SIZE lies outside the array (valid indices are 0 to MAX_SIZE - 1), and no standard convention starts a queue with front = MAX_SIZE and rear = 0.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Inserting into a full queue and deleting from an empty queue are respectively called:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Enqueue on a full queue is overflow; dequeue on an empty queue is underflow.
concept: Overflow means trying to put an element into a structure that has no free space; for a queue that is enqueue on a full queue. Underflow means trying to take an element out of a structure that has nothing in it; for a queue that is dequeue on an empty queue. The same two words are used for a stack: push on a full stack is overflow and pop on an empty stack is underflow.
why: A — Correct. Insert into full = overflow (no room); delete from empty = underflow (nothing to remove).
B — Wrong. The order is reversed. Inserting into a full queue is overflow, not underflow.
C — Wrong. Deleting from an empty queue is not overflow: nothing is spilling over; there is simply nothing to take out, which is underflow.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: OVERflow = too much (no room to add). UNDERflow = too little (nothing to remove).

q: A linear (non-circular) queue is stored in Q[0..MAX_SIZE-1] with front = rear = -1 initially. Which condition makes the next enqueue report overflow?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A linear array queue overflows when rear == MAX_SIZE - 1.
concept: In a linear (non-circular) array queue Q[0..MAX_SIZE-1], rear only moves forward and holds the index of the last element. When rear == MAX_SIZE - 1, rear is already in the last cell, so the next enqueue has no cell to go to: this is the overflow condition. It does not matter where front is, because cells freed at the beginning are never reused. The empty (underflow) test is front == -1.
why: A — Wrong. front == -1 means the queue is EMPTY (nothing inserted yet). An enqueue at that time will succeed, not overflow.
B — Wrong. rear == front happens when the queue has exactly one element (both point to it) or when it is empty (both are -1). It never means full.
C — Correct. When rear == MAX_SIZE - 1 there is no cell after rear, so the next enqueue reports overflow, even if some cells before front are free.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In an array queue with front = rear = -1 initially, which sequence correctly performs enqueue(x) when the queue is not full?
opts: If front == -1 set front = 0; then rear = rear + 1 and Q[rear] = x
More than one of the above
exp: Enqueue sets front = 0 if the queue was empty, then increments rear and stores x at Q[rear].
concept: Enqueue in an array queue that starts with front = rear = -1 has three steps: (1) check for overflow (rear == MAX_SIZE - 1); (2) if the queue was empty (front == -1), set front = 0, because the new element will be the first element; (3) move rear one step forward (rear = rear + 1) and store the new element at Q[rear]. In C this is often written Q[++rear] = x, where ++rear means 'increase rear first, then use it'.
why: A — Correct. It sets front for the very first element, then advances rear and stores x at the new rear position.
B — Wrong. This works at the FRONT, which is the deletion end. Writing at Q[front] would overwrite the element that is waiting to be served (and with front = -1 it would even write to Q[-1]).
C — Wrong. rear = rear - 1 moves rear backwards; on the first enqueue it would become -2 and x would be written outside the array. rear must move forward.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Using front and rear indices (without shifting elements), the time complexities of enqueue and dequeue in an array queue are:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With front and rear indices and no shifting, both enqueue and dequeue are O(1).
concept: In an array queue with front and rear indices, enqueue changes only rear and one array cell, and dequeue changes only front. Neither operation loops over the elements, so each takes constant time, written O(1): the work does not grow when the number of elements n grows.
why: A — Wrong. Enqueue is not O(n). It writes directly into the cell after rear without moving or searching anything. (O(n) enqueue happens, for example, in a linked list without a rear pointer.)
B — Correct. Both operations do a fixed amount of work (one index change and one array access), so both are O(1).
C — Wrong. O(n) dequeue happens only in the design where all elements are shifted left after each dequeue. Here front simply moves forward, so dequeue is O(1).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The main drawback of a linear (non-circular) array queue is that:
opts: Cells freed by dequeue at the front cannot be reused, so overflow may occur even when empty cells exist
Elements cannot be removed in FIFO order
More than one of the above
exp: A linear array queue cannot reuse cells freed at the front, so it can report overflow even when empty cells exist.
concept: In a linear array queue, both front and rear only move forward. When elements are dequeued, the cells before front become empty, but rear can never go back to use them. So once rear reaches the last index, the queue reports overflow even if many cells at the start are empty. This waste of space is the main drawback of the linear queue, and the circular queue was designed to fix it.
why: A — Correct. Freed cells at the front cannot be reused, so a 'false' overflow can happen while empty cells exist.
B — Wrong. Enqueue in an array queue is O(1): increase rear and store the element. No loop is needed.
C — Wrong. A linear queue does remove elements in FIFO order; that is exactly what makes it a queue.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A linear array queue Q[0..9] currently has front = 3 and rear = 7, where front is the index of the first element and rear the index of the last element. How many elements are in the queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Number of elements = rear - front + 1 = 7 - 3 + 1 = 5.
concept: When front is the index of the first element and rear is the index of the last element (and the queue is not empty), the elements fill every index from front to rear, both included. The number of whole numbers from a to b inclusive is b - a + 1. So the number of elements = rear - front + 1.
work:
Elements are at indices 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.
Count = rear - front + 1 = 7 - 3 + 1 = 5.
why: A — Wrong. 4 = rear - front = 7 - 3. This forgets the '+1', the classic fence-post mistake (counting the gaps between posts instead of the posts).
B — Correct. Indices 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 hold elements: 7 - 3 + 1 = 5.
C — Wrong. 6 over-counts by one; it would need indices 3 to 8 (or 2 to 7) to be filled.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Inclusive count = last - first + 1.

q: A linear array queue starts with front = rear = -1. Enqueue sets front = 0 if it is -1 and then does Q[++rear] = x; dequeue simply returns Q[front++] (front and rear are never reset). Which condition(s) mean the queue is empty?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With no index reset, the queue is empty either when front == -1 (nothing inserted yet) or when front > rear (everything removed).
concept: Books detect an empty linear queue in different ways, depending on whether the indices are reset. In this version front and rear are NEVER reset to -1, so the queue can be empty in two ways: (1) nothing has ever been inserted, so front is still -1; (2) everything inserted has been removed, so front has moved past rear (front = rear + 1, i.e. front > rear). Example: enqueue(1), enqueue(2) gives front = 0, rear = 1; two dequeues give front = 2, rear = 1, which is empty. Overflow is a separate test: rear == MAX_SIZE - 1.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because B is also true; so the answer is D. front is -1 only before the first enqueue (the first enqueue sets it to 0 and it is never reset), so front == -1 means nothing has been inserted: empty.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A is also true; so the answer is D. Each dequeue moves front one step right. When the last element is removed, front becomes rear + 1, so front > rear means every element has been removed: empty.
C — Wrong. rear == MAX_SIZE - 1 means rear has reached the last cell. It is the overflow test for enqueue; the queue may still contain elements, so it does not mean empty.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true. (C is false, but two true options are enough.)
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: If indices are never reset, check both: front == -1 OR front > rear.

q: An array queue always keeps its front element at index 0: after every dequeue, all remaining elements are shifted one place to the left. For a queue of n elements, the worst-case time of dequeue is:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Shifting the remaining n - 1 elements after each dequeue makes dequeue O(n).
concept: One simple array design keeps the front element always at index 0. Then every dequeue must shift all remaining elements one place to the left, like everyone in a line taking one step forward. Moving n - 1 elements takes time proportional to n, written O(n). The usual design avoids this by moving the front INDEX instead of the elements, which makes dequeue O(1). Example: [a, b, c, d] -> dequeue a -> b, c, d each move one cell left = 3 moves for n = 4.
why: A — Wrong. O(1) is the time when only the front index changes. In this design all the remaining elements are moved.
B — Wrong. O(log n) appears in algorithms that halve the work at each step (binary search, heap operations). Shifting does not halve anything; it touches every remaining element once.
C — Correct. Shifting n - 1 elements one place left takes time proportional to n, so dequeue is O(n).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A linear queue has MAX_SIZE = 5. (Convention: front = rear = -1 initially; enqueue: if front == -1 set front = 0, then Q[++rear] = x; dequeue: if front == rear set both to -1, otherwise front++.) After enqueue(5), enqueue(10), enqueue(15), dequeue(), enqueue(20), dequeue(), what are front and rear?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After the operations front = 2 and rear = 3 (the queue holds 15 and 20).
concept: This is the standard linear-queue convention. front = rear = -1 means empty. Enqueue: if the queue is empty set front = 0, then increase rear and store. Dequeue: remove Q[front]; if it was the only element (front == rear) reset both to -1, otherwise increase front. front always points to the oldest element and rear to the newest.
work:
enqueue(5): front was -1 so front = 0; [5, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(10): [5, 10, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(15): [5, 10, 15, _, _] front=0 rear=2
dequeue() -> 5: [_, 10, 15, _, _] front=1 rear=2
enqueue(20): [_, 10, 15, 20, _] front=1 rear=3
dequeue() -> 10: [_, _, 15, 20, _] front=2 rear=3
Result: front = 2, rear = 3 (the queue holds 15, 20).
why: A — Wrong. front = 1, rear = 3 is the state after enqueue(20) but BEFORE the last dequeue; it misses the second dequeue.
B — Correct. Two dequeues move front from 0 to 2, and four enqueues move rear from -1 to 3. The queue now holds 15 and 20.
C — Wrong. rear = 4 would need five enqueues. There were four (5, 10, 15, 20), filling indices 0 to 3. This mistake usually comes from numbering the cells from 1.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A linear queue has MAX_SIZE = 6 (indices 0-5). (Convention: front = rear = -1 initially; enqueue: if front == -1 set front = 0, then Q[++rear] = x; dequeue: if front == rear set both to -1, otherwise front++.) Operations: enqueue(3), enqueue(6), enqueue(9), dequeue(), enqueue(12), enqueue(15), dequeue(), dequeue(), enqueue(18). Which element is at the front, and what is rear?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Three dequeues remove 3, 6, 9, so Q[3] = 12 is at the front; the last enqueue puts 18 at index 5, so rear = 5.
concept: Trace a linear array queue by keeping three things after every operation: the array, front and rear. Each enqueue moves rear one step right; each dequeue moves front one step right. The front element is Q[front] and the rear element is Q[rear].
work:
enqueue(3): front was -1 so front = 0; [3, _, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(6): [3, 6, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(9): [3, 6, 9, _, _, _] front=0 rear=2
dequeue() -> 3: [_, 6, 9, _, _, _] front=1 rear=2
enqueue(12): [_, 6, 9, 12, _, _] front=1 rear=3
enqueue(15): [_, 6, 9, 12, 15, _] front=1 rear=4
dequeue() -> 6: [_, _, 9, 12, 15, _] front=2 rear=4
dequeue() -> 9: [_, _, _, 12, 15, _] front=3 rear=4
enqueue(18): [_, _, _, 12, 15, 18] front=3 rear=5
Front element = Q[3] = 12; rear = 5.
why: A — Wrong. 9 was removed by the third dequeue (the dequeues remove 3, 6 and 9 in that order). rear = 5 is right, but the front element is 12.
B — Wrong. 12 is the correct front element, but rear = 4 ignores the final enqueue(18), which put 18 at index 5.
C — Correct. front = 3 so the front element is Q[3] = 12, and the last enqueue(18) made rear = 5.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A linear (non-circular) queue has MAX_SIZE = 4 (indices 0-3). (Convention: front = rear = -1 initially; enqueue: report overflow if rear == MAX_SIZE - 1, otherwise if front == -1 set front = 0, then Q[++rear] = x; dequeue: if front == rear set both to -1, otherwise front++.) Starting from empty: enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), enqueue(4), dequeue(), dequeue(), enqueue(5). What happens on the last operation?
opts: Overflow is reported although two cells are empty
5 is stored at index 2 after shifting
More than one of the above
exp: rear is already MAX_SIZE - 1 = 3, so enqueue(5) reports overflow even though two cells at the start are free.
concept: In a linear queue, rear never moves back. Overflow is reported when rear == MAX_SIZE - 1, no matter where front is. So cells freed at the start by dequeue cannot be reused. This is the 'wasted space' (false overflow) problem of the linear queue, and the circular queue fixes it.
work:
enqueue(1): front was -1 so front = 0; [1, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(2): [1, 2, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(3): [1, 2, 3, _] front=0 rear=2
enqueue(4): [1, 2, 3, 4] front=0 rear=3
dequeue() -> 1: [_, 2, 3, 4] front=1 rear=3
dequeue() -> 2: [_, _, 3, 4] front=2 rear=3
enqueue(5): rear == MAX_SIZE - 1 = 3 -> OVERFLOW, nothing changes; [_, _, 3, 4] front=2 rear=3
So the last operation reports overflow although cells 0 and 1 are empty.
why: A — Wrong. Storing 5 at index 0 is what a CIRCULAR queue would do (rear = (3 + 1) % 4 = 0). A linear queue never wraps around.
B — Correct. rear = 3 = MAX_SIZE - 1, so enqueue(5) reports overflow even though cells 0 and 1 are empty.
C — Wrong. Shifting the elements to the left (compaction) is a separate technique that this enqueue does not perform. The given enqueue only checks rear and reports overflow.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Linear queue: overflow depends only on rear, never on front.

q: A linear (non-circular) array queue Q[0..9] currently has front = 4 and rear = 9. How many more enqueue operations will succeed before overflow is reported (elements are never shifted)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: rear is already at the last index (9), so the next enqueue overflows: 0 more enqueues succeed, which is not listed.
concept: In a linear (non-circular) array queue, an enqueue succeeds only while rear < MAX_SIZE - 1. The value of front does not matter for overflow, because cells freed at the front are never reused (unless elements are shifted). For Q[0..9], MAX_SIZE = 10 and the last index is 9.
work:
Last index = MAX_SIZE - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9.
rear = 9 already equals the last index.
Free cells after rear = 9 - rear = 9 - 9 = 0.
So the very next enqueue reports overflow: 0 more enqueues succeed.
(Cells 0-3 are empty because front = 4, but a linear queue cannot reuse them.)
why: A — Wrong. 4 is the number of empty cells BEFORE front (indices 0, 1, 2, 3). A circular queue could use them, but a linear queue cannot.
B — Wrong. 5 = rear - front = 9 - 4. That is a mix-up with the element count (and even forgets the +1); it says nothing about free space after rear.
C — Wrong. 6 = rear - front + 1 is the number of elements currently in the queue, not the number of free cells.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so there cannot be two correct options.
E — Correct. rear is already 9 = MAX_SIZE - 1, so 0 more enqueues succeed, and 0 is not among A–C.

q: A linear queue has MAX_SIZE = 3. Convention: front = rear = -1 initially; enqueue: if front == -1 set front = 0, then Q[++rear] = x; dequeue: report underflow if front == -1, otherwise if front == rear set both to -1, else front++. Operations: enqueue(7), dequeue(), dequeue(), enqueue(8). Which statement is correct?
opts: The third operation causes underflow; finally front = 0, rear = 0
The third operation causes underflow; finally front = 1, rear = 1
No underflow occurs; finally front = 1, rear = 1
More than one of the above
exp: The second dequeue (third operation) underflows because the queue was reset to empty; enqueue(8) then gives front = rear = 0.
concept: Underflow is an attempt to dequeue from an empty queue. In this convention, when the last element is dequeued (front == rear), both indices are reset to -1, so the queue goes back to its starting state. The next dequeue then finds front == -1 and reports underflow, and a later enqueue starts again from index 0.
work:
op 1: enqueue(7): front was -1 so front = 0; [7, _, _] front=0 rear=0
op 2: dequeue() -> 7: it was the only element (front == rear), reset both to -1; [_, _, _] front=-1 rear=-1
op 3: dequeue(): front == -1 -> UNDERFLOW, nothing changes; [_, _, _] front=-1 rear=-1
op 4: enqueue(8): front was -1 so front = 0; [8, _, _] front=0 rear=0
Operation 3 (the second dequeue) is the underflow. Final: front = 0, rear = 0.
why: A — Correct. The first dequeue empties the queue and resets both indices to -1, so the second dequeue (the third operation) is an underflow. enqueue(8) then sets front = rear = 0.
B — Wrong. The underflow part is right, but front = 1, rear = 1 assumes the indices kept moving forward. Here the indices were reset to -1, so enqueue(8) starts again at index 0.
C — Wrong. Underflow does occur: after the first dequeue the queue is empty, so the second dequeue has nothing to remove. The final indices are also 0, 0, not 1, 1.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many times does the following C program print "Overflow"?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The first 5 enqueues fill the array; the remaining 3 calls (i = 6, 7, 8) print Overflow, so it is printed 3 times.
concept: This enqueue first checks rear == MAX - 1. With MAX = 5 the cells are q[0] to q[4], so exactly 5 values can be stored. Every later call finds rear == 4, prints 'Overflow' and returns without changing anything. No dequeue happens here, so no cell is ever freed.
work:
i = 1: enqueue(1): front was -1 so front = 0; [1, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
i = 2: enqueue(2): [1, 2, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
i = 3: enqueue(3): [1, 2, 3, _, _] front=0 rear=2
i = 4: enqueue(4): [1, 2, 3, 4, _] front=0 rear=3
i = 5: enqueue(5): [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] front=0 rear=4
i = 6: enqueue(6): rear == MAX - 1 = 4 -> OVERFLOW, nothing changes; [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] front=0 rear=4
i = 7: enqueue(7): rear == MAX - 1 = 4 -> OVERFLOW, nothing changes; [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] front=0 rear=4
i = 8: enqueue(8): rear == MAX - 1 = 4 -> OVERFLOW, nothing changes; [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] front=0 rear=4
'Overflow' is printed for i = 6, 7, 8: 3 times.
why: A — Correct. Calls for i = 1 to 5 fill q[0..4]; calls for i = 6, 7 and 8 each find rear == 4 and print Overflow: 3 times.
B — Wrong. 5 is the number of SUCCESSFUL enqueues (the capacity of the array), not the number of failed ones.
C — Wrong. 8 is the total number of calls. The first 5 calls succeed and print nothing.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In the following C program, what is printed by the final printf (ignore the "Underflow" message)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After two enqueues and two successful dequeues, front = 2 and rear = 1; the third dequeue underflows without changing them, so '2 1' is printed.
concept: This dequeue never resets front and rear. It reports underflow when front == -1 (nothing was ever inserted) or front > rear (everything inserted has already been removed). When underflow is detected the function returns early, before front++ runs, so front does not change.
work:
enqueue(1): front was -1 so front = 0; [1, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(2): [1, 2, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
dequeue() -> 1: [_, 2, _, _, _] front=1 rear=1
dequeue() -> 2: [_, _, _, _, _] front=2 rear=1
dequeue(): front (2) > rear (1) -> UNDERFLOW, nothing changes; [_, _, _, _, _] front=2 rear=1
printf prints "2 1".
why: A — Wrong. '-1 -1' would be printed only if the code reset both indices when the queue became empty (as in the other common convention). This code has no reset.
B — Wrong. '3 1' assumes the third dequeue still did front++. But the underflow check returns before front++, so front stays 2.
C — Correct. Two successful dequeues move front from 0 to 2; the third finds front (2) > rear (1), prints Underflow and changes nothing. So '2 1' is printed.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following techniques allow a linear array queue to reuse the cells freed by dequeue operations?
opts: Making it circular, so that rear wraps around to index 0 using the % operator
Shifting all elements towards index 0 when rear reaches the last index
Incrementing front by 2 on every dequeue
More than one of the above
exp: Both making the queue circular (A) and shifting elements back to index 0 (B) let freed cells be reused; C is wrong.
concept: A linear array queue wastes the cells freed at the front, because rear only moves forward. Two standard fixes exist: (1) make the array circular, so that after the last index rear wraps back to 0 using rear = (rear + 1) % MAX_SIZE; (2) compaction: when rear reaches the end, shift all elements left so they start again from index 0 (this costs O(n) time whenever it is done). Both let the freed cells be used again.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because B is also true; so the answer is D. A circular queue wraps rear from the last index back to 0 with the % (remainder) operator, so freed cells at the start are reused.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A is also true; so the answer is D. Shifting all elements towards index 0 moves the free cells to the end of the array, after rear, where enqueue can use them.
C — Wrong. Incrementing front by 2 would skip (lose) an element at every dequeue, breaking FIFO order, and it does not let rear reuse any cell.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true. (C is false, but two true options are enough.)
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Another convention for a linear array queue initialises front = 0 and rear = -1; enqueue does Q[++rear] = x and dequeue does front++ (indices are never reset), and the queue is empty when front > rear. After enqueue(A), enqueue(B), enqueue(C), dequeue(), dequeue(), what are front and rear?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After three enqueues rear = 2 and after two dequeues front = 2, so front = 2, rear = 2, which is not listed.
concept: Another common convention for a linear array queue starts with front = 0 and rear = -1. front is the index of the first element and rear the index of the last element. Enqueue does Q[++rear] = x and dequeue does front++. The queue is empty when front > rear (at the start, 0 > -1), and the number of elements is rear - front + 1.
work:
start: [_, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=-1 (empty, because front > rear)
enqueue(A): [A, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(B): [A, B, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(C): [A, B, C, _, _] front=0 rear=2
dequeue() -> A: [_, B, C, _, _] front=1 rear=2
dequeue() -> B: [_, _, C, _, _] front=2 rear=2
Final: front = 2, rear = 2; only C remains (count = 2 - 2 + 1 = 1).
why: A — Wrong. front = 1, rear = 2 is the state after only ONE dequeue. The second dequeue moves front to 2.
B — Wrong. rear = 3 would need four enqueues. Three enqueues starting from rear = -1 give rear = 0, 1, 2.
C — Wrong. front = 0 is the state before any dequeue. Each dequeue moves front one step forward.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so there cannot be two correct options.
E — Correct. The final state is front = 2, rear = 2 (only C remains), and this pair is not listed in A–C.

q: What is the main reason for using a circular queue instead of a linear array queue?
opts: To allow insertion and deletion at both ends
To reuse the array cells freed at the front by letting the indices wrap around
To serve elements according to their priority
More than one of the above
exp: A circular queue is used to reuse the cells freed at the front by letting the indices wrap around.
concept: A circular queue is an array queue in which the last cell is treated as if it were joined to the first cell, like seats around a round table. When rear (or front) passes the last index it wraps round to index 0 using the modulo operator: index = (index + 1) % n. This lets cells freed by dequeue be reused, which fixes the wasted-space problem of the linear queue.
why: A — Wrong. Insertion and deletion at both ends is a deque (double-ended queue). A circular queue still inserts only at the rear and deletes only at the front.
B — Correct. The indices wrap around, so cells freed at the front are used again by later enqueues.
C — Wrong. Serving elements by priority is a priority queue (usually built with a heap). A circular queue serves strictly in order of arrival (FIFO).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue is also known as a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A circular queue is also known as a ring buffer (circular buffer).
concept: A circular queue is also called a ring buffer or circular buffer, because its cells are used as if they were arranged in a ring: after the last cell comes the first cell again. Ring buffers are widely used in operating systems and device drivers, for example for keyboard input, network packets and audio streams.
why: A — Correct. 'Ring buffer' (or circular buffer) is the standard other name for a circular queue.
B — Wrong. A double-ended queue (deque) allows insertion and deletion at both ends. It is a different ADT; it can be built on a circular array, but 'deque' does not mean circular queue.
C — Wrong. A priority heap (binary heap) is a tree-shaped structure, usually stored in an array, used to build priority queues. It is not a FIFO ring.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a circular queue stored in an array of n cells, the rear index is advanced on enqueue as:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a circular queue, rear is advanced as rear = (rear + 1) % n so that it wraps from n - 1 to 0.
concept: The modulo operator % gives the remainder after division. For an array of n cells, (i + 1) % n equals i + 1 for every i from 0 to n - 2, but equals 0 when i = n - 1. So rear = (rear + 1) % n moves rear forward and wraps it from the last cell back to cell 0. For n = 5, rear goes 3 -> 4 -> 0 -> 1. front is advanced the same way on dequeue: front = (front + 1) % n.
why: A — Wrong. rear = rear + 1 is the linear-queue rule. When rear = n - 1 it gives n, which is outside the array (valid indices are 0 to n - 1), so it never wraps round.
B — Wrong. (rear - 1) % n moves rear backwards. Also, in C, (-1) % n is -1, which is not a valid index.
C — Correct. (rear + 1) % n advances rear by one and wraps it from n - 1 back to 0.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Circular step = (index + 1) % n, for both front and rear.

q: A circular queue of n cells uses the convention front = rear = -1 initially, with all n cells usable. Which condition tells that the queue is FULL?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With all n cells usable, a circular queue is full when (rear + 1) % n == front.
concept: Convention used here: front = rear = -1 means empty; front is the index of the first element and rear the index of the last element; all n cells can be filled. The queue is FULL when the next position after rear (going round the circle) is front: (rear + 1) % n == front. This single test covers both full shapes: front = 0 with rear = n - 1, and front = rear + 1 after wrap-around. The EMPTY test is front == -1.
why: A — Correct. If the cell after rear (circularly) is front, there is no free cell left, so the queue is full.

B — Wrong. rear == n - 1 is the full test of a LINEAR queue. In a circular queue, if some elements have been dequeued (front > 0), rear can wrap to 0 and use the freed cells, so the queue is not full.
C — Wrong. front == rear (not -1) means exactly ONE element, because the first and the last element are in the same cell. It never means full.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue uses the convention front = rear = -1 initially, all n cells usable, and both indices are reset to -1 when the last element is deleted. Which condition tells that the queue is EMPTY?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In the -1 convention, the circular queue is empty exactly when front == -1.
concept: In the convention front = rear = -1 for empty (all n cells usable), the dequeue that removes the last element resets both indices to -1. So EMPTY is tested with front == -1. FULL is (rear + 1) % n == front. front == rear with a value other than -1 means the queue has exactly one element.
why: A — Wrong. front == rear is true when the queue holds exactly one element (both indices point to that cell), so it cannot by itself mean empty. (It means empty only in the OTHER convention, where front = rear = 0 at the start and one cell is kept free.)
B — Correct. The indices are -1 only when the queue is empty (at the start, or after the last element is deleted and the reset happens).
C — Wrong. (rear + 1) % n == front is the FULL test, the opposite state.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue is implemented in an array of 10 cells using the convention that one cell is always kept empty (front == rear means empty). What is the maximum number of elements it can hold at a time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Keeping one cell empty gives a capacity of n - 1 = 9.
concept: In the 'one cell kept empty' convention for a circular queue (front = rear = 0 at the start), front == rear means empty and (rear + 1) % n == front means full. To keep these two states different, the queue is declared full while one cell is still free. So an array of n cells can hold at most n - 1 elements.
work: Capacity = n - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9 elements (one of the 10 cells is always left empty).
why: A — Wrong. 10 is possible only in a convention where all cells are usable (for example front = rear = -1, or keeping a separate count variable). Here one cell is always kept empty.
B — Correct. With one cell always free, the capacity is n - 1 = 9.
C — Wrong. 11 is more than the number of cells; an array of 10 cells can never hold 11 elements.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 'front == rear means empty' convention -> capacity n - 1.

q: A circular queue of n cells uses the convention front = rear = 0 initially, with one cell always kept empty. Which pair of conditions is correct?
opts: Empty: (rear + 1) % n == front;  Full: front == rear
Empty: front == rear;  Full: (rear + 1) % n == front
More than one of the above
exp: With one cell kept empty, the queue is empty when front == rear and full when (rear + 1) % n == front.
concept: Convention: front = rear = 0 at the start, and one cell is always left empty (capacity n - 1). EMPTY: front == rear. FULL: (rear + 1) % n == front, i.e. moving rear one more step would make it equal to front. Because front == rear is reserved for 'empty', the queue must stop one cell early; otherwise a full queue would also show front == rear.
why: A — Wrong. front == -1 is the empty test of a different convention (front = rear = -1); here the indices start at 0 and never become -1. rear == n - 1 is the full test of a linear queue.
B — Wrong. These are the two conditions swapped: (rear + 1) % n == front is the FULL test and front == rear is the EMPTY test.
C — Correct. Empty when front == rear; full when (rear + 1) % n == front.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In the circular-queue convention where front == rear means EMPTY, why is one array cell always left unused?
opts: So that a full queue can be distinguished from an empty one; if all n cells were filled, front would again equal rear
Because the % operator can never produce the index n - 1
To store the count of elements in the queue
More than one of the above
exp: One cell is left unused so that 'full' and 'empty' never both look like front == rear.
concept: If front == rear is used to mean 'empty' and we allowed all n cells to be filled, then after n insertions rear would come all the way round and equal front again. A full queue and an empty queue would then look exactly the same (front == rear), and the program could not tell them apart. Leaving one cell unused solves this. Other solutions are to keep a separate count of elements or a 'full' flag, or to use the front = rear = -1 convention.
why: A — Correct. With one cell kept free, front == rear can only mean empty, so full and empty are always different.
B — Wrong. x % n can produce every value from 0 to n - 1, including n - 1 (for example (n - 2 + 1) % n = n - 1). Every index is reachable.
C — Wrong. The spare cell is left empty; nothing is stored in it. If a count is wanted, it is kept in a separate variable, not inside the array.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue uses an array of n = 8 cells; front is the index of the first element and rear is the index of the next free cell (front == rear means empty, one cell kept free). If front = 6 and rear = 2, how many elements are in the queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Count = (rear - front + n) % n = (2 - 6 + 8) % 8 = 4.
concept: Convention: front = index of the first element, rear = index of the NEXT FREE cell (one past the last element), one cell kept free. Number of elements = (rear - front + n) % n. Adding n before taking % n keeps the result non-negative when rear has wrapped round and is smaller than front.
work:
n = 8, front = 6, rear = 2 (rear has wrapped, so rear < front).
Count = (rear - front + n) % n = (2 - 6 + 8) % 8 = 4 % 8 = 4.
Check: elements are in cells 6, 7, 0, 1; cell 2 is the next free cell.
Queue picture: [x, x, _, _, _, _, x, x] front=6 rear=2 -> 4 elements.
why: A — Wrong. 3 under-counts by one, for example by leaving out cell 6 (the front cell) or cell 1. The filled cells are 6, 7, 0 and 1.
B — Correct. (2 - 6 + 8) % 8 = 4; the elements are in cells 6, 7, 0, 1.
C — Wrong. 5 = (rear - front + n) % n + 1, the formula for the convention where rear is the index of the LAST element. Here rear is the next free cell, so there is no +1.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: rear = next free cell: count = (rear - front + n) % n. rear = last element: add 1.

q: A circular queue of n cells keeps front = index of the first element and rear = index of the last element (all n cells usable; front = rear = -1 when empty). For n = 10, front = 7 and rear = 2, the number of elements is:
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Convention: front = index of the first element, rear = index of the LAST element, all n cells usable. If rear >= front, count = rear - front + 1. If rear has wrapped round (rear < front), count = (n - front) + (rear + 1). One formula covers both cases for a non-empty queue: count = (rear - front + n) % n + 1.
work:
n = 10, front = 7, rear = 2 (wrapped).
Cells used: 7, 8, 9 (n - front = 3 cells) and 0, 1, 2 (rear + 1 = 3 cells).
Count = (rear - front + n) % n + 1 = (2 - 7 + 10) % 10 + 1 = 5 + 1 = 6.
Queue picture: [x, x, x, _, _, _, _, x, x, x] front=7 rear=2 -> 6 elements.
why: A — Correct. The elements fill cells 7, 8, 9, 0, 1, 2: 6 elements.
B — Wrong. 5 = (rear - front + n) % n without the +1. That formula is for the convention where rear is the next free cell; here rear is the last element, so add 1.
C — Wrong. 4 is the number of EMPTY cells (3, 4, 5, 6), not filled ones.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue of n = 7 cells uses the convention front = rear = 0 initially, front == rear means empty and one cell is always left free. After some operations, front = 5 and rear = 5. How many elements does the queue hold?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In this convention front == rear always means empty, so the queue holds 0 elements, which is not listed.
concept: In the 'one cell kept free' convention (front = rear = 0 at the start, capacity n - 1), front == rear ALWAYS means the queue is EMPTY, wherever the two indices happen to be (0, 5 or any other cell). The queue can never hold n elements, so front == rear can never mean full. Count = (rear - front + n) % n.
work:
n = 7, front = 5, rear = 5.
front == rear -> the queue is empty.
Count = (5 - 5 + 7) % 7 = 7 % 7 = 0 elements.
(The maximum possible is n - 1 = 6; 7 is impossible in this convention.)
why: A — Wrong. 7 would mean every cell is filled, but this convention never fills all cells. Here front == rear signals empty, not full.
B — Wrong. 6 is the capacity (n - 1). It is reached when (rear + 1) % n == front, e.g. front = 5, rear = 4, not when front == rear.
C — Wrong. 1 element is what front == rear means in the OTHER convention (front and rear both point to a single element, -1 when empty). Here it means 0 elements.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so there cannot be two correct options.
E — Correct. front == rear means the queue is empty, so it holds 0 elements, and 0 is not among A–C.

q: A circular queue has n = 5 cells. (Convention: front = rear = -1 initially, all n cells can hold elements, full when (rear + 1) % n == front; enqueue: if front == -1 set front = 0, then rear = (rear + 1) % n; dequeue: if front == rear reset both to -1, else front = (front + 1) % n.) Operations: enqueue 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; dequeue(); dequeue(); enqueue(60); enqueue(70). What are front and rear now?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: front = 2 after two dequeues, and rear wraps 4 -> 0 -> 1 for 60 and 70; so front = 2, rear = 1 (the queue is now full).
concept: Circular queue, all n cells usable (front = rear = -1 when empty). Enqueue sets front = 0 if the queue was empty, then rear = (rear + 1) % n and stores. Dequeue removes Q[front]; if front == rear (last element) both are reset to -1, otherwise front = (front + 1) % n. Full when (rear + 1) % n == front. Because of % n, the indices always stay between 0 and n - 1.
work:
enqueue(10): front was -1 so front = 0; rear = (-1 + 1) % 5 = 0; [10, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(20): rear = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1; [10, 20, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(30): rear = (1 + 1) % 5 = 2; [10, 20, 30, _, _] front=0 rear=2
enqueue(40): rear = (2 + 1) % 5 = 3; [10, 20, 30, 40, _] front=0 rear=3
enqueue(50): rear = (3 + 1) % 5 = 4; [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] front=0 rear=4
dequeue() -> 10: front = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1; [_, 20, 30, 40, 50] front=1 rear=4
dequeue() -> 20: front = (1 + 1) % 5 = 2; [_, _, 30, 40, 50] front=2 rear=4
enqueue(60): rear = (4 + 1) % 5 = 0; [60, _, 30, 40, 50] front=2 rear=0
enqueue(70): rear = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1; [60, 70, 30, 40, 50] front=2 rear=1
Final: front = 2, rear = 1. Check: (1 + 1) % 5 = 2 = front, so the queue is now full.
why: A — Wrong. rear = 6 comes from forgetting the modulo (rear + 1 each time: 4 -> 5 -> 6). Index 6 does not exist in a 5-cell array.
B — Wrong. front = 0 ignores the two dequeues, which moved front from 0 to 2. (rear = 1 is right.)
C — Correct. Two dequeues give front = 2; 60 wraps to cell 0 and 70 goes to cell 1, so rear = 1.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue has n = 4 cells. (Convention: front = rear = -1 initially, all n cells can hold elements, full when (rear + 1) % n == front; enqueue: if front == -1 set front = 0, then rear = (rear + 1) % n; dequeue: if front == rear reset both to -1, else front = (front + 1) % n.) Operations: enqueue(A), enqueue(B), enqueue(C), dequeue(), dequeue(), enqueue(D), enqueue(E), dequeue(). Which element is now at the front, and what are front and rear?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The last dequeue removes C, leaving D (cell 3) at the front and E (cell 0) at the rear: front = 3, rear = 0.
concept: In a circular queue the front element is always Q[front], even when rear has wrapped round to a smaller index than front. Trace the array, front and rear after every operation; use (index + 1) % n for each step.
work:
enqueue(A): front was -1 so front = 0; rear = (-1 + 1) % 4 = 0; [A, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(B): rear = (0 + 1) % 4 = 1; [A, B, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(C): rear = (1 + 1) % 4 = 2; [A, B, C, _] front=0 rear=2
dequeue() -> A: front = (0 + 1) % 4 = 1; [_, B, C, _] front=1 rear=2
dequeue() -> B: front = (1 + 1) % 4 = 2; [_, _, C, _] front=2 rear=2
enqueue(D): rear = (2 + 1) % 4 = 3; [_, _, C, D] front=2 rear=3
enqueue(E): rear = (3 + 1) % 4 = 0; [E, _, C, D] front=2 rear=0
dequeue() -> C: front = (2 + 1) % 4 = 3; [E, _, _, D] front=3 rear=0
Front element = Q[3] = D; front = 3, rear = 0.
why: A — Wrong. E is the REAR element (the newest one, in cell 0). front = rear = 0 would mean only one element, but D and E are both present.
B — Wrong. This is the state BEFORE the last dequeue. The final dequeue removes C and moves front to 3.
C — Correct. After the last dequeue, front = 3 and Q[3] = D; E sits in cell 0, so rear = 0.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue is stored in Q[0..3]. (Convention: front = rear = -1 initially, all n cells can hold elements, full when (rear + 1) % n == front; enqueue: if front == -1 set front = 0, then rear = (rear + 1) % n; dequeue: if front == rear reset both to -1, else front = (front + 1) % n.) Operations: enqueue 1, 2, 3, 4; dequeue(); enqueue(5); dequeue(); enqueue(6). What are the array contents Q[0..3] and the value of front?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Q[0..3] = 5 6 3 4 with front = 2 (queue order 3, 4, 5, 6).
concept: In a circular queue the physical order of values in the array is not the same as the queue order. Queue order starts at front and goes round: front, front + 1, ..., wrapping after the last cell, up to rear. Elements are never shifted; a dequeue only moves front, and the freed cell is overwritten by a later enqueue. So track each cell and the indices separately.
work:
enqueue(1): front was -1 so front = 0; rear = (-1 + 1) % 4 = 0; [1, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(2): rear = (0 + 1) % 4 = 1; [1, 2, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(3): rear = (1 + 1) % 4 = 2; [1, 2, 3, _] front=0 rear=2
enqueue(4): rear = (2 + 1) % 4 = 3; [1, 2, 3, 4] front=0 rear=3
dequeue() -> 1: front = (0 + 1) % 4 = 1; [_, 2, 3, 4] front=1 rear=3
enqueue(5): rear = (3 + 1) % 4 = 0; [5, 2, 3, 4] front=1 rear=0
dequeue() -> 2: front = (1 + 1) % 4 = 2; [5, _, 3, 4] front=2 rear=0
enqueue(6): rear = (0 + 1) % 4 = 1; [5, 6, 3, 4] front=2 rear=1
Final array Q[0..3] = 5 6 3 4, front = 2, rear = 1. Queue order from front: 3, 4, 5, 6.
why: A — Correct. The array is 5 6 3 4 and front = 2; the queue order from front is 3, 4, 5, 6.
B — Wrong. 3 4 5 6 is the QUEUE ORDER (reading from front round to rear), not the physical array. Elements are never shifted in a circular queue, and front is 2, not 0.
C — Wrong. The array contents are right, but front = 1 counts only one dequeue. There were two (removing 1 and then 2), so front = 2.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue has n = 6 cells. (Convention: front = rear = -1 initially, all n cells can hold elements, full when (rear + 1) % n == front; enqueue: if front == -1 set front = 0, then rear = (rear + 1) % n; dequeue: if front == rear reset both to -1, else front = (front + 1) % n.) Currently front = 4 and rear = 1 (elements in cells 4, 5, 0, 1). After two more enqueue operations, what is rear, and is the queue full?
opts: rear = 3, the queue is not full
More than one of the above
exp: rear moves 1 -> 2 -> 3; now (3 + 1) % 6 = 4 = front, so the queue is full.
concept: In the all-cells-usable convention, a circular queue is full when (rear + 1) % n == front. Number of elements = (rear - front + n) % n + 1. Cells after the last index continue from 0.
work:
start: [c, d, _, _, a, b] front=4 rear=1 (queue order a, b, c, d; count = (1 - 4 + 6) % 6 + 1 = 4)
enqueue(x): rear = (1 + 1) % 6 = 2; [c, d, x, _, a, b] front=4 rear=2
enqueue(y): rear = (2 + 1) % 6 = 3; [c, d, x, y, a, b] front=4 rear=3
Full test: (3 + 1) % 6 = 4 == front (4) -> FULL. Count = (3 - 4 + 6) % 6 + 1 = 6 = n.
why: A — Wrong. rear = 3 is right, but the queue IS full: 6 elements in 6 cells, and (3 + 1) % 6 = 4 = front.
B — Correct. rear goes 1 -> 2 -> 3, and then (3 + 1) % 6 = 4 = front, so every cell is used: full.
C — Wrong. rear = 2 is the value after only ONE enqueue, and at that point the queue has 5 elements, so it is not yet full.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What does the final printf of this C program print (ignore the "Full" messages)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 10-50 fill the queue (60, 70 print Full); three dequeues give front = 3; 80 and 90 wrap to cells 0 and 1, so '3 1' is printed.
concept: This C code uses the circular convention with front = rear = -1 for empty and all N cells usable. enqueue first checks (rear + 1) % N == front; if true it prints 'Full' and returns without changing anything. Wrap-around is done with % N, so indices stay between 0 and N - 1.
work:
enqueue(10): front was -1 so front = 0; rear = (-1 + 1) % 5 = 0; [10, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=0
enqueue(20): rear = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1; [10, 20, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(30): rear = (1 + 1) % 5 = 2; [10, 20, 30, _, _] front=0 rear=2
enqueue(40): rear = (2 + 1) % 5 = 3; [10, 20, 30, 40, _] front=0 rear=3
enqueue(50): rear = (3 + 1) % 5 = 4; [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] front=0 rear=4
enqueue(60): (4 + 1) % 5 = 0 == front -> prints 'Full', nothing changes; [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] front=0 rear=4
enqueue(70): (4 + 1) % 5 = 0 == front -> prints 'Full', nothing changes; [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] front=0 rear=4
dequeue() -> 10: front = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1; [_, 20, 30, 40, 50] front=1 rear=4
dequeue() -> 20: front = (1 + 1) % 5 = 2; [_, _, 30, 40, 50] front=2 rear=4
dequeue() -> 30: front = (2 + 1) % 5 = 3; [_, _, _, 40, 50] front=3 rear=4
enqueue(80): rear = (4 + 1) % 5 = 0; [80, _, _, 40, 50] front=3 rear=0
enqueue(90): rear = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1; [80, 90, _, 40, 50] front=3 rear=1
printf prints "3 1".
why: A — Wrong. '3 6' forgets the % N: rear would go 4 -> 5 -> 6, which are not valid indices when N = 5.
B — Wrong. '0 1' ignores the three dequeues, which move front 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3. (rear = 1 is right.)
C — Correct. Three dequeues make front = 3; 80 wraps to cell 0 and 90 goes to cell 1, so rear = 1. Output: 3 1.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about a circular queue is/are true?
opts: It reuses array cells by wrapping the indices around with the modulo (%) operator
Its enqueue and dequeue operations take O(1) time
It reports overflow whenever rear reaches index n - 1, regardless of front
More than one of the above
exp: A circular queue wraps indices with % (A) and has O(1) enqueue/dequeue (B); C describes a linear queue.
concept: A circular queue (1) wraps its indices with the % operator, so freed cells are reused; (2) does enqueue and dequeue by changing one index and one cell, so both are O(1); (3) reports full only when there is really no free cell, tested with (rear + 1) % n == front, not merely when rear reaches n - 1.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because B is also true; so the answer is D. Wrapping with (index + 1) % n is exactly how the circular queue reuses cells.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A is also true; so the answer is D. Each operation does a fixed amount of work (one index update and one array access), so both are O(1).
C — Wrong. Overflow at rear == n - 1 regardless of front is the LINEAR queue rule. A circular queue lets rear wrap from n - 1 to 0 if front has moved forward.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true. (C is false, but two true options are enough.)
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following commonly use a circular queue (ring buffer)?
opts: Keyboard and I/O buffers that hold data until it is consumed
Round robin CPU scheduling of processes
Checking for balanced parentheses in an expression
More than one of the above
exp: I/O (keyboard) buffers and round robin scheduling use circular queues; bracket matching uses a stack.
concept: Circular queues (ring buffers) are used wherever data is produced and consumed in arrival order using a fixed amount of memory: keyboard buffers, network and audio/video streaming buffers, and the ready queue of round robin CPU scheduling. In round robin each process gets a small time slice (time quantum) and then goes back to the end of the queue. Problems that match 'last opened, first closed', like balancing brackets, use a stack instead.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because B is also true; so the answer is D. A keyboard buffer stores keystrokes in a fixed-size ring: the keyboard writes at the rear and the program reads at the front, in the order they were typed.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A is also true; so the answer is D. In round robin scheduling the ready processes wait in a circular FIFO queue; when a process's time slice ends it goes to the rear, and the process at the front gets the CPU next.
C — Wrong. Balanced-parentheses checking uses a stack: push each opening bracket, and on a closing bracket pop and match the most recent opening one (LIFO).
D — Correct. A and B are both true, and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true. (C is false, but two true options are enough.)
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Matching / undo / recursion -> stack. Buffering / scheduling / BFS -> queue.

q: A circular queue of n = 12 cells keeps front = index just BEFORE the first element and rear = index of the last element (front == rear means empty; capacity n - 1). If front = 9 and rear = 4, how many elements are present?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: Convention (used in Horowitz-Sahni): front = index one position BEFORE the first element, rear = index of the last element, front == rear means empty, capacity n - 1. The elements occupy cells front + 1, front + 2, ..., rear (going round the circle). Count = (rear - front + n) % n, with no +1, because the cell at front itself is always empty.
work:
n = 12, front = 9, rear = 4.
Elements are in cells 10, 11, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (start one after front, end at rear).
Count = (rear - front + n) % n = (4 - 9 + 12) % 12 = 7 % 12 = 7.
Queue picture: [x, x, x, x, x, _, _, _, _, _, x, x] front=9 rear=4 -> 7 elements (cell 9 is the always-empty cell).
why: A — Wrong. 8 = (rear - front + n) % n + 1; it wrongly counts cell 9 (the front cell), which is always empty in this convention.
B — Wrong. 6 under-counts by one, for example by also leaving out the rear cell 4. The rear cell holds the last element.
C — Correct. Cells 10, 11, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 are filled: (4 - 9 + 12) % 12 = 7.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue has n = 5 cells with front = rear = 0 initially. enqueue(x): if (rear + 1) % n == front report overflow, else rear = (rear + 1) % n and Q[rear] = x. dequeue(): if front == rear report underflow, else front = (front + 1) % n and return Q[front]. Operations: enqueue 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; dequeue(); dequeue(); enqueue 6, 7, 8. How many of the enqueue operations report overflow?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Capacity is n - 1 = 4, so enqueue(5) overflows; after two dequeues, 6 and 7 fit and enqueue(8) overflows: 2 overflows in total.
concept: In this convention (front = rear = 0 at the start), front points one cell BEFORE the first element and rear points to the last element. Enqueue first advances rear and then stores; dequeue first advances front and then reads. The cell at front is always empty, so the capacity is n - 1. Overflow is reported when (rear + 1) % n == front.
work:
(front = rear = 0; the cell at front is always empty, capacity n - 1 = 4.)
enqueue(1): rear = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1, Q[1] = 1; [_, 1, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(2): rear = (1 + 1) % 5 = 2, Q[2] = 2; [_, 1, 2, _, _] front=0 rear=2
enqueue(3): rear = (2 + 1) % 5 = 3, Q[3] = 3; [_, 1, 2, 3, _] front=0 rear=3
enqueue(4): rear = (3 + 1) % 5 = 4, Q[4] = 4; [_, 1, 2, 3, 4] front=0 rear=4
enqueue(5): (4 + 1) % 5 = 0 == front -> OVERFLOW; [_, 1, 2, 3, 4] front=0 rear=4
dequeue() -> 1: front = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1, return Q[1]; [_, _, 2, 3, 4] front=1 rear=4
dequeue() -> 2: front = (1 + 1) % 5 = 2, return Q[2]; [_, _, _, 3, 4] front=2 rear=4
enqueue(6): rear = (4 + 1) % 5 = 0, Q[0] = 6; [6, _, _, 3, 4] front=2 rear=0
enqueue(7): rear = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1, Q[1] = 7; [6, 7, _, 3, 4] front=2 rear=1
enqueue(8): (1 + 1) % 5 = 2 == front -> OVERFLOW; [6, 7, _, 3, 4] front=2 rear=1
Overflow is reported by enqueue(5) and enqueue(8): 2 times.
why: A — Wrong. 1 is what you get if you think all 5 cells can be used (then 5 fits and only 8 fails), or if you miss one of the two overflows. Here the capacity is n - 1 = 4, so both enqueue(5) and enqueue(8) fail.
B — Correct. enqueue(5) overflows (capacity 4), and after 6 and 7 fill the two freed places, enqueue(8) overflows too: 2 times.
C — Wrong. 3 would mean enqueue(6) also failed, but after the two dequeues there are two free places, so 6 and 7 both succeed.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A circular queue has n = 6 cells, front = rear = 0 initially. enqueue stores x at Q[rear] and then rear = (rear + 1) % n; dequeue returns Q[front] and then front = (front + 1) % n. Empty: front == rear; full: (rear + 1) % n == front. Operations: enqueue a, b, c, d, e; three dequeues; enqueue f, g, h. Which is correct now?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: front = 3, rear = 2 and the queue holds 5 elements (d, e, f, g, h); no option states this, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: In this convention rear is the index of the next FREE cell: enqueue writes at Q[rear] and then advances rear; dequeue reads Q[front] and then advances front. One cell is always kept free, so the capacity is n - 1 = 5. Count = (rear - front + n) % n (no +1, because rear is one past the last element).
work:
enqueue(a): Q[0] = a, rear = (0 + 1) % 6 = 1; [a, _, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=1
enqueue(b): Q[1] = b, rear = (1 + 1) % 6 = 2; [a, b, _, _, _, _] front=0 rear=2
enqueue(c): Q[2] = c, rear = (2 + 1) % 6 = 3; [a, b, c, _, _, _] front=0 rear=3
enqueue(d): Q[3] = d, rear = (3 + 1) % 6 = 4; [a, b, c, d, _, _] front=0 rear=4
enqueue(e): Q[4] = e, rear = (4 + 1) % 6 = 5; [a, b, c, d, e, _] front=0 rear=5
dequeue() -> a: front = (0 + 1) % 6 = 1; [_, b, c, d, e, _] front=1 rear=5
dequeue() -> b: front = (1 + 1) % 6 = 2; [_, _, c, d, e, _] front=2 rear=5
dequeue() -> c: front = (2 + 1) % 6 = 3; [_, _, _, d, e, _] front=3 rear=5
enqueue(f): Q[5] = f, rear = (5 + 1) % 6 = 0; [_, _, _, d, e, f] front=3 rear=0
enqueue(g): Q[0] = g, rear = (0 + 1) % 6 = 1; [g, _, _, d, e, f] front=3 rear=1
enqueue(h): Q[1] = h, rear = (1 + 1) % 6 = 2; [g, h, _, d, e, f] front=3 rear=2
Final: front = 3, rear = 2. Count = (2 - 3 + 6) % 6 = 5 (d, e, f, g, h). The queue is now full, since (2 + 1) % 6 = 3 = front.
why: A — Wrong. front = 3 and rear = 2 are right, but there are 5 elements, not 6. The capacity in this convention is n - 1 = 5; the number 6 comes from wrongly adding 1, which is only for the 'rear = last element' convention.
B — Wrong. rear = 3 would need one more enqueue. Also, front == rear means EMPTY in this convention, so it can never go with 5 elements.
C — Wrong. front = 2 counts only two dequeues. Three dequeues move front 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so there cannot be two correct options.
E — Correct. The final state is front = 3, rear = 2 with 5 elements (d, e, f, g, h), which matches none of A–C.

q: A circular queue of n cells uses front = index of the first element and rear = index of the last element; all n cells are usable, front = rear = -1 when empty, and both are reset to -1 when the last element is deleted. Which of the following conditions, whenever true, mean that the queue is FULL?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three conditions mean full: A (no wrap) and B (wrapped) are the two special cases of the general test C.
concept: In the all-cells-usable circular queue (front = first element, rear = last element, both -1 when empty), the number of elements is (rear - front + n) % n + 1, and the queue is full when this equals n. That happens in two shapes: (1) no wrap-around: front = 0 and rear = n - 1; (2) wrapped: rear is just one cell behind front, i.e. front = rear + 1. The single test (rear + 1) % n == front covers both shapes. Many textbooks write the full test as two cases: (front == 0 && rear == n - 1) || (front == rear + 1).
work:
Check with n = 5:
front = 0, rear = 4: count = (4 - 0 + 5) % 5 + 1 = 5 = n -> full; (4 + 1) % 5 = 0 = front.
front = 3, rear = 2: count = (2 - 3 + 5) % 5 + 1 = 5 = n -> full; (2 + 1) % 5 = 3 = front.
Empty (front = rear = -1): A false; B: -1 == 0 false; C: (-1 + 1) % 5 = 0 != -1 false. So none of them is true for an empty queue.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because B and C are also true; so the answer is D. front at index 0 and rear at the last index means every cell from 0 to n - 1 is filled: the non-wrapped full state. Here (rear + 1) % n = 0 = front, so it agrees with C.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A and C are also true; so the answer is D. If rear is just one cell behind front, the elements fill front..n-1 and then 0..rear, which is every cell: count = (n - front) + (rear + 1) = n. For an empty queue front = rear = -1, so -1 == 0 is false and there is no false alarm.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A and B are also true; so the answer is D. This is the general test: the cell after rear (circularly) is front, so there is no free cell. It is never true for an empty queue, because (-1 + 1) % n = 0, not -1.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a linked-list implementation of a queue with pointers front (first node) and rear (last node), where are nodes inserted and deleted?
opts: Inserted after the rear node; deleted at the front node
Inserted before the front node; deleted at the rear node
Inserted and deleted at the front node
More than one of the above
exp: In a linked queue, nodes are inserted after the rear node and deleted at the front node.
concept: In a linked-list queue each element is a node holding the data and a pointer 'next' to the following node. front points to the first node (the oldest) and rear to the last node (the newest). Enqueue creates a node, links it after the rear node and moves rear to it. Dequeue removes the node at front and moves front to the next node.
why: A — Correct. New nodes are linked after rear and removed from front, which gives FIFO order with O(1) operations.
B — Wrong. This reverses the roles. In a singly linked list, deleting the rear node needs its predecessor, which takes O(n) to find, so the standard design deletes at the front.
C — Wrong. Inserting and deleting at the same end (the head) is a linked STACK (LIFO), not a queue.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: If a linked-list queue maintains both front and rear pointers, the time complexities of enqueue and dequeue are:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With front and rear pointers, both enqueue and dequeue of a linked queue are O(1).
concept: With both front and rear pointers: enqueue = create a node, rear->next = new node, rear = new node (a fixed number of steps). Dequeue = temp = front, front = front->next, free(temp) (also a fixed number of steps). So both are O(1). Without a rear pointer, enqueue would have to walk the whole list to find the last node, which is O(n).
why: A — Wrong. O(n) enqueue is the case WITHOUT a rear pointer, when you must traverse the list to find the end. With rear, enqueue is O(1).
B — Wrong. Dequeue just moves front to the next node; no traversal is needed. O(n) deletion would happen only if nodes were deleted at the tail of a singly linked list.
C — Correct. Both operations change only a few pointers, so both are O(1).
