D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a linked-list queue, overflow occurs when:
opts: no memory is available for a new node (malloc returns NULL)
More than one of the above
exp: A linked queue overflows only when memory for a new node cannot be allocated (malloc returns NULL).
concept: A linked-list queue has no fixed maximum size. Nodes are created at run time from free memory (the heap) using malloc in C (or new in C++/Java). So it can overflow only when the system runs out of memory and malloc returns NULL. Underflow is still possible: dequeue when front == NULL.
why: A — Wrong. rear == MAX_SIZE - 1 is the overflow test of an ARRAY (linear) queue, whose size is fixed. In a linked queue rear is a pointer, not an index.
B — Wrong. front == rear (both non-NULL) means the queue has exactly one node; both NULL means empty. Neither is overflow.
C — Correct. A linked queue overflows only when no memory can be allocated for a new node (malloc returns NULL).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are advantages of a linked-list queue over a linear array queue?
opts: No maximum size has to be fixed in advance
Space freed by dequeue is not wasted, because deleted nodes are released
Each element needs less memory, since no pointer is stored
More than one of the above
exp: A linked queue needs no fixed size (A) and releases dequeued nodes (B); C is false because each node stores an extra pointer.
concept: A linked-list queue grows and shrinks at run time, so no maximum size has to be fixed in advance, and each dequeued node is freed (returned to memory), so no space is wasted at the front. The price is that every node stores a 'next' pointer in addition to the data, so it uses more memory per element than an array; nodes are also scattered in memory.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because B is also true; so the answer is D. Nodes are allocated only when needed, so there is no fixed MAX_SIZE.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A is also true; so the answer is D. In a linear array queue the cells before front are wasted; in a linked queue the dequeued node is released with free() (or delete) and that memory can be used again.
C — Wrong. The opposite is true: each node stores an extra pointer (typically 4 or 8 bytes), so a linked queue needs MORE memory per element than an array.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true. (C is false, but two true options are enough.)
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A queue is implemented as a singly linked list that keeps only a pointer to the first node (no rear/tail pointer). Enqueue inserts at the end of the list and dequeue deletes the first node. The time complexities of enqueue and dequeue are:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Without a rear pointer, enqueue must traverse the list (O(n)), while dequeue at the head is O(1).
concept: If a singly linked list queue keeps only a pointer to the first node (front/head), then to enqueue at the end you must start at the head and follow the next pointers until the last node, which takes O(n) time for n nodes. Dequeue deletes the head node, which is O(1). This is why practical linked queues keep a separate rear (tail) pointer.
why: A — Correct. Finding the last node for enqueue takes O(n); deleting the first node for dequeue takes O(1).
B — Wrong. O(1) for both needs a rear pointer (or a circular list with a pointer to the last node). Without it, enqueue must traverse the list.
C — Wrong. This swaps the two. Deleting the first node is O(1) (front = front->next); the O(n) part is finding the end for enqueue.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a singly linked list queue, why is the front of the queue kept at the head of the list and the rear at the tail (and not the other way round)?
opts: Inserting a node at the head of a singly linked list takes O(n) time
Deleting the head node is O(1), whereas deleting the tail node needs its predecessor, which takes O(n) to find
The tail pointer of a list can never be updated after the list is created
More than one of the above
exp: Front is kept at the head because deleting the head is O(1), while deleting the tail of a singly linked list is O(n).
concept: In a singly linked list each node knows only its next node, not the previous one. Inserting at the head, or after the tail when a tail pointer is kept, is O(1), and deleting the head is O(1). But deleting the tail needs the second-last node (to set its next to NULL), and finding it means walking from the head: O(n). Since a queue deletes at the front, the front must be the head (cheap delete) and the rear must be the tail (cheap insert).
why: A — Wrong. Inserting at the head of a singly linked list is O(1): newnode->next = head; head = newnode. (The real problem with the reversed layout is deleting at the tail.)
B — Correct. Deleting the head is O(1), but deleting the tail needs its predecessor, which takes O(n) to find, so deletions (the front) are done at the head.
C — Wrong. A tail pointer is just a variable and can be updated at any time (rear = newnode after every enqueue).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which statement correctly fills the blank in this linked-queue enqueue function?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The new node must be linked after the current last node: rear->next = t, and then rear = t.
concept: Enqueue in a linked queue: create the new node t with t->next = NULL. If the queue is empty (rear == NULL), t becomes both front and rear. Otherwise link it after the current last node (rear->next = t) and then move rear to t. The order matters: link first, then move rear; if rear were moved first, the old last node could no longer be reached to link it.
work:
Example: queue 10 -> 20 (front = node 10, rear = node 20); enqueue(30):
t = new node(30), t->next = NULL
rear->next = t  ->  list 10 -> 20 -> 30
rear = t  ->  front = node 10, rear = node 30
why: A — Wrong. t->next = rear makes the new node point BACK to the old last node, while the old last node's next stays NULL. So t can never be reached from front, and the next dequeues would never find it.
B — Correct. rear->next = t links the new node after the current last node; then rear = t makes it the new last node.

C — Wrong. front->next = t makes the FIRST node point to t, cutting off every node between front and the old rear (they are lost). It happens to work only when the queue has exactly one node (front == rear).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In this linked-queue dequeue function (front and rear are global node pointers), which statement correctly fills the blank?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: When the last node is dequeued, rear must also be set to NULL so that it does not point to freed memory.
concept: Dequeue in a linked queue: save the front node in t, read its data, move front to front->next, then free t. Special case: if the queue had only one node, front becomes NULL, and rear must also be set to NULL. Otherwise rear would still point to the freed node (a dangling pointer, i.e. a pointer to memory that has been released), and the next enqueue would do rear->next = t on freed memory.
work:
Example: the queue has one node holding 5 (front = rear = that node).
t = front; x = 5; front = front->next = NULL
front == NULL  ->  rear = NULL
free(t)  ->  front = NULL, rear = NULL (empty queue)
Next enqueue sees rear == NULL and correctly sets front = rear = new node.
why: A — Correct. When the last node is removed the queue is empty, so rear must also become NULL; then the next enqueue starts a fresh list.
B — Wrong. front = rear would set front back to the node that is about to be freed (rear still points to it), so the queue would look non-empty and point to freed memory.

C — Wrong. rear->next is already NULL (rear is the last node), so this statement changes nothing. rear still points to the node that free(t) releases, leaving a dangling pointer; the next enqueue would then write into freed memory.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A queue is implemented as a linked list with front and rear pointers. Starting from empty: enqueue(4), enqueue(8), enqueue(15), dequeue(), enqueue(16), dequeue(). What data values are in the nodes pointed to by front and rear?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The two dequeues remove 4 and 8, leaving 15 -> 16: front holds 15 and rear holds 16, which is not listed.
concept: In a linked queue, enqueue adds a node after rear and dequeue removes the node at front, so the order of values from front to rear is always the order in which they were inserted. Trace by writing the list from front to rear after each operation.
work:
(List shown from front to rear; front/rear give the data in those nodes.)
enqueue(4): 4   front=4 rear=4
enqueue(8): 4 -> 8   front=4 rear=8
enqueue(15): 4 -> 8 -> 15   front=4 rear=15
dequeue() -> 4: 8 -> 15   front=8 rear=15
enqueue(16): 8 -> 15 -> 16   front=8 rear=16
dequeue() -> 8: 15 -> 16   front=15 rear=16
Final: front node holds 15, rear node holds 16.
why: A — Wrong. 8 was at the front after the FIRST dequeue; the second dequeue removed 8 as well, so front now holds 15.
B — Wrong. 4 was the first value inserted and was removed by the first dequeue.
C — Wrong. The two values are swapped: 16 was enqueued last, so it is at the rear, and 15 is at the front.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is correct, so there cannot be two correct options.
E — Correct. The list is 15 -> 16, so front holds 15 and rear holds 16, and no option says this.

q: A queue is implemented using a circular singly linked list in which only a pointer to the LAST node (rear) is kept, so rear->next is the first node. The time complexities of enqueue and dequeue are:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With a pointer to the last node of a circular list, the first node is rear->next, so both enqueue and dequeue are O(1).
concept: A circular singly linked list joins the last node back to the first. If we keep only a pointer to the LAST node (rear), we still reach the first node in one step as rear->next. Enqueue: t->next = rear->next; rear->next = t; rear = t. Dequeue: first = rear->next; rear->next = first->next; free(first) (and set rear = NULL if it was the only node). Both are a fixed number of pointer changes, so both are O(1).
why: A — Wrong. Dequeue needs only the first node, which is rear->next, so no traversal is needed: it is O(1), not O(n).
B — Correct. Both operations change only a few pointers around rear and rear->next, so both are O(1).

C — Wrong. Enqueue inserts right after rear and moves rear, with no traversal. (If only a pointer to the FIRST node were kept, reaching the last node would need an O(n) walk; that is why the pointer to the last node is the clever choice.)
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Circular list: keep the pointer to the LAST node; you get the first node free as last->next.

q: What does the term 'deque' stand for?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Deque stands for double-ended queue.
concept: Deque (pronounced 'deck') is short for double-ended queue: a linear list in which elements can be inserted and deleted at BOTH ends (front and rear). It is more general than both a stack and a queue. Do not confuse the noun 'deque' with the operation 'dequeue' (remove from the front of a queue).
why: A — Wrong. 'Delete queue' is not a data structure. This confuses 'deque' with the operation 'dequeue'.
B — Correct. Deque = Double-Ended QUEue: insertion and deletion are allowed at both ends.
C — Wrong. A queue built with a linked list is sometimes called a dynamic queue, but that is not what the name 'deque' means.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: DEQUE = Double-Ended QUEue; dequeue = the delete operation.

q: An input-restricted deque is one in which:
opts: Insertion is allowed at only one end, but deletion is allowed at both ends
Deletion is allowed at only one end, but insertion is allowed at both ends
Insertion and deletion are allowed only at the same end
More than one of the above
exp: An input-restricted deque allows insertion at only one end but deletion at both ends.
concept: There are two restricted forms of a deque. In an INPUT-restricted deque, input (insertion) is allowed at only one end, but deletion is allowed at both ends. In an OUTPUT-restricted deque, output (deletion) is allowed at only one end, but insertion is allowed at both ends. The word before 'restricted' tells you which operation is limited.
why: A — Correct. Input (insertion) is restricted to one end, while deletion can happen at both ends.
B — Wrong. Restricting deletion (output) to one end describes an OUTPUT-restricted deque.
C — Wrong. Insertion and deletion only at the same end is a stack, not an input-restricted deque.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Input-restricted: limited INsertion. Output-restricted: limited deletion (taking OUT).

q: An output-restricted deque is one in which:
opts: Insertion is allowed at only one end, but deletion is allowed at both ends
Insertion and deletion are allowed only at the same end
Deletion is allowed at only one end, but insertion is allowed at both ends
More than one of the above
exp: An output-restricted deque allows deletion at only one end but insertion at both ends.
concept: An OUTPUT-restricted deque allows output (deletion) at only one end, but insertion at both ends. An INPUT-restricted deque is the opposite: insertion at only one end, deletion at both ends. The word before 'restricted' names the operation that is limited.
why: A — Wrong. Insertion at only one end with deletion at both ends is an INPUT-restricted deque.
B — Wrong. Insertion and deletion only at the same end is a stack.
C — Correct. Output (deletion) is restricted to one end, while insertion is allowed at both ends.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Output = what comes OUT = deletion.

q: By restricting which ends are used, a deque can directly work as which of the following?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A deque can act as a stack (one end only) or as a queue (insert at one end, delete at the other), but not as a BST.
concept: A deque supports four operations: InsertFront, InsertRear, DeleteFront and DeleteRear. If we use only one end for both insertion and deletion (for example InsertRear + DeleteRear), it behaves as a stack (LIFO). If we insert at one end and delete at the other (InsertRear + DeleteFront), it behaves as a queue (FIFO). So a deque can directly serve as either.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because B is also true; so the answer is D. Using only one end (insert and delete at the rear, say) gives LIFO behaviour: a stack.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself, because A is also true; so the answer is D. Inserting at the rear and deleting at the front gives FIFO behaviour: a queue.

C — Wrong. A binary search tree is a non-linear (tree) structure that keeps keys in sorted order (left < node < right) for fast searching. A deque is a linear list that works only at its two ends; it cannot provide this ordering.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true. (C is false, but two true options are enough.)
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A deque is implemented with a doubly linked list having both head and tail pointers. The time complexity of each of InsertFront, InsertRear, DeleteFront and DeleteRear is:
opts: O(1) for insertions but O(n) for deletions
More than one of the above
exp: With a doubly linked list and head/tail pointers, all four deque operations are O(1).
concept: A doubly linked list node has two pointers: prev and next. With head and tail pointers, every end operation changes only a few pointers: insert at front (link before head), insert at rear (link after tail), delete front (head = head->next; head->prev = NULL), delete rear (tail = tail->prev; tail->next = NULL). The prev pointer is what makes DeleteRear O(1); in a singly linked list DeleteRear would be O(n).
why: A — Wrong. Deletions at both ends are O(1) too, because the prev link gives the second-last node directly. O(n) DeleteRear happens only in a SINGLY linked list.
B — Correct. Both ends are directly reachable and each operation changes a constant number of pointers, so all four are O(1).
C — Wrong. No operation needs to walk through the list, because head and tail point straight to the two ends.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: To check whether a string is a palindrome using a deque, all characters are first inserted at the rear. Then, repeatedly:
opts: one character is removed from the front and one from the rear, and the two are compared
two characters are removed from the front and compared
two characters are removed from the rear and compared
More than one of the above
exp: To test a palindrome with a deque, remove one character from the front and one from the rear and compare them, repeatedly.
concept: A palindrome is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards, like MADAM or LEVEL. Put all the characters into a deque, then repeatedly remove one character from the front and one from the rear and compare them. If any pair differs, the string is not a palindrome; if you reach 0 or 1 remaining characters with all pairs equal, it is a palindrome. Example MADAM: M = M, A = A, D is left alone -> palindrome.
why: A — Correct. Removing one character from each end compares the first with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on: exactly the mirror test.
B — Wrong. Two characters from the front are neighbours (the first and the second, e.g. 'M' and 'A' in MADAM). Comparing neighbours does not test whether the string mirrors itself.
C — Wrong. Two characters from the rear are also neighbours (the last and the second-last), so this does not test the mirror property either.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Starting with an empty deque: InsertRear(7), InsertFront(3), InsertRear(9), DeleteFront(), InsertFront(5). What do getFront() and getRear() now return?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The deque becomes [5, 7, 9], so getFront() = 5 and getRear() = 9.
concept: Deque operations: InsertFront adds at the front, InsertRear adds at the rear, DeleteFront removes the front element, DeleteRear removes the rear element, and getFront / getRear only read the end elements. Trace by writing the deque from front to rear after each step.
work:
InsertRear(7): [7] front=7 rear=7
InsertFront(3): [3, 7] front=3 rear=7
InsertRear(9): [3, 7, 9] front=3 rear=9
DeleteFront() -> 3: [7, 9] front=7 rear=9
InsertFront(5): [5, 7, 9] front=5 rear=9
getFront() = 5, getRear() = 9.
why: A — Correct. The deque is 5, 7, 9 from front to rear, so getFront() = 5 and getRear() = 9.
B — Wrong. 3 and 9 is the state after the third operation. DeleteFront then removed 3, and InsertFront(5) put 5 at the front.
C — Wrong. 7 was the rear only until InsertRear(9); since then 9 has been the rear element.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Starting with an empty deque, the operations InsertRear(10), InsertRear(20), InsertFront(5), InsertFront(1), DeleteRear(), InsertRear(30), DeleteFront() are performed. What are the contents from front to rear?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After all seven operations the deque holds 5, 10, 30 from front to rear.
concept: A deque (double-ended queue, pronounced 'deck') is a linear list in which elements can be inserted and deleted at BOTH ends, the front and the rear. So it has four basic operations: InsertFront, InsertRear, DeleteFront and DeleteRear. Think of a railway coach with doors at both ends: people can get in or get out through either door. To trace a deque, write its contents from front to rear after every operation.
work:
(Deque written from front to rear.)
InsertRear(10): [10]   front = 10, rear = 10
InsertRear(20): [10, 20]   front = 10, rear = 20
InsertFront(5): [5, 10, 20]   front = 5, rear = 20
InsertFront(1): [1, 5, 10, 20]   front = 1, rear = 20
DeleteRear() removes 20: [1, 5, 10]   front = 1, rear = 10
InsertRear(30): [1, 5, 10, 30]   front = 1, rear = 30
DeleteFront() removes 1: [5, 10, 30]   front = 5, rear = 30
Final contents: 5 10 30.
why: A — Wrong. 1 5 10 is the deque just after DeleteRear() (the fifth operation). Stopping there misses the last two steps: InsertRear(30) adds 30 at the rear and DeleteFront() removes 1 from the front.
B — Correct. Following every step gives [5, 10, 30]: 20 was removed from the rear, 1 was removed from the front, and 30 was added at the rear.
C — Wrong. 10 20 30 still contains 20, but 20 was the rear element when DeleteRear() was called, so it was removed. It also leaves out 5, which is still at the front.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Draw the deque as a row and rewrite it after every operation; most mistakes come from skipping a step.

q: Starting with an empty deque: InsertFront(A), InsertFront(B), InsertRear(C), InsertFront(D), DeleteRear(), DeleteRear(). In what order are the elements deleted?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The deque becomes D B A C, so the two rear deletions remove C and then A.
concept: In a deque, DeleteRear() removes the element at the rear end, that is, the last element when the deque is read from front to rear. InsertFront places the new element before the current front, so elements inserted at the front move further away from the rear. To find which elements are deleted, build the deque step by step.
work:
InsertFront(A): [A]   front = A, rear = A
InsertFront(B): [B, A]   front = B, rear = A
InsertRear(C): [B, A, C]   front = B, rear = C
InsertFront(D): [D, B, A, C]   front = D, rear = C
DeleteRear() removes C: [D, B, A]   front = D, rear = A
DeleteRear() removes A: [D, B]   front = D, rear = B
Deleted in order: C, A; left in the deque: D B.
why: A — Wrong. D and B are the two elements LEFT in the deque at the end (D at the front, then B). They would be the deleted ones only if both deletions were made at the front (DeleteFront twice).
B — Wrong. These are the right two elements but in the wrong order. C sits at the rear and is removed first; only after that does A become the rear element.
C — Correct. After the four insertions the deque is [D, B, A, C]. The first DeleteRear() removes C and the second removes A.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In an output-restricted deque, deletion is allowed only at the front. The operations InsertRear(1), InsertFront(2), InsertRear(3), InsertFront(4) are performed, and then all elements are deleted one by one. In what order are they deleted?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The deque is built as 4 2 1 3, and deleting from the front gives 4, 2, 1, 3.
concept: An output-restricted deque allows insertion at both ends but deletion at only one end (here, the front). Elements always leave from the front, but their position in the line depends on which end they were inserted at. When all deletions come after all insertions, the deletion order is simply the deque read from front to rear.
work:
InsertRear(1): [1]   front = 1, rear = 1
InsertFront(2): [2, 1]   front = 2, rear = 1
InsertRear(3): [2, 1, 3]   front = 2, rear = 3
InsertFront(4): [4, 2, 1, 3]   front = 4, rear = 3
DeleteFront() removes 4: [2, 1, 3]   front = 2, rear = 3
DeleteFront() removes 2: [1, 3]   front = 1, rear = 3
DeleteFront() removes 1: [3]   front = 3, rear = 3
DeleteFront() removes 3: []   empty
Deletion order: 4 2 1 3.
why: A — Correct. The insertions build [4, 2, 1, 3] (front to rear), and deleting from the front again and again gives 4, 2, 1, 3.
B — Wrong. 1 2 3 4 is the arrival order. It would be the output of an ordinary queue (all insertions at the rear), but here 2 and 4 were inserted at the front.
C — Wrong. 3 1 2 4 is the deque read from rear to front. That would be the deletion order only if deletions were made at the rear, which this deque does not allow.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Output-restricted: output (deletion) at one end only. Input-restricted: input (insertion) at one end only.

q: An input-restricted deque allows insertion only at the rear. Elements 10, 20, 30, 40 are inserted in this order, and then DeleteRear(), DeleteFront(), DeleteRear() are performed. Which element remains?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The deletions remove 40 (rear), 10 (front) and 30 (rear); only 20 remains, which is not listed.
concept: An input-restricted deque allows insertion at only one end (here, the rear) but deletion at both ends. If 10, 20, 30, 40 are inserted at the rear, the deque is [10, 20, 30, 40] with 10 at the front and 40 at the rear. DeleteRear removes the current rear element and DeleteFront removes the current front element.
work:
InsertRear(10): [10]   front = 10, rear = 10
InsertRear(20): [10, 20]   front = 10, rear = 20
InsertRear(30): [10, 20, 30]   front = 10, rear = 30
InsertRear(40): [10, 20, 30, 40]   front = 10, rear = 40
DeleteRear() removes 40: [10, 20, 30]   front = 10, rear = 30
DeleteFront() removes 10: [20, 30]   front = 20, rear = 30
DeleteRear() removes 30: [20]   front = 20, rear = 20
Deleted: 40, 10, 30. Remaining element: 20.
why: A — Wrong. 10 is the front element, and DeleteFront() removed it.
B — Wrong. After 40 was removed, 30 became the rear element, so the second DeleteRear() removed it.
C — Wrong. 40 was the rear element and was removed by the first DeleteRear().
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The three deletions remove 40, 10 and 30, so the element left is 20, which is not among A–C.

q: A deque is implemented using a singly linked list with head (front) and tail (rear) pointers. Which operation takes O(n) time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only DeleteRear is O(n), because a singly linked list cannot step back from the tail to the second-last node.
concept: In a singly linked list each node points only to the NEXT node, so you can move forward but never backward. With head and tail pointers, inserting at either end and deleting the first node take O(1) time (a fixed number of steps, whatever n is). But deleting the last node needs the second-last node (it becomes the new tail and its next must be set to NULL), and the only way to reach it is to walk from the head, which is O(n). A doubly linked list (each node also has a prev pointer) makes all four deque operations O(1).
why: A — Wrong. InsertFront creates a node, points it to the old head and makes it the new head: a fixed number of steps, O(1).
B — Correct. DeleteRear must find the node just before the tail. A singly linked list has no backward pointer, so we walk from the head through about n nodes: O(n).
C — Wrong. InsertRear sets tail->next to the new node and moves tail to it: O(1). This is exactly why a tail pointer is kept.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: For a deque with all four operations in O(1), use a doubly linked list or a circular array.

q: A deque is stored in a circular array of n cells. On InsertFront (deque neither empty nor full), front is updated as:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: InsertFront moves front one step backward with wrap-around: front = (front - 1 + n) % n.
concept: In a circular array the cells 0 .. n-1 are treated as a ring: after cell n-1 comes cell 0, and before cell 0 comes cell n-1. The modulo operator % makes the index wrap around. Moving forward is (i + 1) % n and moving backward is (i - 1 + n) % n. Adding n before taking % keeps the value non-negative, because in C a negative number % n can be negative (for example, -1 % 5 is -1).
why: A — Wrong. (front + 1) % n moves front one cell FORWARD. That is what DeleteFront does (the front element leaves, so the next cell becomes the front). InsertFront needs the opposite direction.
B — Wrong. Decrementing without wrap-around fails when front is 0: front would become -1, which is outside the array, even though cell n-1 may be free. A circular array must wrap from 0 back to n-1.
C — Correct. (front - 1 + n) % n moves front one cell backward and wraps from 0 to n-1. For example, with n = 5 and front = 0 the new front is (0 - 1 + 5) % 5 = 4.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Forward step: (i + 1) % n. Backward step: (i - 1 + n) % n.

q: A deque is stored in a circular array of n = 5 cells; front = rear = -1 when empty. InsertFront: if empty set front = rear = 0, else front = (front - 1 + n) % n. InsertRear: if empty set front = rear = 0, else rear = (rear + 1) % n. DeleteFront: front = (front + 1) % n. DeleteRear: rear = (rear - 1 + n) % n. Starting empty: InsertRear(10), InsertRear(20), InsertFront(5), InsertFront(3), DeleteRear(), DeleteFront(). What are front and rear now?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: front ends at 4 and rear at 0; the deque holds 5 and 10, wrapping from cell 4 to cell 0.
concept: This deque uses a circular array of 5 cells in which all cells can be used, and front = rear = -1 means empty. InsertRear and DeleteFront move an index forward (+1, wrapping from 4 to 0). InsertFront and DeleteRear move an index backward (-1, wrapping from 0 to 4). Track front and rear after every operation.
work:
(Array shown as Q[0..4]; '_' = free cell.)
InsertRear(10): deque empty, so front = rear = 0; Q[0] = 10   array [10, _, _, _, _]   front = 0, rear = 0
InsertRear(20): rear = (0 + 1) % 5 = 1; Q[1] = 20   array [10, 20, _, _, _]   front = 0, rear = 1
InsertFront(5): front = (0 - 1 + 5) % 5 = 4; Q[4] = 5   array [10, 20, _, _, 5]   front = 4, rear = 1
InsertFront(3): front = (4 - 1 + 5) % 5 = 3; Q[3] = 3   array [10, 20, _, 3, 5]   front = 3, rear = 1
DeleteRear() removes 20: rear = (1 - 1 + 5) % 5 = 0   array [10, _, _, 3, 5]   front = 3, rear = 0
DeleteFront() removes 3: front = (3 + 1) % 5 = 4   array [10, _, _, _, 5]   front = 4, rear = 0
Final: front = 4, rear = 0. Deque from front to rear: Q[4] = 5, Q[0] = 10 (wrapping from cell 4 to cell 0).
why: A — Wrong. front = 3 is the value after the two InsertFront operations; it ignores the final DeleteFront(), which moves front forward to (3 + 1) % 5 = 4. rear = 1 also ignores DeleteRear(), which moves rear back to 0.
B — Wrong. front = 4 is right, but rear = 1 forgets DeleteRear(), which moves rear from 1 back to (1 - 1 + 5) % 5 = 0.
C — Correct. The final state is front = 4, rear = 0. The deque holds 5 (cell 4) followed by 10 (cell 0), wrapping around the end of the array.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is the output of the following C++ code (std::deque)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The deque ends as 4 3 1 5, so the program prints 4 5.
concept: std::deque in C++ (header <deque>) is the standard library's double-ended queue. push_back adds at the rear, push_front adds at the front, pop_back removes the rear element and pop_front removes the front element. front() and back() only READ the first and last elements; they do not remove them.
work:
push_back(1): [1]   front = 1, rear = 1
push_back(2): [1, 2]   front = 1, rear = 2
push_front(3): [3, 1, 2]   front = 3, rear = 2
pop_back() removes 2: [3, 1]   front = 3, rear = 1
push_front(4): [4, 3, 1]   front = 4, rear = 1
push_back(5): [4, 3, 1, 5]   front = 4, rear = 5
d.front() = 4, d.back() = 5 -> prints "4 5".
why: A — Wrong. 3 was the front just before push_front(4). After 4 is added at the front, front() returns 4.
B — Correct. The final deque is [4, 3, 1, 5], so front() is 4 and back() is 5, and the program prints 4 5.
C — Wrong. 2 was removed by pop_back(), and later 5 was pushed at the back, so back() is 5, not 2.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A string is checked for being a palindrome with a deque: repeatedly remove one character from each end and compare them, stopping on a mismatch or when at most one character remains. How many comparisons are made for the string "MALAYALAM"?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: MALAYALAM needs floor(9/2) = 4 comparisons (M-M, A-A, L-L, A-A); 4 is not listed.
concept: A deque makes palindrome checking easy: put all characters into a deque, then repeatedly remove one character from the front and one from the rear and compare them. A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards (MADAM, MALAYALAM), so every pair matches. For a palindrome of length n the number of comparisons is floor(n/2), because each comparison uses up two characters and at most one middle character is left over.
work:
Deque: M A L A Y A L A M (9 characters)
Comparison 1: M (front) vs M (rear) -> match; left: A L A Y A L A
Comparison 2: A (front) vs A (rear) -> match; left: L A Y A L
Comparison 3: L (front) vs L (rear) -> match; left: A Y A
Comparison 4: A (front) vs A (rear) -> match; left: Y
Only 1 character (Y) remains -> stop. Total comparisons = 4 = floor(9/2).
why: A — Wrong. After 3 comparisons the deque still holds 'AYA' (3 characters, more than one), so the process continues and compares A with A. 3 would be the count for a 7-letter palindrome such as RACECAR.
B — Wrong. 5 is ceil(9/2), as if the middle character Y also needed a comparison. The process stops when at most one character remains, so Y is never compared.
C — Wrong. 9 is the length of the string. Each comparison checks two characters at once (one from each end), so far fewer comparisons are needed.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Exactly 4 comparisons are made (floor(9/2) = 4), and 4 is not among A–C.
tip: Deque palindrome check of a palindrome of length n: floor(n/2) comparisons.

q: Which of the following are typical applications of a deque?
opts: Checking whether a string is a palindrome
Finding the maximum of every window of size k (sliding-window maximum)
A-Steal job scheduling, where an idle processor takes work from the back of another processor's deque
More than one of the above
exp: Palindrome checking, sliding-window maximum and A-Steal (work-stealing) scheduling are all standard deque applications.
concept: A deque is useful whenever we must add or remove elements at both ends. Three classic uses: (1) palindrome checking, by removing characters from both ends and comparing; (2) the sliding-window maximum, where a deque holds indices of useful elements in decreasing order of value, so the whole array is processed in O(n); (3) work-stealing schedulers such as A-Steal, where each processor works at one end of its own deque and an idle processor steals tasks from the other end of another processor's deque.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Comparing the first and last characters needs removal from both ends, which a deque gives in O(1) each.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In the sliding-window maximum, the deque keeps candidate indices in decreasing order of value. Indices that slide out of the window are removed from the front; smaller values that can never be the maximum are removed from the rear. Each index enters and leaves once, so the whole algorithm is O(n).

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In work stealing (A-Steal is one such algorithm), each processor pushes and pops its own tasks at one end of its deque, while an idle processor 'steals' a task from the other end of a busy processor's deque. Working at opposite ends reduces clashes between the owner and the thief.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Need to work at both ends? Think deque.

q: A deque is stored in a circular array Q[0..3] (n = 4); front = rear = -1 when empty. InsertFront: if empty set front = rear = 0, else front = (front - 1 + n) % n. InsertRear: if empty set front = rear = 0, else rear = (rear + 1) % n. The element is then stored at Q[front] or Q[rear]. Starting empty: InsertFront(1), InsertFront(2), InsertRear(3), InsertFront(4). What are the array contents Q[0], Q[1], Q[2], Q[3]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The cells are Q[0..3] = 1 3 4 2; the logical order from front (index 2) is 4 2 1 3.
concept: In a circular-array deque, InsertFront moves front backward ((front - 1 + n) % n) and InsertRear moves rear forward ((rear + 1) % n). So elements inserted at the front can end up in the high-numbered cells at the end of the array. The physical array contents (Q[0], Q[1], ...) are therefore not always in the same order as the logical deque from front to rear.
work:
(Array shown as Q[0..3]; '_' = free cell.)
InsertFront(1): deque empty, so front = rear = 0; Q[0] = 1   array [1, _, _, _]   front = 0, rear = 0
InsertFront(2): front = (0 - 1 + 4) % 4 = 3; Q[3] = 2   array [1, _, _, 2]   front = 3, rear = 0
InsertRear(3): rear = (0 + 1) % 4 = 1; Q[1] = 3   array [1, 3, _, 2]   front = 3, rear = 1
InsertFront(4): front = (3 - 1 + 4) % 4 = 2; Q[2] = 4   array [1, 3, 4, 2]   front = 2, rear = 1
Physical cells Q[0], Q[1], Q[2], Q[3] = 1 3 4 2.
Logical order from front (index 2) to rear (index 1) = 4 2 1 3 (this is option A, which answers a different question).
why: A — Wrong. 4 2 1 3 is the LOGICAL order of the deque, read from front (cell 2) to rear (cell 1) with wrap-around: Q[2], Q[3], Q[0], Q[1]. The question asks for the physical cells Q[0] to Q[3] in index order.
B — Wrong. It puts 2 in Q[0] and 4 in Q[1]. But Q[0] keeps 1, the first element; the second InsertFront wraps front from 0 to 3, so 2 goes to Q[3]; InsertRear(3) then fills Q[1]; and 4 goes to Q[2].
C — Correct. Q[0] = 1 (first element, front = rear = 0), Q[3] = 2 (front wraps to 3), Q[1] = 3 (rear moves to 1), Q[2] = 4 (front moves to 2). In index order: 1 3 4 2.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Always check whether a question asks for the array cells in index order or the deque in front-to-rear order.

q: Elements 1, 2, 3, 4 arrive in this order and are passed through an input-restricted deque (insertion only at the rear, deletion at either end); insertions and deletions may be interleaved. Which output sequence can NOT be produced?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 4, 2, 1, 3 is impossible: after 4 leaves, 2 is stuck between 1 and 3.
concept: In an input-restricted deque, elements enter only at the rear, so inside the deque they always stay in arrival order (the oldest at the front). An element can leave from either end. So the next output must be the current front element, the current rear element, or a new element that we insert and immediately delete. To test a sequence, simulate it: insert elements until the wanted one is inside, then check that it is at the front or the rear.
work:
Option A (4, 2, 1, 3): to output 4 first, insert 1, 2, 3, 4 -> [1, 2, 3, 4]; DeleteRear -> 4; deque [1, 2, 3].
  Next wanted 2, but the ends are 1 (front) and 3 (rear); 2 is in the middle -> IMPOSSIBLE.
Option B (4, 1, 3, 2): insert 1, 2, 3, 4 -> [1, 2, 3, 4]; DeleteRear -> 4 [1, 2, 3]; DeleteFront -> 1 [2, 3]; DeleteRear -> 3 [2]; DeleteFront -> 2. Possible.
Option C (2, 4, 1, 3): insert 1, 2 -> [1, 2]; DeleteRear -> 2 [1]; insert 3, 4 -> [1, 3, 4]; DeleteRear -> 4 [1, 3]; DeleteFront -> 1 [3]; DeleteFront -> 3. Possible.
(A full search over all orders of operations confirms: only A cannot be produced.)
why: A — Correct. (A is the sequence that can NOT be produced.) To output 4 first, all of 1, 2, 3, 4 must be inserted, giving [1, 2, 3, 4], and 4 leaves from the rear. Now the deque is [1, 2, 3] and the next output must be 1 (front) or 3 (rear). 2 is stuck in the middle, so 4, 2, 1, 3 is impossible.
B — Wrong. (It can be produced.) Insert 1, 2, 3, 4; DeleteRear gives 4, DeleteFront gives 1, DeleteRear gives 3, and then 2 is left.
C — Wrong. (It can be produced.) Insert 1, 2; DeleteRear gives 2; insert 3, 4 -> [1, 3, 4]; DeleteRear gives 4, DeleteFront gives 1, and then 3.
D — Wrong. Only A cannot be produced; B and C can be produced, so 'More than one of the above' does not fit.
E — Wrong. A can NOT be produced, so an option that fits the stem exists and 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Input-restricted deque: the elements inside stay in arrival order, and only the two end elements can leave.

q: Elements 1, 2, 3, 4 arrive in this order and are passed through an output-restricted deque (insertion at either end, deletion only at the front); insertions and deletions may be interleaved. Which of the following output sequences can NOT be produced?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Both 4, 1, 3, 2 and 4, 2, 3, 1 are impossible (3 would have to sit between 1 and 2), while 4, 2, 1, 3 is possible, so the answer is D.
concept: In an output-restricted deque every element leaves from the front, but a new element can be put at either end. If 4 (the last to arrive) is output first, then all four elements are inside before any deletion, and the rest of the output is just the deque read from front to rear. Since every new element goes to one END of the elements already inside, among 1, 2, 3 the element 3 (inserted last of them) must be at one end of that group, never in the middle.
work:
4 comes out first in all three options, so 1, 2, 3, 4 are all inserted before the first deletion.
Possible arrangements of 1, 2, 3 (3 must be at an end of the group): 3 2 1 / 2 1 3 / 3 1 2 / 1 2 3.
Option A (4, 1, 3, 2): group order 1 3 2 -> 3 in the middle -> IMPOSSIBLE.
Option B (4, 2, 3, 1): group order 2 3 1 -> 3 in the middle -> IMPOSSIBLE.
Option C (4, 2, 1, 3): InsertRear(1) [1]; InsertFront(2) [2, 1]; InsertRear(3) [2, 1, 3]; InsertFront(4) [4, 2, 1, 3]; delete from front: 4, 2, 1, 3. Possible.
(A full search over all orders of operations confirms: A and B cannot be produced, C can.)
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. (Here TRUE means: this sequence can NOT be produced.) The deque would have to read [4, 1, 3, 2], so the group 1, 2, 3 would be in the order 1, 3, 2 with 3 in the middle. But 3 was inserted after 1 and 2, so it went to one end of them. So 4, 1, 3, 2 is impossible.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. (Here TRUE means: this sequence can NOT be produced.) The deque would have to read [4, 2, 3, 1], again with 3 in the middle of the group 1, 2, 3. Impossible for the same reason.
C — Wrong. (It can be produced.) InsertRear(1) -> [1]; InsertFront(2) -> [2, 1]; InsertRear(3) -> [2, 1, 3]; InsertFront(4) -> [4, 2, 1, 3]; deleting from the front gives 4, 2, 1, 3.
D — Correct. A and B both can NOT be produced (both fit the stem), while C can be produced. Two options fit, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B can NOT be produced, so options that fit the stem do exist and 'None of the above' is wrong.
tip: Output-restricted deque: each new element joins at an END of the line, so a later element can never sit between two earlier ones.

q: In a priority queue:
opts: Elements are removed according to their priority rather than strictly by order of arrival
Elements are always removed in LIFO order
Elements can be inserted only at the front
More than one of the above
exp: In a priority queue, the element with the highest priority leaves first, regardless of arrival order.
concept: A priority queue is a collection in which every element has a priority, and the element with the highest priority is removed first, no matter when it arrived. Think of a hospital emergency room: a patient in critical condition is treated before someone with a small cut, even if the small cut came earlier. Arrival order is used only to break ties between equal priorities.
why: A — Correct. This is the definition: the element removed is chosen by its priority, not strictly by its arrival order.
B — Wrong. Always removing the most recently inserted element (LIFO) is the rule of a stack, not of a priority queue.

C — Wrong. A priority queue has no rule that insertion happens only at the front. It is defined by how elements are removed (by priority); where an element is physically stored depends on the implementation (array, linked list, heap).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Priority queue = hospital emergency room.

q: In a descending priority queue, the delete operation removes:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A descending (max) priority queue deletes the largest element.
concept: There are two kinds of priority queue. In an ascending priority queue (also called a min-priority queue) only the smallest element can be removed. In a descending priority queue (max-priority queue) only the largest element can be removed. In both kinds, elements can be inserted in any order.
why: A — Wrong. Removing the smallest element is the rule of an ascending (min) priority queue, the opposite kind.
B — Correct. A descending priority queue gives out its elements from largest to smallest, so each delete removes the current largest element.
C — Wrong. Removing the most recently inserted element is LIFO, the rule of a stack. A priority queue looks at the values, not at the time of insertion.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Ascending PQ: elements come out in ascending order (smallest first). Descending PQ: they come out in descending order (largest first).

q: In an ascending priority queue, the delete operation removes:
opts: the element at the rear of the queue
More than one of the above
exp: An ascending (min) priority queue deletes the smallest element; that is not listed, so the answer is E.
concept: In an ascending priority queue (min-priority queue) the delete operation always removes the SMALLEST element present, so elements come out in ascending order. In a descending (max) priority queue the delete removes the largest element. Neither kind looks at position (front/rear) or at time of insertion.
why: A — Wrong. Removing the largest element is the rule of a descending (max) priority queue.
B — Wrong. A priority queue chooses the element to remove by its value (priority), not by its position. 'Remove the element at the rear' is not how an ascending priority queue is defined.
C — Wrong. Removing the most recently inserted element is LIFO, the rule of a stack.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. An ascending priority queue removes the SMALLEST element, and none of A–C says this.

q: According to the standard definition of a priority queue, two elements having the SAME priority are processed:
opts: in reverse order of their insertion
in the order in which they were inserted (FIFO)
More than one of the above
exp: Elements of equal priority are processed in the order they were inserted (FIFO).
concept: The textbook definition of a priority queue (for example in Lipschutz, Schaum's Outline of Data Structures) has two rules: (1) an element of higher priority is processed before any element of lower priority; (2) two elements with the same priority are processed in the order in which they were added to the queue. So among equal priorities the structure behaves like an ordinary FIFO queue. (A plain binary heap does not keep this tie order by itself; when ties must be FIFO, the arrival number is used as a second key.)
why: A — Wrong. Reverse order of insertion would be LIFO (stack behaviour). The standard definition breaks ties by arrival order, first come first served.
B — Wrong. The definition does not leave ties to chance; it fixes the order as the order of insertion.
C — Correct. Rule 2 of the definition: elements of equal priority are processed first-come-first-served (FIFO).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A max-priority queue is implemented with an UNSORTED array. The worst-case time complexities of insert and delete-max are:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Unsorted array: insert O(1), delete-max O(n).
concept: Big-O notation describes how the running time grows with n, the number of elements. O(1) means constant time (the same small amount of work for any n); O(n) means the work grows in proportion to n. With an UNSORTED array a new element can simply be written into the next free cell, but finding the maximum means looking at every element.
why: A — Wrong. These are the costs for an array kept SORTED in ascending order: insertion must shift elements to keep the order, O(n), and the maximum is the last element, so delete-max is O(1). For an unsorted array the two costs are the other way round.

B — Correct. Insert: write the element into the next free cell, O(1). Delete-max: scan all n elements to find the largest, O(n) (the hole it leaves can be filled by moving the last element into it, O(1)).
C — Wrong. O(log n) for both is what a binary heap gives, not an unsorted array.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Unsorted: fast in, slow out. Sorted: slow in, fast out. Heap: log n both ways.

q: A max-priority queue of n elements is implemented as a binary max-heap. The worst-case complexities of insert, delete-max and find-max (without deleting) are respectively:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Binary max-heap: insert O(log n), delete-max O(log n), find-max O(1).
concept: A binary max-heap is a complete binary tree (every level is full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left) in which every parent is at least as large as its children. So the maximum is always at the root. Because the tree is complete, its height is about log2 n. Insert puts the new key at the end and 'sifts it up' (swaps it with its parent while it is larger); delete-max moves the last element to the root and 'sifts it down'. Each walks along one path of at most about log n levels.
why: A — Correct. Insert O(log n) (sift-up), delete-max O(log n) (sift-down), find-max O(1) (just read the root).

B — Wrong. Insert is not O(1) in the worst case: a new key larger than everything climbs all the way to the root, about log n swaps. And find-max is O(1), not O(log n), because the root is always the maximum.
C — Wrong. Delete-max is not O(1): after the root is removed, the last element is moved to the root and must be sifted down, which takes O(log n).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following algorithms use a priority queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Dijkstra, Huffman and Prim all use a (min) priority queue.
concept: Many greedy algorithms (algorithms that repeatedly make the choice that looks best right now) must pick the 'smallest' item again and again from a changing set. A min-priority queue does exactly that efficiently. Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm, Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm and Huffman coding are the classic examples.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly extracts the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, which is an extract-min on a min-priority queue (with a binary heap the total time is O((V + E) log V)).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Huffman coding repeatedly extracts the two nodes with the lowest frequencies, merges them and inserts the merged node back, all using a min-priority queue keyed on frequency.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Prim's algorithm repeatedly extracts the vertex joined to the growing tree by the cheapest edge, again an extract-min on a priority queue.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Dijkstra, Prim, Huffman: the 'greedy trio' that runs on a priority queue.

q: Which CPU scheduling algorithm directly uses a priority queue to choose the next process?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Priority scheduling uses a priority queue; FCFS and round robin use FIFO queues.
concept: In CPU scheduling, the ready queue holds the processes waiting for the CPU. Different algorithms organise it differently: FCFS (First-Come-First-Served) uses a plain FIFO queue; Round Robin uses a circular FIFO queue with a fixed time slice (time quantum); Priority scheduling always picks the ready process with the highest priority, which is exactly a priority-queue delete.
why: A — Wrong. FCFS runs processes strictly in arrival order, which needs only an ordinary FIFO queue.
B — Correct. Priority scheduling always chooses the process with the highest priority next, which is what a priority queue provides.
C — Wrong. Round robin gives each process a fixed time slice in turn and sends an unfinished process to the rear; it uses a circular FIFO queue, not a priority queue.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In Huffman coding, the min-priority queue (keyed on frequency) is used to repeatedly:
opts: extract the two nodes with the highest frequencies
extract one lowest-frequency and one highest-frequency node
extract the two nodes with the lowest frequencies
More than one of the above
exp: Huffman's algorithm repeatedly extracts the two lowest-frequency nodes from the min-priority queue and merges them.
concept: Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix code (no code word is the beginning of another) for compressing data. It starts with one node per character, keyed on its frequency, in a min-priority queue. At each step it removes the two LOWEST-frequency nodes, makes them the children of a new node whose frequency is their sum, and inserts the new node back. This repeats until one node, the root of the Huffman tree, remains. Rare characters end up deep in the tree (long codes) and frequent characters near the root (short codes).
why: A — Wrong. Merging the highest-frequency nodes first would push the most frequent characters deep into the tree, giving them long codes and poor compression. Also, a min-priority queue gives out the smallest keys, not the largest.
B — Wrong. Huffman's rule never pairs a low-frequency node with a high-frequency node on purpose; it always takes the two smallest.
C — Correct. The greedy step is: extract-min twice, merge the two nodes, and insert their sum back.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which statement about priority queues is TRUE?
opts: A priority queue must always be implemented using a binary heap
Elements are always processed strictly in the order of their arrival
An element of higher priority is processed before an element of lower priority
More than one of the above
exp: In a priority queue a higher-priority element is always processed before a lower-priority one.
concept: A priority queue is an abstract data type (ADT): it is defined by WHAT it does, not by how it is built. Its rule is that a higher-priority element is served before a lower-priority one, and equal priorities are served in arrival order. It can be implemented with an unsorted array, a sorted array, a linked list, a binary heap or other heaps (binomial, Fibonacci); the binary heap is just the most common choice.
why: A — Wrong. A binary heap is the usual implementation because it gives O(log n) insert and delete, but arrays, sorted linked lists and other heaps also work. 'Must always' is false.
B — Wrong. Strict arrival order is the rule of an ordinary queue. In a priority queue, arrival order only breaks ties between equal priorities.
C — Correct. This is the defining property of a priority queue.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A max-priority queue is stored as a binary max-heap in an array (level order): 40 30 15 10 20. The key 35 is inserted (added at the end and sifted up). How many swaps are performed, and what is the resulting array?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 35 swaps once with its parent 15 and stops below 40: 1 swap, array 40 30 35 10 20 15.
concept: A binary heap is stored in an array in level order. With 0-based indexing, the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent of index i is at (i - 1) / 2 (integer division). To insert into a max-heap, put the new key in the first free cell (the end of the array) and then 'sift it up': while the key is larger than its parent, swap the two.
work:
Start (0-based indices): [40, 30, 15, 10, 20]
insert 35: place at index 5 -> [40, 30, 15, 10, 20, 35]
  35 > parent 15 (index 2) -> swap -> [40, 30, 35, 10, 20, 15]
  35 < parent 40 (index 0) -> stop
Total swaps = 1; final array 40 30 35 10 20 15.
why: A — Correct. One swap (35 with its parent 15); then 35 is smaller than its new parent 40, so it stops. Array: 40 30 35 10 20 15.

B — Wrong. This moves 35 up to index 1 and 30 down to index 2, as if 30 were on 35's path to the root. It is not: the path from index 5 goes 5 -> 2 -> 0, and index 1 (30) is in the other subtree. After one swap 35 meets 40 and stops.
C — Wrong. This swaps 35 with 30, but 30 (index 1) is not the parent of index 5; the parent of index 5 is (5 - 1) / 2 = 2, which holds 15.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 0-based heap: parent(i) = (i - 1) / 2, children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

q: Which of the following (insert, delete-max) worst-case complexity pairs for a max-priority queue of n elements is correct?
opts: Array sorted in ascending order: O(1), O(n)
More than one of the above
exp: The correct pairs are: unsorted O(1)/O(n), ascending sorted O(n)/O(1), heap O(log n)/O(log n); every listed pair is wrong.
concept: Costs for a max-priority queue of n elements (insert, delete-max): unsorted array O(1), O(n); array sorted in ascending order O(n), O(1); binary max-heap O(log n), O(log n). A sorted structure pays at insertion time to keep the order, an unsorted one pays at deletion time to search, and a heap balances the two.
why: A — Wrong. The real unsorted-array costs are the other way round: insert O(1) (write into the next free cell) and delete-max O(n) (scan for the largest).

B — Wrong. For an array sorted in ascending order it is again the other way round: insert O(n), because elements must be shifted to make room in the right place, and delete-max O(1), because the largest element is the last one.
C — Wrong. A binary heap needs O(log n) for both: a new key may climb up to log n levels, and after removing the root the replacement may sink log n levels. Only find-max is O(1).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three pairs are wrong (A and B are reversed, and C is too optimistic), so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Which of the following does NOT need a priority queue (a simple FIFO queue is enough)?
opts: Dijkstra's algorithm on a weighted graph
Breadth-first search on an unweighted graph
More than one of the above
exp: BFS needs only a FIFO queue; Dijkstra and Huffman need a priority queue.
concept: Use an ordinary FIFO queue when items must be handled in the order they were found; use a priority queue when you must always pick the item with the best (for example, smallest) key. BFS on an unweighted graph processes vertices in the order they are discovered, which is FIFO. Dijkstra (on a weighted graph) must always pick the closest unvisited vertex, and Huffman must always pick the two smallest frequencies, so both need a min-priority queue.
why: A — Wrong. (It does need a priority queue.) With weighted edges, the vertex discovered first is not necessarily the closest, so Dijkstra must repeatedly extract the vertex with the minimum distance, a priority-queue operation.
B — Wrong. (It does need a priority queue.) Huffman repeatedly takes the two lowest-frequency nodes from a min-priority queue.
C — Correct. BFS visits vertices level by level in discovery order; a plain FIFO queue is enough, and BFS runs in O(V + E).
D — Wrong. Only C works with a simple FIFO queue; A and B need a priority queue.
E — Wrong. C (BFS) does not need a priority queue, so an option fitting the stem exists.
tip: If all edges have the same weight, the vertices come out in the same order whether you use a FIFO queue or a priority queue; that is why BFS needs only a plain queue.

q: A max-priority queue (larger value = higher priority) is initially empty. Operations: insert 15, insert 3, insert 22, insert 8, deleteMax, insert 30, insert 1, deleteMax, deleteMax. Which values are deleted, in order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The three deleteMax operations return 22, 30 and 15.
concept: In a max-priority queue, deleteMax removes the largest value present AT THAT MOMENT - not the largest value ever inserted, and not the oldest one. So when tracing, keep a list of the current contents and, at each delete, pick the largest of them.
work:
(Contents listed in insertion order; each delete picks the LARGEST value present.)
insert 15   contents [15]
insert 3   contents [15, 3]
insert 22   contents [15, 3, 22]
insert 8   contents [15, 3, 22, 8]
deleteMax -> 22   contents [15, 3, 8]
insert 30   contents [15, 3, 8, 30]
insert 1   contents [15, 3, 8, 30, 1]
deleteMax -> 30   contents [15, 3, 8, 1]
deleteMax -> 15   contents [3, 8, 1]
Deleted in order: 22, 30, 15.
why: A — Correct. The deletes return 22 (from 15, 3, 22, 8), then 30 (from 15, 3, 8, 30, 1), then 15 (from 15, 3, 8, 1).
B — Wrong. After 22 and 30 are gone the queue holds 15, 3, 8, 1; the largest is 15, not 8. 8 would come out only after 15.

C — Wrong. A max-priority queue never removes 15 while 22 is present; the first deleteMax returns 22. This option lists the values in increasing order, which is how a min-priority queue would give them out.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An ascending (min) priority queue is initially empty. Operations: insert 7, insert 2, insert 9, deleteMin, insert 1, insert 5, deleteMin, deleteMin. Which values are deleted, in order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: deleteMin returns 2, then 1, then 5 - not listed.
concept: An ascending (min) priority queue removes the smallest element present at the moment of each delete. An element inserted later can be removed earlier if it is smaller - here 1 is inserted after 7 and 9 but leaves before them.
work:
(Contents listed in insertion order; each delete picks the SMALLEST value present.)
insert 7   contents [7]
insert 2   contents [7, 2]
insert 9   contents [7, 2, 9]
deleteMin -> 2   contents [7, 9]
insert 1   contents [7, 9, 1]
insert 5   contents [7, 9, 1, 5]
deleteMin -> 1   contents [7, 9, 5]
deleteMin -> 5   contents [7, 9]
Deleted in order: 2, 1, 5.
why: A — Wrong. The third delete happens when the queue holds 7, 9, 5; the smallest is 5, not 7. 7 is what you get if you forget that 5 was inserted.
B — Wrong. After 2 is removed and 1 and 5 are inserted, the queue holds 7, 9, 1, 5; deleteMin removes 1 before 5.
C — Wrong. 1 is not yet in the queue at the first deleteMin (it is inserted later), so the first deleted value is 2, not 1.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The deleted values are 2, 1, 5, which is not among A–C.

q: Processes arrive in the order P1 (priority 2), P2 (1), P3 (3), P4 (1), P5 (2) and are placed in a priority queue in which a SMALLER number means HIGHER priority and equal priorities are served in order of arrival. All five are in the queue before any of them is served. Which process is served third?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Order of service: P2, P4, P1, P5, P3; the third is P1, which is not listed.
concept: In this priority queue a SMALLER number means a HIGHER priority, so the process with the smallest number is served first. Ties (equal numbers) are broken by arrival order (FIFO). With all processes already in the queue, sort them by priority number and, within the same number, keep the order of arrival.
work:
Priority 1: P2, P4 (P2 arrived before P4)
Priority 2: P1, P5 (P1 arrived before P5)
Priority 3: P3
Service order: 1st P2, 2nd P4, 3rd P1, 4th P5, 5th P3.
Third process served = P1.
why: A — Wrong. P5 has priority 2, the same as P1, but it arrived after P1, so it is served fourth.
B — Wrong. P4 (priority 1) is served second, after P2, which has the same priority but arrived earlier.
C — Wrong. P3 has the lowest priority (the largest number, 3), so it is served last (fifth).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The third process served is P1, which is not among A–C.
tip: Read which way the numbers go: here a smaller number means a higher priority. Some questions use the opposite rule.

q: A max-priority queue is implemented as a binary max-heap stored in an array (level order). Starting from empty, insert 10, 20, 15, 30, 40 (each insert adds the key at the end and sifts it up), then perform one delete-max (move the last element to the root and sift it down). What is the array now?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The inserts give 40 30 15 10 20; delete-max then leaves 30 20 15 10.
concept: To build a max-heap by repeated insertion, put each new key at the end of the array and sift it up while it is larger than its parent. Delete-max removes the root, moves the LAST element to the root, and sifts it down: swap it with its LARGER child while it is smaller than that child. Choosing the larger child keeps every parent at least as large as its children.
work:
insert 10: place at index 0 -> [10]
insert 20: place at index 1 -> [10, 20]
  20 > parent 10 (index 0) -> swap -> [20, 10]
  20 is now the root -> stop
insert 15: place at index 2 -> [20, 10, 15]
  15 < parent 20 (index 0) -> stop
insert 30: place at index 3 -> [20, 10, 15, 30]
  30 > parent 10 (index 1) -> swap -> [20, 30, 15, 10]
  30 > parent 20 (index 0) -> swap -> [30, 20, 15, 10]
  30 is now the root -> stop
insert 40: place at index 4 -> [30, 20, 15, 10, 40]
  40 > parent 20 (index 1) -> swap -> [30, 40, 15, 10, 20]
  40 > parent 30 (index 0) -> swap -> [40, 30, 15, 10, 20]
  40 is now the root -> stop
Heap after all inserts: [40, 30, 15, 10, 20]
delete-max removes 40; move last element 20 to the root -> [20, 30, 15, 10]
  20 at index 0: larger child is 30 (index 1) -> swap -> [30, 20, 15, 10]
  20 at index 1: children [10] are not larger -> stop
Final array: 30 20 15 10.
why: A — Correct. After the inserts the heap is 40 30 15 10 20. Delete-max puts 20 at the root, swaps it with the larger child 30, and stops (its only child, 10, is smaller): 30 20 15 10.

B — Wrong. 30 15 20 10 is also a valid max-heap, but it is not what the algorithm produces. Sift-down never moves 15: 20 swaps only with its larger child 30 and lands at index 1, so index 1 holds 20 and index 2 still holds 15.
C — Wrong. 20 30 15 10 is the array right after 20 is moved to the root, BEFORE sift-down. It breaks the heap property (20 is smaller than its child 30).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a priority queue, each element's priority is set to an insertion counter (1 for the first insertion, 2 for the second, and so on). Such a priority queue can be used to implement:
opts: A stack, if the element with the largest counter is removed first
A queue, if the element with the smallest counter is removed first
A binary search tree, if elements are removed in counter order
More than one of the above
exp: With insertion counters as priorities, largest-first gives a stack and smallest-first gives a queue.
concept: A priority queue can imitate both a stack and a queue if the time of insertion is used as the priority. Give each element a counter 1, 2, 3, ... as it is inserted. Removing the largest counter first means the newest element leaves first (LIFO, a stack). Removing the smallest counter first means the oldest element leaves first (FIFO, a queue).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The largest counter belongs to the most recently inserted element, so removing it first is LIFO - exactly a stack.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The smallest counter belongs to the oldest element, so removing it first is FIFO - exactly a queue.

C — Wrong. A binary search tree (BST) is a tree in which, for every node, smaller keys are in its left subtree and larger keys in its right subtree; it supports searching by value. Removing elements in counter order only controls the order of removal; it builds no tree and gives no search by key, so it does not implement a BST.
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Stack and queue are both special cases of a priority queue.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: What is the minimum number of stacks needed to implement a queue, if only push, pop and isEmpty may be used and recursion is not allowed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Two stacks are the minimum needed to implement a queue without recursion.
concept: A stack lets you reach only its top, which is the newest element, while a queue must remove the oldest element. With one stack and no recursion, the oldest element is at the bottom and cannot be reached without losing the elements above it. With two stacks it works: pouring the elements from one stack into the other reverses their order and brings the oldest element to the top. (If recursion is allowed, one explicit stack is enough, because the function-call stack acts as a hidden second stack.)
why: A — Correct. Two stacks are the minimum: one receives new elements, and the other, filled by reversing the first, gives them out in FIFO order.

B — Wrong. One stack is not enough without recursion: to dequeue you must reach the bottom element, and there is nowhere to keep the elements popped above it. One stack works only with recursion, which secretly uses the call stack as a second stack.
C — Wrong. Three stacks would work, but they are not needed; the question asks for the minimum, which is 2.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: A queue is implemented using two stacks S1 and S2. enqueue(x): move all elements from S1 to S2, push x onto S1, then move all elements back from S2 to S1. dequeue(): pop from S1. For a queue of n elements, the time complexities of enqueue and dequeue are:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Costly-enqueue method: enqueue O(n), dequeue O(1).
concept: This is the 'costly enqueue' way of building a queue from two stacks. Before adding x, all old elements are moved out of S1 into S2 (which reverses them), x is pushed onto the empty S1 so it sits at the bottom, and then the old elements are moved back on top of it. As a result the oldest element is always on top of S1. Enqueue costs about 4n stack operations, O(n), but dequeue is a single pop, O(1).
why: A — Wrong. Cheap enqueue with an O(n) dequeue describes the other method ('costly dequeue', where enqueue is one push and dequeue may have to move elements). In this method it is enqueue that moves all the elements.
B — Correct. Enqueue moves all n elements twice (S1 to S2 and back), O(n); dequeue is one pop from S1, O(1).
C — Wrong. Enqueue cannot be O(1), because it moves every element already in the queue.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: A queue is implemented with two stacks S1 and S2: enqueue(x) pushes x onto S1; dequeue() pops from S2, but if S2 is empty it first moves every element of S1 to S2 (pop from S1, push onto S2). Which of the following statements is/are true?
opts: A single dequeue can take O(n) time in the worst case
Each element is pushed and popped at most twice in total, so the amortised cost per operation is O(1)
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true: one dequeue can be O(n), but the amortised cost is O(1), and enqueue is O(1).
concept: This is the 'lazy transfer' two-stack queue. New elements go onto S1 (the 'in' stack) and elements are taken from S2 (the 'out' stack). Only when S2 is empty is S1 poured into S2, which reverses the order so the oldest element comes to the top. Amortised analysis means averaging the total cost over a whole sequence of operations: one dequeue may be expensive, but expensive ones are rare, so the average per operation is small.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. If S2 is empty and S1 holds n elements, this dequeue pops and pushes all n of them before its own pop: O(n) for that one operation.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each element is pushed onto S1 once, popped from S1 once, pushed onto S2 once and popped from S2 once: at most 2 pushes and 2 pops in its lifetime. So m operations cost at most about 4m stack operations in total, which is O(1) amortised per operation.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Enqueue is just one push onto S1, O(1).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Lazy two-stack queue: worst case O(n) for one dequeue, amortised O(1) per operation.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: A queue is implemented with two stacks S1 and S2: enqueue(x) pushes x onto S1; dequeue() pops from S2, but if S2 is empty it first moves every element of S1 to S2 (pop from S1, push onto S2). Starting empty: enqueue(a), enqueue(b), enqueue(c), dequeue(), enqueue(d). What do the stacks contain now?
opts: S1: d;  S2: c, b (b on top)
S1: d;  S2: b, c (c on top)
S1: b, c, d (d on top);  S2: empty
More than one of the above
exp: S1 = d, and S2 = c, b with b on top.
concept: In the lazy two-stack queue, enqueue pushes onto S1 and dequeue pops from S2. The transfer from S1 to S2 happens only when S2 is empty, and it reverses the order, so the oldest element ends up on top of S2. Elements enqueued after a transfer stay in S1 until S2 becomes empty again.
work:
(Stacks listed bottom to top.)
enqueue(a): push onto S1 (1). Running total 1.   S1: a (top: a) | S2: empty
enqueue(b): push onto S1 (1). Running total 2.   S1: a, b (top: b) | S2: empty
enqueue(c): push onto S1 (1). Running total 3.   S1: a, b, c (top: c) | S2: empty
dequeue() -> a: S2 empty -> move 3 element(s) S1->S2 (3 pops + 3 pushes = 6); pop S2 (1). Cost 7, running total 10.   S1: empty | S2: c, b (top: b)
enqueue(d): push onto S1 (1). Running total 11.   S1: d (top: d) | S2: c, b (top: b)
Final: S1 = d (top: d); S2 = c, b (top: b).
why: A — Correct. After the dequeue removes a, S2 holds c, b with b on top (b is the next to leave), and the new element d waits in S1.

B — Wrong. This has S2 in the wrong order. The transfer pops c first, so c goes to the bottom of S2 and the oldest remaining element, b, is on top. If c were on top, the next dequeue would return c instead of b, breaking FIFO.
C — Wrong. This assumes the remaining elements are put back into S1 after the dequeue. In this method they stay in S2; only new elements go into S1.
