D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: A queue is implemented with two stacks S1 and S2: enqueue(x) pushes x onto S1; dequeue() pops from S2, but if S2 is empty it first moves every element of S1 to S2 (pop from S1, push onto S2). Whenever S2 is not empty, its top element is:
opts: the front (oldest) element of the queue
the largest element of the queue
More than one of the above
exp: The top of S2 is always the front (oldest) element of the queue.
concept: In the lazy two-stack queue, the queue from front to rear is: S2 read from top to bottom, followed by S1 read from bottom to top. Every element in S2 arrived before every element in S1. So the top of S2 is always the oldest element of the whole queue - the front.
why: A — Wrong. The most recently enqueued element is on top of S1 (whenever S1 is non-empty), not on top of S2.
B — Correct. Pouring S1 into S2 reverses it, so the oldest element ends on top; and anything still in S1 is newer than everything in S2. Hence the top of S2 is the front of the queue.
C — Wrong. The stacks keep arrival order, not value order; the top of S2 is the largest only by coincidence. Ordering by value is what a priority queue does.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: The following C++ functions implement a stack using two queues (std::queue). For a stack of n elements, which statement is correct?
opts: push is O(n) and pop is O(1)
push is O(1) and pop is O(n)
both push and pop are O(n)
More than one of the above
exp: This costly-push version has push O(n) and pop O(1).
concept: A stack can be built from two queues in two ways. 'Costly push': on push, put x into the empty q2, move all of q1 behind it, and swap the two queues, so the newest element is always at the front of q1; pop is then a single dequeue. 'Costly pop': push is a single enqueue, and pop moves n - 1 elements to the other queue to reach the newest one. The code here is the costly-push version.
work:
Before push(x): q1 holds the n stack elements (newest at the front), q2 is empty.
q2.push(x): 1 operation.
while loop: moves every element of q1 to q2 -> n iterations.
swap(q1, q2): O(1) for std::queue (it swaps the internal containers, not the elements).
So push = O(n).
pop(): one front() and one pop() on q1 -> O(1).
why: A — Correct. push moves all n elements of q1 into q2 (O(n)); pop just removes the front of q1 (O(1)).
B — Wrong. That is the costly-pop version (push only enqueues; pop moves n - 1 elements). In this code the loop is inside push, not pop.
C — Wrong. pop has no loop: it reads and removes one element, which is O(1).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: These C++ functions implement a stack using two queues. For a stack holding n elements, the time complexities of push and pop are:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Costly-pop version: push O(1), pop O(n).
concept: This is the 'costly pop' way of building a stack from two queues. push simply enqueues into q1, so q1 holds the elements in push order with the newest at the rear. A queue can remove only from its front, so pop must first move the n - 1 older elements to q2, then remove the last one (the newest, which is the stack top), and finally swap the queues.
work:
push(x): one q1.push(x) -> O(1).
pop(): the while loop moves n - 1 elements from q1 to q2 -> O(n);
then one front() + one pop() and an O(1) swap.
So pop = O(n).
why: A — Wrong. pop cannot be O(1): the newest element is at the rear of q1 and a queue removes only from the front, so n - 1 elements must be moved out of the way first.
B — Wrong. That is the cost of the costly-push version. Here push is a single enqueue, O(1).
C — Correct. push is one enqueue, O(1); pop moves n - 1 elements, O(n).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: For the stack-using-two-queues code shown, push(1), push(2), push(3), push(4) are executed on an empty stack, followed by pop(). What value does pop() return, and how many elements are moved from q1 to q2 during this pop?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: pop returns 4 after moving 3 elements (1, 2, 3) to q2.
concept: In the costly-pop stack, q1 holds the elements in push order (oldest at the front, newest at the rear). pop moves all but the last element to q2, removes the last one (the newest, i.e. the stack top), and swaps q1 and q2 so the remaining elements are back in q1.
work:
After push(1..4): q1 = 1 2 3 4 (front at left), q2 = empty
move 1: q1 = 2 3 4 | q2 = 1
move 2: q1 = 3 4 | q2 = 1 2
move 3: q1 = 4 | q2 = 1 2 3
q1.size() == 1 -> loop ends. Remove and return 4. swap -> q1 = 1 2 3, q2 = empty
pop() returns 4; 3 elements were moved.
why: A — Wrong. 1 is the oldest element (front of q1). A stack must return the newest element, 4. Returning 1 would be queue (FIFO) behaviour.
B — Correct. Elements 1, 2, 3 are moved to q2 (3 moves), and 4, the only element left in q1, is returned.
C — Wrong. The loop stops when q1.size() becomes 1, so only n - 1 = 3 elements are moved; 4 is removed directly from q1, not moved.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: A queue is implemented with two stacks S1 and S2. enqueue(x): move every element of S1 to S2 (pop from S1, push onto S2), push x onto S1, then move every element of S2 back to S1. dequeue(): pop from S1. Counting each push and each pop as one operation, how many operations are performed in total by enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), enqueue(4) on an initially empty queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The four enqueues cost 1, 5, 9 and 13 stack operations: 28 in total.
concept: In the costly-enqueue two-stack queue, if the queue already holds k elements, one enqueue does: k pops from S1 and k pushes onto S2 (2k operations), 1 push of x onto S1, then k pops from S2 and k pushes onto S1 (2k operations). Total 4k + 1 stack operations. For several enqueues, add 4k + 1 for k = 0, 1, 2, ...
work:
(Stacks listed bottom to top.)
enqueue(1): k = 0 already present -> 0 pops + 0 pushes (S1->S2), 1 push of 1, 0 pops + 0 pushes (S2->S1) = 4*0 + 1 = 1. Running total 1.   S1: 1 (top: 1)
enqueue(2): k = 1 already present -> 1 pops + 1 pushes (S1->S2), 1 push of 2, 1 pops + 1 pushes (S2->S1) = 4*1 + 1 = 5. Running total 6.   S1: 2, 1 (top: 1)
enqueue(3): k = 2 already present -> 2 pops + 2 pushes (S1->S2), 1 push of 3, 2 pops + 2 pushes (S2->S1) = 4*2 + 1 = 9. Running total 15.   S1: 3, 2, 1 (top: 1)
enqueue(4): k = 3 already present -> 3 pops + 3 pushes (S1->S2), 1 push of 4, 3 pops + 3 pushes (S2->S1) = 4*3 + 1 = 13. Running total 28.   S1: 4, 3, 2, 1 (top: 1)
Total = 1 + 5 + 9 + 13 = 28. (The oldest element, 1, is always on top of S1.)
why: A — Wrong. 16 = 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 is what you get if each element transfer (a pop plus a push) is counted as ONE operation, giving 2k + 1 per enqueue. The question counts every push and every pop separately.
B — Wrong. 10 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 is only the number of pushes onto S1 (the k elements moved back plus x). It leaves out the pops from S1, the pushes onto S2 and the pops from S2.
C — Correct. The four enqueues cost 1, 5, 9 and 13 operations: 1 + 5 + 9 + 13 = 28.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Costly-enqueue method: an enqueue with k elements already present costs 4k + 1 pushes and pops.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: A queue is implemented with two stacks S1 and S2: enqueue(x) pushes x onto S1; dequeue() pops from S2, but if S2 is empty it first moves every element of S1 to S2 (pop from S1, push onto S2). Count each push and each pop as one operation. Starting empty: enqueue 1, 2, 3; dequeue; enqueue 4, 5; dequeue; dequeue; dequeue. What is the total number of push and pop operations performed on the two stacks?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The total is 19 push and pop operations.
concept: In the lazy two-stack queue: enqueue = 1 push. Dequeue = 1 pop if S2 is non-empty; if S2 is empty, first move all m elements of S1 to S2 (m pops + m pushes = 2m operations) and then do 1 pop. Count the operations step by step, checking each time whether S2 is empty.
work:
(Stacks listed bottom to top.)
enqueue(1): push onto S1 (1). Running total 1.   S1: 1 (top: 1) | S2: empty
enqueue(2): push onto S1 (1). Running total 2.   S1: 1, 2 (top: 2) | S2: empty
enqueue(3): push onto S1 (1). Running total 3.   S1: 1, 2, 3 (top: 3) | S2: empty
dequeue() -> 1: S2 empty -> move 3 element(s) S1->S2 (3 pops + 3 pushes = 6); pop S2 (1). Cost 7, running total 10.   S1: empty | S2: 3, 2 (top: 2)
enqueue(4): push onto S1 (1). Running total 11.   S1: 4 (top: 4) | S2: 3, 2 (top: 2)
enqueue(5): push onto S1 (1). Running total 12.   S1: 4, 5 (top: 5) | S2: 3, 2 (top: 2)
dequeue() -> 2: pop S2 (1). Cost 1, running total 13.   S1: 4, 5 (top: 5) | S2: 3 (top: 3)
dequeue() -> 3: pop S2 (1). Cost 1, running total 14.   S1: 4, 5 (top: 5) | S2: empty
dequeue() -> 4: S2 empty -> move 2 element(s) S1->S2 (2 pops + 2 pushes = 4); pop S2 (1). Cost 5, running total 19.   S1: empty | S2: 5 (top: 5)
Total = 3 + 7 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 5 = 19 operations.
why: A — Wrong. 17 is 2 too few. A common slip that gives it is counting the second transfer (moving 4 and 5) as 2 operations instead of 4; each element moved needs a pop from S1 AND a push onto S2.
B — Wrong. 21 is 2 too many. Only a dequeue that finds S2 EMPTY pays for a transfer; here that happens only at the first and the fourth dequeue. The second and third dequeues are single pops.
C — Correct. 3 (enqueues) + 7 (first dequeue) + 2 (enqueues) + 1 + 1 (second and third dequeues) + 5 (fourth dequeue) = 19.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: For the stack-using-two-queues code shown, push(1), push(2), push(3), push(4), push(5) are executed starting with both queues empty. In total, how many elements are moved from q1 to q2 inside the while loop?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Moves = 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 = 5 x 4 / 2, which is not listed.
concept: In the costly-push stack, before the k-th push q1 already holds k - 1 elements, and the while loop moves every one of them to q2. So for n pushes the total number of moves is 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) = n(n - 1)/2.
work:
push(1): q1 had 0 element(s), all moved -> 0 move(s). q1 now 1 (newest at front). Running total 0
push(2): q1 had 1 element(s), all moved -> 1 move(s). q1 now 2 1 (newest at front). Running total 1
push(3): q1 had 2 element(s), all moved -> 2 move(s). q1 now 3 2 1 (newest at front). Running total 3
push(4): q1 had 3 element(s), all moved -> 3 move(s). q1 now 4 3 2 1 (newest at front). Running total 6
push(5): q1 had 4 element(s), all moved -> 4 move(s). q1 now 5 4 3 2 1 (newest at front). Running total 10
Total moves = 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 = 5 x 4 / 2.
why: A — Wrong. 5 is the number of push() calls. The while loop moves the OLD elements of q1, and their number grows with every push.

B — Wrong. 15 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 also counts the new element x each time. But x is put into q2 directly by q2.push(x), before the loop; the loop moves only the elements already in q1: 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.
C — Wrong. 4 counts one move per push after the first, but the k-th push moves k - 1 elements, not just one.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The loop moves 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 elements in total, and 10 is not among A–C.
tip: n pushes in the costly-push stack move n(n - 1)/2 elements in total.

subtopic: Queue using stacks / stack using queues
q: The following C program tries to implement a queue with two stacks, but its dequeue moves S1 into S2 on EVERY call. What does it print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Because the transfer happens on every dequeue, 30 and 40 bury 20, and the output is 10 30 40.
concept: The correct lazy two-stack queue moves S1 into S2 ONLY when S2 is empty. If the transfer is done on every dequeue, newer elements from S1 are piled on top of older elements still waiting in S2, so an old element gets buried and the structure no longer gives FIFO order. In this C code, s1[++top1] = x is a push and s1[top1--] is a pop on an array stack.
work:
(Stacks listed bottom to top.)
enqueue(10): s1: 10 (top: 10) | s2: empty
enqueue(20): s1: 10, 20 (top: 20) | s2: empty
dequeue(): move S1 -> S2: 20, 10; pop s2 -> prints 10.   s1: empty | s2: 20 (top: 20)
enqueue(30): s1: 30 (top: 30) | s2: 20 (top: 20)
enqueue(40): s1: 30, 40 (top: 40) | s2: 20 (top: 20)
dequeue(): move S1 -> S2: 40, 30; pop s2 -> prints 30.   s1: empty | s2: 20, 40 (top: 40)
dequeue(): move nothing (s1 empty); pop s2 -> prints 40.   s1: empty | s2: 20 (top: 20)
Output: 10 30 40 (a correct queue would print 10 20 30).
why: A — Wrong. 10 20 30 is the correct FIFO output that a correct implementation would print. In this buggy code the second dequeue piles 30 and 40 on top of 20, so 20 is not returned second.
B — Wrong. When 30 and 40 are moved, 40 is popped from s1 first and pushed first, so 30 ends up on top of s2 and comes out before 40.
C — Correct. The program prints 10 30 40: 10 is right, but then 40 and 30 are piled above 20, so 30 and 40 come out before 20.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: In the two-stack queue, transfer only when the out-stack is empty.

q: Breadth-first search (BFS) of a graph uses which data structure to hold the vertices waiting to be visited?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: BFS uses a queue.
concept: Breadth-first search (BFS) explores a graph level by level: first the start vertex, then all its neighbours, then their neighbours, and so on. Vertices must be processed in the order in which they were discovered, which is FIFO order, so BFS keeps the waiting vertices in a queue.
why: A — Wrong. A stack makes the search go deep along one path first; that is depth-first search (DFS), not BFS.
B — Correct. BFS enqueues each newly discovered vertex and dequeues vertices in the same order, which gives level-by-level exploration.
C — Wrong. A binary search tree stores keys in sorted order for fast searching. It does not give 'first discovered, first explored' order, so it is not used to drive BFS.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: BFS - Breadth - queue (FIFO). DFS - Depth - stack (LIFO).

q: Level-order traversal of a binary tree is implemented using a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Level-order traversal of a binary tree uses a queue.
concept: Level-order traversal visits a tree level by level, left to right: the root, then its children, then its grandchildren, and so on. It is BFS applied to a tree. Algorithm: enqueue the root; then repeatedly dequeue a node, visit it, and enqueue its left and right children (if any).
why: A — Wrong. A stack is used for depth-first traversals, such as iterative preorder, inorder and postorder.
B — Wrong. A hash table stores key-value pairs for fast lookup; it keeps no visiting order, so it cannot drive a level-by-level traversal.
C — Correct. The queue makes nodes come out in the same order in which they were reached, which is level by level.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is an application of a stack rather than a queue?
opts: Undo operation in a text editor
More than one of the above
exp: Undo is a stack application; printer spooling and BFS use queues.
concept: A stack fits a problem when the most recent item must be handled first (LIFO); a queue fits when the oldest item must be handled first (FIFO). Undo cancels the latest action first, so it uses a stack. Printer jobs and BFS are handled in order of arrival or discovery, so they use queues.
why: A — Correct. Each editing action is pushed onto an undo stack; Undo pops the most recent action and reverses it.
B — Wrong. Printer spooling keeps print jobs in a queue, so documents are printed in the order in which they were sent.
C — Wrong. Breadth-first search uses a queue to visit vertices in the order they were discovered.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are applications of a queue?
opts: Holding processes in the CPU ready queue
Spooling documents sent to a shared printer
Buffering data in asynchronous transfer between processes (e.g. pipes, I/O buffers)
More than one of the above
exp: The CPU ready queue, print spooling and I/O buffers / pipes are all queue applications.
concept: Whenever several requests share one resource and must be served in order of arrival, a queue is used. Common examples are the CPU ready queue, the printer spool, keyboard and I/O buffers, pipes between processes and network packet buffers.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The ready queue holds the processes waiting for the CPU; in FCFS and round robin they are taken in arrival order.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) keeps print jobs in a queue so that the slow printer prints them one by one, in the order they were sent.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. When one process produces data at a different speed or time from the process that consumes it, a FIFO buffer (a queue) holds the data so it is read in the same order it was written. A Unix pipe is exactly such a FIFO.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT an application of a queue?
opts: Checking for balanced parentheses in an expression
Serving requests to a single shared resource in order of arrival
More than one of the above
exp: Checking balanced parentheses uses a stack, not a queue.
concept: Checking balanced parentheses uses a stack: push each opening bracket, and on a closing bracket pop and check that the two match. The most recently opened bracket must be closed first, which is LIFO. Round robin scheduling and serving requests in arrival order are FIFO tasks, so they use queues.
why: A — Wrong. (It IS a queue application.) Round robin keeps the ready processes in a circular queue; a process whose time slice ends goes to the rear.
B — Correct. (It is NOT a queue application.) Bracket matching needs the most recently opened bracket first, so it uses a stack.
C — Wrong. (It IS a queue application.) Serving requests to one shared resource in order of arrival (a printer, a disk, a call centre) is the classic use of a FIFO queue.
D — Wrong. Only B is not a queue application; A and C are queue applications.
E — Wrong. B is not a queue application, so an option that fits the stem exists.

q: Round robin CPU scheduling is usually implemented using a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Round robin CPU scheduling uses a circular queue.
concept: Round robin scheduling gives every ready process a fixed time slice (called a time quantum) in turn. When a process's slice ends and it has not finished, it goes to the rear of the ready queue and the process at the front gets the CPU next. The processes go round and round, so a circular queue is the natural structure.
why: A — Correct. The ready processes are cycled in FIFO order with wrap-around, which is a circular queue.
B — Wrong. A stack would always run the most recently added process, so older processes could wait for ever (starvation). That is not round robin.
C — Wrong. A binary search tree orders items by a key value; round robin does not order processes by value at all, only by turn.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Data produced by a fast device (e.g. the CPU) must be consumed by a slow device (e.g. a printer) in the same order. The buffer between them is best organised as a:
opts: Stack, so that the latest data is used first
Queue, so that data is consumed in the order it was produced
Binary search tree, ordered by data value
More than one of the above
exp: A queue buffer keeps the production order, so it is the right choice.
concept: A buffer is temporary storage between a producer (which makes data) and a consumer (which uses it) that work at different speeds. If the data must be used in the order it was produced, the buffer must be FIFO, i.e. a queue - usually a fixed-size circular queue, also called a ring buffer. Printer buffers, keyboard buffers and network buffers all work this way.
why: A — Wrong. A stack would hand out the latest data first, so, for example, a printer would print the pages in reverse order. The production order would be lost.
B — Correct. A queue gives out data in exactly the order in which it was put in.
C — Wrong. A binary search tree would hand out data in order of value (sorted), not in order of production.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The iterative versions of depth-first search and breadth-first search of a graph use, respectively:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Iterative DFS uses a stack; BFS uses a queue.
concept: Depth-first search (DFS) goes as deep as possible along one path before backtracking, so it always continues from the most recently discovered vertex: LIFO, a stack (the recursive version uses the function-call stack). Breadth-first search (BFS) first explores all vertices one edge away, then two edges away, and so on, so it processes vertices in discovery order: FIFO, a queue.
why: A — Correct. DFS uses a stack and BFS uses a queue.
B — Wrong. This swaps the two. A queue would make 'DFS' behave like BFS, and a stack would make 'BFS' go deep.
C — Wrong. A queue in both would make both searches breadth-first. DFS needs LIFO order.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: DFS - Deep - stack. BFS - Broad - queue.

q: Which problem is most naturally solved using a queue?
opts: Finding the shortest path (fewest edges) between two vertices in an unweighted graph
More than one of the above
exp: The fewest-edge shortest path in an unweighted graph is found by BFS, which uses a queue.
concept: In an unweighted graph, a shortest path is one with the fewest edges. BFS from the source reaches every vertex at distance 1 before any vertex at distance 2, and so on, so the first time BFS reaches a vertex it has found a shortest path to it. BFS uses a queue. Postfix evaluation and string reversal are classic stack problems.
why: A — Wrong. To evaluate a postfix expression such as 2 3 + 4 *, operands are pushed onto a stack, and each operator pops its operands and pushes the result. That is a stack application.
B — Wrong. Pushing all the characters and then popping them gives them in reverse order (LIFO). That is a stack application.
C — Correct. BFS with a queue finds a fewest-edge path in an unweighted graph in O(V + E) time.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT an application of a stack?
opts: Converting an infix expression to postfix
More than one of the above
exp: All three are stack applications, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: A stack is used whenever the most recent pending item must be handled first. Examples: the function-call stack (each call pushes an activation record and each return pops it), backtracking (go back to the most recent choice point) and infix-to-postfix conversion (an operator stack). All three listed items are stack applications.
why: A — Wrong. (It IS a stack application.) Each function call pushes an activation record (return address, parameters, local variables) onto the call stack, and returning pops it. Recursion depends on this.
B — Wrong. (It IS a stack application.) In backtracking, the path taken so far is kept on a stack; at a dead end we pop back to the most recent choice and try another way.
C — Wrong. (It IS a stack application.) The infix-to-postfix algorithm keeps operators and '(' on a stack and pops them according to precedence and brackets.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is a non-stack application, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three are stack applications, so none of A–C fits 'NOT an application of a stack'.
tip: In a 'NOT' question, decide for each option whether it IS the thing; if every option is, the answer is E.

q: Which of the following pairs are correctly matched?
opts: Level-order traversal of a tree - Queue
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are correctly matched; undo/redo uses stacks, not a queue.
concept: Matching applications to structures. Stack (LIFO): function calls and recursion, undo/redo, expression conversion and evaluation, backtracking, DFS. Queue (FIFO): BFS, level-order traversal, CPU and printer scheduling, buffers.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Function calls are managed on the call stack: the most recent call must finish (return) first.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Level-order traversal visits nodes in the order they were discovered, which needs a queue.
C — Wrong. Undo must reverse the MOST RECENT action first, which is LIFO, so editors keep an undo stack (and a separate redo stack). A queue would undo the oldest action first.
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In FIFO page replacement, the pages in memory are kept in a queue. When a page fault occurs and memory is full, which page is replaced?
opts: The page at the rear (most recently loaded)
The page that was used least recently
The page at the front (loaded earliest)
More than one of the above
exp: FIFO page replacement removes the page at the front of the queue (the one loaded earliest).
concept: In FIFO page replacement, the operating system keeps the pages in memory in a queue, in the order in which they were loaded. When memory is full and a page fault occurs (a needed page is not in memory), the page at the front - the one loaded earliest - is removed and the new page joins at the rear. FIFO looks only at loading time, not at how recently or how often a page was used.
why: A — Wrong. The page at the rear was loaded most recently. Removing it would be a LIFO policy, which is not FIFO replacement.
B — Wrong. Replacing the least recently USED page is the LRU (Least Recently Used) policy, a different algorithm. A page loaded long ago may have been used a moment ago; FIFO would still replace it.
C — Correct. FIFO replaces the page that has been in memory the longest, which is the page at the front of the queue.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: FIFO looks at loading time; LRU looks at the time of last use.

q: For a queue of n elements implemented as a circular array (or as a linked list with front and rear pointers), which operation is NOT O(1)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Searching a queue for a value is O(n); enqueue and peek are O(1).
concept: A queue gives O(1) access only at its two ends: enqueue at the rear, and dequeue and peek at the front. It has no quick way to find an arbitrary value; to search, you must look at the elements one by one, which is O(n) in the worst case (the value may be at the rear, or absent).
why: A — Wrong. (It IS O(1).) Enqueue updates rear (rear = (rear + 1) % n, or tail->next = new node) and stores the value: a fixed number of steps.
B — Correct. (It is NOT O(1).) Searching may have to examine all n elements: O(n).
C — Wrong. (It IS O(1).) Peek just reads Q[front] (or front->data).
D — Wrong. Only B is not O(1); A and C are O(1).
E — Wrong. B (searching) is not O(1), so an option that fits the stem exists.

q: Which of the following operations take O(1) time in a circular array queue?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: enqueue, dequeue and isFull are all O(1) in a circular array queue.
concept: In a circular array queue every basic operation touches only a fixed number of variables: enqueue writes one cell and moves rear with %, dequeue reads one cell and moves front with %, and isFull / isEmpty are single comparisons such as (rear + 1) % n == front. No loop over the elements is needed, so all of them are O(1).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. enqueue: rear = (rear + 1) % n and Q[rear] = x - a constant number of steps.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. dequeue: read Q[front] and set front = (front + 1) % n - constant time.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. isFull is one comparison, e.g. (rear + 1) % n == front (or count == n if a counter is kept): O(1).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Elements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are enqueued (in this order) into an empty queue Q. Then all elements are dequeued from Q and pushed onto an empty stack S, after which all elements are popped from S and enqueued back into Q. What does Q contain (front to rear)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Queue -> stack -> queue reverses the queue: 5 4 3 2 1.
concept: A stack reverses order: items pushed as 1, 2, 3 come out as 3, 2, 1. So passing all the elements of a queue through a stack and back into the queue reverses the queue. This is the standard way to reverse a queue.
work:
Q = 1 2 3 4 5 (front at left)
Dequeue all and push: stack (bottom to top) = 1 2 3 4 5, top = 5; Q empty
Pop all and enqueue: pops come out 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 -> Q = 5 4 3 2 1
why: A — Wrong. 1 2 3 4 5 is the original queue. It would come back unchanged only if the middle structure were another queue (FIFO), not a stack.
B — Correct. The stack has 5 on top, so popping gives 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, which are enqueued in that order.
C — Wrong. 1 5 2 4 3 takes elements alternately from the front and the back; one pass through a stack cannot produce such an interleaving.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following can be used to reverse the elements of a queue?
opts: An auxiliary stack: dequeue all elements onto the stack, then pop them back into the queue
Recursion: dequeue an element, reverse the rest recursively, then enqueue the element
An auxiliary min-priority queue keyed on element value
More than one of the above
exp: A stack (A) or recursion (B) reverses a queue; a min-priority queue only sorts it.
concept: Reversing a queue needs a LIFO step. Two standard ways: (1) an explicit stack - dequeue everything onto the stack, then pop everything back into the queue; (2) recursion - remove the front element, reverse the rest recursively, then enqueue the removed element at the rear. The recursive version uses the function-call stack as a hidden stack. Both take O(n) time.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The stack reverses the order: the last element dequeued (the old rear) is popped first and becomes the new front.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each call holds one element while the rest is reversed, and the elements are enqueued while the calls return, in reverse order. The call stack does the job of the explicit stack.

C — Wrong. A min-priority queue gives out elements in increasing order of value, so it SORTS the queue. That equals the reverse only by coincidence (when the queue was in decreasing order). For 3, 1, 2 it gives 1, 2, 3, not the reverse 2, 1, 3.
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), and 'More than one of the above' is right whenever at least two of A–C are true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A queue q contains 10 20 30 40 (front to rear). What does it contain after calling fun(q)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: fun reverses the queue, so it becomes 40 30 20 10.
concept: This recursive function reverses a queue. Each call removes the front element, keeps it in its local variable x, and calls itself on the shorter queue. When the queue becomes empty the calls start returning, and each call puts its x back at the rear. The last element removed is put back first, so the order is reversed. The function-call stack plays the role of an explicit stack.
work:
fun #1: x = 10, queue 20 30 40, call fun
  fun #2: x = 20, queue 30 40, call fun
    fun #3: x = 30, queue 40, call fun
      fun #4: x = 40, queue empty, call fun
        fun #5: queue empty -> return
      fun #4 resumes: push 40 -> 40
    fun #3 resumes: push 30 -> 40 30
  fun #2 resumes: push 20 -> 40 30 20
fun #1 resumes: push 10 -> 40 30 20 10
why: A — Wrong. 10 20 30 40 is the original queue. Because each element is put back only AFTER the recursive call returns, the innermost call (holding 40) puts its element back first, so the order changes.
B — Wrong. 20 10 40 30 swaps neighbouring pairs. This function does not work in pairs; it empties the whole queue first and then refills it in reverse.
C — Correct. The elements are put back in the order 40, 30, 20, 10, so the queue is reversed.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Several queues share one array by dividing it into fixed equal parts, one part per queue. The main drawback of this scheme is:
opts: One queue may overflow even though free cells exist in the other parts
Elements of a queue are no longer removed in FIFO order
More than one of the above
exp: With fixed parts, one queue can overflow while other parts still have free cells.
concept: When several queues share one array, the simplest scheme gives each queue a fixed part (for example, two queues in an array of 100 cells get 50 cells each). It is easy to code, but the space is not shared: if one queue needs more cells than its part, it overflows even though the other parts may be almost empty. Better schemes let the boundaries move (for example, keeping a common pool of free cells as linked nodes).
why: A — Correct. Each queue is limited to its own part, so one queue can overflow while free cells in other parts stay unused; space is wasted.
B — Wrong. Enqueue in each part still just moves that queue's own rear index (circularly within its part): O(1).
C — Wrong. Each part works as an ordinary queue, so FIFO order is kept inside every queue.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An empty queue Q undergoes: enqueue(4), enqueue(7), x = dequeue(), enqueue(x * 2), enqueue(x + 5), y = dequeue(), enqueue(x + y). What does Q contain (front to rear)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: x = 4 and y = 7, so the queue ends as 8 9 11.
concept: When a dequeued value is stored in a variable (x = dequeue()), it can be used later in expressions. In such traces, keep track of both the queue (front to rear) and the variables after every step. New values always join at the rear.
work:
(Q written from front to rear.)
enqueue(4): Q = 4
enqueue(7): Q = 4 7
x = dequeue() = 4: Q = 7
enqueue(x * 2 = 8): Q = 7 8
enqueue(x + 5 = 9): Q = 7 8 9
y = dequeue() = 7: Q = 8 9
enqueue(x + y = 4 + 7 = 11): Q = 8 9 11
Final Q = 8 9 11.
why: A — Correct. x = 4 and y = 7, and the queue ends as 8 9 11.
B — Wrong. This keeps 7 in the queue, but y = dequeue() removed 7 (which was then used in x + y).
C — Wrong. This puts 8 at the rear, but 8 (= x * 2) was enqueued before 9 and 11, so once 7 leaves, 8 is at the front. The order of enqueuing is the order in the queue.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is the output of the following C++ code (std::queue)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Three front-to-rear moves turn 1 2 3 4 5 into 4 5 1 2 3, which is printed.
concept: The statements q.push(q.front()); q.pop(); take the front element and put it at the rear. Doing this k times rotates the queue left by k positions: the first k elements move behind the rest, keeping their original order.
work:
After the first loop: q = 1 2 3 4 5 (front at left)
i = 0: push front (1) to the rear, pop it from the front -> q = 2 3 4 5 1
i = 1: push front (2) to the rear, pop it from the front -> q = 3 4 5 1 2
i = 2: push front (3) to the rear, pop it from the front -> q = 4 5 1 2 3
The while loop prints: 4 5 1 2 3
why: A — Wrong. 3 2 1 5 4 reverses parts of the queue. A rotation never reverses anything; it keeps the cyclic order 1 2 3 4 5.
B — Wrong. 1 2 3 4 5 would be printed only if the loop ran 0 times or 5 times (a full rotation). Three rotations move 1, 2, 3 to the rear.
C — Correct. After three rotations the queue is 4 5 1 2 3, and the last loop prints it from front to rear.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: To reverse the first k elements of a queue: (1) dequeue the first k elements and push them onto a stack; (2) pop all elements from the stack and enqueue them; (3) dequeue the front (n - k) elements and enqueue them again. If the queue is 10 20 30 40 50 60 (front to rear) and k = 4, the final queue is:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The final queue is 40 30 20 10 50 60, which is not listed.
concept: Reversing only the first k elements of a queue uses a stack for those k elements and then a rotation. Step 1 removes the first k elements and pushes them onto a stack. Step 2 pops them back into the queue, so they are now reversed but sitting at the rear. Step 3 moves the n - k untouched elements, one by one, from the front to the rear, so the reversed block comes to the front.
work:
Q = 10 20 30 40 50 60 (front at left), k = 4, n = 6
Step 1: dequeue 4 and push -> stack (bottom to top) 10 20 30 40; Q = 50 60
Step 2: pop all and enqueue (40, 30, 20, 10) -> Q = 50 60 40 30 20 10
Step 3: move 50 from the front to the rear -> Q = 60 40 30 20 10 50
Step 3: move 60 from the front to the rear -> Q = 40 30 20 10 50 60
Final queue: 40 30 20 10 50 60.
why: A — Wrong. 50 60 40 30 20 10 is the queue after step 2. Step 3 then moves 50 and 60 to the rear.
B — Wrong. 60 50 40 30 20 10 reverses the whole queue, as if k = n = 6. Only the first 4 elements are reversed.
C — Wrong. 40 30 20 10 60 50 also reverses 50 and 60, but step 3 moves them one at a time from the front to the rear, which keeps their order 50, 60.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The final queue is 40 30 20 10 50 60, which is not among A–C.

q: People numbered 1 to 6 stand in a queue (1 at the front). Repeatedly: dequeue the front person and enqueue them again at the rear, then dequeue the next person and eliminate them. This continues until one person remains. Who survives?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: People are eliminated in the order 2, 4, 6, 3, 1; person 5 survives, which is not listed.
concept: This is the Josephus problem with every second person eliminated (k = 2), simulated with a queue: move the front person to the rear (they are skipped this time), then remove the next person. For k = 2 there is a formula: write n = 2^m + L with 0 <= L < 2^m; the survivor is 2L + 1. For n = 6: 6 = 4 + 2, so the survivor is 2 x 2 + 1 = 5.
work:
Q = 1 2 3 4 5 6 (front at left)
move 1 to the rear, eliminate 2 -> Q = 3 4 5 6 1
move 3 to the rear, eliminate 4 -> Q = 5 6 1 3
move 5 to the rear, eliminate 6 -> Q = 1 3 5
move 1 to the rear, eliminate 3 -> Q = 5 1
move 5 to the rear, eliminate 1 -> Q = 5
Survivor: 5. Check with the formula: 6 = 4 + 2, survivor = 2 x 2 + 1 = 5.
why: A — Wrong. Person 1 lasts long but is the last one eliminated: when the queue is 5, 1, person 5 is moved to the rear and 1 is removed. (With k = 2, person 1 survives only when n is a power of 2.)
B — Wrong. Person 3 is eliminated in the second round, when the queue is 1, 3, 5 (1 is moved to the rear, then 3 is removed).
C — Wrong. Person 6 is eliminated in the first round, right after 5 is moved to the rear.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The elimination order is 2, 4, 6, 3, 1, so person 5 survives, and 5 is not among A–C.
tip: Josephus with k = 2: if n = 2^m + L (0 <= L < 2^m), the survivor is 2L + 1.

q: In a rooted tree, a node that has no children is called a/an:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A node with no children is a leaf (external node).
concept: A tree in computer science is like a family tree drawn upside down: the root is at the top and each node can have children below it. A node with no children is called a leaf (also called an external or terminal node). A node with at least one child is an internal node. The root is the single node that has no parent.
why: A — Correct. A leaf is exactly a node with no children: it is where a branch ends, like a leaf at the tip of a twig. Leaves are also called external or terminal nodes.
B — Wrong. An internal node is a node that has at least one child, which is the opposite of what the question describes.
C — Wrong. The root is defined by having no PARENT (it is the topmost node), not by having no children. Only in a one-node tree is the root also a leaf.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Root = no parent. Leaf = no children.

q: In a rooted tree, two nodes that have the same parent are called:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Nodes with the same parent are siblings.
concept: Tree relationships use family words. The parent of a node is the node directly above it, and its children are the nodes directly below it. Nodes with the same parent are siblings, like brothers and sisters. Ancestors of a node are all nodes on the path from it up to the root; descendants are all nodes below it in its subtree.
why: A — Wrong. The ancestors of a node are the nodes on the path going up from it to the root (parent, grandparent and so on). Two nodes with the same parent are side by side; neither is above the other.
B — Wrong. The descendants of a node are all the nodes below it (children, grandchildren and so on). Two siblings are at the same level, so neither is a descendant of the other.
C — Correct. Nodes that share the same parent are called siblings, just as children of the same parents in a family are brothers and sisters.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In data-structure terminology, the degree of a node in a tree is:
opts: The number of edges on the path from the root to that node
The number of subtrees (children) of that node
The number of nodes in the subtree rooted at that node
More than one of the above
exp: The degree of a node is the number of its children (subtrees).
concept: In data structures, the degree of a node is the number of children (subtrees) it has. A leaf has degree 0. The degree of a whole tree is the largest degree of any node in it; for example, every node of a binary tree has degree at most 2. (In graph theory 'degree' counts all edges at a vertex, including the edge to the parent; tree questions in data structures use the 'number of children' meaning.)
why: A — Wrong. The number of edges from the root down to a node is that node's depth (also called its level when the root is at level 0), not its degree.
B — Correct. Degree = number of children = number of subtrees hanging directly below the node. A leaf has degree 0; in a binary tree every node has degree 0, 1 or 2.
C — Wrong. The number of nodes in the subtree rooted at a node is the SIZE of that subtree. It counts grandchildren and all lower nodes as well, so it is not the degree.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A tree has 40 nodes. How many edges does it have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges, so this tree has 39 edges, which is not listed.
concept: In a tree, every node except the root has exactly one edge joining it to its parent, and the root has none. So a tree with n nodes always has exactly n − 1 edges. This holds for every tree, binary or not.
work:
Each of the 39 non-root nodes has exactly one edge going up to its parent; the root has none.
Edges = n − 1 = 40 − 1 = 39.
39 is not among 40, 41, 80, so the answer is E.
why: A — Wrong. 40 is the number of nodes. It would be the edge count only if the root also had an edge to a parent, but the root has no parent.
B — Wrong. 41 = n + 1 is the number of NULL child pointers in a linked binary tree with 40 nodes, not the number of edges.
C — Wrong. 80 = 2n is the total number of child pointers (left + right) in a linked binary tree with 40 nodes. Only n − 1 = 39 of them point to real nodes, i.e. are edges.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. A tree with 40 nodes has 40 − 1 = 39 edges, and 39 is not given in A, B or C.
tip: Edges = nodes − 1, because every node except the root has exactly one edge to its parent.

q: Using the convention that the height of a node is the number of edges on the longest downward path from that node to a leaf, which statement is correct?
opts: The height of every leaf is 0
The height of every leaf is 1
A tree consisting of a single node has height 1
More than one of the above
exp: Counting edges, every leaf has height 0, and so does a tree with a single node.
concept: Convention used here: the height of a node is the number of EDGES on the longest downward path from that node to a leaf. A leaf has no edges below it, so its height is 0, and a tree with only one node has height 0. Some books count NODES on the path instead; in that convention a leaf has height 1. Always check which convention the question states.
why: A — Correct. A leaf has no children, so the longest downward path from it contains 0 edges. Its height is therefore 0.
B — Wrong. Height 1 for a leaf belongs to the other convention, where height counts the nodes on the path instead of the edges. This question counts edges.
C — Wrong. A one-node tree is just a single leaf (which is also the root), so its height is 0 edges, not 1. Height 1 again comes from the 'count the nodes' convention.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Edges convention: leaf = 0, empty tree = −1. Nodes convention: leaf = 1, empty tree = 0.

q: A general tree: root A has children B, C and D; B has children E and F; D has children G, H and I; G has one child J. The degree of a node is its number of children and the root has depth 0. Which of the following is true?
opts: The degree of the tree is 3
More than one of the above
exp: Tree degree 3, J at depth 3 and 6 leaves are all correct, so the answer is D.
concept: Degree of a node = its number of children; degree of a tree = the largest degree of any node. Depth of a node = number of edges from the root to it (the question puts the root at depth 0). A leaf is any node with no children, wherever it sits. For such questions, first draw the tree, then check each statement one by one.
work:
Tree (children listed left to right):
A
├─ B
│  ├─ E
│  └─ F
├─ C
└─ D
   ├─ G
   │  └─ J
   ├─ H
   └─ I
Degree of each node (number of children): A = 3, B = 2, C = 0, D = 3, E = 0, F = 0, G = 1, H = 0, I = 0, J = 0.
Degree of the tree = largest node degree = 3.  -> A is true.
Depth of J: path A -> D -> G -> J has 3 edges, so depth 3.  -> B is true.
Leaves (degree 0): C, E, F, H, I, J = 6 leaves.  -> C is true.
All three of A, B, C are true, so the answer is D.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Node A has 3 children (B, C, D) and node D has 3 children (G, H, I); no node has more than 3. So the degree of the tree is 3.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The path from the root to J is A → D → G → J, which has 3 edges, so J is at depth 3.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The nodes with no children are C, E, F, H, I and J: 6 leaves. (C is a leaf even though it is only at depth 1.)
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: A leaf can sit high up in the tree (like C here): 'leaf' only means 'no children'.

q: A general tree: root P has children Q and R; Q has children S, T and U; R has one child V; V has children W and X; X has one child Y. Which option lists exactly the proper ancestors of Y (Y itself excluded)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The proper ancestors of Y are X, V, R and P (option B).
concept: The ancestors of a node are all the nodes on the path from it up to the root: its parent, its grandparent, and so on, up to and including the root. 'Proper' ancestors leave out the node itself. To list them, keep stepping to the parent until you reach the root.
work:
Tree:
P
├─ Q
│  ├─ S
│  ├─ T
│  └─ U
└─ R
   └─ V
      ├─ W
      └─ X
         └─ Y
Walk up from Y, one parent at a time:
parent(Y) = X
parent(X) = V
parent(V) = R
parent(R) = P (the root, stop)
Proper ancestors of Y = {X, V, R, P}. Option B lists exactly these four (order does not matter in a set).
A misses P (the root is an ancestor of every other node); C misses X (the parent is also an ancestor).
why: A — Wrong. X, V, R leaves out the root P. The root is an ancestor of every other node in the tree, so it must be included.
B — Correct. Walking up from Y gives X (its parent), then V, then R, then the root P. These four nodes are exactly the proper ancestors of Y; the order of listing does not matter.
C — Wrong. V, R, P leaves out X, the parent of Y. The parent is the nearest ancestor and must be included.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A general tree: root P has children Q and R; Q has children S, T and U; R has one child V; V has children W and X; X has one child Y. Height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path and the root has depth 0. What are the height of the tree and the depth of W?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Height = 4 (the path down to Y) and depth of W = 3, which is option C.
concept: Convention used here: the root has depth 0, the depth of a node is the number of edges from the root to it, and the height of the tree is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path (which equals the largest depth of any node).
work:
Tree:
P
├─ Q
│  ├─ S
│  ├─ T
│  └─ U
└─ R
   └─ V
      ├─ W
      └─ X
         └─ Y
Depths (root P = 0): Q, R = 1; S, T, U, V = 2; W, X = 3; Y = 4.
Height = largest depth of any leaf = depth of Y = 4 (path P-R-V-X-Y has 4 edges).
Depth of W = 3 (path P-R-V-W has 3 edges).
Answer: height 4, depth of W 3 -> option C.
why: A — Wrong. Height 5 counts the NODES on the longest path P-R-V-X-Y (5 nodes) instead of its edges (4). The question counts edges.
B — Wrong. 3 is the depth of W and X, but Y hangs one level lower (depth 4), so the height of the tree is 4, not 3.
C — Correct. The longest path P → R → V → X → Y has 4 edges, so the height is 4; W is reached by P → R → V → W, 3 edges, so its depth is 3.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a tree, every internal node has exactly 3 children. If the tree has 10 internal nodes, how many leaves does it have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: For a tree where every internal node has 3 children, L = 2I + 1 = 21 leaves.
concept: In a full m-ary tree every internal node has exactly m children. Every node except the root is somebody's child, so the total number of nodes is n = m·I + 1, where I is the number of internal nodes. The number of leaves is L = n − I = (m − 1)·I + 1. For binary trees (m = 2) this becomes the familiar L = I + 1.
work:
m = 3 children per internal node, I = 10 internal nodes.
Children (= edges) = 3 × 10 = 30.
Total nodes n = 30 + 1 (the root is nobody's child) = 31.
Leaves L = n − I = 31 − 10 = 21.
Check with L = (m − 1)·I + 1 = 2 × 10 + 1 = 21.
why: A — Wrong. 20 = 2 × 10 forgets the '+ 1' in L = (m − 1)·I + 1. That + 1 comes from the root, which is not anyone's child.
B — Correct. Using L = (m − 1)·I + 1 with m = 3 and I = 10 gives L = 2 × 10 + 1 = 21.
C — Wrong. 30 is the number of edges (3 children for each of the 10 internal nodes), not the number of leaves. Nine of those 30 children are themselves internal nodes.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Full m-ary tree: L = (m − 1)·I + 1. For binary trees: L = I + 1.

q: Taking the root of a binary tree to be at level 0, what is the maximum number of nodes possible at level 5?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: At most 2^5 = 32 nodes can be on level 5 when the root is at level 0.
concept: Convention used here: the root is at level 0. Each node has at most 2 children, so the largest possible number of nodes doubles from one level to the next: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... At level i (root at level 0) there can be at most 2^i nodes.
work:
Level 0: 1 = 2^0
Level 1: 2 = 2^1
Level 2: 4 = 2^2
Level 3: 8 = 2^3
Level 4: 16 = 2^4
Level 5: 32 = 2^5
why: A — Wrong. 31 = 2^5 − 1 is the largest possible TOTAL number of nodes on levels 0 to 4 together, not the number on level 5 alone.
B — Correct. With the root at level 0, level i holds at most 2^i nodes, so level 5 holds at most 2^5 = 32 nodes.
C — Wrong. 64 = 2^6 is the maximum for level 6, one level too far down.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Root at level 0 → at most 2^i nodes on level i. Root at level 1 → at most 2^(i−1).

q: Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 4?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Maximum nodes for height h is 2^(h+1) − 1 = 31.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a tree of height h has levels 0 to h (that is h + 1 levels). The most nodes are obtained when every level is full: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^h = 2^(h+1) − 1. Such a tree is called a perfect binary tree.
work:
Height 4 → levels 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
All levels full: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31.
Formula: 2^(4+1) − 1 = 32 − 1 = 31.
why: A — Correct. A perfect binary tree of height 4 has 2^(h+1) − 1 = 2^5 − 1 = 31 nodes, the maximum possible.
B — Wrong. 16 = 2^4 is the largest number of nodes on the LAST level (level 4) alone, not the total of all levels.
C — Wrong. 32 = 2^5 forgets the '− 1' in 2^(h+1) − 1. The sum 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 is 31, one less than 32.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Height h (edges): max nodes 2^(h+1) − 1, max leaves 2^h, min nodes h + 1.

q: A binary tree has exactly 20 nodes that have two children. How many leaf nodes does it have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Leaves = (nodes with two children) + 1 = 21.
concept: In every non-empty binary tree, the number of leaves n0 is one more than the number of nodes with two children n2: n0 = n2 + 1. Nodes with exactly one child do not affect this. Reason: count edges two ways. Every node except the root has one parent edge, so edges = n − 1; every edge comes from a parent, so edges = n1 + 2·n2. With n = n0 + n1 + n2 this gives n0 = n2 + 1.
why: A — Correct. Using n0 = n2 + 1 gives 20 + 1 = 21 leaves, no matter how many one-child nodes the tree has.
B — Wrong. 19 = n2 − 1 gets the relation the wrong way round. Leaves are always ONE MORE than the two-child nodes, not one fewer.
C — Wrong. 40 = 2 × 20 counts all the children of the two-child nodes, but many of those children are internal nodes, not leaves.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Leaves = (nodes with 2 children) + 1. One-child nodes do not change it.

q: Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. What is the maximum number of leaves in a binary tree of height 6?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Maximum leaves for height h is 2^h = 64.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. A binary tree of height h has its deepest level at level h, and that level can hold at most 2^h nodes. The perfect binary tree of height h puts all its leaves on level h and reaches 2^h leaves; no binary tree of that height can have more.
work:
Height 6 → the deepest level is level 6.
Level 6 can hold at most 2^6 = 64 nodes.
The perfect binary tree of height 6 has all 64 of them as leaves (plus 63 internal nodes, 127 nodes in total).
why: A — Correct. A perfect binary tree of height 6 has all its leaves on level 6, and that level holds 2^6 = 64 nodes. This is the largest possible number of leaves.
B — Wrong. 127 = 2^7 − 1 is the largest possible TOTAL number of nodes (leaves plus internal nodes) for height 6, not the number of leaves.
C — Wrong. 32 = 2^5 is the maximum number of leaves for height 5, one level less than asked.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: If the root of a binary tree is taken to be at level 1, the maximum number of nodes at level i is:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With the root at level 1, level i holds at most 2^(i−1) nodes.
concept: Convention used here: the root is at level 1 (not 0). Level 1 has at most 1 node, level 2 at most 2, level 3 at most 4. Each level can hold at most twice as many nodes as the level above, so level i holds at most 2^(i−1) nodes.
work:
Level 1: 1 = 2^0
Level 2: 2 = 2^1
Level 3: 4 = 2^2
Level i: 2^(i−1)
why: A — Wrong. 2^i is the formula when the root is at level 0. With the root at level 1 it would give 2 nodes on level 1, but level 1 holds only the root.
B — Wrong. 2^i − 1 is the largest possible TOTAL number of nodes on levels 1 to i together (a perfect tree with i levels), not the number on level i alone.
C — Correct. With the root at level 1, level i holds at most 2^(i−1) nodes: 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Check the level convention first: root at 0 → 2^i; root at 1 → 2^(i−1).

q: Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. What is the minimum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 6?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Minimum nodes for height h is h + 1 = 7, which is not listed, so the answer is E.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. To reach height h the tree needs a path of h edges, and such a path contains h + 1 nodes. A skewed tree (a single chain) has exactly these nodes and nothing more, so the minimum number of nodes for height h is h + 1.
work:
Height 6 needs a root-to-leaf path with 6 edges.
That path contains 6 + 1 = 7 nodes.
A chain of 7 nodes has height 6 and no extra nodes, so the minimum is 7.
7 is not among 6, 13, 127 → E.
why: A — Wrong. 6 nodes can form a path of only 5 edges, so height 6 is impossible with 6 nodes. 6 is what you get if you treat the height as a count of nodes.
B — Wrong. 13 = 2h + 1 is the minimum for a STRICTLY binary tree (every node has 0 or 2 children). An ordinary binary tree may have one-child nodes, so a plain chain of 7 nodes is allowed.
C — Wrong. 127 = 2^7 − 1 is the MAXIMUM number of nodes for height 6 (the perfect tree), not the minimum.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. The minimum is h + 1 = 7 nodes (a chain), and 7 is not given in A, B or C.

q: Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. What is the minimum possible height of a binary tree with 100 nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The minimum height of a binary tree with 100 nodes is ⌊log2 100⌋ = 6.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges. A binary tree of height h holds at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes. So the smallest height that can hold n nodes is the smallest h with 2^(h+1) − 1 ≥ n, which works out to h = ⌊log2 n⌋. The most compact (complete) shape reaches it.
work:
Height 5 → at most 2^6 − 1 = 63 nodes < 100 (not enough)
Height 6 → at most 2^7 − 1 = 127 nodes ≥ 100 (enough)
Minimum height = 6.
Check: ⌊log2 100⌋ = 6, because 2^6 = 64 ≤ 100 < 128 = 2^7.
why: A — Wrong. Height 5 allows at most 63 nodes, fewer than 100, so a binary tree with 100 nodes cannot be that short.
B — Wrong. Height 7 is possible but not the minimum. 7 is the answer if you count height in levels (nodes) instead of edges: 100 nodes need 7 levels.
C — Correct. Height 6 can hold up to 127 nodes, while height 5 cannot hold 100, so the minimum height is 6 = ⌊log2 100⌋.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: For n nodes (height in edges): minimum height ⌊log2 n⌋, maximum height n − 1.

q: A binary tree has 15 leaves and 10 nodes with exactly one child. What is the total number of nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Two-child nodes = 15 − 1 = 14, so the total is 15 + 10 + 14 = 39.
concept: Let n0 = number of leaves, n1 = nodes with exactly one child, n2 = nodes with two children. In every binary tree n0 = n2 + 1, and the total is n = n0 + n1 + n2. Given any two of these counts you can find the rest.
why: A — Wrong. 38 = 15 + 10 + 13 uses n2 = 13. But n2 = n0 − 1 = 14, so the total is 39, not 38.
B — Wrong. 40 = 15 + 10 + 15 assumes n2 = n0. In fact the two-child nodes are always ONE FEWER than the leaves.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A binary tree has 9 nodes with two children and 5 nodes with exactly one child. In its linked representation, how many NULL child pointers are there?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The tree has 10 + 5 + 9 = 24 nodes, so it has n + 1 = 25 NULL pointers.
concept: In the linked representation each node has two child pointers (left and right), so n nodes have 2n pointers. Each edge uses exactly one of them, and there are n − 1 edges, so the other 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1 pointers are NULL. To find n, use n0 = n2 + 1 for the number of leaves.
work:
n2 = 9, n1 = 5
n0 = n2 + 1 = 10
n = 10 + 5 + 9 = 24
Total pointers = 2n = 48; pointers used by edges = n − 1 = 23
NULL pointers = 48 − 23 = 25 = n + 1
Check by counting: each leaf has 2 NULLs (10 × 2 = 20) and each one-child node has 1 NULL (5 × 1 = 5): 20 + 5 = 25.
why: A — Wrong. 24 is the number of nodes n, not the number of NULL pointers (which is n + 1).
B — Correct. With n = 24 nodes there are n + 1 = 25 NULL pointers (also: 2 per leaf + 1 per one-child node = 20 + 5 = 25).
C — Wrong. 20 counts only the NULL pointers of the 10 leaves. Each of the 5 one-child nodes also has one NULL pointer.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: NULL pointers in a linked binary tree = n + 1 (= 2·leaves + one-child nodes).

q: Consider all possible binary trees with exactly 12 nodes (height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path). Which of the following is true?
opts: The maximum possible number of leaves is 6
More than one of the above
exp: Maximum height 11, minimum height 3 and maximum 6 leaves are all correct, so the answer is D.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges. For a binary tree with n nodes, the maximum height is n − 1 (a chain), the minimum height is ⌊log2 n⌋ (a complete tree), and the leaves always satisfy n0 = n2 + 1. To get the most leaves, use as many two-child nodes as possible.
work:
Max height: a chain of 12 nodes has 11 edges → 11. (A true)
Min height: ⌊log2 12⌋ = 3, since 2^3 = 8 ≤ 12 < 16. Height 2 holds at most 7 nodes. (B true)
Max leaves: n = n0 + n1 + n2 and n0 = n2 + 1, so n = 2·n2 + 1 + n1.
  12 = 2·n2 + 1 + n1 → n1 must be odd, so n1 ≥ 1.
  n1 = 1 → n2 = 5 → n0 = 6. (C true)
All three true → D.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A chain (skewed tree) of 12 nodes has 11 edges on its only root-to-leaf path, so the maximum height is 11.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Height 2 allows at most 2^3 − 1 = 7 nodes, too few for 12; height 3 allows up to 15. So the minimum height is 3 = ⌊log2 12⌋.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Since 12 = 2·n2 + 1 + n1, an even total forces at least one one-child node. With n1 = 1 we get n2 = 5 and n0 = n2 + 1 = 6 leaves, the maximum.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: Which of the following is NOT true for every binary tree with n ≥ 1 nodes? (Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.)
opts: In linked representation it has exactly n + 1 NULL child pointers
Its height is at least ⌊log2 n⌋
More than one of the above
exp: Edges = n − 1, NULL pointers = n + 1 and height ≥ ⌊log2 n⌋ hold for every binary tree, so the answer is E.
concept: Three facts hold for EVERY binary tree with n ≥ 1 nodes (height counted in edges): (1) it has n − 1 edges, because every node except the root has one edge to its parent; (2) in linked form it has n + 1 NULL child pointers, because 2n pointers minus the n − 1 used by edges leaves n + 1; (3) its height is at least ⌊log2 n⌋, because a tree of height h holds at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes.
work:
(A) Edges: every node except the root has exactly one parent edge → n − 1. Always true.
(B) Pointers: 2n in total, n − 1 point to children → 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1 are NULL. Always true.
(C) Height h holds at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes, so n ≤ 2^(h+1) − 1 → h ≥ log2(n + 1) − 1 → h ≥ ⌊log2 n⌋. Always true. Example n = 7: ⌊log2 7⌋ = 2, and the perfect tree with 7 nodes has height exactly 2.
None of A–C is a 'NOT true' statement → E.
why: A — Wrong. This statement IS true for every binary tree: each of the n − 1 non-root nodes has exactly one edge to its parent. So it does not satisfy the 'NOT true' stem.
B — Wrong. This statement IS always true: n nodes have 2n child pointers and n − 1 of them are used by edges, so n + 1 are NULL. So it does not satisfy the stem.

C — Wrong. This statement IS always true: a binary tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes, so n nodes need height at least ⌊log2 n⌋ (a complete tree reaches it exactly). So it does not satisfy the stem.
D — Wrong. None of A–C fails for any binary tree, so there are not two (or even one) 'NOT true' statements.
E — Correct. All three statements hold for every binary tree, so none of them is 'NOT true'; the answer is 'None of the above'.
tip: In a 'NOT true' question, if every option is a real theorem, the answer is 'None of the above'.

q: A binary tree in which every node has either 0 or 2 children is called a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A binary tree in which every node has 0 or 2 children is a strictly binary (proper) tree.
concept: A strictly binary tree (also called a proper tree or 2-tree, and in many books a 'full' binary tree) is a binary tree in which every node has either 0 or 2 children, never exactly one. A complete binary tree is about how the levels are filled, and a skewed tree is a single chain.
why: A — Correct. In a strictly binary (proper) tree no node has a single child: every node is either a leaf or has two children. That is exactly the 0-or-2 rule.

B — Wrong. A complete binary tree is defined by level filling: all levels full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. A complete tree can have one node with a single left child, so it is a different idea.
C — Wrong. A skewed tree is a chain in which every internal node has only ONE child (all left or all right), which breaks the 0-or-2 rule.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Careful: many books call the 0-or-2 tree 'full', but Horowitz–Sahni use 'full' to mean 'perfect'. Go by the definition given in the question.

q: Which description defines a complete binary tree?
opts: Every node has either 0 or 2 children
Every level except possibly the last is completely filled, and the nodes of the last level are as far left as possible
All leaves are at the same level and every internal node has two children
More than one of the above
exp: Complete = all levels full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left.
concept: A complete binary tree is one in which every level is completely filled except possibly the last, and the nodes on the last level are packed as far left as possible. This is exactly the shape of a binary heap, and it can be stored in an array with no gaps.
why: A — Wrong. Every node having 0 or 2 children defines a strictly binary (proper) tree. Such a tree can have leaves at very different depths, so it need not be complete.
B — Correct. This is the definition of a complete binary tree: all levels full except maybe the last, and the last level filled from left to right with no gaps.

C — Wrong. All leaves on one level with every internal node having two children describes a PERFECT binary tree. A perfect tree is a special kind of complete tree, but this is not the definition of 'complete', because a complete tree's last level may be only partly filled.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A binary tree with n ≥ 3 nodes has the maximum possible height, n − 1 (counted in edges), when it is a:
opts: Skewed (degenerate) tree in which every internal node has exactly one child
More than one of the above
exp: The maximum height n − 1 is reached only by a skewed (degenerate) chain.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges. A binary tree with n nodes is tallest when it is a single chain, that is, when every internal node has exactly one child (a skewed or degenerate tree); its height is then n − 1. Bushy shapes such as perfect and complete trees are the shortest possible, with height ⌊log2 n⌋.
why: A — Wrong. A perfect binary tree has every level full, so it has the MINIMUM height for its size, not the maximum. For n = 7 its height is 2, while a chain of 7 nodes has height 6.
B — Wrong. A complete binary tree also has the minimum height ⌊log2 n⌋. For n = 3 its height is 1, while the maximum is n − 1 = 2.
C — Correct. When every internal node has only one child, the n nodes form a single chain with n − 1 edges, so the height is n − 1, the largest possible.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A strictly binary tree (every node has 0 or 2 children) has 25 leaves. How many nodes does it have in total?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A strictly binary tree with 25 leaves has 24 internal nodes, 49 nodes in all, which is not listed.
concept: In a strictly binary tree every internal node has exactly 2 children, so there are no one-child nodes. Using leaves = (two-child nodes) + 1, a strictly binary tree with L leaves has L − 1 internal nodes and 2L − 1 nodes in total.
work:
L = 25 leaves
Internal nodes = L − 1 = 24 (each has 2 children)
Total n = 25 + 24 = 49 = 2L − 1
49 is not among 48, 50, 51 → E.
why: A — Wrong. 48 is the number of EDGES of this tree (n − 1 = 49 − 1), not the number of nodes.
B — Wrong. 50 = 2L assumes as many internal nodes as leaves. In fact there is always one fewer internal node than leaves, so the total is 2L − 1 = 49.
C — Wrong. 51 = 2L + 1 assumes one MORE internal node than leaves; the relation is the other way round (internal nodes = leaves − 1).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. The total is 2L − 1 = 49 nodes, which is not given in A, B or C.
tip: Strictly binary tree: n = 2L − 1 = 2I + 1.

q: Which of the following statements is/are true?
opts: Every perfect binary tree is a complete binary tree
Every perfect binary tree is a strictly binary tree (every node has 0 or 2 children)
Every complete binary tree is a perfect binary tree
More than one of the above
exp: Perfect implies complete and strictly binary (A and B), but complete does not imply perfect, so the answer is D.
concept: A perfect binary tree has every level completely full (all leaves on the same level). A complete binary tree has every level full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. A strictly binary tree has 0 or 2 children at every node. Perfect is the strongest of the three: every perfect tree is both complete and strictly binary, but not the other way round.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In a perfect tree every level, including the last, is full, so it certainly satisfies 'all levels full except possibly the last, filled from the left'.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In a perfect tree every internal node has 2 children and every leaf has 0, so the 0-or-2 rule holds.
C — Wrong. A complete tree's last level may be only partly filled. Example: a complete tree with 6 nodes (3 of the 4 places on its last level used) is not perfect.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: Perfect ⊂ Complete and Perfect ⊂ Strictly binary; the reverse inclusions fail.

q: Which of the following is NOT necessarily true for a complete binary tree with n nodes? (Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.)
opts: It can be stored level by level in an array of n cells with no gaps
Every node has either 0 or 2 children
More than one of the above
exp: Height ⌊log2 n⌋ and gap-free array storage always hold, but a complete tree may have a one-child node, so C is the answer.
concept: A complete binary tree with n nodes (height counted in edges) always has height ⌊log2 n⌋ and can be stored level by level in n consecutive array cells with no gaps; this is why heaps are stored in arrays. But completeness does not forbid one-child nodes: when n is even, exactly one node (the parent of the last node) has only a left child.
why: A — Wrong. This IS always true: levels 0 to h − 1 are full and level h has at least one node, so 2^h ≤ n < 2^(h+1), which gives h = ⌊log2 n⌋. So it does not satisfy the 'NOT necessarily true' stem.
B — Wrong. This IS always true: nodes are placed level by level from the left, so array positions 1..n (or 0..n − 1) are all used with no empty cell. So it does not satisfy the stem.

C — Correct. This is NOT necessarily true: a complete tree with 2 nodes (a root with a left child), or any complete tree with an even number of nodes, has one node with exactly one child. So this option satisfies the stem.
D — Wrong. Only C can fail for a complete tree; A and B always hold, so there are not two such statements.
E — Wrong. C does fail for some complete trees, so there is an option that satisfies the stem.

q: A binary tree is height-balanced if, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Which of the following is guaranteed to be height-balanced?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Perfect and complete trees are always height-balanced, but a 3-node chain is not, so the answer is D.
