concept: A binary tree is height-balanced if at EVERY node the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1 (this is the AVL condition). An empty subtree has height −1 in the edges convention. Perfect and complete trees are always height-balanced; a chain of 3 or more nodes is not.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In a perfect tree, at every node the left and right subtrees are perfect trees of the same height, so the difference is 0 everywhere.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In a complete tree only the last level can be partly filled, and it is filled from the left. So at any node the left subtree is either as tall as the right one or one level taller; the difference is at most 1 everywhere.

C — Wrong. At the root of a left-skewed tree with 3 nodes, the left subtree (a chain of 2 nodes) has height 1 and the right subtree is empty (height −1). The difference is 2, so the tree is not height-balanced.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: In a strictly binary tree every node has 0 or 2 children. Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. What is the minimum number of nodes in a strictly binary tree of height 5?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The minimum strictly binary tree of height h has 2h + 1 nodes, so 11 for h = 5.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges. In a strictly binary tree every internal node has 2 children. To reach height h with as few nodes as possible, build one long path of h + 1 nodes and give each of its h internal nodes a single extra leaf as its second child. Minimum nodes = (h + 1) + h = 2h + 1.
work:
Height 5 → a path with 5 edges → 6 nodes on the path: N0-N1-N2-N3-N4-N5.
The 5 internal nodes N0..N4 each need a second child → 5 extra leaves.
Total = 6 + 5 = 11 = 2h + 1.
Shape:
N0
├─ L: N1
│  ├─ L: N2
│  │  ├─ L: N3
│  │  │  ├─ L: N4
│  │  │  │  ├─ L: N5
│  │  │  │  └─ R: leaf
│  │  │  └─ R: leaf
│  │  └─ R: leaf
│  └─ R: leaf
└─ R: leaf
why: A — Wrong. 6 nodes is the minimum for an ORDINARY binary tree of height 5 (a chain), but a chain has one-child nodes, which a strictly binary tree does not allow.
B — Correct. A path of 6 nodes plus one extra leaf for each of its 5 internal nodes gives 6 + 5 = 11 = 2h + 1 nodes, the minimum.
C — Wrong. 63 = 2^6 − 1 is the MAXIMUM number of nodes for height 5 (the perfect tree), not the minimum.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A binary tree is stored in an array with index starting at 0 (root at index 0). The children of the node at index i are at indices:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With 0-based indexing, the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
concept: In the array (sequential) representation, nodes are stored level by level, left to right. With 0-based indexing (root at index 0) the node at index i has its left child at 2i + 1, its right child at 2i + 2 and its parent at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋. With 1-based indexing (root at index 1) the rules become 2i, 2i + 1 and ⌊i/2⌋.
why: A — Wrong. 2i and 2i + 1 is the rule for 1-based indexing (root at index 1). With the root at 0 it would make the root's left child index 0, which is the root itself.
B — Correct. With the root at 0, the root's children are at 1 and 2, node 1's children at 3 and 4, node 2's at 5 and 6; in general 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
C — Wrong. 2i − 1 and 2i is not a standard rule; for the root (i = 0) it gives index −1, which does not exist.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 0-based: children 2i+1, 2i+2; parent ⌊(i−1)/2⌋. 1-based: children 2i, 2i+1; parent ⌊i/2⌋.

q: A binary tree is stored in an array with index starting at 0 (root at index 0). What is the index of the parent of the node at index 18?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With 0-based indexing, parent(18) = ⌊17/2⌋ = 8.
concept: With 0-based array indexing (root at index 0), the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, so the parent of index i is at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋. Using the 1-based formula ⌊i/2⌋ here is a common mistake.
work:
0-based rule: children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, so parent(i) = floor((i - 1) / 2).
parent(18) = floor(17 / 2) = floor(8.5) = 8.
Check: right child of 8 = 2*8 + 2 = 18. Correct.
why: A — Correct. ⌊(18 − 1)/2⌋ = ⌊8.5⌋ = 8, and indeed 2 × 8 + 2 = 18, so index 18 is the right child of index 8.
B — Wrong. 9 = ⌊18/2⌋ uses the 1-based parent rule. With 0-based indexing the children of 9 are 19 and 20, not 18.
C — Wrong. 17 is simply the previous array cell (18 − 1). Neighbouring cells usually hold siblings or cousins, not a parent and its child.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A binary tree is stored in an array with index starting at 1 (root at index 1). For the node at index 13, which of the following is correct?
opts: Its left child is at index 26
Its right child is at index 27
More than one of the above
exp: With 1-based indexing, node 13 has children 26 and 27 and parent 6, so all three are correct (D).
concept: With 1-based indexing (root at index 1), the node at index i has its left child at 2i, its right child at 2i + 1 and its parent at ⌊i/2⌋. These simple formulas are why heaps are often stored starting from index 1.
work:
1-based rules: left(i) = 2i, right(i) = 2i + 1, parent(i) = floor(i / 2).
left(13) = 26  -> A true
right(13) = 27  -> B true
parent(13) = floor(13/2) = floor(6.5) = 6  -> C true
Check: 13 = 2*6 + 1, so 13 is the right child of 6.
All three true, so the answer is D.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Left child = 2i = 2 × 13 = 26.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Right child = 2i + 1 = 2 × 13 + 1 = 27.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Parent = ⌊13/2⌋ = ⌊6.5⌋ = 6. Check: 2 × 6 + 1 = 13, so 13 is the right child of 6.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: The sequential (array) representation of a binary tree wastes the least space when the tree is a:
opts: Sparse binary tree of large height
More than one of the above
exp: Array storage wastes no space only for a complete binary tree.
concept: In the array representation every node's position is fixed by where it would be in a full tree (children of i at 2i and 2i + 1). A missing node still uses up an empty cell. A complete tree has no missing positions before its last node, so it uses cells 1..n with no waste. Tall, thin trees waste the most: a skewed tree with n nodes can need 2^n − 1 cells.
why: A — Correct. A complete tree fills positions 1..n level by level from the left, so no cell is wasted. This is why heaps are kept in arrays.
B — Wrong. A right-skewed tree is the worst case: its nodes sit at indices 1, 3, 7, 15, ..., so n nodes need 2^n − 1 cells, almost all of them empty.
C — Wrong. A sparse, tall tree leaves most cells empty, because the array must be long enough to reach the position of its deepest node.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A right-skewed binary tree with 5 nodes (every internal node has only a right child) is stored in an array with index starting at 1. What is the minimum array size needed (cells 1..m)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A right-skewed tree of 5 nodes needs indices up to 2^5 − 1 = 31.
concept: Convention used here: 1-based indexing, with the right child of index i at 2i + 1. In a right-skewed tree each node is the right child of the one before, so the indices grow as 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ... (= 2^k − 1). A right-skewed tree with n nodes therefore needs an array of 2^n − 1 cells.
work:
1-based: the right child of i is at 2i + 1. Follow the chain of right children:
node 1 at index 1
node 2 at 2*1 + 1 = 3
node 3 at 2*3 + 1 = 7
node 4 at 2*7 + 1 = 15
node 5 at 2*15 + 1 = 31
The last node sits at index 31, so cells 1..31 are needed: m = 31 (only 5 of them are used, 26 are empty).
General rule: a right-skewed tree of n nodes needs 2^n - 1 cells (2^5 - 1 = 31).
why: A — Wrong. 5 cells would be enough only if the nodes could be stored without gaps, which is the case for a complete tree. A right-skewed tree puts its 5th node at index 31.
B — Wrong. 16 = 2^4 is where the 5th node of a LEFT-skewed tree goes (indices 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, since left children are at 2i). Here every child is a right child, at 2i + 1.
C — Correct. The indices go 1 → 3 → 7 → 15 → 31; the last node is at index 31, so the array needs 31 cells (2^5 − 1).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Skewed tree with n nodes (1-based): left-skewed needs 2^(n−1) cells, right-skewed needs 2^n − 1 cells.

q: Binary tree: Root A has left child B and right child C; B has only a right child D; C has only a left child E; D has only a left child F; all other nodes are leaves. It is stored in an array with index starting at 1 (root at 1, children of i at 2i and 2i + 1). At which index is F stored, and how many cells among indices 1 to that index are left empty?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: F is stored at index 10, and 4 of the cells 1..10 are empty.
concept: In the 1-based array representation the root is at index 1, the left child of index i is at 2i and the right child at 2i + 1. A missing node leaves its cell empty. To find a node's index, follow its path from the root, doubling for a left step and doubling plus one for a right step.
work:
Tree:
A
├─ L: B
│  └─ R: D
│     └─ L: F
└─ R: C
   └─ L: E
1-based: left(i) = 2i, right(i) = 2i + 1.
A -> 1
B = left of A -> 2*1 = 2
C = right of A -> 2*1 + 1 = 3
D = right of B -> 2*2 + 1 = 5
E = left of C -> 2*3 = 6
F = left of D -> 2*5 = 10
Cells 1..10: 1 A | 2 B | 3 C | 4 empty | 5 D | 6 E | 7 empty | 8 empty | 9 empty | 10 F
F is at index 10 and 4 cells (4, 7, 8, 9) are empty -> option A.
why: A — Correct. F is reached by A → B (left) → D (right) → F (left), i.e. 1 → 2 → 5 → 10. Among cells 1..10, cells 4, 7, 8 and 9 are empty: 4 empty cells.
B — Wrong. Index 11 would be the RIGHT child of D (2 × 5 + 1). F is D's LEFT child, so it is at 2 × 5 = 10.
C — Wrong. Index 10 is right, but cells 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 10 are used (6 nodes), so only 10 − 6 = 4 cells are empty, not 5.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A binary tree is stored in an array with index starting at 1 (children of i at 2i and 2i + 1): index 1 = 10, 2 = 20, 3 = 30, 4 = 40, 6 = 50, 7 = 60, 9 = 70; all other cells are empty. What is the inorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Rebuilding the tree from the array shows 70 is 40's right child, so the inorder is 40, 70, 20, 10, 50, 30, 60.
concept: To read a tree stored in an array (1-based), remember that the children of cell i are cells 2i and 2i + 1, and an empty cell means 'no child there'. First rebuild the tree from the array, then traverse it. Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree (L N R).
work:
Rebuild the tree from the array (children of i at 2i and 2i + 1):
index 1 = 10 (root); its children: index 2 = 20 (left), index 3 = 30 (right)
index 2 = 20: children index 4 = 40 (left), index 5 empty (no right child)
index 3 = 30: children index 6 = 50 (left), index 7 = 60 (right)
index 4 = 40: children index 8 empty (no left child), index 9 = 70 (right)
Tree:
10
├─ L: 20
│  └─ L: 40
│     └─ R: 70
└─ R: 30
   ├─ L: 50
   └─ R: 60
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(40) = 40 + In(70) = 40, 70   [40 has no left child]
In(20) = In(40) + 20 = 40, 70, 20   [20 has no right child]
In(30) = In(50) + 30 + In(60) = 50, 30, 60
In(10) = In(20) + 10 + In(30) = 40, 70, 20, 10, 50, 30, 60
Inorder: 40, 70, 20, 10, 50, 30, 60
why: A — Wrong. This puts 70 after 20, as if 70 were the right child of 20 (index 5). But 70 is at index 9 = 2 × 4 + 1, the right child of 40, so it comes straight after 40.
B — Wrong. This puts 70 first, as if it were the LEFT child of 40 (index 8). Index 9 is a right child, so inorder visits 40 before 70.
C — Correct. The tree is 10 → (20, 30), 20 has left child 40, 40 has right child 70, and 30 → (50, 60). Its inorder is 40, 70, 20, 10, 50, 30, 60.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A left-skewed binary tree with 6 nodes (every internal node has only a left child) is stored in an array with index starting at 0. What is the minimum number of array cells needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The 6 nodes are at indices 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, so 32 cells are needed, which is not listed.
concept: Convention used here: 0-based indexing, with the left child of index i at 2i + 1. In a left-skewed tree the indices go 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ... (= 2^k − 1). The number of cells needed is (last index + 1), because index 0 is also a cell.
work:
0-based: the left child of i is at 2i + 1. Follow the chain of left children:
node 1 at index 0
node 2 at 2*0 + 1 = 1
node 3 at 2*1 + 1 = 3
node 4 at 2*3 + 1 = 7
node 5 at 2*7 + 1 = 15
node 6 at 2*15 + 1 = 31
The last node is at index 31, so indices 0..31 are needed = 32 cells.
32 is not among 31, 63, 64, so the answer is E. (31 is the last INDEX, not the number of cells; 63 = 2^6 - 1 is what a RIGHT-skewed 6-node tree would need, since right children are at 2i + 2: indices 0, 2, 6, 14, 30, 62.)
why: A — Wrong. 31 is the INDEX of the 6th node, but indices 0..31 make 32 cells. Forgetting cell 0 gives 31.
B — Wrong. 63 = 2^6 − 1 is the size a RIGHT-skewed 6-node tree would need (0-based indices 0, 2, 6, 14, 30, 62). Left children are placed lower, so a left-skewed tree needs less.
C — Wrong. 64 = 2^6 overestimates. It would be the size only if the last node were at index 63.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. The last node is at index 31, so indices 0..31 = 32 cells are needed, and 32 is not given in A, B or C.

q: Which data structures are normally used for (i) iterative (non-recursive) inorder traversal and (ii) level-order traversal of a binary tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Iterative inorder uses a stack; level-order traversal uses a queue.
concept: Depth-first traversals (preorder, inorder, postorder) go deep down one branch before coming back, so they must remember the nodes to return to. The node saved last is the first one needed again, which is LIFO, a stack (recursive code uses the system's call stack). Level-order (breadth-first) traversal visits nodes in the order they were found, level by level, which is FIFO, a queue.
why: A — Wrong. This swaps the two. A queue visits nodes in the order they were discovered, which produces level order, not inorder; and a stack cannot produce level order.
B — Correct. Iterative inorder pushes nodes while going left and pops them to visit them: a stack (LIFO). Level order removes a node from the front and adds its children at the back: a queue (FIFO).

C — Wrong. A stack is right for (i), but level order needs FIFO behaviour. With a stack, the most recently added child would be visited first and the traversal would dive deep instead of finishing each level.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: DFS (pre/in/post) → stack. BFS (level order) → queue.

q: Binary tree: Root A has left child B and right child C; B has left child D and right child E; all other nodes are leaves. What is the preorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Preorder (node, left, right) gives A, B, D, E, C.
concept: Preorder traversal visits a node first, then its whole left subtree (in preorder), then its whole right subtree (in preorder): N L R. So the root is always the first node in preorder.
work:
Tree:
A
├─ L: B
│  ├─ L: D
│  └─ R: E
└─ R: C
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(B) = B + Pre(D) + Pre(E) = B, D, E
Pre(A) = A + Pre(B) + Pre(C) = A, B, D, E, C
Preorder: A, B, D, E, C
why: A — Correct. Root A first, then B's subtree in preorder (B, D, E), then C: A, B, D, E, C.
B — Wrong. D, B, E, A, C is the inorder traversal (L N R): the root A sits in the middle.
C — Wrong. A, B, C, D, E is the level-order traversal (level by level), not preorder.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root 1 has left child 2 and right child 3; 2 has only a right child 4; 3 has left child 5 and right child 6; all other nodes are leaves. What is the inorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Inorder (left, node, right) gives 2, 4, 1, 5, 3, 6.
concept: Inorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree (L N R). When a node has only a RIGHT child, the node comes BEFORE that child; when it has only a LEFT child, the node comes after it.
work:
Tree:
1
├─ L: 2
│  └─ R: 4
└─ R: 3
   ├─ L: 5
   └─ R: 6
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(2) = 2 + In(4) = 2, 4   [2 has no left child]
In(3) = In(5) + 3 + In(6) = 5, 3, 6
In(1) = In(2) + 1 + In(3) = 2, 4, 1, 5, 3, 6
Inorder: 2, 4, 1, 5, 3, 6
why: A — Wrong. 4, 2, ... treats 4 as the LEFT child of 2. Since 4 is the right child, inorder prints 2 first, then 4.
B — Correct. In(2) = 2, 4 (no left child, then the right child); In(3) = 5, 3, 6; so In(1) = 2, 4, 1, 5, 3, 6.
C — Wrong. This visits 3 before 5, but 5 is the LEFT child of 3, so inorder must print 5 before 3.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root P has left child Q and right child R; Q has left child S and right child T; R has left child U and right child V; all other nodes are leaves. What is the postorder traversal?
opts: S, Q, T, P, U, R, V
S, T, U, V, Q, R, P
S, T, Q, U, V, R, P
More than one of the above
exp: Postorder (left, right, node) gives S, T, Q, U, V, R, P.
concept: Postorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the node itself (L R N). The root is always the LAST node in postorder, and every node comes after all of its descendants.
work:
Tree:
P
├─ L: Q
│  ├─ L: S
│  └─ R: T
└─ R: R
   ├─ L: U
   └─ R: V
Postorder = left subtree, then right subtree, then node (L R N). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Post(Q) = Post(S) + Post(T) + Q = S, T, Q
Post(R) = Post(U) + Post(V) + R = U, V, R
Post(P) = Post(Q) + Post(R) + P = S, T, Q, U, V, R, P
Postorder: S, T, Q, U, V, R, P
why: A — Wrong. S, Q, T, P, U, R, V is the inorder traversal (L N R), with the root P in the middle.
B — Wrong. This prints U and V before Q, mixing the two subtrees. Postorder must finish Q's whole subtree (S, T, Q) before it starts R's subtree.
C — Correct. Post(Q) = S, T, Q; Post(R) = U, V, R; then the root: S, T, Q, U, V, R, P.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root 15 has left child 8 and right child 20; 8 has left child 4 and right child 12; 20 has only a right child 25; 12 has only a left child 10; 25 has only a left child 22; all other nodes are leaves. What is the level-order (left to right) traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Level order reads the levels {15}, {8, 20}, {4, 12, 25}, {10, 22} from left to right.
concept: Level-order (breadth-first) traversal visits the root, then all nodes at depth 1 from left to right, then all nodes at depth 2, and so on. It is done with a queue: take the node at the front, visit it, then add its left and right children at the back.
work:
Tree:
15
├─ L: 8
│  ├─ L: 4
│  └─ R: 12
│     └─ L: 10
└─ R: 20
   └─ R: 25
      └─ L: 22
Level order reads the tree level by level, each level from left to right (a queue does this: take a node from the front, put its left child then its right child at the back).
Level 0: 15
Level 1: 8, 20
Level 2: 4, 12, 25
Level 3: 10, 22
Level order: 15, 8, 20, 4, 12, 25, 10, 22
why: A — Correct. Levels: {15}, {8, 20}, {4, 12, 25}, {10, 22}. Reading each level left to right gives 15, 8, 20, 4, 12, 25, 10, 22.
B — Wrong. 15, 8, 4, 12, 10, 20, 25, 22 is the preorder traversal (depth-first), not level order.
C — Wrong. This swaps the last two nodes. On the deepest level, 10 is in the root's left half (under 12) and 22 is in the right half (under 25), so 10 comes before 22.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root A has left child B and right child C; B has only a left child D; C has left child E and right child F; D has only a right child G; E has only a left child H; F has only a right child I; all other nodes are leaves. What is the inorder traversal?
opts: D, G, B, A, E, H, C, F, I
G, D, B, A, H, E, C, F, I
D, G, B, A, H, E, C, F, I
More than one of the above
exp: Inorder gives D, G, B, A, H, E, C, F, I.
concept: Inorder = left subtree, node, right subtree (L N R). The side of a single child matters: a node with only a right child is printed BEFORE that child, and a node with only a left child is printed AFTER it.
work:
Tree:
A
├─ L: B
│  └─ L: D
│     └─ R: G
└─ R: C
   ├─ L: E
   │  └─ L: H
   └─ R: F
      └─ R: I
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(D) = D + In(G) = D, G   [D has no left child]
In(B) = In(D) + B = D, G, B   [B has no right child]
In(E) = In(H) + E = H, E   [E has no right child]
In(F) = F + In(I) = F, I   [F has no left child]
In(C) = In(E) + C + In(F) = H, E, C, F, I
In(A) = In(B) + A + In(C) = D, G, B, A, H, E, C, F, I
Inorder: D, G, B, A, H, E, C, F, I
why: A — Wrong. This prints E before H. But H is E's LEFT child, so inorder must print H first, then E.
B — Wrong. This prints G before D. But G is D's RIGHT child, so D comes first, then G.
C — Correct. In(B) = D, G, B and In(C) = H, E, C, F, I, so the inorder is D, G, B, A, H, E, C, F, I.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root 1 has left child 2 and right child 3; 2 has left child 4 and right child 5; 3 has only a right child 6; 4 has only a left child 7; 5 has left child 8 and right child 9; 6 has only a left child 10; all other nodes are leaves. Which node is visited 6th in postorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Postorder is 7, 4, 8, 9, 5, 2, 10, 6, 3, 1, so the 6th node visited is 2.
concept: Postorder = left subtree, right subtree, node (L R N). To find the k-th node visited, write out the whole postorder (building it up subtree by subtree) and then count.
work:
Tree:
1
├─ L: 2
│  ├─ L: 4
│  │  └─ L: 7
│  └─ R: 5
│     ├─ L: 8
│     └─ R: 9
└─ R: 3
   └─ R: 6
      └─ L: 10
Postorder = left subtree, then right subtree, then node (L R N). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Post(4) = Post(7) + 4 = 7, 4   [4 has no right child]
Post(5) = Post(8) + Post(9) + 5 = 8, 9, 5
Post(2) = Post(4) + Post(5) + 2 = 7, 4, 8, 9, 5, 2
Post(6) = Post(10) + 6 = 10, 6   [6 has no right child]
Post(3) = Post(6) + 3 = 10, 6, 3   [3 has no left child]
Post(1) = Post(2) + Post(3) + 1 = 7, 4, 8, 9, 5, 2, 10, 6, 3, 1
Postorder: 7, 4, 8, 9, 5, 2, 10, 6, 3, 1
Numbering the postorder: 1:7, 2:4, 3:8, 4:9, 5:5, 6:2, 7:10, 8:6, 9:3, 10:1
The 6th node visited is 2.
why: A — Wrong. 9 is the 4th node in postorder (7, 4, 8, 9, ...). It is the 6th node in INORDER (7, 4, 2, 8, 5, 9, ...).
B — Correct. The postorder is 7, 4, 8, 9, 5, 2, 10, 6, 3, 1; the 6th node is 2, printed just as the root's whole left subtree is finished.
C — Wrong. 8 is the 3rd node in postorder. It is the 6th node in PREORDER (1, 2, 4, 7, 5, 8, ...).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root P has left child Q and right child R; Q has left child S and right child T; R has only a right child U; S has only a right child V; T has left child W and right child X; U has only a left child Y; all other nodes are leaves. In inorder traversal, which node is visited immediately after X?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: X is the last node of P's left subtree, so P is visited immediately after X.
concept: In inorder, the node visited right after X is X's inorder successor. If X has a right subtree, the successor is the leftmost node of that subtree. If X has no right child, move up through the ancestors until you arrive at one from its LEFT side; that ancestor is the successor.
work:
Tree:
P
├─ L: Q
│  ├─ L: S
│  │  └─ R: V
│  └─ R: T
│     ├─ L: W
│     └─ R: X
└─ R: R
   └─ R: U
      └─ L: Y
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(S) = S + In(V) = S, V   [S has no left child]
In(T) = In(W) + T + In(X) = W, T, X
In(Q) = In(S) + Q + In(T) = S, V, Q, W, T, X
In(U) = In(Y) + U = Y, U   [U has no right child]
In(R) = R + In(U) = R, Y, U   [R has no left child]
In(P) = In(Q) + P + In(R) = S, V, Q, W, T, X, P, R, Y, U
Inorder: S, V, Q, W, T, X, P, R, Y, U
In this sequence X is followed by P.
why: A — Correct. X has no right child. Going up: X is the right child of T, T is the right child of Q, and Q is the LEFT child of P. So P comes next. The full inorder is S, V, Q, W, T, X, P, R, Y, U.
B — Wrong. T is X's parent, but X is T's RIGHT child, so T is printed BEFORE X (W, T, X), not after it.
C — Wrong. R comes after P in inorder. P must be printed first, because X is the last node of P's left subtree.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root A has left child B and right child C; B has left child D and right child E; C has only a left child F; D has only a right child G; E has left child H and right child I; F has only a right child J; all other nodes are leaves. Which node is visited last in preorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Preorder is A, B, D, G, E, H, I, C, F, J, so the last node is J.
concept: Preorder = node, left subtree, right subtree (N L R). The last node in preorder can be found by starting at the root and repeatedly moving to the right child if there is one, otherwise to the left child, until you reach a leaf.
work:
Tree:
A
├─ L: B
│  ├─ L: D
│  │  └─ R: G
│  └─ R: E
│     ├─ L: H
│     └─ R: I
└─ R: C
   └─ L: F
      └─ R: J
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(D) = D + Pre(G) = D, G   [D has no left child]
Pre(E) = E + Pre(H) + Pre(I) = E, H, I
Pre(B) = B + Pre(D) + Pre(E) = B, D, G, E, H, I
Pre(F) = F + Pre(J) = F, J   [F has no left child]
Pre(C) = C + Pre(F) = C, F, J   [C has no right child]
Pre(A) = A + Pre(B) + Pre(C) = A, B, D, G, E, H, I, C, F, J
Preorder: A, B, D, G, E, H, I, C, F, J
The last node visited is J.
why: A — Wrong. I is the last node of the root's LEFT subtree (B's subtree). After it, preorder still visits the whole right subtree C, F, J.
B — Wrong. C is the first node of the right subtree. It is visited right after I, and its own subtree (F, J) follows it.
C — Correct. The full preorder is A, B, D, G, E, H, I, C, F, J. Path to the last node: A → C (right child) → F (C has only a left child) → J (F's right child).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Last in preorder: from the root go right when possible, else left, until a leaf.

q: Binary tree: Root 10 has left child 20 and right child 30; 20 has only a left child 40; 30 has left child 50 and right child 60; 40 has only a right child 70; 60 has only a left child 80; all other nodes are leaves. Which of the following statements is/are correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The preorder (A) and postorder (B) are correct; the inorder in C is wrong, so the answer is D.
concept: Preorder = N L R, postorder = L R N, inorder = L N R. Every traversal must respect whether a single child is a LEFT or a RIGHT child; for inorder this decides whether the node is printed before or after that child.
work:
Tree:
10
├─ L: 20
│  └─ L: 40
│     └─ R: 70
└─ R: 30
   ├─ L: 50
   └─ R: 60
      └─ L: 80
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(40) = 40 + Pre(70) = 40, 70   [40 has no left child]
Pre(20) = 20 + Pre(40) = 20, 40, 70   [20 has no right child]
Pre(60) = 60 + Pre(80) = 60, 80   [60 has no right child]
Pre(30) = 30 + Pre(50) + Pre(60) = 30, 50, 60, 80
Pre(10) = 10 + Pre(20) + Pre(30) = 10, 20, 40, 70, 30, 50, 60, 80
Preorder: 10, 20, 40, 70, 30, 50, 60, 80
Postorder = left subtree, then right subtree, then node (L R N). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Post(40) = Post(70) + 40 = 70, 40   [40 has no left child]
Post(20) = Post(40) + 20 = 70, 40, 20   [20 has no right child]
Post(60) = Post(80) + 60 = 80, 60   [60 has no right child]
Post(30) = Post(50) + Post(60) + 30 = 50, 80, 60, 30
Post(10) = Post(20) + Post(30) + 10 = 70, 40, 20, 50, 80, 60, 30, 10
Postorder: 70, 40, 20, 50, 80, 60, 30, 10
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(40) = 40 + In(70) = 40, 70   [40 has no left child]
In(20) = In(40) + 20 = 40, 70, 20   [20 has no right child]
In(60) = In(80) + 60 = 80, 60   [60 has no right child]
In(30) = In(50) + 30 + In(60) = 50, 30, 80, 60
In(10) = In(20) + 10 + In(30) = 40, 70, 20, 10, 50, 30, 80, 60
Inorder: 40, 70, 20, 10, 50, 30, 80, 60
Compare: A matches the preorder, B matches the postorder, C does not match the inorder (C puts 60 before 80, but 80 is the LEFT child of 60, so 80 comes first).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Pre(20) = 20, 40, 70 and Pre(30) = 30, 50, 60, 80, so the preorder is 10, 20, 40, 70, 30, 50, 60, 80.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Post(20) = 70, 40, 20 and Post(30) = 50, 80, 60, 30, so the postorder is 70, 40, 20, 50, 80, 60, 30, 10.
C — Wrong. The correct inorder ends with 80, 60, because 80 is the LEFT child of 60 (L N R puts 80 first). The option writes 60, 80, as if 80 were a right child.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: Binary tree (left-skewed): Root 5 has only a left child 4; 4 has only a left child 3; 3 has only a left child 2; 2 has only a left child 1; all other nodes are leaves. The sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is produced by which traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a left-skewed chain, inorder and postorder both give 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, so the answer is D.
concept: In a left-skewed tree every node has only a left child. Preorder (N L R) prints each node before its subtree, so it goes from the top down. Inorder (L N R) and postorder (L R N) both print the whole left subtree before the node, and there is no right subtree, so both go from the bottom up and give the same sequence.
work:
Tree:
5
└─ L: 4
   └─ L: 3
      └─ L: 2
         └─ L: 1
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(2) = 2 + Pre(1) = 2, 1   [2 has no right child]
Pre(3) = 3 + Pre(2) = 3, 2, 1   [3 has no right child]
Pre(4) = 4 + Pre(3) = 4, 3, 2, 1   [4 has no right child]
Pre(5) = 5 + Pre(4) = 5, 4, 3, 2, 1   [5 has no right child]
Preorder: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(2) = In(1) + 2 = 1, 2   [2 has no right child]
In(3) = In(2) + 3 = 1, 2, 3   [3 has no right child]
In(4) = In(3) + 4 = 1, 2, 3, 4   [4 has no right child]
In(5) = In(4) + 5 = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5   [5 has no right child]
Inorder: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Postorder = left subtree, then right subtree, then node (L R N). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Post(2) = Post(1) + 2 = 1, 2   [2 has no right child]
Post(3) = Post(2) + 3 = 1, 2, 3   [3 has no right child]
Post(4) = Post(3) + 4 = 1, 2, 3, 4   [4 has no right child]
Post(5) = Post(4) + 5 = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5   [5 has no right child]
Postorder: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Inorder and postorder both give 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (no node has a right child, so 'L N' and 'L R N' are the same).
why: A — Wrong. Preorder prints each node before its subtree, so it gives 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, the reverse of the required sequence.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Inorder prints the left subtree first and then the node: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Postorder prints the left subtree, the (empty) right subtree, then the node: also 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
D — Correct. B and C are both true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. B and C are true, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: No right children anywhere → inorder = postorder. No left children anywhere → preorder = inorder.

q: Binary tree: Root J has left child E and right child N; E has left child B and right child H; N has left child L and right child Q; B has left child A and right child C; H has only a left child G; L has only a right child M; all other nodes are leaves. Which traversal of this tree produces the sequence J, E, B, A, C, H, G, N, L, M, Q?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The given sequence is the preorder of the tree.
concept: A sequence that starts with the root and then goes deep into the left side before moving to the right is a preorder (N L R). Inorder puts the root in the middle, and level order lists both children of the root right after it.
work:
Tree:
J
├─ L: E
│  ├─ L: B
│  │  ├─ L: A
│  │  └─ R: C
│  └─ R: H
│     └─ L: G
└─ R: N
   ├─ L: L
   │  └─ R: M
   └─ R: Q
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(B) = B + Pre(A) + Pre(C) = B, A, C
Pre(H) = H + Pre(G) = H, G   [H has no right child]
Pre(E) = E + Pre(B) + Pre(H) = E, B, A, C, H, G
Pre(L) = L + Pre(M) = L, M   [L has no left child]
Pre(N) = N + Pre(L) + Pre(Q) = N, L, M, Q
Pre(J) = J + Pre(E) + Pre(N) = J, E, B, A, C, H, G, N, L, M, Q
Preorder: J, E, B, A, C, H, G, N, L, M, Q
Inorder (for comparison): A, B, C, E, G, H, J, L, M, N, Q
Level order (for comparison): J, E, N, B, H, L, Q, A, C, G, M
Only the preorder equals J, E, B, A, C, H, G, N, L, M, Q.
why: A — Wrong. Inorder would start with the leftmost node A and put J in the middle: A, B, C, E, G, H, J, L, M, N, Q.
B — Correct. Pre(E) = E, B, A, C, H, G and Pre(N) = N, L, M, Q, so the preorder is J, E, B, A, C, H, G, N, L, M, Q, which is the given sequence.
C — Wrong. Level order would list both of J's children next: J, E, N, B, H, L, Q, A, C, G, M.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root 9 has left child 4 and right child 7; 4 has only a right child 2; 7 has left child 6 and right child 8; 2 has left child 1 and right child 3; 8 has only a left child 5; all other nodes are leaves. What is the postorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The postorder is 1, 3, 2, 4, 6, 5, 8, 7, 9, which is not listed, so the answer is E.
concept: Postorder = left subtree, right subtree, node (L R N). Every node comes after all of its descendants, and the left child's whole subtree comes before the right child's subtree.
work:
Tree:
9
├─ L: 4
│  └─ R: 2
│     ├─ L: 1
│     └─ R: 3
└─ R: 7
   ├─ L: 6
   └─ R: 8
      └─ L: 5
Postorder = left subtree, then right subtree, then node (L R N). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Post(2) = Post(1) + Post(3) + 2 = 1, 3, 2
Post(4) = Post(2) + 4 = 1, 3, 2, 4   [4 has no left child]
Post(8) = Post(5) + 8 = 5, 8   [8 has no right child]
Post(7) = Post(6) + Post(8) + 7 = 6, 5, 8, 7
Post(9) = Post(4) + Post(7) + 9 = 1, 3, 2, 4, 6, 5, 8, 7, 9
Postorder: 1, 3, 2, 4, 6, 5, 8, 7, 9
This sequence is not any of A, B, C.
why: A — Wrong. This prints 8 before its child 5. In postorder a parent always comes after its children, so it must be 5, then 8.
B — Wrong. This prints 3 before 1. Both are children of 2, and the left child 1 must come before the right child 3.
C — Wrong. This prints 2 before its child 3. A parent must come after all of its children in postorder.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. The correct postorder is 1, 3, 2, 4, 6, 5, 8, 7, 9, which matches none of A, B, C.

q: Binary tree: Root 5 has left child 3 and right child 8; 3 has left child 1 and right child 4; 8 has left child 7 and right child 11; 1 has only a right child 2; 7 has only a left child 6; 11 has left child 9 and right child 12; all other nodes are leaves. What is the level-order (left to right) traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Level order reads {5}, {3, 8}, {1, 4, 7, 11}, {2, 6, 9, 12} from left to right.
concept: Level-order traversal visits the tree level by level from the top, reading each level from left to right. A queue does this naturally: remove the front node, visit it, and add its left and then right child at the back.
work:
Tree:
5
├─ L: 3
│  ├─ L: 1
│  │  └─ R: 2
│  └─ R: 4
└─ R: 8
   ├─ L: 7
   │  └─ L: 6
   └─ R: 11
      ├─ L: 9
      └─ R: 12
Level order reads the tree level by level, each level from left to right (a queue does this: take a node from the front, put its left child then its right child at the back).
Level 0: 5
Level 1: 3, 8
Level 2: 1, 4, 7, 11
Level 3: 2, 6, 9, 12
Level order: 5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 11, 2, 6, 9, 12
why: A — Wrong. This reads each level from RIGHT to left (5 | 8, 3 | 11, 7, 4, 1 | ...). Standard level order reads each level from left to right.
B — Wrong. 5, 3, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6, 11, 9, 12 is the preorder, a depth-first order.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root M has left child K and right child T; K has left child F and right child L; T has left child P and right child W; F has only a left child C; L has only a right child N; P has only a right child R; W has only a left child V; all other nodes are leaves. What is the postorder traversal?
opts: C, F, N, L, K, P, R, V, W, T, M
C, F, L, N, K, R, P, V, W, T, M
C, F, N, L, K, R, P, W, V, T, M
More than one of the above
exp: The postorder is C, F, N, L, K, R, P, V, W, T, M, which is not listed, so the answer is E.
concept: Postorder = left subtree, right subtree, node (L R N). Each node is printed only after all of its descendants, so a quick check is: no node may appear before any of its children.
work:
Tree:
M
├─ L: K
│  ├─ L: F
│  │  └─ L: C
│  └─ R: L
│     └─ R: N
└─ R: T
   ├─ L: P
   │  └─ R: R
   └─ R: W
      └─ L: V
Postorder = left subtree, then right subtree, then node (L R N). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Post(F) = Post(C) + F = C, F   [F has no right child]
Post(L) = Post(N) + L = N, L   [L has no left child]
Post(K) = Post(F) + Post(L) + K = C, F, N, L, K
Post(P) = Post(R) + P = R, P   [P has no left child]
Post(W) = Post(V) + W = V, W   [W has no right child]
Post(T) = Post(P) + Post(W) + T = R, P, V, W, T
Post(M) = Post(K) + Post(T) + M = C, F, N, L, K, R, P, V, W, T, M
Postorder: C, F, N, L, K, R, P, V, W, T, M
This sequence is not any of A, B, C.
why: A — Wrong. This prints P before its child R. In postorder a parent comes after its children, so it must be R, then P.
B — Wrong. This prints L before its child N. N is L's right child, so the order must be N, L.
C — Wrong. This prints W before its child V. V is W's left child, so the order must be V, W.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. The correct postorder is C, F, N, L, K, R, P, V, W, T, M, which matches none of A, B, C.
tip: Quick postorder check: every node must appear AFTER all of its children.

q: Binary tree: Root A has left child B and right child C; B has only a left child D; C has left child E and right child F; D has left child G and right child H; F has only a right child I; I has only a left child J; all other nodes are leaves. Which node is visited 5th in inorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A's left subtree has 4 nodes, so A is the 5th node in inorder.
concept: Inorder = left subtree, node, right subtree (L N R). The root's position in the inorder equals (number of nodes in its left subtree) + 1. Here the root A has 4 nodes in its left subtree, so A is visited 5th.
work:
Tree:
A
├─ L: B
│  └─ L: D
│     ├─ L: G
│     └─ R: H
└─ R: C
   ├─ L: E
   └─ R: F
      └─ R: I
         └─ L: J
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(D) = In(G) + D + In(H) = G, D, H
In(B) = In(D) + B = G, D, H, B   [B has no right child]
In(I) = In(J) + I = J, I   [I has no right child]
In(F) = F + In(I) = F, J, I   [F has no left child]
In(C) = In(E) + C + In(F) = E, C, F, J, I
In(A) = In(B) + A + In(C) = G, D, H, B, A, E, C, F, J, I
Inorder: G, D, H, B, A, E, C, F, J, I
Numbering the inorder: 1:G, 2:D, 3:H, 4:B, 5:A, 6:E, 7:C, 8:F, 9:J, 10:I
The 5th node visited is A.
why: A — Correct. The inorder is G, D, H, B, A, E, C, F, J, I. A's left subtree has 4 nodes (G, D, H, B), so A is the 5th node visited.
B — Wrong. B is the 4th node: it comes right after its left subtree G, D, H, and B has no right subtree.
C — Wrong. E is the 6th node, the first node of A's right subtree, visited just after A.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary tree: Root 1 has left child 2 and right child 3; 2 has left child 4 and right child 5; 3 has only a right child 6; 5 has only a left child 7; all other nodes are leaves. What does the call f(root) print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: f visits node, right, left, so it prints 1 3 6 2 5 7 4.
concept: A recursive traversal is defined by where the 'visit' (here printf) is placed relative to the two recursive calls. This f prints the node, then goes to the RIGHT subtree, then to the LEFT subtree (N R L). That is the preorder of the mirror image of the tree, and it is exactly the reverse of the postorder.
work:
Tree:
1
├─ L: 2
│  ├─ L: 4
│  └─ R: 5
│     └─ L: 7
└─ R: 3
   └─ R: 6
f prints the node FIRST, then calls f on the RIGHT subtree, then on the LEFT subtree (order N R L).
f(1): print 1; f(3); f(2)
  f(3): print 3; f(6) -> print 6 (6 is a leaf); f(NULL) returns   => 3 6
  f(2): print 2; f(5); f(4)
    f(5): print 5; f(NULL) returns; f(7) -> print 7   => 5 7
    f(4): print 4   => 4
  so f(2) prints 2 5 7 4
Output: 1 3 6 2 5 7 4
why: A — Wrong. 1 2 4 5 7 3 6 is the ordinary preorder (N L R). f visits the right subtree first, so 3 comes straight after 1.
B — Correct. N R L gives 1, then the right subtree (3, 6), then the left subtree (2, then its right part 5, 7, then 4): 1 3 6 2 5 7 4.
C — Wrong. 6 3 7 5 4 2 1 prints children before parents (right subtree, left subtree, node: R L N). f prints a node BEFORE its subtrees, so 1 must come first.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Node-Right-Left is the reverse of postorder: read f's output backwards and you get the postorder 4 7 5 2 6 3 1.

q: Binary tree (a zig-zag chain): Root 1 has only a left child 2; 2 has only a right child 3; 3 has only a left child 4; 4 has only a right child 5; 5 has only a left child 6; all other nodes are leaves. What is the inorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The inorder of the zig-zag chain is 2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 1, which is not listed.
concept: Inorder = left subtree, node, right subtree (L N R). In a zig-zag chain, a node whose only child is on the RIGHT is printed before that child's subtree, while a node whose only child is on the LEFT is printed after it. Work from the bottom up.
work:
Tree:
1
└─ L: 2
   └─ R: 3
      └─ L: 4
         └─ R: 5
            └─ L: 6
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(5) = In(6) + 5 = 6, 5   [5 has no right child]
In(4) = 4 + In(5) = 4, 6, 5   [4 has no left child]
In(3) = In(4) + 3 = 4, 6, 5, 3   [3 has no right child]
In(2) = 2 + In(3) = 2, 4, 6, 5, 3   [2 has no left child]
In(1) = In(2) + 1 = 2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 1   [1 has no right child]
Inorder: 2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 1
For comparison: preorder = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, postorder = 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
why: A — Wrong. 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 is the postorder of this chain (every node after its only child).
B — Wrong. This prints 5 before 6. But 6 is the LEFT child of 5, so inorder must print 6 first, then 5.
C — Wrong. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 is the preorder (every node before its only child).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. The inorder is 2, 4, 6, 5, 3, 1, which matches none of A, B, C.

q: Binary tree: Root 1 has left child 2 and right child 3; 2 has left child 4 and right child 5; all other nodes are leaves. What does the call g(root) print?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Each node is printed on arrival and again after its left subtree: 1 2 4 4 2 5 5 1 3 3.
concept: g prints each node twice: once when the node is first reached (its preorder position) and once more after its left subtree is finished (its inorder position). For a node with an empty left subtree the two prints come one right after the other.
work:
Tree:
1
├─ L: 2
│  ├─ L: 4
│  └─ R: 5
└─ R: 3
g prints the node, calls g(left), prints the node AGAIN, then calls g(right).
g(1): print 1 | g(2) | print 1 | g(3)
  g(2): print 2 | g(4) | print 2 | g(5)
    g(4): print 4 | g(NULL) | print 4 | g(NULL)  => 4 4
    g(5): print 5 | g(NULL) | print 5 | g(NULL)  => 5 5
    so g(2) prints 2 4 4 2 5 5
  g(3): print 3 | g(NULL) | print 3 | g(NULL)  => 3 3
Output: 1 | 2 4 4 2 5 5 | 1 | 3 3  =  1 2 4 4 2 5 5 1 3 3
why: A — Wrong. This has only 8 numbers. Each of the 5 nodes is printed twice, so the output must contain 10 numbers.
B — Wrong. This prints 5 5 before the second 2. But g(2) prints 2 again right after finishing its LEFT subtree (node 4), before it goes to the right subtree (node 5).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Keep only the first copy of each node → preorder 1 2 4 5 3; keep only the second copy → inorder 4 2 5 1 3.

q: Assuming all node labels are distinct, which pair of traversal sequences does NOT, in general, determine a unique binary tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Preorder + postorder cannot tell left children from right children; any pair that includes inorder can, so the answer is A.
concept: To rebuild a binary tree we must know, at each node, which nodes go to its left and which to its right. Inorder gives exactly this split once the root is known, and preorder, postorder or level order tell us the root. So inorder together with any one of the others fixes the tree (labels distinct). Preorder + postorder cannot tell whether a lone child is a left or a right child.
why: A — Correct. This pair does NOT always determine the tree. Example: preorder A, B and postorder B, A fit both 'B is the left child of A' and 'B is the right child of A'. So this option satisfies the stem.

B — Wrong. Inorder + level order DOES determine the tree: the first level-order node is the root, the inorder splits the remaining nodes into left and right parts, and each part keeps its level order. So it does not satisfy the stem.

C — Wrong. Inorder + postorder DOES determine the tree: the last postorder node is the root, the inorder splits the others into left and right parts, and this repeats. So it does not satisfy the stem.
D — Wrong. Only A fails to fix a unique tree; B and C both determine it, so there are not two such pairs.
E — Wrong. A really does fail to determine a unique tree, so there is an option that satisfies the stem.
tip: A unique tree needs INORDER plus one more traversal. Preorder + postorder works only for strictly binary (0-or-2 children) trees.

q: The inorder traversal of a binary tree is D, B, G, E, A, C, H, F and its preorder traversal is A, B, D, E, G, C, F, H. What is its postorder traversal?
opts: D, E, G, B, F, H, C, A
D, G, E, B, H, F, C, A
G, D, E, B, H, F, C, A
More than one of the above
exp: Rebuilding the tree and reading it left-right-node gives D, G, E, B, H, F, C, A.
concept: To rebuild a tree from preorder + inorder: the first preorder node is the root; find it in the inorder, and everything to its left forms the left subtree while everything to its right forms the right subtree. Repeat on each part. Then read the required traversal off the rebuilt tree.
work:
Rule: the first preorder node is the root; it splits the inorder into left part | right part. Repeat on each part.
Preorder [A, B, D, E, G, C, F, H] starts with A, so A is the root here. In inorder [D, B, G, E, A, C, H, F], left of A: {D, B, G, E}; right of A: {C, H, F}.
  Preorder [B, D, E, G] starts with B, so B is the root here. In inorder [D, B, G, E], left of B: {D}; right of B: {G, E}.
    Preorder [D] starts with D, so D is the root here. In inorder [D], left of D: nothing; right of D: nothing.
    Preorder [E, G] starts with E, so E is the root here. In inorder [G, E], left of E: {G}; right of E: nothing.
      Preorder [G] starts with G, so G is the root here. In inorder [G], left of G: nothing; right of G: nothing.
  Preorder [C, F, H] starts with C, so C is the root here. In inorder [C, H, F], left of C: nothing; right of C: {H, F}.
    Preorder [F, H] starts with F, so F is the root here. In inorder [H, F], left of F: {H}; right of F: nothing.
      Preorder [H] starts with H, so H is the root here. In inorder [H], left of H: nothing; right of H: nothing.
Tree:
A
├─ L: B
│  ├─ L: D
│  └─ R: E
│     └─ L: G
└─ R: C
   └─ R: F
      └─ L: H
Postorder = left subtree, then right subtree, then node (L R N). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Post(E) = Post(G) + E = G, E   [E has no right child]
Post(B) = Post(D) + Post(E) + B = D, G, E, B
Post(F) = Post(H) + F = H, F   [F has no right child]
Post(C) = Post(F) + C = H, F, C   [C has no left child]
Post(A) = Post(B) + Post(C) + A = D, G, E, B, H, F, C, A
Postorder: D, G, E, B, H, F, C, A
why: A — Wrong. This puts E before G. G is the LEFT child of E, so in postorder G must come before E.
B — Correct. The rebuilt tree is A → (B, C), B → (D, E), E has left child G, C has right child F, and F has left child H. Its postorder is D, G, E, B, H, F, C, A.
C — Wrong. This starts with G. But B's left subtree (just D) must be finished before its right subtree (G, E), so D comes before G.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The inorder traversal of a binary tree is 9, 2, 3, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 1 and its postorder traversal is 2, 9, 3, 6, 7, 4, 1, 5, 8. What is its preorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Rebuilding from postorder (root last) and inorder gives preorder 8, 3, 9, 2, 5, 7, 6, 1, 4.
concept: To rebuild a tree from postorder + inorder: the LAST postorder node is the root; it splits the inorder into the left subtree (before it) and the right subtree (after it). Repeat on each part. Then write the preorder (N L R).
work:
Rule: the LAST postorder node is the root; it splits the inorder into left part | right part. Repeat on each part.
Postorder [2, 9, 3, 6, 7, 4, 1, 5, 8] ends with 8, so 8 is the root here. In inorder [9, 2, 3, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 1], left of 8: {9, 2, 3}; right of 8: {7, 6, 5, 4, 1}.
  Postorder [2, 9, 3] ends with 3, so 3 is the root here. In inorder [9, 2, 3], left of 3: {9, 2}; right of 3: nothing.
    Postorder [2, 9] ends with 9, so 9 is the root here. In inorder [9, 2], left of 9: nothing; right of 9: {2}.
      Postorder [2] ends with 2, so 2 is the root here. In inorder [2], left of 2: nothing; right of 2: nothing.
  Postorder [6, 7, 4, 1, 5] ends with 5, so 5 is the root here. In inorder [7, 6, 5, 4, 1], left of 5: {7, 6}; right of 5: {4, 1}.
    Postorder [6, 7] ends with 7, so 7 is the root here. In inorder [7, 6], left of 7: nothing; right of 7: {6}.
      Postorder [6] ends with 6, so 6 is the root here. In inorder [6], left of 6: nothing; right of 6: nothing.
    Postorder [4, 1] ends with 1, so 1 is the root here. In inorder [4, 1], left of 1: {4}; right of 1: nothing.
      Postorder [4] ends with 4, so 4 is the root here. In inorder [4], left of 4: nothing; right of 4: nothing.
Tree:
8
├─ L: 3
│  └─ L: 9
│     └─ R: 2
└─ R: 5
   ├─ L: 7
   │  └─ R: 6
   └─ R: 1
      └─ L: 4
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(9) = 9 + Pre(2) = 9, 2   [9 has no left child]
Pre(3) = 3 + Pre(9) = 3, 9, 2   [3 has no right child]
Pre(7) = 7 + Pre(6) = 7, 6   [7 has no left child]
Pre(1) = 1 + Pre(4) = 1, 4   [1 has no right child]
Pre(5) = 5 + Pre(7) + Pre(1) = 5, 7, 6, 1, 4
Pre(8) = 8 + Pre(3) + Pre(5) = 8, 3, 9, 2, 5, 7, 6, 1, 4
Preorder: 8, 3, 9, 2, 5, 7, 6, 1, 4
why: A — Wrong. This prints 2 before 9, as if 2 were the parent. Actually 9 is the parent and 2 is its right child, so preorder gives 9, 2.
B — Wrong. The left part 8, 3, 9, 2 is right, but in the right part 7 is the parent of 6 and 1 is the parent of 4, so the correct order there is 5, 7, 6, 1, 4, not 5, 6, 7, 4, 1.
C — Correct. The tree is 8 → (3, 5), 3 has left child 9, 9 has right child 2, 5 → (7, 1), 7 has right child 6, 1 has left child 4. Preorder: 8, 3, 9, 2, 5, 7, 6, 1, 4.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The inorder traversal of a binary tree is A, B, C, D, E, F, H, I, J, K, M and its postorder traversal is A, C, B, E, F, D, I, J, M, K, H. What is the root of the left subtree of the root, and how many nodes are in the right subtree of the root?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The left subtree of root H is rooted at D, and the right subtree has 4 nodes.
concept: In postorder the root is the last node. Find it in the inorder: the nodes before it form the left subtree and the nodes after it form the right subtree. In the postorder, the left subtree's nodes come first as one block, and the last node of that block is the root of the left subtree.
work:
Rule: the LAST postorder node is the root; it splits the inorder into left part | right part.
Postorder [A, C, B, E, F, D, I, J, M, K, H] ends with H, so H is the root here. In inorder [A, B, C, D, E, F, H, I, J, K, M], left of H: {A, B, C, D, E, F}; right of H: {I, J, K, M}.
Left part in postorder order is A, C, B, E, F, D (the first 6 postorder entries); its last entry D is the root of the left subtree.
Right part {I, J, K, M} has 4 nodes.
Full reconstruction (for checking):
  Postorder [A, C, B, E, F, D] ends with D, so D is the root here. In inorder [A, B, C, D, E, F], left of D: {A, B, C}; right of D: {E, F}.
    Postorder [A, C, B] ends with B, so B is the root here. In inorder [A, B, C], left of B: {A}; right of B: {C}.
      Postorder [A] ends with A, so A is the root here. In inorder [A], left of A: nothing; right of A: nothing.
      Postorder [C] ends with C, so C is the root here. In inorder [C], left of C: nothing; right of C: nothing.
    Postorder [E, F] ends with F, so F is the root here. In inorder [E, F], left of F: {E}; right of F: nothing.
      Postorder [E] ends with E, so E is the root here. In inorder [E], left of E: nothing; right of E: nothing.
  Postorder [I, J, M, K] ends with K, so K is the root here. In inorder [I, J, K, M], left of K: {I, J}; right of K: {M}.
    Postorder [I, J] ends with J, so J is the root here. In inorder [I, J], left of J: {I}; right of J: nothing.
      Postorder [I] ends with I, so I is the root here. In inorder [I], left of I: nothing; right of I: nothing.
    Postorder [M] ends with M, so M is the root here. In inorder [M], left of M: nothing; right of M: nothing.
Tree:
H
├─ L: D
│  ├─ L: B
│  │  ├─ L: A
│  │  └─ R: C
│  └─ R: F
│     └─ L: E
└─ R: K
   ├─ L: J
   │  └─ L: I
   └─ R: M
Root of left subtree = D; nodes in right subtree = 4 -> option A.
why: A — Correct. Root H splits the inorder into {A, B, C, D, E, F} and {I, J, K, M}. The left block of the postorder is A, C, B, E, F, D, which ends with D, so D is the left subtree's root; the right subtree has 4 nodes.
B — Wrong. B is the root of D's left subtree, one level lower; it is not the root of H's left subtree. The count 4 is right, but the root is wrong.
C — Wrong. D is right, but the right subtree {I, J, K, M} has 4 nodes, not 5. Counting the root H as well would give 5.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The inorder traversal of a binary tree is 2, 5, 4, 6, 7, 1, 8, 3 and its preorder traversal is 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 3, 8. Taking height as the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path, what is the height of the tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The longest root-to-leaf path is 1-2-4-6-7 with 4 edges, so the height is 4.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. First rebuild the tree from preorder + inorder (first preorder node = root; inorder splits left and right), then find the deepest node.
work:
Rule: the first preorder node is the root; it splits the inorder into left part | right part.
Preorder [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 3, 8] starts with 1, so 1 is the root here. In inorder [2, 5, 4, 6, 7, 1, 8, 3], left of 1: {2, 5, 4, 6, 7}; right of 1: {8, 3}.
  Preorder [2, 4, 5, 6, 7] starts with 2, so 2 is the root here. In inorder [2, 5, 4, 6, 7], left of 2: nothing; right of 2: {5, 4, 6, 7}.
    Preorder [4, 5, 6, 7] starts with 4, so 4 is the root here. In inorder [5, 4, 6, 7], left of 4: {5}; right of 4: {6, 7}.
      Preorder [5] starts with 5, so 5 is the root here. In inorder [5], left of 5: nothing; right of 5: nothing.
      Preorder [6, 7] starts with 6, so 6 is the root here. In inorder [6, 7], left of 6: nothing; right of 6: {7}.
        Preorder [7] starts with 7, so 7 is the root here. In inorder [7], left of 7: nothing; right of 7: nothing.
  Preorder [3, 8] starts with 3, so 3 is the root here. In inorder [8, 3], left of 3: {8}; right of 3: nothing.
    Preorder [8] starts with 8, so 8 is the root here. In inorder [8], left of 8: nothing; right of 8: nothing.
Tree:
1
├─ L: 2
│  └─ R: 4
│     ├─ L: 5
│     └─ R: 6
│        └─ R: 7
└─ R: 3
   └─ L: 8
Depths: 1 = 0; 2, 3 = 1; 4, 8 = 2; 5, 6 = 3; 7 = 4.
Longest root-to-leaf path 1-2-4-6-7 has 4 edges, so height = 4.
why: A — Wrong. Height 3 misses the deepest node 7, which is at depth 4 (path 1-2-4-6-7).
B — Correct. The rebuilt tree is 1 → (2, 3), 2 has right child 4, 4 → (5, 6), 6 has right child 7, 3 has left child 8. The longest path 1-2-4-6-7 has 4 edges.
C — Wrong. 5 counts the NODES on the longest path (1, 2, 4, 6, 7) instead of the edges. The question counts edges, so the height is 4.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The inorder traversal of a binary tree is U, S, X, V, Y, R, W, Z, T and its preorder traversal is R, S, U, V, X, Y, T, W, Z. Which of the following is true about this tree?
opts: The parent of Z is W
Node T has only a left child
More than one of the above
exp: The rebuilt tree makes all three statements true, so the answer is D.
concept: To rebuild a tree from preorder + inorder: the first preorder node is the root; in the inorder, the nodes to its left form the left subtree and the nodes to its right form the right subtree. Repeat on each part, then check each statement against the rebuilt tree.
work:
Rule: the first preorder node is the root; it splits the inorder into left part | right part.
Preorder [R, S, U, V, X, Y, T, W, Z] starts with R, so R is the root here. In inorder [U, S, X, V, Y, R, W, Z, T], left of R: {U, S, X, V, Y}; right of R: {W, Z, T}.
  Preorder [S, U, V, X, Y] starts with S, so S is the root here. In inorder [U, S, X, V, Y], left of S: {U}; right of S: {X, V, Y}.
    Preorder [U] starts with U, so U is the root here. In inorder [U], left of U: nothing; right of U: nothing.
    Preorder [V, X, Y] starts with V, so V is the root here. In inorder [X, V, Y], left of V: {X}; right of V: {Y}.
      Preorder [X] starts with X, so X is the root here. In inorder [X], left of X: nothing; right of X: nothing.
      Preorder [Y] starts with Y, so Y is the root here. In inorder [Y], left of Y: nothing; right of Y: nothing.
  Preorder [T, W, Z] starts with T, so T is the root here. In inorder [W, Z, T], left of T: {W, Z}; right of T: nothing.
    Preorder [W, Z] starts with W, so W is the root here. In inorder [W, Z], left of W: nothing; right of W: {Z}.
      Preorder [Z] starts with Z, so Z is the root here. In inorder [Z], left of Z: nothing; right of Z: nothing.
Tree:
R
├─ L: S
│  ├─ L: U
│  └─ R: V
│     ├─ L: X
│     └─ R: Y
└─ R: T
   └─ L: W
      └─ R: Z
A: Z is the right child of W, so parent(Z) = W -> true.
B: T has left child W and no right child -> true.
C: leaves are U, X, Y, Z = 4 -> true.
All three true -> D.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In T's part (preorder T, W, Z; inorder W, Z, T), W is T's left child, and Z comes after W in the inorder, so Z is W's right child: parent(Z) = W.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In the inorder, T is the last node of R's right part (W, Z, T), so all the other nodes of that part are to T's left. T therefore has only a left child, W.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The nodes with no children are U, X, Y and Z: 4 leaves.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: The inorder traversal of a binary tree is 60, 20, 30, 10, 50, 40, 80, 70, 90 and its preorder traversal is 50, 10, 20, 60, 30, 40, 70, 80, 90. What is its level-order traversal (left to right)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The rebuilt tree has levels {50}, {10, 40}, {20, 70}, {60, 30, 80, 90}, so the level order is option A.
concept: First rebuild the tree from preorder + inorder (the first preorder node is the root; the inorder splits the rest into left and right parts; repeat). Then list the nodes level by level, reading each level from left to right.
work:
Rule: the first preorder node is the root; it splits the inorder into left part | right part.
Preorder [50, 10, 20, 60, 30, 40, 70, 80, 90] starts with 50, so 50 is the root here. In inorder [60, 20, 30, 10, 50, 40, 80, 70, 90], left of 50: {60, 20, 30, 10}; right of 50: {40, 80, 70, 90}.
  Preorder [10, 20, 60, 30] starts with 10, so 10 is the root here. In inorder [60, 20, 30, 10], left of 10: {60, 20, 30}; right of 10: nothing.
    Preorder [20, 60, 30] starts with 20, so 20 is the root here. In inorder [60, 20, 30], left of 20: {60}; right of 20: {30}.
      Preorder [60] starts with 60, so 60 is the root here. In inorder [60], left of 60: nothing; right of 60: nothing.
      Preorder [30] starts with 30, so 30 is the root here. In inorder [30], left of 30: nothing; right of 30: nothing.
  Preorder [40, 70, 80, 90] starts with 40, so 40 is the root here. In inorder [40, 80, 70, 90], left of 40: nothing; right of 40: {80, 70, 90}.
    Preorder [70, 80, 90] starts with 70, so 70 is the root here. In inorder [80, 70, 90], left of 70: {80}; right of 70: {90}.
      Preorder [80] starts with 80, so 80 is the root here. In inorder [80], left of 80: nothing; right of 80: nothing.
      Preorder [90] starts with 90, so 90 is the root here. In inorder [90], left of 90: nothing; right of 90: nothing.
Tree:
50
├─ L: 10
│  └─ L: 20
│     ├─ L: 60
│     └─ R: 30
└─ R: 40
   └─ R: 70
      ├─ L: 80
      └─ R: 90
Level order reads the tree level by level, each level from left to right (a queue does this: take a node from the front, put its left child then its right child at the back).
Level 0: 50
Level 1: 10, 40
Level 2: 20, 70
Level 3: 60, 30, 80, 90
Level order: 50, 10, 40, 20, 70, 60, 30, 80, 90
why: B — Wrong. This lists 20 before 40. But 40 is the root's right child (level 1) while 20 is 10's child (level 2), and level order finishes level 1 before starting level 2.
C — Wrong. This reads every level from RIGHT to left. Level order reads each level from left to right.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A strictly binary tree (every node has 0 or 2 children) has preorder A, B, D, E, F, G, C, H, I and postorder D, F, G, E, B, H, I, C, A. What is its inorder traversal?
opts: D, B, E, F, G, A, H, C, I
B, D, F, E, G, A, H, C, I
D, B, F, E, G, A, H, C, I
More than one of the above
exp: For a strictly binary tree, preorder + postorder fix the tree; its inorder is D, B, F, E, G, A, H, C, I.
concept: Preorder + postorder usually do NOT fix a binary tree, but they DO when the tree is strictly binary (every node has 0 or 2 children). Then the node right after the root in preorder must be the root's left child; find it in the postorder, and everything up to and including it there forms the left subtree.
work:
Because every internal node has exactly 2 children, the node right after the root in preorder must be the LEFT child, and in postorder the left subtree ends exactly at that node.
Root A (first in preorder [A, B, D, E, F, G, C, H, I]). Next preorder node B is the root of the LEFT subtree. In postorder [D, F, G, E, B, H, I, C, A], B ends the left subtree: left = {D, F, G, E, B}, right = {H, I, C}.
  Root B (first in preorder [B, D, E, F, G]). Next preorder node D is the root of the LEFT subtree. In postorder [D, F, G, E, B], D ends the left subtree: left = {D}, right = {F, G, E}.
    D alone -> leaf.
    Root E (first in preorder [E, F, G]). Next preorder node F is the root of the LEFT subtree. In postorder [F, G, E], F ends the left subtree: left = {F}, right = {G}.
      F alone -> leaf.
      G alone -> leaf.
  Root C (first in preorder [C, H, I]). Next preorder node H is the root of the LEFT subtree. In postorder [H, I, C], H ends the left subtree: left = {H}, right = {I}.
    H alone -> leaf.
    I alone -> leaf.
Tree:
A
├─ L: B
│  ├─ L: D
│  └─ R: E
│     ├─ L: F
│     └─ R: G
└─ R: C
   ├─ L: H
   └─ R: I
Inorder = left subtree, then node, then right subtree (L N R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
In(E) = In(F) + E + In(G) = F, E, G
In(B) = In(D) + B + In(E) = D, B, F, E, G
In(C) = In(H) + C + In(I) = H, C, I
In(A) = In(B) + A + In(C) = D, B, F, E, G, A, H, C, I
Inorder: D, B, F, E, G, A, H, C, I
why: A — Wrong. This puts E before F. F is E's LEFT child, so inorder must print F, then E, then G.
B — Wrong. This puts B before D. D is B's left child, so D must come first in inorder.
C — Correct. The rebuilt tree is A → (B, C), B → (D, E), E → (F, G), C → (H, I). Its inorder is D, B, F, E, G, A, H, C, I.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many different binary trees have preorder traversal A, B, C and postorder traversal C, B, A?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The tree must be the chain A-B-C, and each of the two links can go left or right, so there are 4 trees (not listed).
concept: Preorder and postorder together cannot tell whether a lone child is on the left or the right. If the tree is a chain in which every internal node has exactly one child, each of those children can independently be a left or a right child, so several different trees share the same preorder and postorder.
work:
Preorder A, B, C: A is the root. Postorder C, B, A: A is last (consistent).
If A had two children, they would be the leaves B (left) and C (right), giving postorder B, C, A. The given postorder is C, B, A, so A has exactly ONE child, B (the next node in preorder).
B's subtree then holds B and C, with C below B: B has exactly one child, C. The tree is a chain A - B - C.
Choices: B is the left or right child of A (2 ways); C is the left or right child of B (2 ways).
The 4 trees:
1) A
   └─ L: B
      └─ L: C
2) A
   └─ L: B
      └─ R: C
3) A
   └─ R: B
      └─ L: C
4) A
   └─ R: B
      └─ R: C
All four give preorder A, B, C and postorder C, B, A. Count = 2 x 2 = 4, not in A-C -> E.
why: A — Wrong. 1 would be right only for a strictly binary tree. Here A and B each have a single child, and each such child can be on either side.
B — Wrong. 2 counts only the choice for B (left or right of A) and forgets that C can also be either a left or a right child of B.
C — Wrong. 3 does not match the count: the two independent left/right choices give 2 × 2 = 4 trees.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. There are 2 × 2 = 4 such trees, and 4 is not given in A, B or C.

q: Which condition defines a binary search tree (all keys distinct)?
opts: For every node X, every key in X's left subtree is smaller than X and every key in X's right subtree is larger than X
For every node X, its left child (if any) is smaller than X and its right child (if any) is larger than X
For every node X, the key of X is larger than the keys of both of its children
More than one of the above
exp: In a BST, every key in a node's left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger.
concept: A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree in which, for every node X, ALL keys in X's left subtree are smaller than X and ALL keys in X's right subtree are larger. Because of this, an inorder traversal lists the keys in sorted order, and a search can throw away one whole subtree at every step.
why: A — Correct. This is the BST property. It is about the whole subtrees, not only the immediate children.

B — Wrong. Checking only the immediate children is not enough. Example: 10 with left child 5, and 5 with right child 15. Every parent-child pair passes B, but 15 sits in 10's left subtree, so a search for 15 would go right at 10 and never find it.
C — Wrong. A node larger than both of its children is the max-heap property. A heap is a different structure, used for priority queues, not for searching.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: BST rule = whole subtrees. Checking only children is the classic trap.

q: For a binary search tree with n nodes, what is the average-case search time when the keys were inserted in random order, and the worst-case search time when the keys were inserted in sorted order?
opts: O(log n) and O(n log n)
More than one of the above
exp: Random insertion order gives O(log n) average search; sorted insertion order gives a chain and O(n) search.
concept: Searching a BST takes time proportional to its height. If keys are inserted in random order, the average depth of a node is about 2·ln n ≈ 1.39·log2 n (and the expected height is also O(log n)), so the average search is O(log n). If the keys are inserted in sorted order, each new key goes to the right of the previous one, giving a chain of height n − 1, so the worst-case search is O(n).
why: A — Wrong. This swaps the two cases. Random order gives a bushy tree, O(log n); sorted order gives a chain, O(n).
B — Correct. Average O(log n) when keys arrive in random order; worst case O(n) when sorted input builds a skewed chain.
C — Wrong. O(n log n) is about the time to BUILD a BST by n insertions (on average), not the time for one search. A single search can never cost more than O(n), the number of nodes.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Given only the preorder traversal of a binary search tree with distinct keys, the tree:
opts: Can be reconstructed uniquely, because its inorder traversal is simply the keys in sorted order
Cannot be reconstructed unless the postorder traversal is also given
Can be reconstructed uniquely only if the tree is complete
More than one of the above
exp: A BST's inorder is its sorted keys, so its preorder alone rebuilds it uniquely.
concept: For a BST with distinct keys, the inorder traversal is simply the keys in sorted order. So the preorder alone is enough: sort the keys to get the inorder, then rebuild from preorder + inorder. An even simpler way is to insert the preorder keys one by one into an empty BST; this gives back the same tree.
why: A — Correct. Sorting the keys gives the inorder for free, and preorder + inorder determines a binary tree uniquely. So the BST can be rebuilt.
B — Wrong. The postorder is not needed. For a BST, the preorder alone already fixes the tree (and so does the postorder alone).
C — Wrong. Completeness is not needed. A BST of any shape can be rebuilt from its preorder.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is/are true for every binary search tree with distinct keys?
opts: Inorder traversal lists the keys in ascending order
The minimum key is found by following left pointers from the root until a node with no left child is reached
The node with the maximum key is always a leaf
More than one of the above
exp: Sorted inorder (A) and 'go left for the minimum' (B) always hold, but the maximum need not be a leaf, so the answer is D.
concept: In a BST, smaller keys are always to the left and larger keys to the right. So the inorder (L N R) lists the keys in ascending order, the minimum is the leftmost node (keep going left), and the maximum is the rightmost node (keep going right). The rightmost node has no RIGHT child, but it may still have a LEFT child.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Inorder visits the left subtree (smaller keys), then the node, then the right subtree (larger keys), so the keys come out in ascending order.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The minimum has nothing smaller than it, so it has no left child; going left from the root until there is no left child reaches it.
C — Wrong. The maximum has no right child, but it may have a left child. Example: insert 50, 70, 60. The maximum 70 has left child 60, so 70 is not a leaf.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: The keys 45, 28, 67, 12, 35, 52, 80, 31 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree (no balancing). What is the preorder traversal of the resulting tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Inserting the keys builds 45 → (28, 67) with 31 under 35; its preorder is 45, 28, 12, 35, 31, 67, 52, 80.
concept: To insert into a BST: start at the root; if the new key is smaller go left, otherwise go right; repeat until you reach an empty place and put the key there. The insertion order decides the shape of the tree. Preorder then lists node, left subtree, right subtree (N L R).
work:
Insert each key: start at the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty spot is found.
insert 45: tree empty, 45 becomes the root
insert 28: compare 45; becomes left child of 45
insert 67: compare 45; becomes right child of 45
insert 12: compare 45 -> 28; becomes left child of 28
insert 35: compare 45 -> 28; becomes right child of 28
insert 52: compare 45 -> 67; becomes left child of 67
insert 80: compare 45 -> 67; becomes right child of 67
insert 31: compare 45 -> 28 -> 35; becomes left child of 35
Final tree:
45
├─ L: 28
│  ├─ L: 12
│  └─ R: 35
│     └─ L: 31
└─ R: 67
   ├─ L: 52
   └─ R: 80
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(35) = 35 + Pre(31) = 35, 31   [35 has no right child]
