Pre(28) = 28 + Pre(12) + Pre(35) = 28, 12, 35, 31
Pre(67) = 67 + Pre(52) + Pre(80) = 67, 52, 80
Pre(45) = 45 + Pre(28) + Pre(67) = 45, 28, 12, 35, 31, 67, 52, 80
Preorder: 45, 28, 12, 35, 31, 67, 52, 80
why: B — Wrong. This is just the insertion order (here it is also the level order). Preorder goes deep into the left subtree first, so 12 comes before 67.
C — Wrong. This prints 31 before 35. 31 is 35's LEFT child, so in preorder 35 comes first, then 31. (31, 35 is the inorder order of these two.)
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The keys 40, 25, 60, 10, 30, 55, 70, 5, 27, 35, 33 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree (no balancing). Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. What is the height of the tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The deepest node 33 is 4 edges below the root, so the height is 4.
concept: Convention used here: height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. Build the BST by inserting the keys one at a time (smaller → left, larger → right), then find the deepest node.
work:
Insert each key: start at the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty spot is found.
insert 40: tree empty, 40 becomes the root
insert 25: compare 40; becomes left child of 40
insert 60: compare 40; becomes right child of 40
insert 10: compare 40 -> 25; becomes left child of 25
insert 30: compare 40 -> 25; becomes right child of 25
insert 55: compare 40 -> 60; becomes left child of 60
insert 70: compare 40 -> 60; becomes right child of 60
insert 5: compare 40 -> 25 -> 10; becomes left child of 10
insert 27: compare 40 -> 25 -> 30; becomes left child of 30
insert 35: compare 40 -> 25 -> 30; becomes right child of 30
insert 33: compare 40 -> 25 -> 30 -> 35; becomes left child of 35
Final tree:
40
├─ L: 25
│  ├─ L: 10
│  │  └─ L: 5
│  └─ R: 30
│     ├─ L: 27
│     └─ R: 35
│        └─ L: 33
└─ R: 60
   ├─ L: 55
   └─ R: 70
Depths: 40 = 0; 25, 60 = 1; 10, 30, 55, 70 = 2; 5, 27, 35 = 3; 33 = 4.
Deepest node 33 (path 40-25-30-35-33, 4 edges), so height = 4.
why: A — Wrong. 3 is the depth of 5, 27 and 35, but 33 was inserted below 35, one level deeper.
B — Wrong. 5 counts the NODES on the longest path 40-25-30-35-33 instead of its edges. The question counts edges, so the height is 4.
C — Correct. The deepest node is 33, reached by 40 → 25 → 30 → 35 → 33: 4 edges, so the height is 4.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The keys 15, 10, 20, 8, 12, 17, 25, 6, 11, 13 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree (no balancing). Which node is the parent of 11?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 11 goes 15 → 10 → 12 and becomes 12's left child, so its parent is 12.
concept: A new key in a BST always becomes a leaf. Its parent is the last node visited on its search path, the node where the path stopped because the child it needed was empty.
work:
Insert each key: start at the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty spot is found.
insert 15: tree empty, 15 becomes the root
insert 10: compare 15; becomes left child of 15
insert 20: compare 15; becomes right child of 15
insert 8: compare 15 -> 10; becomes left child of 10
insert 12: compare 15 -> 10; becomes right child of 10
insert 17: compare 15 -> 20; becomes left child of 20
insert 25: compare 15 -> 20; becomes right child of 20
insert 6: compare 15 -> 10 -> 8; becomes left child of 8
insert 11: compare 15 -> 10 -> 12; becomes left child of 12
insert 13: compare 15 -> 10 -> 12; becomes right child of 12
Final tree:
15
├─ L: 10
│  ├─ L: 8
│  │  └─ L: 6
│  └─ R: 12
│     ├─ L: 11
│     └─ R: 13
└─ R: 20
   ├─ L: 17
   └─ R: 25
11 was attached as the left child of 12, so parent(11) = 12.
why: A — Wrong. 10 is on the path (15 → 10 → 12), but at 10 the key 11 goes right, to 12, which already exists, so the path continues past 10.
B — Correct. 15 → 10 (11 < 15) → 12 (11 > 10) → the empty left spot of 12 (11 < 12). So 11 becomes 12's left child.
C — Wrong. 13 is 12's right child, a sibling of 11, not its parent. 13 is also inserted after 11.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The keys 30, 50, 20, 40, 10, 45, 25, 60, 35 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree (no balancing). What is the level-order traversal (left to right) of the resulting tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The final tree's levels are {30}, {20, 50}, {10, 25, 40, 60}, {35, 45}, giving option B.
concept: Build the BST by inserting the keys in the given order, then read the final tree level by level, each level from left to right. The level order depends on the final tree, not on the order in which keys were inserted.
work:
Insert each key: start at the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty spot is found.
insert 30: tree empty, 30 becomes the root
insert 50: compare 30; becomes right child of 30
insert 20: compare 30; becomes left child of 30
insert 40: compare 30 -> 50; becomes left child of 50
insert 10: compare 30 -> 20; becomes left child of 20
insert 45: compare 30 -> 50 -> 40; becomes right child of 40
insert 25: compare 30 -> 20; becomes right child of 20
insert 60: compare 30 -> 50; becomes right child of 50
insert 35: compare 30 -> 50 -> 40; becomes left child of 40
Final tree:
30
├─ L: 20
│  ├─ L: 10
│  └─ R: 25
└─ R: 50
   ├─ L: 40
   │  ├─ L: 35
   │  └─ R: 45
   └─ R: 60
Level order reads the tree level by level, each level from left to right (a queue does this: take a node from the front, put its left child then its right child at the back).
Level 0: 30
Level 1: 20, 50
Level 2: 10, 25, 40, 60
Level 3: 35, 45
Level order: 30, 20, 50, 10, 25, 40, 60, 35, 45
why: A — Wrong. This is just the insertion order. In level order each level is read from left to right, so 20 (left child of 30) must come before 50 (right child).
C — Wrong. This lists 45 before 35 on the last level. 35 is 40's LEFT child and 45 its right child, so 35 comes first.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The keys 62, 31, 85, 17, 48, 70, 93, 40, 55, 74 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree (no balancing). How many leaf nodes does the resulting tree have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The leaves are 17, 40, 55, 74 and 93, five in all, which is not listed.
concept: Build the BST by inserting the keys in order (smaller → left, larger → right). Then count the leaves, the nodes with no children. Leaves can be on different levels, so check every node, not only the deepest ones.
work:
Insert each key: start at the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty spot is found.
insert 62: tree empty, 62 becomes the root
insert 31: compare 62; becomes left child of 62
insert 85: compare 62; becomes right child of 62
insert 17: compare 62 -> 31; becomes left child of 31
insert 48: compare 62 -> 31; becomes right child of 31
insert 70: compare 62 -> 85; becomes left child of 85
insert 93: compare 62 -> 85; becomes right child of 85
insert 40: compare 62 -> 31 -> 48; becomes left child of 48
insert 55: compare 62 -> 31 -> 48; becomes right child of 48
insert 74: compare 62 -> 85 -> 70; becomes right child of 70
Final tree:
62
├─ L: 31
│  ├─ L: 17
│  └─ R: 48
│     ├─ L: 40
│     └─ R: 55
└─ R: 85
   ├─ L: 70
   │  └─ R: 74
   └─ R: 93
Leaves (no children): 17, 40, 55, 74, 93 -> 5 leaves. 5 is not among 4, 6, 3 -> E.
why: A — Wrong. 4 misses one of the 5 leaves (17, 40, 55, 74, 93). For example, 17 and 93 are easy to forget because they were inserted early, yet nothing was ever placed below them.
B — Wrong. 6 would also count 70 as a leaf, but 70 has a right child (74), so it is an internal node.
C — Wrong. 3 counts only the leaves on the deepest level (40, 55, 74). 17 and 93 have no children either.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. The tree has 5 leaves (17, 40, 55, 74, 93), and 5 is not given in A, B or C.

q: The keys 70, 35, 90, 20, 50, 80, 95, 45, 60, 47 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree (no balancing). Which sequence of nodes is examined when searching for 47?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The search for 47 visits 70, 35, 50, 45, 47.
concept: To search a BST, compare the key with the current node: if equal, stop; if smaller, go left; if larger, go right. The search examines exactly the nodes on the path from the root down to the key.
work:
Insert each key: start at the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty spot is found.
insert 70: tree empty, 70 becomes the root
insert 35: compare 70; becomes left child of 70
insert 90: compare 70; becomes right child of 70
insert 20: compare 70 -> 35; becomes left child of 35
insert 50: compare 70 -> 35; becomes right child of 35
insert 80: compare 70 -> 90; becomes left child of 90
insert 95: compare 70 -> 90; becomes right child of 90
insert 45: compare 70 -> 35 -> 50; becomes left child of 50
insert 60: compare 70 -> 35 -> 50; becomes right child of 50
insert 47: compare 70 -> 35 -> 50 -> 45; becomes right child of 45
Final tree:
70
├─ L: 35
│  ├─ L: 20
│  └─ R: 50
│     ├─ L: 45
│     │  └─ R: 47
│     └─ R: 60
└─ R: 90
   ├─ L: 80
   └─ R: 95
Search 47: at 70, 47 < 70 go left -> 35; 47 > 35 go right -> 50; 47 < 50 go left -> 45; 47 > 45 go right -> 47 found.
Nodes examined: 70, 35, 50, 45, 47
why: A — Correct. 47 < 70 → left to 35; 47 > 35 → right to 50; 47 < 50 → left to 45; 47 > 45 → right to 47. Path: 70, 35, 50, 45, 47.
B — Wrong. This skips 50. 45 is not a child of 35; it is 50's left child, so the search must pass through 50.
C — Wrong. This skips 35. 50 is not a child of 70; the root's left child is 35, so 35 is examined first.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The preorder traversal of a binary search tree is 40, 20, 10, 30, 25, 35, 60, 50, 70, 65. What is its postorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Rebuilding the BST from its preorder and reading left-right-node gives 10, 25, 35, 30, 20, 50, 65, 70, 60, 40.
concept: The preorder of a BST fixes the tree: insert the keys in preorder order into an empty BST (equivalently: the first key is the root, the smaller keys form the left subtree and the larger keys the right subtree, recursively). Then write the postorder (L R N).
work:
Inserting the preorder keys one by one into an empty BST rebuilds the same BST (every node comes after its ancestors in preorder).
insert 40: tree empty, 40 becomes the root
insert 20: compare 40; becomes left child of 40
insert 10: compare 40 -> 20; becomes left child of 20
insert 30: compare 40 -> 20; becomes right child of 20
insert 25: compare 40 -> 20 -> 30; becomes left child of 30
insert 35: compare 40 -> 20 -> 30; becomes right child of 30
insert 60: compare 40; becomes right child of 40
insert 50: compare 40 -> 60; becomes left child of 60
insert 70: compare 40 -> 60; becomes right child of 60
insert 65: compare 40 -> 60 -> 70; becomes left child of 70
Tree:
40
├─ L: 20
│  ├─ L: 10
│  └─ R: 30
│     ├─ L: 25
│     └─ R: 35
└─ R: 60
   ├─ L: 50
   └─ R: 70
      └─ L: 65
Postorder = left subtree, then right subtree, then node (L R N). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Post(30) = Post(25) + Post(35) + 30 = 25, 35, 30
Post(20) = Post(10) + Post(30) + 20 = 10, 25, 35, 30, 20
Post(70) = Post(65) + 70 = 65, 70   [70 has no right child]
Post(60) = Post(50) + Post(70) + 60 = 50, 65, 70, 60
Post(40) = Post(20) + Post(60) + 40 = 10, 25, 35, 30, 20, 50, 65, 70, 60, 40
Postorder: 10, 25, 35, 30, 20, 50, 65, 70, 60, 40
why: A — Wrong. 10, 20, 25, ..., 70 is the keys in sorted order, which is the INORDER of any BST, not the postorder.
B — Wrong. This prints 30 before its child 35. In postorder 30 must come after both of its children, 25 and 35.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The postorder traversal of a binary search tree is 5, 15, 12, 25, 22, 20, 35, 45, 40, 30. What is its preorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The rebuilt BST has preorder 30, 20, 12, 5, 15, 22, 25, 40, 35, 45, which is not listed.
concept: The postorder of a BST fixes the tree: the last key is the root; the keys smaller than it (which appear first) form the left subtree and the larger keys form the right subtree, each still in postorder. Repeat on each part, then write the preorder (N L R).
work:
Root = last postorder key = 30. Keys < 30 form the left subtree, keys > 30 the right subtree; each part keeps its postorder order.
Left part (postorder): 5, 15, 12, 25, 22, 20 -> its root is 20 (last). Keys < 20: 5, 15, 12 ; keys > 20: 25, 22.
  5, 15, 12 -> root 12; left 5, right 15.
  25, 22 -> root 22; 25 > 22 so 25 is the right child of 22.
Right part (postorder): 35, 45, 40 -> root 40; left 35, right 45.
Tree:
30
├─ L: 20
│  ├─ L: 12
│  │  ├─ L: 5
│  │  └─ R: 15
│  └─ R: 22
│     └─ R: 25
└─ R: 40
   ├─ L: 35
   └─ R: 45
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(12) = 12 + Pre(5) + Pre(15) = 12, 5, 15
Pre(22) = 22 + Pre(25) = 22, 25   [22 has no left child]
Pre(20) = 20 + Pre(12) + Pre(22) = 20, 12, 5, 15, 22, 25
Pre(40) = 40 + Pre(35) + Pre(45) = 40, 35, 45
Pre(30) = 30 + Pre(20) + Pre(40) = 30, 20, 12, 5, 15, 22, 25, 40, 35, 45
Preorder: 30, 20, 12, 5, 15, 22, 25, 40, 35, 45
This is not any of A, B, C (A has 25, 22 instead of 22, 25; B and C put wrong nodes at the top of a subtree).
why: A — Wrong. This prints 25 before 22. 25 is 22's RIGHT child, so in preorder 22 comes first, then 25.
B — Wrong. This makes 5 the root of 20's left subtree. But that subtree's postorder 5, 15, 12 ends with 12, so 12 is its root and preorder must give 12, 5, 15.
C — Wrong. This makes 12 the root's left child. But the left part's postorder (5, 15, 12, 25, 22, 20) ends with 20, so 20 is the root's left child.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. The correct preorder is 30, 20, 12, 5, 15, 22, 25, 40, 35, 45, which matches none of A, B, C.

q: The keys 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 65, 75 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree (no balancing). The root 50 is then deleted, replacing it by its inorder successor. What is the preorder traversal of the resulting tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Deleting 50 brings its successor 60 to the root and moves 65 up; the preorder is 60, 30, 20, 40, 70, 65, 80, 75.
concept: To delete a BST node that has two children: replace its key by its inorder successor (the smallest key in its right subtree: go right once, then left as far as possible), then remove that successor from its old place. The successor has no left child, so removing it is easy: its right child, if any, moves up into its place.
work:
Insert each key: start at the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty spot is found.
insert 50: tree empty, 50 becomes the root
insert 30: compare 50; becomes left child of 50
insert 70: compare 50; becomes right child of 50
insert 20: compare 50 -> 30; becomes left child of 30
insert 40: compare 50 -> 30; becomes right child of 30
insert 60: compare 50 -> 70; becomes left child of 70
insert 80: compare 50 -> 70; becomes right child of 70
insert 65: compare 50 -> 70 -> 60; becomes right child of 60
insert 75: compare 50 -> 70 -> 80; becomes left child of 80
Tree before deletion:
50
├─ L: 30
│  ├─ L: 20
│  └─ R: 40
└─ R: 70
   ├─ L: 60
   │  └─ R: 65
   └─ R: 80
      └─ L: 75
Delete 50 (two children). Inorder successor = smallest key in the right subtree: go right to 70, then left as far as possible: 70 -> 60 (60 has no left child). Successor = 60.
Copy 60 into the root. Remove the old 60: it has one child (right child 65), so 65 moves up to take its place as the left child of 70.
Tree after deletion:
60
├─ L: 30
│  ├─ L: 20
│  └─ R: 40
└─ R: 70
   ├─ L: 65
   └─ R: 80
      └─ L: 75
Preorder = node, then left subtree, then right subtree (N L R). A leaf on its own gives just itself. Working from the smallest subtrees upwards:
Pre(30) = 30 + Pre(20) + Pre(40) = 30, 20, 40
Pre(80) = 80 + Pre(75) = 80, 75   [80 has no right child]
Pre(70) = 70 + Pre(65) + Pre(80) = 70, 65, 80, 75
Pre(60) = 60 + Pre(30) + Pre(70) = 60, 30, 20, 40, 70, 65, 80, 75
Preorder: 60, 30, 20, 40, 70, 65, 80, 75
why: A — Wrong. This is the result of using the inorder PREDECESSOR 40 (the largest key in the left subtree). The question asks for the successor.
B — Wrong. 65 is not the inorder successor of 50. The successor is the smallest key larger than 50, which is 60 (65 is larger than 60).
C — Correct. The successor of 50 is 60. 60 moves to the root, and its right child 65 takes its old place under 70. Preorder: 60, 30, 20, 40, 70, 65, 80, 75.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Successor = right once, then left all the way. Predecessor = left once, then right all the way.

q: The keys 44, 22, 66, 11, 33, 55, 77, 30, 38 are inserted in this order into an initially empty binary search tree (no balancing). Node 22 is then deleted, replacing it by its inorder predecessor. What is the level-order traversal of the resulting tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 22 is replaced by its predecessor 11, giving level order 44, 11, 66, 33, 55, 77, 30, 38.
concept: To delete a BST node with two children using the inorder predecessor: replace its key by the largest key in its LEFT subtree (go left once, then right as far as possible), then remove that predecessor from its old place.
work:
Insert each key: start at the root, go left if smaller, right if larger, until an empty spot is found.
insert 44: tree empty, 44 becomes the root
insert 22: compare 44; becomes left child of 44
insert 66: compare 44; becomes right child of 44
insert 11: compare 44 -> 22; becomes left child of 22
insert 33: compare 44 -> 22; becomes right child of 22
insert 55: compare 44 -> 66; becomes left child of 66
insert 77: compare 44 -> 66; becomes right child of 66
insert 30: compare 44 -> 22 -> 33; becomes left child of 33
insert 38: compare 44 -> 22 -> 33; becomes right child of 33
Tree before deletion:
44
├─ L: 22
│  ├─ L: 11
│  └─ R: 33
│     ├─ L: 30
│     └─ R: 38
└─ R: 66
   ├─ L: 55
   └─ R: 77
Delete 22 (two children: 11 and 33). Inorder predecessor = largest key in the left subtree: go left to 11, then right as far as possible; 11 has no right child, so predecessor = 11.
Copy 11 into 22's place and remove the old leaf 11. The new node 11 has no left child and keeps 33 as its right child.
Tree after deletion:
44
├─ L: 11
│  └─ R: 33
│     ├─ L: 30
│     └─ R: 38
└─ R: 66
   ├─ L: 55
   └─ R: 77
Level order reads the tree level by level, each level from left to right (a queue does this: take a node from the front, put its left child then its right child at the back).
Level 0: 44
Level 1: 11, 66
Level 2: 33, 55, 77
Level 3: 30, 38
Level order: 44, 11, 66, 33, 55, 77, 30, 38
why: A — Wrong. This uses the inorder SUCCESSOR 30 (the smallest key in 22's right subtree). The question asks for the predecessor.
B — Correct. 22's predecessor is 11 (its left subtree is just 11). 11 takes 22's place, keeping 33 as its right child. Level order: 44, 11, 66, 33, 55, 77, 30, 38.

C — Wrong. This puts 33 in 22's place, as if 22's right child simply moved up. That shortcut is allowed only when the deleted node has one child; 22 has two children, so it must be replaced by its predecessor 11 (or, with the other method, its successor 30).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following insertion orders (into an initially empty BST) produce exactly the same BST as the order 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Orders A and B insert every key after its ancestors and rebuild the same BST; C starts with 20 and does not, so the answer is D.
concept: A newly inserted key always becomes a leaf below the keys already in the BST. So an insertion order builds a given BST exactly when every key is inserted after all of its ancestors (parent, grandparent, ..., root) in that tree. In particular the root must come first; the order among unrelated nodes, such as siblings, does not matter.
work:
Reference order 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70 gives:
40
├─ L: 20
│  ├─ L: 10
│  └─ R: 30
└─ R: 60
   ├─ L: 50
   └─ R: 70
Key idea: the same BST is produced by any order in which every key comes after all of its ancestors (parent, grandparent, ...).
A: 40, 60, 20, 70, 50, 30, 10 -> 40 root; 60 R of 40; 20 L of 40; 70 R of 60; 50 L of 60; 30 R of 20; 10 L of 20. Same tree -> true.
B: 40, 20, 10, 30, 60, 50, 70 -> 40 root; 20 L; 10 L of 20; 30 R of 20; 60 R; 50 L of 60; 70 R of 60. Same tree -> true.
C: 20 comes first, so 20 becomes the root:
20
├─ L: 10
└─ R: 40
   ├─ L: 30
   └─ R: 60
      ├─ L: 50
      └─ R: 70
Different tree -> false.
A and B true -> D.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 40 comes first and every other key comes after its ancestors (20 and 60 before their children). It builds 40 → (20, 60), 20 → (10, 30), 60 → (50, 70), the same tree.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 40 first, 20 before 10 and 30, 60 before 50 and 70: every key follows its ancestors, so it builds the same tree.
C — Wrong. 20 is inserted first, so 20 becomes the root, but the target tree has 40 at the root. The resulting tree is different.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is false.
tip: Same BST ⇔ same root first, and every key inserted after all of its ancestors.

q: A BST contains integer keys. Which of the following could NOT be the sequence of nodes examined while searching for the key 55?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In C, 45 appears after the search went right at 50, which is impossible; A and B are valid paths.
concept: When you search a BST for a key, each comparison narrows the range of values the remaining nodes can have. After going right at node x, every later node must be larger than x; after going left at x, every later node must be smaller than x. A sequence is a possible search path only if every node lies inside the current range.
work:
While searching for 55, every node visited narrows the allowed range (low, high) for the nodes that follow:
A: 90 (55 < 90, go left: range (-inf, 90)); 20 in range, 55 > 20 go right: (20, 90); 70 in range, go left: (20, 70); 30 in range, go right: (30, 70); 60 in range, go left: (30, 60); 55 in range -> found. Possible.
B: 10 -> go right (10, inf); 80 ok -> go left (10, 80); 30 ok -> go right (30, 80); 70 ok -> go left (30, 70); 40 ok -> go right (40, 70); 55 ok -> found. Possible.
C: 50 -> go right (50, inf); 80 ok -> go left (50, 80); 60 ok -> go left (50, 60); 45 is NOT between 50 and 60 -> impossible. (45 < 50 would have to be in 50's LEFT subtree, but we went right at 50.)
Only C could NOT be a search sequence -> answer C.
why: A — Wrong. This IS a possible path: the range shrinks (−∞, 90) → (20, 90) → (20, 70) → (30, 70) → (30, 60), and every next node lies inside it. So A does not satisfy the 'could NOT' stem.
B — Wrong. This IS a possible path: (10, ∞) → (10, 80) → (30, 80) → (30, 70) → (40, 70), and every next node lies inside the range. So B does not satisfy the stem.

C — Correct. This could NOT be a search path: after 50 (go right) and 60 (go left) every later node must be between 50 and 60, but 45 < 50. A key smaller than 50 can only be in 50's LEFT subtree, which the search has already left. So C satisfies the stem.
D — Wrong. Only C is an impossible sequence; A and B are possible, so there are not two such options.
E — Wrong. C is impossible, so there is an option that satisfies the stem.
tip: Keep a (low, high) window: each 'go right' raises low, each 'go left' lowers high. A node outside the window makes the sequence impossible.

q: How many structurally different (unlabelled) binary trees can be formed with 3 nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: There are C(3) = 5 binary tree shapes with 3 nodes.
concept: The number of structurally different binary trees with n nodes is the Catalan number C(n) = (2n)! / ((n + 1)! · n!). The first values are 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 for n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. 'Structurally different' means we compare shapes only, ignoring labels, and a left child is different from a right child.
work:
Shapes with 3 nodes:
1) root → left child → its left child (chain L-L)
2) root → left child → its right child (chain L-R)
3) root → right child → its left child (chain R-L)
4) root → right child → its right child (chain R-R)
5) root with both a left and a right child
Total = 5 = C(3) = 6! / (4! · 3!) = 720 / 144.
why: A — Correct. There are 4 chain shapes (each of the two lower nodes hangs left or right: 2 × 2) plus 1 shape in which the root has two children: 5, the Catalan number C(3).
B — Wrong. 6 = 3! counts the ways to arrange 3 labels, not the number of shapes.
C — Wrong. 3 undercounts. In a binary tree a left child and a right child are different positions, so the four chains L-L, L-R, R-L and R-R are all different, plus the shape with two children.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Catalan numbers: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132 for n = 0..6.

q: The number of structurally different binary trees with n nodes is given by:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Both A and B are formulas for the Catalan number; 2^n − 1 is not, so the answer is D.
concept: The number of distinct binary tree shapes with n nodes is the n-th Catalan number. It can be written in two equivalent ways: (2n)! / ((n + 1)! · n!) or C(2n, n) / (n + 1), because C(2n, n) = (2n)! / (n! · n!) and n! · (n + 1) = (n + 1)!.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. (2n)! / ((n + 1)! · n!) is the Catalan number; for n = 3 it gives 720 / (24 × 6) = 5.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. C(2n, n) / (n + 1) = (2n)! / (n! · n! · (n + 1)) = (2n)! / ((n + 1)! · n!), the same Catalan number; for n = 3: 20 / 4 = 5.
C — Wrong. 2^n − 1 is wrong: n = 3 gives 7 (true count 5) and n = 4 gives 15 (true count 14). 2^n − 1 is the number of nodes in a perfect binary tree with n levels.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so more than one of A–C holds and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: How many structurally different binary search trees can be built with the 4 distinct keys 1, 2, 3, 4?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The number of BSTs on 4 distinct keys is C(4) = 14.
concept: For a fixed set of n distinct keys, each binary tree SHAPE can be filled with the keys in exactly one way that obeys the BST rule (the inorder must be sorted). So the number of different BSTs on n distinct keys equals the number of shapes, the Catalan number C(n). C(4) = 14.
work:
C(4) = 8! / (5! · 4!) = 40320 / (120 · 24) = 14
Or by choosing the root k (left gets k − 1 keys, right gets 4 − k keys):
root 1 → C(0)·C(3) = 1·5 = 5
root 2 → C(1)·C(2) = 1·2 = 2
root 3 → C(2)·C(1) = 2·1 = 2
root 4 → C(3)·C(0) = 5·1 = 5
Total = 14
why: A — Wrong. 24 = 4! is the number of insertion ORDERS. Different orders often build the same BST (for example 2, 1, 3, 4 and 2, 3, 1, 4), so 24 overcounts.
B — Correct. The number of BSTs on 4 distinct keys is the Catalan number C(4) = 14.
C — Wrong. 16 = 2^4 is not a tree-counting formula; the correct count is the Catalan number 14.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Number of BSTs on n distinct keys = number of binary tree shapes = Catalan C(n).

q: How many structurally different binary search trees can be built with the 5 distinct keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The count is the Catalan number C(5) = 42, which is not listed.
concept: The number of different BSTs that can be built from n distinct keys is the Catalan number C(n) = (2n)! / ((n + 1)! · n!), because each tree shape can be filled with the sorted keys in exactly one valid way. For n = 5 this is 42.
why: A — Wrong. 120 = 5! counts insertion orders; many different orders build the same BST, so this overcounts.
B — Wrong. 32 = 2^5 is not a tree-counting formula.
C — Wrong. 14 is C(4), the count for 4 keys, one key too few.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be true.
E — Correct. There are C(5) = 42 BSTs on 5 distinct keys, and 42 is not given in A, B or C.

q: How many different labelled binary trees can be formed with 3 nodes carrying the distinct labels X, Y, Z?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 5 shapes × 3! labellings = 30 labelled binary trees.
concept: For labelled binary trees, count the shapes and then the ways to place the labels on each shape. With n distinct labels, each of the C(n) shapes can be labelled in n! ways, so there are C(n) · n! = (2n)! / (n + 1)! labelled binary trees. (This differs from BSTs, where the BST rule allows only one labelling per shape.)
work:
Shapes: C(3) = 5
Labellings per shape: 3! = 6
Total = 5 × 6 = 30 (= 6! / 4! = 720 / 24)
why: A — Wrong. 6 = 3! counts only the ways to place the labels on ONE fixed shape.
B — Wrong. 5 is the number of unlabelled shapes (it is also the number of BSTs on 3 keys), where each shape is counted only once.
C — Correct. 5 shapes × 6 labellings each = 30 labelled binary trees.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Unlabelled shapes: C(n). BSTs on n keys: C(n). Labelled trees with any placement: C(n) × n!.

q: How many distinct binary search trees with the keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 have 3 as the root?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With root 3, each side has 2 keys and 2 possible shapes, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 BSTs.
concept: In a BST on the keys 1..n with root k, the left subtree must contain exactly the keys 1..k − 1 and the right subtree exactly k + 1..n. Each side can be shaped independently, so the number of such BSTs is C(k − 1) × C(n − k), using Catalan numbers. Adding this over all roots k gives C(n).
work:
Root 3 → left keys {1, 2}: C(2) = 2 BSTs (1 with right child 2, or 2 with left child 1)
right keys {4, 5}: C(2) = 2 BSTs (4 with right child 5, or 5 with left child 4)
Total = 2 × 2 = 4
why: A — Wrong. 5 is C(3), the count for a 3-key set. Here each side has only 2 keys.
B — Correct. The left side {1, 2} has 2 shapes and the right side {4, 5} has 2 shapes; they combine freely: 2 × 2 = 4.
C — Wrong. 2 counts only one side's choices. The left and right subtrees are chosen independently, so their counts multiply: 2 × 2 = 4.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In an inorder threaded binary tree, a NULL right-child pointer of a node is replaced by a thread pointing to the node's:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In an inorder threaded tree, a NULL right pointer becomes a thread to the inorder successor.
concept: A binary tree with n nodes has n + 1 NULL child pointers. A threaded binary tree reuses them. In an inorder threaded tree, a NULL right pointer is made to point to the node's inorder successor, and a NULL left pointer to its inorder predecessor; a flag bit tells whether a pointer is a real child or a thread. This allows inorder traversal without a stack or recursion.
why: A — Wrong. The inorder predecessor is stored in a NULL LEFT pointer (a left thread), not in the right pointer.
B — Correct. A NULL right pointer becomes a right thread to the inorder successor, the node that comes next in inorder.
C — Wrong. A pointer to the parent is used in some other designs (trees with parent pointers), but it is not what an inorder thread stores.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Right thread → successor (next). Left thread → predecessor (previous).

q: The postfix expression  a b c * + d e / −  is converted into an expression tree (operands are leaves, operators are internal nodes). What is the preorder traversal of this tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The tree is −( +(a, *(b, c)), /(d, e) ), whose preorder is − + a * b c / d e.
concept: An expression tree has operands as leaves and operators as internal nodes. To build it from postfix, scan left to right with a stack: push each operand as a one-node tree; for an operator, pop two trees (the first one popped becomes the RIGHT child), join them under the operator and push the result. The preorder of an expression tree is the prefix (Polish) form of the expression.
work:
Scan the postfix left to right with a stack of subtrees:
a -> push a                         stack: [a]
b -> push b                         stack: [a, b]
c -> push c                         stack: [a, b, c]
* -> pop c (right), pop b (left), push (b * c)          stack: [a, (b*c)]
+ -> pop (b*c) (right), pop a (left), push (a + (b*c))  stack: [(a+b*c)]
d -> push d                         stack: [(a+b*c), d]
e -> push e                         stack: [(a+b*c), d, e]
/ -> pop e, pop d, push (d / e)     stack: [(a+b*c), (d/e)]
− -> pop (d/e) (right), pop (a+b*c) (left), push the tree rooted at −   stack: [whole tree]
Tree:
−
├─ L: +
│  ├─ L: a
│  └─ R: *
│     ├─ L: b
│     └─ R: c
└─ R: /
   ├─ L: d
   └─ R: e
Preorder (node, left, right): − , then preorder of + subtree (+ a * b c), then preorder of / subtree (/ d e)
Preorder: − + a * b c / d e
why: A — Correct. The root − has left subtree + (with a and the subtree b * c) and right subtree / (with d and e). Preorder: − + a * b c / d e.
B — Wrong. This puts * before a, as if the expression were (a * b) + c. In the postfix a b c * +, the * joins b and c, and then + joins a with (b * c).
C — Wrong. This makes + the root. The last operator in the postfix is −, so − is the root of the tree.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The LAST operator of a postfix expression (or the FIRST of a prefix one) is the root of the expression tree.

q: A general (ordered) tree has root A with children B, C, D (left to right); B has children E, F; D has one child G. It is converted to a binary tree using the left-child right-sibling representation. Which statement about the binary tree is correct?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In the left-child right-sibling form, C's right pointer goes to its next sibling D; the other two statements are false.
concept: Any ordered general tree can be stored as a binary tree using the left-child right-sibling (LCRS) rule: a node's LEFT pointer points to its first (leftmost) child, and its RIGHT pointer points to its next sibling. The root has no siblings, so the root's right pointer is always NULL.
work:
General tree:
A
├─ B
│  ├─ E
│  └─ F
├─ C
└─ D
   └─ G
Left-child right-sibling rule: left pointer -> FIRST child; right pointer -> NEXT sibling (the brother/sister just to the right).
A: first child B -> A.left = B; A is the root and has no sibling -> A.right = NULL
B: first child E -> B.left = E; next sibling C -> B.right = C
C: no child -> C.left = NULL; next sibling D -> C.right = D
D: first child G -> D.left = G; no next sibling -> D.right = NULL
E: no child; next sibling F -> E.right = F
Binary tree:
A
└─ L: B
   ├─ L: E
   │  └─ R: F
   └─ R: C
      └─ R: D
         └─ L: G
A says A.right = B: false (A.right is NULL; B is A's LEFT child).
B says B.left = C: false (B.left = E; C is B's RIGHT pointer).
C says C.right = D: true.  -> answer C.
why: A — Wrong. B is A's first child, so B goes in A's LEFT pointer. A is the root and has no sibling, so A's right pointer is NULL.
B — Wrong. B's left pointer points to B's first child, E. C is B's next SIBLING, so C goes in B's RIGHT pointer.
C — Correct. C's next sibling (just to its right) is D, so C's right pointer points to D.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: LCRS: Left = first child, Right = next sibling. The root's right pointer is always NULL.

q: An expression tree is built for the infix expression (a + b) * (c − d / e) using the usual precedence rules. What is its postorder traversal?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The tree has root * with subtrees (a + b) and c − d / e; its postorder is a b + c d e / − *.
concept: To build an expression tree from infix, bracket the expression fully using precedence (* and / before + and −). The operator applied LAST becomes the root, with its two operands as the left and right subtrees. The postorder of the tree is the postfix form, and the preorder is the prefix form.
work:
Fully bracket using precedence (/ before −; brackets first): (a + b) * (c − (d / e))
The operator applied LAST is the root: * (it joins the two bracketed groups).
Left subtree: a + b -> + with children a, b.
Right subtree: c − (d / e) -> − with left c and right (d / e); the / node has children d, e.
Tree:
*
├─ L: +
│  ├─ L: a
│  └─ R: b
└─ R: −
   ├─ L: c
   └─ R: /
      ├─ L: d
      └─ R: e
Postorder (left, right, node):
Post(+) = a b +
Post(/) = d e /
Post(−) = c, Post(/), − = c d e / −
Post(*) = Post(+), Post(−), * = a b + c d e / − *
why: A — Correct. The root * has left subtree (a + b) and right subtree c − (d / e). Postorder: a b +, then c d e / −, then *: a b + c d e / − *.
B — Wrong. a b + c d − e / * stands for (a + b) * ((c − d) / e), which does the − before the /. Precedence makes d / e happen first.
C — Wrong. * + a b − c / d e is the PREORDER (prefix form) of the same tree, not the postorder.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In an AVL tree, the balance factor of a node is computed from:
opts: the heights of its left and right subtrees
the numbers of nodes in its left and right subtrees
its own depth and the height of the whole tree
More than one of the above
exp: Balance factor = height of the left subtree − height of the right subtree.
concept: An AVL tree is a binary search tree that keeps itself balanced. For every node it computes the balance factor = height of the left subtree − height of the right subtree (some books use right − left). The height of a subtree is the number of edges on its longest downward path. If any balance factor goes outside −1, 0, +1, the tree is repaired by rotations.
why: A — Correct. The balance factor of a node is height(left subtree) − height(right subtree). Only heights are used, because AVL balance is about how tall the two sides are.
B — Wrong. Comparing the numbers of nodes on each side describes weight-balanced (size-balanced) trees, not AVL trees. Two subtrees can have very different node counts but the same height.
C — Wrong. The depth of a node (its distance from the root) and the height of the whole tree are not used. The balance factor depends only on the node's own two subtrees.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: AVL = heights. Measure how tall each side is, do not count nodes.

q: Which set contains exactly the balance-factor values permitted at every node of an AVL tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The permitted balance factors in an AVL tree are −1, 0 and +1 only.
concept: In an AVL tree the heights of the left and right subtrees of every node may differ by at most 1. So every balance factor must be −1 (right side taller by one), 0 (equal) or +1 (left side taller by one). A value of +2 or −2 means the node has become unbalanced and must be fixed with a rotation.
why: A — Wrong. {0, 1, 2} wrongly allows +2 (an imbalance) and wrongly leaves out −1, which is allowed when the right subtree is one level taller.
B — Wrong. This set includes ±2. A balance factor of ±2 is exactly the signal that a rotation is needed, so it is not permitted in a finished AVL tree.
C — Correct. |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1 means the difference can only be −1, 0 or +1.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Like a see-saw that may tilt by one notch either way, never by two.

q: An AVL tree with n nodes is always:
opts: a perfect binary tree (all leaves at the same level)
a full binary tree (every node has 0 or 2 children)
More than one of the above
exp: AVL trees are height-balanced, but they are not necessarily complete, perfect or full.
concept: An AVL tree is only height-balanced: at every node the two subtree heights differ by at most 1. It does NOT have to be complete (levels filled left to right), perfect (all leaves on one level) or full (every node has 0 or 2 children). Example: root 20 with children 10 and 30, where 30 has only a right child 40, is a valid AVL tree but is none of these three.
why: A — Wrong. A complete binary tree has every level full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. In the example (20; 10, 30; 30 has only a right child 40), 10 has no children while 30 has one, so the last level is not filled from the left, yet the tree is AVL.
B — Wrong. A perfect binary tree has all leaves on the same level and exactly 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes. An AVL tree with, say, 4 nodes cannot be perfect, and its leaves are often on two different levels.
C — Wrong. A full binary tree has every node with 0 or 2 children. AVL trees often contain nodes with exactly one child (node 30 in the example), as long as the heights differ by at most 1.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. An AVL tree is guaranteed only to be height-balanced; it need not be complete, perfect or full, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Which AVL imbalance case is fixed by first rotating right at the unbalanced node's right child and then rotating left at the unbalanced node?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A right rotation at the right child followed by a left rotation at the node is the RL double rotation.
concept: AVL imbalance cases are named by the first two steps of the path from the unbalanced node towards the new key. LL and RR are fixed by one single rotation. LR and RL are zig-zag shapes and need a double rotation. In the RL case (key in the Left subtree of the Right child), we first rotate right at the right child to make a straight right-right chain, then rotate left at the unbalanced node.
why: A — Wrong. The LL case (key in the left subtree of the left child) is fixed by one single right rotation at the unbalanced node; no second rotation is needed.
B — Wrong. The LR case is the mirror image: rotate LEFT at the left child first, then RIGHT at the unbalanced node.

C — Correct. The right rotation at the right child turns the zig-zag (right, then left) into a straight right-right chain, and the left rotation at the unbalanced node then balances it. This is the RL case.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: For double rotations the rotation directions follow the letters of the case name: RL → Right rotation (at the child), then Left rotation (at the node).

q: Let N(h) be the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h. Which recurrence does N(h) satisfy for h ≥ 2?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Minimum nodes: N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 (a root plus two sparsest subtrees whose heights differ by 1).
concept: To get an AVL tree of height h with the fewest nodes, make it as lopsided as the rule allows: a root, one subtree of height h−1 and the other of height h−2, each itself as sparse as possible. So N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1, with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2. These numbers grow like Fibonacci numbers, which is why the height of an AVL tree is O(log n).
why: A — Correct. Root (1 node) + the sparsest subtree of height h−1 + the sparsest subtree of height h−2. The two subtree heights differ by exactly 1, the most AVL allows.
B — Wrong. 2·N(h−1) + 1 gives the MAXIMUM number of nodes (a perfect tree, where both subtrees have height h−1), which is 2^(h+1) − 1, not the minimum.
C — Wrong. N(h−1) + 1 describes a chain (every node has one child). A chain of height 2 or more is not AVL, because its top node has balance factor ±2.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: N(h) + 1 is a Fibonacci number: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …

q: Which of the following operations take O(log n) time in the worst case on an AVL tree with n nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Search, insertion and deletion are all O(log n) in the worst case, because an AVL tree's height is always O(log n).
concept: An AVL tree always has height O(log n), about 1.44·log2 n at worst. Search walks one root-to-leaf path. Insertion and deletion also walk one path, then go back up updating heights and doing rotations, and each rotation costs O(1). So all three basic operations take O(log n) time in the worst case.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Search compares the key at each level and goes left or right, visiting at most height + 1 nodes, which is O(log n).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Insertion walks down one path (O(log n)), then walks back up updating heights; at most one single or double rotation is needed, each O(1). Total O(log n).

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Deletion also walks one path and may rotate at several ancestors on the way back up, but there are only O(log n) ancestors and each rotation is O(1). Total O(log n).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The tight worst-case height of an AVL tree with n nodes is approximately:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The worst-case height of an AVL tree is about 1.44·log2 n.
concept: The tallest AVL tree for n nodes is the sparsest one, where N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1. These numbers grow like Fibonacci numbers, roughly 1.618^h. Solving gives h < 1.44·log2(n + 2), so the worst-case height is about 1.44·log2 n — at most about 44% taller than a perfectly balanced tree.
why: A — Wrong. log2 n is the height of a perfectly balanced tree, i.e. the BEST case. AVL trees can be taller than this.
B — Correct. From the Fibonacci-like growth of N(h), h ≈ 1.44·log2 n is the tight worst-case height.
C — Wrong. √n is far too large; AVL height grows logarithmically, not like a power of n.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 1.44 ≈ 1/log2(1.618), where 1.618 is the golden ratio.

q: After inserting a single key into an AVL tree, what is the maximum number of single rotations needed to restore balance?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: AVL insertion needs at most one double rotation, i.e. at most 2 single rotations.
concept: After an insertion only the lowest unbalanced ancestor of the new node needs fixing. It is fixed by one single rotation (LL or RR case) or one double rotation (LR or RL case), and a double rotation is just two single rotations. After this fix the subtree gets back its old height, so no ancestor higher up stays unbalanced. Hence an insertion needs at most 2 single rotations.
why: A — Wrong. One rotation is enough only for the LL and RR cases. The LR and RL cases need a double rotation, which is two single rotations.
B — Correct. A double rotation (LR or RL) = 2 single rotations, and after it the subtree height is restored, so no further rotation is ever needed.
C — Wrong. 3 never happens for an insertion. (Deletion is different: it can need rotations at several levels.)
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path (a single node has height 0). What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 5?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 5 is N(5) = 20.
concept: The minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h follows N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1, with N(0) = 1 (a single node) and N(1) = 2 (a root with one child). Compute the values step by step up to the required height.
why: A — Wrong. 12 is N(4), the minimum for height 4 — one step short.
C — Wrong. 33 is N(6), the minimum for height 6 — one step too far.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Each option describes a binary search tree. Which one is NOT a valid AVL tree?
opts: Root 40; left child 20 (which has a left child 10); right child 60
Root 40; left child 20 (children 10 and 30); right child 60 (right child 70)
Root 40; left child 20 (left child 10, whose left child is 5); right child 60
More than one of the above
exp: In C, nodes 20 and 40 both have balance factor +2, so C is not an AVL tree.
concept: To check whether a BST is an AVL tree, compute the balance factor (left height − right height) of EVERY node, not just the root. If any node has a balance factor of +2, −2 or worse, the tree is not AVL. Use height(empty subtree) = −1 and height(leaf) = 0.
why: A — Wrong. All balance factors are 0 or +1 (20 has +1 because of its left child 10; the root 40 has +1). It is a valid AVL tree, so it does not answer a 'NOT' question.
B — Wrong. Every node has balance factor −1, 0 or +1 (60 has −1 because of its right child 70; the root has 0). It is valid, so it is not the answer.
C — Correct. Node 20 has a left subtree of height 1 (10 → 5) and no right subtree (height −1), so bf(20) = +2; the root 40 is also +2. This BST is NOT an AVL tree.
D — Wrong. Only C is not a valid AVL tree; A and B are valid, so 'More than one of the above' does not fit.
E — Wrong. C is not a valid AVL tree, so one option does satisfy the stem.

q: During AVL insertion, calling the function below once on the unbalanced node (and doing nothing else) fixes which imbalance case?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The code is a single right rotation, which fixes the LL case.
concept: A right rotation at node y lifts its left child x into y's place. y becomes x's right child, and x's old right subtree (keys between x and y) becomes y's new left subtree. The in-order (sorted) order of the keys does not change. A single right rotation repairs the LL case: a node that is too heavy on the left because of its left child's left subtree.
work:
Before: y has left child x; x has right subtree t.
x = y->left; t = x->right
x->right = y   (y moves down to the right of x)
y->left = t    (t, whose keys lie between x and y, hangs on y's left)
return x       (x is the new root of this subtree)
This is a single RIGHT rotation at y.
why: A — Wrong. The RR case (too heavy on the right-right side) needs a LEFT rotation, which would use y->right, not y->left.

B — Wrong. The RL case needs a double rotation: a right rotation at the right child and then a left rotation at the node. One call of this function does only a single right rotation at the unbalanced node.
C — Correct. The function performs a single right rotation, and one right rotation at the unbalanced node is exactly the fix for the LL case.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Right rotation fixes Left-Left; left rotation fixes Right-Right.

q: Keys 50, 40, 30, 20, 10 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. Which rotations are performed, and what is the final root?
opts: Two single left rotations (RR cases); root 40
Two single right rotations (LL cases); root 40
More than one of the above
exp: Two LL cases → two single right rotations; the final tree is 40(20(10, 30), 50) with root 40.
concept: Inserting keys in decreasing order into an AVL tree keeps creating left-left chains. Each time a node gets balance factor +2 while its left child has +1, it is the LL case, fixed by one single right rotation at that node. Always fix the LOWEST unbalanced node on the path.
work:
Balance factor (bf) = height(left subtree) − height(right subtree); height of an empty subtree = −1, of a single node = 0.
Insert 50: becomes the root. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  50 (bf 0)
Insert 40: path 50, attached as the left child of 50. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  50 (bf +1)
    L: 40 (bf 0)
Insert 30: path 50 → 40, attached as the left child of 40. Node 50 has bf +2 and its left child 40 has bf +1 → LL case → single right rotation at 50.
  40 (bf 0)
    L: 30 (bf 0)
    R: 50 (bf 0)
Insert 20: path 40 → 30, attached as the left child of 30. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  40 (bf +1)
    L: 30 (bf +1)
      L: 20 (bf 0)
    R: 50 (bf 0)
Insert 10: path 40 → 30 → 20, attached as the left child of 20. Node 30 has bf +2 and its left child 20 has bf +1 → LL case → single right rotation at 30.
  40 (bf +1)
    L: 20 (bf 0)
      L: 10 (bf 0)
      R: 30 (bf 0)
    R: 50 (bf 0)
Result: two single right rotations (both LL cases); final root 40.
why: A — Wrong. Left rotations (RR cases) happen when keys are inserted in increasing order. Here the keys decrease, so every new key goes to the left.
B — Correct. Inserting 30 gives LL at 50 (right rotation) and inserting 10 gives LL at 30 (right rotation). The root stays 40.
C — Wrong. A double rotation (LR) needs a zig-zag shape (left child, then right grandchild). Decreasing keys always go left-left, so no LR case occurs, and the root is 40, not 30.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 50, 20, 40 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. Which imbalance case occurs at node 50, and what is the root afterwards?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: LR case at 50; after the double rotation the root is 40.
concept: When a node becomes unbalanced, look at the path from it towards the new key. 50 → left to 20 → right to 40 is Left then Right: the LR case. LR is fixed by a double rotation: a left rotation at the left child, then a right rotation at the unbalanced node. The middle key (40) ends up on top.
work:
Balance factor (bf) = height(left subtree) − height(right subtree); height of an empty subtree = −1, of a single node = 0.
Insert 50: becomes the root. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  50 (bf 0)
Insert 20: path 50, attached as the left child of 50. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  50 (bf +1)
    L: 20 (bf 0)
Insert 40: path 50 → 20, attached as the right child of 20. Node 50 has bf +2 and its left child 20 has bf −1 → LR case → left rotation at 20, then right rotation at 50.
  40 (bf 0)
    L: 20 (bf 0)
    R: 50 (bf 0)
Result: LR case at 50; final root 40 with children 20 and 50.
why: A — Wrong. LL would need the new key in the LEFT subtree of 20 (for example 10). 40 > 20, so it went to the right of 20. Also, the root becomes 40, not 20.
B — Correct. The path 50 → L → 20 → R → 40 is the LR case; the double rotation makes the middle value 40 the root with children 20 and 50.
C — Wrong. RL would need the new key in the left subtree of a RIGHT child. Here 20 is the LEFT child of 50, so the case is LR, not RL (the root 40 is right, but the case name is wrong).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: For three keys in a zig-zag, the middle value always becomes the root.

q: Keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. What does the final tree look like at the top?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The final AVL tree is perfect: root 4 with children 2 and 6.
concept: Inserting keys in increasing order keeps creating right-right chains, which are fixed by single left rotations (RR case). A plain BST would become a long chain, but the AVL tree stays balanced. Inserting 1 to 7 in order ends with a perfect tree of height 2.
work:
Balance factor (bf) = height(left subtree) − height(right subtree); height of an empty subtree = −1, of a single node = 0.
Insert 1: becomes the root. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  1 (bf 0)
Insert 2: path 1, attached as the right child of 1. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  1 (bf −1)
    R: 2 (bf 0)
Insert 3: path 1 → 2, attached as the right child of 2. Node 1 has bf −2 and its right child 2 has bf −1 → RR case → single left rotation at 1.
  2 (bf 0)
    L: 1 (bf 0)
    R: 3 (bf 0)
Insert 4: path 2 → 3, attached as the right child of 3. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  2 (bf −1)
    L: 1 (bf 0)
    R: 3 (bf −1)
      R: 4 (bf 0)
Insert 5: path 2 → 3 → 4, attached as the right child of 4. Node 3 has bf −2 and its right child 4 has bf −1 → RR case → single left rotation at 3.
  2 (bf −1)
    L: 1 (bf 0)
    R: 4 (bf 0)
      L: 3 (bf 0)
      R: 5 (bf 0)
Insert 6: path 2 → 4 → 5, attached as the right child of 5. Node 2 has bf −2 and its right child 4 has bf −1 → RR case → single left rotation at 2.
  4 (bf 0)
    L: 2 (bf 0)
      L: 1 (bf 0)
      R: 3 (bf 0)
    R: 5 (bf −1)
      R: 6 (bf 0)
Insert 7: path 4 → 5 → 6, attached as the right child of 6. Node 5 has bf −2 and its right child 6 has bf −1 → RR case → single left rotation at 5.
  4 (bf 0)
    L: 2 (bf 0)
      L: 1 (bf 0)
      R: 3 (bf 0)
    R: 6 (bf 0)
      L: 5 (bf 0)
      R: 7 (bf 0)
Result: four RR rotations; the final tree is perfect with root 4, children 2 and 6.
why: A — Correct. After four RR rotations the tree is 4(2(1, 3), 6(5, 7)): root 4 with children 2 and 6.
B — Wrong. Root 4 with children 2 and 5 is the state just after inserting 6. Inserting 7 makes 5 unbalanced (RR), and a left rotation at 5 lifts 6 into its place.
C — Wrong. Root 2 with children 1 and 4 is the state after inserting 5. Inserting 6 makes node 2 unbalanced, and a left rotation lifts 4 to the root.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An AVL tree has root 20 with left child 10 and right child 30; node 10 has a single left child 5. Key 30 is deleted and the tree is rebalanced. What is the new root?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Delete 30 → LL imbalance at 20 → right rotation → the new root is 10.
concept: Deletion from an AVL tree first works like ordinary BST deletion, then walks back up checking balance factors. The same four cases (LL, LR, RR, RL) are used. After a deletion, the case is decided by the balance factor of the child on the TALLER side: here the left child 10 has bf +1, so it is the LL case.
work:
Balance factor (bf) = height(left subtree) − height(right subtree); height of an empty subtree = −1, of a single node = 0.
Starting tree:
  20 (bf +1)
    L: 10 (bf +1)
      L: 5 (bf 0)
    R: 30 (bf 0)
Delete 30: it is a leaf, so it is simply removed. Walking back up: Node 20 has bf +2 and its left child 10 has bf +1 → LL case → single right rotation at 20.
  10 (bf 0)
    L: 5 (bf 0)
    R: 20 (bf 0)
Result: new root 10 (children 5 and 20).
why: A — Wrong. 5 does not become the root; it ends up as the left child of the new root 10. A single right rotation lifts the left child (10), not the grandchild.
B — Correct. Removing 30 makes bf(20) = +2 with left child 10 at +1 (LL case). A right rotation at 20 makes 10 the root with children 5 and 20.
C — Wrong. 20 cannot stay the root: after removing 30 its balance factor is +2, which breaks the AVL rule.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Unlike insertion, deleting a key from an AVL tree with n nodes may trigger rotations at several ancestors. In the worst case, the number of rotations caused by a single deletion is proportional to:
opts: the height of the tree, i.e. log n
More than one of the above
exp: A single AVL deletion may need up to O(log n) rotations, one per level on the path to the root.
concept: After an insertion, one (single or double) rotation restores the subtree's old height, so nothing above changes. After a deletion, a rotation can leave the subtree one level SHORTER than before, which may unbalance the next ancestor up. This can repeat at every level on the path to the root. An AVL path has O(log n) nodes, so a deletion needs O(log n) rotations in the worst case.
why: A — Wrong. 'At most 2' (one double rotation) is true for insertion, not for deletion. A deletion can cause rotations at many levels, one after another.
B — Wrong. Rotations happen only at ancestors of the deleted node, and there are only O(log n) of them, so the count can never grow in proportion to n.
C — Correct. In the worst case a rotation is needed at each level on the path up to the root, about one per level = O(log n). Sparsest (Fibonacci-shaped) AVL trees show this really happens.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Insertion: rotate once and stop. Deletion: may keep rotating all the way up.

q: Keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. When 25 is inserted, which imbalance occurs and what is the final root?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Inserting 25 causes an RL case at node 20; the final root is 30.
concept: Insert the keys one by one, and after each insertion find the lowest node whose balance factor becomes ±2. Read the case from the first two steps of the path from that node towards the new key: Right then Left = RL. RL is fixed by a right rotation at the right child, then a left rotation at the unbalanced node.
work:
Balance factor (bf) = height(left subtree) − height(right subtree); height of an empty subtree = −1, of a single node = 0.
Insert 10: becomes the root. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  10 (bf 0)
Insert 20: path 10, attached as the right child of 10. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  10 (bf −1)
    R: 20 (bf 0)
Insert 30: path 10 → 20, attached as the right child of 20. Node 10 has bf −2 and its right child 20 has bf −1 → RR case → single left rotation at 10.
  20 (bf 0)
    L: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 30 (bf 0)
Insert 40: path 20 → 30, attached as the right child of 30. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  20 (bf −1)
    L: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 30 (bf −1)
      R: 40 (bf 0)
Insert 50: path 20 → 30 → 40, attached as the right child of 40. Node 30 has bf −2 and its right child 40 has bf −1 → RR case → single left rotation at 30.
  20 (bf −1)
    L: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 40 (bf 0)
      L: 30 (bf 0)
      R: 50 (bf 0)
Insert 25: path 20 → 40 → 30, attached as the left child of 30. Node 20 has bf −2 and its right child 40 has bf +1 → RL case → right rotation at 40, then left rotation at 20.
  30 (bf 0)
    L: 20 (bf 0)
      L: 10 (bf 0)
      R: 25 (bf 0)
    R: 40 (bf −1)
      R: 50 (bf 0)
Result: inserting 25 causes an RL case at node 20; final root 30.
why: A — Wrong. Node 20 is unbalanced (bf −2), but its right child 40 has bf +1 because 25 went into 40's LEFT subtree. That is RL, not RR, and a single left rotation would not balance it. The final root is 30, not 40.
B — Wrong. The heavy side is the right side of 20 (bf −2). Node 40 itself has bf +1, which is allowed, so there is no imbalance at 40 and no LR case.
C — Correct. Path 20 → R → 40 → L → 30 → L → 25: right then left from node 20, so RL at 20. After the double rotation, 30 (the middle of 20, 30, 40) becomes the root.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 21, 26, 30, 9, 4, 14, 28, 18, 15, 10, 2, 3, 7 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. What are the root and its two children in the final tree?

  21 (bf 0)

    R: 28 (bf 0)

Insert 10: path 21 → 9 → 15 → 14, attached as the left child of 14. Node 9 has bf −2 and its right child 15 has bf +1 → RL case → right rotation at 15, then left rotation at 9.
  21 (bf +1)
    L: 14 (bf 0)

  14 (bf 0)
    L: 9 (bf +1)
      L: 4 (bf +1)
        L: 2 (bf 0)
      R: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 21 (bf 0)
      L: 15 (bf −1)
        R: 18 (bf 0)
      R: 28 (bf 0)
        L: 26 (bf 0)
        R: 30 (bf 0)
Insert 3: path 14 → 9 → 4 → 2, attached as the right child of 2. Node 4 has bf +2 and its left child 2 has bf −1 → LR case → left rotation at 2, then right rotation at 4.
  14 (bf 0)
    L: 9 (bf +1)
      L: 3 (bf 0)
        L: 2 (bf 0)
        R: 4 (bf 0)
      R: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 21 (bf 0)
      L: 15 (bf −1)
        R: 18 (bf 0)
      R: 28 (bf 0)
        L: 26 (bf 0)
        R: 30 (bf 0)
Insert 7: path 14 → 9 → 3 → 4, attached as the right child of 4. Node 9 has bf +2 and its left child 3 has bf −1 → LR case → left rotation at 3, then right rotation at 9.
  14 (bf 0)
    L: 4 (bf 0)
      L: 3 (bf +1)
        L: 2 (bf 0)
      R: 9 (bf 0)
        L: 7 (bf 0)
        R: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 21 (bf 0)
      L: 15 (bf −1)
        R: 18 (bf 0)
      R: 28 (bf 0)
        L: 26 (bf 0)
        R: 30 (bf 0)
Result: root 14 with children 4 and 21.
why: A — Wrong. Root 21 with children 14 and 28 is the state after inserting 10. Inserting 2 then makes 21 unbalanced (LL case), and a right rotation makes 14 the root.
B — Wrong. Root 14 with children 9 and 21 is the state after inserting 2 and 3. Inserting 7 makes node 9 unbalanced (LR case), and the double rotation moves 4 up to become 14's left child.
C — Correct. After all 13 insertions (with 9 rebalancing steps) the tree is 14(4(3(2, –), 9(7, 10)), 21(15(–, 18), 28(26, 30))): root 14 with children 4 and 21.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 40, 20, 10, 25, 30, 22, 50 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. What is the preorder traversal of the final tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The final tree is 25(20(10, 22), 40(30, 50)); its preorder 25 20 10 22 40 30 50 is not listed.
concept: Preorder traversal visits the root, then the whole left subtree, then the whole right subtree. For an AVL tree, first build the final tree carefully (one insertion and its rotation at a time), then read the nodes in root-left-right order.
work:
Balance factor (bf) = height(left subtree) − height(right subtree); height of an empty subtree = −1, of a single node = 0.
Insert 40: becomes the root. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  40 (bf 0)
Insert 20: path 40, attached as the left child of 40. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  40 (bf +1)
    L: 20 (bf 0)
Insert 10: path 40 → 20, attached as the left child of 20. Node 40 has bf +2 and its left child 20 has bf +1 → LL case → single right rotation at 40.
  20 (bf 0)
    L: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 40 (bf 0)
Insert 25: path 20 → 40, attached as the left child of 40. All balance factors are −1, 0 or +1, so no rotation.
  20 (bf −1)
    L: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 40 (bf +1)
      L: 25 (bf 0)
Insert 30: path 20 → 40 → 25, attached as the right child of 25. Node 40 has bf +2 and its left child 25 has bf −1 → LR case → left rotation at 25, then right rotation at 40.
  20 (bf −1)
    L: 10 (bf 0)
    R: 30 (bf 0)
      L: 25 (bf 0)
      R: 40 (bf 0)
Insert 22: path 20 → 30 → 25, attached as the left child of 25. Node 20 has bf −2 and its right child 30 has bf +1 → RL case → right rotation at 30, then left rotation at 20.
  25 (bf 0)
    L: 20 (bf 0)
      L: 10 (bf 0)
      R: 22 (bf 0)
    R: 30 (bf −1)
      R: 40 (bf 0)
Insert 50: path 25 → 30 → 40, attached as the right child of 40. Node 30 has bf −2 and its right child 40 has bf −1 → RR case → single left rotation at 30.
  25 (bf 0)
    L: 20 (bf 0)
      L: 10 (bf 0)
      R: 22 (bf 0)
    R: 40 (bf 0)
      L: 30 (bf 0)
      R: 50 (bf 0)
Preorder (root, left, right) of the final tree: 25 20 10 22 40 30 50 (not among A–C).
why: A — Wrong. 25 20 10 22 30 40 50 is the preorder of the tree just before the last rotation: 50 hangs under 40, which hangs under 30 (bf(30) = −2). The RR rotation at 30 lifts 40, so the true preorder has 40 before 30.
B — Wrong. 40 20 10 25 22 30 50 is the preorder of the plain BST built from these keys with no rotations at all.
C — Wrong. This keeps 20 as the root with right subtree 25(22, 40(30, 50)), which gives node 20 a balance factor of −2, so it is not even an AVL tree. In fact inserting 22 makes 25 the root.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 25 20 10 22 40 30 50), so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path (a single node has height 0). What is the maximum possible height of an AVL tree with 32 nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: N(5) = 20 ≤ 32 < N(6) = 33, so the maximum height is 5, which is not listed.
concept: The maximum height of an AVL tree with n nodes is the largest h whose minimum node count N(h) is still ≤ n. Use N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2. Here height counts edges.
work:
N(0..6) = 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33
N(5) = 20 ≤ 32, so height 5 is possible.
N(6) = 33 > 32, so height 6 is impossible.
Maximum height = 5.
Also, any binary tree of height 4 holds at most 2^5 − 1 = 31 nodes < 32, so the height is at least 5.
So every AVL tree with 32 nodes has height exactly 5.
why: A — Wrong. Height 4 is impossible: a binary tree of height 4 holds at most 31 nodes, and there are 32.
B — Wrong. Height 6 needs at least N(6) = 33 nodes, but there are only 32. (6 is what you get if you count height in levels instead of edges.)
C — Wrong. 7 is roughly 1.44·log2 32 ≈ 7.2. That formula is only an approximate upper bound; the exact maximum comes from the N(h) table.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 5), so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Max AVL height for n nodes: the largest h with N(h) ≤ n, where N = 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, …

q: What happens to the colour of the very first key inserted into an empty red-black tree?
opts: It is inserted red and stays red
It is inserted black and its NIL children are coloured red
It is inserted red and then recoloured black because it is the root
More than one of the above
exp: The first key is inserted red and immediately recoloured black because it is the root.
concept: In a red-black tree every new key is inserted as a RED node, because adding a red node never changes the number of black nodes on any path (the black height). A fix-up step then repairs any broken rule. One rule says the root must be black, so when the tree was empty, the new red root is simply recoloured black.
why: A — Wrong. It cannot stay red, because the root of a red-black tree must be black.
B — Wrong. New nodes are always inserted red, not black. NIL leaves are ALWAYS black; they are never coloured red.
C — Correct. The new node is inserted red like every other new node, and the fix-up then colours the root black.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a property of a red-black tree?
opts: Every red node has two red children
More than one of the above
exp: 'Every red node has two red children' is not a property; a red node's children must be black.
concept: A red-black tree is a BST in which every node is red or black and: (1) the root is black; (2) every NIL (empty) leaf is black; (3) a red node cannot have a red child; (4) every path from a node down to a NIL leaf has the same number of black nodes. Rules 3 and 4 together keep the tree roughly balanced.
why: A — Correct. This is the opposite of the real rule. Both children of a red node must be BLACK; two reds in a row are not allowed. So this is NOT a property, and it answers the question.
B — Wrong. 'The root is black' is a genuine red-black property, so it does not answer a 'NOT' question.
C — Wrong. 'Every NIL leaf is black' is a genuine property: the empty leaves are treated as black nodes.
D — Wrong. Only A is not a property; B and C are real properties, so 'More than one of the above' does not fit.
E — Wrong. A is not a property of red-black trees, so one option does satisfy the stem.
tip: Red rule: never two reds in a row.

q: The black height bh(x) of a node x in a red-black tree is:
opts: the total number of black nodes in the subtree rooted at x
the number of black nodes on any path from x down to a NIL leaf, not counting x
the number of red nodes on the longest path from x down to a leaf
More than one of the above
exp: bh(x) = the number of black nodes on any downward path from x to a NIL leaf, not counting x.
concept: The black height bh(x) of a node x is the number of black nodes on a path from x down to a NIL leaf, NOT counting x itself (but counting the black NIL leaf). The red-black rules make every such path from x contain the same number of black nodes, so bh(x) is well defined.
why: A — Wrong. The total number of black nodes in the whole subtree adds up all paths together; black height is measured along ONE path.
B — Correct. This is the standard (Cormen) definition: black nodes on any path from x down to a leaf, excluding x.
C — Wrong. Black height counts BLACK nodes, not red ones, and it is the same on every path, so 'longest path' is not needed.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A red-black tree with n internal (key) nodes has height at most:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The height of a red-black tree with n keys is at most 2·log2(n + 1).
concept: A subtree whose root has black height bh contains at least 2^bh − 1 key nodes. No two reds are adjacent, so at least half of the nodes on any root-to-leaf path are black, i.e. bh ≥ h/2. Putting these together, n ≥ 2^(h/2) − 1, so h ≤ 2·log2(n + 1).
work:
Lemma: a subtree with black height bh has at least 2^bh − 1 internal nodes.
No two reds in a row → at least half of the nodes on a root-to-leaf path are black → bh(root) ≥ h/2.
So n ≥ 2^(h/2) − 1 → n + 1 ≥ 2^(h/2) → log2(n + 1) ≥ h/2 → h ≤ 2·log2(n + 1).
why: A — Wrong. log2(n + 1) is about the height of a perfectly balanced tree. A red-black tree can be taller: for example, 6 keys can form a valid red-black tree of height 3, while log2 7 ≈ 2.8.
B — Wrong. (1/2)·log2(n + 1) is, for large n, smaller than the height of even a perfectly balanced tree (about log2 n), so no binary tree could stay within it.
C — Correct. This is the standard bound h ≤ 2·log2(n + 1), proved from the black-height lemma.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: AVL height ≈ 1.44·log2 n at worst; red-black height ≤ 2·log2(n + 1).

q: Red-black trees are used in which of the following?
opts: Typical implementations of the C++ STL std::map and std::set
The Linux kernel's Completely Fair Scheduler, to order runnable tasks
More than one of the above
exp: STL map/set, the Linux CFS scheduler and Java's TreeMap/TreeSet all use red-black trees.
concept: Red-black trees are the most widely used balanced BST in practice, because they keep O(log n) height while needing few rotations on updates. Ordered maps and sets in standard libraries and some operating-system schedulers use them.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. GCC's libstdc++, LLVM's libc++ and Microsoft's STL all implement std::map and std::set as red-black trees (the C++ standard itself only fixes the O(log n) complexity).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Linux's Completely Fair Scheduler kept runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime and ran the leftmost (smallest) task next.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Java's TreeMap is documented as a red-black tree implementation, and TreeSet is built on a TreeMap.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What are the tight worst-case time complexities of search, insertion and deletion (in that order) in a red-black tree with n nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Search, insertion and deletion are all O(log n) in a red-black tree, so none of the listed triples is correct.
concept: A red-black tree has height at most 2·log2(n + 1), which is O(log n). Search walks down one path: O(log n).
