Insertion and deletion must first FIND the position (O(log n)), then recolour and rotate (at most 2 rotations for insertion and 3 for deletion, plus recolouring that may climb the tree). So all three operations take O(log n) time in the worst case.
why: A — Wrong. Search is not O(1): it must walk down the tree, which takes O(log n).
B — Wrong. Deletion is not O(1): the key must first be found (O(log n)), and recolouring may move up the tree. Only the number of ROTATIONS is O(1).
C — Wrong. Insertion is not O(1) for the same reason: finding the place and recolouring take O(log n), even though at most 2 rotations are done.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is O(log n), O(log n), O(log n)), so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: A constant number of rotations does not mean O(1) time: you still have to find the node.

q: What is the smallest factor k such that, in every red-black tree, the longest root-to-NIL path is at most k times as long as the shortest root-to-NIL path?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a red-black tree the longest root-to-NIL path is at most twice the shortest, and the factor 2 can be reached.
concept: In a red-black tree every root-to-NIL path has the same number of black nodes, and red nodes cannot be next to each other. The shortest possible path is all black; the longest alternates black and red. So the longest path is at most twice as long as the shortest.
work:
Let every root-to-NIL path contain b black nodes (root and NIL included).
Shortest path: only black nodes → b − 1 edges.
Longest path: a red node can sit in each of the b − 1 gaps between consecutive blacks → 2b − 1 nodes → 2b − 2 edges.
Ratio = (2b − 2)/(b − 1) = 2.
Example reaching 2: a black root with one red child has 1 edge to the NIL on one side and 2 edges on the other.
why: A — Wrong. 1.5 is too small: a black root with one red child already has paths of 1 and 2 edges, a ratio of 2.
B — Correct. Longest ≤ 2 × shortest, and the factor 2 is actually reached, so 2 is the smallest such factor.
C — Wrong. 3 is a valid bound but not the smallest one; the true limit is 2.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Compared with AVL trees, red-black trees:
opts: usually perform fewer rotations during insertion and deletion
are more strictly balanced, so their searches are faster
cannot guarantee O(log n) worst-case search time
More than one of the above
exp: Red-black trees usually need fewer rotations than AVL trees; both give O(log n) search.
concept: AVL trees keep strict balance (subtree heights differ by at most 1), so they are shorter but need more rotations when keys are added or removed. Red-black trees allow more imbalance (height up to 2·log2(n + 1)), so they rotate less: at most 2 rotations per insertion and 3 per deletion. Both guarantee O(log n) search.
why: A — Correct. Red-black trees tolerate more imbalance, so insertions and deletions trigger fewer rotations than in AVL trees.
B — Wrong. It is the other way round: AVL trees are the more strictly balanced ones, so AVL searches are usually slightly faster.
C — Wrong. Red-black trees do guarantee O(log n) worst-case search, because their height is at most 2·log2(n + 1).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Many lookups → AVL. Many updates → red-black.

q: During red-black insertion, the new red node z has a red parent and a red uncle. What is the correct fix-up step?
opts: Recolour parent and uncle black, grandparent red; repeat from the grandparent
Rotate at the grandparent and swap colours of parent and grandparent; stop
Colour z black, leaving the parent and uncle red; stop
More than one of the above
exp: Red parent and red uncle: recolour (parent and uncle black, grandparent red) and continue from the grandparent.
concept: During red-black insertion, a red-red conflict (a red node with a red parent) is fixed by looking at the UNCLE (the parent's sibling). If the uncle is red, only recolour: parent and uncle become black, the grandparent becomes red, and the check continues from the grandparent, which may now have a red parent. If the uncle is black, rotations are used.
why: A — Correct. Red uncle → recolour the parent and uncle black and the grandparent red. Black heights stay the same, and the check repeats from the grandparent.
B — Wrong. A rotation at the grandparent with a colour swap is the fix when the uncle is BLACK (outer-child case), not when it is red.
C — Wrong. Colouring z black would add an extra black node only on z's paths, breaking the equal-black-height rule.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Uncle red → recolour. Uncle black → rotate.

q: An application performs millions of searches but very few insertions and deletions. Which balanced BST is generally the better choice, and why?
opts: Red-black tree, because its height is always smaller than an AVL tree's
AVL tree, because it is more strictly balanced and so has smaller height
Red-black tree, because its search runs in O(1) time
More than one of the above
exp: For many searches and few updates, choose an AVL tree, because its stricter balance gives a smaller height.
concept: Search time depends on the height of the tree. AVL trees are more strictly balanced (height about 1.44·log2 n at worst) than red-black trees (height up to 2·log2(n + 1)). So for search-heavy work AVL trees are slightly faster, while red-black trees win when there are many insertions and deletions, because they rotate less.
why: A — Wrong. It is the opposite: a red-black tree may be TALLER than an AVL tree holding the same keys.
B — Correct. AVL trees are more strictly balanced, so their height (and the number of comparisons per search) is smaller, which suits search-heavy applications.
C — Wrong. No balanced BST searches in O(1); red-black search is O(log n).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A BST is coloured as follows: root 20 (black) with children 10 (red) and 30 (red); node 10 has a single left child 5 (red); all NIL leaves are black. Which red-black property does it violate?
opts: Every root-to-NIL path must contain the same number of black nodes
A red node cannot have a red child
More than one of the above
exp: Red node 10 has a red child 5, so the 'no red node has a red child' rule is broken.
concept: To check a coloured BST, test each red-black rule in turn: root black; NIL leaves black; no red node with a red child; and the same number of black nodes on every root-to-NIL path. Then name exactly which rule is broken.
work:
Root 20 is black → rule satisfied.
Red node 10 has red child 5 → red-red violation.
Black nodes on each root-to-NIL path (not counting the root): 20→10→5→NIL: 1 (the NIL); 20→10→NIL: 1; 20→30→NIL: 1. All equal → black-height rule satisfied.
why: A — Wrong. The root 20 is black, so this rule is satisfied.
B — Wrong. Every path from the root to a NIL leaf has the same number of black nodes (only the root and the NIL are black on each path), so this rule holds.
C — Correct. Node 10 is red and its child 5 is also red: two reds in a row, which is not allowed.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 10, 20, 30, 40 are inserted in this order into an empty red-black tree using standard insertion (new node red, then fix-up). Which describes the final tree?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Final tree: root 20 (black) with black children 10 and 30, and 40 (red) as the right child of 30.
concept: Red-black insertion: insert as in a BST and colour the new node red, then fix any red-red conflict. Red uncle → recolour the parent and uncle black and the grandparent red, and continue upward. Black uncle → rotate at the grandparent (with a colour swap). Finally colour the root black.
work:
Standard insertion: insert as in a BST, colour the new node red, then fix up (red uncle → recolour; black uncle → rotate).
Insert 10: 10 becomes the root (inserted red). The root 10 is red → recolour it black. Rotations so far: 0.
  10 (black)
Insert 20: 20 is inserted red as the right child of 10 (black). Its parent is black, so no fix-up is needed. Rotations so far: 0.
  10 (black)
    R: 20 (red)
Insert 30: 30 is inserted red as the right child of 20 (red). Red parent 20, uncle NIL (black), 30 is an outer (right) child: colour 20 black, 10 red, left rotation at 10. Rotations so far: 1.
  20 (black)
    L: 10 (red)
    R: 30 (red)
Insert 40: 40 is inserted red as the right child of 30 (red). Red parent 30 and red uncle 10: recolour 30 and 10 black, grandparent 20 red; continue from 20. The root 20 is red → recolour it black. Rotations so far: 1.
  20 (black)
    L: 10 (black)
    R: 30 (black)
      R: 40 (red)
why: A — Correct. After 30, a left rotation gives 20 (black) with red children 10 and 30. Inserting 40 meets a red uncle (10), so 10 and 30 become black and 20 red; then the root 20 is recoloured black. 40 stays red.
B — Wrong. This forgets to recolour the uncle 10. With 10 red and 30 black, the path 20→10→NIL has fewer black nodes than 20→30→NIL, breaking the black-height rule.
C — Wrong. The root stays 20. Inserting 40 needs only recolouring (red uncle), not a rotation that would make 30 the root.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 are inserted in this order into an empty red-black tree using standard insertion. How many rotations are performed in total, and what is the final root?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Two rotations (at 10 and at 30); the final root is 20.
concept: Count rotations by tracing each insertion separately. With a red uncle only recolouring happens (no rotation). With a black uncle (a NIL counts as black) there is one rotation for an outer child and two for an inner child. Increasing keys always give the outer-child case.
work:
Standard insertion: insert as in a BST, colour the new node red, then fix up (red uncle → recolour; black uncle → rotate).
Insert 10: 10 becomes the root (inserted red). The root 10 is red → recolour it black. Rotations so far: 0.
  10 (black)
Insert 20: 20 is inserted red as the right child of 10 (black). Its parent is black, so no fix-up is needed. Rotations so far: 0.
  10 (black)
    R: 20 (red)
Insert 30: 30 is inserted red as the right child of 20 (red). Red parent 20, uncle NIL (black), 30 is an outer (right) child: colour 20 black, 10 red, left rotation at 10. Rotations so far: 1.
  20 (black)
    L: 10 (red)
    R: 30 (red)
Insert 40: 40 is inserted red as the right child of 30 (red). Red parent 30 and red uncle 10: recolour 30 and 10 black, grandparent 20 red; continue from 20. The root 20 is red → recolour it black. Rotations so far: 1.
  20 (black)
    L: 10 (black)
    R: 30 (black)
      R: 40 (red)
Insert 50: 50 is inserted red as the right child of 40 (red). Red parent 40, uncle NIL (black), 50 is an outer (right) child: colour 40 black, 30 red, left rotation at 30. Rotations so far: 2.
  20 (black)
    L: 10 (black)
    R: 40 (black)
      L: 30 (red)
      R: 50 (red)
Total rotations: 2 (one while inserting 30, one while inserting 50). Final root 20.
why: A — Wrong. 1 rotation is the count after 4 insertions. Inserting 50 makes 40 and 50 a red-red pair with a black (NIL) uncle, which needs another rotation.
B — Correct. Rotations happen when 30 is inserted (left rotation at 10) and when 50 is inserted (left rotation at 30). 40 needs only recolouring. The root stays 20.
C — Wrong. There are 2 rotations, but the second one is at 30, deep in the tree, so the root does not change; it stays 20.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The black height of the root of a red-black tree is 4 (black nodes on a root-to-NIL path, counting the NIL leaf but not the root). What is the minimum possible number of internal (key) nodes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The minimum number of internal nodes is 2^4 − 1 = 15, which is not listed.
concept: A key fact of red-black trees: a subtree whose root has black height bh has at least 2^bh − 1 internal (key) nodes. The fewest nodes occur when the tree is all black and perfect. Here bh counts the NIL leaf but not the root.
work:
Minimum internal nodes = 2^bh − 1 = 2^4 − 1 = 15.
It is reached by an all-black perfect tree with 4 levels of key nodes (1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15): each root-to-NIL path has 3 black key nodes below the root plus the NIL leaf = 4.
why: A — Wrong. 7 = 2^3 − 1 is the minimum for black height 3; it comes from counting one black level too few.
B — Wrong. 16 = 2^4 forgets the '− 1' in 2^bh − 1.
C — Wrong. 31 = 2^5 − 1 is what you get if you also count the root, as if the black height were 5.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 15), so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: In a binary max-heap, which condition must hold for every node other than the root?
opts: Its key is less than or equal to its parent's key
Its key is greater than or equal to its parent's key
Its key is less than its right sibling's key
More than one of the above
exp: In a max-heap every non-root key is ≤ its parent's key.
concept: A binary max-heap satisfies the heap-order property: every parent's key is greater than or equal to its children's keys. Seen from the child's side, every node except the root has a key ≤ its parent's key. So the largest key is always at the root. Nothing is said about the order between siblings.
why: A — Correct. This is the max-heap property seen from the child's side: each child ≤ its parent.
B — Wrong. Child ≥ parent is the MIN-heap property, where the smallest key is at the root.
C — Wrong. Heaps do not order siblings; the left child may be larger or smaller than the right child.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In terms of shape, a binary heap with n elements is always a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In shape, a binary heap is always a complete binary tree.
concept: A binary heap must satisfy a shape rule: it is a complete binary tree, meaning every level is full except possibly the last, and the last level is filled from left to right. This shape lets the heap be stored in an array with no gaps.
why: A — Wrong. A full binary tree needs every node to have 0 or 2 children. A heap with an even number of elements has one node with only a left child, so a heap is not always full.
B — Wrong. In a BST, left < node < right. A heap only needs parent ≥ children (in a max-heap), so its keys are not in BST order.
C — Correct. Every heap is a complete binary tree: all levels full except possibly the last, which fills from the left.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Heap = complete shape + heap order.

q: A binary heap is stored in an array whose indices start at 0. The children of the node at index i are at indices:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a 0-based heap the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
concept: A complete binary tree can be stored level by level in an array. With indices starting at 0, the node at index i has its left child at 2i + 1, its right child at 2i + 2 and its parent at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋. With indices starting at 1, the formulas are 2i, 2i + 1 and ⌊i/2⌋.
why: A — Wrong. 2i and 2i + 1 are the child formulas for 1-based arrays. With 0-based indexing, 2i would make the root (i = 0) its own child.
B — Correct. For 0-based arrays, left = 2i + 1 and right = 2i + 2. Check: the root at index 0 has children at 1 and 2.
C — Wrong. i + 1 and i + 2 are just the next positions in the array; that describes a linear list, not a tree.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Test any formula on the root: index 0 must have children 1 and 2.

q: Which data structure is most commonly used to implement a priority queue that supports insert and delete-max in O(log n) time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A binary heap is the usual way to build a priority queue with O(log n) insert and delete-max.
concept: A priority queue always serves the most important item first, like a hospital emergency ward that treats the most serious patient first. A binary heap supports insert and delete-max in O(log n) and find-max in O(1), so it is the standard implementation.
why: A — Correct. A binary heap does insert (sift-up) and delete-max (sift-down) in O(log n) each, and it is the usual priority-queue implementation.
B — Wrong. A sorted array gives the maximum in O(1), but inserting a new element needs shifting other elements, which is O(n).
C — Wrong. An unsorted linked list inserts in O(1), but finding and deleting the maximum needs a full scan, which is O(n).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: To sort an array in ascending order in place, heap sort first builds a ____ and then repeatedly swaps the root with the last element of the heap.
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Ascending heap sort builds a max-heap and repeatedly moves the root (the maximum) to the end.
concept: Heap sort works in two phases. First it builds a max-heap from the array. Then it repeatedly swaps the root (the current maximum) with the last element of the heap, shrinks the heap by one and sifts the new root down. The largest values collect at the end of the array, so the result is in ascending order.
why: A — Wrong. Used in the same way, a min-heap puts the SMALLEST remaining value at the end each time, giving descending order.
B — Correct. A max-heap moves the largest remaining value to the end on each pass, so the array ends up in ascending order, in place.
C — Wrong. A binary search tree is used in tree sort, not in heap sort, and it is not built inside the array.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Swap-root-to-end heap sort: max-heap → ascending; min-heap → descending.

q: What is the tightest worst-case time to build a binary heap from n unsorted elements using the bottom-up method (sift-down from the last internal node back to the root)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Bottom-up heap construction takes O(n) time.
concept: Bottom-up build-heap runs sift-down from the last internal node back to the root. Most nodes are near the bottom and can move down only a few levels: about n/2 nodes move 0 levels, n/4 at most 1, n/8 at most 2, and so on. The total work n·(1/4 + 2/8 + 3/16 + …) is at most n, so the whole build takes O(n) time.
work: Total work ≤ Σ (number of nodes at height h) × h ≈ Σ (n / 2^(h+1)) × h = (n/2) × Σ h/2^h ≤ (n/2) × 2 = n → O(n).
why: A — Wrong. O(log n) is the cost of ONE sift-down. Building a heap must at least look at all n elements, so it cannot be faster than O(n).
B — Correct. Because most nodes are close to the leaves, the total sift-down work is linear: O(n).
C — Wrong. O(n log n) is the cost of inserting the n elements one at a time (top-down build). It is a valid upper bound for the bottom-up method too, but not the tightest.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a binary max-heap with n distinct elements, what are the worst-case times to find the maximum and to find the minimum element?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In a max-heap, find-max is O(1) and find-min is O(n).
concept: In a max-heap the largest element is always at the root, so finding it takes O(1). The smallest element must be a leaf (any node with a child is larger than that child), but it can be ANY of the about n/2 leaves, and the heap gives no clue which one. So finding the minimum takes O(n).
why: A — Correct. Maximum: read a[0], O(1). Minimum: scan the ⌈n/2⌉ leaves, O(n).
B — Wrong. The minimum cannot be found in O(log n); no single path leads to it, because siblings and cousins are not ordered.
C — Wrong. The maximum is at the root, so it takes O(1), not O(log n); and the minimum needs O(n), not O(log n).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following operations take O(log n) worst-case time on a binary max-heap of n elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Insert and delete-max are O(log n); searching for an arbitrary key is O(n).
concept: A binary heap is only partly ordered: each parent beats its children, but there is no left-right order. Insert and delete-max move one element along a single root-to-leaf path (height ⌊log2 n⌋), so they are O(log n). Searching for an arbitrary key may require checking every element, which is O(n).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Insert appends at the end and sifts up along one path to the root: at most ⌊log2 n⌋ swaps, O(log n).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Delete-max moves the last element to the root and sifts it down along one path: O(log n).
C — Wrong. A heap has no search order (unlike a BST), so an arbitrary key may be anywhere; the worst case is O(n).
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about heap sort are true?
opts: Its worst-case time complexity is O(n log n)
It sorts in place using O(1) extra space
It is a stable sorting algorithm
More than one of the above
exp: Heap sort is O(n log n) in the worst case and in place, but not stable.
concept: Heap sort builds a max-heap in O(n) and then performs n − 1 delete-max steps of O(log n) each, so it is O(n log n) in every case. It rearranges the array itself and needs only a few extra variables, so it is in place. It is NOT stable: equal keys can change their relative order because of the long-distance swaps.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Build-heap O(n) + (n − 1) sift-downs of O(log n) each = O(n log n), even in the worst case.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Heap sort works inside the same array and uses only a constant number of extra variables (with an iterative sift-down).
C — Wrong. Swapping the root with the last heap element moves elements over long distances, so two equal keys can swap their order. Heap sort is not stable.
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Stable: bubble, insertion, merge. Not stable: heap, quick, selection.

q: A binary heap is stored in an array whose indices start at 1. What is the index of the parent of the node at index 13?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The parent of index 13 in a 1-based heap is ⌊13/2⌋ = 6.
concept: With 1-based array indexing, the node at index i has children at 2i and 2i + 1, and its parent is at ⌊i/2⌋ (integer division, rounding down).
work:
parent(13) = ⌊13/2⌋ = ⌊6.5⌋ = 6
Check: the children of index 6 are 2·6 = 12 and 2·6 + 1 = 13.
why: A — Correct. ⌊13/2⌋ = 6, and node 6 indeed has children 12 and 13.
B — Wrong. 7 comes from rounding 6.5 UP; the parent formula uses the floor. Node 7's children are 14 and 15.
C — Wrong. 12 is just i − 1, the previous array position (13's sibling), not its parent.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many leaves does a binary heap with 25 elements have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A heap with 25 elements has ⌈25/2⌉ = 13 leaves, which is not listed.
concept: In a heap (complete binary tree) with n elements, using 1-based indices, the internal (non-leaf) nodes are indices 1 to ⌊n/2⌋ and the leaves are indices ⌊n/2⌋ + 1 to n. So the number of leaves is n − ⌊n/2⌋ = ⌈n/2⌉.
work:
n = 25
Internal nodes = ⌊25/2⌋ = 12 (indices 1–12)
Leaves = 25 − 12 = 13 (indices 13–25)
Level check: levels 0–3 hold 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes; the bottom level holds 10; on level 3, indices 13, 14, 15 have no children → 10 + 3 = 13 leaves.
why: A — Wrong. 12 = ⌊n/2⌋ is the number of INTERNAL nodes, not leaves.
B — Wrong. 14 does not match: the leaves are exactly indices 13 to 25, which is 13 nodes.
C — Wrong. 16 = 2^4 would be a completely filled bottom level (a 31-node heap). With 25 nodes the bottom level holds only 10 nodes, and 3 nodes of the level above are also leaves (10 + 3 = 13).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 13), so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: In a heap: leaves = ⌈n/2⌉, internal nodes = ⌊n/2⌋.

q: What is the height of a binary heap with 100 elements? (Height = number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The height of a 100-element heap is ⌊log2 100⌋ = 6.
concept: A heap is a complete binary tree, so its height (in edges) is ⌊log2 n⌋. All levels are full except perhaps the last, so a heap of height h has between 2^h and 2^(h+1) − 1 elements.
work:
2^6 = 64 ≤ 100 < 128 = 2^7
height = ⌊log2 100⌋ = 6
(Levels 0–5 hold 63 nodes; the remaining 37 are on level 6.)
why: A — Wrong. A heap of height 5 holds at most 2^6 − 1 = 63 elements, fewer than 100.
B — Correct. ⌊log2 100⌋ = 6, because 64 ≤ 100 < 128.
C — Wrong. 7 is the number of LEVELS (levels 0 to 6), i.e. the height counted in nodes instead of edges.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: buildHeap below is called with n = 20 (elements a[0] to a[19]). At which index does the loop start, and how many times does the loop call heapify?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The loop starts at index 9 and calls heapify 10 times.
concept: In a 0-based heap of n elements, indices ⌊n/2⌋ to n − 1 are leaves, and a single leaf is already a heap. So bottom-up build-heap only needs to sift down at indices ⌊n/2⌋ − 1 down to 0, which is ⌊n/2⌋ calls.
work:
n = 20 → the loop starts at i = 20/2 − 1 = 9
Last element index 19 → its parent = ⌊(19 − 1)/2⌋ = 9 (the last internal node)
The loop runs i = 9, 8, …, 0 → 10 calls of heapify
why: A — Wrong. 10 is n/2 without the '− 1'. Index 10 is a leaf (its left child would be 21, beyond 19), so it is not visited; and there are 10 calls, not 11.
B — Wrong. Starting at 19 would also process all the leaves, which is unnecessary; the code starts at n/2 − 1 = 9.
C — Correct. i starts at 9 and goes down to 0, which is 10 calls.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Array a[0..n−1] (n ≥ 1) holds a max-heap with distinct keys. What does f return?
opts: The minimum element of the heap
The second-largest element of the heap
The smallest key among the non-leaf nodes
More than one of the above
exp: f returns the minimum element of the max-heap by scanning only the leaves.
concept: In a 0-based heap with n elements, indices ⌊n/2⌋ to n − 1 are exactly the leaves. In a max-heap every internal node is larger than its child, so the smallest element can never be an internal node; it must be a leaf. Scanning only the leaves finds the minimum with about n/2 comparisons.
work:
Example: a = [90, 70, 80, 40, 50, 60, 75, 10], n = 8
n/2 = 4 → m = a[4] = 50; scan i = 5, 6, 7: 60, 75, 10 → m = 10
The minimum of the heap is 10 (the compiled C code also prints 10).
n = 1: m = a[0] and the loop does not run → returns the only element.
why: A — Correct. f scans exactly the leaves a[n/2..n−1] and returns the smallest of them, which is the minimum of the whole heap.
B — Wrong. The second-largest element is one of the root's children, a[1] or a[2]; it is not found by scanning the leaves.
C — Wrong. f never looks at the non-leaf nodes (indices 0 to n/2 − 1); it looks only at the leaves.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following arrays represents a valid binary max-heap? (Array index 0 = root.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only C satisfies parent ≥ children everywhere.
concept: To check a max-heap array (0-based), check every parent–child pair: a[i] ≥ a[2i + 1] and a[i] ≥ a[2i + 2] wherever those children exist. The shape is automatically complete, because an array has no gaps.
why: A — Wrong. 40 at index 1 has the child 45 at index 3, and 40 < 45 breaks the max-heap rule.
B — Wrong. 30 at index 1 has the child 35 at index 3, and 40 at index 2 has the child 45 at index 5; both break the rule.
C — Correct. Every parent is at least as large as its children, so this is a valid max-heap.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following arrays represent valid binary min-heaps? (Array index 0 = root.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A and B are valid min-heaps; C is not.
concept: A min-heap array (0-based) must satisfy a[i] ≤ a[2i + 1] and a[i] ≤ a[2i + 2] for every parent. Check every parent, not just the root; siblings may be in any order.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Every parent is ≤ its children (2 ≤ 5, 3; 5 ≤ 9, 6; 3 ≤ 4).
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Every parent is ≤ its children (1 ≤ 3, 2; 3 ≤ 7, 4; 2 ≤ 8, 5).
C — Wrong. 4 at index 1 has the child 3 at index 3; 4 > 3 breaks the min-heap rule.
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Key 85 is inserted into the max-heap [90, 70, 80, 40, 50, 60, 75] by appending it at the end and sifting it up. What is the resulting array? (Array index 0 = root.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After sift-up the heap is [90, 85, 80, 70, 50, 60, 75, 40].
concept: To insert into a max-heap, put the new key in the next free position (the end of the array), then sift it up: while it is larger than its parent (at index ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋), swap them. Stop when the parent is larger or the key reaches the root. This takes at most ⌊log2 n⌋ swaps.
work:
Start: [90, 70, 80, 40, 50, 60, 75]
Append 85 at the end (index 7): [90, 70, 80, 40, 50, 60, 75, 85]
85 at index 7, parent 40 at index 3: swap → [90, 70, 80, 85, 50, 60, 75, 40]
85 at index 3, parent 70 at index 1: swap → [90, 85, 80, 70, 50, 60, 75, 40]
85 at index 1, parent 90 at index 0: parent is larger, stop.
Result: [90, 85, 80, 70, 50, 60, 75, 40]
why: A — Correct. 85 moves from index 7 to index 3 (swap with 40), then to index 1 (swap with 70), and stops below 90.
B — Wrong. This stops after the first swap, but 85 is still larger than its new parent 70, so sifting must continue.

C — Wrong. Here 70 has jumped to the end while 40 is still at index 3, which is not what sift-up does (and 40 would then be the parent of 70, which is invalid). 85 passes through index 3, pushing 40 down to index 7 and 70 down to index 3.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Key 3 is inserted into the min-heap [5, 10, 8, 20, 15, 12] by appending it and sifting it up. What is the resulting array? (Array index 0 = root.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After sift-up the min-heap is [3, 10, 5, 20, 15, 12, 8].
concept: Inserting into a min-heap: append the key at the end, then sift it up — swap it with its parent while it is SMALLER than the parent. A new minimum climbs all the way to the root, and only the nodes on its path move down.
work:
Start: [5, 10, 8, 20, 15, 12]
Append 3 at the end (index 6): [5, 10, 8, 20, 15, 12, 3]
3 at index 6, parent 8 at index 2: swap → [5, 10, 3, 20, 15, 12, 8]
3 at index 2, parent 5 at index 0: swap → [3, 10, 5, 20, 15, 12, 8]
3 has reached the root (index 0), stop.
Result: [3, 10, 5, 20, 15, 12, 8]
why: A — Wrong. 3 travels along the path index 6 → 2 → 0, so only 8 and 5 move. This array instead moves 10 to the end and 5 to index 1, which are not on that path.
B — Correct. 3 swaps with 8 (index 2), then with 5 (index 0): [3, 10, 5, 20, 15, 12, 8].
C — Wrong. This stops after one swap, but 3 is still smaller than its new parent 5, so it must keep moving up.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Delete-max is performed on the max-heap [100, 80, 90, 40, 70, 60, 30]: the last element replaces the root and is sifted down. What is the resulting array? (Array index 0 = root.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The correct result is [90, 80, 60, 40, 70, 30], which is not listed.
concept: Delete-max from a max-heap: remove the root, move the LAST element to the root, then sift it down: swap it with its LARGER child while it is smaller than that child. Swapping with the larger child is essential, so that the new parent is bigger than both children.
work:
Start: [100, 80, 90, 40, 70, 60, 30]
Remove the root 100; move the last element 30 to the root: [30, 80, 90, 40, 70, 60]
30 at index 0: children 80 (index 1), 90 (index 2); larger child is 90 → swap → [90, 80, 30, 40, 70, 60]
30 at index 2: children 60 (index 5); larger child is 60 → swap → [90, 80, 60, 40, 70, 30]
30 at index 5: no children (leaf), stop.
Result: [90, 80, 60, 40, 70, 30]
why: A — Wrong. This stops after one swap. 30 at index 2 still has a larger child, 60 at index 5, so it must sift down once more.
B — Wrong. Here 30 was first swapped with the left child 80 instead of the larger child 90, which leaves 90 below 80 and breaks the heap property.
C — Wrong. This is not a valid max-heap: 70 at index 1 has the child 80 at index 4.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is [90, 80, 60, 40, 70, 30]), so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Sift-down in a max-heap: always swap with the LARGER child.

q: What is the output of the following C program?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The program prints 9 5 8 4 3 7 6.
concept: heapify (sift-down) at index i compares a[i] with its children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, swaps it with the largest one if needed, and then continues recursively at the child's position. It stops when the element is larger than both children or reaches a leaf.
work:
Start: [3, 9, 8, 4, 5, 7, 6]; heapify(a, 7, 0). Children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
3 at index 0: children 9 (index 1), 8 (index 2); larger child is 9 → swap → [9, 3, 8, 4, 5, 7, 6]
3 at index 1: children 4 (index 3), 5 (index 4); larger child is 5 → swap → [9, 5, 8, 4, 3, 7, 6]
3 at index 4: no children (leaf), stop.
Printed: 9 5 8 4 3 7 6
why: A — Wrong. This shows only the first swap. The recursive call heapify(a, n, 1) then moves 3 below 5.
B — Correct. 3 swaps with 9 (index 1), then with 5 (index 4); index 4 has no children, so it stops: 9 5 8 4 3 7 6.
C — Wrong. This wrongly moves 8 to index 1. 8 is the root's right child (index 2) and never moves, because the root swaps only with its larger child 9.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 are inserted one at a time (append, then sift up) into an initially empty max-heap. What is the final array? (Array index 0 = root.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Repeated insertion gives [50, 40, 20, 10, 30].
concept: Building a heap by inserting one key at a time: each key is appended at the end and sifted up. With increasing keys, every new key is the largest so far and climbs to the root, pushing the old ancestors down. The result can differ from the bottom-up build-heap method applied to the same keys.
work:
Insert 10: append → [10]
  heap now [10]
Insert 20: append → [10, 20]
  20 at index 1, parent 10 at index 0: swap → [20, 10]
  20 has reached the root (index 0), stop.
  heap now [20, 10]
Insert 30: append → [20, 10, 30]
  30 at index 2, parent 20 at index 0: swap → [30, 10, 20]
  30 has reached the root (index 0), stop.
  heap now [30, 10, 20]
Insert 40: append → [30, 10, 20, 40]
  40 at index 3, parent 10 at index 1: swap → [30, 40, 20, 10]
  40 at index 1, parent 30 at index 0: swap → [40, 30, 20, 10]
  40 has reached the root (index 0), stop.
  heap now [40, 30, 20, 10]
Insert 50: append → [40, 30, 20, 10, 50]
  50 at index 4, parent 30 at index 1: swap → [40, 50, 20, 10, 30]
  50 at index 1, parent 40 at index 0: swap → [50, 40, 20, 10, 30]
  50 has reached the root (index 0), stop.
  heap now [50, 40, 20, 10, 30]
Result: [50, 40, 20, 10, 30]
why: A — Wrong. [50, 40, 30, 10, 20] is the heap produced by the bottom-up build-heap method on [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], not by repeated insertion.
B — Wrong. [50, 30, 40, 20, 10] is a valid max-heap, but not the one these insertions produce: once 30 is inserted, 20 sits at index 2 and never moves again.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: One-by-one insertion and bottom-up build-heap can give DIFFERENT valid heaps for the same keys.

q: Bottom-up build-heap (sift-down at indices ⌊n/2⌋ − 1 down to 0) is applied to [5, 12, 3, 8, 20, 7, 15, 1, 9] to form a max-heap. What is the resulting array? (Array index 0 = root.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Bottom-up build-heap gives [20, 12, 15, 9, 5, 7, 3, 1, 8].
concept: Bottom-up build-heap: for i = ⌊n/2⌋ − 1 down to 0, sift a[i] down (swap it with the larger child until it is larger than both children). Leaves are skipped because a single node is already a heap. An element may move down more than one level, as 5 does here.
work:
Start: [5, 12, 3, 8, 20, 7, 15, 1, 9], n = 9, so sift-down runs at indices 3, 2, 1, 0 (indices 4 to 8 are leaves).
i = 3:
  8 at index 3: children 1 (index 7), 9 (index 8); larger child is 9 → swap → [5, 12, 3, 9, 20, 7, 15, 1, 8]
  8 at index 8: no children (leaf), stop.
i = 2:
  3 at index 2: children 7 (index 5), 15 (index 6); larger child is 15 → swap → [5, 12, 15, 9, 20, 7, 3, 1, 8]
  3 at index 6: no children (leaf), stop.
i = 1:
  12 at index 1: children 9 (index 3), 20 (index 4); larger child is 20 → swap → [5, 20, 15, 9, 12, 7, 3, 1, 8]
  12 at index 4: no children (leaf), stop.
i = 0:
  5 at index 0: children 20 (index 1), 15 (index 2); larger child is 20 → swap → [20, 5, 15, 9, 12, 7, 3, 1, 8]
  5 at index 1: children 9 (index 3), 12 (index 4); larger child is 12 → swap → [20, 12, 15, 9, 5, 7, 3, 1, 8]
  5 at index 4: no children (leaf), stop.
Result: [20, 12, 15, 9, 5, 7, 3, 1, 8]
why: A — Correct. Sift-down at indices 3, 2, 1, 0 gives [20, 12, 15, 9, 5, 7, 3, 1, 8].
B — Wrong. [20, 12, 15, 9, 8, 3, 7, 1, 5] is the heap you get by inserting the keys one at a time with sift-up, not by bottom-up build-heap.
C — Wrong. This is simply the keys in descending order. It is a valid max-heap, but build-heap does not sort the array.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Take the order m of a B-tree to be the maximum number of children of a node. The maximum number of keys a node of a B-tree of order m can hold is:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A node of a B-tree of order m holds at most m − 1 keys.
concept: In a B-tree, a node with k keys has k + 1 children, because k keys divide the key range into k + 1 parts. So if the order m is the maximum number of children, a node holds at most m − 1 keys. Every non-root node must also hold at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys.
why: A — Wrong. m keys would need m + 1 children, which is more than the order m allows.
B — Correct. Keys = children − 1, so a node holds at most m − 1 keys.
C — Wrong. ⌈m/2⌉ is the MINIMUM number of children of a non-root internal node, not the maximum number of keys.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: k dividers cut a line into k + 1 pieces: k keys → k + 1 children.

q: B-trees are primarily designed to:
opts: allow O(1) search of any key held in main memory
keep every internal node with exactly two children
minimise disk (block) accesses for large data on secondary storage
More than one of the above
exp: B-trees are designed to minimise disk (block) accesses.
concept: A B-tree is a balanced search tree designed for data stored on disk. Reading a disk block is far slower than reading main memory, so each node is made as large as one disk block and holds many keys. With such a large branching factor the tree is very short, and a search reads only a few blocks.
why: A — Wrong. B-tree search is O(log n) (with a very large logarithm base), not O(1). O(1) average-case search is what hashing aims for.
B — Wrong. B-tree nodes have MANY children (up to m), not exactly two. Exactly two children for every internal node describes a full binary tree.
C — Correct. Large, block-sized nodes make the tree shallow, so few disk blocks are read per search.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Take the order m of a B-tree to be the maximum number of children of a node. In a B-tree of order m, the root, when it is not a leaf, must have at least:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A non-leaf root of a B-tree needs at least 2 children.
concept: In a B-tree of order m, every internal node except the root must have at least ⌈m/2⌉ children (it must be at least half full). The root is an exception: it may hold just one key, so a non-leaf root needs only 2 children. This lets the tree grow taller by splitting the root.
why: A — Correct. The root may hold a single key, which gives it 2 children; that is the minimum for a non-leaf root.
B — Wrong. ⌈m/2⌉ is the minimum for the other internal nodes; the root is exempt from this rule.
C — Wrong. m − 1 is the maximum number of KEYS in a node, not a minimum number of children.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a B+ tree, where are the data records (or the pointers to the records) stored?
opts: In every node, together with its keys
More than one of the above
exp: In a B+ tree, records are stored only in the leaf nodes.
concept: A B+ tree is a B-tree variant used for database indexes. Internal nodes contain only routing keys (signposts) and child pointers. All data records, or pointers to them, are stored in the leaf nodes, and the leaves are linked together in key order.
why: A — Wrong. Storing data with the keys in every node describes an ordinary B-tree, not a B+ tree.
B — Correct. In a B+ tree all records (or record pointers) are in the leaves; internal nodes only guide the search.
C — Wrong. Internal nodes hold only routing keys; keeping the data only there would be the opposite of a B+ tree.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: B+ tree: signposts above, data at the bottom, leaves linked like a chain.

q: Take the order m of a B-tree to be the maximum number of children of a node. Which of the following hold for every B-tree of order m?
opts: All leaves appear at the same level
The keys inside every node are kept in sorted order
Every node other than the root has at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys
More than one of the above
exp: All three are standard properties of every B-tree.
concept: A B-tree of order m follows these rules: all leaves are on the same level (it is perfectly height-balanced); keys inside a node are sorted; every node has at most m − 1 keys; every non-root node has at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys; and the root has at least 1 key. The tree grows by splitting the root, which keeps all the leaves level.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. All leaves are at the same depth, because the tree only grows at the top (by splitting the root) and shrinks at the top (by merging into the root).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Keys within a node are kept in increasing order, so the node can be searched and the correct child chosen.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Every non-root node must be at least about half full: at least ⌈m/2⌉ − 1 keys.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Take the order m of a B-tree to be the maximum number of children of a node. For a B-tree of order 9, what are the maximum number of keys in any node and the minimum number of keys in a non-root node?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Order 9: at most 8 keys in a node, and at least 4 keys in a non-root node.
concept: For a B-tree of order m (maximum number of children): maximum keys per node = m − 1; minimum children of a non-root internal node = ⌈m/2⌉; minimum keys of a non-root node = ⌈m/2⌉ − 1.
work:
m = 9
Maximum keys = 9 − 1 = 8
Minimum keys (non-root) = ⌈9/2⌉ − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4
why: A — Correct. Maximum keys 9 − 1 = 8; minimum keys ⌈9/2⌉ − 1 = 4.
B — Wrong. 9 is the maximum number of CHILDREN; the maximum number of keys is one less, 8.
C — Wrong. 5 = ⌈9/2⌉ is the minimum number of CHILDREN of a non-root internal node; the minimum number of keys is 4.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Most database systems use B+ trees for their indexes. Which feature of a B+ tree especially helps a range query such as salary BETWEEN 20000 AND 40000?
opts: B+ trees never need to split nodes
Internal nodes hold the full records, so leaves need not be visited
Leaf nodes are linked in key order, so the range is scanned sequentially
More than one of the above
exp: Leaves linked in key order make range queries fast in a B+ tree.
concept: In a B+ tree every key appears in the leaves, and the leaves are linked in sorted order like a chain. A range query finds the first key ≥ 20000 with one root-to-leaf search, then simply walks along the leaf chain until the keys pass 40000, without going back up the tree.
why: A — Wrong. B+ trees do split nodes when they overflow, just like B-trees.
B — Wrong. Internal nodes of a B+ tree hold only keys and pointers; the records are in the leaves, so the leaves must be visited.
C — Correct. Linked leaves let the query scan the whole range sequentially after a single search.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following correctly describe ways in which a B+ tree differs from a B-tree?
opts: Internal nodes hold only keys and child pointers, so more keys fit in a disk block (higher fan-out)
Every successful search must go all the way down to a leaf
The leaf level contains every key of the tree, in sorted order
More than one of the above
exp: All three statements describe how a B+ tree differs from a B-tree.
concept: Main differences of a B+ tree from a B-tree: (1) internal nodes store only keys and child pointers, no data, so more keys fit in a block and the tree is shorter; (2) all data is in the leaves, so every search goes down to a leaf; (3) the leaf level contains every key in sorted order, and the leaves are linked, which makes range scans easy. Some keys therefore appear twice (in an internal node and in a leaf).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. With no records inside internal nodes, each block holds more keys, which gives a higher fan-out and a shorter tree.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Records are only in the leaves, so even if the key matches a routing key in an internal node, the search continues to the leaf. In a B-tree a search can stop at an internal node.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Every key is present at the leaf level, in sorted order (and the leaves are linked).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 are inserted in this order into an empty B-tree of order 5 (at most 4 keys per node). A node that overflows to 5 keys is split and its middle key moves up to the parent. What are the keys in the root at the end?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: At the end the root holds the keys 30 and 60.
concept: B-tree insertion always adds the key to a leaf. If the leaf overflows (here, 5 keys when the maximum is 4), it is split into two nodes and the middle key moves up into the parent. If the root splits, a new root is created, and the tree grows one level taller.
work:
At most 4 keys per node.
Insert 10, 20, 30, 40: [10, 20, 30, 40]
Insert 50: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] overflows → middle key 30 moves up → root [30]; leaves [10, 20] [40, 50]
Insert 60: leaf [40, 50, 60]
Insert 70: leaf [40, 50, 60, 70]
Insert 80: [40, 50, 60, 70, 80] overflows → middle key 60 moves up → root [30, 60]; leaves [10, 20] [40, 50] [70, 80]
why: A — Wrong. [30] is the root after inserting 50. The later overflow when 80 is inserted pushes 60 up into the root as well.
B — Wrong. 40 and 70 are never the middle key of an overflowing node. The overflowing nodes are [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] (middle 30) and [40, 50, 60, 70, 80] (middle 60).
C — Correct. 30 moves up when 50 is inserted, and 60 moves up when 80 is inserted, so the root holds 30 and 60.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Take the order m of a B-tree to be the maximum number of children of a node. A B-tree of order 5 has height 2 (root at level 0, leaves at level 2). What is the maximum number of keys it can store?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The maximum number of keys is 5^3 − 1 = 124, which is not listed.
concept: A B-tree holds the most keys when every node is full: m − 1 keys and m children. With the root at level 0 and the leaves at level h, there are 1 + m + m² + … + m^h nodes. Multiplying by m − 1 keys per node gives m^(h+1) − 1 keys.
work:
Order 5: at most 4 keys and 5 children per node.
Level 0: 1 node; level 1: 5 nodes; level 2: 25 nodes → 31 nodes
Keys = 31 × 4 = 124 = 5^3 − 1
why: A — Wrong. 31 is the number of NODES, not keys. Each full node holds 4 keys.
B — Wrong. 120 = 30 × 4 forgets the root node (5 + 25 = 30 nodes). With the root there are 31 nodes and 124 keys.
C — Wrong. 155 = 31 × 5 uses 5 keys per node, but order 5 allows at most 4 keys (5 is the number of children).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 124), so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Maximum keys in a B-tree of order m and height h = m^(h+1) − 1.

q: For which of the following tasks is a trie (prefix tree) a natural choice?
opts: Autocomplete: listing all stored words that begin with a given prefix
Checking whether a word exists in a dictionary (spell checking)
Longest-prefix matching of IP addresses in routers
More than one of the above
exp: Autocomplete, dictionary lookup and IP longest-prefix matching all use tries naturally.
concept: A trie (prefix tree, from 'retrieval') stores strings character by character: each edge is one character, and all words with the same prefix share the same path from the root. This makes prefix-based tasks natural: look up a word, list all words with a prefix, or find the longest stored prefix of a string.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Walk down the path of the prefix, then list every word in that subtree. This is how autocomplete works.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Checking a word is one walk of L steps from the root; if the path exists and ends at a node marked 'end of word', the word is in the dictionary.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Routers store network prefixes in binary tries (each edge is one bit); following the address bit by bit finds the longest matching prefix.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A trie stores n words over a fixed alphabet, and each node keeps an array of child pointers. The worst-case time to search for a word of length L:
opts: depends only on n, and is O(log n)
depends on both n and L, and is O(n·L)
depends only on L, and is O(L)
More than one of the above
exp: Searching a trie takes O(L) time, where L is the length of the word.
concept: To search a word of length L in a trie, follow one edge per character from the root. With an array of child pointers (one slot per letter of the fixed alphabet), each step is a direct array index, O(1). So the search takes O(L), however many words n are stored.
why: A — Wrong. The search never compares the word with other stored words, so n does not matter. O(log n) comparisons is the cost of searching a balanced BST.
B — Wrong. The search time does not depend on n at all; n·L would be the cost of comparing the word with every stored word one by one.
C — Correct. One O(1) step per character → O(L), independent of n.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which statement about Huffman coding is correct?
opts: It builds the code tree greedily by repeatedly merging the two lowest-frequency nodes
It assigns longer codewords to more frequent characters
It may produce a codeword that is a prefix of another codeword
More than one of the above
exp: Huffman coding builds its tree greedily by repeatedly merging the two lowest-frequency nodes.
concept: Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix code. It repeatedly takes the two nodes with the lowest frequencies and merges them under a new parent whose frequency is their sum — a greedy choice. Characters end up only at the leaves, so no codeword is a prefix of another. Frequent characters end up near the root and get short codes.
why: A — Correct. Huffman's algorithm is greedy: at every step it merges the two least frequent nodes.
B — Wrong. It is the opposite: more frequent characters get SHORTER (or equal) codewords, and rare characters get longer ones.
C — Wrong. Huffman codes are prefix-free: every character is a leaf, so no codeword can be the beginning of another, and decoding is unambiguous.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A 100-character message uses only the symbols P, Q, R, S, T with frequencies 40, 25, 20, 10 and 5. How many bits are needed to encode the whole message with a Huffman code?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Huffman code needs 210 bits, which is not listed.
concept: Total Huffman bits = Σ (frequency × code length). A shortcut: the total also equals the sum of the weights of all merged (internal) nodes. Always merge the two smallest weights available at that moment.
work:
Frequencies: P 40, Q 25, R 20, S 10, T 5
Merge 5 (T) + 10 (S) = 15
Merge 15 + 20 (R) = 35
Merge 25 (Q) + 35 = 60
Merge 40 (P) + 60 = 100 (root)
Code lengths: P 1, Q 2, R 3, S 4, T 4
Bits = 40×1 + 25×2 + 20×3 + 10×4 + 5×4 = 40 + 50 + 60 + 40 + 20 = 210
Check: sum of merged weights = 15 + 35 + 60 + 100 = 210
why: A — Wrong. 200 bits would be an average of 2 bits per symbol. The Huffman code is optimal and needs 210 bits, so no prefix code can do it in 200.
B — Wrong. 225 is more than the optimal 210; it does not come from the Huffman tree.
C — Wrong. 300 = 100 × 3 is the cost of a FIXED-length 3-bit code (5 symbols need 3 bits each), not of Huffman coding.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 210 bits), so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Huffman total bits = the sum of all merged (internal node) weights.

q: In a full 4-ary tree every internal node has exactly 4 children. If such a tree has 25 leaves, how many internal nodes and how many nodes in total does it have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Full 4-ary tree: i = (L − 1)/(m − 1) = 8 internal nodes and n = 4·8 + 1 = 33 nodes.
concept: In a full m-ary tree every internal node has exactly m children (a full binary tree is the case m = 2). Every node except the root is the child of exactly one internal node, so n = m·i + 1, where n is the number of nodes and i the number of internal nodes. Since n = i + L (L = number of leaves), it follows that L = (m − 1)·i + 1. For m = 2 this is the familiar 'leaves = internal nodes + 1'. Knowing any one of n, i or L gives the other two.
why: A — Wrong. 6 internal nodes comes from dividing 24 by m = 4 instead of by m − 1 = 3. A full 4-ary tree with 6 internal nodes would have only 3 × 6 + 1 = 19 leaves.
B — Wrong. 8 internal nodes is right, but the total m·i = 32 forgets the root. Every node except the root is a child of some internal node, so n = m·i + 1 = 33.
C — Correct. i = (25 − 1)/(4 − 1) = 8 and n = 4 × 8 + 1 = 33, which also equals i + L = 8 + 25.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Full m-ary tree: n = m·i + 1 and L = (m − 1)·i + 1.

q: A full 5-ary tree (every internal node has exactly 5 children) has 9 internal nodes. How many leaves does it have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Leaves = (5 − 1) × 9 + 1 = 37, which is not listed.
concept: In a full m-ary tree every internal node has exactly m children (a full binary tree is the case m = 2). Every node except the root is the child of exactly one internal node, so n = m·i + 1, where n is the number of nodes and i the number of internal nodes. Since n = i + L (L = number of leaves), it follows that L = (m − 1)·i + 1. For m = 2 this is the familiar 'leaves = internal nodes + 1'. Knowing any one of n, i or L gives the other two.
work:
L = (m − 1)·i + 1 = (5 − 1) × 9 + 1 = 36 + 1 = 37
Total nodes n = m·i + 1 = 5 × 9 + 1 = 46 = 9 internal + 37 leaves
why: A — Wrong. 36 = (5 − 1) × 9 forgets the '+ 1' in L = (m − 1)·i + 1. A single internal node already shows the '+ 1': a root with 5 children has 4 × 1 + 1 = 5 leaves.
B — Wrong. 45 = 5 × 9 is the number of children of all the internal nodes, i.e. the number of edges (n − 1). Some of those children are themselves internal nodes, so they are not all leaves.
C — Wrong. 46 = 5 × 9 + 1 is the TOTAL number of nodes n, which includes the 9 internal nodes. Leaves = 46 − 9 = 37.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true. L = (m − 1)·i + 1 = 4 × 9 + 1 = 37, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: A forest has three ordered trees: T1 has root A with children B and C (left to right); T2 has root D with one child E; T3 is the single node F. The forest is converted to one binary tree by the standard rule: a node's first child becomes its left child, its next sibling becomes its right child, and the root of each following tree is treated as the next sibling of the previous tree's root. What is the inorder traversal of the binary tree?
opts: B C A E D F
B A C E D F
A B C D E F
More than one of the above
exp: Left = first child, right = next sibling; the inorder of the resulting binary tree is B C A E D F.
concept: A forest is a collection of disjoint trees (in graph terms, an acyclic graph whose connected components are trees). Any ordered forest can be stored as a single binary tree with the left-child, right-sibling rule: left pointer = first child, right pointer = next sibling, with the roots of the trees treated as siblings. This is how a general tree or a forest is stored with only two pointers per node. Useful facts: the preorder of the binary tree equals the preorder of the forest, and the inorder of the binary tree equals the postorder of the forest.
work:
Binary tree: A.left = B (first child of A), A.right = D (root of the next tree)
B.right = C (next sibling of B)
D.left = E (first child of D), D.right = F (root of the next tree)
Inorder (Left, Root, Right) from A: inorder of B's subtree = B C, then A, then inorder of D's subtree = E D F
Inorder = B C A E D F (equal to the forest's postorder)
Preorder = A B C D E F
why: A — Correct. Inorder visits A's left subtree (B, then B's right child C), then A, then A's right subtree (E, D, F): B C A E D F.
B — Wrong. This treats C as A's right child, as if B and C were the two children of A in the binary tree. With the sibling rule, C is the RIGHT child of B, so C is visited before A.
C — Wrong. A B C D E F is the PREORDER of the binary tree (which is also the preorder of the forest), not the inorder.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Forest → binary tree: preorder is unchanged; inorder of the binary tree = postorder of the forest.

q: Which of the following statements correctly compares a tree with a general graph?
opts: A tree may contain a cycle, as long as all its edges are directed
A tree with n vertices always has exactly n − 1 edges, whereas a simple graph with n vertices can have anywhere from 0 to n(n − 1)/2 edges
Between two vertices of a tree there can be several different simple paths
More than one of the above
exp: A tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices; a general graph has no such restrictions.
concept: A tree is a special kind of graph: a connected graph with no cycles. Because of this, a tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges and there is exactly one simple path between any two of its vertices. A general graph may be disconnected, may contain cycles and may have many paths between two vertices; a simple undirected graph can have up to n(n − 1)/2 edges. Every tree is a graph, but not every graph is a tree. In data structures trees are usually rooted and model hierarchies, while graphs model networks.
why: A — Wrong. A tree has no cycle at all. A directed graph with no directed cycle is a DAG, and a DAG need not be a tree (one vertex may have two parents, giving two different paths to it).

B — Correct. Being connected and acyclic forces exactly n − 1 edges in a tree. A simple graph has no such rule: it can range from the edgeless graph (0 edges) to the complete graph Kn (n(n − 1)/2 edges).
C — Wrong. In a tree the simple path between two vertices is unique. If there were two different paths, together they would form a cycle.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT true for every tree (a connected, acyclic undirected graph) with n ≥ 2 vertices?
opts: There is exactly one simple path between any two vertices
Removing any one edge disconnects it
More than one of the above
exp: All three are true properties of every tree, so none of them is 'NOT true' — the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: A tree is minimally connected and maximally acyclic. Minimally connected: it is connected, but removing ANY edge disconnects it (every edge is a bridge). Maximally acyclic: it has no cycle, but adding ANY new edge between two of its vertices creates exactly one cycle. These facts, 'n − 1 edges' and 'a unique path between every pair of vertices' are all equivalent ways of describing a tree.
why: A — Wrong. This is TRUE for every tree (connected and acyclic forces n − 1 edges), so it is not a 'NOT true' statement.
B — Wrong. This is TRUE for every tree: two different paths between the same pair of vertices would together form a cycle, and a tree has none. So it does not answer the question.
C — Wrong. This is TRUE for every tree: each edge of a tree is a bridge (cut edge), because its two ends are joined by no other path. So it is not a 'NOT true' statement.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is a false statement about trees, so 'More than one of the above' (two or more NOT-true statements) is also wrong.
E — Correct. All three statements A, B and C hold for every tree, so none of them is 'NOT true'. Hence 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: In a 'Which is NOT true' question, an option is the answer only if it is FALSE.

q: Keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 are inserted in this order into an empty B-tree of order 3 (at most 2 keys and 3 children per node). When a node overflows to 3 keys it is split: the middle key moves up to the parent and the other two keys form two separate nodes. After all insertions, what is the height of the tree (number of edges on a root-to-leaf path) and how many leaf nodes does it have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The final tree has root [40], level 1 [20] [60] and leaves [10] [30] [50] [70]: height 2 with 4 leaves.
concept: Insertion into a B-tree always starts at a leaf. If the leaf has room, the key is placed there in sorted order. If the leaf overflows (in a B-tree of order 3, when it gets 3 keys), it splits into two nodes and its middle key moves up into the parent. The parent may overflow in turn and split, so one insertion can cause a chain (cascade) of splits. When the root splits, a new root is created holding the middle key, and the height grows by one — a B-tree grows at the root, which keeps all leaves on the same level.
work:
Insert 10, 20 → leaf [10 20]
Insert 30 → [10 20 30] overflows → split: 20 moves up → root [20], leaves [10] [30]
Insert 40 → leaf [30 40]
Insert 50 → [30 40 50] overflows → 40 moves up → root [20 40], leaves [10] [30] [50]
Insert 60 → leaf [50 60]
Insert 70 → [50 60 70] overflows → 60 moves up → root [20 40 60] overflows
Root split: 40 moves up into a NEW root → root [40], children [20] and [60]
Final: root [40]; level 1: [20] [60]; leaves: [10] [30] [50] [70] → height 2 (3 levels), 4 leaves, 4 splits in all
why: A — Wrong. This is the tree just before the last split: root [20 40 60] over the leaves [10] [30] [50] [70]. But an order-3 node may hold only 2 keys, so the root with 3 keys must split, which adds a new level.
B — Wrong. 3 is the number of LEVELS (root, middle level, leaves). Counted in edges from the root to a leaf, the height is 2.
C — Correct. After the root [20 40 60] splits, the tree is root [40], middle level [20] [60], and leaves [10] [30] [50] [70]: height 2 with 4 leaves.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: A B-tree gets taller only when its root splits.

q: Keys 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 10 are inserted in this order into an empty B-tree of order 3 (at most 2 keys per node; a node that overflows to 3 keys is split and its middle key moves up). How many node splits take place in total? (A split of the root counts as a split.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 70 → 1 split, 40 → 1 split, 80 → 2 splits (leaf and root), 10 → none: 4 splits in all.
concept: Insertion into a B-tree always starts at a leaf. If the leaf has room, the key is placed there in sorted order. If the leaf overflows (in a B-tree of order 3, when it gets 3 keys), it splits into two nodes and its middle key moves up into the parent. The parent may overflow in turn and split, so one insertion can cause a chain (cascade) of splits. When the root splits, a new root is created holding the middle key, and the height grows by one — a B-tree grows at the root, which keeps all leaves on the same level.
work:
50, 30 → [30 50]
70 → [30 50 70] overflows → split 1: root [50], leaves [30] [70]
20 → [20 30]
40 → [20 30 40] overflows → split 2: 30 moves up → root [30 50], leaves [20] [40] [70]
60 → [60 70]
80 → [60 70 80] overflows → split 3: 70 moves up → root [30 50 70] overflows → split 4: 50 becomes the new root
Now: root [50]; level 1: [30] [70]; leaves [20] [40] [60] [80]
10 → leaf [10 20] (room, no split)
Total splits = 4
why: A — Wrong. 3 misses the cascade when 80 is inserted: the leaf [60 70 80] splits, and the 70 pushed up makes the root [30 50 70] overflow, so the root splits as well. That second split also counts.
B — Correct. Splits happen when inserting 70 (one), 40 (one) and 80 (two: the leaf, then the root). Inserting 10 into the leaf [20] needs no split. Total = 4.
C — Wrong. 5 would need one more split, but the last key, 10, goes into the leaf [20], which still has room for a second key.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Linear search is performed on an array of n elements. How many key comparisons are made in the worst case (key absent or at the last position)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In the worst case linear search compares the key with every element, so it makes n comparisons.
concept: Linear (sequential) search checks the elements one by one from the start, like looking for a name in an unsorted attendance register by reading every line. If the key is at the last position or is not present at all, every one of the n elements must be compared before the search can stop, so the worst case needs n comparisons. Key properties: best case 1 comparison (Θ(1)), average about (n + 1)/2 comparisons for a successful search, worst case n comparisons (Θ(n)); extra space O(1); works on unsorted data and linked lists.
work:
Key at position 1 → 1 comparison (best case)
Key at position n → n comparisons
Key absent → all n elements are compared, none matches → n comparisons
Worst case = n
why: A — Wrong. n/2 is roughly the AVERAGE number of comparisons for a successful search ((n + 1)/2 to be exact), not the worst case. In the worst case nothing lets the search stop half-way.

B — Wrong. log₂ n is (roughly) the worst-case number of probes of BINARY search, which halves a sorted array at every step. Linear search does not halve anything; it moves forward one element at a time.
C — Correct. When the key is in the last position or absent, linear search must compare the key with all n elements before it can stop, so it makes n comparisons.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Linear search: best 1, average about n/2, worst n comparisons.

q: What is the best-case time complexity of linear search on an array of n elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The best case is the key at the first position: one comparison, so Θ(1).
concept: The best case of an algorithm is the input on which it does the least work. For linear search the best case is when the key is the very first element: one comparison and the search stops, whatever the size of the array. Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Θ(1) means a fixed, constant amount of work. Key properties of linear search: best Θ(1), average and worst Θ(n), extra space O(1).
why: A — Correct. If a[0] equals the key, the search stops after a single comparison, no matter how large n is. Constant work is Θ(1).
B — Wrong. Θ(log n) is the average and worst-case time of binary search on a sorted array. Linear search never halves the array, and its best case does not grow with n at all.
C — Wrong. Θ(n) is the AVERAGE and WORST-case time of linear search (key near the end, or missing), not its best case.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Best case of almost any search = 'found at the first look' = constant time.

q: Linear (sequential) search can be correctly applied to which of the following?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Linear search needs only sequential access, so it works on unsorted arrays, sorted arrays and singly linked lists; more than one option is correct.
concept: Linear search only needs to visit the elements one after another and compare each one with the key. It needs neither sorted order nor random access (jumping directly to the i-th element). So it works on unsorted arrays, sorted arrays and linked lists alike. Binary search, in contrast, needs both sorted data and random access.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Linear search makes no assumption about order; it simply checks every element in turn until it finds the key or reaches the end, so an unsorted array is fine.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A sorted array is still just a sequence of elements, so linear search works on it too. (On sorted data it can even stop early once it passes the place where the key would be, but the worst case is still Θ(n).)

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. A singly linked list can be walked from the head by following the next pointers, which is exactly the one-by-one visiting that linear search needs. (Binary search is not practical on a linked list, because reaching the middle node alone takes Θ(n) steps.)
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array holds 9 distinct elements. The key is known to be present and is equally likely to be at any position. What is the average number of comparisons made by linear search?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Average comparisons = (n + 1)/2 = (9 + 1)/2 = 5, which is not listed.
concept: If the key is present and equally likely to be at each of the n positions, linear search needs i comparisons when the key is at position i (counting positions from 1). The average is (1 + 2 + … + n)/n = (n + 1)/2. For n = 9 this is 10/2 = 5.
work:
Comparisons if the key is at position 1, 2, …, 9: 1, 2, …, 9
Sum = 9 × 10 / 2 = 45
Average = 45 / 9 = 5 = (n + 1)/2
5 is not among the options
why: A — Wrong. 4 is (n − 1)/2. You get it by counting positions from 0 (0 + 1 + … + 8 = 36, and 36/9 = 4), as if finding the key at index 0 cost no comparison. It still costs one comparison.
B — Wrong. 4.5 is n/2, the popular rough estimate. The exact average is (n + 1)/2 = 5, because the costs run from 1 to n, not from 0 to n.
C — Wrong. 9 is the WORST case (key at the last position), not the average.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The exact average is (9 + 1)/2 = 5, which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Average successful linear search = (n + 1)/2, not n/2.

q: What is printed by the following C code?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: There is no break, so all 5 iterations run and pos keeps the last match: the output is 3 5.
concept: This loop is a linear search WITHOUT a break. It visits all 5 elements, so count becomes 5. Because pos is overwritten at every match, it ends up holding the index of the LAST occurrence of 3, not the first. To get the first occurrence, the loop must stop (break) at the first match.
work:
i=0: count=1, a[0]=7 ≠ 3
i=1: count=2, a[1]=3 → pos=1
i=2: count=3, a[2]=9 ≠ 3
i=3: count=4, a[3]=3 → pos=3 (overwrites 1)
i=4: count=5, a[4]=5 ≠ 3
Loop ends: pos=3, count=5 → prints 3 5 (confirmed by compiling with gcc)
why: A — Wrong. '1 2' would be printed if the loop had a break right after the first match (pos = 1 after 2 iterations). There is no break, so the loop continues to the end.
B — Correct. The loop runs all 5 times, so count = 5, and the last match (a[3] = 3) sets pos = 3. The output is 3 5.
C — Wrong. '1 5' mixes the two ideas: it keeps the first match (1) but counts all 5 iterations. Without a break, the second match at index 3 overwrites pos.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: No break in a search loop → you get the LAST match, not the first.
