q: In sentinel linear search, the key is first stored at a[n] (one position after the last element) and the loop simply runs while a[i] != key. What is the main advantage of this technique?
opts: It removes the index-bound check (i < n) from every loop iteration
It reduces the worst-case time complexity to O(log n)
It reduces the space complexity from O(n) to O(1)
More than one of the above
exp: The sentinel guarantees that the loop stops, so the i < n check is removed from every iteration; the complexity stays Θ(n).
concept: In ordinary linear search each loop step makes two tests: 'is i still inside the array (i < n)?' and 'is a[i] equal to the key?'. In sentinel search we first put the key itself at a[n], an extra slot just after the last element. Now the loop is certain to stop at the key, at a[n] at the latest, so the bound test can be dropped and each step makes only one test. The time is still Θ(n); only the constant factor improves. After the loop, i == n means the key was not really in the array.
why: A — Correct. Because the sentinel guarantees that a[i] == key becomes true by i = n at the latest, the loop can never run past the array. So the i < n check is unnecessary, which removes one of the two tests in every iteration.

B — Wrong. The sentinel does not change the order of growth: in the worst case the loop still visits every element, so it stays Θ(n). Only searches that skip elements on sorted data (like binary search) reach Θ(log n).
C — Wrong. Ordinary linear search already uses O(1) extra space (just an index variable), so there is nothing to reduce. Sentinel search actually needs one extra array slot for the sentinel.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following search techniques work correctly only when the array is sorted?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Binary, interpolation and jump search all rely on sorted order to skip elements, so more than one option is correct.
concept: Binary search, interpolation search and jump search all skip parts of the array: they compare the key with a chosen element and conclude that the key cannot lie in the skipped part. That conclusion is valid only if the elements are in sorted order. On unsorted data they can miss a key that is present. Linear search is the common search that works on unsorted data.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Binary search compares the key with the middle element and throws away the half that cannot contain the key. This is valid only if everything to the left of the middle is smaller and everything to the right is larger, that is, if the array is sorted.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Interpolation search guesses the position from the key's value (like opening a dictionary near the end for a word starting with 'w'). Both the guess and the narrowing of the range assume sorted order.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Jump search jumps ahead block by block (every m-th element) until it reaches an element ≥ the key, then searches that one block linearly. Stopping at the first larger element makes sense only when the array is sorted.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Any search that 'skips' elements needs sorted data; only linear search does not.

q: The best-case and worst-case time complexities of binary search on n sorted elements are, respectively:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Binary search: best case Θ(1) (key at the first middle), worst case Θ(log n).
concept: Binary search looks at the middle element of a sorted range; if it is not the key, it discards the half that cannot contain the key. Best case: the very first middle element is the key, so one comparison, Θ(1). Worst case: the range keeps halving until a single element is left, which takes ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 probes, i.e. Θ(log n). Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Key properties of binary search: best Θ(1), average and worst Θ(log n); extra space O(1) when written with a loop; needs sorted data with random access.
why: A — Correct. The best case is finding the key at the first middle position (one comparison); the worst case needs about log₂ n halvings. So the pair is Θ(1) and Θ(log n).
B — Wrong. The worst case is Θ(log n), but the best case is not: if the key happens to be the first middle element, the search ends after one comparison, which is Θ(1).
C — Wrong. The best case Θ(1) is right, but Θ(n) is the worst case of LINEAR search. Binary search halves the range each time, so it never looks at all n elements.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In a C binary search with int variables low and high (0 ≤ low ≤ high), which statement computes the middle index without the risk of integer overflow?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: mid = low + (high − low)/2 gives the same middle index without forming low + high, so it cannot overflow.
concept: In C an int can hold values only up to INT_MAX (2,147,483,647 for a 32-bit int). If low and high are both large, low + high can exceed INT_MAX and overflow, giving a negative or wrong mid. Writing mid = low + (high − low)/2 gives the same middle index but never forms the big sum, because high − low is at most the size of the array. This exact bug sat for years in the binary search of Java's standard library.
work:
32-bit int: INT_MAX = 2,147,483,647
Example: low = 2,000,000,000, high = 2,100,000,000
A: low + high = 4,100,000,000 > INT_MAX → overflow (wrong, possibly negative mid)
B: high − low = 100,000,000; /2 = 50,000,000; low + 50,000,000 = 2,050,000,000 (correct, no overflow)
C: (high − low)/2 = 50,000,000, an offset, not an index between low and high
why: A — Wrong. This is the textbook formula and gives the right index for small values, but it computes low + high first. For very large arrays that sum can exceed INT_MAX and overflow, so it does carry the risk the question asks us to avoid.

B — Correct. high − low cannot overflow (it lies between 0 and the array size); half of it is added to low, and the result lies between low and high. For non-negative values it equals (low + high)/2 but never forms the big sum.

C — Wrong. (high − low)/2 is only the distance from low to the middle (an offset), not the middle index itself. For example, low = 10 and high = 20 give 5, which is not even inside the range. low must be added to it.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Middle index = low plus half the gap.

q: Binary search is used on a sorted array of 100 elements. Counting one comparison per probe (each probe examines one array element), what is the maximum number of comparisons needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Maximum binary-search probes = ⌊log₂ 100⌋ + 1 = 7.
concept: Each probe of binary search halves the remaining range. The maximum number of probes for n elements is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1, which is the height of its binary decision tree. For n = 100: 2⁶ = 64 ≤ 100 < 128 = 2⁷, so ⌊log₂ 100⌋ = 6 and the maximum is 6 + 1 = 7.
work:
Worst case, the search always continues in the larger half:
range sizes 100 → 50 → 25 → 12 → 6 → 3 → 1 (one probe at each size)
That is 7 probes
Formula: ⌊log₂ 100⌋ + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7
why: A — Correct. ⌊log₂ 100⌋ + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7. Seven halvings are always enough to empty a range of 100, and some keys do need all 7.
B — Wrong. 6 is ⌊log₂ 100⌋ without the + 1. Six probes can cover at most 2⁶ − 1 = 63 elements, fewer than 100.
C — Wrong. 50 is n/2, about the average cost of LINEAR search, not the worst case of binary search.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Worst-case binary search probes = number of bits needed to write n in binary (100 = 1100100, 7 bits).

q: A sorted array contains 1000 elements. In the worst case, how many array elements does binary search examine before it finds the key or reports failure?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Worst-case binary search on 1000 elements examines ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = 10 elements, which is not listed.
concept: The worst-case number of elements binary search examines on n sorted elements is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1, the same whether the search succeeds or fails. For n = 1000: 2⁹ = 512 ≤ 1000 < 1024 = 2¹⁰, so ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ = 9 and the worst case is 9 + 1 = 10.
work:
Worst-case range sizes: 1000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1
One element examined at each size → 10 elements
Formula: ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10
10 is not among the options
why: A — Wrong. 9 is ⌊log₂ 1000⌋, the formula without the + 1. Nine probes can handle at most 2⁹ − 1 = 511 elements.
B — Wrong. 11 is one too many: 11 probes are needed only when n is between 1024 and 2047. Since 1000 < 1024 = 2¹⁰, ten probes are enough.
C — Wrong. 500 is n/2, roughly the average cost of LINEAR search, not the worst case of binary search.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The worst case is ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = 10, which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Binary search with mid = (low + high)/2 (integer division) is applied to [3, 8, 15, 21, 27, 34, 40, 46, 52, 60] (indices 0–9) to search for 52. Which elements are compared with the key, in order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The probes are a[4] = 27, a[7] = 46 and a[8] = 52, so the sequence is 27, 46, 52.
concept: Binary search on a sorted array keeps a range [low, high]. It compares the key with a[mid]: if the key is larger it sets low = mid + 1, if smaller it sets high = mid − 1, and it stops when they are equal. With mid = (low + high)/2 in integer division, the middle is rounded DOWN when the range has an even number of elements.
work:
low=0, high=9 → mid=4, a[4]=27 < 52 → low=5
low=5, high=9 → mid=7, a[7]=46 < 52 → low=8
low=8, high=9 → mid=8, a[8]=52 = key → found at index 8
Elements compared: 27, 46, 52
why: A — Wrong. 34 is a[5]. It would be the first probe only if mid were rounded up ((0 + 9)/2 = 4.5 → 5). C's integer division rounds down, so the first probe is a[4] = 27.
B — Wrong. 27 and 52 are right, but 40 (a[6]) is never probed. After 27 the range is 5..9, so mid = (5 + 9)/2 = 7 and the probe is a[7] = 46.
C — Correct. mid = 4 (27), then mid = 7 (46), then mid = 8 (52, found). This is exactly the order of comparisons.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Binary search with mid = (low + high)/2 (integer division) searches for 40 in [5, 12, 17, 23, 38, 44, 51, 67, 72, 88, 95] (indices 0–10). Which elements are compared with the key before the search reports failure?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The search probes 44, 17, 23 and 38; then low > high and it reports failure.
concept: An unsuccessful binary search keeps narrowing the range until low becomes greater than high. Every middle element visited on the way is compared with the key, so even a failed search makes about log₂ n comparisons. Here n = 11, so at most ⌊log₂ 11⌋ + 1 = 4 comparisons are made.
work:
low=0, high=10 → mid=5, a[5]=44 > 40 → high=4
low=0, high=4 → mid=2, a[2]=17 < 40 → low=3
low=3, high=4 → mid=3, a[3]=23 < 40 → low=4
low=4, high=4 → mid=4, a[4]=38 < 40 → low=5
low=5 > high=4 → stop, key not found
Elements compared: 44, 17, 23, 38
why: A — Wrong. This skips 23. After comparing 17 the range is indices 3..4, so mid = (3 + 4)/2 = 3 and a[3] = 23 must be compared before 38.
B — Correct. Following low, mid and high step by step gives 44, 17, 23, 38, after which low (5) exceeds high (4) and the search reports failure.
C — Wrong. This skips 17. After 44 the range is 0..4, so the next probe is mid = 2, which holds 17, not 23.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Standard binary search (mid = (low + high)/2, return as soon as a[mid] equals the key) searches for 5 in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15] (indices 0–14). Which index is returned?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The search probes indices 7, 3 and then 5, where it finds 5 and returns index 5.
concept: Plain binary search returns the first index it happens to probe that holds the key. When the key appears several times (here at indices 4, 5 and 6), this need not be the first or the last occurrence. To find the first occurrence, a modified search remembers a match and keeps searching to the left (high = mid − 1); for the last occurrence it keeps searching to the right.
work:
low=0, high=14 → mid=7, a[7]=8 > 5 → high=6
low=0, high=6 → mid=3, a[3]=4 < 5 → low=4
low=4, high=6 → mid=5, a[5]=5 = key → return 5
why: A — Wrong. Index 4 is the FIRST occurrence of 5. Standard binary search does not look for the first occurrence; it stops at index 5 because that is the first probe that matches.
B — Correct. The probes are indices 7, 3 and 5. a[5] = 5 matches, so the search returns 5 immediately.
C — Wrong. Index 6 is the LAST occurrence of 5, which would need a 'last occurrence' variant. The standard search never even probes index 6 here.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Duplicates + plain binary search = some occurrence, not necessarily the first.

q: What is printed by the following C code?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The probes are indices 4, 7 and 5; the key is found at index 5 on the third step, so the code prints 5 3.
concept: Here steps is increased once per loop iteration, before the comparison, so it counts how many middle elements were probed, including the one that matched. The break leaves mid holding the index where the key was found. mid = low + (high − low)/2 is the overflow-safe way of writing the middle index.
work:
low=0, high=9: mid=0+(9−0)/2=4, steps=1, a[4]=16 < 23 → low=5
low=5, high=9: mid=5+(9−5)/2=7, steps=2, a[7]=56 > 23 → high=6
low=5, high=6: mid=5+(6−5)/2=5, steps=3, a[5]=23 = key → break
Prints mid=5, steps=3 → 5 3 (confirmed with gcc)
why: A — Wrong. '5 2' has the right index but one step too few: the key is found on the THIRD probe (after 16 and 56), and steps is incremented before the break.
B — Wrong. 6 is the index of 38. The third probe is mid = 5 + (6 − 5)/2 = 5 + 0 = 5, because integer division turns 1/2 into 0.
C — Correct. Three probes (16, 56, 23) are made and the key is found at index 5, so the output is 5 3.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A sorted array has 15 distinct elements (indices 0–14). Binary search uses mid = (low + high)/2. How many of the 15 elements are found using exactly 3 probes (comparisons with array elements)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Level 3 of the perfect decision tree for 15 elements has 4 nodes, so 4 elements need exactly 3 probes.
concept: The probes of binary search form a binary decision tree: the first middle element is the root, the middles of the two halves are its children, and so on. For 15 = 2⁴ − 1 elements this tree is perfect: 1 element on level 1, 2 on level 2, 4 on level 3 and 8 on level 4. An element on level k is found after exactly k probes, and level k holds 2^(k−1) elements.
work:
Level 1 (1 probe): index 7
Level 2 (2 probes): indices 3, 11
Level 3 (3 probes): indices 1, 5, 9, 13
Level 4 (4 probes): indices 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14
Check: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15
Exactly 3 probes: 4 elements (confirmed by simulating all 15 searches)
why: A — Wrong. 2 is the number of elements found in exactly 2 probes (indices 3 and 11).
B — Wrong. 8 is the number of elements found in exactly 4 probes (the leaves of the tree).
C — Correct. Level 3 of the decision tree holds 2² = 4 elements (indices 1, 5, 9, 13), and each is found after exactly 3 probes.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Level k of the decision tree has 2^(k−1) elements.

q: What is the auxiliary space complexity of the following recursive binary search on n elements (counting the call stack)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The recursion depth is about log₂ n with constant space per call, so the extra space is Θ(log n).
concept: Each recursive call puts a new frame (its parameters and the local variable mid) on the call stack, and the frame stays there until that call returns. Every call halves the range, so the deepest chain of calls is about log₂ n frames, each of fixed size. So the auxiliary (extra) space is Θ(log n). Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. The iterative (loop) version of binary search needs only Θ(1) extra space because it reuses the same few variables.
work:
Range sizes along the deepest chain: n → n/2 → n/4 → … → 1 → empty
Number of nested calls ≈ log₂ n + 2 (the last call sees low > high and returns −1)
Each call uses a constant-size frame → total Θ(log n)
why: A — Wrong. Θ(1) is the extra space of the ITERATIVE version (a loop with low, high and mid). This version is recursive and every pending call keeps its own stack frame. (A compiler may optimise these tail calls into a loop, but the question asks us to count the call stack.)
B — Correct. The recursion depth is about log₂ n because the range halves at every call, and each frame takes constant space, giving Θ(log n).
C — Wrong. Θ(n) depth would happen only if each call reduced the range by ONE element, as in a recursive linear search. Here each call halves the range.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: For a sorted array whose keys are uniformly distributed, the average-case time complexity of interpolation search is:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: On uniformly distributed sorted keys, interpolation search makes Θ(log log n) probes on average.
concept: Interpolation search guesses where the key should be from its value, the way you open a telephone directory near the end for a name starting with 'S'. It probes pos = low + (key − a[low]) × (high − low) / (a[high] − a[low]). If the keys are uniformly (evenly) spread, each guess shrinks the range very fast and the average number of probes is Θ(log log n). If the values are very uneven, the guesses can be poor and the worst case is Θ(n). Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Key properties: average Θ(log log n) on uniform data, worst Θ(n), extra space O(1), needs sorted data.
why: A — Correct. For uniformly distributed sorted keys, the expected number of probes of interpolation search is about log₂(log₂ n), i.e. Θ(log log n). This is even faster than binary search.
B — Wrong. Θ(log n) is the average and worst case of BINARY search, which always probes the middle and ignores the key's value.
C — Wrong. Θ(√n) is the time of JUMP search with block size √n.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Interpolation: log log n average (n worst); binary: log n; jump: √n.

q: Interpolation search probes pos = low + ((key − a[low]) × (high − low)) / (a[high] − a[low]) using integer division. For a = [10, 12, 13, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 33, 35, 42, 47] (indices 0–14) and key = 18, which index is probed first?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: pos = 0 + (8 × 14)/37 = 112/37 = 3 in integer division, so index 3 is probed first.
concept: Interpolation search estimates the position by assuming the values grow evenly from a[low] to a[high]. The key's distance from a[low], as a fraction of the whole spread a[high] − a[low], tells how far into the index range to look. In C the formula uses integer division, so the estimate is rounded down.
work:
low=0, high=14, a[low]=10, a[high]=47, key=18
pos = 0 + ((18 − 10) × (14 − 0)) / (47 − 10)
    = (8 × 14) / 37 = 112 / 37 = 3 (integer division; 112/37 ≈ 3.03)
First probe: index 3 (a[3] = 16 < 18)
Next range 4..14: pos = 4 + (0 × 10)/29 = 4, a[4] = 18 → found on the second probe
why: A — Correct. 8 × 14 = 112 and 112 / 37 = 3 in integer division, so the first probe is index 3.
B — Wrong. Index 4 is where 18 actually sits, and it is the SECOND probe. The first estimate (≈ 3.03) is rounded down to 3.
C — Wrong. Index 7 is the middle index (0 + 14)/2 that BINARY search would probe first. Interpolation search does not use the middle.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Jump search on a sorted array of 256 elements checks every m-th element and then searches linearly inside one block. Which block size m minimises the worst-case number of comparisons?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Jump search is fastest with block size √n = 16, which is not listed.
concept: Jump search with block size m first jumps through the sorted array checking every m-th element (at most about n/m checks), then searches linearly inside one block (at most m − 1 checks). The worst case is about n/m + m − 1 comparisons. This is smallest when n/m = m, that is m = √n. For n = 256 the best block size is √256 = 16. Key properties: Θ(√n) time with m = √n, extra space O(1), needs sorted data.
work:
Worst case f(m) ≈ n/m + (m − 1), with n = 256
m = 8: 32 + 7 = 39
m = 16: 16 + 15 = 31 (smallest)
m = 32: 8 + 31 = 39
m = 128: 2 + 127 = 129
Best m = √256 = 16, which is not listed
why: A — Wrong. With m = 8 there are too many jumps: up to 256/8 = 32 jumps plus 7 linear checks = 39 comparisons, worse than m = 16 (31).
B — Wrong. With m = 32 there are only 8 jumps, but the linear scan inside a block can need 31 checks: 39 in total, again worse than m = 16.
C — Wrong. m = 128 = n/2 makes the linear part huge (up to 127 checks), about 129 comparisons in the worst case.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The best block size is m = √n = √256 = 16, which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Jump search: block size √n, time Θ(√n).

q: Which of the following are true for bubble sort that swaps adjacent elements only when a[j] > a[j+1]?
opts: It is a stable sorting algorithm
It sorts in place using O(1) extra space
Its worst-case time complexity is O(n²)
More than one of the above
exp: Bubble sort with a strict > is stable, sorts in place with O(1) extra space, and is O(n²) in the worst case: all three are true.
concept: Bubble sort repeatedly compares neighbouring elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order, so in each pass the largest remaining element 'bubbles' to the end. A sort is STABLE if equal elements keep their original relative order. Swapping only when a[j] > a[j+1] (strictly greater) never swaps two equal elements, so bubble sort is stable. Key properties: best Θ(n) with a swapped flag (Θ(n²) without), average and worst Θ(n²); extra space O(1); stable: yes; in-place: yes; adaptive: only with the flag.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Equal neighbours are never swapped because the test is a strict >, and an element moves only one step at a time, so two equal keys can never jump over each other. Their original order is kept.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Bubble sort rearranges the elements inside the same array and needs only one temporary variable for the swap, so the extra space is O(1). That is what 'in place' means.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. On a reverse-sorted array every pair is out of order, so bubble sort makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons and n(n − 1)/2 swaps, which is O(n²).
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The following bubble sort stops when a pass makes no swap. What is its time complexity when the input array of n elements is already sorted?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: On sorted input the first pass makes no swap, so the flag stops the sort after n − 1 comparisons: Θ(n).
concept: The swapped flag makes bubble sort ADAPTIVE (faster on input that is already in order): if a whole pass makes no swap, the array is already sorted and the loop stops. On a sorted array the very first pass makes n − 1 comparisons and no swaps, so the sort ends after one pass: Θ(n). Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Without the flag, bubble sort always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, even on sorted input.
work:
Sorted input, pass i = 0: j = 0 … n−2 → n − 1 comparisons, 0 swaps
swapped == 0 → break
Total = n − 1 comparisons → Θ(n)
(Checked with gcc: a sorted array of 100 elements needs 99 comparisons.)
why: A — Correct. One pass of n − 1 comparisons finds no swap, and the break ends the sort, so the time is Θ(n).
B — Wrong. Θ(n log n) is the running time of merge sort or heap sort. Bubble sort never splits the array, and on sorted input this version does even less work than that.
C — Wrong. Θ(n²) is the best case only for bubble sort WITHOUT the swapped flag (and the worst case of both versions). Here the break stops the loop after the first pass.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Bubble sort best case: Θ(n) with the flag, Θ(n²) without it.

q: During ascending-order bubble sort (each pass moves the larger element of each adjacent pair towards the end), which statement is ALWAYS true after the k-th pass?
opts: The k smallest elements are in their final positions at the start of the array
The k largest elements are in their final positions at the end of the array
The first k elements are in sorted order among themselves
More than one of the above
exp: After k passes of bubble sort the k largest elements are in their final places at the end; nothing is guaranteed at the front.
concept: In ascending bubble sort each pass carries the largest element of the unsorted part to the end, like the biggest bubble rising to the top. So after k passes the last k positions hold the k largest elements, in their final places. The front of the array gets no such guarantee, because a small element moves left only one position per pass.
why: A — Wrong. This is the guarantee of SELECTION sort, which puts the minimum at the front in each pass. In bubble sort, [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] after 1 pass is [4, 3, 2, 1, 5]: the smallest element 1 is not at the front.
B — Correct. Each pass moves the largest element of the unsorted part to the end of that part, so after k passes the k largest elements sit at the end in their final places.

C — Wrong. The first k elements need not be sorted. Example: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] after 2 passes is [3, 2, 1, 4, 5]; the first two elements 3, 2 are out of order. (Insertion sort is the algorithm whose front part is always sorted.)
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Bubble sort fixes the END first; selection sort fixes the FRONT first.

q: Basic bubble sort without an early-exit flag (pass i, for i = 0 … n−2, compares a[j] with a[j+1] for j = 0 … n−2−i) is run on 10 elements. How many comparisons does it make, whatever the input order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Basic bubble sort makes n(n − 1)/2 = 45 comparisons on 10 elements, whatever the input.
concept: Without an early-exit flag, bubble sort always does all n − 1 passes. Pass i compares n − 1 − i pairs, so the total is (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2, no matter how the input is arranged. Only the number of SWAPS depends on the input.
why: A — Wrong. 90 = n(n − 1) = 10 × 9. You get it by forgetting the division by 2 in n(n − 1)/2 (each pass is shorter than the one before).
B — Wrong. 100 = n² is only the rough order of growth, not the exact count of comparisons.
C — Correct. 9 + 8 + … + 1 = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 comparisons, for every input order.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 appears in bubble, selection and insertion sort counts.

q: Bubble sort (ascending; each pass compares adjacent pairs from left to right and swaps if a[j] > a[j+1]) is applied to [6, 2, 9, 1, 5, 3]. What is the array after the second pass?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pass 1 gives [2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 9] and pass 2 gives [2, 1, 5, 3, 6, 9].
concept: In each pass of bubble sort the larger element of every adjacent pair moves right, so the largest unsorted element ends up at the end of the unsorted part. After pass 1 the maximum (9) is last; after pass 2 the second largest (6) is in the second-last place.
why: A — Wrong. [2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 9] is the array after the FIRST pass; one more pass is needed.
B — Correct. Pass 2 on [2, 6, 1, 5, 3, 9] moves 6 right past 1, 5 and 3, giving [2, 1, 5, 3, 6, 9].
C — Wrong. [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9] is the fully sorted array. More passes are needed before 1 reaches the front, because a small element moves left only one place per pass.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Bubble sort (ascending; adjacent left-to-right comparisons, swap if a[j] > a[j+1]) is applied to [15, 3, 27, 8, 12, 1]. What is the array after the third pass?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pass 3 gives [3, 8, 1, 12, 15, 27], which matches none of A–C.
concept: Trace bubble sort one pass at a time. In every pass the largest unsorted element is carried all the way to the right end, while a small element near the end (here 1) moves left by only ONE position per pass. A common exam slip is to stop one pass too early or too late.
why: A — Wrong. [3, 8, 12, 1, 15, 27] is the array after pass 2, one pass too early.
B — Wrong. [3, 1, 8, 12, 15, 27] is the array after pass 4, one pass too late. In pass 3, the 1 moves only one step left (past 12).
C — Wrong. [1, 3, 8, 12, 15, 27] is the fully sorted array, reached only after pass 5, because 1 starts at the far right and moves one place left per pass.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. After the third pass the array is [3, 8, 1, 12, 15, 27], which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: In bubble sort a small element near the end crawls left only one place per pass.

q: How many swaps does bubble sort perform to sort [4, 2, 6, 1, 3] in ascending order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Bubble sort makes one swap per inversion, and [4, 2, 6, 1, 3] has 6 inversions.
concept: An inversion is a pair of elements in the wrong order (a bigger one before a smaller one). Each bubble-sort swap exchanges two neighbours that form an inversion; this removes exactly that one inversion and leaves every other pair unchanged. So the number of swaps bubble sort makes equals the number of inversions in the input.
work:
Inversions of [4, 2, 6, 1, 3]:
4 before 2, 1, 3 → 3
2 before 1 → 1
6 before 1, 3 → 2
1 before 3 → 0
Total = 6
Simulation: pass 1 → [2, 4, 1, 3, 6] (3 swaps); pass 2 → [2, 1, 3, 4, 6] (2 swaps); pass 3 → [1, 2, 3, 4, 6] (1 swap); pass 4 → no swap. Total 6 swaps
why: A — Wrong. 4 = n − 1 is the number of passes, not the number of swaps; the first pass alone already makes 3 swaps.
B — Wrong. 5 is just n, the number of elements. The swap count depends on how disordered the array is (its inversions), not on its size.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Bubble-sort swaps = insertion-sort shifts = number of inversions.

q: How many swaps does bubble sort make to sort a reverse-sorted array of 6 distinct elements, such as [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1], into ascending order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A reverse-sorted array of 6 elements has 6 × 5 / 2 = 15 inversions, so bubble sort makes 15 swaps.
concept: In a reverse-sorted array every pair of elements is in the wrong order, so the number of inversions equals the number of pairs, n(n − 1)/2. Bubble sort removes exactly one inversion per swap, so it makes n(n − 1)/2 swaps. This is bubble sort's worst case.
work:
n = 6, reverse sorted → every pair is an inversion
Pairs = 6 × 5 / 2 = 15
Swaps per pass: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 (every comparison causes a swap)
why: A — Correct. 6 × 5 / 2 = 15 inversions, and each swap removes one, so there are 15 swaps.
B — Wrong. 6 is just n. The first pass alone makes 5 swaps, and later passes add 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 more.
C — Wrong. 30 = n(n − 1) forgets the division by 2: each pair of elements is swapped only once, not twice.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The function below sorts a[0..n−1] in ascending order. After the first iteration of the outer loop (i = 0) finishes, which statement is ALWAYS true?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After the first bubble-sort pass the maximum is guaranteed to be in a[n − 1]; nothing is guaranteed about the front.
concept: This function is bubble sort without a flag. In the first pass (i = 0), j runs over every adjacent pair from left to right and the larger element of each pair is carried forward, so the maximum is pushed step by step all the way to a[n − 1]. Nothing similar is guaranteed for the minimum, which moves left by at most one position per pass.
work:
Counter-example [3, 4, 1, 2], pass i = 0 (checked with gcc):
3<4 keep → [3, 4, 1, 2]; 4>1 swap → [3, 1, 4, 2]; 4>2 swap → [3, 1, 2, 4]
a[3] = 4 is the maximum (A holds)
a[0] = 3 is not the minimum 1 (B fails)
a[0..2] = 3, 1, 2 is not sorted (C fails)
why: A — Correct. Once the pass reaches the maximum, it is the larger element in every later comparison, so it is swapped one step right each time and ends in a[n − 1].

B — Wrong. The minimum moves left only one position per pass. In [3, 4, 1, 2] the first pass gives [3, 1, 2, 4]; a[0] is still 3, not 1. (Putting the minimum at a[0] in one pass is what selection sort does.)
C — Wrong. The rest of the array is generally not sorted after one pass: [3, 4, 1, 2] becomes [3, 1, 2, 4], and 3, 1, 2 is out of order.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Optimised bubble sort (pass i compares a[j], a[j+1] for j = 0 … n−2−i, and the sort stops after the first pass that makes no swap) is applied to [1, 2, 3, 5, 4]. How many comparisons are made in total?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pass 0 makes 4 comparisons and one swap; pass 1 makes 3 comparisons and no swap, so the sort stops: 7 in total.
concept: Optimised bubble sort stops after the first pass that makes no swap. Pass 0 compares n − 1 pairs, pass 1 compares n − 2 pairs, and so on. To count comparisons, add the comparisons of every pass that runs, INCLUDING the final pass that finds no swap, because the algorithm needs that clean pass to know the array is sorted.
work:
Pass 0 (j = 0..3): 1<2, 2<3, 3<5, 5>4 swap → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; 4 comparisons, 1 swap
Pass 1 (j = 0..2): 1<2, 2<3, 3<4; 3 comparisons, 0 swaps → stop
Total = 4 + 3 = 7
why: A — Wrong. 4 counts only the first pass. The algorithm does not know the array is sorted until a pass makes no swap, so pass 1 (3 comparisons) also runs.
B — Correct. 4 comparisons in pass 0 (one swap) plus 3 comparisons in pass 1 (no swap, so it stops) = 7.
C — Wrong. 10 = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 is the count for bubble sort WITHOUT the early-exit flag.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Selection sort is often preferred over bubble sort and insertion sort when:
opts: the input is already nearly sorted
writing to memory (swapping elements) is very costly
More than one of the above
exp: Selection sort makes at most n − 1 swaps, so it is preferred when writing (swapping) is expensive.
concept: Selection sort finds the smallest element of the unsorted part and swaps it into place, once per pass. So it makes at most n − 1 swaps, only O(n) writes, while bubble sort and insertion sort can make Θ(n²) swaps or shifts. That makes selection sort attractive when writing to memory is expensive (for example flash memory, which wears out with writes). Key properties: Θ(n²) comparisons in every case; at most n − 1 swaps; extra space O(1); stable: no; in-place: yes; adaptive: no.
why: A — Wrong. Nearly sorted input favours INSERTION sort, which then runs in almost linear time. Selection sort is not adaptive: it always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, even on sorted input.
B — Correct. Selection sort makes at most one swap per pass, so at most n − 1 swaps in total (O(n) writes), far fewer than the Θ(n²) swaps or shifts that bubble or insertion sort may need.
C — Wrong. Standard selection sort is NOT stable: a long-distance swap can carry an element past another equal element. Bubble sort and insertion sort are the stable ones among these.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Selection sort = fewest swaps; insertion sort = best on nearly sorted data.

q: What is the best-case time complexity of selection sort on n elements (for example, when the input is already sorted)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Selection sort always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, so even its best case is Θ(n²), which is not listed.
concept: Selection sort always scans the whole unsorted part to find its minimum, because it cannot know the minimum without looking at every element. This happens even if the array is already sorted, so it always makes (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 comparisons. Its best, average and worst cases are all Θ(n²). Key properties: Θ(n²) in every case; at most n − 1 swaps; extra space O(1); stable: no; in-place: yes; adaptive: no.
why: A — Wrong. O(n) is the best case of insertion sort and of bubble sort with a swapped flag. Selection sort has no early exit: even on sorted input every pass scans the rest of the array.
B — Wrong. O(n log n) is the time of merge sort and heap sort (and the average of quick sort), not of selection sort.
C — Wrong. O(log n) is impossible for any sort: a sorting algorithm must at least look at all n elements.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Even on sorted input selection sort makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, so its best case is Θ(n²), which is not among A–C. 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Selection sort: n² in every case, but at most n − 1 swaps.

q: Which of the following statements are true for the standard (swap-based) selection sort?
opts: It performs at most n − 1 swaps
More than one of the above
exp: Selection sort is in place and makes at most n − 1 swaps, but it is not stable: B and C are true.
concept: Standard selection sort finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it with the first unsorted element. Only one temporary variable is needed for the swap, so it sorts in place, and there is at most one swap per pass, so at most n − 1 swaps. But the long-distance swap can carry an element past another element equal to it, so it is not stable. Example: [2a, 2b, 1] → swap 2a with 1 → [1, 2b, 2a]; now 2b comes before 2a.
why: A — Wrong. Selection sort is NOT stable. In [2a, 2b, 1] the first pass swaps 2a with 1, giving [1, 2b, 2a], so the two equal keys change their relative order. (A stable variant that shifts elements instead of swapping exists, but it is not the standard swap-based version.)

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. All the work happens inside the original array with one temporary variable, so the extra space is O(1).

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. There are n − 1 passes and each makes at most one swap, so there are at most n − 1 swaps.
D — Correct. B and C are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. B and C are both true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Selection sort (ascending; pass i finds the minimum of a[i..n−1] and swaps it with a[i]) is applied to [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]. What is the array after the second pass?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pass 1 gives [10, 29, 14, 37, 13] and pass 2 swaps 13 into index 1: [10, 13, 14, 37, 29].
concept: Selection sort grows a sorted part at the front. In pass i it looks through a[i..n−1], finds the smallest element and swaps it with a[i]. After pass k the first k elements are the k smallest, in their final order.
why: A — Correct. Pass 1 brings 10 to the front; pass 2 picks 13, the smallest of [29, 14, 37, 13], and swaps it with 29, giving [10, 13, 14, 37, 29].

B — Wrong. [10, 14, 29, 37, 13] is what INSERTION sort gives after two passes (inserting 10, then 14, into the front). Selection sort's second pass must bring the second-smallest value, 13, to index 1.
C — Wrong. [10, 29, 14, 37, 13] is the array after the FIRST pass only.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Selection sort (ascending; the minimum of the unsorted part is swapped to its front in each pass) is applied to [45, 20, 50, 15, 30, 10, 40]. What is the array after three passes?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After three passes the three smallest values 10, 15, 20 are at the front: [10, 15, 20, 50, 30, 45, 40].
concept: In each pass selection sort swaps the minimum of the unsorted part into the next front position; only two elements change places per pass. The element that is swapped out (like 45 in pass 1) jumps to wherever the minimum was, which can be far away.
why: A — Wrong. [10, 15, 50, 20, 30, 45, 40] is the array after only TWO passes.
B — Wrong. [10, 15, 20, 30, 50, 45, 40] is the array after FOUR passes (pass 4 swaps 30 with 50).
C — Correct. Pass 3 swaps 20, the minimum of [50, 20, 30, 45, 40], with 50, giving [10, 15, 20, 50, 30, 45, 40].
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many element comparisons does selection sort make on an array of 8 elements, whatever their initial order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Selection sort always makes n(n − 1)/2 = 28 comparisons on 8 elements.
concept: Pass i of selection sort compares the current minimum with each remaining element of the unsorted part: n − 1 comparisons in the first pass, n − 2 in the second, …, 1 in the last. The total n(n − 1)/2 does not depend on the input order, because the scan never stops early.
why: A — Correct. 7 + 6 + … + 1 = 8 × 7 / 2 = 28 comparisons, for every input.
B — Wrong. 7 = n − 1 is the number of passes (and the maximum number of swaps), not the number of comparisons.
C — Wrong. 64 = n² is only the rough order of growth; the exact count is n(n − 1)/2.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Selection sort (ascending) swaps a[i] with the minimum of a[i..n−1] only when that minimum is not already at index i. How many swaps are performed on [3, 5, 1, 2, 4]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Selection sort swaps in passes 1, 2 and 4 only, so it makes 3 swaps.
concept: In this version a pass swaps only when the minimum of the unsorted part is not already at its front. So count the passes in which the minimum is somewhere else. Selection sort never makes more than n − 1 swaps; here only 3. (Bubble sort on the same array would need 5 swaps, one per inversion.)
work:
Start: [3, 5, 1, 2, 4]
Pass 1: min 1 at index 2 ≠ 0 → swap → [1, 5, 3, 2, 4] (swaps = 1)
Pass 2: min of a[1..4] is 2 at index 3 ≠ 1 → swap → [1, 2, 3, 5, 4] (swaps = 2)
Pass 3: min of a[2..4] is 3 at index 2 → already in place, no swap
Pass 4: min of a[3..4] is 4 at index 4 ≠ 3 → swap → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (swaps = 3)
Total = 3
why: A — Wrong. 5 is the number of inversions in [3, 5, 1, 2, 4]; that is the swap count of BUBBLE sort (one swap per inversion), not of selection sort.
B — Wrong. 4 = n − 1 would be right only if every pass swapped. Pass 3 finds 3 already in place, so it makes no swap.
C — Correct. Passes 1, 2 and 4 make a swap; pass 3 does not. Total 3 swaps.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Selection sort (pass i finds the first minimum of a[i..n−1] using strict <, then swaps it with a[i]) sorts [4a, 3, 4b, 1], where 4a and 4b are equal keys labelled to show their original order. What is the final array?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Selection sort's first swap moves 4a behind 4b, giving [1, 3, 4b, 4a]; this shows it is unstable.
concept: Labelling equal keys (4a, 4b) is the standard way to test stability: a stable sort must keep 4a before 4b. Selection sort swaps the minimum into the front position, and such a long-distance swap can throw an element (here 4a) behind an equal one. So selection sort is not stable.
work:
Start: [4a, 3, 4b, 1]
Pass 1 (i=0): minimum is 1 (index 3); swap a[0]↔a[3] → [1, 3, 4b, 4a] (4a jumps behind 4b)
Pass 2 (i=1): minimum of [3, 4b, 4a] is 3 (index 1); no change
Pass 3 (i=2): with strict <, the first minimum of [4b, 4a] is 4b (4a is not smaller); no change
Final: [1, 3, 4b, 4a]
why: A — Wrong. [1, 3, 4a, 4b] is what a STABLE sort (insertion sort or merge sort, for example) would produce. Selection sort's first swap moves 4a from the front to the last position, behind 4b.
B — Correct. The first swap exchanges 4a and 1, giving [1, 3, 4b, 4a]; the later passes change nothing, so 4b stays before 4a.
C — Wrong. [1, 4a, 3, 4b] is not even sorted (a 4 comes before 3), so it cannot be the final result of a correct sort.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Long-distance swaps (selection, quick, heap sort) break stability.

q: Insertion sort attains its best case when the input array of n elements is already sorted. What is that best-case time complexity?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: On sorted input insertion sort makes n − 1 comparisons and no shifts: Θ(n).
concept: Insertion sort takes the next element and moves it left past larger elements into its place in the sorted front part, like arranging playing cards in your hand. On an already sorted array each new element is compared once with its left neighbour, found to be in place, and nothing moves: n − 1 comparisons, Θ(n). Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Key properties: best Θ(n), average and worst Θ(n²); extra space O(1); stable: yes; in-place: yes; adaptive: yes; online: yes.
why: A — Wrong. Θ(1) would mean not even looking at all the elements. Any sort must check every element at least once, so no sort finishes in constant time for large n.
B — Correct. Each of the n − 1 elements a[1..n−1] needs exactly one comparison and no shift, so the best case is Θ(n).
C — Wrong. Θ(n log n) is the time of merge sort and heap sort in every case. Insertion sort's best case is even better, Θ(n).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following properties does insertion sort have?
opts: It is online (it can sort elements as they arrive)
More than one of the above
exp: Insertion sort is stable, in place and online, so more than one option is correct.
concept: Insertion sort keeps a sorted part at the front and inserts each new element into it, like a card player sorting cards as they are dealt. It moves an element left only past STRICTLY greater elements, so equal elements keep their order (stable). It works inside the array with one extra variable (in place). And because each step needs only the elements seen so far, it can sort data as it arrives (online). Key properties: best Θ(n), average and worst Θ(n²); extra space O(1); stable: yes; in-place: yes; adaptive: yes; online: yes.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The inner loop shifts elements only while a[j] > key, so it stops at an equal element and the new element is placed after it. Equal keys keep their original order, so insertion sort is stable.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Only one variable (key) holds the element being inserted; everything else is shifted inside the same array, so the extra space is O(1).

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each step needs only the already sorted prefix and the next element, so elements can be inserted as they arrive, without seeing the whole input first. That is what 'online' means.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Insertion sort (ascending; pass i inserts a[i] into the sorted part a[0..i−1], i = 1, 2, …) is applied to [7, 4, 9, 2, 6, 1]. What is the array after pass 3?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After pass 3 the first four elements are sorted: [2, 4, 7, 9, 6, 1].
concept: In pass i, insertion sort takes a[i] (the 'key'), shifts every larger element of the sorted part a[0..i−1] one place right, and drops the key into the gap. After pass i the first i + 1 elements are sorted among themselves (though not necessarily in their final places), and the rest are untouched.
work:
Start: [7, 4, 9, 2, 6, 1]
Pass 1 (key 4): 7 shifts right → [4, 7, 9, 2, 6, 1]
Pass 2 (key 9): 7 < 9, nothing shifts → [4, 7, 9, 2, 6, 1]
Pass 3 (key 2): 9, 7, 4 shift right → [2, 4, 7, 9, 6, 1]
why: A — Wrong. [4, 7, 9, 2, 6, 1] is the array after passes 1 and 2 (pass 2 changes nothing). Pass 3 still has to insert 2.
B — Correct. Pass 3 inserts 2 at the front of [4, 7, 9], giving [2, 4, 7, 9, 6, 1].
C — Wrong. [2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 1] is the array after pass 4, when 6 has also been inserted.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Insertion sort (ascending; pass i inserts a[i] into the sorted part a[0..i−1]) is applied to [20, 12, 35, 5, 18, 9]. What is the array after pass 4?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pass 4 inserts 18 between 12 and 20, giving [5, 12, 18, 20, 35, 9], which is not listed.
concept: After pass i of insertion sort, the first i + 1 elements are sorted and the remaining elements are untouched, still in their original order. So after pass 4 on six elements, the first five must be sorted and the last original element (9) must still be at the end.
why: A — Wrong. [5, 12, 20, 35, 18, 9] is the array after pass 3, one pass too early.
B — Wrong. [5, 9, 12, 18, 20, 35] is the fully sorted array, reached only after pass 5, when 9 is inserted.

C — Wrong. This array has 9 inside the front part and 35 at the end. But 9 is not touched until pass 5, so after pass 4 it must still be at the end, with the first five elements sorted and ending in 35.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. After pass 4 the array is [5, 12, 18, 20, 35, 9], which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: How many element shifts does insertion sort perform to sort [4, 3, 2, 10, 12, 1, 5, 6] in ascending order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Insertion sort makes one shift per inversion, and the array has 12 inversions.
concept: Each shift in insertion sort moves one larger element one place right past the key, and this fixes exactly one inversion (a pair in the wrong order). So the total number of shifts equals the number of inversions in the input. Counting inversions is often quicker than tracing every pass.
why: A — Correct. Shifts = inversions = 3 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 3 = 12.
B — Wrong. 10 is too small. Every one of the 12 inversions costs exactly one shift, so the total cannot be 10; a typical slip is to forget that 1 must move past all five larger elements before it.
C — Wrong. 14 is too large. 1 causes 5 shifts, 5 and 6 cause only 2 each (past 12 and 10), and 3 and 2 cause 1 + 2 = 3: 5 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 12.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Shifts in insertion sort = inversions in the input.

q: How many key comparisons does insertion sort make on an already sorted array of 10 elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: On sorted input insertion sort makes n − 1 = 9 comparisons.
concept: On a sorted array, insertion sort compares each new element a[i] with its left neighbour a[i−1] once, finds that the neighbour is not larger, and stops. Elements a[1] to a[n−1] each need one comparison, so there are n − 1 comparisons and no shifts. This is insertion sort's best case.
work:
n = 10, sorted input
Pass i = 1..9: test a[i−1] > a[i] → false → stop (1 comparison per pass)
Total = 9 comparisons, 0 shifts
why: A — Wrong. 45 = 10 × 9 / 2 is the WORST case (reverse-sorted input), where every key is compared with all the earlier elements.
B — Wrong. 0 is impossible: the algorithm cannot know the array is sorted without comparing neighbours, so every pass makes at least one comparison.
C — Correct. Each of the 9 passes makes exactly one comparison and finds the element already in place: 9 comparisons.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: For a small array, or one that is already nearly sorted, which of these simple algorithms is usually the best choice (it is also used for small sub-arrays inside hybrid sorts)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Insertion sort is fast on small or nearly sorted arrays, which is why hybrid sorts use it for small pieces.
concept: Insertion sort runs in Θ(n + I) time, where I is the number of inversions (pairs out of order). On nearly sorted data I is small, so it is almost linear, and on small arrays its very simple loop has tiny overhead. That is why hybrid sorts such as Timsort (used in Python and Java) and introsort (used in C++ std::sort) switch to insertion sort for small sub-arrays of a few dozen elements.
why: A — Correct. Insertion sort adapts to existing order (Θ(n) on sorted input) and has very low overhead, so it is the usual choice for small or nearly sorted arrays and inside hybrid sorts.
B — Wrong. Selection sort is not adaptive: it always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, even on sorted input. Its only advantage is its small number of swaps.
C — Wrong. Heap sort is not a simple algorithm for small arrays: building and maintaining the heap adds overhead, and it takes Θ(n log n) even on sorted data, so it gains nothing from existing order.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Small or nearly sorted? Use insertion sort.

q: What is printed by the following C code?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The shift counter equals the number of inversions, which is 9.
concept: The variable shifts is increased each time an element moves one place right inside the while loop. Each such move fixes one inversion, so the program prints the number of inversions in [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3].
work:
i=1 key 2: shift 5 → [2, 5, 4, 6, 1, 3], shifts=1
i=2 key 4: shift 5 → [2, 4, 5, 6, 1, 3], shifts=2
i=3 key 6: no shift, shifts=2
i=4 key 1: shift 6, 5, 4, 2 → [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 3], shifts=6
i=5 key 3: shift 6, 5, 4 → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], shifts=9
Prints 9 (confirmed with gcc)
why: A — Correct. 1 + 1 + 0 + 4 + 3 = 9 shifts, which equals the 9 inversions of the input.
B — Wrong. 8 misses one shift; for example, forgetting that 3 must move past all three of 6, 5 and 4 in the last pass.
C — Wrong. 15 = 6 × 5 / 2 is the WORST-case number of shifts, for a reverse-sorted array of 6 elements.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many element shifts does insertion sort make when sorting a reverse-sorted array of 7 distinct elements into ascending order?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Reverse-sorted input needs 1 + 2 + … + 6 = 21 shifts.
concept: In a reverse-sorted array each new element is smaller than everything before it, so in pass i it must be shifted past all i earlier elements. The total is 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2, the worst case of insertion sort (and equal to the number of inversions).
work:
n = 7, reverse sorted
Shifts in passes 1..6: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21 = 7 × 6 / 2
why: A — Wrong. 6 = n − 1 is the number of passes (or the number of comparisons on SORTED input), not the shifts on reverse-sorted input.
B — Wrong. 42 = n(n − 1) forgets to divide by 2.
C — Correct. 1 + 2 + … + 6 = 21 shifts.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Insertion sort is modified so that each insertion position is found by binary search on the sorted part. What is the worst-case time complexity of this binary insertion sort?
opts: O(n log n), since comparisons drop to O(n log n)
O(n²), since elements must still be shifted
O(n), since each binary search takes O(log n)
More than one of the above
exp: Binary search reduces only the comparisons; the shifting still costs Θ(n²), so the worst case stays O(n²).
concept: Binary insertion sort uses binary search to find where each new element belongs in the sorted part. This cuts the comparisons to about log₂ i per element, Θ(n log n) in total. But it still has to make room by shifting every larger element one place right, and on reverse-sorted input that is 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = Θ(n²) moves. So the worst-case running time stays Θ(n²).
why: A — Wrong. The comparison count does drop to O(n log n), but running time counts ALL the work, including moving elements. The shifts alone can cost Θ(n²).
B — Correct. Shifting elements to open a gap still costs up to i moves in pass i, which sums to Θ(n²) in the worst case, so the total stays O(n²).
C — Wrong. Θ(n) is wrong twice over: n binary searches alone already cost Θ(n log n), and the shifting costs Θ(n²) in the worst case.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Fewer comparisons do not mean less time if the moves dominate.

q: Merge sort is based on which algorithm design technique?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Merge sort splits the array into halves, sorts them recursively and merges them: divide and conquer.
concept: Divide and conquer solves a problem in three steps: DIVIDE it into smaller sub-problems, CONQUER them recursively, and COMBINE their answers. Merge sort divides the array into two halves, sorts each half recursively, and combines them by merging two sorted lists into one. Quick sort and binary search are also divide-and-conquer algorithms.
why: A — Wrong. The greedy method builds a solution by taking the best-looking choice at each step and never going back (for example Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms, Huffman coding). Merge sort does not work that way.

B — Wrong. Dynamic programming solves OVERLAPPING sub-problems once and stores their answers in a table (for example Fibonacci with memoisation, 0/1 knapsack). Merge sort's two halves are independent and never repeat, so no table is needed.
C — Correct. Merge sort divides the array into halves, conquers them by sorting recursively, and combines them with the merge step: divide and conquer.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which recurrence describes the running time of merge sort on n elements, together with its solution?
opts: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), giving Θ(n log n)
More than one of the above
exp: Merge sort satisfies T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), which solves to Θ(n log n).
concept: A recurrence describes running time in terms of smaller inputs. Merge sort makes two recursive calls on halves (2T(n/2)) and then merges in linear time (Θ(n)), so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n). The recursion has about log₂ n levels and each level does Θ(n) merging work in total, giving Θ(n log n) (case 2 of the master theorem).
why: A — Correct. Two half-size sub-problems plus a linear merge give T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n), whose solution is Θ(n log n).
B — Wrong. This recurrence has only ONE recursive call. Its solution Θ(n) is right for it (n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n), but merge sort recurses on BOTH halves.

C — Wrong. Here the combine step takes constant time. Θ(n) is the right solution of this recurrence (it fits, for example, finding the maximum by divide and conquer), but merging two halves takes linear time, not constant.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: 2T(n/2) + n → n log n (merge sort); T(n − 1) + n → n² (worst-case quick sort).

q: What is the best-case time complexity of standard (top-down) merge sort on n elements, for example when the input is already sorted?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Merge sort does Θ(n log n) work on every input, so its best case, Θ(n log n), is not listed.
concept: Standard top-down merge sort always splits the array all the way down to single elements and merges at every level, whatever the input order. There are about log₂ n levels and each level does Θ(n) work, so the best, average and worst cases are all Θ(n log n). On sorted input the merges make fewer comparisons, but every element is still copied at every level. Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Key properties: Θ(n log n) in every case; extra space Θ(n) for arrays; stable: yes; in-place: no; adaptive: no (standard version).
why: A — Wrong. Θ(n) is the best case of insertion sort, and of 'natural' merge sort variants that detect already sorted runs. Standard merge sort still splits and merges at all log₂ n levels, copying every element at each level.
B — Wrong. Θ(log n) is far too small: merge sort must at least copy every element while merging, which already costs Θ(n).
C — Wrong. Θ(n²) is the worst case of bubble, insertion, selection and quick sort. Merge sort never goes beyond Θ(n log n), and its best case is not worse than its worst case.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Merge sort's best case is Θ(n log n), which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Merge sort and heap sort: n log n always.

q: How much auxiliary space does standard merge sort need to sort an array of n elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Merging needs a temporary array of size n, so array merge sort uses O(n) extra space.
concept: Merging two sorted halves needs a temporary array to hold the merged result, because the halves cannot be overwritten while they are still being read. At the top level this temporary array holds n elements, so standard array merge sort uses Θ(n) auxiliary space, plus an O(log n) recursion stack. That is why merge sort is not an in-place sort. (On a linked list, merging can be done by relinking nodes, without an extra array.)
why: A — Wrong. O(1) extra space is achieved by heap sort, insertion sort, selection sort and bubble sort. The standard merge needs a temporary array. (Complicated in-place merging methods exist, but they are not standard merge sort.)

B — Wrong. O(log n) is only the recursion stack (the depth of the halving). It leaves out the temporary array used by merging, which is the dominant Θ(n) part. O(log n) on average is the extra space of QUICK sort.
C — Correct. The merge step needs a temporary array of up to n elements, so the auxiliary space is O(n).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Merge sort is a preferred choice in which of the following situations?
opts: Sorting data too large to fit in main memory (external sorting)
When a stable sort with O(n log n) worst-case time is required
More than one of the above
exp: Merge sort suits external sorting, linked lists and stable O(n log n) sorting, so all three situations apply.
concept: Merge sort reads its inputs sequentially (front to back) while merging and never needs random access. It is stable and guaranteed Θ(n log n). These properties make it the natural choice for external sorting (data on disk, sorted in chunks that are then merged), for linked lists (merging only relinks nodes, so no extra array is needed), and whenever a stable sort with an O(n log n) worst case is required.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. External sorting sorts chunks that fit in memory, writes them to disk as sorted 'runs', and then merges the runs while reading each file sequentially. That is exactly merge sort's merging step, so (multi-way) merge sort is the standard external sort.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Merge sort needs no random access, and merging two linked lists only changes next pointers, so it sorts a singly linked list in O(n log n) time without an extra array. Quick sort and heap sort rely on random access and suit linked lists poorly.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Merge sort is stable (it takes from the left half on ties) and its worst case is Θ(n log n). Quick sort can degrade to O(n²) and heap sort is unstable, so merge sort is the usual choice when both properties are needed.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is the maximum number of comparisons needed to merge two sorted lists of sizes 5 and 7 into one sorted list?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Merging sorted lists of sizes 5 and 7 needs at most 5 + 7 − 1 = 11 comparisons.
concept: The merge procedure compares the front elements of the two lists and outputs the smaller one, so each comparison outputs exactly one element. Once one list is empty, the rest of the other list is copied without comparisons. In the worst case both lists stay non-empty until only one element is left, so merging m and n elements takes at most m + n − 1 comparisons. The minimum is min(m, n), when the whole shorter list is smaller than every element of the other.
work:
Total elements = 5 + 7 = 12
Worst case: comparisons continue until 1 element remains → 12 − 1 = 11
Example: [1, 3, 5, 7, 12] with [2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11] → 11 comparisons (12 is copied at the end)
Best case: min(5, 7) = 5 comparisons
why: A — Correct. Each comparison outputs one element and the last element needs no comparison, so at most 5 + 7 − 1 = 11 comparisons.
B — Wrong. 12 = m + n is one too many: when only one element is left there is nothing to compare it with, so it is copied without a comparison.
C — Wrong. 35 = 5 × 7 would be the count if every element of one list were compared with every element of the other. Merging only ever compares the two front elements.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Merging m and n elements: at most m + n − 1, at least min(m, n) comparisons.

q: The standard merge procedure (compare the front elements, output the smaller, and copy the rest once one list becomes empty) merges [10, 20, 30, 40] and [1, 2, 25]. How many comparisons are made?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Five comparisons output 1, 2, 10, 20 and 25; the rest are copied without comparisons.
concept: In the standard merge, count comparisons only while BOTH lists still have elements. Each comparison outputs one element. As soon as one list runs out, the remaining elements of the other list are copied without any comparison.
work:
L = [10, 20, 30, 40], R = [1, 2, 25]
1) 10 vs 1 → output 1
2) 10 vs 2 → output 2
3) 10 vs 25 → output 10
4) 20 vs 25 → output 20
5) 30 vs 25 → output 25; R is now empty
Copy 30, 40 without comparisons
Result [1, 2, 10, 20, 25, 30, 40]; comparisons = 5
why: A — Wrong. 3 = the size of the shorter list, which is the MINIMUM possible (when the whole shorter list is smaller than the other list). Here 25 is larger than 10 and 20, so more comparisons are needed.
B — Correct. Five comparisons are made (outputting 1, 2, 10, 20 and 25); then R is empty and 30, 40 are copied for free.
C — Wrong. 6 = 4 + 3 − 1 is the WORST-case bound for these sizes. It is reached only if both lists last until the very end; here R runs out while two elements of L remain.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Bottom-up (iterative) merge sort first merges runs of size 1, then 2, then 4, and so on. How many merge passes are needed to sort 20 elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Bottom-up merge sort needs ⌈log₂ 20⌉ = 5 passes.
concept: Bottom-up merge sort starts with n runs of size 1 and in each pass merges neighbouring runs, doubling the run size: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → … The array is sorted once a single run covers all n elements. So the number of passes is ⌈log₂ n⌉ (log₂ n rounded UP).
work:
Run size after each pass: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32
After pass 4 the runs are 16 long (< 20), so the last 4 elements are still a separate run
Pass 5 merges the 16-run with the 4-run → sorted
Passes = ⌈log₂ 20⌉ = 5 (2⁴ = 16 < 20 ≤ 32 = 2⁵)
why: A — Wrong. 4 = ⌊log₂ 20⌋, rounded down instead of up. After 4 passes the runs are only 16 long, and the last 4 elements still form a separate run, so one more pass is needed.
B — Wrong. 10 = n/2 is the number of merges in the FIRST pass (pairs of single elements), not the number of passes.
C — Correct. Run sizes 2, 4, 8, 16, 32: the fifth pass is the first whose run size covers all 20 elements, so 5 passes are needed.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Bottom-up merge sort (pass 1 merges adjacent runs of size 1, pass 2 merges adjacent runs of size 2, …) is applied to [45, 12, 78, 34, 23, 56, 9, 67]. What is the array after pass 2?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Pass 2 merges sorted pairs into sorted groups of four: [12, 34, 45, 78, 9, 23, 56, 67].
concept: In pass 1, bottom-up merge sort merges neighbouring single elements into sorted pairs. In pass 2 it merges neighbouring pairs into sorted groups of 4, and so on. After pass k, every block of 2^k elements is sorted (but the blocks are not yet merged with each other).
why: A — Wrong. [12, 45, 34, 78, 23, 56, 9, 67] is the array after pass 1 (sorted pairs).
B — Correct. Merging the pairs gives [12, 34, 45, 78] and [9, 23, 56, 67], so the array is [12, 34, 45, 78, 9, 23, 56, 67].
C — Wrong. [9, 12, 23, 34, 45, 56, 67, 78] is the fully sorted array, reached after pass 3 (merging the two groups of four).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Top-down merge sort splits n elements into two halves, and each merge stops comparing as soon as one list is empty. For n = 8 distinct elements, what is the worst-case total number of comparisons?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Worst case = 4 × 1 + 2 × 3 + 1 × 7 = 17 comparisons, which is not listed.
concept: Count comparisons merge by merge. Merging two sorted lists of sizes p and q takes at most p + q − 1 comparisons (worst case) and at least min(p, q) (best case). For n = 8, top-down merge sort performs four 1+1 merges, two 2+2 merges and one 4+4 merge.
work:
Four 1+1 merges: worst 1 each → 4
Two 2+2 merges: worst 3 each → 6
One 4+4 merge: worst 7 → 7
Worst total = 4 + 6 + 7 = 17 (confirmed by trying all 8! = 40320 orderings)
Best total = 4×1 + 2×2 + 1×4 = 12
why: A — Wrong. 12 is the BEST case: 4 × 1 + 2 × 2 + 1 × 4 (each merge uses only min(p, q) comparisons, for example on sorted input).
B — Wrong. 24 = n log₂ n = 8 × 3 is only an approximate estimate. The exact worst case is smaller, because a merge of p + q elements costs at most p + q − 1 comparisons, not p + q.
C — Wrong. 28 = 8 × 7 / 2 is the comparison count of selection sort (and the worst case of bubble or insertion sort), not of merge sort.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The worst-case total is 4 + 6 + 7 = 17, which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: In quick sort, most of the work of sorting is done in which step?
opts: Building a heap from the array
Partitioning the array around a pivot
More than one of the above
exp: Quick sort does its work in the partition step; no merging is needed afterwards.
concept: Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer sort that does its real work while DIVIDING. It picks a pivot and partitions the array: smaller elements go to the left of the pivot and larger ones to the right, and the pivot lands in its final position. Then the two sides are sorted recursively, and nothing needs to be combined afterwards. Merge sort is the opposite: its divide step is trivial and its work is in combining (merging).
why: A — Wrong. Merging sorted sub-arrays is the main work of MERGE sort. Quick sort has no merge step: once both sides are sorted, the whole array is already sorted.
B — Wrong. Building a heap is the first phase of HEAP sort, not part of quick sort.
C — Correct. Partitioning places the pivot in its final position with smaller elements on one side and larger ones on the other; this is where quick sort does its comparing and swapping.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Quick sort: hard divide, easy combine. Merge sort: easy divide, hard combine.

q: What is the average-case time complexity of quick sort on n elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Quick sort's average case is Θ(n log n); Θ(n²) is only its worst case.
concept: On average (for example, over random input orders) quick sort's pivots split the array reasonably evenly, so the recursion is about log n levels deep and each level does Θ(n) partitioning work in total. The average is therefore Θ(n log n), about 1.39 n log₂ n comparisons. Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Key properties: best and average Θ(n log n), worst Θ(n²); extra space O(log n) average stack (O(n) worst); stable: no; in-place: yes; adaptive: no.
why: A — Wrong. Θ(n) is too small for a comparison sort: on distinct keys any comparison sort needs about n log₂ n comparisons even on average, and quick sort's partitioning costs Θ(n) per level of recursion.
B — Correct. Partitions that are balanced on average give about log n levels with Θ(n) work each: Θ(n log n).
C — Wrong. Θ(n²) is quick sort's WORST case (very unbalanced splits, e.g. sorted input with a first- or last-element pivot), not its average.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Quick sort that always chooses the last element as the pivot is run on an already sorted array of n elements. What is its running time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: On sorted input a last-element pivot gives (n − 1, 0) splits every time, so the running time is O(n²).
concept: If the pivot is always the last element and the array is already sorted, the pivot is always the LARGEST element of its sub-array. Partitioning then puts everything on one side: the split is (n − 1, 0). The next call works on n − 1 elements, then n − 2, and so on, so the comparisons add up to (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2, which is O(n²). This is quick sort's worst case.
work:
Sizes of the sub-arrays partitioned: n, n − 1, n − 2, …, 2
Comparisons: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 → O(n²)
why: A — Correct. Each partition removes only the pivot, so there are about n levels with n − 1, n − 2, … comparisons: n(n − 1)/2 = O(n²).
B — Wrong. O(n log n) needs reasonably balanced splits. Here every split is completely unbalanced (n − 1 and 0).
C — Wrong. O(n) would be possible only if the algorithm detected sorted input and stopped early. Quick sort has no such check and keeps partitioning.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
