E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Sorted input + first or last element as pivot = quick sort's worst case.

q: Which recurrence describes the worst-case running time of quick sort (the pivot always ends up at one end of the sub-array)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Worst-case quick sort satisfies T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n), which is Θ(n²).
concept: In the worst case of quick sort the pivot lands at one end of the sub-array every time, so one side is empty and the other has n − 1 elements. Partitioning n elements costs Θ(n). So T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n), which unrolls to n + (n − 1) + … + 1 = Θ(n²).
why: A — Wrong. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) describes two equal halves: the BEST case of quick sort (and every case of merge sort), with solution Θ(n log n).
B — Correct. One sub-problem of size n − 1 plus Θ(n) partitioning work gives T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n) = Θ(n²).
C — Wrong. T(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(1) would mean partitioning costs constant time; it solves to only Θ(n). Partitioning must look at every element, so it costs Θ(n), not Θ(1).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Lomuto partition is applied to [24, 9, 29, 14, 19, 27, 21]: pivot = last element; i = low − 1; for j = low … high−1, if a[j] ≤ pivot then i++ and swap a[i], a[j]; finally swap a[i+1] with a[high]. What is the array after this partition?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After Lomuto partition the array is [9, 14, 19, 21, 29, 27, 24], with the pivot 21 at index 3.
concept: Lomuto partition keeps a boundary i: everything in a[low..i] is ≤ pivot. It scans j from left to right; whenever a[j] ≤ pivot it grows the boundary (i++) and swaps a[j] into it. Finally it swaps the pivot into position i + 1, so the pivot lands in its final sorted place, with smaller-or-equal elements on its left and larger ones on its right. The two sides are not sorted yet.
why: A — Wrong. [9, 14, 19, 21, 24, 27, 29] is the fully sorted array. One partition only places the pivot; the right side (29, 27, 24) is still unsorted.
B — Wrong. [9, 19, 14, 21, 29, 27, 24] has 19 and 14 in the wrong order. Lomuto moves the ≤ elements to the front in the order it meets them (9, then 14, then 19), so 14 comes before 19.
C — Correct. The scan gives [9, 14, 19, 24, 29, 27, 21]; swapping a[3] = 24 with the pivot then gives [9, 14, 19, 21, 29, 27, 24].
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Lomuto partition with the last element as pivot is applied to [35, 12, 60, 8, 47, 25, 3, 30] (indices 0–7). At which index does the pivot end up?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Four elements are smaller than 30, so the pivot ends at index 4.
concept: After a partition the pivot sits in its final sorted position, so its index equals the number of elements that go to its left. In Lomuto partition (test a[j] ≤ pivot) that is the number of other elements ≤ pivot, counted from index low.
why: A — Wrong. Index 3 is the final value of i (the last slot holding an element ≤ pivot); the pivot goes one place after it, to i + 1 = 4.
B — Correct. Four elements (12, 8, 25, 3) are ≤ 30, so they fill indices 0–3 and the pivot lands at index 4.
C — Wrong. Index 5 would need five elements ≤ 30; only four exist.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Pivot's final index = low + number of other elements that go to its left.

q: The partition function below (first element as pivot) is called as partition(a, 0, 6) with a = {50, 70, 20, 90, 40, 10, 60}. What is the array after the call?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After the swaps 70↔10 and 90↔40 and the final pivot swap, the array is [40, 10, 20, 50, 90, 70, 60].
concept: This is a Hoare-style partition with the first element as pivot. Index i moves right past elements smaller than the pivot, index j moves left past elements larger than the pivot; when both stop and i < j, the two elements are swapped. When the indices cross, the pivot is swapped with a[j], which puts it in its final place: elements ≤ pivot on its left, elements ≥ pivot on its right.
why: A — Correct. The two swaps (70↔10 and 90↔40) and the final pivot swap (50↔40) give [40, 10, 20, 50, 90, 70, 60].
B — Wrong. [10, 20, 40, 50, 90, 70, 60] has the left side sorted, but one partition does not sort the sides. The final swap puts 40 (the old a[3]) at index 0, so the left side is 40, 10, 20.
C — Wrong. [40, 10, 20, 50, 60, 70, 90] has the right side sorted. After the second swap the partition never touches 90, 70, 60, so they stay in that order.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many times is the comparison a[j] <= pivot executed when this Lomuto partition function is called on a sub-array of n elements (high − low + 1 = n)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: j takes n − 1 values (every element except the pivot), so the comparison runs n − 1 times.
concept: In Lomuto partition the for loop runs j from low to high − 1, that is over every element of the sub-array except the pivot a[high]. The test a[j] <= pivot runs once per iteration, whatever the data, so a sub-array of n elements always costs n − 1 comparisons. This fact is used when counting quick sort's total comparisons.
work:
Iterations: j = low, low+1, …, high−1 → high − low = n − 1 values
(Checked with gcc: sub-arrays of 1..10 elements give 0..9 comparisons.)
why: A — Correct. The loop covers every element except the pivot, so the comparison runs n − 1 times.
B — Wrong. n would count the pivot too, but the pivot is never compared with itself: the loop stops at high − 1.
C — Wrong. n/2 would mean only half of the elements are examined. Partitioning must check every non-pivot element to know which side it belongs to.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about quick sort on arrays are correct?
opts: It sorts in place, needing only the recursion stack as extra space
It is not a stable sort
Its worst-case time complexity is O(n log n)
More than one of the above
exp: Quick sort is in place and unstable (A and B are true), but its worst case is O(n²), not O(n log n).
concept: Quick sort rearranges elements inside the array itself, so apart from a few variables it needs only the recursion stack (O(log n) on average). Its long-distance swaps during partitioning can carry an element past an equal one, so it is not stable. Its worst case is Θ(n²), when the pivots keep splitting the array very unevenly. Key properties: best and average Θ(n log n), worst Θ(n²); extra space O(log n) average stack; stable: no; in-place: yes; adaptive: no.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Partitioning swaps elements within the array, so no second array is needed. The only extra space is the recursion stack (O(log n) on average), which is why quick sort is called in place.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Partitioning swaps elements over long distances. Example: Lomuto partition of [2a, 2b, 1] with pivot 1 swaps 1 with 2a, giving [1, 2b, 2a], and the final result keeps 2b before 2a. Equal keys can change order, so quick sort is not stable.
C — Wrong. The worst case of quick sort is O(n²), for example on sorted input with a first- or last-element pivot. O(n log n) is only its best and average case.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are both true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is the average-case extra space used by the recursion stack of quick sort?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: On average quick sort's recursion is about log n deep, so the stack uses Θ(log n) space.
concept: Quick sort needs no extra array, but each pending recursive call keeps a frame on the call stack. With reasonably balanced partitions (the average case) the recursion depth is about log n, so the stack uses Θ(log n) space on average. In the worst case (very unbalanced splits) the depth can reach n, unless the implementation always recurses on the smaller part first and loops on the larger part, which keeps the depth O(log n). Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower.
why: A — Wrong. Θ(1) would mean no recursion stack at all. Quick sort makes nested recursive calls, and the pending ones must be remembered.
B — Wrong. Θ(n) stack depth happens in the WORST case (splits of n − 1 and 0), not on average.
C — Correct. Balanced splits on average give a recursion depth of about log n with constant space per frame: Θ(log n).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Quick sort is modified to pick its pivot uniformly at random from the current sub-array. Which statement is correct?
opts: Its expected running time is O(n log n) for every input
Its worst-case running time becomes O(n log n)
It becomes a stable sorting algorithm
More than one of the above
exp: A random pivot gives O(n log n) expected time on every input, but the worst case is still O(n²) and the sort is still unstable.
concept: Randomised quick sort picks its pivot at random. Then no particular input (such as sorted data) is always bad: the running time depends on the random choices, and its EXPECTED value (the average over those random choices) is O(n log n) for every input. But an unlucky run of random pivots can still give unbalanced splits, so the worst case is still O(n²), although it is extremely unlikely. Randomisation does not affect stability.
why: A — Correct. For any fixed input, the expected running time over the random pivot choices is O(n log n); the input order no longer matters.

B — Wrong. The worst case is still O(n²): if the random pivot happens to be the smallest or largest element again and again, the splits are (n − 1, 0) as before. Randomisation makes this very unlikely, not impossible. A guaranteed O(n log n) worst case needs the true median as pivot (e.g. the median-of-medians method) or a different algorithm such as heap sort or merge sort.
C — Wrong. Stability depends on how elements are moved, not on how the pivot is chosen. Partitioning still swaps elements over long distances, so randomised quick sort is still unstable.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In quick sort, choosing the pivot as the median of the first, middle and last elements mainly helps to:
opts: avoid O(n²) behaviour on already sorted or reverse-sorted input
reduce the extra space to O(1) in every case
More than one of the above
exp: Median-of-three gives balanced partitions on sorted or reverse-sorted input, avoiding the O(n²) behaviour.
concept: Median-of-three takes the first, middle and last elements and uses their median (the middle value of the three) as the pivot. On sorted or reverse-sorted input this picks the true middle element, giving balanced splits instead of the (n − 1, 0) splits that a first- or last-element pivot causes. It does not make the worst case impossible (special 'killer' inputs exist), and it changes neither stability nor the need for a recursion stack.
why: A — Wrong. Stability depends on how elements are moved during partitioning. Median-of-three changes only the choice of pivot, so quick sort remains unstable.
B — Correct. On sorted or reverse-sorted data the median of the first, middle and last elements is the middle value, so the partitions are balanced and the O(n²) behaviour is avoided.
C — Wrong. The recursion stack still needs space (O(log n) with balanced splits, possibly more on bad inputs). No pivot rule makes quick sort use O(1) extra space in every case.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Quick sort with Lomuto partition (last element as pivot) sorts an already sorted array of 9 distinct elements. How many element-to-pivot comparisons are made in total?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Sorted input gives partitions of 9, 8, …, 2 elements: 8 + 7 + … + 1 = 36 comparisons.
concept: Each Lomuto partition of k elements makes exactly k − 1 comparisons. On sorted input the last element is always the maximum, so the pivot stays at the end and the next call works on k − 1 elements. The total is (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2.
work:
n = 9, sorted
Partition sizes: 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 (a size-1 sub-array needs no partition)
Comparisons: 8 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 36 = 9 × 8 / 2 (confirmed by simulation)
why: A — Wrong. 45 = 9 × 10 / 2 counts k comparisons per partition instead of k − 1 (as if the pivot were compared with itself).
B — Wrong. 81 = n² is only the rough order of growth, not the exact count.
C — Correct. 8 + 7 + … + 1 = 36 comparisons.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Quick sort with Lomuto partition (last element as pivot, test a[j] ≤ pivot) is applied to an array of n elements that are all equal. What is its running time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With all keys equal, Lomuto partition gives (n − 1, 0) splits every time, so quick sort takes Θ(n²), which is not listed.
concept: When all elements are equal, every element passes the test a[j] ≤ pivot. So in Lomuto partition every element goes to the left side and the pivot ends at the right end: the split is (n − 1, 0) every time, exactly like sorted input. That gives n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, Θ(n²). Hoare partition, or three-way partitioning (the 'Dutch national flag' method, which keeps equal keys in a middle group), handles many equal keys much better.
work:
All n elements equal: every test a[j] ≤ pivot is true
Pivot ends at index high → split (n − 1, 0)
Comparisons: (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 → Θ(n²)
why: A — Wrong. O(n) would be possible with three-way partitioning (all equal keys go into the middle group in one pass). Lomuto with ≤ does not separate equal keys, so it keeps recursing on n − 1 elements.
B — Wrong. O(log n) is impossible: even one partition must look at all n elements.
C — Wrong. O(n log n) needs balanced splits. Here every split is (n − 1, 0), the worst possible.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The running time is Θ(n²), which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: Many duplicate keys? Use three-way partitioning.

q: For n distinct keys, the best-case and worst-case running times of heap sort are, respectively:
opts: Θ(n log n) and Θ(n log n)
More than one of the above
exp: Heap sort is Θ(n log n) in both the best and the worst case for distinct keys.
concept: Heap sort first builds a max-heap (Θ(n)), then n − 1 times swaps the root (the maximum) to the end and sifts the new root down, which costs O(log n) each time. For distinct keys it has been proved that even the best input needs about n log₂ n comparisons, because the element moved to the root comes from the bottom of the heap and usually has to sift far down again. So best, average and worst cases are all Θ(n log n). Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Key properties: Θ(n log n) in every case (distinct keys); extra space O(1); stable: no; in-place: yes; adaptive: no.
why: A — Wrong. Heap sort's best case is not Θ(n) for distinct keys: even on sorted input most extractions sift down about log n levels. (Linear time is possible only in special cases such as all keys equal, which the stem excludes.)
B — Correct. Both are Θ(n log n): building the heap is Θ(n), and the n − 1 extractions cost about log n each, whatever the input order.

C — Wrong. The best case Θ(n log n) is right, but the worst case is not Θ(n²): each sift-down is limited by the heap height (about log₂ n), so heap sort never exceeds O(n log n). Θ(n²) is QUICK sort's worst case.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are true about heap sort?
opts: It sorts in place with O(1) extra space
It is not a stable sort
It needs a separate output array of size n
More than one of the above
exp: Heap sort is in place with O(1) extra space and is not stable; it needs no output array (A and B are true).
concept: Heap sort keeps the heap inside the input array itself: the heap occupies a[0..k−1] and the sorted elements collect at the end, a[k..n−1]. Only a few variables are needed (O(1) extra space with a loop-based sift-down), so it is in place. Swapping the root with the last heap element moves elements over long distances, so equal keys can change order: it is not stable.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The heap and the sorted part share the same array, and a loop-based sift-down needs only a few variables, so the extra space is O(1).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Heap sort is unstable. Example: [2a, 2b, 1] is already a max-heap; heap sort produces [1, 2b, 2a], so the two equal 2s end up reversed.
C — Wrong. No separate output array is needed: each extracted maximum is swapped into the free slot at the end of the same array, just after the shrinking heap.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are both true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The first phase of heap sort builds a max-heap from n unordered elements using bottom-up heapify (sift-down from the last internal node back to the root). What is the tightest upper bound on the time of this phase?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Bottom-up heap construction takes O(n) time, because most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a little.
concept: Bottom-up heap construction (Floyd's method) calls sift-down on each internal node, from the last one back to the root. A node at height h can sift down at most h levels, and most nodes are near the bottom: about n/2 leaves need no work, n/4 nodes move at most 1 level, n/8 at most 2, and so on. The total n/4·1 + n/8·2 + n/16·3 + … is less than n, so building the heap takes O(n). Building it by n separate insertions would cost O(n log n).
why: A — Correct. Adding up the possible sift-down distances of all nodes gives fewer than n steps, so the tightest bound is O(n).
B — Wrong. O(log n) is the cost of ONE sift-down or one insertion, not of building a whole heap of n elements (every element must at least be looked at).

C — Wrong. O(n log n) is a correct but loose upper bound (n/2 sift-downs × log n each); it is also the cost of building a heap by n successive insertions. The careful sum shows the bottom-up method is O(n), which is tighter.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Build-heap O(n); each delete-max O(log n); heap sort O(n log n).

q: A max-heap is built from [3, 9, 2, 1, 4, 5] (array representation, children of index i at 2i+1 and 2i+2) by bottom-up heapify: sift down the nodes at indices 2, 1, 0 in that order. What is the resulting array?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Bottom-up heapify gives [9, 4, 5, 1, 3, 2]: 2↔5 at index 2, then the root 3 sifts down past 9 and 4.
concept: In a heap stored in an array, the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. In a max-heap every parent is ≥ its children. Bottom-up heapify fixes the nodes from the last internal node (index n/2 − 1) back to the root. Sift-down swaps a node with its LARGER child and keeps going down until the node is ≥ both children or becomes a leaf.
work:
n = 6, internal nodes: indices 2, 1, 0
Index 2 (value 2): only child index 5 (value 5) → 5 > 2, swap → [3, 9, 5, 1, 4, 2]
Index 1 (value 9): children 1 (index 3) and 4 (index 4) → 9 is larger, no change
Index 0 (value 3): children 9 and 5 → swap with 9 → [9, 3, 5, 1, 4, 2]
  continue at index 1 (value 3): children 1 and 4 → swap with 4 → [9, 4, 5, 1, 3, 2]
Result: [9, 4, 5, 1, 3, 2]
why: A — Wrong. [9, 3, 5, 1, 4, 2] stops the root's sift-down too early. After 3 moves down to index 1, its child 4 (index 4) is larger, so it must sift down once more.

B — Wrong. [9, 5, 4, 1, 3, 2] is a valid max-heap, but not the one this procedure produces. Once index 2 is fixed, 5 stays at index 2; the root's 3 goes down the LEFT side (through index 1) and 4 moves up there.
C — Correct. Fixing index 2 (2↔5), leaving index 1 alone, then sifting the root 3 down twice (3↔9, then 3↔4) gives [9, 4, 5, 1, 3, 2].
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Sift-down always swaps with the LARGER child and continues until it can stop.

q: Heap sort (ascending) works on the max-heap [20, 15, 18, 7, 10, 12, 4]. One step swaps the root with the last element of the heap and then sifts the new root down within the remaining 6-element heap. What is the array after this first step?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After swapping 20 to the end and sifting 4 down past 18 and 12, the array is [18, 15, 12, 7, 10, 4, 20].
concept: Each step of heap sort's second phase swaps the root (the maximum) with the last element of the heap, shrinks the heap by one (the maximum is now in its final place at the end), and sifts the new root down inside the smaller heap to restore the max-heap property.
work:
Max-heap: [20, 15, 18, 7, 10, 12, 4]
Swap root 20 with last element 4 → [4, 15, 18, 7, 10, 12, 20]; heap is now indices 0–5
Sift 4 down: children 15 (index 1) and 18 (index 2) → swap with 18 → [18, 15, 4, 7, 10, 12, 20]
At index 2: child 12 (index 5); index 6 is outside the heap → 12 > 4, swap → [18, 15, 12, 7, 10, 4, 20]
Result: [18, 15, 12, 7, 10, 4, 20]
why: A — Wrong. [18, 15, 4, 7, 10, 12, 20] stops the sift-down after one level. At index 2, 4 still has a larger child, 12 at index 5, so it must go down again.
B — Correct. Swap 20 with 4, then sift 4 down: 4↔18, then 4↔12, giving [18, 15, 12, 7, 10, 4, 20].

C — Wrong. [15, 18, 12, 7, 10, 4, 20] puts 15 at the root although its child 18 is larger, which breaks the max-heap property. Sift-down must swap with the LARGER child (18), not simply the left child.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Heap sort is said to be NOT adaptive. What does this mean?
opts: Its running time does not improve significantly when the input is already nearly sorted
It cannot be used to sort linked lists
It needs to know the range of key values in advance
More than one of the above
exp: 'Not adaptive' means heap sort does not run noticeably faster on nearly sorted input.
concept: An adaptive sorting algorithm runs faster when the input already has some order (for example, when it is nearly sorted). Insertion sort is the classic example: Θ(n) on sorted input. Heap sort is not adaptive: building the heap scrambles any existing order, so it takes Θ(n log n) even when the input is already sorted. Adaptiveness has nothing to do with linked lists or key ranges.
why: A — Correct. This is exactly what 'not adaptive' means: heap sort's running time stays about n log n even on sorted or nearly sorted input.

B — Wrong. Heap sort's need for random access (jumping from a parent to its children by index) does make it awkward for linked lists, but that is a separate issue. 'Adaptive' is about benefiting from existing order.

C — Wrong. Needing the range of key values in advance is a property of counting sort and other non-comparison sorts, not the meaning of 'adaptive'. Heap sort is a comparison sort and needs no key range.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Adaptive = rewards existing order (insertion sort, bubble sort with a flag).

q: What is the time complexity of counting sort for n integers whose values lie in the range 0 to k?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Counting sort takes Θ(n + k): Θ(n) to count and place the elements and Θ(k) for the count array.
concept: Counting sort does not compare elements. It counts how many times each value 0..k occurs (Θ(n)), turns the counts into prefix sums that give each value's final position (Θ(k)), and then places each element in an output array (Θ(n)). The total is Θ(n + k), which is linear when k = O(n). Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower. Key properties: Θ(n + k) time; Θ(n + k) extra space; stable: yes (output filled from right to left); in-place: no; not comparison-based.
why: A — Wrong. Θ(nk) would mean checking all k possible values for each of the n elements. Counting sort instead uses the key directly as an index (count[a[i]]++), which is one step per element.
B — Wrong. Θ(n log n) is the best possible worst case for COMPARISON sorts (merge sort, heap sort). Counting sort makes no comparisons, so that limit does not apply to it.
C — Correct. Θ(n) to count, Θ(k) for the prefix sums and Θ(n) to place the elements give Θ(n + k).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about counting sort are true?
opts: It does not compare elements with each other
It can be implemented as a stable sort
It requires the range of key values to be known in advance
More than one of the above
exp: Counting sort compares no elements, can be stable, and needs the key range to size its count array: all three are true.
concept: Counting sort uses each key directly as an index into a count array, so it never compares two elements with each other. After the counts are turned into prefix sums, it places the elements by scanning the input from right to left, which keeps equal keys in their original order (stable). The count array has one slot per possible key value, so the range 0..k must be known before counting starts. Key properties: Θ(n + k) time and space; stable: yes; in-place: no; not comparison-based.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Counting sort does count[a[i]]++ for each element; it never asks 'is a[i] < a[j]?'. That is why it can beat the Ω(n log n) limit of comparison sorts.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Placing elements by scanning the input from right to left, each at position --count[key], keeps equal keys in their original order, so counting sort can be (and usually is) stable. This is what makes it usable inside radix sort.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The count array needs one slot for every possible key value, so the range must be known before counting starts (given in the problem, or found first with an extra pass for the minimum and maximum). Counting sort is practical only when this range is small.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Counting sort is applied to [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 0, 3, 1] with keys in the range 0–5. After counting and taking prefix (cumulative) sums, what is the count array C[0..5]?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The counts [1, 3, 0, 2, 1, 1] become [1, 4, 4, 6, 7, 8] after prefix sums.
concept: Counting sort first counts how many times each key occurs: C[x] = number of elements equal to x. Then it takes prefix (running) sums, so C[x] becomes the number of elements ≤ x. This tells where each key's block ends in the sorted output: the last copy of key x goes to position C[x] (counting from 1).
why: A — Wrong. [1, 3, 0, 2, 1, 1] is the plain count array BEFORE the prefix sums are taken.
B — Correct. Running sums of the counts give [1, 4, 4, 6, 7, 8]; the last value, 8, equals n, as it must.
C — Wrong. [1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] wrongly gives C[2] = 5. No element equals 2, so the running sum must stay at 4 for index 2.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: The last prefix sum always equals n: a quick self-check.

q: LSD (least significant digit first) radix sort in base 10 is used to sort integers in the range 0 to 99999. How many passes (one stable sort per digit) are needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Keys up to 99999 have 5 decimal digits, so base-10 LSD radix sort needs 5 passes.
concept: LSD radix sort sorts numbers one digit at a time, starting from the least significant (units) digit, using a stable sort for each digit. The number of passes equals the number of digits d in the largest key. Numbers from 0 to 99999 have at most 5 decimal digits (shorter numbers are treated as having leading zeros), so 5 passes are needed. Key properties: Θ(d(n + b)) time for d digits in base b; extra space Θ(n + b); stable: yes; in-place: no; not comparison-based.
work:
Largest key 99999 has 5 decimal digits
Passes: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands → 5
Time Θ(d(n + b)) = Θ(5(n + 10))
why: A — Correct. Five decimal digits → five stable passes (units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands).
B — Wrong. 10 is the base b (the number of possible digit values 0–9, i.e. the number of buckets in each pass), not the number of passes.
C — Wrong. 17 is the number of BINARY digits (bits) needed for 99999 (2¹⁶ = 65536 ≤ 99999 < 131072 = 2¹⁷). It would be the pass count for base-2 radix sort, not base 10.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In LSD radix sort, the algorithm used to sort the keys on each individual digit must be:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Each digit pass must be stable so that it keeps the order produced by the earlier, less significant digits.
concept: LSD radix sort sorts by the least significant digit first, then the next digit, and so on. Each later pass must keep the order created by the earlier passes whenever two keys have the same digit in the current position; otherwise the earlier work is lost. A sort that keeps equal keys in their existing order is called stable, so the per-digit sort must be stable. Counting sort is the usual choice: it is stable, but it is neither in place nor comparison-based.
why: A — Wrong. In-place is not required: counting sort, the usual per-digit sort, uses an extra output array and works perfectly.

B — Correct. Stability is essential. Example: after the units pass, [12, 11] becomes [11, 12]. In the tens pass both keys have digit 1; a stable sort keeps [11, 12], but an unstable one could output [12, 11], undoing the units pass.
C — Wrong. It need not be comparison-based. In fact the usual choice, counting sort, makes no comparisons at all, which is why radix sort can run in linear time.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: LSD radix sort (base 10) is applied to [512, 87, 230, 45, 391, 608, 74]. What is the array after the first pass (stable sort on the units digit)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Sorting by the units digit gives [230, 391, 512, 74, 45, 87, 608].
concept: In the first pass of LSD radix sort the numbers are distributed by their units digit (0 to 9) and collected in order of that digit. Because the pass is stable, numbers with the same units digit keep their original relative order. Only the units digit matters in this pass; the rest of each number is ignored.
why: A — Correct. Ordering by units digit 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 gives [230, 391, 512, 74, 45, 87, 608].
B — Wrong. [230, 391, 512, 45, 74, 87, 608] puts 45 (units digit 5) before 74 (units digit 4). In the first pass only the units digit counts, so 74 must come first.
C — Wrong. [45, 74, 87, 230, 391, 512, 608] is the fully sorted array, reached only after all three passes.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: LSD radix sort (base 10, stable sort on each digit) is applied to [263, 418, 127, 905, 341, 76, 580]. What is the array after the second pass (tens digit)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: After the tens-digit pass the array is [905, 418, 127, 341, 263, 76, 580], which is not listed.
concept: In pass 2 of LSD radix sort the keys are ordered by their tens digit, starting from the order produced by pass 1. Keys with equal tens digits keep their pass-1 order (stability). A shorter number such as 76 is treated as 076: tens digit 7, hundreds digit 0.
why: A — Wrong. [580, 341, 263, 905, 76, 127, 418] is the array after the FIRST pass (units digit), not the second.
B — Wrong. This is almost right but swaps the last two: 76 has tens digit 7 and 580 has tens digit 8, so 76 must come before 580.
C — Wrong. [76, 127, 263, 341, 418, 580, 905] is the fully sorted array, reached only after the third pass (hundreds digit).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. After the tens pass the array is [905, 418, 127, 341, 263, 76, 580], which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Bucket sort runs in O(n) average time when:
opts: the input is uniformly distributed over a known range
More than one of the above
exp: Bucket sort runs in O(n) average time when the input is uniformly distributed over a known range.
concept: Bucket sort divides the known range of values into n equal buckets, drops each element into its bucket, sorts each bucket (usually with insertion sort) and then joins the buckets in order. If the input is uniformly distributed (spread evenly) over the range, each bucket gets about one element on average, so the expected total time is Θ(n). If the data is skewed, many elements can land in one bucket and the time can degrade to Θ(n²) with insertion sort. Key properties: average Θ(n) for uniform input, worst Θ(n²); extra space Θ(n + number of buckets); stable if the per-bucket sort is stable.
why: A — Wrong. Distinct keys can still be badly clustered: 0.500, 0.501, 0.502, … all fall into the same bucket. What matters is how evenly the values are spread, not whether they are distinct.
B — Wrong. Sorted input does not help: if the sorted values are clustered they still crowd into a few buckets. Bucket sort's speed depends on the distribution of values, not on their initial order.
C — Correct. With a uniform distribution each of the n buckets receives about one element on average, so sorting the buckets and joining them takes Θ(n) expected time.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The Ω(n log n) lower bound on the worst-case number of comparisons holds for which of the following algorithms?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The Ω(n log n) lower bound applies to every comparison sort, including merge, heap and quick sort.
concept: Any comparison-based sort can be drawn as a decision tree: each internal node is a comparison and each leaf is one possible sorted order. With n distinct keys there are n! possible orders, so the tree needs at least n! leaves, and its height (the worst-case number of comparisons) is at least log₂(n!) = Ω(n log n). This lower bound applies to EVERY comparison sort, fast or slow. It does not apply to non-comparison sorts such as counting, radix and bucket sort.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Merge sort is a comparison sort, so it needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. It meets the bound exactly (Θ(n log n)), which makes it asymptotically optimal.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Heap sort is a comparison sort whose worst case is Θ(n log n), so the lower bound holds and is met.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Quick sort is a comparison sort too. Its worst case is Θ(n²), even more than n log n, so the Ω(n log n) lower bound certainly holds for it. (A lower bound says 'at least'; being slower never violates it.)
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Ω is a floor: a slower algorithm never breaks a lower bound.

q: By the decision-tree argument, what is the minimum number of comparisons that any comparison-based algorithm needs in the worst case to sort 5 distinct elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The decision tree needs 5! = 120 leaves, so at least ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7 comparisons are needed.
concept: A comparison sort on n distinct elements must be able to produce any of the n! orderings, so its decision tree needs at least n! leaves. A binary tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves, so 2^h ≥ n!, i.e. h ≥ ⌈log₂(n!)⌉. For n = 5: 5! = 120 and 2⁶ = 64 < 120 ≤ 128 = 2⁷, so at least 7 comparisons are needed in the worst case. (Seven is actually achievable, by the Ford–Johnson merge-insertion method.)
work:
5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120 possible orderings
2⁶ = 64 < 120 ≤ 128 = 2⁷
Minimum worst-case comparisons = ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7
why: A — Wrong. 5 is just n. Five comparisons can distinguish at most 2⁵ = 32 cases, far fewer than the 120 possible orderings.
B — Correct. ⌈log₂ 5!⌉ = ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7: 2⁶ = 64 leaves are too few and 2⁷ = 128 are enough.

C — Wrong. 10 = 5 × 4 / 2 is the number of comparisons selection sort makes (and the worst case of bubble and insertion sort). It is what those algorithms need, not the minimum that any algorithm needs.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Shell sort can best be described as:
opts: insertion sort applied to elements a gap apart, with the gap reduced until it becomes 1
selection sort applied to sub-arrays of decreasing size
merge sort that merges more than two runs at a time
More than one of the above
exp: Shell sort is insertion sort on elements a gap apart, with the gap reduced until it becomes 1.
concept: Shell sort (Donald Shell, 1959) improves insertion sort. It first insertion-sorts elements that are a gap h apart, which moves elements long distances in few steps, and then repeats with smaller and smaller gaps. The last pass uses gap 1, which is ordinary insertion sort, but by then the array is nearly sorted, so that pass is fast. Key properties: time depends on the gap sequence (Θ(n²) worst case with gaps n/2, n/4, …, 1; about O(n^1.5) with Knuth's gaps 1, 4, 13, 40, …); extra space O(1); stable: no; in-place: yes.
why: A — Correct. Shell sort is gapped insertion sort: insertion sort on elements h apart, with h shrinking until a final pass with h = 1.
B — Wrong. Shell sort is built on insertion sort, not selection sort, and its groups are interleaved elements a gap apart, not sub-arrays of decreasing size.
C — Wrong. Merging more than two runs at a time is k-way merge sort, used in external sorting. Shell sort does no merging.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Shell sort is applied to [35, 33, 42, 10, 14, 19, 27, 44, 26, 31] (indices 0–9). What is the array after the first pass with gap 5 (insertion sort on each group of elements 5 positions apart)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Only the groups (35, 19) and (33, 27) are out of order; fixing them gives [19, 27, 42, 10, 14, 35, 33, 44, 26, 31].
concept: With gap 5, the array splits into 5 interleaved groups: indices (0, 5), (1, 6), (2, 7), (3, 8) and (4, 9). Each group is insertion-sorted on its own; elements of different groups are never compared in this pass. With only two elements per group, each group is simply put in order.
why: A — Wrong. [19, 33, 42, 10, 14, 35, 27, 44, 26, 31] fixes only the first group (35, 19). The group (33, 27) at indices 1 and 6 is also out of order and must be swapped.
B — Wrong. [19, 27, 42, 26, 14, 35, 33, 44, 10, 31] also swaps 10 and 26 (indices 3 and 8), but 10 < 26 is already in order, so that group must not change.
C — Correct. Swapping only the out-of-order groups (35, 19) and (33, 27) gives [19, 27, 42, 10, 14, 35, 33, 44, 26, 31].
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about Shell sort?
opts: Its final pass uses a gap of 1
Its running time depends on the gap sequence used
More than one of the above
exp: All three statements about Shell sort are true, so none of A–C answers the 'NOT true' question.
concept: This is a 'NOT true' question: an option satisfies the stem only if it is FALSE about Shell sort. Shell sort rearranges elements inside the array with O(1) extra space (in place), must finish with a gap-1 pass (plain insertion sort) to guarantee a fully sorted result, and its running time depends strongly on the gap sequence (Θ(n²) worst case for Shell's original gaps n/2, n/4, …; about O(n^1.5) for Knuth's gaps; O(n log² n) for Pratt's gaps). A genuinely false statement would be 'Shell sort is stable'; it is not stable.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true, so it does not satisfy the 'NOT true' stem. Shell sort only moves elements inside the array and needs a few variables: O(1) extra space.
B — Wrong. This statement is true, so it does not satisfy the stem. A final gap-1 pass is essential: it is an ordinary insertion sort that guarantees the whole array ends up sorted.

C — Wrong. This statement is true, so it does not satisfy the stem. Shell's original gaps n/2, n/4, … give Θ(n²) in the worst case, while better sequences such as Knuth's (1, 4, 13, 40, …) give about O(n^1.5).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is a false statement, so no option satisfies the 'NOT true' stem, let alone more than one.
E — Correct. All three statements are true about Shell sort, so none of them is 'NOT true' and the answer is 'None of the above'. (A NOT-true statement would be 'Shell sort is stable'.)
tip: In NOT questions, first mark each option true or false, then look for the false ones.

q: Which of the following sorting algorithms is NOT stable in its standard form?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Merge, insertion and bubble sort are all stable, so none of A–C is an unstable sort.
concept: A sorting algorithm is stable if equal keys keep their original relative order. This matters when records are sorted by one field after another (for example, sort by name, then stably by marks, so students with equal marks stay in name order). The standard stable sorts are bubble, insertion, merge, counting and radix sort; the usual unstable ones are selection, quick, heap and Shell sort. Here the stem asks for an UNSTABLE algorithm.
why: A — Wrong. Merge sort is stable: when the front elements of the two halves are equal, the standard merge takes the one from the LEFT half first (using ≤), so equal keys keep their order. It does not satisfy the stem.
B — Wrong. Insertion sort is stable: it shifts only strictly greater elements, so a new element stops just after any equal element. It does not satisfy the stem.
C — Wrong. Bubble sort is stable: it swaps neighbours only when a[j] > a[j+1], so equal neighbours are never exchanged. It does not satisfy the stem.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is unstable, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. Merge, insertion and bubble sort are all stable, so none of them is 'NOT stable' and the answer is 'None of the above'. (Selection, quick, heap or Shell sort would have been NOT stable.)
tip: Unstable: selection, quick, heap, Shell. Stable: bubble, insertion, merge, counting, radix.

q: Which of the following is NOT an in-place sorting algorithm when sorting an array?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Standard array merge sort needs O(n) extra space, so it is the one that is not in place.
concept: An in-place sort uses only O(1) extra memory (many books also accept the O(log n) recursion stack, so quick sort counts as in place). Heap sort, insertion sort, bubble sort and selection sort are in place. Standard merge sort on an array needs an auxiliary array of n elements for merging, so it is NOT in place.
why: A — Wrong. Heap sort IS in place: the heap lives inside the input array and only O(1) extra space is used, so it does not satisfy the stem.
B — Wrong. Insertion sort IS in place: it shifts elements within the array using one extra variable, so it does not satisfy the stem.
C — Correct. Merge sort needs an O(n) temporary array to merge two halves, so it is not in place and satisfies the stem.
D — Wrong. Only C (merge sort) is not in place; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to satisfy the stem.
E — Wrong. Merge sort (C) is not an in-place sort, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following sorting algorithms are adaptive, i.e. run in O(n) time on an already sorted array of n elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Insertion sort and flagged bubble sort run in O(n) on sorted input; selection sort does not.
concept: An adaptive sort takes advantage of existing order. On an already sorted array, insertion sort makes n − 1 comparisons and no shifts (Θ(n)), and bubble sort with a 'swapped' flag stops after one pass with no swaps (Θ(n)). Selection sort is not adaptive: it always scans the whole unsorted part to find the minimum, so it takes Θ(n²) even on sorted input.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Each element is compared once with its left neighbour and nothing moves, so insertion sort takes Θ(n) on sorted input.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The first pass makes n − 1 comparisons and no swap, so the flag ends the sort: Θ(n). (Without the flag bubble sort is not adaptive.)
C — Wrong. Selection sort always makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, because finding a minimum requires looking at every remaining element. It is Θ(n²) even on sorted input.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are both true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An array must be sorted with guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case time using only O(1) extra memory; stability is not needed. Which algorithm fits best?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Heap sort is the only option with both a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case and O(1) extra space.
concept: Match each requirement to the algorithms. Guaranteed O(n log n) worst case: merge sort and heap sort. O(1) extra memory: heap sort, insertion, selection and bubble sort (quick sort needs a recursion stack). Only heap sort meets both, and its weakness, instability, does not matter here. (Introsort, used in C++ std::sort, falls back from quick sort to heap sort for exactly this reason.)
why: A — Wrong. Merge sort has a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case but needs O(n) extra space for merging, so it fails the memory requirement.
B — Wrong. Quick sort works inside the array, but its worst case is O(n²), so it fails the time guarantee; its recursion stack also needs at least O(log n) space, not O(1).
C — Correct. Heap sort runs in O(n log n) in the worst case and sorts in place with O(1) extra space; it is unstable, but stability is not needed here.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: One million exam scores, each an integer from 0 to 100, must be sorted. Which algorithm sorts them in linear time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Scores 0–100 form a small known range, so counting sort sorts them in Θ(n + k) = Θ(n) time.
concept: When the keys are integers in a small known range, a non-comparison sort can beat n log n. Counting sort counts how many times each of the k + 1 possible values occurs and writes them out in order, in Θ(n + k) time. Here n = 1,000,000 and the scores 0–100 give only 101 possible values, so the time is Θ(n): linear. Comparison sorts such as quick sort and heap sort compare pairs of elements and take about n log n steps.
why: A — Wrong. Quick sort compares elements and takes Θ(n log n) time on average, not linear time. With so many repeated values, simple versions (such as Lomuto partition) can even slow down towards Θ(n²).
B — Wrong. Heap sort compares elements and takes Θ(n log n) time; it makes no use of the fact that the scores lie in a small range.
C — Correct. With 101 possible scores, counting sort takes Θ(n + k) = Θ(n) time: one pass to count, a short pass over 101 counters, and one pass to write the output.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An inversion is a pair (i, j) with i < j and a[i] > a[j]. How many inversions does the array [3, 7, 1, 8, 5, 2] contain?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: [3, 7, 1, 8, 5, 2] has 8 inversions, which is not listed.
concept: An inversion is a pair of positions (i, j) with i < j but a[i] > a[j], i.e. a pair in the wrong order. To count them, take each element in turn and count the smaller elements to its right. The inversion count measures how unsorted an array is: 0 for a sorted array and n(n − 1)/2 for a reverse-sorted one.
why: A — Wrong. 6 is too small: it misses two of the eight pairs, typically far-apart ones such as (3, 2) and (7, 2).
B — Wrong. 7 misses one pair, typically a far-apart one such as (3, 2).
C — Wrong. 9 counts one pair too many, for example (1, 2); but 1 < 2, so that pair is in the right order and is not an inversion.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. The array has 2 + 3 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 8 inversions, which is not among A–C, so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: For each element, count the smaller elements to its right, then add up.

q: What is the maximum possible number of inversions in an array of 12 distinct elements?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The maximum number of inversions is n(n − 1)/2 = 12 × 11 / 2 = 66.
concept: Each pair of positions can form at most one inversion. The maximum is reached when EVERY pair is out of order, that is when the array is sorted in reverse. The number of pairs that can be chosen from n elements is C(n, 2) = n(n − 1)/2.
work:
n = 12, reverse sorted → every pair is an inversion
C(12, 2) = 12 × 11 / 2 = 66
why: A — Wrong. 132 = 12 × 11 counts each pair twice (once as (i, j) and once as (j, i)); an inversion needs i < j, so divide by 2.
B — Correct. All C(12, 2) = 66 pairs are inverted in a reverse-sorted array, which is the maximum.
C — Wrong. 144 = 12² counts every ordered pair, including each element paired with itself; it is not the number of pairs with i < j.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following sorting algorithms have a worst-case time complexity of O(n²)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Quick sort, insertion sort and bubble sort all have O(n²) worst cases.
concept: Θ(n²) worst cases occur in the simple sorts and in quick sort. Quick sort reaches it when the pivots keep producing very unbalanced splits; insertion and bubble sort reach it on reverse-sorted input (n(n − 1)/2 shifts or swaps). Merge sort and heap sort are the common comparison sorts with an O(n log n) worst case.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Quick sort's worst case is O(n²), for example on sorted input with a first- or last-element pivot: splits of (n − 1, 0) at every level.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Insertion sort's worst case is O(n²): on reverse-sorted input each new element is shifted past all earlier ones, n(n − 1)/2 shifts in total.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Bubble sort's worst case is O(n²): on reverse-sorted input every comparison causes a swap, n(n − 1)/2 swaps in total.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Insertion sort is run on an array of n elements that contains at most 5 inversions. What is its running time?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Insertion sort runs in Θ(n + I); with at most 5 inversions this is Θ(n).
concept: Insertion sort's running time is Θ(n + I), where I is the number of inversions: there are n − 1 passes with at least one comparison each, and every shift removes exactly one inversion. If I is at most a constant (here 5), the total work is at most about (n − 1) + 2 × 5 steps, which is Θ(n). This is why insertion sort is excellent for nearly sorted data. Θ (theta) is a tight bound: Θ(f(n)) means the cost grows exactly like f(n), neither faster nor slower.
work:
Shifts = I ≤ 5
Comparisons ≤ (n − 1) + I ≤ n + 4
Total work = Θ(n + I) = Θ(n)
why: A — Wrong. Θ(n²) is insertion sort's worst case, which needs about n²/2 inversions (reverse-sorted input). With at most 5 inversions there are at most 5 shifts in total.
B — Wrong. Θ(n log n) is the time of merge sort or heap sort. Insertion sort does even better here, because almost nothing needs to move.
C — Correct. n − 1 passes with at most 5 shifts in total give Θ(n + 5) = Θ(n).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Insertion sort time = n + number of inversions.

q: The naive (brute-force) string-matching algorithm slides the pattern P over the text T one position at a time and, at each shift, compares characters from left to right, stopping at the first mismatch. How many character comparisons does it make for T = AAAAAAA (7 characters) and P = AAB?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 5 shifts × 3 comparisons each = 15 comparisons.
concept: The naive algorithm tries every shift s = 0, 1, …, n − m of the pattern (n = text length, m = pattern length) and compares P with T[s..s + m − 1] character by character. Its worst case is (n − m + 1)·m comparisons, i.e. Θ((n − m + 1)m) = O(nm). The worst case happens on inputs like this one, where almost the whole pattern matches at every shift and the mismatch is found only at the last character.
work:
Number of shifts = n − m + 1 = 7 − 3 + 1 = 5 (s = 0 … 4)
At each shift: A = A (1), A = A (2), A ≠ B (3) → 3 comparisons, mismatch at the last character
Total = 5 × 3 = 15 comparisons; the pattern is never found
why: A — Correct. There are 5 shifts and each one needs 3 comparisons (the mismatch is found only at B), so 5 × 3 = 15.
B — Wrong. 21 = 7 × 3 assumes 7 shifts. The pattern cannot start after position n − m = 4, so there are only n − m + 1 = 5 shifts.
C — Wrong. 5 is the number of shifts, not the number of comparisons. At every shift the first two A's match, so 3 comparisons are made, not 1.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: For a text of length n and a pattern of length m (m ≤ n), what is the worst-case running time of the naive string-matching algorithm?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Naive matching: n − m + 1 shifts × up to m comparisons = Θ((n − m + 1)m), i.e. O(nm).
concept: The naive matcher checks each of the n − m + 1 possible shifts, and at each shift it may compare up to m characters, so its worst case is Θ((n − m + 1)·m), which is O(nm) (and Θ(n²) when m is about n/2). It needs no preprocessing. Smarter algorithms do better: KMP runs in Θ(n + m) in the worst case, and Rabin–Karp and Boyer–Moore are usually fast in practice.
why: A — Wrong. Θ(n + m) is the worst case of the Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) algorithm, which uses the prefix function to avoid re-comparing text characters. The naive method has no such preprocessing.
B — Wrong. Θ(n log m) is not the cost of any standard string-matching method; nothing in the naive algorithm is halved repeatedly.
C — Correct. There are n − m + 1 shifts and each may need up to m comparisons (for example T = AAA…A and P = AA…AB), giving Θ((n − m + 1)·m).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In the KMP algorithm, the prefix (failure) function π[q] is the length of the longest PROPER prefix of P[0..q] that is also a suffix of P[0..q] (indices start at 0). What is π for the pattern P = ABABCABAB?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: π(ABABCABAB) = 0 0 1 2 0 1 2 3 4.
concept: The Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) algorithm first computes the prefix function (also called the failure function or LPS array) of the pattern. π[q] is the length of the longest PROPER prefix of P[0..q] that is also a suffix of P[0..q] ('proper' means it cannot be the whole string). After a mismatch, π tells how much of the pattern is still matched, so the pattern can be shifted forward without moving back in the text. π[q] can grow by at most 1 from π[q − 1]; when the next character breaks the match, the algorithm falls back to a shorter border, k = π[k − 1], and tries again. Computing π takes Θ(m) time. A character that occurs nowhere else at the start of the pattern (like C here) resets π to 0.
work:
q: P[0..q] → longest proper prefix that is also a suffix → π[q]
0: A → none → 0
1: AB → none → 0
2: ABA → A → 1
3: ABAB → AB → 2
4: ABABC → none (no prefix ends with C) → 0
5: ABABCA → A → 1
6: ABABCAB → AB → 2
7: ABABCABA → ABA → 3
8: ABABCABAB → ABAB → 4
π = 0 0 1 2 0 1 2 3 4
why: A — Wrong. π[4] cannot be 3. P[0..4] = ABABC ends with C, and no proper prefix of ABABC ends with C, so π[4] = 0. This option kept counting as if the match had continued.
B — Correct. Each value is the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix: A → 0, AB → 0, ABA → 1, ABAB → 2, ABABC → 0, then ABABCA, …, ABABCABAB → 1, 2, 3, 4.
C — Wrong. These values are shifted one place to the right (π[q − 1] written at position q), as in some 'next array' conventions. With the definition given, π[2] for ABA is 1, not 0.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: π can rise by at most 1 per step; a mismatch makes it fall back using π itself.

q: Using the same definition (π[q] = length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..q] that is also a suffix of P[0..q]), what is the KMP prefix function of P = AABAAAB?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: π(AABAAAB) = 0 1 0 1 2 2 3, which is not listed.
concept: The Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) algorithm first computes the prefix function (also called the failure function or LPS array) of the pattern. π[q] is the length of the longest PROPER prefix of P[0..q] that is also a suffix of P[0..q] ('proper' means it cannot be the whole string). After a mismatch, π tells how much of the pattern is still matched, so the pattern can be shifted forward without moving back in the text. π[q] can grow by at most 1 from π[q − 1]; when the next character breaks the match, the algorithm falls back to a shorter border, k = π[k − 1], and tries again. Computing π takes Θ(m) time. Example from this pattern: after AABAA (π = 2, the border 'AA'), the next pattern character is P[2] = B, but the new character is A, so k falls back to π[1] = 1; now P[1] = A matches, so π[5] = 2.
work:
0: A → 0
1: AA → A → 1
2: AAB → none → 0
3: AABA → A → 1
4: AABAA → AA → 2
5: AABAAA → AA (AAB is not a suffix; AAA is not a prefix) → 2
6: AABAAAB → AAB → 3
π = 0 1 0 1 2 2 3 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. π[5] is not 3: the prefix of length 3 is AAB, but AABAAA does not end with AAB. The longest border of AABAAA is AA, so π[5] = 2.

B — Wrong. π[5] is not 1: AABAAA both begins and ends with AA, so the border has length 2 (falling back to k = π[1] = 1 and then matching P[1] = A gives 2). Its π[6] = 2 is also wrong; AABAAAB ends with AAB, so π[6] = 3.
C — Wrong. π[1] is not 0: AA has the proper prefix A, which is also a suffix, so π[1] = 1.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true. The correct prefix function is 0 1 0 1 2 2 3, which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: What is the worst-case time complexity of the Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) algorithm, including the computation of the prefix function, for a text of length n and a pattern of length m?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: KMP: Θ(m) preprocessing + Θ(n) matching = Θ(n + m).
concept: KMP has two phases. Preprocessing computes the prefix function of the pattern in Θ(m) time. Matching scans the text once: the text pointer never moves backwards, and every fall-back through π is paid for by earlier forward steps, so matching takes Θ(n). The total is Θ(n + m) even in the worst case — much better than the naive Θ((n − m + 1)m).
why: A — Correct. Θ(m) for the prefix function plus Θ(n) for the single scan of the text gives Θ(n + m), even in the worst case.
B — Wrong. Θ(n·m) is the worst case of the naive algorithm (and of Rabin–Karp when there are many spurious hits). KMP avoids it because it never re-reads text characters.
C — Wrong. Θ(n log m) is not the cost of KMP; nothing in KMP is repeatedly halved.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Rabin–Karp is used to search for P = 26 in the digit string T = 31415926535. Each 2-digit window is hashed as (its numeric value) mod 11. How many spurious hits occur?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Hash 4 appears for 15, 59, 92 and 26; three of these are not the pattern, so there are 3 spurious hits.
concept: Rabin–Karp compares a hash value of the pattern with a hash of each window of the text (updated in O(1) time by a rolling hash). If the hashes differ, the window cannot match. If they are equal, the characters must still be checked, because different strings can have the same hash. A spurious hit is a window whose hash equals the pattern's hash but whose characters do not match. Many spurious hits push the worst case up to Θ((n − m + 1)m); the expected time with a good modulus is O(n + m).
work:
Hash of P: 26 mod 11 = 4
Windows (value → value mod 11): 31→9, 14→3, 41→8, 15→4, 59→4, 92→4, 26→4, 65→10, 53→9, 35→2
Hash equal to 4 for 15, 59, 92, 26 → 4 hash hits
Character check: 15, 59, 92 are not '26' → 3 spurious hits; 26 (shift 6) is the real match
why: A — Wrong. 4 is the number of hash HITS, including the genuine match 26 at shift 6. A spurious hit is a hit whose characters do NOT match, so the real occurrence must not be counted.
B — Wrong. 1 is the number of valid matches (the window 26). The question asks for the false alarms, of which there are 3.
C — Correct. Windows 15, 59 and 92 have hash 4, like the pattern, but they are not '26', so they are spurious hits; 26 itself is a valid hit.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is the main idea of the Boyer–Moore string-matching algorithm?
opts: Compare the hash value of each text window with the hash value of the pattern
Compare the pattern with the text from RIGHT to LEFT and, on a mismatch, use the bad-character (and good-suffix) rule to shift the pattern forward, often by many positions
Precompute a prefix function so that the pattern is compared from left to right and the text pointer never moves backwards
More than one of the above
exp: Boyer–Moore scans the pattern right to left and uses the bad-character and good-suffix rules to make long shifts.
concept: Boyer–Moore lines the pattern up with the text but compares characters starting from the LAST character of the pattern and moving left. When a mismatch occurs at text character c, the bad-character rule shifts the pattern so that the rightmost occurrence of c in the pattern lines up with it — or right past c if c does not occur in the pattern at all. The good-suffix rule uses the part that has already matched. Because a shift can be as long as the whole pattern, Boyer–Moore often skips large parts of the text and is very fast in practice.
why: A — Wrong. Comparing hash values of windows is the idea of the Rabin–Karp algorithm.

B — Correct. Right-to-left comparison with bad-character and good-suffix shifts is exactly the Boyer–Moore idea; a mismatch on a character that does not occur in the pattern lets the pattern jump right past it.
C — Wrong. A prefix (failure) function with left-to-right comparison and no backing up in the text describes the Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) algorithm.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about string-matching algorithms are TRUE? (n = text length, m = pattern length)
opts: Rabin–Karp can take Θ((n − m + 1)·m) time in the worst case, when there are many spurious hits
In the matching phase of KMP, the pointer into the text never moves backwards
Boyer–Moore compares the characters of the pattern from left to right
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are true; Boyer–Moore compares right to left, so C is false.
concept: Summary of the four standard methods. Naive: tries every shift; worst case Θ((n − m + 1)m); no preprocessing. Rabin–Karp: rolling hash; expected O(n + m), but worst case Θ((n − m + 1)m) when many windows collide with the pattern's hash (spurious hits). KMP: prefix function in Θ(m), then a single left-to-right scan of the text that never backs up; Θ(n + m) in the worst case. Boyer–Moore: compares the pattern right to left and uses bad-character/good-suffix shifts; very fast in practice.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Every hash hit must be checked character by character. If almost every window has the same hash as the pattern, each costs Θ(m), giving Θ((n − m + 1)m) — the same as the naive method.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. After a mismatch KMP shifts the pattern using the prefix function and continues from the same text character; it never re-reads earlier text characters, which is why matching takes Θ(n).
C — Wrong. Boyer–Moore compares from RIGHT to LEFT, starting with the last character of the pattern; that is what lets it skip ahead with the bad-character rule.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which statement about internal and external sorting is correct?
opts: External sorting is used when the data is too large to fit in main memory; it sorts pieces (runs) in memory and then merges the sorted runs stored on disk
Internal sorting keeps the data on disk and brings only one record into memory at a time
Bubble sort and insertion sort are standard external sorting algorithms
More than one of the above
exp: External sorting handles data larger than main memory, typically by sorting runs and merging them; internal sorting works entirely in RAM.
concept: Internal sorting: all the data fits in main memory (RAM) while it is being sorted — bubble, insertion, selection, quick, heap and merge sort on arrays are internal sorts. External sorting: the data is too large for main memory and lives on disk or tape, so the algorithm must keep slow disk accesses to a minimum. The standard method is external merge sort: read as much as fits in memory, sort it, write it out as a sorted run, and then merge the runs (often k at a time).
why: A — Correct. When data does not fit in RAM it is sorted chunk by chunk into runs, and the runs are merged — this is external (merge) sorting.
B — Wrong. This describes the opposite. In internal sorting the whole data set is in main memory while it is being sorted.

C — Wrong. Bubble sort and insertion sort need repeated access to all elements and many passes, which would be extremely slow on disk; they are internal sorts. External sorting is normally based on merging.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: An online sorting algorithm can process its input piece by piece, keeping the items received so far in sorted order, without needing the whole input at the start. Which of the following is an online sorting algorithm?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Insertion sort is online: every new item is inserted into the sorted part as it arrives.
concept: An online algorithm handles its input one item at a time, in the order it arrives, without knowing the future items. Insertion sort is online: when a new item arrives, it is simply inserted into the correct place among the items already sorted. Selection sort is not online, because its very first step — finding the minimum of ALL the items — needs the whole input. Standard heap sort first builds a heap of all n items and then repeatedly removes the maximum, so it also needs the complete input.
why: A — Wrong. Selection sort's first pass selects the minimum of all n elements, so it cannot place anything until it has seen the whole input.
B — Wrong. Standard heap sort builds a heap from the complete array before removing elements one by one, so it is not online.
C — Correct. Each newly arriving item is inserted into the already sorted part, so the items seen so far are always in order — insertion sort is online.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which sorting algorithm is generally the best choice for sorting a singly linked list of n nodes, giving Θ(n log n) time even in the worst case?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Merge sort is the standard choice for linked lists: Θ(n log n) worst case with only sequential access.
concept: A linked list has no random access: reaching the i-th node takes Θ(i) time. Merge sort suits linked lists very well: the list is split into halves (for example with slow and fast pointers), each half is sorted recursively, and two sorted lists are merged just by relinking nodes, without any extra array. It runs in Θ(n log n) in the worst case and is stable. Heap sort depends on array indexing (children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2), and quick sort's worst case is Θ(n²).
why: A — Wrong. Quick sort can be written for linked lists, but its worst case is still Θ(n²) (for example, taking the first node as pivot on an already sorted list), so it does not guarantee Θ(n log n).
B — Correct. Merge sort needs only sequential access: split, sort the halves and merge by relinking nodes. It is Θ(n log n) in the worst case and needs no extra array for lists.
C — Wrong. Heap sort relies on jumping to array positions (parent at (i − 1)/2, children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2). On a linked list each such jump takes linear time, so the Θ(n log n) bound is lost.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A simple graph is an undirected graph that has:
opts: no self-loops and no parallel (multiple) edges
the same degree at every vertex
More than one of the above
exp: A simple graph has no self-loops and no parallel edges; it may still have cycles and unequal degrees.
concept: A graph is a set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines). A self-loop is an edge that starts and ends at the same vertex, and parallel (multiple) edges are two or more edges joining the same pair of vertices. A simple graph has neither: at most one edge between any two different vertices and no loops. A simple graph may still contain cycles, and its vertices may have different degrees.
why: A — Correct. This is exactly the definition of a simple graph: no self-loops and no parallel edges. Think of a road map where no road comes back to its own town and no two towns have two separate direct roads.
B — Wrong. A graph with no cycles is called acyclic; an acyclic undirected graph is a forest (and a connected one is a tree). A simple graph is allowed to have cycles, for example the triangle 1-2-3.
C — Wrong. A graph in which every vertex has the same degree (number of edges at it) is called a regular graph. A simple graph can have different degrees; the path 1-2-3 has degrees 1, 2, 1.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Simple = no loops + no multi-edges. Nothing else is required.

q: An undirected graph on vertices {1, 2, 3} has the edge list (1,2), (2,3), (2,3), (3,3). Which of the following is true about this graph?
opts: It contains a pair of parallel (multiple) edges
More than one of the above
exp: The repeated edge (2,3) gives parallel edges and (3,3) is a self-loop, so A and B are true and the graph is not simple.
concept: Two or more edges with the same pair of end vertices are called parallel (multiple) edges, and an edge whose two ends are the same vertex is a self-loop. A graph with parallel edges but no loops is called a multigraph; a graph that may also have loops is often called a pseudograph. A graph is simple only when it has neither.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The edge (2,3) is listed twice, so vertices 2 and 3 are joined by two separate edges. These are parallel (multiple) edges.
B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. The edge (3,3) begins and ends at vertex 3, so it is a self-loop.
C — Wrong. A simple graph must have no loops and no parallel edges. This graph has both, so it is not simple (it is a pseudograph).
D — Correct. A and B are both true and C is false, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A graph in which every vertex has the same degree k is called a:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Equal degree k at every vertex defines a k-regular graph.
concept: The degree of a vertex in an undirected graph is the number of edges touching it. If every vertex has the same degree k, the graph is called k-regular (regular of degree k). For example, every cycle is 2-regular and the cube graph is 3-regular. A complete graph K_n is one special regular graph (it is (n − 1)-regular), but most regular graphs are not complete.
why: A — Wrong. A complete graph has an edge between every pair of distinct vertices. K_n is (n − 1)-regular, but the reverse is not true: the 6-cycle is 2-regular and is not complete. So 'every vertex has degree k' does not make a graph complete.
B — Correct. This is the definition: 'every vertex has degree k' is exactly what k-regular means.

C — Wrong. A bipartite graph is one whose vertices can be split into two groups so that every edge goes between the groups. That has nothing to do with equal degrees; the triangle is 2-regular but not bipartite.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Regular = same degree everywhere. Complete = every pair joined.

q: A graph G has 5 vertices and no edges (an edgeless or null graph). Which of the following is true?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With no edges there can be no cycle, so G is a forest (5 one-vertex trees); it is disconnected and 0-regular.
concept: An edgeless graph (also called a null or empty graph) has vertices but no edges. A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices; with no edges and more than one vertex this is impossible. A forest is any graph with no cycles; each connected piece of a forest is a tree, and a single vertex on its own counts as a (trivial) tree.
why: A — Wrong. Connected means there is a path between every two vertices. With 5 vertices and no edges, no two vertices are joined, so G has 5 separate components and is disconnected.
B — Wrong. 1-regular means every vertex has degree 1. Here every vertex has degree 0, so G is 0-regular, not 1-regular.
C — Correct. A forest is a graph with no cycles. A graph with no edges cannot contain a cycle, so G is a forest made of 5 single-vertex trees.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: No edges -> no cycles -> forest. Only the 1-vertex trivial graph is both edgeless and connected.

q: A directed graph is called strongly connected if:
opts: for every ordered pair of vertices (u, v) there is a directed path from u to v
its underlying undirected graph is connected
every vertex has in-degree equal to its out-degree
More than one of the above
