So Bellman–Ford cannot give shortest paths on an undirected graph with a negative edge — it reports a negative cycle.
work:
Directed edges (relaxed in this order): A→B 4, B→A 4, B→C −2, C→B −2, A→C 5, C→A 5
Start: A = 0, B = ∞, C = ∞
Round 1: A→B: B = 4; B→C: C = 2; C→B: B = 0 → (A, B, C) = (0, 0, 2)
Round 2 (V − 1 = 2): B→C: C = −2; C→B: B = −4 → (0, −4, −2)
Extra check: B→C would give −4 − 2 = −6 < −2 → a distance can still decrease → negative-weight cycle reported
Cause: B→C→B has weight −2 + (−2) = −4 < 0
why: A — Wrong. These are the values after relaxing only A→B and then B→C once. Relaxation does not stop there: going back and forth along the −2 edge keeps lowering the distances of B and C, so no final distances exist.
B — Wrong. 5 is just the direct edge A–C. Even ignoring the cycle, A→B→C (4 − 2 = 2) is shorter. In fact there is a negative cycle, so no finite shortest distances exist.

C — Correct. The edge B–C becomes B→C and C→B, each of weight −2, forming the cycle B→C→B of weight −4. Bellman–Ford's extra check finds that a distance can still decrease and reports a negative-weight cycle.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Undirected graph + a negative edge ⇒ a negative cycle for Bellman–Ford.

q: Which of the following statements are TRUE?
opts: The complete graph K4 has 16 different spanning trees
If Kruskal's algorithm is run on a disconnected weighted graph, it produces a minimum spanning forest (a minimum spanning tree of each connected component)
To obtain a spanning tree from a connected graph with n vertices and e edges, exactly e − n − 1 edges must be removed
More than one of the above
exp: A and B are true (K4 has 4² = 16 spanning trees; Kruskal gives a minimum spanning forest); C is false — the number of edges removed is e − n + 1.
concept: A spanning tree of a connected graph with n vertices has n − 1 edges, so e − (n − 1) = e − n + 1 edges must be removed from the graph to get one. Cayley's formula: the complete graph Kn has n^(n−2) spanning trees (K4: 4² = 16). Prim's algorithm grows ONE tree from a start vertex, so on a disconnected graph it covers only that vertex's component. Kruskal's algorithm scans all the edges in increasing order of weight and adds every edge that joins two different components; on a disconnected graph it therefore builds a minimum spanning forest with n − c edges (c = number of components).
work:
A: Cayley: n^(n−2) = 4² = 16
B: Kruskal on a graph with n vertices and c components picks n − c edges (one MST per component)
C: edges to remove = e − (n − 1) = e − n + 1; for K4: 6 − 4 + 1 = 3 (not 6 − 4 − 1 = 1)
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. By Cayley's formula Kn has n^(n−2) spanning trees; for n = 4 that is 4² = 16.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Kruskal's algorithm never needs the graph to be connected: it keeps adding the cheapest edge that joins two different components and ends with one minimum spanning tree per component (n − c edges in all).
C — Wrong. A spanning tree keeps n − 1 of the e edges, so e − (n − 1) = e − n + 1 edges are removed, not e − n − 1. For K4: 6 − 4 + 1 = 3.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements is TRUE?
opts: A pendant vertex is a vertex of degree 0
An isolated vertex is a vertex of degree 1
In a directed graph, a sink is a vertex whose in-degree is 0
More than one of the above
exp: Pendant = degree 1, isolated = degree 0, sink = out-degree 0; all three options swap these definitions, so none is true.
concept: Vertex types by degree: an isolated vertex has degree 0 (no edge touches it); a pendant (end) vertex has degree exactly 1. In a directed graph, a source has in-degree 0 (edges only leave it) and a sink has out-degree 0 (edges only enter it).
why: A — Wrong. Degree 0 describes an ISOLATED vertex. A pendant vertex has degree exactly 1 — it hangs from the graph by one edge.
B — Wrong. Degree 1 describes a PENDANT vertex. An isolated vertex has degree 0 — no edge touches it.
C — Wrong. In-degree 0 describes a SOURCE. A sink has out-degree 0: edges come into it, but none leave it.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.

E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true: each option swaps two definitions. Correctly, a pendant vertex has degree 1, an isolated vertex has degree 0, and a sink has out-degree 0. So 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: In hashing, what is the job of the hash function?
opts: It maps a key to a slot (index) of the hash table
It arranges the keys of the table in sorted order
It encrypts a key so that it can be decrypted later
More than one of the above
exp: A hash function maps each key to a slot (index) of the hash table.
concept: Hashing stores and finds keys quickly by computing their position instead of searching for it. A hash function h takes a key k and returns an index h(k) between 0 and m − 1, where m is the number of slots in the hash table. The key is stored in that slot (or near it, if there is a collision). For example, with h(k) = k mod 10 the key 47 goes to slot 7.
why: A — Correct. The hash function maps (converts) a key to a slot index of the hash table, so the key can be stored and found there directly.
B — Wrong. A hash function scatters keys over the table; it does not keep them in sorted order. Sorted order is given by structures such as a BST or a sorted array, not by hashing.

C — Wrong. Encryption is reversible with a secret key, so the original can be recovered (decrypted). A hash function is not meant to be reversed; it only computes an index (or a fixed-size 'fingerprint') from the key.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is a desirable property of a good hash function?
opts: It spreads the keys uniformly over all slots
It is fast and simple to compute
It always returns the same index for the same key
More than one of the above
exp: A good hash function spreads keys uniformly, is quick to compute, and always gives the same index for the same key.
concept: A good hash function should (1) spread the keys uniformly over all slots, so that collisions are rare; (2) be fast and simple to compute, because it runs on every insert, search and delete; and (3) be deterministic — the same key must always give the same index, otherwise a stored key could never be found again. It should also use every part of the key.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true, but B and C are true too, so the answer is D, not A alone. Uniform spreading keeps chains and probe sequences short, which keeps operations close to O(1).

B — Wrong. This statement is true, but A and C are true too, so the answer is D, not B alone. The hash is computed on every operation, so it must be cheap; a slow hash function would destroy the speed advantage of hashing.

C — Wrong. This statement is true, but A and B are true too, so the answer is D, not C alone. Determinism is essential: if the same key gave different indices at different times, a search would look in the wrong slot and miss a key that is stored.
D — Correct. All three of A–C are desirable properties, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: For the division method h(k) = k mod m, which table size m is generally recommended?
opts: A prime number not close to an exact power of 2
More than one of the above
exp: For the division method, choose the table size m as a prime not close to a power of 2.
concept: In the division method h(k) = k mod m, the result depends on the choice of m. If m = 2^p, then k mod m is just the lowest p bits of k; if m = 10^p, it is just the last p decimal digits. The rest of the key is ignored, so keys that share their last bits or digits collide (with m = 100, the keys 1234, 5634 and 9934 all go to slot 34). Choosing m as a prime not too close to a power of 2 makes the remainder depend on all digits of the key and spreads the keys better (Cormen).
why: A — Wrong. With m = 2^p (e.g. 1024 = 2^10), k mod m keeps only the lowest 10 bits of the key, so keys that differ only in their higher bits all collide.
B — Correct. A prime m not close to a power of 2 makes h(k) depend on all the bits/digits of k, so the keys are spread more evenly.
C — Wrong. With m = 1000, k mod 1000 is just the last three digits of the key, so keys such as 21456 and 98456 collide even though they are very different.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Division method → prime table size.

q: Using the division method h(k) = k mod 13, at which index is the key 100 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: The division method computes h(k) = k mod m: the remainder when the key k is divided by the table size m. The result is always between 0 and m − 1, so it is always a valid slot index.
why: A — Wrong. 7 is the quotient (100 ÷ 13 = 7 remainder 9). The hash is the remainder, not the quotient.
B — Wrong. 8 is the remainder of 99 ÷ 13, not of 100 ÷ 13 (an off-by-one slip).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: mod gives the remainder, never the quotient.

q: Using the mid-square method, the key 4567 is squared and the middle two digits of the square are taken as the address. What is the address?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 4567² = 20857489, and its middle two digits are 57.
concept: In the mid-square method, the key is squared and a fixed number of digits is taken from the middle of the square as the address. The middle digits depend on every digit of the key, so keys are spread well. The same digit positions must be used for every key.
work:
4567² = 4567 × 4567 = 20857489 (8 digits)
Positions: 2(1) 0(2) 8(3) 5(4) 7(5) 4(6) 8(7) 9(8)
Middle two of 8 digits = positions 4 and 5 → 5, 7
Address = 57
why: A — Correct. The square is 20857489 and its middle two digits (the 4th and 5th of 8) are 5 and 7, giving 57.
B — Wrong. 85 takes the 3rd and 4th digits, one place to the left of the middle.
C — Wrong. 74 takes the 5th and 6th digits, one place to the right of the middle.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The key 123456789 is hashed by the shift-folding method into a table with addresses 000–999: the key is split into 3-digit parts that are added, and any carry beyond three digits is discarded. What is the address?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Shift folding: 123 + 456 + 789 = 1368; dropping the carry gives 368.
concept: In the folding method the key is cut into parts of equal size (here 3 digits) and the parts are added. In shift folding the parts are added as they are; in boundary folding every alternate part is reversed before adding. If the sum has more digits than the address allows, the extra leading digit (the carry) is dropped.
work:
Key 123456789 → parts 123 | 456 | 789
Shift folding: 123 + 456 + 789 = 1368
Addresses have 3 digits (000–999), so drop the carry 1 → 368
Address = 368
why: A — Wrong. 1368 is the sum before the carry is dropped; it has four digits and is outside the address range 000–999.
B — Correct. 123 + 456 + 789 = 1368, and discarding the carry gives 368.
C — Wrong. 566 comes from boundary folding, where the middle part is reversed: 123 + 654 + 789 = 1566 → 566. The question asks for shift folding.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Shift folding = add the parts as they are. Boundary folding = reverse alternate parts, then add.

q: Using the multiplication method h(k) = ⌊m · (kA mod 1)⌋ with m = 100 and A = 0.618, what is h(40)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 40 × 0.618 = 24.72; the fractional part is 0.72; 100 × 0.72 = 72, which is not listed.
concept: In the multiplication method, multiply the key k by a constant A (0 < A < 1), keep only the fractional part of kA (that is what 'kA mod 1' means), multiply that fraction by the table size m, and take the floor. Knuth suggests A ≈ 0.618 (related to the golden ratio). In this method the value of m is not critical; a power of 2 is commonly used.
why: A — Wrong. 24 is the integer part of 24.72. The method keeps the fractional part (0.72), not the integer part.
B — Wrong. 27 does not come from the formula (it is 72 with its digits reversed). The correct value is ⌊100 × 0.72⌋ = 72.
C — Wrong. 62 is about 100 × 0.618 = 61.8 rounded up; it leaves out the key 40 altogether.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above', which needs at least two true options, is false.
E — Correct. The correct value is h(40) = 72, which is not among A–C.

q: What value does hash("CAT", 10) return for the C function below? (ASCII: 'A' = 65, 'C' = 67, 'T' = 84)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The sum of the ASCII codes is 216, and 216 % 10 = 6.
concept: A simple string hash adds up the character codes of all characters and takes the remainder modulo the table size. In C a char is stored as its ASCII number, so sum += *s++ adds the code of the current character and then moves s to the next character. The loop stops at the terminating '\0' character.
why: A — Wrong. 21 is 216 / 10, the quotient of integer division. The function uses %, which gives the remainder.
C — Wrong. 16 is 216 % 100 (the last two digits). The table size passed here is 10, not 100.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Such an additive hash gives the same value for anagrams ("CAT" and "ACT") — a known weakness.

q: In hashing, a collision occurs when:
opts: two different keys hash to the same slot
the same key is inserted into the table twice
the hash table becomes completely full
More than one of the above
exp: A collision occurs when two different keys hash to the same slot.
concept: A hash table has far fewer slots than there are possible keys, so different keys must sometimes get the same index. A collision happens when two different keys k1 ≠ k2 have h(k1) = h(k2). Collisions are normal and are handled by collision-resolution techniques such as separate chaining or open addressing (probing).
why: A — Correct. A collision is two distinct keys hashing to the same slot; e.g. with h(k) = k mod 10, the keys 25 and 35 both go to slot 5.
B — Wrong. Inserting the same key twice is a duplicate key, not a collision; the table normally just updates the stored value or rejects the duplicate.
C — Wrong. A completely full table is overflow (in open addressing no more keys can be inserted). Collisions can happen long before the table is full — even with only two keys.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following is NOT a collision-resolution technique?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Linear probing, separate chaining and double hashing are all collision-resolution techniques.
concept: Collision-resolution techniques come in two families. Separate chaining (open hashing) keeps all keys that hash to the same slot in a linked list attached to that slot. Open addressing (closed hashing) keeps every key inside the table and, on a collision, probes other slots: linear probing, quadratic probing and double hashing.
why: A — Wrong. Linear probing IS a collision-resolution technique: on a collision, try the next slot, then the next, and so on.
B — Wrong. Separate chaining IS a collision-resolution technique: colliding keys are kept in a linked list at the same slot.
C — Wrong. Double hashing IS a collision-resolution technique: a second hash function decides the step size between probes.
D — Wrong. None of A–C satisfies 'NOT a collision-resolution technique', so 'More than one of the above' cannot be the answer.
E — Correct. All three are collision-resolution techniques, so none of them satisfies the stem.

q: A hash table has 40 slots and currently stores 30 keys. What is its load factor α?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: α = keys / slots = 30 / 40 = 0.75.
concept: The load factor α (alpha) measures how full a hash table is: α = n / m, where n is the number of keys stored and m is the number of slots. A larger α means more collisions and slower operations, so tables are usually enlarged (rehashed) when α crosses a threshold such as 0.75.
work:
n = 30 keys, m = 40 slots
α = n / m = 30 / 40 = 0.75
why: A — Wrong. 1.33 is 40 / 30, i.e. slots divided by keys — the fraction upside down.
B — Wrong. 0.25 is 10 / 40, the fraction of slots that are still empty, not the load factor.
C — Correct. α = n / m = 30 / 40 = 0.75, i.e. three quarters of the slots are in use.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Load factor: keys on top, slots below.

q: Which of the following statements about separate chaining are correct?
opts: The load factor α can be greater than 1
Each table slot points to a linked list of the keys that hash to it
Inserting a new key at the head of its chain takes O(1) time
More than one of the above
exp: In separate chaining each slot points to a linked list, α can exceed 1, and insertion at the head of a chain is O(1).
concept: In separate chaining, each slot of the table holds a pointer to a linked list (a chain) of all the keys that hash to that slot. Because a list can grow as long as needed, the table can hold more keys than it has slots, so α = n/m may be greater than 1. A new key can be added at the head of its chain in O(1) time (if we do not first check for a duplicate).
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true, but B and C are true too, so the answer is D, not A alone. Keys live in the lists, not in the slots themselves, so n can exceed m and α can be greater than 1 (e.g. 20 keys in 10 slots gives α = 2).

B — Wrong. This statement is true, but A and C are true too, so the answer is D, not B alone. This is the definition of separate chaining: each slot points to a linked list of the keys with that hash value.
C — Wrong. This statement is true, but A and B are true too, so the answer is D, not C alone. Adding a node at the head of a linked list needs only a couple of pointer changes, which is O(1).
D — Correct. All three statements are correct, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: With separate chaining under simple uniform hashing (load factor α = n/m), the expected time for a search is:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With chaining and simple uniform hashing, a search takes Θ(1 + α) expected time.
concept: Simple uniform hashing assumes that every key is equally likely to go to any of the m slots. With n keys the average chain length is then n/m = α. A search computes the hash and reaches the slot (constant time, the '1'), then scans a chain of expected length α, so the expected search time is Θ(1 + α) (Cormen). If α is kept bounded (e.g. α ≤ 1), this is O(1). In the worst case, when all keys fall into one chain, a search is Θ(n).
why: A — Wrong. Θ(log n) is the search time of a balanced binary search tree or of binary search, not of hashing with chaining.
B — Correct. Expected cost = 1 (compute the hash, reach the slot) + α (scan the chain): Θ(1 + α).
C — Wrong. There is no log n factor: a chain is scanned one node at a time, and its expected length is α.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The keys 15, 11, 27, 8, 12, 33, 20, 34, 3 are inserted (in this order) into a hash table of 7 slots (0–6) using h(k) = k mod 7 and separate chaining. Which slot has the longest chain, and what is its length?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Slot 6 holds 27, 20 and 34, a chain of length 3, and no option says that.
concept: In separate chaining, compute h(k) for every key and add the key to the list of that slot. The chain length of a slot is the number of keys that hash to it. To find the longest chain, simply count how many keys share each slot.
work:
h(k) = k mod 7:
15 → 1, 11 → 4, 27 → 6, 8 → 1, 12 → 5, 33 → 5, 20 → 6, 34 → 6, 3 → 3
slot 0: empty
slot 1: 15 → 8 (length 2)
slot 2: empty
slot 3: 3 (length 1)
slot 4: 11 (length 1)
slot 5: 12 → 33 (length 2)
slot 6: 27 → 20 → 34 (length 3)
Longest chain: slot 6, length 3
why: A — Wrong. Slot 1 does have a chain of length 2 (15, 8), but it is not the longest; slot 6 holds 3 keys.
B — Wrong. Slot 5 also has length 2 (12, 33), but slot 6 is longer.
C — Wrong. Slot 6 is the right slot, but its length is 3 (27, 20, 34), not 4. The key 3 goes to slot 3 (3 mod 7 = 3), not slot 6.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above', which needs at least two true options, is false.
E — Correct. The longest chain is at slot 6 with length 3, which none of A–C states.

q: The keys 12, 7, 22, 3, 17 are inserted (in this order) into a table of 5 slots using h(k) = k mod 5 and separate chaining, where each new key is inserted at the HEAD of its chain. Reading from the head, what is the chain at slot 2?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Head insertion reverses the arrival order, so slot 2 reads 17 → 22 → 7 → 12.
concept: In separate chaining a new key can be added at the head (front) or at the tail (end) of its chain. Head insertion is O(1) and puts the newest key first, so reading a chain from the head gives its keys in reverse order of insertion.
work:
h(k) = k mod 5: 12 → 2, 7 → 2, 22 → 2, 3 → 3, 17 → 2
Slot 2, inserting each key at the head:
insert 12 → 12
insert 7 → 7 → 12
insert 22 → 22 → 7 → 12
(3 goes to slot 3)
insert 17 → 17 → 22 → 7 → 12
why: A — Wrong. 12 → 7 → 22 → 17 is the order you get with insertion at the TAIL of the chain.
B — Correct. With head insertion the newest key comes first: 17 → 22 → 7 → 12.
C — Wrong. 17 → 7 → 22 → 12 has 7 and 22 in the wrong order: 22 was inserted after 7, so with head insertion 22 must come before 7.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The term 'open hashing' refers to which collision-resolution technique?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Open hashing means separate chaining.
concept: 'Open hashing' is another name for separate chaining: keys are kept outside the table array, in linked lists hanging from the slots. 'Closed hashing' is another name for open addressing: all keys are kept inside the table, and probing (linear, quadratic, double hashing) finds a free slot. The names are easy to confuse because 'open hashing' and 'open addressing' are opposites.
why: A — Wrong. Linear probing is an open-addressing (closed hashing) method: the keys stay inside the table.
B — Wrong. Double hashing is also an open-addressing (closed hashing) method.
C — Correct. Open hashing = separate chaining (keys are stored outside the table, in lists).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Open HASHING: the chains hang open, outside the table. Open ADDRESSING: a key may end up at any open address inside the table.

q: Which of the following pairs are synonyms in standard hashing terminology?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Open hashing = closed addressing = separate chaining, and closed hashing = open addressing, so all three pairs are synonyms.
concept: There are two families of collision resolution, each with more than one name. (1) Separate chaining = open hashing = closed addressing: keys live in lists outside the table, and each key always stays at its own home address (the address is 'closed', i.e. fixed). (2) Open addressing = closed hashing: all keys are kept inside the table (closed within it), and a key may end up at any address found by probing (the address is 'open').
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true, but B and C are true too, so the answer is D, not A alone. Open hashing and separate chaining are the same thing.
B — Wrong. This statement is true, but A and C are true too, so the answer is D, not B alone. Closed hashing and open addressing are the same thing.

C — Wrong. This statement is true, but A and B are true too, so the answer is D, not C alone. Closed addressing is another name for separate chaining, because each key stays in the chain of its own home address.
D — Correct. All three pairs are synonyms, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In open addressing, every key is stored inside the table itself. Hence the load factor α always satisfies:
opts: α can exceed 1 when collisions are frequent
More than one of the above
exp: In open addressing each slot holds at most one key, so α ≤ 1.
concept: In open addressing all keys are stored in the table's own slots, one key per slot, with no lists outside. A table with m slots can therefore hold at most m keys, so the load factor α = n/m can never exceed 1. In practice α is kept well below 1 (often around 0.5 to 0.7), because probing becomes slow as the table fills up.
why: A — Correct. n ≤ m, so α = n/m ≤ 1.
B — Wrong. α ≥ 1 would mean at least as many keys as slots. α = 1 is a completely full table, and more keys than slots is impossible in open addressing.
C — Wrong. Frequent collisions only make probing slower; they cannot create extra slots. α > 1 is possible only with separate chaining.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which probe sequence is used by quadratic probing (i = 0, 1, 2, …)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Quadratic probing uses h(k, i) = (h(k) + i²) mod m.
concept: Open addressing resolves a collision by trying a sequence of slots, called the probe sequence, for i = 0, 1, 2, …. Linear probing uses (h(k) + i) mod m. Quadratic probing uses (h(k) + i²) mod m (more generally h(k) + c1·i + c2·i²). Double hashing uses (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod m.
why: A — Wrong. (h(k) + i) mod m adds 0, 1, 2, 3, … to the home slot; that is linear probing.
B — Correct. (h(k) + i²) mod m adds 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, …; that is quadratic probing.
C — Wrong. (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod m uses a second hash function as the step size; that is double hashing.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Linear: +1, +2, +3. Quadratic: +1, +4, +9. Double hashing: +h2, +2·h2, +3·h2.

q: Primary clustering — long runs of consecutive occupied slots that keep growing — is a characteristic drawback of:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Primary clustering is a drawback of linear probing.
concept: Primary clustering happens in linear probing. A run of consecutive occupied slots attracts new keys: any key whose home slot falls anywhere inside the run slides to the end of the run and makes it one slot longer, and neighbouring runs join together. If a run has length r, the empty slot just after it is filled next with probability (r + 1)/m instead of 1/m. Long runs make both searches and insertions slow.
why: A — Wrong. Separate chaining keeps colliding keys in a list at their own slot; keys never move into neighbouring slots, so no runs form.
B — Wrong. Double hashing uses a key-dependent step size, so colliding keys jump to different places; it avoids primary (and secondary) clustering.
C — Correct. Primary clustering is the typical weakness of linear probing, because a collision always moves the key to the very next slot.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Quadratic probing removes primary clustering but still suffers from secondary clustering. Secondary clustering means that:
opts: keys with the same home slot follow exactly the same probe sequence
keys with different home slots always probe identical slots
the table has to be resized after every collision
More than one of the above
exp: Secondary clustering means keys with the same home slot follow exactly the same probe sequence.
concept: In quadratic probing the probe sequence is h(k), h(k) + 1, h(k) + 4, h(k) + 9, … (mod m). This sequence depends only on the home slot h(k), not on the key itself. So all keys with the same home slot follow exactly the same sequence of slots and keep colliding with each other. This milder problem is called secondary clustering. Double hashing removes it, because its step size depends on the key.
why: A — Correct. This is exactly secondary clustering: keys with the same home slot follow the same probe sequence.

B — Wrong. Keys with different home slots start at different places, so their probe sequences differ. Runs that grow from many different home slots are primary clustering (linear probing), which quadratic probing reduces.
C — Wrong. A table is resized (rehashed) when its load factor becomes too high, not after every collision; resizing has nothing to do with the definition of secondary clustering.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which collision-resolution technique avoids both primary and secondary clustering?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Double hashing avoids both primary and secondary clustering.
concept: Linear probing suffers from primary clustering (long runs of occupied slots). Quadratic probing removes primary clustering but still has secondary clustering (keys with the same home slot follow the same path). Double hashing uses a step size h2(k) that depends on the key, so even keys with the same home slot usually follow different probe sequences; it avoids both kinds of clustering. With a good h2 it produces about m² different probe sequences, against only m for linear or quadratic probing.
why: A — Wrong. Linear probing has primary clustering (and secondary clustering too, since keys with the same home slot follow the same path).
B — Correct. Double hashing avoids both primary and secondary clustering, because the step size depends on the key.
C — Wrong. Quadratic probing avoids primary clustering but still suffers from secondary clustering.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In double hashing, h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod m. Which of the following are requirements on the secondary hash function h2?
opts: h2(k) should be relatively prime to the table size m
h2(k) must be equal to h1(k) for every key
More than one of the above
exp: h2(k) must never be 0 and should be relatively prime to m; it should not be equal to h1(k).
concept: In double hashing the second hash function h2(k) gives the step size between probes. If h2(k) = 0, the probe sequence stays on the same slot forever. If h2(k) and m share a common factor d > 1, only m/d of the slots can ever be reached. So h2(k) must be non-zero and relatively prime to m (gcd = 1). Common choices: m prime with 1 ≤ h2(k) < m, or m a power of 2 with h2(k) always odd. h2 should be independent of (different from) h1.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true, but B is true too, so the answer is D, not A alone. If h2(k) = 0, every probe is h1(k) + i·0 = h1(k): the same slot is tried again and again.

B — Wrong. This statement is true, but A is true too, so the answer is D, not B alone. If gcd(h2(k), m) = 1, the probe sequence visits all m slots, so a free slot is found whenever one exists; otherwise some slots are never probed.

C — Wrong. h2 should be independent of h1. If h2(k) = h1(k), keys with the same home slot get the same step size, bringing back secondary clustering — and a key with h1(k) = 0 would get h2(k) = 0, which is not allowed.
D — Correct. A and B are both requirements, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: With quadratic probing h(k, i) = (h(k) + i²) mod 10, how many distinct slots can ever be examined for a key whose home slot is 0?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: i² mod 10 takes only the values 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 and 9, so only 6 slots can ever be examined.
concept: Quadratic probing visits (h(k) + i²) mod m. The values of i² mod m repeat, and when m is not chosen carefully they cannot cover all m slots. For m = 10, a square can only end in the digit 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, so 4 of the 10 slots are never examined. That is why quadratic probing is used with a prime m and a load factor of at most 1/2: then a free slot is guaranteed to be found.
work:
Home slot 0, so probe i examines i² mod 10:
i = 0 → 0
i = 1 → 1
i = 2 → 4
i = 3 → 9
i = 4 → 16 mod 10 = 6
i = 5 → 25 mod 10 = 5
i = 6 → 36 mod 10 = 6
i = 7 → 49 mod 10 = 9
i = 8 → 64 mod 10 = 4
i = 9 → 81 mod 10 = 1
i = 10 → 100 mod 10 = 0 (the pattern repeats)
Distinct slots: {0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9} → 6
Never examined: 2, 3, 7, 8
why: A — Wrong. 10 would mean every slot is reached, but slots 2, 3, 7 and 8 are never probed, because no square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8.
B — Wrong. 5 is too few: i = 0 to 5 already gives the six different slots 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5. (About m/2 distinct probes is the guarantee for a PRIME table size; it is not this count.)
C — Correct. Exactly 6 distinct slots can be examined: 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A linear-probing hash table of size 10 has only slots 2, 3 and 4 occupied. If the next key's home slot is equally likely to be any of the 10 slots, what is the probability that the key ends up in slot 5?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Home slots 2, 3, 4 and 5 all end in slot 5, so the probability is 4/10 = 0.4.
concept: Linear probing causes primary clustering: a run of occupied slots acts like a funnel. Any key whose home slot falls inside the run slides forward to the first empty slot after it. So the empty slot just after a run is much more likely to be filled next than an isolated empty slot. If every home slot is equally likely, the chance that a particular empty slot is filled next = (number of home slots that lead to it) / m.
work:
Occupied: 2, 3, 4. Each home slot has probability 1/10.
Home 5 → slot 5 is empty → placed in 5
Home 4 → 4 full → 5
Home 3 → 3, 4 full → 5
Home 2 → 2, 3, 4 full → 5
Home 0, 1, 6, 7, 8, 9 → that slot is empty → the key stays there
Home slots leading to slot 5: {2, 3, 4, 5} → 4 of 10
Probability = 4/10 = 0.4
why: A — Correct. Four home slots (2, 3, 4 and 5) lead to slot 5, so the probability is 4/10 = 0.4.
B — Wrong. 0.1 = 1/10 counts only home slot 5 itself and forgets the keys that hit the cluster 2–4 and slide to slot 5. (0.1 is the right probability for an isolated empty slot such as slot 8.)
C — Wrong. 0.3 counts only the three home slots inside the cluster (2, 3, 4) and forgets the key whose home slot is 5 itself.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 42, 52, 63, 72, 15 are inserted in this order into an empty hash table of size 10 (slots 0–9) with h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing. In which slot is 15 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 72 has already taken slot 5, so 15 goes to the next slot, 6.
concept: In linear probing a key first tries its home slot h(k). If that slot is occupied it tries the next slot, then the next, wrapping around from the last slot to slot 0, until it finds an empty slot. In trace questions, write down the table after every insertion, because earlier keys decide where later keys go.
work:
42: h = 2 → probes 2 → slot 2
52: h = 2 → probes 2 (full), 3 → slot 3
63: h = 3 → probes 3 (full), 4 → slot 4
72: h = 2 → probes 2, 3, 4 (full), 5 → slot 5
15: h = 5 → probes 5 (full), 6 → slot 6
Table: 2 = 42, 3 = 52, 4 = 63, 5 = 72, 6 = 15
why: A — Wrong. Slot 5 is the home slot of 15, but 72 already occupies it (72 slid there from slot 2).
B — Correct. 15's home slot 5 is taken by 72, so 15 moves to the next slot, 6, which is empty.
C — Wrong. Slot 7 would need slot 6 to be occupied as well, but slot 6 is empty when 15 arrives.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 19, 26, 13, 48, 17 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 7 (slots 0–6) with h(k) = k mod 7 and linear probing (wrapping around from slot 6 to slot 0). In which slot is 48 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 48 probes slot 6 (taken by 26) and slot 0 (taken by 13), and lands in slot 1, which is not listed.
concept: In linear probing a key first tries its home slot h(k). If that slot is occupied it tries the next slot, then the next, wrapping around from the last slot to slot 0, until it finds an empty slot. In trace questions, write down the table after every insertion, because earlier keys decide where later keys go.
work:
19: h = 19 mod 7 = 5 → slot 5
26: h = 5 → probes 5 (full), 6 → slot 6
13: h = 6 → probes 6 (full), 0 (wrap) → slot 0
48: h = 48 mod 7 = 6 → probes 6 (full), 0 (full), 1 → slot 1
17: h = 3 → slot 3
Final table: [13, 48, –, 17, –, 19, 26]
why: A — Wrong. Slot 6 is 48's home slot (48 = 6 × 7 + 6), but 26 already occupies it.
B — Wrong. Slot 0 is the next slot after wrapping around, but 13 already occupies it.
C — Wrong. 48 stops at the first empty slot it meets, which is slot 1; it never reaches slot 2.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above', which needs at least two true options, is false.
E — Correct. 48 is stored in slot 1, which is not among A–C.

q: Keys 12, 18, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 15 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 10 with h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing. How many probes (slots examined, including the slot where it is finally placed) are needed to insert 15?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 15 checks slots 5, 6, 7 and 8 (all occupied) and is placed in 9: 5 probes.
concept: A probe is one slot examined. In linear probing, the number of probes for an insertion = the number of occupied slots passed + 1 (the empty slot where the key is finally placed). Long runs of occupied slots (primary clustering) make this number grow quickly.
work:
12: h = 2 → slot 2
18: h = 8 → slot 8
13: h = 3 → slot 3
2: h = 2 → 2, 3 full → slot 4
3: h = 3 → 3, 4 full → slot 5
23: h = 3 → 3, 4, 5 full → slot 6
5: h = 5 → 5, 6 full → slot 7
Before 15: 2 = 12, 3 = 13, 4 = 2, 5 = 3, 6 = 23, 7 = 5, 8 = 18
15: h = 5 → probe 1: slot 5 (full), probe 2: 6 (full), probe 3: 7 (full), probe 4: 8 (full), probe 5: 9 (empty) → slot 9
Probes = 5
why: A — Wrong. 4 counts only the occupied slots 5, 6, 7 and 8 and forgets slot 9, where 15 is placed; the question says to include it.
B — Correct. 15 examines slots 5, 6, 7, 8 (all occupied) and 9 (empty): 5 probes.
C — Wrong. 6 would need one more occupied slot, but slot 9 is empty, so the search stops there.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 12, 5, 19, 26, 8, 3 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 7 (slots 0–6) with h(k) = k mod 7 and linear probing. What is the final table (slot 0 first, – = empty)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Linear probing gives the table [19, 26, 8, 3, –, 12, 5].
concept: In linear probing a key first tries its home slot h(k). If that slot is occupied it tries the next slot, then the next, wrapping around from the last slot to slot 0, until it finds an empty slot. In trace questions, write down the table after every insertion, because earlier keys decide where later keys go.
work:
12: h = 5 → slot 5
5: h = 5 → 5 full → slot 6
19: h = 5 → 5, 6 full → wrap → slot 0
26: h = 5 → 5, 6, 0 full → slot 1
8: h = 1 → 1 full → slot 2
3: h = 3 → slot 3
Final: [19, 26, 8, 3, –, 12, 5]
why: A — Wrong. [26, 8, 19, 3, –, 12, 5] is the table that QUADRATIC probing would give (19 jumps to (5 + 4) mod 7 = 2 and 26 to (5 + 9) mod 7 = 0), not linear probing.
B — Wrong. [26, 19, 8, …] puts 26 before 19. But 19 is inserted first and takes slot 0, so 26 must go to slot 1.
C — Correct. Tracing linear probing step by step gives [19, 26, 8, 3, –, 12, 5].
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 17, 25, 9, 33, 14, 30, 6 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 8 (slots 0–7) with h(k) = k mod 8 and linear probing. Which slot remains empty?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Slots 0–4, 6 and 7 are filled, so slot 5 stays empty.
concept: In linear probing a key first tries its home slot h(k). If that slot is occupied it tries the next slot, then the next, wrapping around from the last slot to slot 0, until it finds an empty slot. In trace questions, write down the table after every insertion, because earlier keys decide where later keys go.
work:
17: h = 1 → slot 1
25: h = 1 → 1 full → slot 2
9: h = 1 → 1, 2 full → slot 3
33: h = 1 → 1, 2, 3 full → slot 4
14: h = 6 → slot 6
30: h = 6 → 6 full → slot 7
6: h = 6 → 6, 7 full → wrap → slot 0
Final: [6, 17, 25, 9, 33, –, 14, 30] → slot 5 is empty
why: A — Correct. The 7 keys fill slots 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7; slot 5 is the only one left empty.
B — Wrong. Slot 0 is filled by 6, which wraps around after finding slots 6 and 7 full.
C — Wrong. Slot 7 is filled by 30 (its home slot 6 was already taken by 14).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 27, 40, 53, 15, 66 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 13 with h(k) = k mod 13 and linear probing. An unsuccessful search is then made for 79. How many slots are examined (count the empty slot that ends the search)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The search for 79 checks slots 1 to 5 (all occupied) and stops at the empty slot 6: 6 slots.
concept: In linear probing, an unsuccessful search starts at the key's home slot and checks slots one by one. It can stop only when it reaches an EMPTY slot, because if the key were in the table it would have been placed at or before the first empty slot of its probe sequence. So an unsuccessful search examines the whole run of occupied slots starting at the home slot, plus the empty slot that ends it.
work:
Insert with h(k) = k mod 13:
27: h = 1 → slot 1
40: h = 1 → slot 2
53: h = 1 → slot 3
15: h = 2 → 2, 3 full → slot 4
66: h = 1 → 1, 2, 3, 4 full → slot 5
Search 79: h = 79 mod 13 = 1 (79 = 6 × 13 + 1)
examine 1 (27), 2 (40), 3 (53), 4 (15), 5 (66) — none is 79
examine 6 → empty → stop: 79 is not in the table
Slots examined = 6
why: A — Wrong. 1 would be right only if the home slot 1 were empty, but it holds 27.
B — Wrong. 5 counts only the occupied slots 1–5 and forgets the empty slot 6 that ends the search, which the question says to count.
C — Correct. 5 occupied slots + 1 empty slot = 6 slots examined.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 4, 7, 14, 9, 24, 17 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 10 using h(k) = (2k + 3) mod 10 and linear probing. In which slot is 24 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: h(24) = 51 mod 10 = 1; slots 1, 2 and 3 are taken, so 24 goes to slot 4.
concept: The hash function need not be just k mod m; here it is h(k) = (2k + 3) mod 10. Compute it carefully for each key, then apply linear probing as usual. Notice that four of the keys (4, 14, 9, 24) share home slot 1 — a poor hash function creates clusters very quickly.
work:
h(k) = (2k + 3) mod 10
4: 11 mod 10 = 1 → slot 1
7: 17 mod 10 = 7 → slot 7
14: 31 mod 10 = 1 → 1 full → slot 2
9: 21 mod 10 = 1 → 1, 2 full → slot 3
24: 51 mod 10 = 1 → 1, 2, 3 full → slot 4
(17: 37 mod 10 = 7 → 7 full → slot 8)
24 is in slot 4
why: A — Wrong. Slot 1 is the home slot of 24, but it was taken by 4 (and slots 2 and 3 by 14 and 9).
B — Correct. 24 probes slots 1, 2, 3 (all full) and goes to slot 4.
C — Wrong. Slot 5 would need slot 4 to be occupied, but slot 4 is empty when 24 arrives.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 22, 32, 42, 52, 62 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 10 with h(k) = k mod 10 and quadratic probing h(k, i) = (h(k) + i²) mod 10. In which slot is 52 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 52 probes 2, 3 and 6 and lands in (2 + 9) mod 10 = 1.
concept: In quadratic probing the i-th probe is (h(k) + i²) mod m: the offsets from the home slot are 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, … instead of 0, 1, 2, 3, …. Keys with the same home slot follow the same sequence (secondary clustering), so here each new key goes one step further along the same path.
work:
Every key has home slot 2 (k mod 10 = 2).
Sequence from 2: 2, 2+1 = 3, 2+4 = 6, 2+9 = 11 mod 10 = 1, 2+16 = 18 mod 10 = 8, …
22: slot 2
32: 2 full → slot 3
42: 2, 3 full → slot 6
52: 2, 3, 6 full → slot 1
(62: 2, 3, 6, 1 full → slot 8)
52 is in slot 1
why: A — Correct. 52 probes 2, 3, 6 (all full) and then (2 + 9) mod 10 = 1, which is free.
B — Wrong. Slot 5 is the linear-probing answer (22 → 2, 32 → 3, 42 → 4, 52 → 5). Quadratic probing jumps by squares instead.
C — Wrong. Slot 8 is where the next key, 62, goes: (2 + 16) mod 10 = 8.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 33, 44, 55, 23, 12 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 11 with h(k) = k mod 11 and quadratic probing (h(k) + i²) mod 11. In which slot is 12 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 12 probes slot 1, slot 2 and then slot 5, where it is stored.
concept: Quadratic probing tries h(k), h(k) + 1, h(k) + 4, h(k) + 9, … (mod m). Keys with different home slots can still land in each other's way, so keep track of the whole table, not just the keys with the same home slot.
why: A — Wrong. Slot 2 is 12's second probe (1 + 1), but 23 already occupies it.
B — Wrong. Slot 3 is what you get by stepping linearly from slot 1 (1, 2, 3). Quadratic probing jumps from 1 + 1 = 2 to 1 + 4 = 5.
C — Correct. 12 probes slot 1 (full), slot 2 (full) and then 1 + 4 = 5, which is free.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 18, 29, 40, 51, 7 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 11 with h(k) = k mod 11 and quadratic probing (h(k) + i²) mod 11. How many probes (slots examined, including the final one) are needed to insert 7?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Key 7 checks slots 7, 8, 0 and 5 and is placed in slot 1: 5 probes.
concept: Count every slot examined, including the last one where the key is placed. All five keys here have home slot 7, so each follows the same quadratic sequence 7, 8, 0, 5, 1, … (secondary clustering), and each new key needs one more probe than the one before it.
work:
h(k) = k mod 11; 18, 29, 40, 51 and 7 all have home slot 7
Sequence from 7: 7, 8, 7+4 = 11 mod 11 = 0, 7+9 = 16 mod 11 = 5, 7+16 = 23 mod 11 = 1
18 → slot 7
29 → 7 full → slot 8
40 → 7, 8 full → slot 0
51 → 7, 8, 0 full → slot 5
7 → probe 1: 7 (full), probe 2: 8 (full), probe 3: 0 (full), probe 4: 5 (full), probe 5: 1 (empty) → slot 1
Probes = 5
why: A — Wrong. 3 probes would end at slot 0, which is already occupied by 40.
B — Wrong. 4 counts only the occupied slots 7, 8, 0, 5 and forgets the final slot 1, where 7 is placed.
C — Correct. Key 7 examines slots 7, 8, 0, 5 (all full) and 1 (empty): 5 probes.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 37, 24, 50, 63, 76, 11 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 13 with h(k) = k mod 13 and quadratic probing (h(k) + i²) mod 13. In which slot is 11 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Key 11 probes 11, 12, 2, 7 and 1, and lands in (11 + 25) mod 13 = 10, which is not listed.
concept: All keys here share home slot 11, so each follows the quadratic sequence 11, 12, 2, 7, 1, 10, … and takes the next unused position in it. Always reduce (h(k) + i²) modulo the table size; a slot number must lie between 0 and m − 1.
why: A — Wrong. Slot 0 does not appear in this probe sequence before slot 10 (the sequence is 11, 12, 2, 7, 1, 10). Slot 0 would be the third slot under linear probing (11, 12, 0).
B — Wrong. Slot 3 is the linear-probing answer: the first five keys would fill 11, 12, 0, 1, 2, and the sixth key would go to 3.
C — Wrong. 36 is 11 + 5² before taking mod 13. A table of size 13 has slots 0–12 only; 36 mod 13 = 10.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above', which needs at least two true options, is false.
E — Correct. 11 is stored in slot 10, which is not among A–C.

q: Keys 79, 69, 98, 72, 14 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 13 using double hashing with h1(k) = k mod 13, h2(k) = 1 + (k mod 11) and h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod 13. In which slot is 14 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 14 probes slot 1 (full) and then 1 + 4 = 5, which is free; slot 5 is not listed.
concept: In double hashing the i-th probe is (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod m. The first probe is the home slot h1(k); after that the key jumps in steps of h2(k), which depends on the key. You only need h2 when the home slot is occupied. The order of insertion matters: the same keys inserted in a different order can produce a different table.
why: A — Wrong. Slot 2 is what linear probing would give (the slot after 1). In double hashing the step for 14 is h2(14) = 4, not 1.

B — Wrong. Slot 9 is the answer in Cormen's well-known figure (Fig. 11.5), where 98 sits in slot 5 — which happens when 98 is inserted after 72. Here 98 is inserted before 72 and takes its home slot 7, so slot 5 is still free and 14 stops there.
C — Wrong. Slot 10 comes from forgetting the '1 +' in h2: a step of 14 mod 11 = 3 gives probes 1, 4, 7, 10. The correct step is 1 + 3 = 4.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above', which needs at least two true options, is false.
E — Correct. 14 is stored in slot 5, which is not among A–C.

q: Keys 27, 16, 49 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 11 using double hashing with h1(k) = k mod 11, h2(k) = 7 − (k mod 7) and h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod 11. In which slot is 49 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: h1(49) = 5 is taken and h2(49) = 7, so 49 goes to (5 + 7) mod 11 = 1.
concept: Double hashing probes h1(k), h1(k) + h2(k), h1(k) + 2·h2(k), … (mod m). A secondary function of the form h2(k) = R − (k mod R), with R a prime smaller than m, always gives a value from 1 to R, so it is never 0, as required.
why: A — Correct. 49's home slot 5 is full; with step h2(49) = 7 the next probe is (5 + 7) mod 11 = 1, which is free.
B — Wrong. Slot 6 is the next slot after 5, i.e. linear probing with step 1. In double hashing the step is h2(49) = 7.
C — Wrong. Slot 9 is what quadratic probing would give (27 → 5, 16 → 6, 49 → 5 + 4 = 9). In double hashing 49 goes to (5 + 7) mod 11 = 1.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 14, 27, 18, 47 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 11 using double hashing with h1(k) = k mod 11, h2(k) = 7 − (k mod 7). How many probes (slots examined, including the final one) are needed to insert 47?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: With step 2, 47 checks slots 3, 5 and 7 and is placed in slot 9: 4 probes.
concept: Count every slot examined, including the one where the key is finally placed. In double hashing the key moves in steps of h2(k); here the step h2(47) = 2 happens to land on three occupied slots before reaching a free one.
work:
h1(k) = k mod 11, h2(k) = 7 − (k mod 7)
14: h1 = 3 → slot 3
27: h1 = 5 → slot 5
18: h1 = 7 → slot 7
47: h1 = 47 mod 11 = 3; h2 = 7 − (47 mod 7) = 7 − 5 = 2
probe 1: 3 (full); probe 2: 3 + 2 = 5 (full); probe 3: 3 + 4 = 7 (full); probe 4: 3 + 6 = 9 (free) → slot 9
Probes = 4
why: A — Wrong. 2 probes would place 47 in slot 5, but 27 occupies it.
B — Wrong. 3 counts only the occupied slots 3, 5 and 7 and forgets slot 9, where 47 is placed.
C — Correct. 47 examines slots 3, 5, 7 (all full) and 9 (free): 4 probes.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A table of size 10 uses double hashing with h1(k) = k mod 10, h2(k) = 1 + (k mod 7) and h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i·h2(k)) mod 10. Keys 15 and 20 are inserted, then key 25 is inserted. What happens to 25?
opts: It cannot be placed: its probe sequence visits only slots 5 and 0
More than one of the above
exp: h2(25) = 5 shares the factor 5 with m = 10, so 25 only probes slots 5 and 0 (both full) and cannot be placed.
concept: In double hashing the step size h2(k) must be relatively prime to the table size m. If gcd(h2(k), m) = d > 1, the probe sequence visits only m/d slots and then repeats. If all of those slots are full, the key cannot be inserted even though the table still has free space.
work:
h1(k) = k mod 10, h2(k) = 1 + (k mod 7)
15: h1 = 5 → slot 5
20: h1 = 0 → slot 0
25: h1 = 5 (full); h2 = 1 + (25 mod 7) = 1 + 4 = 5
i = 1: 5 + 5 = 10 mod 10 = 0 (full)
i = 2: 5 + 10 = 15 mod 10 = 5 (full)
i = 3: 5 + 15 = 20 mod 10 = 0 (full) … the sequence repeats 5, 0, 5, 0, …
gcd(5, 10) = 5 → only 10 / 5 = 2 slots are ever visited
25 cannot be placed, although 8 slots are empty
why: A — Wrong. Slot 6 is the linear-probing answer (the slot after 5). With a step of 5 the sequence never reaches slot 6.
B — Wrong. Slot 1 is never reached either: every probe is 5 + 5i, which is always 5 or 0 (mod 10).
C — Correct. With h2(25) = 5 and m = 10 the probes are 5, 0, 5, 0, …; both slots are occupied, so 25 cannot be placed.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Make m prime (or make h2 always odd when m is a power of 2) so that every step size is relatively prime to m.

q: Keys 24, 35, 46, 57 are inserted in this order into an empty table of size 11 with h(k) = k mod 11. In which slot does 57 end up with linear probing, and in which with quadratic probing (h(k) + i²) mod 11?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Linear probing puts 57 in slot 5; quadratic probing puts it in (2 + 9) mod 11 = 0.
concept: Linear probing adds 1, 2, 3, … to the home slot; quadratic probing adds 1, 4, 9, …. In both cases the result is taken mod m, so (h(k) + i²) can wrap around to the start of the table.
why: A — Correct. Linear probing puts 57 in slot 5, and quadratic probing puts it in (2 + 9) mod 11 = 0.
B — Wrong. The linear part is right, but 11 is (2 + 9) before taking mod 11. A table of size 11 has slots 0–10 only, so the slot is 0.
C — Wrong. Linear probing gives 5, not 6: the earlier keys fill slots 2, 3, 4, and 57 takes the next slot, 5. (Slot 6 is where 46 goes under quadratic probing.)
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In open addressing, deleted keys are usually marked with a special DELETED (tombstone) marker instead of emptying the slot. Which statements about a DELETED slot are correct?
opts: A search treats it as occupied and continues probing past it
An insertion may reuse the slot for a new key
An unsuccessful search should stop as soon as it reaches it
More than one of the above
exp: A search passes over DELETED slots and an insertion may reuse them; only an empty slot stops a search.
concept: In open addressing a search stops when it reaches an empty slot. If we simply emptied the slot of a deleted key, a later search for another key that had probed past that slot would stop too early and wrongly report 'not found'. So the slot is marked DELETED (a 'tombstone') instead. Searches treat a DELETED slot as occupied and keep probing past it; insertions may reuse it.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true, but B is true too, so the answer is D, not A alone. A search must treat a DELETED slot as 'occupied, keep going', because keys stored after it in the probe sequence must still be reachable.
B — Wrong. This statement is true, but A is true too, so the answer is D, not B alone. A DELETED slot holds no live key, so an insertion can put a new key there and reuse the space.
C — Wrong. If an unsuccessful search stopped at a DELETED slot, a search for a key stored beyond it would also stop there and give a wrong 'not found'. Only an EMPTY (never-used) slot ends a search.
D — Correct. A and B are both correct, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 31, 41, 51, 61 are inserted into an empty table of size 10 with h(k) = k mod 10 and linear probing. Then 41 is deleted by marking its slot DELETED, and 71 is inserted (an insertion may reuse a DELETED slot). In which slot is 71 stored?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 71 passes slot 1 (occupied) and reuses the DELETED slot 2.
concept: When a key is deleted in open addressing, its slot is marked DELETED. A later insertion follows the normal probe sequence and may place the new key in the first DELETED or empty slot it meets, which reuses space and keeps runs short. (A careful implementation first checks the rest of the probe sequence to make sure the key is not already present, but the new key still goes into the first reusable slot.)
work:
31: h = 1 → slot 1
41: h = 1 → 1 full → slot 2
51: h = 1 → 1, 2 full → slot 3
61: h = 1 → 1, 2, 3 full → slot 4
Delete 41 → slot 2 = DELETED
71: h = 1 → slot 1 occupied (31) → slot 2 DELETED → reuse → slot 2
why: A — Correct. 71's probe sequence is 1 (occupied by 31), then 2 (DELETED, reusable), so 71 goes into slot 2.
B — Wrong. Slot 5 is the answer only if a DELETED slot is treated as occupied for insertion too; the question says an insertion may reuse it.
C — Wrong. Slot 1 is 71's home slot, but it still holds 31.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: When the load factor of a hash table exceeds a threshold, the table is rehashed. Rehashing means:
opts: sorting the keys within the same table to reduce collisions
creating a larger table and re-inserting every key using the hash function for the new size
deleting the oldest keys so that the load factor decreases
More than one of the above
exp: Rehashing builds a larger table and re-inserts every key using the hash function for the new size.
concept: As keys are added, the load factor α = n/m grows and operations slow down. When α crosses a threshold (e.g. 0.75 for chaining, often 0.5 for open addressing), the table is rehashed: a new, larger table is created (often about twice the size, frequently a prime), and every key is inserted again using the hash function for the new size. Keys must be re-inserted because h(k) = k mod m changes when m changes. Rehashing costs O(n), but it happens rarely, so the average (amortised) cost per insertion stays O(1).
why: A — Wrong. Sorting keys inside the same table does not help: each key's slot is decided by the hash function, and sorting would break that link. The table size also stays the same, so α does not fall.
B — Correct. Rehashing creates a larger table and re-inserts every key with the hash function for the new size, which lowers α.
C — Wrong. A hash table must not throw away keys the user has stored. Removing old entries is what a cache with an eviction policy (such as LRU) does; it is not rehashing.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A table of size 5 using h(k) = k mod 5 and linear probing holds 12, 17, 22 (inserted in this order). It is rehashed into a new table of size 11 using h(k) = k mod 11 and linear probing, re-inserting the keys in the same order. In which slot is 22 now?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: In the new table 22 mod 11 = 0 with no collision, so 22 is in slot 0.
concept: During rehashing each key's position is computed afresh with the new hash function; its old slot number means nothing in the new table. A larger table often removes collisions that happened in the old one.
work:
Old table (size 5, h = k mod 5): 12 → 2; 17 → 2 full → 3; 22 → 2, 3 full → 4
New table (size 11, h = k mod 11), same order:
12 → 12 mod 11 = 1 → slot 1
17 → 17 mod 11 = 6 → slot 6
22 → 22 mod 11 = 0 → slot 0 (free)
22 is now in slot 0
why: A — Wrong. 4 is 22's slot in the OLD table (after linear probing). Rehashing recomputes the slot with the new hash function.
B — Correct. 22 mod 11 = 0, and slot 0 is free, so 22 goes to slot 0.
C — Wrong. 2 is 22's home slot in the old table (22 mod 5 = 2), not in the new one.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Perfect hashing guarantees which of the following?
opts: O(1) worst-case search for any set of keys that changes frequently
That every key is stored in sorted order of its hash value
O(1) worst-case search for a static (fixed) set of keys, with no collisions
More than one of the above
exp: Perfect hashing gives collision-free, O(1) worst-case search for a static set of keys.
concept: Perfect hashing is used when the set of keys is static — fixed in advance and not changed later (for example the reserved words of a programming language, or the file names stored on a CD-ROM). A hash function is built specially for that set so that no two keys collide. The classic method (Fredman–Komlós–Szemerédi, described in Cormen) uses two levels of universal hashing with O(n) total space and gives O(1) worst-case search.
why: A — Wrong. Classic perfect hashing is designed for a static set. If keys are inserted and deleted often, the collision-free function would have to be rebuilt, so there is no such guarantee for a frequently changing set.
B — Wrong. Hashing, including perfect hashing, scatters keys over the table; it does not store them in sorted order.
C — Correct. For a fixed set of keys, perfect hashing gives no collisions and O(1) worst-case search.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In universal hashing, the hash function is:
opts: chosen at random from a family in which any two distinct keys collide with probability at most 1/m
a single fixed function that is collision-free for every possible set of keys
chosen so that all keys collide and are stored in one universal list
More than one of the above
exp: Universal hashing picks the hash function at random from a family in which two distinct keys collide with probability at most 1/m.
concept: With any single fixed hash function, someone can choose keys that all collide and make the table slow (O(n) per operation). Universal hashing avoids this by choosing the hash function at random, when the program starts, from a carefully designed family H. The family is universal if, for any two different keys, the chance that a randomly chosen h sends them to the same slot is at most 1/m. Then the expected performance is good for every input. A standard family is h(k) = ((a·k + b) mod p) mod m, with a prime p and random a, b.
why: A — Correct. This is the definition: h is picked at random from a family in which any two distinct keys collide with probability at most 1/m.

B — Wrong. No single fixed function can avoid collisions for every possible set of keys, because there are more possible keys than slots (pigeonhole principle). Universal hashing relies on randomness instead.
C — Wrong. Making all keys collide is the worst case — the exact opposite of what any hashing scheme wants.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What are the average-case and worst-case times to search for a key in a hash table with n keys (assuming a good hash function and a bounded load factor)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Searching a hash table takes O(1) time on average and O(n) in the worst case.
concept: With a good hash function and a bounded load factor, a search looks at only a constant number of slots or list nodes on average, so the average time is O(1). In the worst case, however, all n keys can hash to the same slot (one long chain or one long probe run), and a search must check all of them: O(n).
why: A — Correct. The average is O(1) because keys are spread evenly; the worst case is O(n) when all keys collide.
B — Wrong. O(log n) average is the search time of a balanced binary search tree (or binary search), not of a hash table.

C — Wrong. A standard hash table (linked-list chains or open addressing) has worst case O(n), not O(log n), because all keys may collide. (Some libraries, e.g. Java 8's HashMap, turn very long chains into balanced trees to get O(log n), but that is a special optimisation, not the standard answer.)
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are common applications of hashing?
opts: Storing passwords in a login system
More than one of the above
exp: Symbol tables, caches and password storage are all common applications of hashing.
concept: Hashing is used wherever fast lookup by key is needed, and also to make short 'fingerprints' of data. Examples: compilers keep identifiers in a hash-based symbol table; caches and in-memory key–value stores use hash maps; login systems store a hash of each password instead of the password itself; databases use hash indexes; downloaded files are checked with checksums.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is true, but B and C are true too, so the answer is D, not A alone. A compiler's symbol table maps each identifier name to its details (type, scope, address), and it is usually a hash table so that each lookup is O(1) on average.

B — Wrong. This statement is true, but A and C are true too, so the answer is D, not B alone. Caches (for example memcached, or a dictionary/HashMap inside a program) use hashing to find an item by its key in O(1) average time.

C — Wrong. This statement is true, but A and B are true too, so the answer is D, not C alone. Login systems store a cryptographic hash (ideally salted) of each password; at login the entered password is hashed and compared with it.
D — Correct. All three are applications of hashing, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are all true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A system stores only the hash of each user's password. Which statement is correct?
opts: The original password can be recovered by applying the inverse of the hash function
Login works by hashing the entered password and comparing it with the stored hash
Hashing is a form of symmetric encryption that uses a secret key for decryption
More than one of the above
exp: Login works by hashing the entered password and comparing it with the stored hash; the password itself is never recovered.
concept: A cryptographic hash function is one-way: it is easy to compute the hash of a password, but practically impossible to get the password back from the hash. So a system stores only the hash (usually with a random 'salt' added). At login it hashes the password the user typed and compares the result with the stored hash; if they match, the password was right. Hashing is not encryption: encryption uses a key and can be reversed (decrypted), while hashing uses no key and cannot be decrypted.
why: A — Wrong. A cryptographic hash has no inverse: many inputs can give the same hash, and the function is designed so that the input cannot be worked out from the output. Attackers can only guess passwords and hash each guess.
B — Correct. The entered password is hashed with the same function (and the same salt) and compared with the stored hash.
C — Wrong. Hashing is not encryption. Symmetric encryption (such as AES) uses a secret key and can be decrypted; a hash uses no key and cannot be decrypted.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is a true statement, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The property that every step of an algorithm must be precisely and unambiguously specified is called:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Definiteness is the property that every step of an algorithm is precise and unambiguous.
concept: Every algorithm must have five standard characteristics (as listed by Knuth): Input (zero or more), Output (at least one), Definiteness (every step is precise and unambiguous), Finiteness (it stops after a finite number of steps) and Effectiveness (every step is basic enough to be carried out exactly, in finite time, even with pencil and paper). Definiteness means no step can be read in two different ways.
why: A — Wrong. Finiteness means the algorithm must terminate after a finite number of steps. It is about stopping, not about clarity.
B — Correct. Definiteness means each step is precisely and unambiguously defined, so there is only one way to carry it out.
C — Wrong. Effectiveness means each step is simple enough to be performed exactly in a finite amount of time. A step can be clear yet not effective (for example, 'write down the exact value of π').
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Five properties: Input, Output, Definiteness, Finiteness, Effectiveness.

q: Which of the following is NOT a required property of an algorithm?
opts: It must terminate after a finite number of steps
It must produce at least one output
It must be written in a high-level programming language
More than one of the above
exp: An algorithm is language-independent, so being written in a high-level language is not required; finiteness and at least one output are required.
concept: An algorithm is a finite, step-by-step method for solving a problem, and it does not depend on any programming language. It can be written in plain English, in pseudocode or as a flowchart. A program is an algorithm expressed in a particular programming language. The required properties are input, output, definiteness, finiteness and effectiveness.
why: A — Wrong. Terminating after a finite number of steps (finiteness) IS a required property, so it does not answer this 'NOT required' question.
B — Wrong. Producing at least one output IS required; an algorithm that gives no result is of no use.
C — Correct. Being written in a high-level programming language is NOT required. An algorithm can be expressed in pseudocode, a flowchart or ordinary English.
D — Wrong. Only C is 'not required'; A and B are genuine requirements, so 'More than one of the above' is false.
E — Wrong. C is not a required property, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: As per the standard characteristics of an algorithm, how many inputs and outputs must it have?
opts: Zero or more inputs and at least one output
At least one input and zero or more outputs
Exactly one input and exactly one output
More than one of the above
exp: An algorithm has zero or more inputs and at least one output.
concept: An algorithm takes zero or more inputs and must produce at least one output. Zero inputs is allowed: for example, an algorithm that prints the first ten prime numbers needs no input. But it must produce some output, otherwise it achieves nothing.
why: A — Correct. Zero or more inputs and at least one output is the standard characteristic.
B — Wrong. It has the two parts reversed: inputs may be zero, but outputs must be at least one.
C — Wrong. This is too strict. Many algorithms take several inputs (GCD needs two numbers) or give several outputs (sorting outputs a whole list).
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The time complexity of an algorithm is usually expressed as:
opts: the running time in seconds measured on a particular computer
the number of basic operations executed, as a function of the input size n
the number of lines in the program's source code
More than one of the above
exp: Time complexity counts the basic operations performed as a function of the input size n, independent of any machine.
concept: Time complexity measures how the work done by an algorithm grows with the input size n. We count basic operations (comparisons, assignments, arithmetic) as a function T(n), instead of measuring seconds, so the result does not depend on a particular computer, compiler or programming language. T(n) is then described with O, Ω or Θ for large n.
why: A — Wrong. Seconds on one computer depend on the processor, the compiler and the system load. That is an experimental measurement (a posteriori testing), not time complexity.
B — Correct. Time complexity is the number of basic operations executed, written as a function of the input size n.
C — Wrong. The length of the source code says nothing about running time: a three-line loop can execute millions of steps.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following contribute to the variable (instance-dependent) part of an algorithm's space requirement?
opts: Recursion stack space that depends on the input size
Memory allocated dynamically according to the input size n
Space occupied by the program's instructions (code)
More than one of the above
exp: Recursion stack space and memory allocated according to n are instance-dependent; the code space is part of the fixed part.
concept: The space needed by a program P can be written as S(P) = c + S_P (Sahni/Horowitz). The fixed part c does not depend on the input: it includes the space for the instructions (code), simple variables and constants. The variable part S_P depends on the particular problem instance: memory allocated according to n, and the recursion stack, whose depth may grow with the input.
why: A — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so A alone is not the answer (choose D). Each active recursive call keeps an activation record on the stack, so if the recursion depth grows with n, this space grows with n.

B — Wrong. This option is true, but it is not the only true option, so B alone is not the answer (choose D). Memory allocated at run time according to n (for example an array of n elements made with malloc()) belongs to the variable part.
C — Wrong. The space for the program's instructions is the same for every input, so it belongs to the FIXED part, not the variable part.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so more than one of A–C is true.
E — Wrong. A and B are true statements, so 'None of the above' is false.

q: Worst-case analysis of an algorithm gives:
opts: an upper bound on the running time over all inputs of size n
the running time averaged over all inputs of size n
the minimum running time over all inputs of size n
More than one of the above
exp: Worst-case analysis gives the maximum running time for inputs of size n, an upper bound that holds for every input of that size.
concept: For a fixed input size n, different inputs can take different times. The worst case is the MAXIMUM time over all inputs of size n, the best case is the MINIMUM, and the average case is the expected time when inputs occur with given probabilities. Because no input of size n can take longer than the worst case, the worst-case time is an upper bound and a guarantee.
why: A — Correct. The worst case is the maximum time over all inputs of size n, so it bounds the running time of every such input from above.
B — Wrong. Averaging the running time over all inputs of size n is the AVERAGE-case analysis.
C — Wrong. The minimum running time over all inputs of size n is the BEST-case analysis.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In linear search on an array of n distinct elements, if the key is present and equally likely to be at any of the n positions, the average number of key comparisons is:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: On average the key is found after (1 + 2 + … + n)/n = (n + 1)/2 comparisons.
concept: Linear search compares the key with the elements one by one from the start. If the key is at position i, it needs i comparisons. When the key is present and equally likely to be at any of the n positions, the average number of comparisons is the average of 1, 2, …, n.
work:
Comparisons if key is at position i = i, each position with probability 1/n
Average = (1 + 2 + … + n) / n = [n(n + 1)/2] / n = (n + 1)/2
Check n = 5: (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5)/5 = 15/5 = 3 = (5 + 1)/2
