B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two least frequent nodes — a greedy choice.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly finalises the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance — a greedy choice.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: For which problem does the greedy strategy of taking items in decreasing order of value/weight ratio ALWAYS give an optimal solution?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The value/weight greedy rule is always optimal only for the fractional knapsack.
concept: In the fractional knapsack problem you may take part of an item, like pouring out some grain. Taking items in decreasing order of value per unit weight (value/weight ratio), plus a fraction of the last one, is always optimal. In 0/1 knapsack items cannot be broken, the same greedy rule can fail, and dynamic programming is used instead.
why: A — Wrong. For 0/1 knapsack the ratio rule can fail. Example: capacity 50 with items (60, 10), (100, 20), (120, 30): greedy takes 60 + 100 = 160, but the best is 100 + 120 = 220.
B — Wrong. The travelling salesman problem is NP-hard; no greedy rule (such as 'go to the nearest city') is guaranteed to find the optimal tour.
C — Correct. Fractional knapsack is solved optimally by the value/weight greedy rule.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Fractional knapsack: capacity 50; items (value, weight) = (60, 10), (100, 20), (120, 30). What is the maximum total value?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The maximum fractional-knapsack value is 240.
concept: Fractional knapsack: compute value/weight for each item, take items in decreasing order of this ratio, and when the next item does not fit completely, take the fraction that exactly fills the remaining capacity.
work:
Ratios: (60, 10) → 6; (100, 20) → 5; (120, 30) → 4
Take (60, 10) fully: value 60, capacity left 40
Take (100, 20) fully: value 160, capacity left 20
Take 20/30 of (120, 30): value 160 + 80 = 240, capacity left 0
Maximum value = 240
why: A — Wrong. 220 = 100 + 120 is the 0/1 knapsack answer (whole items only). Allowing fractions gives 240.
C — Wrong. 180 = 60 + 120 uses two whole items; it skips the higher-ratio item (100, 20) and the fractional part.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Fractional knapsack: capacity 15; items (value, weight) = (10, 2), (5, 3), (15, 5), (7, 7), (6, 1), (18, 4), (3, 1). What is the maximum total value?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The maximum value is about 55.33.
concept: Fractional knapsack: sort the items by value/weight ratio (highest first), take whole items while they fit, then take a fraction of the next item to fill the knapsack exactly. Items with equal ratios can be taken in either order.
work:
Ratios: (6, 1) 6; (10, 2) 5; (18, 4) 4.5; (15, 5) 3; (3, 1) 3; (5, 3) 1.67; (7, 7) 1
Take (6, 1): value 6, capacity left 14
Take (10, 2): value 16, left 12
Take (18, 4): value 34, left 8
Take (15, 5): value 49, left 3
Take (3, 1): value 52, left 2
Take 2/3 of (5, 3): value 52 + 3.33 = 55.33, left 0
Maximum value ≈ 55.33
why: A — Correct. Whole items worth 52 fill 13 units; the last 2 units take 2/3 of (5, 3), adding 3.33, for a total of 55.33.
B — Wrong. 52 is the value before the last 2 units are filled. In fractional knapsack the leftover capacity must be used.
C — Wrong. 49 is the value after only the first four items; it stops too early.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Activity selection: the activities (start, finish) are (1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11), (8,12), (2,14), (12,16). An activity may start when another finishes. What is the maximum number of mutually compatible activities?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The maximum is 4 activities — (1,4), (5,7), (8,11), (12,16) — which is not listed.
concept: Activity selection: sort the activities by finishing time and repeatedly pick the next activity that starts no earlier than the finish of the last chosen one. Picking the earliest finish leaves the most time for the rest, and this greedy choice is proven optimal.
work:
Sorted by finish: (1,4) (3,5) (0,6) (5,7) (3,9) (5,9) (6,10) (8,11) (8,12) (2,14) (12,16)
Pick (1,4); last finish 4
Skip (3,5), (0,6) (they start before 4); pick (5,7); last finish 7
Skip (3,9), (5,9), (6,10); pick (8,11); last finish 11
Skip (8,12), (2,14); pick (12,16)
Chosen: (1,4), (5,7), (8,11), (12,16) → 4 activities (a check of all subsets confirms that 4 is the maximum)
why: A — Wrong. 3 is too few; the greedy choice already finds 4 compatible activities.
B — Wrong. 5 mutually compatible activities do not exist; checking all subsets shows the maximum is 4.
C — Wrong. 6 is impossible for the same reason; at most 4 activities can be chosen without overlap.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 4), so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: The greedy algorithm for the activity-selection problem repeatedly picks:
opts: the compatible activity that finishes earliest
More than one of the above
exp: Activity selection greedily picks the compatible activity that finishes earliest.
concept: For activity selection the proven greedy rule is: always choose the compatible activity that FINISHES earliest. It leaves the largest possible free time for the remaining activities. Other natural rules (shortest activity first, earliest start first) can fail.
why: A — Wrong. Shortest-first can fail: a short activity in the middle can block two longer ones. With (1,5), (4,7), (6,10), shortest-first picks (4,7) and gets only 1 activity, while (1,5) and (6,10) give 2.
B — Correct. Earliest finish time is the rule proven optimal (Cormen).
C — Wrong. Earliest-start can fail: one long activity that starts first, such as (0,10), blocks many short ones such as (1,2) and (3,4).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Job sequencing with deadlines (each job takes one unit of time): jobs (profit, deadline) = J1 (100, 2), J2 (19, 1), J3 (27, 2), J4 (25, 1), J5 (15, 3). What is the maximum total profit?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The maximum profit is 142 (jobs J3, J1, J5).
concept: Job sequencing with deadlines: sort the jobs by profit (highest first). Put each job in the latest free time slot on or before its deadline; if no such slot is free, reject the job. Each job takes one unit of time.
work:
Sorted by profit: J1 (100, 2), J3 (27, 2), J4 (25, 1), J2 (19, 1), J5 (15, 3)
J1 → slot 2
J3 → slot 1 (slot 2 is taken)
J4 (deadline 1) → slot 1 is taken → rejected
J2 (deadline 1) → rejected
J5 → slot 3
Profit = 100 + 27 + 15 = 142
why: A — Correct. J3, J1 and J5 in slots 1, 2 and 3 earn 27 + 100 + 15 = 142.
B — Wrong. 127 = 100 + 27 forgets J5, which still fits in slot 3 (deadline 3).
C — Wrong. 152 = 100 + 27 + 25 would need J1, J3 and J4 all finished by time 2, but there are only 2 time slots up to then.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Coins of value 1, 3 and 4 are available in unlimited supply. To make 6, the greedy method (always take the largest coin that fits) uses how many coins, and what is the minimum possible?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Greedy uses 3 coins but the minimum is 2, so greedy is not optimal for coins 1, 3, 4.
concept: The greedy coin rule (always take the largest coin that fits) is optimal for 'canonical' coin systems such as 1, 2, 5, 10, but not for every set of coins. When it fails, dynamic programming finds the true minimum.
work:
Greedy for 6: take 4 (left 2), take 1 (left 1), take 1 (left 0) → 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins
Best: 3 + 3 = 2 coins (DP: minimum coins for amounts 0..6 = 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2)
why: A — Wrong. Greedy cannot finish in 2 coins here: it first takes 4, and the remaining 2 needs 1 + 1.
B — Wrong. The minimum is not 3: 3 + 3 = 6 uses only 2 coins.
C — Correct. Greedy uses 3 coins (4 + 1 + 1), but the optimum is 2 coins (3 + 3).
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Characters a, b, c, d, e, f occur with frequencies 5, 9, 12, 13, 16 and 45. Using Huffman coding, what is the total number of bits needed to encode all the characters?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Huffman coding needs 224 bits in total.
concept: Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two least frequent nodes. The total number of bits = Σ (frequency × code length), which also equals the sum of the weights of all merged nodes.
why: A — Correct. Σ frequency × code length = 224 (also the sum of the merged weights).
B — Wrong. 300 = 100 × 3 is a fixed-length 3-bit code for 6 characters, not Huffman.
C — Wrong. 241 is more than the optimal 224; it does not come from the Huffman tree.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms is NOT true?
opts: Kruskal's algorithm considers edges in increasing order of weight
Prim's algorithm grows a single tree from a starting vertex
On the same connected graph they may produce MSTs of different total weight
More than one of the above
exp: C is not true: Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms always give MSTs of the same total weight.
concept: Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms both find a minimum spanning tree (MST). Kruskal sorts the edges by weight and adds the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle (it may hold several separate pieces for a while). Prim grows one tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge leaving the tree. With equal weights they may choose different MSTs, but every MST of a graph has the same total weight.
why: A — Wrong. This is true: Kruskal processes edges in increasing order of weight. A true statement does not answer a 'NOT true' question.
B — Wrong. This is true: Prim keeps a single tree and grows it one vertex at a time.
C — Correct. This is NOT true. Both produce a minimum spanning tree, and all MSTs of a graph have the same (minimum) total weight; only the chosen edges may differ when weights tie.
D — Wrong. Only C is a false statement; A and B are true, so 'More than one of the above' does not fit.
E — Wrong. C is a false statement, so one option does satisfy 'NOT true'.

q: Which two properties indicate that a problem can be solved by dynamic programming?
opts: Independent subproblems and a combine step
More than one of the above
exp: DP needs overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
concept: Dynamic programming (DP) fits a problem when (1) it has overlapping subproblems — the same smaller problems come up again and again — and (2) optimal substructure — the best solution is built from best solutions of subproblems. DP solves each subproblem once and stores the result in a table.
why: A — Correct. Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure are the two hallmarks of DP.
B — Wrong. The greedy-choice property and optimal substructure are the conditions for a greedy algorithm.
C — Wrong. Independent (non-overlapping) subproblems with a combine step describe divide and conquer.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which statement correctly compares memoization and tabulation?
opts: Memoization is bottom-up; tabulation is top-down
Memoization is top-down with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up with a table
More than one of the above
exp: Memoization is top-down with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up with a table.
concept: DP can be written in two ways. Memoization is top-down: write the natural recursion and keep a cache (memo), so each subproblem is computed only once. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table with loops, starting from the smallest subproblems, until the final answer is reached.
why: A — Wrong. This swaps the two: memoization is top-down and tabulation is bottom-up.
B — Correct. Memoization = recursion + cache (top-down); tabulation = loops filling a table (bottom-up).
C — Wrong. Both are dynamic programming techniques, not greedy ones.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: Memoization = 'make a memo' (a note) of each answer while recursing down.

q: Which of the following problems are classically solved using dynamic programming?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 0/1 knapsack, LCS and matrix chain multiplication are all classic DP problems.
concept: Classic dynamic programming problems include 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence (LCS), matrix chain multiplication, Floyd–Warshall, Bellman–Ford, optimal BST and edit distance. Each fills a table of subproblem answers built from smaller entries.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. 0/1 knapsack uses a table K[i][w] = best value using the first i items with capacity w.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. LCS uses a table L[i][j] = LCS length of the first i characters of X and the first j characters of Y.

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Matrix chain multiplication uses m[i][j] = minimum cost of multiplying matrices i to j.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How does dynamic programming differ from ordinary divide and conquer?
opts: Divide and conquer stores subproblem results while DP recomputes them
DP cannot be applied to optimisation problems
DP is used when subproblems overlap, so their results are stored and reused
More than one of the above
exp: DP is used when subproblems overlap, so each result is stored once and reused.
concept: Divide and conquer and DP both break a problem into subproblems. In divide and conquer the subproblems are independent (they share no sub-subproblems), so each is solved once anyway. When subproblems overlap, plain recursion would solve the same thing many times; DP stores each answer and reuses it.
why: A — Wrong. This is reversed: DP stores results, while plain divide and conquer recomputes any repeated subproblem.
B — Wrong. DP is used mainly FOR optimisation problems (knapsack, shortest paths, matrix chain).
C — Correct. DP is the right choice when subproblems overlap; storing and reusing their results avoids repeated work.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is the length of the longest common subsequence of X = ABCBDAB and Y = BDCABA?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The LCS length is 4 (for example BCBA), which is not listed.
concept: A subsequence keeps the order of the characters but may skip some (unlike a substring, which must be continuous). The LCS table: L[i][j] = L[i−1][j−1] + 1 if the i-th character of X equals the j-th character of Y, otherwise max(L[i−1][j], L[i][j−1]). The bottom-right cell gives the LCS length.
work:
Rows: X = A B C B D A B; columns: Y = B D C A B A
      B D C A B A
A:    0 0 0 1 1 1
B:    1 1 1 1 2 2
C:    1 1 2 2 2 2
B:    1 1 2 2 3 3
D:    1 2 2 2 3 3
A:    1 2 2 3 3 4
B:    1 2 2 3 4 4
L[7][6] = 4; one LCS is BCBA (others: BDAB, BCAB)
why: A — Wrong. 3 is too short; BCBA is a common subsequence of length 4.
B — Wrong. 5 is too long: the final cell of the DP table is 4, so no common subsequence of length 5 exists.
C — Wrong. 6 is the length of Y itself, and Y is not a subsequence of X.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 4), so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: What is the length of the longest common subsequence of AGGTAB and GXTXAYB?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The LCS of AGGTAB and GXTXAYB is GTAB, of length 4.
concept: A subsequence keeps the order of the characters but may skip some (unlike a substring, which must be continuous). The LCS table: L[i][j] = L[i−1][j−1] + 1 if the i-th character of X equals the j-th character of Y, otherwise max(L[i−1][j], L[i][j−1]). The bottom-right cell gives the LCS length.
work:
Rows: X = A G G T A B; columns: Y = G X T X A Y B
      G X T X A Y B
A:    0 0 0 0 1 1 1
G:    1 1 1 1 1 1 1
G:    1 1 1 1 1 1 1
T:    1 1 2 2 2 2 2
A:    1 1 2 2 3 3 3
B:    1 1 2 2 3 3 4
L[6][7] = 4; LCS = GTAB
why: A — Wrong. 3 is too short: GTA is common, but B also matches after it, giving GTAB.
B — Correct. GTAB appears in order in both strings, and the DP table confirms that 4 is the maximum.
C — Wrong. 5 is too long; the final table cell is 4.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: 0/1 knapsack: capacity 5; items (weight, value) = (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 6). What is the maximum value?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The maximum value is 7.
concept: 0/1 knapsack: each item is taken whole or not at all. The DP table K[i][w] = max(K[i−1][w], value_i + K[i−1][w − weight_i]), where the second choice is allowed only if item i fits. The answer is in the last cell.
why: A — Correct. Items (2, 3) and (3, 4) fit exactly (weight 5) for a value of 7.
B — Wrong. 6 is the value of the single item (5, 6); the pair (2, 3) + (3, 4) is better.
C — Wrong. 8 = 3 + 5 needs items of weight 2 + 4 = 6, which exceeds the capacity 5.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: 0/1 knapsack: capacity 10; items (weight, value) = (5, 10), (4, 40), (6, 30), (3, 50). What is the maximum value?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The maximum value is 90.
concept: 0/1 knapsack: each item is taken whole or not at all. The DP table K[i][w] = max(K[i−1][w], value_i + K[i−1][w − weight_i]), where the second choice is allowed only if item i fits. The answer is in the last cell. Items cannot be split, so the greedy ratio rule is not guaranteed to work (here it happens to give the same answer).
why: A — Wrong. 100 = 50 + 40 + 10 needs weight 3 + 4 + 5 = 12, which is more than 10.
B — Wrong. 80 = 50 + 30 (weight 3 + 6 = 9) is feasible but not the best.
C — Correct. Items (4, 40) and (3, 50) weigh 7 and are worth 90; no other feasible combination does better.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Matrices A (10 × 30), B (30 × 5) and C (5 × 60) are to be multiplied. What is the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The best order (AB)C needs 4500 scalar multiplications.
concept: Multiplying a p × q matrix by a q × r matrix needs p·q·r scalar multiplications. Matrix multiplication is associative, so the brackets can be placed in any order, and different orders can cost very different amounts. With three matrices there are only two orders, so compare both.
why: A — Wrong. 27000 is the cost of A(BC), the expensive order.
B — Correct. (AB)C costs 1500 + 3000 = 4500, the minimum.
C — Wrong. 9000 is only the cost of computing BC, which is just part of the A(BC) order.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Four matrices have dimensions 40 × 20, 20 × 30, 30 × 10 and 10 × 30. What is the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to multiply them?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The minimum number of scalar multiplications is 26000.
concept: Multiplying a p × q matrix by a q × r matrix needs p·q·r scalar multiplications. Matrix multiplication is associative, so the brackets can be placed in any order, and different orders can cost very different amounts. Matrix chain DP: m[i][j] = min over k of m[i][k] + m[k+1][j] + p(i−1)·p(k)·p(j), where matrix i has size p(i−1) × p(i). Fill the table for chains of length 2, then 3, then 4.
why: A — Wrong. 30000 does not match any bracketing; the five possible totals are 26000, 36000, 48000, 51000 and 69000.
B — Wrong. 24000 is only m[1,2], the cost of multiplying the first two matrices.
C — Correct. The DP gives m[1,4] = 26000 with the order (A1(A2A3))A4.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The naive recursive Fibonacci function takes exponential time. What is the time complexity of computing the nth Fibonacci number with memoization?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Memoized Fibonacci runs in Θ(n) time.
concept: Naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values again and again, which takes exponential time. With memoization, each fib(k) for k = 0..n is computed once and stored; later calls just look it up. So there are about n real computations, each O(1) (assuming constant-time addition): Θ(n).
work:
Naive: T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) + O(1) → exponential (about 1.618ⁿ calls)
Memoized: fib(n), fib(n − 1), …, fib(0) are each computed once → n + 1 computations → Θ(n)
why: A — Correct. Each of the n + 1 values is computed once, so the time is Θ(n).
B — Wrong. Θ(2ⁿ) (more exactly about 1.618ⁿ) describes the naive recursion without memoization.
C — Wrong. Θ(n²) would mean about n work per value; with memoization each value needs only one addition after two look-ups.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following algorithms are based on dynamic programming?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Floyd–Warshall and Bellman–Ford are based on DP; Prim's algorithm is greedy.
concept: Floyd–Warshall finds shortest paths allowing only vertices 1..k as intermediate stops, increasing k step by step (DP over k). Bellman–Ford finds the shortest paths that use at most i edges, for i = 1 to V − 1 (DP over the number of edges). Prim's algorithm is greedy: it always adds the cheapest edge leaving the current tree.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Floyd–Warshall: d_k[i][j] = min(d_(k−1)[i][j], d_(k−1)[i][k] + d_(k−1)[k][j]) — a classic DP recurrence.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Bellman–Ford relaxes all edges V − 1 times; after round i, the best paths using at most i edges are known — a DP over path length.
C — Wrong. Prim's algorithm is greedy, not dynamic programming.
D — Correct. A and B are both true (C is false), so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In what order does a backtracking algorithm explore the state-space tree?
opts: In increasing order of estimated cost
More than one of the above
exp: Backtracking explores the state-space tree depth-first.
concept: Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time, going as deep as possible (depth-first). When a partial solution breaks a constraint, it goes back (backtracks) to the last choice and tries the next option — like walking through a maze, following a path to a dead end and returning to the last junction.
why: A — Wrong. Breadth-first (level by level) order is used by FIFO branch and bound, not by backtracking.
B — Correct. Backtracking is a depth-first search of the state-space tree with pruning.
C — Wrong. Expanding nodes in increasing order of estimated cost is least-cost (LC) branch and bound.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are classic backtracking problems?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: N-Queens, sum of subsets and graph colouring are all classic backtracking problems.
concept: Backtracking suits problems where we must find arrangements that satisfy constraints: make choices one by one, and undo the last choice when a constraint is broken. Classic examples are N-Queens, sum of subsets, graph colouring, Hamiltonian cycles and Sudoku.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. N-Queens places one queen per row and backtracks when the new queen is attacked.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Sum of subsets includes or excludes each number and backtracks when the partial sum exceeds the target (or can no longer reach it).

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Graph (m-)colouring gives each vertex a colour in turn and backtracks when two adjacent vertices get the same colour.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many distinct solutions does the 4-Queens problem have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The 4-Queens problem has 2 solutions.
concept: N-Queens: place N queens on an N × N board so that no two share a row, column or diagonal. Backtracking places one queen per row. For N = 4 there are exactly 2 solutions, and they are mirror images of each other.
work:
Column of the queen in rows 1–4:
Solution 1: 2, 4, 1, 3
Solution 2: 3, 1, 4, 2
Every other placement fails (a backtracking program finds exactly 2 solutions).
why: A — Wrong. 1 is the count if mirror images are treated as the same solution; as distinct boards there are 2.
B — Correct. (2, 4, 1, 3) and (3, 1, 4, 2) are the only two solutions.
C — Wrong. 4 is too many; only two arrangements work.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: How many distinct solutions does the 8-Queens problem have?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The 8-Queens problem has 92 distinct solutions, which is not listed.
concept: The 8-Queens problem has 92 distinct solutions. If solutions that are rotations or reflections of each other are counted as the same, there are 12 'fundamental' solutions.
work:
A backtracking program counts 92 solutions.
Grouping by symmetry: 11 fundamental solutions have 8 versions each and 1 has only 4 → 11 × 8 + 4 = 92.
why: A — Wrong. 64 is the number of squares on the board, not the number of solutions.
B — Wrong. 12 is the number of fundamental solutions (up to rotation and reflection). The word 'only' makes it wrong: there are 92 distinct solutions.
C — Wrong. 96 = 12 × 8 assumes every fundamental solution has 8 versions, but one of them is symmetric under a half-turn and has only 4 (11 × 8 + 4 = 92).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so there cannot be two true options.
E — Correct. None of A–C is true (the correct answer is 92), so 'None of the above' is the answer.
tip: 4-Queens: 2 solutions. 8-Queens: 92 (12 fundamental).

q: Branch and bound differs from backtracking mainly because branch and bound:
opts: uses a bound on the best achievable cost of each node to prune it, and is mainly used for optimisation problems
always explores the state-space tree depth-first
never prunes any node of the state-space tree
More than one of the above
exp: Branch and bound prunes nodes using a bound on the best achievable cost, and it is used mainly for optimisation problems.
concept: Branch and bound (B&B) explores a state-space tree like backtracking but is used for optimisation (finding the best solution). At each node it computes a bound: the best value any solution below that node could reach. If this bound is no better than the best solution found so far, the whole subtree is pruned. Live nodes can be expanded in FIFO, LIFO or least-cost order.
why: A — Correct. B&B uses bounds to prune nodes that cannot beat the current best, and it is used mainly for optimisation problems (TSP, 0/1 knapsack, job assignment).
B — Wrong. B&B does not always go depth-first: FIFO B&B explores breadth-first and LC B&B picks the cheapest node. Depth-first order is typical of backtracking.
C — Wrong. Pruning is the whole point of B&B; without it, it would just be brute force.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In least-cost (LC) branch and bound, which live node is expanded next?
opts: The most recently generated live node
The live node with the lowest estimated cost
More than one of the above
exp: LC branch and bound expands the live node with the lowest estimated cost.
concept: In branch and bound, 'live' nodes are generated but not yet expanded. The method decides which live node to expand next: FIFO B&B uses a queue (oldest first), LIFO B&B uses a stack (newest first), and least-cost (LC) B&B uses a priority queue and expands the live node with the lowest estimated cost.
why: A — Wrong. Taking the most recently generated node is LIFO (stack-based) branch and bound.
B — Wrong. Taking the oldest live node is FIFO (queue-based) branch and bound.
C — Correct. LC branch and bound expands the live node with the smallest estimated cost.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The complexity class P consists of decision problems that:
opts: can be solved by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time
can only be verified, never solved
cannot be solved by any algorithm
More than one of the above
exp: P = decision problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time.
concept: P is the class of decision (yes/no) problems that an ordinary (deterministic) computer can solve in polynomial time, i.e. O(n^k) for some fixed k. Examples: sorting, shortest paths, minimum spanning tree. These are considered 'efficiently solvable'.
why: A — Correct. This is the definition of P.
B — Wrong. Every problem in P can be solved (and so also verified) in polynomial time; 'can only be verified, never solved' does not describe P.
C — Wrong. Problems that no algorithm can solve are undecidable (like the halting problem); they lie outside P.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The class NP consists of decision problems:
opts: that are 'Not Polynomial' and always need exponential time
whose proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time
that can be solved only on quantum computers
More than one of the above
exp: NP = decision problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time.
concept: NP stands for 'Nondeterministic Polynomial time'. A decision problem is in NP if, whenever the answer is 'yes', a proposed solution (certificate) can be checked in polynomial time. For example, checking a filled Sudoku grid is fast even when finding it is hard. Every problem in P is also in NP.
why: A — Wrong. NP does NOT mean 'Not Polynomial'. P ⊆ NP, so many NP problems (all of P) are solvable in polynomial time.
B — Correct. NP = problems whose 'yes' certificates can be verified in polynomial time.
C — Wrong. NP is defined with ordinary (nondeterministic) Turing machines; it has nothing to do with quantum computers.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements is correct?
opts: Every NP-hard problem is in NP
NP-complete problems are exactly those that are both in NP and NP-hard
More than one of the above
exp: NP-complete problems are exactly those that are both in NP and NP-hard.
concept: NP-hard means 'at least as hard as every problem in NP': every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. An NP-hard problem need not be in NP (the halting problem is NP-hard but undecidable). NP-complete problems are those that are both in NP and NP-hard: NP-complete = NP ∩ NP-hard. NP is NOT a subset of NP-hard.
why: A — Wrong. Many NP problems are easy (every problem in P is also in NP), and an easy problem is not NP-hard unless P = NP. So NP is not a subset of NP-hard.
B — Wrong. Some NP-hard problems are not in NP at all: the halting problem is NP-hard but undecidable, so it cannot be in NP.
C — Correct. NP-complete = NP ∩ NP-hard: in NP and at least as hard as every NP problem.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: NP-complete = NP ∩ NP-hard. NP-hard problems may lie outside NP.

q: Which problem was the first to be proved NP-complete (Cook–Levin theorem)?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SAT was the first problem proved NP-complete (Cook–Levin theorem).
concept: The Cook–Levin theorem (Stephen Cook 1971, and Leonid Levin independently) proved that Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete by showing that every NP problem can be converted to SAT in polynomial time. After that, other problems were proved NP-complete by reducing SAT (or another known NP-complete problem) to them; Richard Karp listed 21 such problems in 1972.
why: A — Wrong. The decision version of TSP is NP-complete, but this was shown later by reduction (via Hamiltonian cycle), not by the Cook–Levin theorem.
B — Correct. SAT was the first problem proved NP-complete (Cook–Levin theorem).
C — Wrong. Graph colouring (with k ≥ 3 colours) is NP-complete, but it was proved later by reduction (it is among Karp's 21 problems).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following problems are in P?
opts: Single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights
More than one of the above
exp: Sorting, shortest paths with non-negative weights and minimum spanning tree are all in P.
concept: A problem is in P if some algorithm solves it in polynomial time. Sorting (O(n log n)), single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights (Dijkstra) and minimum spanning tree (Kruskal or Prim) all have polynomial algorithms. (Strictly, P contains decision versions, such as 'is there a path of length at most k?'.)
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Merge sort or heap sort sort n numbers in O(n log n), which is polynomial.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Dijkstra's algorithm solves it in O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap — polynomial.
C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm finds an MST in O(E log V) — polynomial.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all true, so more than one of A–C is true and 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following problems is NOT NP-complete? (Assume P ≠ NP.)
opts: More than one of the above
exp: 2-SAT is solvable in polynomial time, so (assuming P ≠ NP) it is not NP-complete.
concept: SAT asks whether a Boolean formula can be made true. 3-SAT (every clause has 3 literals) is NP-complete. 2-SAT (every clause has 2 literals) is much easier: it can be solved in linear time using an implication graph and strongly connected components, so it is in P. Assuming P ≠ NP, a problem in P is not NP-complete.
why: A — Wrong. 3-SAT is NP-complete (shown by reduction from SAT, one of the earliest NP-completeness results).
B — Wrong. Vertex cover (decision version: is there a cover with at most k vertices?) is NP-complete; it is one of Karp's 21 problems.
C — Correct. 2-SAT is in P (linear time via strongly connected components), so with P ≠ NP it is not NP-complete.
D — Wrong. Only C is not NP-complete; A and B are NP-complete, so 'More than one of the above' does not fit.
E — Wrong. C (2-SAT) is not NP-complete, so one option does satisfy the stem.
tip: 2-SAT: easy (in P). 3-SAT: NP-complete.

q: The halting problem is:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The halting problem is undecidable.
concept: A problem is undecidable if no algorithm can give the correct yes/no answer for every input, no matter how much time it is allowed. Alan Turing proved in 1936 that the halting problem — 'does this program stop on this input?' — is undecidable. It is NP-hard (every NP problem reduces to it) but not in NP, so it is not NP-complete.
why: A — Wrong. NP-complete problems must be in NP, which means they are decidable. The halting problem is not even decidable, so it is not NP-complete (it is NP-hard).
B — Wrong. No algorithm solves the halting problem at all, let alone in polynomial time.
C — Correct. Turing proved that no algorithm can decide halting for all programs and inputs.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: If any one NP-complete problem is solved in polynomial time, then:
opts: only that one problem moves into P
More than one of the above
exp: A polynomial-time algorithm for any NP-complete problem would prove P = NP.
concept: Every problem in NP reduces in polynomial time to any NP-complete problem. So if one NP-complete problem had a polynomial-time algorithm, every NP problem could be solved in polynomial time by first reducing it to that problem. That would mean P = NP. This is why NP-complete problems are called the hardest problems in NP.
why: A — Correct. All of NP reduces to that problem, so all of NP would be in P, i.e. P = NP.
B — Wrong. It would prove the opposite: P = NP, not P ≠ NP.
C — Wrong. Because every NP problem reduces to it, the effect spreads to the whole of NP, not just to that one problem.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Problem X reduces to problem Y in polynomial time (X ≤ₚ Y). If Y is in P, then:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: If X ≤p Y and Y is in P, then X is also in P.
concept: X ≤p Y means any instance of X can be converted in polynomial time into an instance of Y with the same answer, so Y is at least as hard as X. If Y is easy (in P), X is easy too: convert, then solve Y. If X is hard (NP-hard), Y is hard too. Easiness flows from Y back to X; hardness flows from X to Y.
why: A — Wrong. Nothing here makes Y NP-hard; Y is in P. (Y would be NP-hard only if an NP-hard problem reduced to it.)
B — Correct. Solve X by converting it to Y in polynomial time and running Y's polynomial algorithm: X is in P.
C — Wrong. X is in P, so it need not be NP-complete; X can be any easy problem.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
tip: X ≤p Y: Y easy → X easy; X hard → Y hard.

q: Which of the following decision problems is NOT NP-complete?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: All three are NP-complete, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: Many famous decision problems are NP-complete: SAT, 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover, independent set, Hamiltonian cycle, TSP (decision), subset sum, 0/1 knapsack (decision) and graph colouring with k ≥ 3. All of them are in NP, and every NP problem reduces to each of them.
why: A — Wrong. Hamiltonian cycle (is there a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once?) is NP-complete, so it does not answer the 'NOT' question.
B — Wrong. Clique (is there a complete subgraph with k vertices?) is NP-complete.
C — Wrong. Subset sum (is there a subset adding up to exactly t?) is NP-complete; its DP is only pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial in the input size.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is 'NOT NP-complete', so there cannot be two such options.
E — Correct. Hamiltonian cycle, clique and subset sum are all NP-complete, so none of them fits 'NOT NP-complete', and 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: In a multistage graph the vertices are divided into k ≥ 2 stages, and every edge goes from a vertex in stage i to a vertex in stage i + 1. The problem of finding a minimum-cost path from the source (stage 1) to the sink (stage k) is classically solved by:
opts: dynamic programming, computing for each vertex j: cost(j) = min over edges j→l of [c(j, l) + cost(l)], stage by stage
the greedy method of always taking the cheapest edge out of the current vertex
backtracking over all possible orders of the stages
More than one of the above
exp: The multistage-graph shortest path is a standard dynamic-programming problem, solved stage by stage with cost(j) = min[c(j, l) + cost(l)].
concept: A multistage graph is a directed graph whose vertices are split into stages V1, V2, …, Vk, with only the source in V1 and only the sink in Vk; every edge goes from one stage to the next. Every source-to-sink path passes through exactly one vertex of each stage, so the best path can be built stage by stage. In the forward approach (Horowitz–Sahni), cost(j) is the cheapest cost from vertex j to the sink, computed from the last stage backwards: cost(j) = min over edges j→l of [c(j, l) + cost(l)]. The backward approach does the same from the source. With adjacency lists this takes Θ(V + E) time. Resource-allocation problems are often modelled as multistage graphs.
why: A — Correct. The principle of optimality holds: a best path from any vertex to the sink is one edge followed by a best path from the next stage, so DP computes every vertex's cost once and combines them.

B — Wrong. Taking the cheapest edge at each step can lead into an expensive later stage — for example, an edge of cost 1 followed by edges of cost 7 and 5 (total 13) is worse than 3 + 2 + 2 = 7. Greedy does not guarantee the optimum here.

C — Wrong. The order of the stages is fixed (1, 2, …, k), so there is nothing to permute. Trying all paths by backtracking would take exponential time, while DP needs only time linear in the size of the graph.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A 4-stage graph has source S (stage 1), vertices A, B, C (stage 2), D, E (stage 3) and sink T (stage 4). Edge costs: S→A 2, S→B 1, S→C 3; A→D 4, A→E 6, B→D 7, B→E 9, C→D 3, C→E 2; D→T 5, E→T 2. What is the minimum cost from S to T, and along which path?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: DP gives cost(S) = 7 along S–C–E–T; the greedy choice S–B–D–T costs 13.
concept: Solve a multistage graph backwards: first find the cost from each stage-(k − 1) vertex to the sink, then use those values to get the costs of the stage before, and so on back to the source. At each vertex keep the cheapest choice 'edge cost + cost of the next vertex', and remember which next vertex gave it, so the best path can be read off at the end.
work:
Stage 3 (cost to T): cost(D) = 5, cost(E) = 2
Stage 2: cost(A) = min(4 + 5, 6 + 2) = min(9, 8) = 8 (via E)
cost(B) = min(7 + 5, 9 + 2) = min(12, 11) = 11 (via E)
cost(C) = min(3 + 5, 2 + 2) = min(8, 4) = 4 (via E)
Stage 1: cost(S) = min(2 + 8, 1 + 11, 3 + 4) = min(10, 12, 7) = 7 (via C)
Path: S → C → E → T = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7
Greedy (cheapest edge each time): S→B (1), B→D (7), D→T (5) = 13
why: A — Wrong. 13 is what the greedy method gives: the cheapest first edge S→B (1), then B→D (7) and D→T (5). The cheap first edge leads into an expensive part of the graph.
B — Wrong. S–A–E–T costs 2 + 6 + 2 = 10. It is a valid path but not the cheapest; S–C–E–T costs only 7.
C — Correct. Working backwards: cost(E) = 2, cost(C) = min(3 + 5, 2 + 2) = 4, and cost(S) = min(2 + 8, 1 + 11, 3 + 4) = 7, reached through C and then E.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: In the reliability design problem, a system consists of n devices connected in series, and at stage i there are m_i copies of device i connected in parallel. If each copy of device i works with probability r_i (independently of the others), what is the reliability of stage i?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: A parallel stage works unless all its copies fail: φ_i = 1 − (1 − r_i)^(m_i).
concept: In reliability design we want the most reliable system within a cost limit. Devices connected in series must all work, so the system reliability is the PRODUCT of the stage reliabilities. To make a stage more reliable, several copies of its device are connected in parallel: the stage fails only if ALL its m copies fail, which has probability (1 − r)^m, so the stage works with probability 1 − (1 − r)^m. Choosing how many copies to buy for each stage under a total budget is solved by dynamic programming.
why: A — Wrong. r^m is the probability that ALL m copies work. A parallel stage needs only ONE working copy, so its reliability is higher than r, whereas r^m is lower than r.
B — Correct. The stage fails only if every copy fails, which has probability (1 − r_i)^(m_i); so it works with probability 1 − (1 − r_i)^(m_i).
C — Wrong. m·r can exceed 1 (for example 3 × 0.9 = 2.7), so it cannot be a probability. Reliabilities of parallel copies are not simply added.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: A system has three stages connected in series. The devices have reliabilities 0.9, 0.8 and 0.5, and the design uses 1, 2 and 2 copies of them in parallel, respectively. What is the reliability of the whole system?
opts: More than one of the above
concept: In reliability design we want the most reliable system within a cost limit. Devices connected in series must all work, so the system reliability is the PRODUCT of the stage reliabilities. To make a stage more reliable, several copies of its device are connected in parallel: the stage fails only if ALL its m copies fail, which has probability (1 − r)^m, so the stage works with probability 1 − (1 − r)^m. Choosing how many copies to buy for each stage under a total budget is solved by dynamic programming. So: parallel copies → 1 − (1 − r)^m for the stage; series stages → multiply.
why: A — Correct. The stage reliabilities are 0.9, 0.96 and 0.75, and their product is 0.648.
B — Wrong. 0.36 = 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.5 is the reliability with only ONE copy of each device; it ignores the extra parallel copies.
C — Wrong. 0.144 = 0.9 × 0.8² × 0.5² treats the copies as if they were in series (all must work). Parallel copies increase reliability; they do not reduce it.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Keys 10 < 20 < 30 are searched with frequencies 3, 2 and 5 (only successful searches). The cost of a BST is Σ frequency × (level of the key), with the root at level 1. What is the minimum possible cost, i.e. the cost of the optimal BST?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The optimal BST has root 30, left child 10 and 20 as the right child of 10, with cost 17.
concept: An optimal binary search tree (OBST) is the BST that minimises the total (or expected) search cost Σ f(k) × level(k) for the given search frequencies. A balanced shape is not always best: a frequently searched key should be near the root. The DP recurrence is cost(i, j) = W(i, j) + min over roots r of [cost(i, r − 1) + cost(r + 1, j)], where W(i, j) is the sum of the frequencies of keys i..j; the straightforward algorithm takes O(n³) time.
work:
All 5 BSTs on 3 keys (cost = Σ f × level):
Root 20 (10 left, 30 right): 2×1 + 3×2 + 5×2 = 18
Root 30, 10 left, 20 right child of 10: 5×1 + 3×2 + 2×3 = 17 ← minimum
Root 30, 20 left, 10 left child of 20: 5×1 + 2×2 + 3×3 = 18
Root 10, 30 right, 20 left child of 30: 3×1 + 5×2 + 2×3 = 19
Root 10, 20 right, 30 right child of 20: 3×1 + 2×2 + 5×3 = 22
DP check: W = 3 + 2 + 5 = 10; roots 10, 20, 30 give 0 + c(20,30) = 9, c(10) + c(30) = 3 + 5 = 8, c(10,20) + 0 = 7
cost = 10 + min(9, 8, 7) = 17 (root 30)
why: A — Wrong. 18 is the cost of the perfectly balanced tree with 20 at the root (2 + 3×2 + 5×2). Balance is not the goal; the heavy key 30 should be closer to the root.
B — Correct. With 30 at the root, 10 as its left child and 20 as the right child of 10, the cost is 5×1 + 3×2 + 2×3 = 17, the smallest of all five possible BSTs.
C — Wrong. 22 is the worst choice: the chain 10 → 20 → 30 puts the most frequent key, 30, at the deepest level (3×1 + 2×2 + 5×3 = 22).
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which statement about the optimal binary search tree (OBST) problem is TRUE?
opts: It finds the BST with the minimum expected search cost for given search probabilities, and it is solved by dynamic programming
The optimal BST always has the most frequently searched key at its root
It is solved optimally by a greedy method that inserts the keys in decreasing order of frequency
More than one of the above
exp: OBST minimises the expected search cost and is solved by dynamic programming; greedy 'most frequent key at the root' rules can fail.
concept: Given sorted keys and the probability (frequency) of searching for each key (and, in the full version, for each gap between keys), the OBST problem asks for the BST with the smallest expected search cost. The left and right subtrees of an optimal tree must themselves be optimal (optimal substructure), and the same ranges of keys are needed again and again (overlapping subproblems), so dynamic programming is used: cost(i, j) = W(i, j) + min over r of [cost(i, r − 1) + cost(r + 1, j)]. Simple greedy rules such as 'put the most frequent key at the root' can fail.
why: A — Correct. OBST minimises the expected (weighted) search cost; a DP table over ranges of keys gives the optimum in O(n³) time (O(n²) with Knuth's improvement).

B — Wrong. Not always. With keys 1 < 2 < 3 and frequencies 34, 33, 33, putting key 1 at the root gives at best 34 + 33×2 + 33×3 = 199, while putting 2 at the root gives 33 + 2×(34 + 33) = 167. The middle key wins even though key 1 is the most frequent.

C — Wrong. Inserting keys in decreasing order of frequency is a greedy heuristic that can give a lopsided tree; with frequencies 34, 33, 33 it builds the chain 1 → 2 → 3 of cost 199 instead of the optimum 167. Only DP guarantees the optimum.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: What is the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (LIS) of the sequence 5, 2, 8, 6, 3, 6, 9, 7?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: LIS = 4 (for example 2, 3, 6, 9).
concept: A subsequence keeps the order of the elements but may skip some of them (it need not be contiguous). The DP solution computes L[i], the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ENDS at a[i], as 1 + the largest L[j] over earlier elements with a[j] < a[i] (or 1 if there is none). The answer is the maximum L[i]. This takes Θ(n²) time; a cleverer method using binary search takes Θ(n log n).
work:
L[i] = 1 + max{L[j] : j < i and a[j] < a[i]} (1 if no such j)
a: 5 2 8 6 3 6 9 7
L: 1 1 2 2 2 3 4 4
5 → 1; 2 → 1; 8 (after 5 or 2) → 2; 6 (after 5 or 2) → 2; 3 (after 2) → 2; 6 (after 3) → 3; 9 (after the second 6) → 4; 7 (after the second 6) → 4
LIS length = max L = 4, e.g. 2, 3, 6, 9 or 2, 3, 6, 7
why: A — Wrong. 3 is the length of increasing subsequences such as 5, 8, 9 or 2, 6, 9, but a longer one exists: 2, 3, 6, 9.
B — Correct. The DP table L = 1 1 2 2 2 3 4 4 has maximum 4, reached by 2, 3, 6, 9 (or 2, 3, 6, 7).
C — Wrong. 5 would need, for example, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9 — but 9 comes before 7 in the sequence, so that is not a subsequence. No element has L greater than 4.
D — Wrong. Only B is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. B is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The edit distance (Levenshtein distance) between two strings is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to change one into the other. What is the edit distance between SUNDAY and SATURDAY?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: SUNDAY → SATURDAY needs 3 edits (two insertions and one substitution); 3 is not listed.
concept: Edit distance is a classic dynamic-programming problem. D[i][j] = edit distance between the first i characters of s and the first j characters of t, with D[i][0] = i and D[0][j] = j, and D[i][j] = min(D[i−1][j] + 1 (delete), D[i][j−1] + 1 (insert), D[i−1][j−1] + (0 if the characters are equal, else 1) (match or substitute)). The table has (m + 1)(n + 1) entries, so the time is Θ(mn). The difference in the lengths of the strings is always a lower bound.
work:
SATURDAY has 8 letters and SUNDAY 6 → at least 2 insertions are needed
Alignment:  S - - U N D A Y
            S A T U R D A Y
Insert A and T after S, substitute N → R; S, U, D, A, Y stay
Edit distance = 3 (DP table entry D[6][8] = 3), which is not listed
why: A — Wrong. 2 is only the difference in lengths (8 − 6), i.e. the two insertions. After inserting two letters, the word still differs from SATURDAY at N/R, so a third operation (a substitution) is needed.
B — Wrong. 4 is not the minimum: inserting A and T and substituting N by R (3 operations) is enough.
C — Wrong. 5 counts unnecessary operations, for example replacing letters that already match. The DP table gives 3.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.
E — Correct. None of A, B or C is true. The minimum is 3 (insert A, insert T, substitute N → R), which is not listed, so 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Coins of 2, 3 and 5 rupees are available in unlimited numbers. In how many different ways can an amount of 10 rupees be made, if the order of the coins does NOT matter?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Order-independent combinations: {2,2,2,2,2}, {2,2,3,3}, {2,3,5}, {5,5} — 4 ways.
concept: The coin-change counting problem asks for the number of different combinations of coins that make an amount N. DP: ways[0] = 1, and for each coin c (outer loop) and each amount x from c to N (inner loop), ways[x] += ways[x − c]. Putting the coins in the OUTER loop counts each combination once, whatever the order; swapping the two loops would count ordered sequences instead. Time Θ(k·N) for k coin types. (The related 'minimum number of coins' problem is also solved by DP, because the greedy method can fail.)
work:
DP over coins: ways[0] = 1; for each coin c, for x = c … 10: ways[x] += ways[x − c]
After coin 2: ways[10] = 1 (2+2+2+2+2)
After coin 3: ways[10] = 2 (adds 2+2+3+3)
After coin 5: ways[10] = 4 (adds 5+5 and 2+3+5)
The 4 ways: {2,2,2,2,2}, {2,2,3,3}, {2,3,5}, {5,5}
(If order mattered, e.g. 2+3+5 and 5+3+2 counted separately, there would be 14 sequences.)
why: A — Correct. The combinations are {2,2,2,2,2}, {2,2,3,3}, {2,3,5} and {5,5}: four ways.
B — Wrong. 14 counts ORDERED sequences (2+3+5, 2+5+3, 3+2+5, … are counted separately). The question says the order does not matter.
C — Wrong. 3 misses the mixed combination {2, 3, 5}, which uses one coin of each value.
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following are classic applications of dynamic programming?
opts: Longest increasing subsequence of n numbers, in Θ(n²) time
Edit distance between strings of lengths m and n, in Θ(mn) time
Counting the ways to make change for an amount N with k coin types, in Θ(kN) time
More than one of the above
exp: LIS, edit distance and coin-change counting are all classic dynamic-programming problems.
concept: Dynamic programming fits problems with optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Classic DP problems include 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, matrix-chain multiplication, multistage graphs, reliability design, optimal BST, Floyd–Warshall and Bellman–Ford — and also the three listed here. LIS uses L[i] = 1 + max L[j] (j < i, a[j] < a[i]); edit distance fills an (m + 1) × (n + 1) table; coin-change counting uses ways[x] += ways[x − c]. (Θ(kN) for coin change is called pseudo-polynomial, because it grows with the VALUE N rather than with the number of digits of N.)
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. L[i] depends on the L-values of earlier elements, which are reused many times; filling the table takes Θ(n²) time (Θ(n log n) with binary search).

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. D[i][j] uses D[i−1][j], D[i][j−1] and D[i−1][j−1]; there are (m + 1)(n + 1) entries, each found in O(1), giving Θ(mn).

C — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. ways[x] is built from ways[x − c] for each coin c; with k coin types and amounts 0..N this takes Θ(kN) time.
D — Correct. A, B and C are all three true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A, B and C are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following problems is NOT usually solved by backtracking?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: Rat in a maze, knight's tour and Hamiltonian cycle are all classic backtracking problems, so the answer is 'None of the above'.
concept: Backtracking builds a solution step by step (depth-first through the state-space tree) and abandons a partial solution as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer, then goes back and tries the next choice. Classic backtracking problems: N-Queens, sum of subsets, graph (m-)colouring, Hamiltonian cycle, rat in a maze, knight's tour, and generating all k-ary strings or permutations. Rat in a maze: find a path through the open cells of a grid. Knight's tour: move a knight so that it visits every square of the board exactly once (a Hamiltonian path in the 'knight's graph'). Hamiltonian cycle: a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once.
why: A — Wrong. Rat in a maze IS a standard backtracking problem: the rat tries a move, and if it reaches a dead end it backs up and tries the next direction. So it does not answer the question.
B — Wrong. Knight's tour IS a standard backtracking problem: the knight moves to an unvisited square, and the move is undone when no further move is possible. So it is not a 'NOT' item.

C — Wrong. Hamiltonian cycle IS a standard backtracking problem: the path is extended one vertex at a time and the algorithm backs up when the next vertex would repeat or no edge exists. So it does not answer the question.
D — Wrong. None of A–C is a problem that is NOT solved by backtracking, so 'More than one of the above' is also wrong.
E — Correct. All three — rat in a maze, knight's tour and Hamiltonian cycle — are classic backtracking problems, so none of them is a 'NOT' item. Hence 'None of the above' is the answer.

q:
A rat starts at the top-left cell (0, 0) of the 4 × 4 maze below (1 = open, 0 = wall) and must reach the bottom-right cell (3, 3), moving only RIGHT or DOWN through open cells. How many different paths are there?
Row 0: 1 1 0 1
Row 1: 1 1 1 1
Row 2: 0 1 0 1
Row 3: 1 1 1 1
opts: More than one of the above
exp: There are 4 right/down paths through the open cells.
concept: In the rat-in-a-maze problem, backtracking moves the rat one step at a time into an open cell. If the rat reaches a dead end (no allowed move leads to the goal), the algorithm undoes the last move and tries the next direction. To count all paths, the search continues after each success instead of stopping. With only right/down moves the count also follows the simple recurrence paths(i, j) = paths(i + 1, j) + paths(i, j + 1).
work:
paths(i, j) = paths(i + 1, j) + paths(i, j + 1) for an open cell; paths(3, 3) = 1; a wall or outside cell gives 0
(2,1): down to (3,1), then right, right → 1; (2,3): down → 1
(1,3) → 1; (1,2): right to (1,3) → 1 (down (2,2) is a wall); (1,1): right (1,2) = 1 + down (2,1) = 1 → 2
(1,0): right (1,1) = 2 (down (2,0) is a wall) → 2
(0,1): down (1,1) = 2 (right (0,2) is a wall) → 2; (0,0): right (0,1) = 2 + down (1,0) = 2 → 4
The 4 paths: R D R R D D, R D D D R R, D R R R D D, D R D D R R
(Backtracking that tries RIGHT before DOWN finds R D R R D D first.)
why: A — Wrong. 2 counts only the paths that begin with one of the two first moves. Both first moves, right to (0,1) and down to (1,0), lead to 2 paths each.
B — Wrong. 3 usually misses a path that goes down column 1 to the bottom row (R D D D R R or D R D D R R): cell (2,1) is open even though (2,0) and (2,2) are walls.
C — Correct. Both (0,1) and (1,0) lead to cell (1,1), from which there are 2 ways on (along row 1 then down column 3, or down column 1 then along row 3), giving 2 + 2 = 4 paths.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: The m-colouring backtracking algorithm is run for m = 1, 2, 3, … on the wheel graph W: vertices 1–5 form the cycle 1-2-3-4-5-1, and a hub vertex 6 is joined to every one of 1–5. What is the smallest m for which a valid colouring (adjacent vertices get different colours) is found, i.e. the chromatic number of W?
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The odd 5-cycle rim needs 3 colours and the hub needs a 4th: χ = 4, which is not listed.
concept: Graph m-colouring asks whether the vertices can be coloured with at most m colours so that adjacent vertices get different colours; the smallest such m is the chromatic number χ(G). Backtracking colours the vertices one by one, trying colours 1..m for each and backing up when a vertex has no allowed colour. Useful facts: an even cycle needs 2 colours, an odd cycle needs 3, and a vertex adjacent to every vertex of a subgraph needs one colour more than that subgraph.
work:
The rim 1-2-3-4-5-1 is an odd cycle (5 vertices) → it needs 3 colours on its own
The hub 6 is adjacent to all 5 rim vertices → it needs a colour different from all of them → a 4th colour
m = 3 fails (backtracking tries every choice and backs up); m = 4 succeeds, e.g. rim 1, 2, 1, 2, 3 and hub 4
Chromatic number χ(W) = 4 (not among the options)
why: A — Wrong. 2 colours work only for bipartite graphs. The rim is a 5-cycle (odd), so it cannot be 2-coloured, and there are also triangles such as 1-2-6.
B — Wrong. 3 colours are enough for the rim alone, but the hub 6 touches all the rim vertices, which already use 3 colours, so the hub needs a fourth.
C — Wrong. 5 colours certainly work, but they are not the minimum; 4 colours already give a valid colouring (rim 1, 2, 1, 2, 3 and hub 4).
D — Wrong. None of A–C is true, so 'More than one of the above' (which needs at least two true options) is also false.

E — Correct. None of A, B or C is the smallest m. The odd rim needs 3 colours and the hub needs a different one, so the chromatic number is 4, which is not listed. Hence 'None of the above' is the answer.

q: Which of the following graphs has a Hamiltonian cycle (a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start)?
opts: A star: centre 1 joined to 2, 3, 4 and 5
More than one of the above
exp: Only graph A has a Hamiltonian cycle (1-2-3-4-5-1); the star has degree-1 vertices and the two triangles share a cut vertex.
concept: A Hamiltonian cycle visits every VERTEX exactly once (compare an Euler circuit, which uses every EDGE exactly once). Deciding whether one exists is NP-complete, and backtracking is the standard exact method: extend a path one vertex at a time and back up when stuck. Quick tests that rule one out: a vertex of degree 1, or a cut vertex (a graph with a Hamiltonian cycle has no cut vertex).
work:
A: the cycle 1-2-3-4-5-1 uses only edges of the graph and visits all 5 vertices → Hamiltonian
B: vertices 2–5 have degree 1; a Hamiltonian cycle needs every vertex to have degree ≥ 2 → none
C: vertex 3 is a cut vertex; a cycle that leaves {1, 2} through 3 must come back through 3 → 3 would be visited twice → none
why: A — Correct. 1-2-3-4-5-1 is a cycle through all five vertices using edges of the graph, so the graph is Hamiltonian (the extra edge 1-3 is not even needed).
B — Wrong. In a star the leaves 2, 3, 4, 5 have degree 1. A cycle must enter and leave every vertex, which needs degree at least 2, so no Hamiltonian cycle exists.
C — Wrong. Vertex 3 is a cut vertex: to visit both triangles the cycle would have to pass through 3 twice. (This graph has an Euler circuit, since all its degrees are even, but no Hamiltonian cycle.)
D — Wrong. Only A is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. A is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: While searching a state-space tree, a node that has been generated and whose children are being generated right now is called the:
opts: More than one of the above
exp: The node currently being expanded is the E-node; other unexpanded nodes are live; finished or pruned nodes are dead.
concept: Terms used in state-space search (Horowitz–Sahni). Live node: a node that has been generated but not all of whose children have been generated yet. E-node (expanding node): the live node whose children are currently being generated. Dead node: a generated node that will not be expanded further — either it was killed by the bounding function or all its children have been generated. Backtracking and branch and bound differ in how they choose the next E-node.
why: A — Wrong. A live node is waiting: it has been generated but not fully expanded. Many nodes can be live at once; the one being expanded right now is the E-node.
B — Wrong. A dead node will not be expanded any more — it was pruned by the bounding function or all of its children have already been generated.
C — Correct. The E-node is exactly the live node that is currently being expanded, i.e. whose children are being generated.
D — Wrong. Only C is true; 'More than one of the above' needs at least two of A–C to be true.
E — Wrong. C is true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.

q: Which of the following statements about state-space search are TRUE?
opts: In backtracking, as soon as a new child of the current E-node is generated, that child becomes the new E-node (depth-first generation)
In branch and bound, the E-node remains the E-node until it is dead, i.e. all its children are generated before another live node is expanded
A dead node is a node that is still waiting in the list of live nodes to be expanded
More than one of the above
exp: A and B correctly describe backtracking and branch and bound; C describes a live node, not a dead node.
concept: Terms used in state-space search (Horowitz–Sahni). Live node: a node that has been generated but not all of whose children have been generated yet. E-node (expanding node): the live node whose children are currently being generated. Dead node: a generated node that will not be expanded further — either it was killed by the bounding function or all its children have been generated. Backtracking is depth-first: the newest child immediately becomes the E-node, and the parent becomes the E-node again only after that child's subtree is finished. Branch and bound generates ALL the children of the E-node first, adds them to the list of live nodes, and then picks the next E-node from that list — FIFO (queue, breadth-first), LIFO (stack) or least cost (priority queue). Both use bounding functions to kill nodes that cannot lead to an (optimal) answer.
why: A — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. Backtracking explores depth-first: it moves to a newly generated child at once and returns to the parent only after the child's subtree has been explored or killed.

B — Wrong. This statement is TRUE, but it is not the answer by itself; since more than one of A–C is true, the answer is D. In branch and bound the E-node generates all of its children (which become live nodes) before it dies; the next E-node is then chosen from the live-node list by FIFO, LIFO or least cost.
C — Wrong. A node still waiting to be expanded is a LIVE node. A dead node will never be expanded: it was killed by the bounding function or all its children have been generated.
D — Correct. A and B are both true, so 'More than one of the above' is the answer.
E — Wrong. A and B are true, so 'None of the above' cannot be the answer.
